stem: A chest X-ray showed a fluid level behind the heart. What is the most likely diagnosis driving his recent deterioration?
explanation:
Oesophageal carcinoma
Although this man has had a very long history of symptoms of gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GORD) and a hiatus hernia, the features described here (i.e. X-ray changes, the history of weight loss and his rapidly progressive dysphagia) should raise significant suspicions of oesophageal carcinoma. Further suspicion is raised by the fact that he is anaemic and has a raised ESR. Long-term GORD is the most common predisposing factor for oesophageal carcinoma. Endoscopy with biopsy is the investigation of choice for this patient.

Achalasia
Achalasia is incorrect. Although chronic dysphagia to solids and liquids is a common symptom of achalasia, the rapidly progressive dysphagia described for this man – coupled with his other symptoms, such as weight loss – are much more suggestive of increasing mechanical obstruction of the oesophagus.

Oesophageal diverticulum
Oesophageal diverticulum is incorrect. An oesophageal diverticulum may cause symptoms including regurgitation, nocturnal cough and aspiration, but would not explain rapidly progressive dysphagia and weight loss.

Pharyngeal pouch
Pharyngeal pouch is incorrect. A pharyngeal pouch may cause regurgitation and intermittent dysphagia, but would not explain rapidly progressive dysphagia and weight loss.

Rolling hiatus hernia
Rolling hiatus hernia is incorrect. While a rolling hiatus hernia could explain reflux symptoms, the rapidly progressive dysphagia described for this man is much less consistent with this diagnosis, which – coupled with his other symptoms, such as weight loss – are much more suggestive of increasing mechanical obstruction of the oesophagus.

stem: A 43-year-old lady with chronic liver disease secondary to autoimmune hepatitis presents with haematemesis and melaena. Gastroscopy shows bleeding oesophageal varices that are banded and portal hypertensive gastropathy. On examination she is jaundiced, has palmar erythema and a distended abdomen with shifting dullness. She was enquiring about the possibility of getting a transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt. Which of the following is an indication for a transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPSS)?
explanation:
Refractory ascites
A transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPSS) involves the formation of a low-resistance channel between the hepatic vein and the intrahepatic portion of the portal vein. This reduces portal hypertension, and therefore the complications associated with portal hypertension. From all of the options listed, only refractory ascites is an indication for TIPSS.

Encephalopathy
Encephalopathy is incorrect. TIPSS can precipitate or worsen hepatic encephalopathy.

Portal hypertensive gastropathy
Portal hypertensive gastropathy is incorrect. Portal hypertensive gastropathy is not an indication for TIPSS.

Primary prophylaxis of oesophageal varices
Primary prophylaxis of oesophageal varices is incorrect. There is no role for TIPSS in primary prophylaxis of varices. TIPSS can be used to treat acutely bleeding oesophageal varices that are refractory to medical treatment, or to prevent rebleeding from varices. Ascites A 49-year-old bar owner with a known history of liver cirrhosis presents with increased abdominal swelling and pain, accompanied by worsening confusion. He has apparently continued to drink one bottle of wine per day and one-third of a bottle of whisky, despite being advised to stop by his GP. On examination his BP is 105/65 mmHg, pulse 92 bpm and regular, and temperature 37.9°C. He is confused and has a liver flap. There are changes consistent with chronic liver disease, and he has tense painful ascites. Investigations:

Severe heart failure
Severe heart failure is incorrect. Severe heart failure is a contraindication to TIPSS. Other absolute contraindications include multiple hepatic cysts, uncontrolled systemic infection or sepsis, unrelieved biliary obstruction and severe pulmonary hypertension.

stem: A 34-year-old man with profuse watery diarrhoea was referred for assessment of a possible neuroendocrine tumour of the gastrointestinal tract. Which statement correctly describes the action of gastrointestinal hormones?
options: Enteroglucagon increases the small-bowel transit rate
Pancreatic polypeptide stimulates pancreatic bicarbonate secretion
explanation:
Gastrin increases gastric motor activity
Gastrin (secreted by gastric antral G cells) causes acid secretion, mucosal growth and smooth muscle contraction.

Enteroglucagon increases the small-bowel transit rate
Enteroglucagon increases the small-bowel transit rate is incorrect. Enteroglucagon is released in response to food, promoting mucosal growth and slowing transit of the gastrointestinal tract (rather than increasing it, making this option incorrect), and therefore enhances food absorption.

Pancreatic polypeptide stimulates pancreatic bicarbonate secretion
Pancreatic polypeptide stimulates pancreatic bicarbonate secretion is incorrect. Pancreatic polypeptide inhibits pancreatic enzyme secretion (rather than increases it, making this option incorrect).

Secretin maintains mucosal growth
Secretin maintains mucosal growth is incorrect. Secretin stimulates pancreatic secretions (as well as reduces acid secretion from gastric parietal cells) in response to the presence of duodenal acid. It has no direct effect on mucosal growth. Neuroendocrine Tumours

Somatostatin increases gastrin secretion
Somatostatin increases gastrin secretion is incorrect. Somatostatin reduces gastrointestinal motility, and also reduces secretion of gastrin (rather than increases it, making this option incorrect). It also down-regulates portal blood flow and all gastrointestinal tract secretions.

stem: A 23-year-old woman complains of intermittent diarrhoea containing blood and mucus, tiredness and anorexia going back over the past 2 to 3 months. Her abdomen is soft and non-tender. Cultures of stool samples are negative. Examination is unremarkable. What is the most appropriate investigation?
options: Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy with duodenal biopsy
explanation:
Colonoscopy and biopsies
A history of a young person with chronic rectal bleeding and systemic symptoms that may represent anaemia is very suggestive of ulcerative colitis (UC). Colonoscopy will allow endoscopic views of the mucosa and biopsies that will be definitive in confirming the diagnosis, and will also allow staging of the extent and severity of disease.

Barium enema
Barium enema is incorrect. Barium enema is helpful for looking for significant structural lesions of the colon (eg tumours, diverticular disease etc), but does not allow assessment of the colonic mucosa or give the ability to take biopsies, limiting its role in cases of suspected UC.

Hydrogen breath test
Hydrogen breath test is incorrect. A glucose-hydrogen breath test is useful in cases of suspected small bowel bacterial overgrowth, but again the presence of rectal bleeding is inconsistent with this as the underlying diagnosis.

Plain X-ray of the abdomen
Plain X-ray of the abdomen is incorrect. X-ray of the abdomen is helpful when looking for dilated bowel loops in cases of suspected intestinal obstruction, but is unlikely to be of any benefit here. Ulcerative Colitis A 72-year-old man with a long history of indigestion presents to the gastroenterology clinic. He also describes episodes of regurgitation that help to relieve his feelings of fullness and retrosternal pain. When questioned more deeply, he describes dysphagia to both solids and liquids, with little pattern. His weight has been stable for the past 6 months. On examination his BP is 155/82 mmHg, pulse is 72 beats per min and regular, and his BMI is 32. Except for obesity there are no other significant findings on physical examination Investigations:

Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy with duodenal biopsy
Upper gastrointestinal (GI) endoscopy with duodenal biopsy is incorrect. Upper GI endoscopy with duodenal biopsy is the reference standard for diagnosis of coeliac disease and other enteric causes of malabsorption. However, rectal bleeding clearly suggests a lower gastrointestinal source of her symptoms, so this investigation is unlikely to be of any benefit here.

stem: A 49-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with 200 ml upper gastrointestinal haemorrhage. He is known to have alcohol-related liver cirrhosis and oesophageal varices. He has continued to drink 15–20 units of alcohol per day. On examination, his blood pressure is 90/50 mmHg, and his heart rate is 95 bpm and regular. His abdomen is generally tender, particularly in the epigastrium. Arterial blood gas monitoring reveals a haemoglobin level of 85 g/l. Intravenous fluid replacement is commenced. Given the most likely cause, which of the following is most likely to stop the bleeding?
explanation:
Band ligation
Band ligation is the first-line endoscopic therapy for oesophageal varices once initial circulatory resuscitation has been performed. Some studies suggest the success rate of band ligation is around 90%. Oesophageal varices are seen in patients with cirrhosis, leading to raised portal venous pressure. In this case, long-term alcohol dependence has led to cirrhosis of the liver. The band captures the varices, causing complete closure of the aperture and cessation of bleeding. The band will eventually slough off after a few days, leaving behind a mucosal ulceration, which will heal with time.

Prothrombin complex concentrate
Prothrombin complex concentrate is useful where rapid reversal of vitamin K anticoagulants, such as warfarin, is required. While prothrombin complex concentrate may help in some cases to stabilise the patient, it is not a definitive treatment for haemostasis. As per the British National Formulary, indications for the use of prothrombin complex concentrate include perioperative management of patients with congenital deficiencies of clotting factors II, VII, IX or X and major bleeding for patients on warfarin.

Sclerotherapy
N-butyl-2-cyanoacrylate is usually considered the first line for gastric varices. The most likely cause of the bleeding here is the known oesophageal varices, for which band ligation has superior efficacy. According to guidance from the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence, banding of gastric varices is unlikely to be successful. There is a risk of N-butyl-2-cyanoacrylate pulmonary embolism, with risk factors including the size of the vein and the volume injected.

Terlipressin
Terlipressin reduces all-cause mortality and, as per National Institute for Health and Care Excellence guidelines, should be offered to patients with suspected variceal bleeding at presentation. It is not, however, the most likely treatment to stop the bleeding. Terlipressin should be stopped after definitive haemostasis has been achieved, or after five days unless there is another indication for its use. Portal Hypertension A 36-year-old woman with a history of well-controlled ulcerative colitis (UC) comes to the clinic for review. She has started passing 8-10 bowel motions per day over the past few days, with bloody diarrhoea. She continues to take regular mesalazine. Her lifestyle has recently changed, in that she has given up smoking, changed to a vegetarian diet, begun exercising and started taking B vitamin supplements. She has a recent knee injury for which she has been taking intermittent paracetamol and ibuprofen.

Tranexamic acid
There is no evidence that tranexamic acid reduces bleeding or mortality in patients with gastrointestinal bleeding, according to the HALT-IT trial. Tranexamic acid is commonly used to prevent excess blood loss from major trauma. It can also be used for heavy menstruation, postpartum bleeding, epistaxis and some surgical procedures.

stem: A 36-year-old woman with a history of well-controlled ulcerative colitis (UC) comes to the clinic for review. She has started passing 8-10 bowel motions per day over the past few days, with bloody diarrhoea. She continues to take regular mesalazine. Her lifestyle has recently changed, in that she has given up smoking, changed to a vegetarian diet, begun exercising and started taking B vitamin supplements. She has a recent knee injury for which she has been taking intermittent paracetamol and ibuprofen. Which of the following is the most likely reason for her relapse?
explanation:
Stopping smoking
Whereas smoking worsens Crohn’s disease, it is thought to control in patients with a history of ulcerative colitis, possibly because of alterations in the colonic microbiota.

B vitamin supplements
B vitamin supplements is incorrect. These do not alter the course of UC activity.

Increased exercise
Increase exercise is incorrect. There is no evidence that exercise is linked to disease activity in UC.

Use of NSAIDs
Use of NSAIDs is incorrect. Long-term regular use of NSAIDs can lead to the development of a microscopic colitis, but short-term ad hoc use is very unlikely to result in the worsening of symptoms seen here. Ulcerative Colitis You are asked to review a 52-year-old man who is on the gastroenterology ward with end stage alcoholic liver disease and encephalopathy. He is drowsy and disorientated when you review him but he complains bitterly of itching. On examination is BP is 95/50 mmHg, pulse is 82/min and regular. There is ascites on abdominal examination and bilateral pitting oedema affecting both legs. Investigations reveal plasma sodium of 131 mmol/l.

Vegetarian diet
Vegetarian diet is incorrect. There is little evidence that dietary changes can affect disease activity.

stem: You are asked to review a 52-year-old man who is on the gastroenterology ward with end stage alcoholic liver disease and encephalopathy. He is drowsy and disorientated when you review him but he complains bitterly of itching. On examination is BP is 95/50 mmHg, pulse is 82/min and regular. There is ascites on abdominal examination and bilateral pitting oedema affecting both legs. Investigations reveal plasma sodium of 131 mmol/l. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial therapy to treat his itching?
explanation:
Cholestyramine
Cholestyramine is a resin historically used in the treatment of hypercholesterolaemia, which binds bile acids. It is not absorbed from the GI tract, which means it is a relatively safe option in patients with severe hepatic impairment. In patients with hepatic impairment itching is driven by bile acid accumulation, and Cholestyramine helps reduce bile acid accumulation.

Calamine lotion
Calamine lotion is incorrect. Calamine lotion does have a local soothing effect, but in reality it will be insufficient and impossible to cover such a wide area of the body in this situation.

Cetirizine
Cetirizine is incorrect. Cetirizine is non-sedating anti-histamine which can be used in patients with hepatic impairment but should be dose adjusted and used with caution. As such in this case it is best avoided during acute decompensation.

Chlorpheniramine
Chlorpheniramine is incorrect. Chlorpheniramine is a sedating anti-histamine and is therefore best avoided in this situation because of the risk of increasing drowsiness and confusion.

Ketotifen
Ketotifen is incorrect. Ketotifen undergoes significant first pass hepatic metabolism and is at risk of significant accumulation in patients with hepatic failure and should therefore be avoided. She unfortunately continues to have diarrhoea, and is opening her bowels some 4-6 times per day. There is no abdominal pain and she has increased in weight since her surgery and has been able to return to work. On examination her BP is 122/72 mmHg, pulse is 74/min and regular. Her abdomen is soft and nontender and the laparotomy scar is healing well. Her BMI is 23. Investigations reveal.

stem: A 23-year-old woman experiences nausea, vomiting and abdominal cramps 4 hours after eating a salad and a hamburger in a local restaurant. Watery diarrhoea begins a few hours later. She looks dehydrated but her vital observations are stable and there is no postural BP drop. On examination her abdomen is soft, with some mild generalised discomfort to deep palpation; bowel sounds are frequent. What is the most likely causative organism?
explanation:
Staphylococcus aureus
Staphylococcal food poisoning leads to profuse vomiting that occurs 2–4 hours after eating food (often premade salads, meat or dairy products) that is contaminated by an enterotoxin. Diarrhoea occurs a few hours later and is profuse and watery.

Salmonella enteritidis
Salmonella enteritidis is incorrect. Salmonella enteritidis food poisoning usually occurs following ingestion of contaminated poultry, eggs or milk, with symptoms starting from 12–72 hours. It is usually associated with a fever and bloody diarrhoea due to the ability of the organism to invade the mucosa.

Listeria monocytogenes
Listeria monocytogenes is incorrect. Listeria monocytogenes food poisoning usually occurs following ingestion of contaminated unpasteurised dairy products. Patients may present with mild diarrhoea and features of CNS listeria infection including headache and confusion. It is more commonly seen as a cause of sepsis in the elderly and pregnant women.

Clostridium perfringens
Clostridium perfringens is incorrect. Clostridium perfringens food poisoning typically presents from 6–12 hours after eating the contaminated food. GastroenteritisA 36-year-old nurse with a 15-year history of ulcerative colitis developed abnormal liver enzymes: ALT, 154 U/l; ALP, 354 U/l; bilirubin, 12 μmol/l. An ultrasound of the liver was normal. Her anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA) test was positive and anti-mitochondrial antibody (AMA) negative.

Yersinia enterocolitica
Yersinia enterocolitica is incorrect. Yersinia is most commonly associated with the ingestion of improperly cooked meat, but symptoms generally begin more than 1 day after ingestion of the contaminated food (average of 4 days incubation period).

stem: A 41-year-old man has a BMI of 38. He is normotensive and a non-smoker. A fasting blood glucose is measured at 6.2 mmol/l. Which of the following is the risk factor increasing mortality in obese patients when compared to patients with normal weight?
options: Microvascular complications of type 2 diabetes mellitus
explanation:
Cardiovascular disease
This patient has significant obesity coupled with impaired fasting blood glucose on blood testing, both pointers to an insulin-resistant state. Insulin resistance drives hypertension, dyslipidaemia and a pro-coagulant state, increasing the risk of cardiovascular disease.

Carcinoma of colon
Carcinoma of the colon is incorrect. Obesity is related to increased risk of colon cancer; the risk is particularly associated with abdominal obesity, again a sign of insulin resistance. Overall however the greater increased risk of mortality is for cardiovascular disease.

Chronic respiratory disease
Chronic respiratory disease is incorrect. Obesity hypoventilation syndrome and sleep apnoea are features of respiratory disease associated with severe obesity, but they primarily drive morbidity.

Pancreatic cancer
Pancreatic cancer is incorrect. Pancreatic cancer is primarily associated with type 2 diabetes, potentially related to increased demands upon both endocrine and exocrine pancreatic tissue. Nutritional Assessment, Malabsorption and FeedingMicrovascular complications of type 2 diabetes mellitus
Microvascular complications of type 2 diabetes mellitus is incorrect. Microvascular complications of diabetes are most strongly associated with fasting blood glucose levels above 7.0 mmol/l.

stem: A 72-year-old man with a history of type 2 diabetes comes to the Emergency department with severe abdominal pain and diarrhoea mixed with dark blood. He reports paroxysms of lower abdominal pain occurring after meals some 6-8 times over the past few months. On examination his temperature is 37.9 oC, BP is 100/60 mmHg, pulse is 95/min and regular. His abdomen is generally tender with quiet bowel sounds. Arterial blood gasses show a pH of 7.15 and a marked elevation in serum lactate. You suspect ischaemic colitis. Where is the most likely affected area?
explanation:
Splenic flexure
This patient has chronic ischemic colitis, with clues that point to the diagnosis including the age, history of diabetes, and symptoms of abdominal pain and PR blood occurring in association with meals. There is often a history of vascular disease or diabetes, and it sometimes may follow aneurysm surgery and ligation of the inferior mesenteric artery. The superior mesenteric artery supplies the ascending and transverse colon and the inferior mesenteric artery supplies the descending and sigmoid colon. The splenic flexure and sigmoid colon are regions where the two circulations meet each other and have limited collateral networks making ischemic damage more common in these areas (watershed areas).

Ascending colon
Ascending colon is incorrect. Ischemic colitis occurs on the right side of the colon in about 10% of cases and is less common than left sided ischemic colitis. This is because there is often increased tortuosity of long colonic arteries and the superior rectal artery.

Descending colon
Descending colon is incorrect. Descending colon ischaemic colitis is the next most common after splenic flexure colitis because of superior rectal artery fibromuscular dysplasia.

Hepatic flexure
Hepatic flexure is incorrect. The hepatic flexure receives its blood supply from the superior mesenteric artery, which is subject to much lower levels of atherosclerosis. Bowel IschaemiaA 65-year-old woman with scleroderma and Raynaud’s phenomenon complained of weight loss and was referred for further investigation. Which of the following conditions is most strongly associated with progressive systemic sclerosis?

Transverse colon
Transverse colon is incorrect. The lack of tortuosity of the blood supply to the transverse colon means it is rarely interrupted.

stem: Which of the following is the most logical next investigation?
explanation:
Anti–tissue transglutaminase antibodies
This lady has undiagnosed coeliac disease, an autoimmune disease affecting the small bowel. It is increasingly recognised that occult coeliac disease is an important cause of anaemia in patients of this age group. This is because the inflammatory process causes villous atrophy, disrupting the structure and function of the small bowel, resulting in malabsorption of multiple nutrients, minerals and fat soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K). The cause of coeliac disease is thought to be multi-factorial with a strong genetic susceptibility; 95% of patients have either the HLA-DQ2 or HLA-DQ8 protein present. The symptoms of coeliac disease are very varied; common complaints are fatigue, anaemia, large volume loose stool or steatorrhoea, abdominal pain and bloating, and weight loss. Some patients also report mouth ulcers. The gastrointestinal symptoms of coeliac disease can be incorrectly labelled as irritable bowel syndrome (as in this patient). The evidence of iron deficiency anaemia in someone with this history should therefore alert you to the possible diagnosis of coeliac disease, and this should be investigated. Anti-TTG antibody screening is seen as the initial screening investigation of choice for patients with possible coeliac disease. Total serum immunoglobulin A (IgA) levels should be checked in parallel as 2% of people have IgA deficiency resulting in a false negative result. In these patients, IgG-TTG should be checked. The only effective treatment for coeliac disease is a gluten free diet, which must be strictly adhered to. If untreated, it can increase the risk of intestinal lymphoma. Coeliac disease is associated with other autoimmune conditions such as type one diabetes, vitiligo, hypothyroidism and dermatitis herpetiformis; NICE recommends screening in these patients, as well in firstdegree relatives of those with confirmed coeliac disease, patients with newly diagnosed chronic fatigue syndrome and irritable bowel syndrome.

Anti-parietal cell antibodies
Anti-parietal cell antibodies is incorrect. This is a test for pernicious anaemia, an autoimmune disease causing atrophy of all layers of the body and fundus of the stomach, ultimately causing a loss of intrinsic factor. This is required for vitamin B 12 absorption. Pernicious anaemia therefore causes a macrocytic, megaloblastic anaemia. Although the vitamin B 12 level is slightly low in this case, the history, age of patient and iron deficiency anaemia make coeliac disease a more likely diagnosis, and testing for anti-TTG antibodies the most logical next investigation.

Colonoscopy
Colonoscopy is incorrect. Nothing in the history suggests a lower GI cause for her symptoms. However, if all other investigations are negative, this may well be required at a later stage. Additionally, if this patient had any red flag symptoms, or was an elderly patient presenting with iron deficiency anaemia, a colonoscopy may be indicated earlier on in the patients work up.

Faecal elastase
Faecal elastase is incorrect. This is a test for pancreatic insufficiency. Nothing in this patient’s history suggests this as a diagnosis.

Upper GI endoscopy
Upper GI endoscopy is incorrect. While this may be done with small bowel sampling to confirm the diagnosis, serological testing is the first line investigation for coeliac disease. It is important to note that multiple (4–8) biopsy sites are needed for confirming coeliac disease as not all areas may be equally affected. Multiple sites reduce the risk of false negatives.

stem: A 57-year-old man was brought to the Emergency Department by his wife, who reported that he had become increasingly drowsy and difficult to rouse. There was no history of head injury. He had recently had problems with sleeping and had been given zopiclone by his general practitioner; his pills had been counted and it did not appear that he had taken an overdose. He had a background of previous alcohol dependence, for which he had recently been treated with detoxification. On examination, he clearly had ascites, and his abdomen was generally tender. There was no evidence of a focal neurological deficit. Blood tests revealed an iron-deficiency picture, elevated transaminases and a bilirubin of 145 μmol/l; a random blood glucose concentration was 6.7 mmol/l. He had a mildly elevated white blood cell count. What is the most likely explanation for his drowsiness?
explanation:
Hepatic encephalopathy
The history of previous alcohol dependence, together with ascites, is suggestive of this man having alcoholrelated cirrhosis and portal hypertension. The description of tender ascites and a raised white cell count raises the possibility of spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP), a well-recognised potential complication of chronic liver disease. Hepatic encephalopathy is another common complication of cirrhosis, and this man has at least two obvious risk factors for it, namely his recent use of sedatives (zopiclone) and the possibility of SBP; as such, this is the most likely diagnosis here. Hepatic encephalopathy is usually graded from 1 to 4, with 1 being mild obtundation and 4 being deep coma. Precipitating factors for encephalopathy in patients with underlying cirrhosis include: Upper gastrointestinal tract bleeding Sepsis Medications – in particular, analgesic and sedative drugs Electrolytes abnormalities – including hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia Alkalosis. Management of hepatic encephalopathy involves identification and treatment of any precipitating factors, along with medications to purge the bowel of nitrogenous material (as such material may be converted to ammonia, which is one of the key drivers of encephalopathy). Such treatments include oral lactulose solution, phosphate enemas and non-absorbable antibiotics (i.e. rifaximin).

Hypoglycaemia
Hypoglycaemia is incorrect. The fact that this man is drowsy even when a random blood glucose is normal makes hypoglycaemia unlikely to be the explanation.

Metastatic carcinoma
Metastatic carcinoma is incorrect. No information is given that might support a diagnosis of metastatic carcinoma, and the absence of focal neurological deficit would be somewhat unusual if he was suffering from brain metastases.

Subdural haematoma
Subdural haematoma is incorrect. Although people with a history of alcohol excess are at higher risk of subdural haematoma, the absence of any head injury makes this unlikely to be the explanation here; furthermore, if he did have a haematoma that was large enough to impair his consciousness, it might be expected for him to have other localising neurological signs. Hepatic EncephalopathyZopiclone overdose
Zopiclone overdose is incorrect. The normal pill count of his tablets makes zopiclone overdose very unlikely.

stem: A 65-year-old man with long-standing insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus was referred with nausea and recurrent vomiting. At endoscopy, a large gastric food residue was noted despite a 6-hour fast. What would the most useful diagnostic test be?
explanation:
Gamma scintigraphy, gastric emptying study.
Diabetes-associated gastroparesis occurs in ~10% of diabetics after 10 years. It appears to be very underdiagnosed, and probably represents the most common gastrointestinal complication of the condition. Other causes of gastroparesis include post-operative (particularly related to gastric and thoracic surgery), medications (such as anti-muscarinic medications and calcium channel blockers) and neurological conditions, although a significant proportion of cases are apparently idiopathic. Scintigraphic gastric emptying studies are the most reliable diagnostic test. Management is with prokinetics (domperidone and erythromycin). Gastric pacing is also possible.

Barium meal and follow-through
Barium meal and follow-through is incorrect. A barium meal and follow-through may be useful for excluding obstruction of the upper gastrointestinal tract (which may present with similar symptoms), but is not the best test for diagnosing the dysmotility of gastroparesis.

Lactose hydrogen breath test
Lactose hydrogen breath test is incorrect. Diabetes is a risk factor for small bowel bacterial overgrowth, but this is a much less common cause of these symptoms than gastroparesis in a patient such as this, and the lactose hydrogen breath test is therefore likely to be normal.

Lying and standing blood pressure
Lying and standing blood pressure is incorrect. A proportion of patients will have an autonomic neuropathy but not all, so a postural drop in blood pressure is unlikely to be found. Diabetic NeuropathyA 42-year-old woman who drinks 1.5 bottles of wine per day is reviewed in the liver clinic. Her GP is concerned because of a rise in her transaminases that he has documented over the past few months. Her medical history includes hypertension. She has been consuming half a bottle of wine every day since a divorce some 5 years earlier. Examination reveals a BP of 152/90 mmHg, with pulse is 85 bpm and regular. Her BMI is 34. Her abdomen is soft and non-tender, with no other remarkable findings. Investigations reveal:

Oesophageal manometry
Oesophageal manometry is incorrect. Oesophageal manometry is helpful in investigating oesophageal symptoms (such as reflux and dysphagia), but is unlikely to be of any benefit here.

stem: A 22-year-old woman was reviewed in the clinic. She was pregnant and in the third month of gestation, but had recently been having trouble with severe morning sickness with vomiting. Her general practitioner had requested blood tests, and had found an alanine aminotransferase (ALT) of 64 U/l, normal alkaline phosphatase level and a bilirubin of 35 μmol/l. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Hyperemesis gravidarum
Severe hyperemesis (hyperemesis gravidarum) is common in pregnancy, and is associated with mild liver abnormalities in around 0.5–1% of pregnancies. Her ALT of 64 and bilirubin of 35 are only modestly above the upper limits of normal, which are the typical levels that may be found in hyperemesis. All of the other options given are associated with a different complex of symptoms and/or different patterns of liver biochemistry. If hyperemesis continues for a prolonged period then it can result in a lower birthweight baby, but this is rare.

Acute fatty liver of pregnancy
Acute fatty liver of pregnancy is incorrect. Acute fatty liver of pregnancy typically presents in the third trimester of pregnancy, causing a potentially life-threatening syndrome of liver failure that may progress to jaundice, coagulopathy, profoundly abnormal liver enzymes and encephalopathy. It is associated with fetal and maternal mortalities of up to 20%. This woman is at the wrong stage of her gestation for this to be the diagnosis; furthermore, her liver chemistry would be expected to be much more abnormal were this the diagnosis here.

Biliary tract disease
Biliary tract disease is incorrect. Biliary tract disease would typically be accompanied by a rise in cholestatic liver enzymes like ALP, and often also by a more marked rise in the bilirubin than that described here.

Cholecystitis
Cholecystitis is incorrect. Cholecystitis is usually accompanied by marked upper abdominal pain, raised inflammatory markers, and also often a rise in ALP (as gallstones enter the biliary tree); the absence of any of these features makes this unlikely to be the diagnosis here. Pregnancy-related Liver DiseaseIntrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy
Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy is incorrect. Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy most commonly occurs in the second or third trimesters, with pruritus often being the major symptom. Left untreated, the condition may be serious; it is associated with stillbirth, prematurity and a fetal mortality rate of up to 3.5%. This woman is somewhat earlier in her pregnancy than people typically affected by the condition, and the information that her major symptom is vomiting (rather than pruritus) would also seem to make this option unlikely.

stem: A 63-year-old patient has had a one-year history of iron deficiency anaemia which has not fully resolved on iron therapy. He denies any GI symptoms or any melena, haematemesis or haematuria.A colonoscopy is unremarkable. A gastroscopy shows multiple dilated vessels in the stomach which resembles a ‘watermelon’. He has a past medical history of diabetes and hypertension. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Gastric antral vascular ectasia (GAVE)
GAVE, also known as ‘watermelon stomach’ is a rare but significant cause of acute and chronic upper GI blood loss. It has the name ‘watermelon’ stomach because of the endoscopic appearance of columns of red tortuous ectatic vessels along longitudinal folds of the antrum that resemble watermelon stripes. These vessels frequently bleed leading to occult GI loss that may necessitate blood transfusions or treatment with radio frequency ablation at endoscopy.

Portal hypertensive gastropathy
Portal hypertensive gastropathy is incorrect. Portal hypertensive gastropathy can cause iron deficiency anaemia but is unlikely in the absence of portal hypertension. Endoscopic appearances include erythematous and oedematous mucosa with a snakeskin or mosaic pattern.

Duodenal ulcer
Duodenal ulcer is incorrect. A small bleeding duodenal ulcer can cause iron deficiency anaemia over time, but you would not expect to find the dilated tortuous vessels described in this case.

Gastritis
Gastritis is incorrect. Gastritis is very rarely a cause of iron deficiency anaemia. Gastrointestinal BleedingFlashcards

Pancreatic rest
Pancreatic rest is incorrect. A pancreatic rest is a benign submucosal lesion usually located in the stomach, made up of pancreatic ectopic tissue. They very rarely bleed.

stem: A 22-year-old man presented with unexplained jaundice that occurred repeatedly during episodes of fasting (starvation). What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Gilbert syndrome
The answer is Gilbert syndrome (Option B). One of the classic features of Gilbert syndrome is an increase in serum bilirubin during episodes of starvation, making option B the correct answer here. Gilbert syndrome is a mild unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia; the cause of the condition is inheritance of a form of the enzyme glucuronyltransferase that has reduced activity for conjugation of bilirubin. Factors that are associated with a particular reduction in enzyme activity – and consequent elevation in serum bilirubin – include fasting, infection and haemolysis. The syndrome is not associated with any adverse effects. The male to female ratio is 7:2.

Alcohol abuse
Alcohol abuse (Option A) is incorrect. Alcohol abuse may cause a wide range of liver disease. However, there is no association between starvation in this condition and an increase in serum bilirubin, ruling out this option.

Haemochromatosis
Haemochromatosis (Option C) is incorrect. Haemochromatosis may cause a wide range of liver disease. However, there is no association between starvation in this condition and an increase in serum bilirubin, ruling out this option.

Hepatitis B virus infection
Hepatitis B infection (Option D) is incorrect. Hepatitis B virus infection may cause a wide range of liver disease. However, there is no association between starvation in this condition and an increase in serum bilirubin, ruling out this option. JaundiceWilson's disease
Wilson’s disease (Option E) is incorrect. Wilson's disease may cause a wide range of liver disease. However, there is no association between starvation in this condition and an increase in serum bilirubin, ruling out this option.

stem: A 28-year-old woman visits her GP some 10 days after returning from honeymoon in Mauritius. During the trip she admits to eating food from local street stalls, and now complains of symptoms consistent with an irritable bowel type picture, with alternating constipation and diarrhoea, coupled with abdominal bloating. She is given a course of tinidazole but returns some 2 weeks later with the diarrhoea. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Lactose intolerance
Giardia is a common infection transmitted via the faeco-oral route, and in this situation it is reasonable to treat empirically with a single dose of tinidazole. The persistence of symptoms is not likely to be due to tinidazole resistance. Lactose intolerance is commonly seen following giardia infection and may persist for many weeks after the initial insult. Symptoms usually resolve after a period of abstinence from lactose containing foods.

Gluten intolerance
Gluten intolerance is incorrect. Although gluten intolerance may present with symptoms of diarrhoea, it is lactose intolerance which is more strongly associated with previous giardia infection.

Irritable bowel syndrome
Irritable bowel syndrome is incorrect. Irritable bowel syndrome shouldn’t be diagnosed so close to an episode of giardiasis until other causes of GI upset have been ruled out first.

Protein intolerance
Protein intolerance is incorrect. Protein intolerance is usually manifest by diarrhoea a few hours after eating, rather than by the intermittent diarrhoea and bloating seen here. GiardiasisA 28-year-old woman presented to the Gastroenterology Clinic with weight loss, intermittent, oily diarrhoea and malaise. Blood testing revealed folate and iron deficiency. There was also mild hypocalcaemia on biochemistry screening. She had type 1 diabetes of 10 years’ duration and was stable on a basal-bolus insulin regime. Otherwise, her past medical history was unremarkable.

Tinidazole resistant infection
Tinidazole resistant infection is incorrect. Tinidazole resistant giardiasis is virtually never reported.

stem: A 28-year-old woman presented to the Gastroenterology Clinic with weight loss, intermittent, oily diarrhoea and malaise. Blood testing revealed folate and iron deficiency. There was also mild hypocalcaemia on biochemistry screening. She had type 1 diabetes of 10 years’ duration and was stable on a basal-bolus insulin regime. Otherwise, her past medical history was unremarkable. What is the most specific antibody test for confirming the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Anti-tissue transglutaminase antibodies
The scenario is very suggestive of underlying coeliac disease. Coeliac disease is slightly more common in women, with the peak ages of presentation being in the third and seventh decades. The condition is often found in association with other conditions with an immunological basis, such as type 1 diabetes or Grave’s disease. Pathologically, the condition is characterised by autoimmune small-bowel villous atrophy, which can be confirmed on duodenal biopsy. Although antigliadin, anti-endomysial and anti-tissue transglutaminase antibodies are all relatively specific tests for coeliac disease, it is anti-tissue transglutaminase that has the highest overall sensitivity and specificity for the condition, and is therefore the preferred test at present. The association between coeliac disease and other autoimmune/immunological conditions means that it is not unusual to detect either anti-thyroid or anti-nuclear antibodies in the serum of people with coeliac disease. However, neither antibody is specific for the diagnosis of coeliac disease, and therefore they have no role in making the diagnosis of the condition.

Antigliadin IgA and IgG antibodies
Antigliadin IgA and IgG antibodies is incorrect. Anti-tissue transglutaminase antibody has a higher sensitivity and specificity for coeliac disease.

Anti-nuclear antibodies
Anti-nuclear antibodies is incorrect. Anti-nuclear antibody is not specific for the diagnosis of coeliac disease.

Anti-smooth muscle antibodies
Anti-smooth muscle antibodies is incorrect. Anti-tissue transglutaminase antibody has a higher sensitivity and specificity for coeliac disease.

Anti-thyroid antibodies
Anti-thyroid antibodies is incorrect. Anti-thyroid antibody is not specific for the diagnosis of coeliac disease. Nutritional Assessment, Malabsorption and FeedingA 45-year-old man who was HIV-positive presented with diarrhoea. He had lost 12 kg in weight during the past 2 months and looked cachetic. He was passing voluminous diarrhoea 6–10 times per day and during the night, but denied either abdominal pain or fever. He was known to be only intermittently compliant with antiretroviral therapy. He had not travelled abroad for over 10 years. His CD4 count on admission was 80.

stem: A 45-year-old man who was HIV-positive presented with diarrhoea. He had lost 12 kg in weight during the past 2 months and looked cachetic. He was passing voluminous diarrhoea 6–10 times per day and during the night, but denied either abdominal pain or fever. He was known to be only intermittently compliant with antiretroviral therapy. He had not travelled abroad for over 10 years. His CD4 count on admission was 80. What is the most likely causative organism?
explanation:
A cryptosporidium
Cryptosporidium infection in HIV-positive patients is typically associated with moderate to severe diarrhoea, but there is often little or no abdominal pain and no fever. Severe weight loss is also a common feature. Cryptosporidium infection particularly occurs when the CD4 count is low (<100).

A microsporidium
A microsporidium is incorrect. Microsporidiosis is a possibility in this scenario but tends only to occur in HIVpositive people with very severe immunodeficiency (i.e. CD4 count <50), and is usually associated with abdominal pain.

Cytomegalovirus
Cytomegalovirus (CMV) is incorrect. CMV infection is also a relatively common cause of diarrhoea in people with HIV with low CD4 counts; however, CMV infection tends to present with abdominal pain and fever, and a slightly lower stool frequency than that found in Cryptosporidium infection.

Isospora belli
Isospora belli is incorrect. Isospora may certainly cause diarrhoea and weight loss in people with HIV infection, but is usually acquired in tropical or subtropical regions; in the absence of a relevant travel history, this is less likely to be the correct diagnosis here. GastroenteritisA 32-year-old man presented with a six month history of diarrhoea with mucus and abdominal pain. He had no past medical history. Examination was normal. Investigations: Colonoscopy Proctosigmoiditis Colonic biopsy Crypt abscesses, inflammatory cell infiltrate in the lamina propria Which of the following are associated with this patient’s condition?

Mycobacterium avium intracellulare
Mycobacterium avium intracellulare (MAI) is incorrect. MAI infection is a possibility in this scenario, but tends to occur only in HIV-positive people with very severe immunodeficiency (ie CD4 count <50), and is usually associated with abdominal pain. Furthermore, MAI infection would also be often associated with disease in other organ systems, and particularly a tuberculosis-like condition affecting the lungs.

stem: Which of the following statements fits best with the use of lactulose in this patient?
options: It is not absorbed from the gut
It does not cause abdominal cramps
It begins to work after 2 hours
It increases systemic absorption of ammonia
explanation:
It is not absorbed from the gut
This patient has decompensated liver disease and hepatic encephalopathy (HE) secondary to a UTI and constipation (the constipation may have well caused the UTI, or they may be two separate events). Lactulose is a synthetic disaccharide; there are no disaccharidases on the enterocytes in the small intestine, that can hydrolyse lactulose therefore it is not absorbed from the gut.

It significantly increases blood glucose
It significantly increases blood glucose is incorrect. There is little significant systemic absorption of lactulose, therefore serum glucose is not impacted.

It does not cause abdominal cramps
It does not cause abdominal cramps is incorrect. Common side effects include nausea, bloating and abdominal cramps.

It begins to work after 2 hours
It begins to work after 2 hours is incorrect. Lactulose begins to work after 8 hours. Hepatic EncephalopathyA 61-year-old man with Type 2 diabetes comes to the Emergency department with epigastric pain and severe vomiting. He takes metformin, liraglutide, atorvastatin, Ramipril and aspirin. He admits to drinking 4 pints of beer each evening. On examination his BP is 105/80, pulse is 85 and regular. He is very tender in the epigastrium. Investigations:

It increases systemic absorption of ammonia
It increases systemic absorption of ammonia is incorrect. Its metabolism by colonic bacteria leads to production of lactic acid and other organic acids which cause a fall in colonic pH. This leads to increased ionisation of the feely diffusible ammonia, into ammonium which cannot diffuse back into the blood therefore lactulose reduces systemic absorption of ammonia. Since some of the pathogenesis of HE may involve an excess of nitrogenous compounds accessing the brain, lactulose is used to reduce the amount of nitrogenous content in the blood.

stem: A 24-year-old student presented to his general practitioner with lethargy and malaise following a ‘flu-like’ illness. His general practitioner noticed that he had jaundiced sclerae and arranged blood tests. These revealed that his bilirubin was 65 μmol/l; alkaline phosphatase, albumin, transaminases and clotting were normal. A full blood count and haptoglobins were also normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Gilbert syndrome
Gilbert syndrome is a genetic disorder of bilirubin conjugation, with an autosomal recessive pattern of inheritance. It affects more than 5% of the population and has a male to female preponderance of 3:1. Alcohol consumption and periods of fasting (often associated with illnesses like influenza) can be associated with worsening jaundice. Phenobarbitone may help bilirubin conjugation; however, Gilbert syndrome is of no pathological significance, and no treatment is required.

Acute viral hepatitis
Acute viral hepatitis is incorrect. Although the description of a ‘flu-like’ illness followed by jaundice may sound suggestive of acute viral hepatitis, the normal level of transaminases helps to exclude this option.

Cirrhosis
Cirrhosis is incorrect. No risk factors for or clinical features of cirrhosis are described; furthermore, the normal albumin level and clotting would also be unusual for someone with cirrhosis.

Haemolytic anaemia
Haemolytic anaemia is incorrect. Haemolytic anaemia will cause an increase in bilirubin, but the normal full blood count and haptoglobins mean that this cannot be the diagnosis here. JaundicePancreatic carcinoma
Pancreatic carcinoma is incorrect. Pancreatic cancer would be very unusual in someone of this age; in addition, cancer of the head of the pancreas causing biliary obstruction would be associated with a rise in alkaline phosphatase as well as bilirubin, and this therefore can be ruled out.

stem: A 54-year-old woman was brought to the Emergency Department by her relatives. The family had returned from a holiday in Morocco some 2 weeks earlier. She was intermittently confused, but a history taken from her relatives confirmed that she had suffered a prolonged fever, myalgia, headaches and cough for some days. She had also noticed some diarrhoea after returning home, but this had settled. On examination, there were several faint rose spots, which blanched, on her chest. Blood tests revealed neutropaenia. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Typhoid fever
This scenario is very suggestive of typhoid fever. Typhoid can have an incubation period of anything from a few days to a few weeks, with transmission occurring faeco-orally, and particularly in countries with poor sanitation. Diarrhoea or constipation is common at the outset of the illness, but then often settles; later symptoms include fever, malaise, headache, cough, anorexia, sore throat, and the characteristic maculopapular rose spots, which blanch on pressure. Laboratory testing may reveal raised transaminases, and neutropaenia is also a common finding. Multiple blood, stool and urine cultures are sometimes needed to identify the causative organism, Salmonella typhi. Acute treatment for severe disease is with a third-generation cephalosporin (eg ceftriaxone). Second-line options include ciprofloxacin, but fluoroquinolone resistance is increasing and recent guidelines suggest they should only be used when other treatments are not suitable.

Amoebic liver abscess
Amoebic liver abscess is incorrect. Morocco is not a typical endemic area for amoebiasis; furthermore, the onset of symptoms in amoebic liver abscess tends to be over several months (rather than several weeks, as is the case here), and right upper quadrant pain is a frequent finding – making this unlikely to be the diagnosis.

Brucellosis
Brucellosis is incorrect. Brucellosis may have a very variable clinical presentation, but fever and myalgia are certainly common symptoms; however, this condition has no association with rose spots, ruling this out.

Malaria
Malaria is incorrect. Malaria is exceptionally rare in Morocco, so is very unlikely to be the explanation here.

Tuberculosis
Tuberculosis is incorrect. Although not impossible, this illness is more acute than typically described for tuberculosis, and the lack of prominent respiratory symptoms also make it less likely.

stem: A chest X-ray shows bilateral pulmonary infiltrates. He becomes more short of breath and his hypoxia worsens. Given the likely diagnosis underlying his hypoxia, which of the following findings is most characteristic?
explanation:
Protein-rich oedema fluid
Oedema fluid tends to be protein-rich as a result of the increased alveolar permeability. This patient has acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), which is a recognised complication of acute pancreatitis that affects 15–20% of patients and has a mortality around 30–50%. Clinical features include severe dyspnoea and hypoxaemia refractory to a high-inspired oxygen concentration. Chest imaging findings suggestive of the diagnosis includes multilobar pulmonary infiltrates in patients with previous normal radiographs. The lungs are characterised by increased alveolar-capillary permeability with interstitial oedema.

Excess production of surfactant
Excess production of surfactant is incorrect. It is thought that the pancreatic enzymes damage pulmonary surfactant, which then reduces lung compliance.

Increased lung compliance
Increased lung compliance is incorrect. Lung compliance is reduced and not increased.

Haemorrhagic oedema fluid
Haemorrhagic oedema fluid is incorrect. Oedema fluid that shows marked haemorrhage or very large numbers of white cells are not characteristic of ARDS and may suggest an alternative diagnosis. Acute PancreatitisFlashcards

Raised pulmonary capillary wedge pressure
Raised pulmonary capillary wedge pressure is incorrect. The capillary wedge pressure tends to be normal and not elevated in ARDS.

stem: A 25-year-old cook applied for a job at a cafeteria. He gave a history of having had enteric fever 2 years ago. Which of the following investigations is most likely to indicate a chronic carrier status?
explanation:
Culture of intestinal secretions
Salmonella typhi can be cultured from intestinal secretions, faeces or urine in chronic carriers, and it is this investigation that is recommended to confirm chronic carrier status.

Blood culture
Blood culture is incorrect. Blood cultures will invariably be negative in chronic carriers, because the organism resides mainly in the gallbladder.

Full blood count
Full blood count is incorrect. A full blood count may be useful in acute typhoid (since leucopaenia is a common feature), but this is not found in chronic carriers, making this test redundant here.

Vi agglutination test
Vi agglutination test is incorrect. Vi agglutination demonstration is a screening test that can be positive in around 80% of cases, but lacks the sensitivity and specificity of culture techniques in making the diagnosis of chronic carriage. The Vi (virulence) antigen is a polysaccharide on the exterior of the cell wall; the antigen prevents O antibodies from binding to the O antigen. GastroenteritisA 28-year-old man, who had a history of perioral and buccal pigmentation, intermittent gastrointestinal bleeding and multiple polyposis, was diagnosed with Peutz–Jeghers syndrome. He had met a partner and wanted to start a family, and they attended for genetic counselling. What is the usual inheritance pattern for Peutz–Jeghers syndrome?

Widal antigen test
Widal antigen test is incorrect. Serological tests (such as the Widal antigen test) may be of merit in acute disease, but are not useful for detecting chronic carriage.

stem: A 28-year-old man, who had a history of perioral and buccal pigmentation, intermittent gastrointestinal bleeding and multiple polyposis, was diagnosed with Peutz–Jeghers syndrome. He had met a partner and wanted to start a family, and they attended for genetic counselling. What is the usual inheritance pattern for Peutz–Jeghers syndrome?
explanation:
Autosomal dominant
Peutz-Jeghers syndrome (PJS) is inherited in an autosomal dominant manner. Its cause appears to be a mutation in the STK11/LKB1 gene (the serine/threonine kinase 11 gene) in most cases, a gene that is located on chromosome 19. The gene has variable penetrance, so the pattern of polyposis and cancers can vary between family groups and between patients within families. Around 50% of people with PJS have developed gastrointestinal carcinoma by the time they get to the age of 57. Regular screening is required, and upper and lower gastrointestinal endoscopy, pancreatic ultrasound, testicular ultrasound and small bowel radiography/enteroscopy have been suggested as an appropriate regimen for cancer surveillance within these patients.

Autosomal recessive
Autosomal recessive is incorrect. Peutz-Jeghers syndrome (PJS) is inherited in an autosomal dominant manner.

Mitochondrial
Mitochondrial is incorrect. Peutz-Jeghers syndrome (PJS) is inherited in an autosomal dominant manner.

X-linked dominant
X-linked dominant is incorrect. Peutz-Jeghers syndrome (PJS) is inherited in an autosomal dominant manner. Peutz-Jeghers SyndromeA 60-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes complains of blood-stained diarrhoea and cramping abdominal pain of several months’ duration. She underwent a hysterectomy and radiotherapy 8 months ago for endometrial carcinoma and her diarrhoea began a short period after this.

X-linked recessive
X-linked recessive is incorrect. Peutz-Jeghers syndrome (PJS) is inherited in an autosomal dominant manner.

stem: What is the best follow-up test to confirm the underlying diagnosis?
explanation:
Stool antigen test
This patient has symptoms suggestive of giardiasis; three stool samples are required for culture in order to give a sensitivity of 90%. However, stool antigen testing is more convenient and has a greater sensitivity and specificity than three stool cultures.

Duodenal aspiration
Duodenal aspiration is incorrect. Duodenal aspiration to demonstrate the presence of the trophozoites can be used, but is an invasive investigation.

Hydrogen breath test
Hydrogen breath test is incorrect. This is used to diagnose small bowel bacterial overgrowth and has no role in the detection of giardiasis.

Faecal calprotectin
Faecal calprotectin is a marker of white blood cell activity and is used in the diagnosis of inflammatory bowel disease. GiardiasisFlexible sigmoidoscopy
Flexible sigmoidoscopy is incorrect. This would be unable to diagnose giardiasis, as the protozoan attaches to the duodenum. A flexible sigmoidoscopy would be more useful if suspecting IBD.

stem: As it is the weekend, she is given an 'off-the-shelf' standard bag of total parenteral nutrition (TPN), giving her 2200 calories and 9 g of nitrogen. On Monday she develops severe congestive cardiac failure. This might have been prevented by pretreating her before the start of TPN with which of the following?
explanation:
Intravenous phosphate
Intravenous phosphate with AI This patient has refeeding syndrome, which consists of metabolic disturbances that occur asChat a result ofTutor reinstitution of nutrition to patients who are starved or severely malnourished. During starvation the body uses fatty acids or amino acids as the main energy source, which suppresses insulin release and reduces intracellular minerals (particularly phosphate). During refeeding, insulin secretion increases in response to glucose, resulting in increased glycogen, fat and protein synthesis, which requires phosphate, magnesium and potassium, stores of which are already depleted. Body fluid and electrolyte fluxes that occur after feeding may result in cardiac failure, cardiac arrhythmias, hypotension, kidney disease and death. For this reason electrolyte disorders and fluid balance must be corrected prior to feeding. The hallmark biochemical feature of refeeding syndrome is hypophosphataemia, and so the most important electrolyte to replace is phosphate.

Intravenous calcium
Intravenous calcium is incorrect. Intravenous calcium can be used to optimise serum calcium, but this does not prevent refeeding syndrome.

Intravenous potassium
Intravenous potassium is incorrect. Intravenous potassium administration to correct hypokalaemia is important as consequences of K + < 3 mmol/l include: arrhythmias, hypotension and cardiac arrest, weakness, paralysis, metabolic alkalosis, ileus and constipation. The rate should not exceed 20 mmol/h if administered by peripheral infusion. However, correcting potassium alone would not prevent refeeding syndrome.

Intravenous sodium
Intravenous sodium is incorrect. Changes in carbohydrate metabolism have a profound effect on sodium and water balance, and correcting sodium usually requires correction of fluid balance prior to feeding. Again, correcting sodium balance alone would not prevent refeeding syndrome. Nutritional Assessment, Malabsorption and FeedingIntravenous thiamine
Intravenous thiamine is incorrect. Thiamine deficiency is common in patients with prolonged malnutrition, and introducing carbohydrate causes increased cellular thiamine utilisation. This can precipitate Wernick’s encephalopathy (ocular disturbance, confusion, ataxia and coma), and so thiamine supplementation is important in preventing this. It does not, however, prevent refeeding syndrome.

stem: An obese woman attends your clinic asking for dietary advice, but unfortunately the dietician is unavailable. Which of the following has the most calories per gram of weight?
explanation:
Hard cheese
Fats and alcohols contain the greatest amount of energy per gramme of mass: around 9 kcal/g for fat and around 7kcal/g for alcohols. Typically, hard cheese consists of approximately 40% water, 25% protein and 33% fat; it is the high fat content that drives its high total calories.

Pasta
Pasta is incorrect. Pasta comprises carbohydrate, which contains around 4 kcal/g.

White bread
White bread is incorrect. Like pasta, it comprises mainly carbohydrate, with smaller amounts of protein and fat.

Sugar
Sugar is incorrect. It is a carbohydrate and therefore at the lower end of the energy per gramme scale.

Lean red meat
Lean red meat with Tutor 0.8 Lean red meat is incorrect. It contains protein-to-fat in the ratio of approximately 2 : 1, vs theChat ratio ofAI around : 1 for hard cheese. Nutritional Assessment,.

stem: Which one of these statements about irritable bowel syndrome is correct?
options: A diet high in soluble fibre is often prescribed for the treatment of the syndrome
If abdominal discomfort is eased by opening bowels, the diagnosis should be reconsidered
Weight loss becomes more evident as the disease runs a chronic course
explanation:
A diet high in soluble fibre is often prescribed for the treatment of the syndrome
Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) is a functional intestinal disorder that is characterised by abdominal discomfort (often eased by opening bowels), and alteration of stool form and/or frequency (either constipation or diarrhoea). Importantly, the diagnosis is made based on the pattern of symptoms, and there are no significant physical, laboratory or histological abnormalities. Anaemia, occult blood in the stool, weight loss or nocturnal symptoms cannot be attributed to irritable bowel syndrome, and should prompt investigations for structural gut disease. A diet high in soluble fibre may be useful in some patients, whereas others seem to gain benefit from excluding dairy foods.

Characterised by nocturnal diarrhoea
Characterised by nocturnal diarrhoea is incorrect. Nocturnal symptoms cannot be attributed to irritable bowel syndrome.

If abdominal discomfort is eased by opening bowels, the diagnosis should be reconsidered
If abdominal discomfort is eased by opening bowels, the diagnosis should be reconsidered is incorrect. Abdominal discomfort that is eased by opening the bowels is characteristic of irritable bowel syndrome.

Sigmoidoscopy findings are often diagnostic
Sigmoidoscopy findings are often diagnostic is incorrect. There are no significant physical, laboratory or histological findings in irritable bowel syndrome. The diagnosis is made based upon the pattern of symptoms. Functional Bowel DiseaseWeight loss becomes more evident as the disease runs a chronic course
Weight loss becomes more evident as the disease runs a chronic course is incorrect. Weight loss cannot be attributed to irritable bowel syndrome; it should prompt investigation for structural gut disease.

stem: A 32-year-old man is admitted to the acute medical unit with jaundice and lethargy. He drinks 40 units of alcohol per week. Transaminases, bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase are all markedly elevated and a diagnosis of acute fulminant hepatitis is made. What is the predominant pathological process occurring in this condition?
explanation:
Necrosis
Necrosis is cell death which occurs due to accumulated toxins, infection or trauma. This fits best with a diagnosis of alcoholic hepatitis.

Apoptosis
Apoptosis is incorrect. Apoptosis is the process of programmed cell death, and can occur in response to extrinsic signals such as hormones, growth factors or cytokines, or as a response to intracellular signalling.

De-differentiation
De-differentiation is incorrect. De-differentiation is loss of factors which differentiate one cell type from another, which usually occurs in response to an external stimulus. An example of de-differentiation is the fact that beta cells may lose their ability to produce insulin in response to autoimmune attack.

Ischaemia
Ischaemia is incorrect. Hepatic ischaemia is seen in response to right heart failure, or due to embolism. Drug-Induced Liver InjuryAn 18-year-old student – who had just returned from a gap-year trip to India – presented to the Emergency Department. He reported profound tiredness and a lack of appetite for the last week of his travels, and had noticed that he had developed jaundice just before he was due to return home. He had previously also felt feverish, but this appeared to have subsided once the jaundice appeared. He denied any sexual contacts while abroad. He did not have a blood transfusion or any tattoos during his trip, and denied ever using recreational drugs. Blood tests revealed an alanine aminotransferase (ALT) of 950 U/l, bilirubin of 240 μmol/l and an elevated alkaline phosphatase that was just outside the upper limit of normal. White blood cell count, albumin level and prothrombin time were all normal.

Senescence
Senescence is incorrect. Senescence is cellular loss of function which occurs due to natural aging.

stem: A 37-year-old homeless patient is found on the floor confused and unwell. He is bought to the emergency department by the police. After some prompting he denies any past medical history or regular medications. He says he hasn’t eaten in nearly 2 weeks. On examination, His BP is 100/80, pulse is 95 bpm. He looks malnourished and weak with a BMI of 17. He is admitted on the wards and a dietician makes a plan with the ward team on the best way to reinstitute feeding. Which of the following are you most concerned about?
explanation:
Hypophosphataemia
In this situation, with a prolonged period of low calorie intake, re-feeding syndrome is a possibility. This is characterised by hypophosphataemia which can drive generalised muscle weakness, cardiac failure and rhythm disturbance and is a potentially fatal condition. A hypophosphatamic state normally develops within 4 days of feeding commencing in at risk patients. These patients require close monitoring of blood biochemistry with dietician involvement.

Hypocalcaemia
Hypocalcaemia is incorrect. Hypocalcaemia is commonly found in hypoparathyroidism, chronic kidney disease, vitamin D, and phosphate deficiency. In malnutrition, low plasma calcium levels may occur due to reduced serum protein (particularly albumin); this is known as pseudohypocalceaemia. In this situation the free calcium may not be truly reflected. Calcium levels are not of primary concern in re-feeding syndrome.

Hypokalaemia
Hypokalaemia is incorrect. Although hypokalaemia is a consequence of re-feeding syndrome, it would be considered less dangerous than hypophosphataemia.

Hypomagnesaemia
Hypomagnesaemia is incorrect. Hypomagnesaemia is seen most commonly in patients with a history of diarrhoea.

Hyponatraemia
Hyponatraemia is incorrect. This is a feature of hypoadrenalism and syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone (SIADH), and isn’t necessarily associated with malnutrition.

stem: A 67-year-old man with a history of atrial fibrillation and cardiovascular disease was brought into hospital by his relatives with acute abdominal pain and vomiting. On examination, he was drowsy and looked unwell. His blood pressure was 105/60 mmHg, his pulse was 110 bpm, and he was in atrial fibrillation. His abdomen was generally tender. Initial blood tests revealed an amylase of 500 U/l (NR 25–170 U/l), neutrophilia and kidney disease, with a creatinine of 350 μmol/l (NR 60–110 μmol/l) and a urea of 12.5 mmol/l (NR 2.5–7.5 mmol/l). Further questioning revealed that he has complained of intermittent lower abdominal pain and diarrhoea after dinner over the past few months. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Acute-on-chronic mesenteric ischaemia
This scenario describes features consistent with both acute and chronic mesenteric ischaemia: Acute mesenteric ischaemia is a cause of elevated serum amylase that is unrelated to pancreatitis. The classic presentation is with acute abdominal pain and vomiting. Arterial embolus related to atrial fibrillation is the most common cause, with subsequent occlusion of the superior mesenteric artery. Abdominal examination usually reveals generalised tenderness, with distension and absence of bowel sounds. The mortality approaches 90%, and is related to multi-organ failure. Survivors have a high chance of developing short bowel syndrome, the severity of which is related to the length of bowel resection. There is also evidence of chronic small bowel ischaemia in this case, indicated by this man’s abdominal pain after meals over the past few months. Clinical signs of bowel ischaemia might be absent in the chronic phase due to the development of an adequate collateral circulation. Bruits may occasionally be heard over the abdomen, but are also found in many normal individuals.

Acute pancreatitis
Acute pancreatitis is incorrect. Although this man has an elevated serum amylase, he does not describe the history of acute severe upper abdominal pain that normally typifies acute pancreatitis. There are other conditions that may be associated with a rise in serum amylase other than pancreatitis, including acute mesenteric ischaemia. In addition, no risk factors are described for acute pancreatitis (alcohol excess and/or a history of gallstone disease would be those most commonly seen in practice).

Chronic pancreatitis
Chronic pancreatitis is incorrect. Chronic pancreatitis typically presents with features that are very different to those described here, including chronic upper abdominal pain, weight loss, diarrhoea/steatorrhoea and/or recent onset of diabetes mellitus. Serum amylase may be raised, but may also be normal. Furthermore, no risk factors for chronic pancreatitis are described (alcohol excess is the one most commonly seen in practice).

Chronic mesenteric ischaemia
Chronic mesenteric ischaemia is incorrect. Although this scenario describes features consistent with chronic mesenteric ischaemia (ie abdominal pain after meals in a patient with known vascular disease), his acute symptoms, tachycardia and abnormal blood tests all imply that he has acute mesenteric ischaemia as well.

Mesenteric vasculitis
Mesenteric vasculitis is incorrect. Although mesenteric vasculitis may cause clinical features similar to those described, this condition is very much less common than mesenteric ischaemia. The fact that this patient has a background of atrial fibrillation and cardiovascular disease is entirely consistent with this man having underlying mesenteric ischaemia. Bowel IschaemiaA 21-year-old student, who had recently returned from summer travels in the Far East, presented with acuteonset bloody diarrhoea, fever and abdominal pain. She had a raised, red rash on her shins. She described two previous attacks of acute bloody diarrhoea in the past 2 years that resolved over a period of a few weeks.

stem: A 23-year-old woman was in her 29th week of pregnancy. She had been suffering from itching for 3 weeks, which was getting progressively worse. She had now developed mild jaundice. Her bilirubin was raised at around 80 μmol/l and her alanine aminotransferase (ALT) raised at 82 U/l, whereas her full blood count was normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy
The combination of jaundice and pruritus in someone at this stage of their pregnancy is very suggestive of intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy, a condition that occurs in approximately 0.2% of pregnancies, and particularly affects woman in their second or third trimesters. Pruritus is the most common clinical feature of this condition, and jaundice may develop at approximately 1–4 weeks after this. Characteristic laboratory features include a rise in alanine aminotransferase (ALT), bilirubin and bile acid levels. Liver biopsy is not indicated, but the underlying pathology would show centrilobular cholestasis. The disease is associated with increased rates of stillbirth, prematurity and a fetal mortality rate of around 3.5%. Treatment is with the bile salt ursodeoxycholic acid, which appears to bile flow. There is a tendency for the cholestasis to recur in subsequent pregnancies, or after using the oral contraceptive pill.

Acute fatty liver of pregnancy
Acute fatty liver of pregnancy is incorrect. Acute fatty liver of pregnancy typically presents in the third trimester of pregnancy, causing a potentially life-threatening syndrome of liver failure that may progress to jaundice, coagulopathy, profoundly abnormal liver enzymes and encephalopathy. It is associated with fetal and maternal mortalities of up to 20%. Pruritus is not a typical feature of acute fatty liver of pregnancy; furthermore, this condition is typically associated with higher bilirubin and transaminase levels than is the case here.

Cholecystitis
Cholecystitis is incorrect. Cholecystitis is associated with a variable pattern of bilirubin and liver enzymes, but almost always with sharp upper abdominal pain; the lack of such features here makes this unlikely to be the diagnosis.

HELLP syndrome
HELLP syndrome is incorrect. HELLP syndrome (haemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, and low platelets) is a potentially life-threatening syndrome characterised by microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia, abnormalities in liver enzymes and a reduced platelet count; the normal full blood count result rules this out as a possibility here.

Hyperemesis gravidarum
Hyperemesis gravidarum is incorrect. The cardinal feature of hyperemesis gravidarum is severe vomiting, which is not described in the scenario and therefore unlikely to be the explanation here; in addition, hyperemesis is associated with only minor abnormalities in liver enzymes, and the level of bilirubin and ALT described here are slightly higher than would be typically expected of the condition.

stem: A 45-year-old woman presented with night sweats, right upper-quadrant abdominal pain, weight loss and anorexia. A scan revealed a liver abscess consistent with bacterial infection. Her past history of note included Crohn’s disease, which may have been a possible contributing cause. She was known to be allergic to penicillin, describing that she developed diarrhoea as a child after taking amoxicillin. Which of the following intravenous antibiotic regimens would be most appropriate as an empirical regimen?
explanation:
Ceftriaxone + metronidazole
Many different organisms can cause liver abscess, but the most frequently implicated are Gram-negative bacteria, Gram-positive anaerobes and other anaerobic organisms, so the initial choice of antibiotic treatment should reflect this. Ideally, a penicillin-based β-lactam antibiotic – combined with metronidazole to provide anaerobic cover – would be the treatment of choice. In this patient, where penicillin allergy is actually unlikely given the report of diarrhoea only, substituting the penicillin-based antibiotic with a cephalosporin would be a reasonable choice. Local hospital prescribing policies vary according to resistance patterns, however, and the choice suggested here would not necessarily be used in every hospital. In addition, cephalosporins as a group are less used than they were in the past because of the associated risk of Clostridium difficile colitis. The duration of the antibiotic course is also the subject of debate, but between 2–6 weeks of therapy is recommended after percutaneous drainage of the abscess.

Azithromycin + clindamycin
Azithromycin + clindamycin is incorrect. Gram-positive anaerobes are a relatively common cause of pyogenic liver abscess, and this regimen does not provide sufficient cover for these (clindamycin mostly targets Gramnegative anaerobes rather than Gram-positive); a regimen containing metronidazole would be preferable.

Clindamycin + ciprofloxacin
Clindamycin + ciprofloxacin is incorrect. Gram-positive anaerobes are a relatively common cause of pyogenic liver abscess, and this regimen does not provide sufficient cover for these (clindamycin mostly targets Gramnegative anaerobes rather than Gram-positive); a regimen containing metronidazole would be preferable.

Clindamycin + metronidazole
Clindamycin + metronidazole is incorrect. Although this regimen may be suitable, liver abscess is a potentially life-threatening condition, and very potent intravenous antibiotics are preferred, at least initially. Ceftriaxone is typically much more potent than clindamycin for this purpose. Liver AbscessA 55-year-old Vietnamese businessman relocated to the UK and presented with several months of diarrhoea, anorexia and weight loss. On examination, he had some non-specific abdominal tenderness and distension. He also had a little increased pigmentation, and glossitis was noted on examining his oropharynx. Rectal examination revealed steatorrhoea. Blood tests demonstrated megaloblastic anaemia, with vitamin B12 and folate deficiencies.

Vancomycin + meropenem
Vancomycin + meropenem is incorrect. This regimen provides good cover for Gram-positive bacteria (including anaerobes), but does not provide optimal cover for the Gram-negative bacteria that may cause pyogenic liver abscess.

stem: A 39-year-old patient presents to the emergency department with jaundice and mild left upper quadrant pain radiating to his back, and vomiting. He has no significant past medical history. He drinks 12 units of alcohol a week and is a non-smoker. On examination, he has upper abdominal tenderness and bruising in his flanks. Which of the following conditions can cause pancreatitis?
explanation:
IgG4 related disease
IgG4 related disease is a multi-organ immune mediated condition that can affect almost any organ and has been recognized increasingly in the last few years. It is characterised by elevated serum levels of IgG4 and inflammation in affected tissues with typical histological features of IgG4 bearing plasma cells, storiform fibrosis and obliterate phlebitis. The aetiology is unclear. It is a recognised cause of auto immune pancreatitis,usually resulting in chronic pancreatitis. Treatment is with steroids.

Hypoparathyroidism
Hypoparathyroidism is incorrect. Hyperparathyroidism and not hypoparathyroidism is a cause of acute pancreatitis.

Diabetes mellitus
Diabetes mellitus is incorrect. Diabetes mellitus is not a cause of acute pancreatitis. It can be a consequence of chronic pancreatitis.

Rubella
Rubella is incorrect. There are several infections linked with acute pancreatitis including Coxsackie virus, mumps, CMV, HIV, varicella, toxoplasma and a few others but rubella is not one of them. Acute PancreatitisFlashcards An 18-year-old man who is known to have Down syndrome presents to the Emergency department with acute abdominal pain and vomiting. He has not opened his bowels for the past 36hrs. On examination his temperature is 37.8 oC, BP is 105/60 mmHg, pulse is 85/min and regular.
