His abdomen is mildly distended and tender, tympanic to percussion. Bowel sounds are sluggish. An abdominal x-ray reveals dilated loops of small bowel. Investigations reveal:

Hypocalcemia
Hypocalcemia is incorrect. Hypercalcemia and not hypocalcemia can cause acute pancreatitis.

stem: A 48-year-old man is recovering on the gastroenterology ward after suffering from a large variceal haemorrhage. He is found to have grade II varices on endoscopy, which are banded. Which of the following is recommended with respect to long term prophylaxis against further bleeding?
explanation:
Propranolol
Non-selective beta-blockers reduce portal blood pressure and are therefore potentially useful with respect to prophylaxis against further variceal bleeds. As such they are the long term intervention of choice.

Bendroflumethiazide
Bendroflumethiazide is incorrect. Thiazides are not a first choice agent in the management of cirrhosis and portal hypertension.

Omeprazole
Omeprazole is incorrect. Although omeprazole is highly effective in reducing gastric acid production, it has no impact in reducing portal blood pressure.

Spironolactone
Spironolactone is incorrect. Whilst spironolactone is useful for addressing oedema associated with cirrhosis, it is less effective in reducing portal blood pressure.

Terlipressin
Terlipressin is incorrect. Terlipressin is used for the acute treatment of variceal haemorrhage.

stem: A 56 year old watercress farmer is admitted for worsening jaundice, pruritis and some right upper quadrant discomfort. He has dark urine and pale stools. There is no history of alcohol or IVDU use and no recent foreign travel. He occasionally takes NSAIDS for headaches, and St John's wort for depression. On examination he is afebrile, icteric, has some tenderness in the RUQ and hepatomegaly. US abdomen shows no gallstones, although intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts are dilated. What does the differential diagnosis include?
explanation:
Cholangiocarcinoma
Whilst all of the options can present with obstructive jaundice, only PSC and cholangiocarcinoma can give rise to intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile duct dilatation. Cholangiocarcinoma is a malignancy of the bile ducts, and usually presents late. PSC is the most common predisposing factor for cholangiocarcinoma. Liver fluke and industrial chemical exposure are other potential problems, and of course farming in a wet environment increases exposure to liver fluke. The only curative options are surgical resection or neoadjuvant chemotherapy followed by liver transplantation.

Drug-induced cholestasis
Drug-induced cholestasis is incorrect. Dug induced cholestasis can result in acute or chronic liver disease, or may be asymptomatic with only a raised ALP to indicate the presence of disease. Some of the common culprits include; Azathioprine, Isoniazid, Halothane, NSAIDS, macrolide antibiotics and tricyclic antidepressants. Resolution occurs after withdrawal of the offending drug – but may not be an immediate effect.

Viral hepatitis
Chronic viral hepatitis is more likely to be associated with features of fibrosis and hepatic cirrhosis, rather than intra and extra hepatic duct dilatation. We are also given no evidence of exposure to viral hepatitis given the absence of drug abuse history here.

Autoimmune hepatitis
Autoimmune hepatitis is incorrect. Autoimmune hepatitis isn't associated with hepatic bile duct dilatation, therefore the scenario isn't consistent with this as an underlying diagnosis. Hepatobiliary Tumours A nursing-home resident was brought by his carers to the Emergency Department because they were concerned that he was finding it difficult to eat. His past history of note included the use of a corticosteroid inhaler for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. On examination of his oropharynx, there were several areas of erythema, and a number of white plaques accompanied by some white, curd-like material.

Primary biliary cholangitis (PBC)
Primary biliary cholangitis (PBC) is incorrect. PBC is an autoimmune condition characterised by destruction of the intrahepatic bile ducts, eventually leading to chronic liver disease. IgM and ANA is often elevated, and antimitochondrial antibodies are found in 95% of patients. Only liver transplant is potentially curative.

stem: What would you expect to see on the blood film?
explanation:
Schistocytes
The clinical picture of bloody diarrhoea following a petting zoo visit, with findings of anaemia, thrombocytopenia and renal failure, is consistent with haemaolytic uraemic syndrome (HUS). This usually occurs in children and is caused by an E. coli 0157 infection. HUS is characterised by a micro-angiopathic haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia and renal failure (urine dip would be positive for protein and blood). The mechanism of the anaemia is via ‘shearing’ of red cells due to the presence of capillary microthrombi, making them fragmented. These are described as schistocytes on a blood film.

Elliptocytes
Elliptocytes is incorrect. Elliptocytes are seen in hereditary elliptocytosis which is caused by mutation in genes encoding RBC membrane proteins.

Target cells
Target cells is incorrect. These describe red blood cells that look thin and have precipitated haemaglobin in the centre. Causes include iron deficiency anaemia, sickle cell disease, thalassaemia and liver disease.

Giant platelets
Giant platelets is incorrect. These are seen in idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura or the rare inherited disorder Bernard-Soulier disease. E. coli InfectionRouleaux formation
Rouleaux formation is incorrect. Rouleaux formation describes the appearance of stacked red cells, which occurs due to hyperviscosity; these are typically seen in multiple myeloma.

stem: A 75-year-old man with a history of atrial fibrillation and peripheral vascular disease presented to the Emergency Department. His abdomen was distended and tender. A plain abdominal radiograph showed thumb-printing at the site of the splenic flexure. Blood testing revealed evidence of mild dehydration, and a slightly raised neutrophil count. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Ischaemic colitis
The combination of acute abdominal pain, raised inflammatory markers and the radiographic features described in a patient with established cardiovascular disease is a very typical presentation for ischaemic colitis. Risk factors for this condition (starting with the most common first) include: pre-existing vascular disease/cardiac arrhythmias (particularly atrial fibrillation) people with a thrombophilia syndrome women taking the oral contraceptive pill. The plain abdominal film is characteristic, with ‘thumb-printing’ occuring at the site of the splenic flexure. Thumb-printing represents underlying colonic oedema, which arises in the context of inadequate perfusion of the colon. The splenic flexure is particularly vulnerable to colonic ischaemia as it is a so-called ‘watershed’ area of the gut, ie sited at an overlap area between two sources of colonic perfusion (the superior and inferior mesenteric arteries), but with neither artery perfusing the area particularly well, and creating a propensity to hypoperfusion. Management of the condition is usually conservative, with intravenous rehydration and supportive management, but the condition may progress to gangrene and perforation, and require surgical colonic resection. A long-standing consequence of a resolved episode is stricture formation in the previously ischaemic area.

Colonic carcinoma
Colonic carcinoma is incorrect. Colonic carcinoma would not typically cause acute abdominal pain, and is not associated with colonic oedema.

Diverticular abscess
Diverticular abscess is incorrect. Diverticular abscess is unlikely given that his neutrophilia is only middle, and that there is no description of fever or any other features of sepsis.

Diverticulitis
Diverticulitis is incorrect. Diverticulitis is unlikely for a number of reasons, not least the lack of any apparent history of diverticular disease. Bowel IschaemiaUlcerative colitis
Ulcerative colitis is incorrect. The typical major clinical feature of a flare of ulcerative colitis is bloody diarrhoea, which is not described here; furthermore, the initial onset of ulcerative colitis is typically at a somewhat younger age than that of this patient.

stem: A 45-year-old bar owner from Tenerife presented for review. He reported being very tired and feeling ‘washed out’. He attended with his girlfriend, who was concerned that he was impotent and had lost interest in sex. He had a past history of joint pains and mild arthritis, particularly affecting his knees. There is a family history of autoimmune disease, with type 1 diabetes in one first-degree relative and hypothyroidism in another. On examination, he looked deeply tanned, there was loss of body hair, and he had testicular atrophy. His fasting blood glucose concentration was 8.4 mmol/l, and alkaline phosphatase and transaminase levels were raised. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Haemochromatosis
All of the clinical features described in this scenario may be found in haemochromatosis, making this the correct answer. Haemochromatosis often presents in the fifth decade in men, but women typically present later as menstruation acts as a natural form of venesection. The incidence is around 1 in 300 in white populations. The condition has an autosomal recessive pattern of inheritance, and the relevant gene mutations (the most common of which are C282Y and H63D) may now be screened for. The mutations associated with haemocromatosis result in increased iron absorption despite the existence of excessive iron stores; this results in the accumulation of iron in different organs of the body, and particularly in the liver. Typical clinical features of haemochromatosis include arthropathy, diabetes mellitus, impotence and increased pigmentation of the skin (the condition is sometimes referred to as ‘bronze diabetes’). Progressive iron deposition within the liver results in progressive fibrosis, which if untreated may lead to cirrhosis and its complications. Phlebotomy is the treatment of choice, generally aiming to reduce the haematocrit to below 40%. The prognosis is usually good if treatment is commenced before the development of advanced cirrhosis.

Alcohol-related cirrhosis
Alcohol-related cirrhosis is incorrect. Alcohol-related cirrhosis causes chronic liver disease and could potentially explain the abnormal liver enzymes described; however; the condition is not associated with any of the extrahepatic manifestations of haemochromatosis as described in this scenario, and therefore is not likely to be the underlying diagnosis here.

Diabetes mellitus
Diabetes mellitus is incorrect. Diabetes mellitus would clearly explain this man’s raised blood glucose (and could potentially explain his impotence), but could not account for his arthropathy, tanned appearance or apparent liver disease.

Primary adrenal failure
Primary adrenal failure is incorrect. Although primary adrenal failure (Addison’s disease) is often characterised by hyperpigmentation, it could not explain any of the clinical features described in this scenario; in particular, Addison’s disease is associated with hypoglycaemia rather than hyperglycaemia. Hereditary Haemochromatosis A 34-year-old man with a history of ulcerative colitis attends the Emergency Department. He was started on high-dose oral corticosteroids in the gastroenterology clinic 3 days earlier because he was opening his bowels 6-10 times per day with bloody diarrhoea. His symptoms have not improved; if anything his abdomen is more distended and there has been no difference in his bowel frequency. Examination reveals a BP of 105/70 mmHg, his pulse is 95/min and regular, and temperature is elevated at 38.2°C. His abdomen is distended and diffusely tender, and he has active bowel sounds. Investigations show:

Wilson’s disease
Wilson’s disease is incorrect. Wilson’s disease causes chronic liver disease and could potentially explain the abnormal liver enzymes described; however; the condition is not associated with any of the extra-hepatic manifestations of haemochromatosis as described in this scenario, and therefore is not likely to be the underlying diagnosis here.

stem: A 40-year-old woman attended the Emergency Department because of easy bruising. She had been diagnosed with Crohn’s disease 3 months earlier, and initiated on sulfasalazine at the time of diagnosis. Her bowel symptoms had much improved since starting on medication. On examination, she had a number of bruises. Blood testing revealed a pancytopaenia. Which of the following is the most likely cause of her pancytopaenia?
explanation:
Sulfasalazine therapy
Sulfasalazine therapy can lead to isolated falls in the numbers of red blood cells, white cells or platelets, or may alternatively lead to a pancytopaenia. The close temporal association between this woman starting sulfasalazine and her presentation with pancytopaenia suggests that sulfasalazine therapy is the correct answer here. As such, patients taking sulfasalazine are recommended to report any unexplained bleeding, bruising, purpura, sore throat, fever or malaise, so that a full blood count may be arranged; the medication should be suspended pending the result. Other side-effects of sulfasalazine therapy include: Hypersensitivity reactions Periorbital oedema Stomatitis Parotitis Cautions for sulfasalazine use include: Renal and hepatic insufficiency Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency Slow acetylator status

Acute leukaemia
Acute leukaemia is incorrect. Although acute leukaemia may cause a pancytopaenia, this is also often accompanied by other constitutional symptoms (e.g. fever), which is evidently not the case here. Furthermore, the clear close relationship in the time frame between this woman starting sulfasalazine and the development of pancytopaenia also means that acute leukaemia is unlikely to be the diagnosis here.

Immune (idiopathic) thrombocytopaenia
Immune (idiopathic) thrombocytopaenia is incorrect. Immune (idiopathic) thrombocytopaenia is characterised by an isolated thrombocytopaenia; a pancytopaenia would not be typical of the condition.

Viral infection
Viral infection is incorrect. Although certain viral infections (include Epstein–Barr virus, HIV or hepatitis) may cause a pancytopaenia, they are also often accompanied by other constitutional symptoms (eg fever), which is evidently not the case here. Furthermore, the clear close relationship in the time frame between this woman starting sulfasalazine and the development of pancytopaenia also means that viral infection is unlikely to be the diagnosis here. Crohn’s Disease A 56-year-old woman who has a history of systemic sclerosis comes to the clinic. She is currently managed with amlodipine for symptoms of Raynaud’s disease and omeprazole for gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GORD), but over the past few months she has suffered from increasing symptoms of abdominal bloating, intermittent diarrhoea and constipation. She is also increasingly nauseated despite taking her omeprazole regularly. On examination she has a slightly distended abdomen, which is soft with only mild tenderness. Investigations show:

Worsening of her Crohn’s disease
Worsening of her Crohn’s disease is incorrect. The information that her bowel symptoms have settled would be inconsistent with her Crohn’s disease worsening.

stem: A 67-year-old woman is admitted with iron deficiency anaemia. She has an ejection systolic murmur radiating to both carotids. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy and colonoscopy are normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next investigation?
explanation:
Repeat colonoscopy
This woman presents with an iron deficiency anaemia and also has features of aortic stenosis. Her upper gastrointestinal endoscopy and colonoscopy were reported as normal The most likely diagnosis is angiodysplasia. Angiodysplasia is the most common vascular lesion of the gastrointestinal tract; the condition may be asymptomatic, or it may cause gastrointestinal bleeding (estimated incidence of active bleeding being about 10% of affected cases). The most commonly affected site is the large bowel: 77% of angiodysplasia cases are located in the caecum and ascending colon, 15% in the jejunum and ileum, and the remainder distributed throughout the alimentary tract. Angiodysplasia is associated with aortic stenosis, making it even more likely that this is the diagnosis here. Pick up of colonic angiodysplasia, (sensitivity), is only 80% by colonoscopy however, this is why it is advisable to move to a repeat colonoscopy. Once two colonoscopies have taken place, moving to capsule endoscopy is a usual next step.

Barium enema
Barium enema is incorrect. Barium enema is a test that is helpful when looking for structural colonic abnormalities, but is not good at identifying subtle mucosal abnormalities such as angiodysplasia. Given that this woman’s colonoscopy has already excluded significant structural colonic disease, there is no additional merit in a barium enema.

Bone marrow examination
Bone marrow examination is incorrect. Although bone marrow examination may be an appropriate test to investigate unexplained cases of anaemia, iron deficiency anaemia in a woman of this age is much more likely to reflect blood loss than marrow failure.

Repeat upper gastrointestinal endoscopy
Repeat upper GI endoscopy is incorrect. If this woman’s previous upper gastrointestinal endoscopy had good views of the whole mucosa, it is likely to have been sufficient to confidently rule out an upper gastrointestinal tract lesion as the source of her anaemia. Vascular Lesions of the ColonA 17-year-old girl presented with lethargy and chronic nausea. She had been unable to complete her school examinations and her mother was worried that she might be depressed. On examination, there were signs of chronic liver disease and a brown-green ring at the periphery of the iris in both eyes. Her serum copper level was low.

Selective mesenteric angiography
Selective mesenteric angiography is incorrect. It is less successful in the diagnosis of chronic bleeding, because chronic blood loss over time is very difficult to see on mesenteric angiography.

stem: A 19-year-old student returned early from a cricket tour of India. He has recently played in a cricket match in Chennai, but had to leave the game early owing to sudden onset of painless, voluminous diarrhoea. There is no associated fever but he is complaining of abdominal cramps. He was advised to get on a plane home and collapsed as a result of dehydration soon after leaving the plane at Heathrow. On questioning he reported opening his bowels 20 times in 24 hours. A sample collected in the Emergency Department revealed a ricewater appearance. Vibrio cholerae were identified in the stool sample. Which of the following is the most appropriate antibiotic in this case?
explanation:
Oral doxycycline
The priority is to hydrate the patient and correct electrolyte imbalances. Antibiotic therapy can be started after rehydration and cessation of vomiting. Antibiotic use in cholera infection leads to a shortening of the duration of diarrhoea and an improved recovery versus oral rehydration alone. There is no evidence that intravenous administration incurs any advantages over the oral route. 300mg of doxycline given as a single dose is the recommended regimen. Alternatives include oral tetracycline or oral ciprofloxacin.

IV Ceftriaxone
IV Ceftriaxone is incorrect. Ceftriaxone is primarily used in the treatment of meningitis related to E coli rather than cholera related diarrhoea.

IV Ciprofloxacin
IV Ciprofloxacin is incorrect. Ciprofloxacin is a treatment option for salmonella infection, rather than cholera.

Oral amoxicillin
Oral amoxicillin is incorrect. Amoxicillin is a treatment option for listeria infection. Vibrio cholera is a gram negative comma shaped rod that spreads via the faecal-oral route. The incubation period ranges from 12 hours to 5 days. Symptoms can be mild- moderate watery diarrhoea but left untreated rapid dehydration can cause death. Diagnosis is by stool microscopy and culture. GastroenteritisAn 18-year-old media studies student was admitted to hospital at the end of the first week of his university course with severe epigastric pain. He was tender in the epigastrium. Investigations:

Oral metronidazole
Oral metronidazole is incorrect. Metronidazole is used for the treatment of giardia infection.

stem: A 52-year-old man is reviewed in the Emergency Department after being admitted with a bleeding duodenal ulcer. He was admitted with epigastric pain and diagnosed with duodenitis two years ago, but self-discharged from the hospital before therapy options could be discussed with him. Which of the following is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
explanation:
Helicobacter pylori
Helicobacter pylori is a well-known cause of duodenitis and duodenal ulceration and is probably the cause of his original presentation with epigastric pain. National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guidelines recommend H. pylori eradication therapy with a 7-day course of twice-daily proton pump inhibitor, amoxicillin and clarithromycin or metronidazole.

Campylobacter jejuni
Campylobacter jejuni is a common cause of gastroenteritis. Infection is usually related to under-cooked poultry. Most patients recover spontaneously over a few days, although some patients who are immunocompromised, elderly or have significant chronic morbidities require treatment with antibiotics. Azithromycin is the usual first choice.

Escherichia coli
Escherichia coli is one possible cause of bacterial overgrowth syndrome; it does not impact on the risk of duodenitis. Symptoms of bacterial overgrowth syndrome are similar to those of irritable bowel syndrome with bloating, abdominal pain and intermittent diarrhoea. Rifaximin is one potential option for treatment of bacterial overgrowth syndrome.

Streptococcus gallolyticus
Streptococcus gallolyticus is a recognised cause of bacterial endocarditis. When identified, it raises suspicions of either an underlying colonic neoplasm or abnormal architecture of the biliary tree prompting haematological spread of bacteria from the biliary tree. All cases of S. gallolyticus endocarditis should be investigated for an underlying cancer, preferably with a colonoscopy.

stem: Which one of the following factors will his prognosis depend on?
options: Degree of inflammation seen on computed tomography
explanation:
Partial pressure of oxygen (paO2)
The combination of acute severe epigastric pain and raised amylase level is consistent with a diagnosis of acute pancreatitis. It is likely that alcohol misuse is the cause for this. A number of different prognostic scoring systems for acute pancreatitis have been established, with hypoxia/reduced p aO 2 having been consistently identified to be an adverse prognostic factor.

Degree of inflammation seen on computed tomography
Degree of inflammation seen on computed tomography is incorrect. CT imaging of the pancreas is useful in people with acute pancreatitis as it allows for assessment of pseudocysts, abscesses and necrosis, all of which are associated with a worse prognosis. However, the degree of pancreatic inflammation in itself does not appear to be a prognostic factor.

Degree of opiate use
Degree of opiate use is incorrect. The degree of opiate use has not been shown to affect the prognosis of acute pancreatitis.

Pain severity
Pain severity is incorrect. The severity of pain has not been shown to affect the prognosis of acute pancreatitis. Acute PancreatitisFlashcards A 35-year-old Irish woman presents to the Haematology Clinic with unexplained megaloblastic anaemia. She has a history of peptic ulcer disease at age 23, for which she underwent Helicobacter pylori eradication. Over the past five months she has lost 3 kg in weight. There is no history of diarrhoea or abdominal bloating. On examination, her BP is 112/80 mmHg, with pulse 80/min and regular. She looks pale and you notice areas of vitiligo. Her BMI is 22. Investigations show:

Previous alcohol intake
Previous alcohol intake is incorrect. The patient’s previous alcohol intake has not been shown to affect the prognosis of acute pancreatitis.

stem: A 45-year-old man with a history of alcohol-related cirrhosis presented to the Emergency Department with massive upper gastrointestinal haemorrhage. It was suspected that he may have oesophageal varices. Which of the following fits best with the clinical features of varices?
options: Band ligation is successful in stopping acute bleeding in around 60% of patients
Emergency surgical portocaval shunting has a mortality of around 20%
Oesophageal transection has an operative mortality of around 5%
Overall mortality from bleeding varices is around 30%
Rebleeds occur within the first year in around 50% of survivors after oesophageal transection
explanation:
Overall mortality from bleeding varices is around 30%
The overall mortality rate from variceal haemorrhage is around 30%. The mortality rate is highest in patients with the most severe liver disease (Child–Pugh grade C).

Band ligation is successful in stopping acute bleeding in around 60% of patients
Band ligation is successful in stopping acute bleeding in around 60% of patients is incorrect. Success rates for band ligation in causing cessation of variceal bleeding are around 90%. This compares to approximately 80% success for balloon tamponade, and around 65% for medical therapy alone (vasopressin, nitrates, etc).

Emergency surgical portocaval shunting has a mortality of around 20%
Emergency surgical portocaval shunting has a mortality of around 20% is incorrect. While emergency surgical portocaval shunting controls bleeding in 95% of patients in which it is used, it has a periprocedural mortality of up to 40%. Although this partly reflects the invasive nature of the procedure, it also reflects the high acuity of the patients in which portocaval shunting is suitable. Where available, a radiologically guided shunt is preferred (transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic stent shunt [TIPSS]), as this is much less invasive than surgical portocaval shunting.

Oesophageal transection has an operative mortality of around 5%
Oesophageal transection has an operative mortality of around 5% is incorrect. Oesophageal transection has an operative mortality of around 10–20%. Alcoholic Liver Disease and Alcoholism

Rebleeds occur within the first year in around 50% of survivors after oesophageal transection
Rebleeds occur within the first year in around 50% of survivors after oesophageal transection is incorrect. Rebleeding occurs in up to 80% of people treated with oesophageal transection by 1 year post-operatively.

stem: Which of the following is the recommended next step to achieve sustained remission in this patient?
explanation:
Azathioprine
Azathioprine is recommended in patients with ulcerative colitis who fail to gain remission on mesalazine alone, or fail to tolerate mesalazine therapy. In patients with UC a Cochrane meta-analysis suggested ofTutor patients Chat56% with AI remained remission free treated with azathioprine vs 35% of placebo. It is also recommended in Crohn’s disease where two or more courses of corticosteroids are required per year. Of note 5-ASA’s have no role in small bowel Crohn’s disease. Before commencing azathioprine, thiopurine methyltransferase levels (TPMT) should be routinely tested in everyone as about 11% of the population have reduced TPMT activity and 0.3% have a TPMT deficiency. In these patients, active 6 mercaptopurine can accumulate and a larger proportion is converted to 6-thioguanine analogues which increase the risk of myelotoxicity.

Continuous low-dose corticosteroids
Continuous low-dose corticosteroids is incorrect. Continuous low dose steroids is rarely an option in IBD, due to the side effect profile. A short course of tapering steroids can be appropriate to induce remission in moderate to severe disease, with a view of instigating immunomodulators (the therapeutic action of which take weeks to months to achieve) and as such has been described as ‘bridging’ therapy.

Ciclosporin
Ciclosporin is incorrect. Ciclosporin is a calcineurin inhibitor which reduces the production of inflammatory cytokines. It is mainly used as rescue therapy in acute severe ulcerative colitis, as it has been proven to reduce the need for colectomy. Intravenous therapy is then usually followed by oral ciclosporin. There is a limited role in Crohn’s disease.

Infliximab
Infliximab is incorrect. Infliximab is an anti-TNF monoclonal antibody used to downregulate inflammation in IBD. It is used when immunomodulators such as azathioprine or methotrexate fail, or first line in fistulating disease.

stem: A 26-year-old woman presented to her general practititioner complaining of 6 months of intermittent uncomfortable abdominal distension and bloating, which changed with her menstrual cycle. These symptoms were interspersed with bouts of loose motions. She worked as a trader in a busy office and found work very stressful; she had previously taken a course of fluoxetine for anxiety and depression. Examination, blood test results and sigmoidoscopy were all normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Irritable bowel syndrome
Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) has a female to male preponderance of 2:1, and is found at higher rates in people with a background of affective disorders. Symptoms that change at different points in the menstrual cycle are not an unusual finding in IBS (although abdominal/pelvic symptoms affected by the menstrual cycle should also make clincians consider endometriosis as a possible diagnosis). Physical examination and investigations are invariably normal in IBS. Being able to differentiate functional from structural bowel disease is important; any history of unintentional weight loss, rectal bleeding, nocturnal diarrhoea, faecal incontinence or onset of persistent GI symptoms at >40 years of age is not consistent with functional disease, and requires further assessment. Management of IBS includes dietary modification (e.g. change in fibre, cutting out dairy foods, etc) and pharmacological therapy. Pharmacological options include anti-spasmodics (such as peppermint oil), antidiarrhoeals (e.g. loperamide) and laxatives. There is also a potential role for anti-depressants (including tricyclic antidepressants and selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors) in functional bowel disease, for treating the ‘visceral hypersensitvity’ that may be found in the condition.

Chronic pancreatitis
Chronic pancreatitis is incorrect. No risk factors for chronic pancreatitis (e.g. alcohol excess) are described; furthermore, the typical clinical features of chronic pancreatitis are severe upper abdominal pain radiating through to the back, and possible steatorrhoea in advanced disease, neither of which is described here.

Diverticulitis
Diverticulitis is incorrect. Diverticular disease tends to occur in people who are much older than this woman, with diverticulitis manifesting as acute-onset lower abdominal pain, altered bowel habit, rectal bleeding and fever, none of which fits with the scenario described here.

Peptic ulcer disease
Peptic ulcer disease is incorrect. Peptic ulcer disease typically presents with upper abdominal discomfort related to eating, and without any consistent disturbance of bowel habit; this clearly also does not fit with the symptoms outlined. Functional Bowel DiseaseA 56-year-old man with severe exertional dyspnoea is admitted with jaundice and ascites. He has recently been diagnosed with COPD by his GP, although he insists that he only smokes occasional cigars. His father died of respiratory illness at 54 years of age. Bilirubin, aspartate transaminase (AST) and alkaline phosphatase levels are elevated and liver biopsy reveals the presence of periodic acid–Schiff- (PAS-) positive, diastaseresistant globules in periportal hepatocytes.

Ulcerative colitis
Ulcerative colitis is incorrect. The characteristic presentation of ulcerative colitis includes diarrhoea, rectal bleeding and tenesmus, with raised inflammatory markers on blood tests; although this woman’s symptoms could potentially fit with this diagnosis, the normal blood test results and sigmoidoscopy help to rule this out.

stem: A 40-year-old woman with pernicious anaemia is admitted with jaundice. She drinks 10 units of alcohol per week. Examination shows bruises on her arms and legs, palmar erythema, spider naevi and hepatosplenomegaly. She also complains of joint pains and amenorrhoea of recent onset. She is on long-term nitrofurantoin for recurrent urinary tract infection. Investigations show a mild, normochromic, normocytic anaemia, bilirubin 89 μmol/l (normal range < 17 μmol/l) and aspartate transaminase (AST) 450 U/l (10–40 U/l). What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Nitrofurantoin-induced chronic active hepatitis
A huge range of different drugs have been recognised to potentially cause drug-induced liver injury (DILI). The clinical spectrum of this may range from a small perturbation of liver enzymes through to more dramatic presentations, including acute liver failure. Nitrofurantoin is one of the more common causes of DILI, and may cause a chronic active hepatitis syndrome, which results in symptoms and signs of decompensated chronic liver disease. Improvement is likely to occur following the withdrawal of nitrofurantoin. This chronic active hepatitis may be accompanied by features of autoimmune disease; common clinical features include symptoms such as the joint pain described here, and autoantibodies (eg anti-liver/kidney microsomal antibodies) may be positive. The normocytic anaemia may also be consistent with anaemia of chronic disease, whereas amenorrhoea may reflect chronic liver disease.

Alcoholic liver disease
Alcoholic liver disease is incorrect. This woman has features of chronic liver disease, but drinks alcohol within recommended limits, meaning this is unlikely to be the diagnosis.

Idiopathic cirrhosis
Idiopathic cirrhosis is incorrect. Although a small number of cases of cirrhosis are idiopathic, the constellation of features of chronic liver disease, features suggestive of immune overactivity (pernicious anaemia, joint pains, etc) and the use of nitrofurantoin collectively mean that nitrofurantoin-induced chronic active hepatitis is far more likely than idiopathic cirrhosis.

Primary biliary cholangitis
Primary biliary cholangitis is incorrect. Primary biliary cholangitis (PBC; until recently known as ‘primary biliary cirrhosis’) may present with non-specific symptoms, although fatigue and pruritus are common. PBC is a cholestatic liver disease, so typically manifests with a raised alkaline phosphatase but normal transaminases; an AST of 450 U/l would be inconsistent with the diagnosis of PBC, and much more consistent with a form of hepatitis, making Option A incorrect. Anti-mitochondrial antibody (AMA) would be the test of choice to assess for suspected PBC. Drug-Induced Liver InjuryA 36-year-old man with ulcerative colitis was admitted with abdominal pain and an amylase level of 1433 U/l. Which medication is most likely to be a cause of his symptoms?

Viral hepatitis
Viral hepatitis is incorrect. Her raised bilirubin and AST indicate a hepatitic process, but no risk factors for viral hepatitis are described.

stem: A 24-year-old woman presented as an emergency to her general practitioner with acute vomiting. Her symptoms began about 3–4 hours after attending an afternoon meeting. Cream cakes were served during the tea break. Which of the following organisms is the most likely cause of this acute attack of vomiting?
explanation:
Staphylococcus aureus
This question describes a typical scenario of Staphylococcus aureus food poisoning. This organism causes up to 2–5% of cases of bacterial food poisoning. The organisms multiply rapidly in foods that are rich in carbohydrates and salt (e.g. dairy products, cold meats or mayonnaise) kept at room temperature. They produce a heat-stable endotoxin that causes nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea typically 1–6 hours after the ingestion of contaminated food. Fever is uncommon, and only supportive treatment is usually required.

Bacillus cereus
Bacillus cereus is incorrect. Rather than dairy products, Bacillus cereus infection is particularly associated with slow-cooked food and reheated rice (making it a common problem with takeaway food). The bacterium produces an emetic toxin that leads to vomiting in 1–5 hours or diarrhoea after 8–16 hours.

Campylobacter spp.
Campylobacter spp is incorrect. Campylobacter infection has an incubation period of 3-7 days. Campylobacter infection leads to flu-like symptoms, abdominal pain and diarrhoea.

Salmonella spp.
Salmonella spp is incorrect. Salmonella infections normally lead to gastroenteritis at 8-48 hours after the ingestion of infected food. GastroenteritisYersinia enterocolitica
Yersinia enterocolitica is incorrect. Yersinia infection typically leads to bloody diarrhoea rather than vomiting. Furthermore, Yersinia’s incubation period is about 4-10 days.

stem: Which of the following is likely to be the most appropriate treatment for his symptoms?
explanation:
Phosphate supplementation
This patient has refeeding syndrome, which consists of metabolic disturbances that occur as a result of reinstitution of nutrition to patients who are starved or severely malnourished. During starvation, the body uses fatty acids or amino acids as the main energy source, which suppresses insulin release and reduces intracellular minerals (particularly phosphate). During refeeding, insulin secretion increases in response to glucose, resulting in increased glycogen, fat and protein synthesis, which requires phosphate, magnesium and potassium, stores of which are already depleted. Body fluid and electrolyte fluxes that occur after feeding may result in muscle weakness, depressed myocardial contractility and rhabdomyolysis, in conjunction with acute hypophosphataemia. The most important electrolyte to replace is phosphate.

Calcium supplementation
Calcium supplementation is incorrect. In refeeding syndrome, calcium fluxes do not occur as dramatically as fluxes in serum phosphate, and there is no place for treating with calcium alone.

Magnesium supplementation
Magnesium supplementation is incorrect. Magnesium is an important salt to replace but because the hallmark biochemical feature of refeeding syndrome is hypophosphataemia, phosphate replacement is more important in treatment.

Potassium supplementation
Phosphate supplementation is incorrect. Potassium is also an important salt to replace, but from the options listed, phosphate is the single best answer Nutritional Assessment, Malabsorption and FeedingA 45-year-old publican collapsed while closing up his pub and is taken to the Emergency Department. His wife tells you that he has recently been referred by his GP to the hospital because of abnormal liver function tests. On examination he looks pale and his blood pressure is 130/90 mmHg, with a postural drop of 30 mmHg on standing; his pulse is 95 bpm and regular. There are signs of chronic liver disease. Which of the following blood results would be most suggestive of an upper gastrointestinal (GI) bleed?

Vitamin B supplementation
Vitamin B supplementation is incorrect. Vitamin B replacement is used in the prophylaxis or treatment of Wernicke’s encephalopathy, which can also be precipitated in malnourished patients.

stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management?
explanation:
Magnesium sulphate
This woman is suffering from HELLP (i.e. Haemolysis–Elevated Liver enzymes–Low Platelets). The key management step in pregnancy is to plan for delivery, as this is the definitive management of the condition. The immediate risk prior to obstetric review is one of eclampsia-related seizures, and so magnesium is given as an infusion pre-delivery, during delivery and in the immediate post-partum period, regardless of blood pressure.

Dexamethasone
Dexamethasone is incorrect. This woman is suffering from HELLP (i.e. Haemolysis–Elevated Liver enzymes–Low Platelets). A number of studies have examined the role of dexamethasone in treating HELLP syndrome; there have been some contradictions in results, but overall it appears that steroids are unlikely to be of significant benefit.

Intravenous heparin
Intravenous heparin is incorrect. This woman is suffering from HELLP (i.e. Haemolysis–Elevated Liver enzymes– Low Platelets). Despite previous interest, there is no good evidence that intravenous heparin is a useful treatment for HELLP syndrome.

Normal human immunoglobulin
Normal human immunoglobulin is incorrect. This woman is suffering from HELLP (i.e. Haemolysis–Elevated Liver enzymes–Low Platelets). There is little evidence to suggest that human immunoglobulin is a useful treatment for HELLP syndrome. HELLP SyndromePlasma exchange
Plasma exchange is incorrect. This woman is suffering from HELLP (i.e. Haemolysis–Elevated;Liver enzymes– LowPlatelets). While plasma exchange is effective for treating thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP), there is little evidence to suggest that it is a useful treatment for HELLP syndrome.

stem: A 28-year-old woman who is 32 weeks pregnant with her second child presents to the Emergency department with jaundice. She is very concerned that this may result in the termination of her pregnancy. The only significant medical history is that she has returned from a holiday to Southern Spain a few days earlier. Which one of the following statements can be used to reassure her?
options: Acute fatty liver usually follows a benign course in pregnancy
Acute viral hepatitis always follows a benign course in pregnancy
No further intervention is usually required after investigation
Obstetric cholestasis doesn’t recur in subsequent pregnancies
Treatment with anti-histamines without investigation is all that is required
explanation:
No further intervention is usually required after investigation
Obstetric cholestasis occurs late in pregnancy and is a form of obstructive cholestasis. It is unclear whether it is associated with significant risks to the fetus, it may be associated with increased risks of bleeding for the mother.

Acute fatty liver usually follows a benign course in pregnancy
Acute fatty liver usually follows a benign course in pregnancy is incorrect. Acute fatty liver is progressive resulting in liver failure and encephalitis, the only possible intervention being delivery of the child.

Acute viral hepatitis always follows a benign course in pregnancy
Acute viral hepatitis always follows a benign course in pregnancy is incorrect. Both hepatitis A and hepatitis E are associated with much more significant liver damage when they occur in pregnancy.

Obstetric cholestasis doesn’t recur in subsequent pregnancies
Obstetric cholestasis doesn’t recur in subsequent pregnancies is incorrect. Obstetric cholestasis does have a tendency to recur in subsequent pregnancies. Pregnancy-related Liver DiseaseTreatment with anti-histamines without investigation is all that is required
Treatment with anti-histamines is all that is required is incorrect. It’s important to define the cause of jaundice before advising on necessary intervention.

stem: A 36-year-old nurse with a 15-year history of ulcerative colitis developed abnormal liver enzymes: ALT, 154 U/l; ALP, 354 U/l; bilirubin, 12 μmol/l. An ultrasound of the liver was normal. Her anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA) test was positive and anti-mitochondrial antibody (AMA) negative. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Primary sclerosing cholangitis
This woman is likely to have primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC). PSC is a condition of complex aetiology (although appears to have an autoimmune component) that is strongly associated with inflammatory bowel disease (and especially ulcerative colitis). It is characterised by inflammation and stricturing of both the intraand extrahepatic biliary tree. The condition is usually first suspected in people with inflammatory bowel disease who develop cholestatic liver enzymes without an alternative explanation; ultrasound, magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) and occasionally endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) are useful for making the diagnosis, with imaging showing characteristic ‘beading’ and stricturing of the biliary tree. Rarely, the condition may just affect the intrahepatic biliary tree (so-called ‘small duct PSC’), with liver biopsy being required to confirm the diagnosis. PSC may be complicated by recurrent episodes of cholangitis, requiring frequent episodes of antibiotics and occasionally - endoscopic stenting. The other major potential complication of PSC is a range of malignancies, including colorectal cancer, cholangiocarcinoma, gallbladder malignancy and – for those with PSC who develop significant hepatic fibrosis – hepatocellular carcinoma. As such, people with PSC require surveillance for colorectal cancer via annual colonoscopy, as well as regular ultrasound of the liver/MRCP to screen for hepatobiliary malignancies.

Chronic active hepatitis
Chronic active hepatitis is incorrect. This woman has a raised ALT and ALP, but a disproportionately elevated ALP; as such, she is likely to have a cholestatic rather than a hepatic liver disease.

Gallstones
Gallstones is incorrect. Although this woman’s blood test results could be consistent with a flare of gallstone disease, the absence of any abdominal pain and the lack of any gallstones on ultrasound suggest that this is unlikely to be the diagnosis.

Mesalamine hepatitis
Mesalamine hepatitis is incorrect. This woman has a raised ALT and ALP, but a disproportionately elevated ALP; as such, she is likely to have a cholestatic rather than a hepatic liver disease.

Primary biliary cholangitis
Primary biliary cirrhosis is incorrect. While primary biliary cholangitis (PBC; previously called ‘primary biliary cirrhosis’) could explain this woman’s cholestatic blood tests, the negative anti-mitochondrial antibody result effectively rules out this condition.

stem: A 54-year-old man attends his GP with feelings of lethargy. Routine screening reveals raised gammaglutamyltransferase (GGT). Which of following statements concerning GGT is true?
options: Increased GGT is found in cases of fatty liver
Isolated elevation of GGT in a patient with prostatic carcinoma indicates the presence of hepatic
It is a better indicator of infectious hepatitis than of cholestasis
It is only present in liver
Serum activity is typically elevated in pregnancy
explanation:
Increased GGT is found in cases of fatty liver
GGT may be raised in fatty liver disease.

Isolated elevation of GGT in a patient with prostatic carcinoma indicates the presence of hepatic
Isolated elevation of GGT in a patient with prostatic carcinoma indicates the presence of hepatic metastases Isolated elevation of GGT in a patient with prostatic carcinoma indicates the presence of hepatic metastases is incorrect. Any rise in GGT because of hepatic metastases would be expected to be accompanied by a rise in alkaline phosphatase.

It is a better indicator of infectious hepatitis than of cholestasis
It is a better indicator of infectious hepatitis than of cholestasis is incorrect. Infectious hepatitis is most associated with rises in serum transaminases, whilst raised GGT is more typically a marker of cholestasis. However, GGT it is not a highly sensitive and specific marker for cholestasis, and raised levels need to be interpreted within the clinical context. For instance, GGT can be induced by drugs such as phenytoin and alcohol; mild raises in GGT can occur with any alcohol intake, and a rise does not always indicate liver pathology.

It is only present in liver
It is only present in liver is incorrect. GGT is a microsomal enzyme that is present in many tissues, including the liver. Non-alcoholic

Serum activity is typically elevated in pregnancy
Serum activity is typically elevated in pregnancy is incorrect. Alkaline phosphatase is typically elevated in pregnancy (as the placenta is a source of it), but GGT is not.

stem: A 17-year-old girl is admitted to the medical ward for feeding because an eating disorder has left her severely undernourished. Her BMI is 14 and she looks pale and weak. On examination, her BP is 90/65 mmHg, pulse is 45bpm and temperature is 36 °C. Which of the following statements regarding feeding is true?
options: If her thiamine levels are normal, no supplementation is necessary
Nasogastric tube feeding should be attempted first, given her psychiatric background
The patient should be made fluid and electrolyte replete alongside feeding
Hyperkalemia is the hallmark of refeeding syndrome
She is in a high catabolic state and will require higher than average energy requirements
explanation:
The patient should be made fluid and electrolyte replete alongside feeding
This patient is high risk for re-feeding syndrome and so electrolytes and fluid balance must be corrected alongside feeding. The rate of feeding should be slowed down. . This reduces the risk of major body fluxes occurring and causing disturbances that can be seen in re-feeding syndrome such as cardiac failure, fluid overload, hypotension, pre-kidney disease and sudden death.

If her thiamine levels are normal, no supplementation is necessary
If her thiamine levels are normal, no supplementation is necessary is incorrect. Thiamine should be given to all patients suspected to be at risk of re-feeding syndrome regardless of the serum levels.

Nasogastric tube feeding should be attempted first, given her psychiatric background
Nasogastric tube feeding should be attempted first, given her psychiatric background is incorrect. Oral feeding should always be attempted before tube feeding unless there is a contraindication.

Hyperkalemia is the hallmark of refeeding syndrome
Hyperkalemia is the hallmark of refeeding syndrome is incorrect. Hypophosphatemia is the hallmark of refeeding syndrome. It usually co-exists with hypokalaemia. Refeeding SyndromeA 45-year-old man with a long history of Crohn’s disease presents to the Gastroenterology Clinic with lethargy and progressively increasing generalised itching over the past 6 months. His Crohn’s is quiescent and he is maintained on a small dose of Mesalazine only. He opens his bowels normally 2-3 times per day. Examination reveals a BP of 110/72 mmHg; pulse is 70/min and regular. Abdomen is soft and non-tender, apart from some vague pain in the right upper quadrant. His BMI is 22. There are generalised scratch marks and he has jaundiced sclerae. Investigations;

She is in a high catabolic state and will require higher than average energy requirements
She is in a high catabolic state and will require higher than average energy requirements is incorrect. Prolonged inadequate dietary intake predisposes to a low catabolic state. Examples of high catabolic states include intensive care unit patients, septic patients or those with malignancies, and these groups would have higher calorie requirements.

stem: A 51-year-old man presents with weight loss and is found on examination to have hepatomegaly. He complains of flushing and wheeze. Blood testing reveals a mild normochromic normocytic anaemia (Hb 108 g/l) and elevated liver transaminases. Imaging reveals multiple hepatic lesions. Urinary 5-HIAA levels are found to be elevated. Given the likely diagnosis, which additional clinical feature is the most likely to be present?
explanation:
Diarrhoea
The diagnosis here is carcinoid syndrome. It is a paraneoplastic syndrome comprising the signs and symptoms that occur secondary to carcinoid tumors. The syndrome includes flushing and diarrhea, and, less frequently, heart failure and bronchoconstriction. It is caused by endogenous secretion of mainly serotonin and kallikrein.

Abdominal pain
Abdominal pain is incorrect. This is not a common feature of carcinoid syndrome, occurring in less than 10% of cases.

Hypertension
Hypertension is incorrect. This is not a feature of carcinoid syndrome, the likely diagnosis in this case. Flushing in carcinoid may be accompanied by tachycardia, while the blood pressure usually falls or does not change.

Skin rash
Skin rash is incorrect. This is not a typical feature of carcinoid syndrome, the likely diagnosis in this case. It can occur in the setting of pellagra from niacin deficiency in carcinoid. You do get skin flushing and telangiectasias. Carcinoid syndrome Malignant carcinoid syndrome is characterized by an array of signs and symptoms—in particular, hot, red flushing of the face; severe and debilitating diarrhea; and wheeze, caused by vasoactive hormones secreted by metastases from carcinoid tumours. Typically, 90% of carcinoid tumors originate from the distal ileum or appendix. Carcinoid tumors represent 90% of appendiceal tumors. Carcinoids do not produce the malignant carcinoid syndrome until they are no longer confined to the small bowel or mesentery. The somatostatin analogs octreotide and lanreotide are used to control carcinoid symptoms and tumor progression in advanced inoperable disease. Neuroendocrine Tumours A 72-year-old man with a history of type 2 diabetes comes to the Emergency department with severe abdominal pain and diarrhoea mixed with dark blood. He reports paroxysms of lower abdominal pain occurring after meals some 6-8 times over the past few months. On examination his temperature is 37.9 oC, BP is 100/60 mmHg, pulse is 95/min and regular. His abdomen is generally tender with quiet bowel sounds. Arterial blood gasses show a pH of 7.15 and a marked elevation in serum lactate. You suspect ischaemic colitis. Where is the most likely affected area?

Headache
Headache is incorrect. This is not a typical feature of carcinoid syndrome, the likely diagnosis in this case.

stem: A 65-year-old woman with scleroderma and Raynaud’s phenomenon complained of weight loss and was referred for further investigation. Which of the following conditions is most strongly associated with progressive systemic sclerosis?
explanation:
Oesophageal stricture
Systemic sclerosis results in vascular damage, fibrosis, alterations in gastrointestinal tract motility and an activated immune system. Gastrointestinal tract involvement includes: Oesophageal strictures Malabsorption – including small-bowel bacterial overgrowth Intestinal pseudo-obstruction Anal incontinence. As such, oesophageal stricture is the correct choice here.

Abnormal exocrine pancreatic function
Abnormal exocrine pancreatic function is incorrect. Although systemic sclerosis is associated with certain causes of malabsorption (including small-bowel bacterial overgrowth), it is not strongly associated with pancreatic exocrine failure.

Diverticulitis
Diverticulitis is incorrect. Diverticulitis has no consistent association with systemic sclerosis.

Primary sclerosing cholangitis
Primary sclerosing cholangitis is incorrect. The CREST variant of systemic sclerosis (ie Calcinosis cutis, Raynaud’s phenomenon, oEsophageal hypomobility, Sclerodactyly and Telangiectasia) is linked with primary biliary cholangitis but not with sclerosing cholangitis. Systemic Sclerosis Which statement about alcohol-related liver disease is correct?

Small-bowel lymphoma
Small-bowel lymphoma is incorrect. Small-bowel lymphoma has no consistent association with systemic sclerosis.

stem: Which statement about alcohol-related liver disease is correct?
options: Alcohol-related fatty infiltration is irreversible once established
Hepatic iron overload is indicative of concomitant heterozygote haemochromatosis
In alcoholic hepatitis the aspartate aminotransferase to alanine aminotransferase (AST:ALT) ratio is
Men are more susceptible than women
Unlike other causes of liver cirrhosis, alcohol-related cirrhosis does not progress to hepatoma
explanation:
In alcoholic hepatitis the aspartate aminotransferase to alanine aminotransferase (AST:ALT) ratio is
In alcoholic hepatitis the aspartate aminotransferase to alanine aminotransferase (AST:ALT) ratio is 2:1 Alcohol-related liver disease is a term that describes a spectrum of disorders including simple steatosis of the liver, acute alcoholic hepatitis, steatohepatitis and alcohol-related cirrhosis. Alcohol remains the most common cause of cirrhosis in developed countries at present. Although liver enzymes may be variable in other forms of alcohol-related liver disease, it is well-recognised that alcoholic hepatitis is associated with a reversed AST:ALT ratio of 2:1.

Alcohol-related fatty infiltration is irreversible once established
Alcohol-related fatty infiltration is irreversible once established is incorrect. Alcohol-related fatty infiltration appears to be reversible with abstinence and adequate nutrition.

Hepatic iron overload is indicative of concomitant heterozygote haemochromatosis
Hepatic iron overload is indicative of concomitant heterozygote haemochromatosis is incorrect. Transferrin saturation and serum ferritin are commonly increased in alcohol-related liver disease, and minor degrees of iron overload are common within the condition, allowing this option to be ruled out.

Men are more susceptible than women
Men are more susceptible than women is incorrect. Women are more susceptible to alcohol-related liver disease than men, even when consumption is corrected for body weight. Alcoholic Liver Disease and Alcoholism A 43-year-old woman presented with a three month history of diarrhoea and abdominal pain. She also reported flushing after drinking alcohol. On examination blood pressure was 128/72mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min. She had a flushed face, facial telangiectasia and mild hepatomegaly.

Unlike other causes of liver cirrhosis, alcohol-related cirrhosis does not progress to hepatoma
Unlike other causes of liver cirrhosis, alcohol-related cirrhosis does not progress to hepatoma is incorrect. It is well established that alcohol-related cirrhosis may progress to hepatoma.

stem: A 43-year-old woman presented with a three month history of diarrhoea and abdominal pain. She also reported flushing after drinking alcohol. On examination blood pressure was 128/72mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min. She had a flushed face, facial telangiectasia and mild hepatomegaly. What is the most appropriate investigation?
options: Stool microscopy for ova and parasites
explanation:
24 hour urinary 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid
This patient has symptoms and signs suggestive of carcinoid syndrome, and detection of 5-HIAA in the urine is an appropriate diagnostic test.

24 hour urinary metanephrine
24 hour urinary metanephrine is incorrect. This would be an appropriate investigation for phaeochromocytoma; however, this would present with hypertension (this patient is normotensive), sweating, tremor and headaches, none of which are reported by this patient. This patient has symptoms and signs consistent with carcinoid syndrome, and the appropriate investigation would be 24 hour urinary 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid.

24 hour urinary uroporphyrin
24 hour urinary uroporphyrin is incorrect. This test can be used to diagnose porphyria, though it can be inappropriately slow for the diagnosis of an acute attack of porphyria, when a random urine test is sufficient for diagnosis. This patient does not have symptoms and signs consistent with porphyria; instead, it is more suggestive of carcinoid syndrome. The most appropriate test for carcinoid syndrome is 24 hour collection of 5hydroxyindoleacetic acid.

Follicle stimulating hormone levels
Follicle stimulating hormone levels is incorrect. This can be used to confirm the menopause in patients aged between 40 and 45 years old experiencing symptoms of menopause. Although this patient has flushing, diarrhoea and abdominal pain are not symptoms of menopause. You would not expect facial flushing, telangiectasia and hepatomegaly in menopause; this patient’s symptoms and signs are more suggestive of carcinoid syndrome, for which the appropriate diagnostic test is 24 hour urine collection for 5hydroxyindoleacetic acid. Neuroendocrine Tumours

Stool microscopy for ova and parasites
Stool microscopy for ova and parasites is incorrect. Stool microscopy can be appropriate in the investigation of prolonged diarrhoea; however, parasitic infection would not explain the flushing and facial telangiectasia in this patient. A more likely explanation is carcinoid syndrome, for which the most appropriate investigation is 24 urine collection for 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid.

stem: A 54-year-old man with long-standing ulcerative colitis is seen in the Gastroenterology Clinic. His general practitioner has noticed that he has abnormal liver enzymes, and also that he has lost weight. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Biliary tract carcinoma
Ulcerative colitis (UC) is associated with a number of different conditions, including erythema nodosum, pyoderma gangrenosum, uveitis, scleritis, episcleritis and primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC). PSC is a chronic disease of unclear aetiology that is characterised by inflammation, scarring and stricturing of the biliary tree. The diagnosis is usually first suspected from the finding of cholestatic liver enzymes in people with inflammatory bowel disease, with the identification of biliary stricturing on cholangiography (such as by MRCP or ERCP) helping to confirm the diagnosis. It is usually the medium and large biliary ducts of both the intra- and extrahepatic biliary tree that are affected in PSC, although a small number of people with the condition have involvement of the intrahepatic biliary tree only (‘small duct PSC’); such patients require a liver biopsy to confirm the diagnosis. PSC has a number of well-recognised complications, particularly an increased risk of colonic cancer (meaning that an annual colonoscopy is required as surveillance). PSC with intrahepatic duct involvement is also a risk factor for chronic liver disease and its complications, including hepatocellular carcinoma. One other well-recognised complication of PSC is cholangiocarcinoma (biliary tract malignancy), and regular imaging of the biliary tree is indicated as surveillance. The description in this question of a man with UC who has abnormalities in liver enzymes and weight loss makes biliary tract carcinoma the correct answer here.

Non-specific urethritis
Non-specific urethritis is incorrect. Non-specific urethritis would not explain this man’s symptoms, and is also not a condition related to inflammatory bowel disease.

Primary biliary cholangitis
Primary biliary cholangitis (PBC) is incorrect. PBC is much less likely to be associated with inflammatory bowel disease versus PSC.

Seropositive arthritis
Seropositive arthritis is incorrect. A seronegative arthritis may occur in association with inflammatory bowel disease (so-called ‘enteropathic arthritis’), but there is no strong association with seropositive disease. Primary Sclerosing Cholangitis A 24-year-old man presented with malaise, mild fever, loss of weight and anorexia. On examination, his sclerae appeared yellow. Serum bilirubin was elevated at 85 μmol/l (normal range 1–22 μmol/l), enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) for IgG anti-HEV (anti-hepatitis E virus) was positive, and HEV RNA was detectable in serum by polymerase chain reaction (PCR). What would the characteristic finding on liver biopsy be in this case?

Small-bowel lymphoma
Small-bowel lymphoma is incorrect. The risk of small bowel lymphoma is increased in people with inflammatory bowel disease, although they are still rare malignancies. They occur against a background of poorly controlled coeliac disease in many cases.

stem: A 28-year-old woman comes to the obesity clinic for advice. Her BMI is 39 and she maintains she has always been overweight, with a consistency to gain weight throughout her life. Her mother is also significantly overweight, as are her two sisters. She wants to know why she is overweight. Which of the following is the most important causative factor in the development of obesity in the majority of patients?
options: Energy intake in excess of expenditure
explanation:
Energy intake in excess of expenditure
The ultimate cause of weight gain is energy intake in excess of expenditure for the majority of patients. Varying underlying aetiologies are proposed, with the most likely cause being behavioural factors coupled with a minor influence from a number of different genes. Decreased overall energy expenditure, decreased energy expenditure after a period of exercise, and increased energy intake can all contribute to weight gain.

Insulin resistance
Insulin resistance is incorrect. Insulin resistance is primarily a consequence of obesity rather than a cause of it, although in patients with type 2 diabetes and obesity it is insulin resistance that drives the need for quite large doses of exogenous insulin to achieve glycaemic control.

Intrauterine malnutrition
Intrauterine malnutrition is incorrect. Intrauterine malnutrition may contribute to obesity in some patients (but not the majority) because of intrauterine programming driving chronic overeating.

Leptin deficiency
Leptin deficiency is incorrect. Deficiency of leptin, or inadequate action of leptin, may drive lipodystrophy, which often is not associated with overall BMI in the obesity range. Nutritional Assessment, Malabsorption and FeedingMelanocortin 4 receptor null mutations
Melanocortin 4 receptor null mutations is incorrect. Melanocortin 4 receptor null mutations are rare, but they do lead to significant weight gain. Partial loss of function mutations are more common as a cause of obesity.

stem: A 45-year-old man presented to his general practitioner with epigastric pain. He worked as a company sales manager, drank 35 units of alcohol per week and smoked 10 cigarettes per day. He denied using NSAIDs. Screening for Helicobacter pylori was negative. He succeeded in giving up smoking, reduced his alcohol intake and was given a trial of lansoprazole by his doctor. Three months later, he presented to the Emergency Department with haematemesis. Endoscopy showed multiple duodenal ulcers. What is the most appropriate management plan?
options: Consider screening for multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2
Discharge home and continue low-dose lansoprazole
Measure his serum gastrin level and consider an octreotide scan or endoscopic ultrasound, then give
Measure his serum vasoactive intestinal polypeptide level
Treat for Helicobacter pylori, even if repeat screen is negative
explanation:
Measure his serum gastrin level and consider an octreotide scan or endoscopic ultrasound, then give
Measure his serum gastrin level and consider an octreotide scan or endoscopic ultrasound, then give him a high-dose proton-pump inhibitor The presence of recurrent peptic ulcer disease in a young person without an obvious alternative explanation raises the possibility of gastrinoma; when a gastrinoma leads to hypersecretion of gastric acid and multiple duodenal ulcers this is known as the Zollinger–Ellison syndrome. Gastrinoma is rare (accounting for 1 in 1000 cases of duodenal ulceration), but should always be considered in scenarios such as this; as such, measuring serum gastrin level with consideration of an octreotide scan for endoscopic ultrasound, then giving him a highdose proton-pump inhibitor, is the correct answer. High-dose proton-pump inhibitors can suppress symptoms, but surgical resection is the only curative option.

Consider screening for multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2
Consider screening for multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 (MEN 2) is incorrect. Gastrinomas may also occur as part of the autosomal dominant multiple endocrine neoplasia 1 (MEN-1) syndrome (i.e. the ‘three Ps’ – parathyroid, pituitary and pancreatic tumours), but are not associated with MEN-2 syndrome.

Discharge home and continue low-dose lansoprazole
Discharge home and continue low-dose lansoprazole is incorrect. Given that this man reduced his risk factors for peptic ulceration and used lansoprazole, but still had significant peptic ulcer disease, it is clear that this would not be appropriate.

Measure his serum vasoactive intestinal polypeptide level
Measure his serum vasoactive intestinal polypeptide (VIP) level is incorrect. VIPomas are – like gastrinomas – a form of neuroendocrine tumour that may arise from the pancreas; unlike them, however, the major clinical manifestation they give is diarrhoea rather than peptic ulcer disease. Peptic Ulcer Disease and Gastritis

Treat for Helicobacter pylori, even if repeat screen is negative
Treat for Helicobacter pylori, even if repeat screen is negative is incorrect. Currently available tests for H. pylori are so sensitive that it is unlikely that he has underlying infection which has been hitherto missed.

stem: A 24-year-old man presented with malaise, mild fever, loss of weight and anorexia. On examination, his sclerae appeared yellow. Serum bilirubin was elevated at 85 μmol/l (normal range 1–22 μmol/l), enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) for IgG anti-HEV (anti-hepatitis E virus) was positive, and HEV RNA was detectable in serum by polymerase chain reaction (PCR). What would the characteristic finding on liver biopsy be in this case?
options: Marked increase in the activation of sinusoidal lining cells
explanation:
Marked cholestasis
The diagnosis in this case is acute hepatitis E infection. Marked cholestasis is a hallmark histological finding in hepatitis E virus infection.

Ground-glass hepatocytes
Ground-glass hepatocytes is incorrect. Ground-glass hepatocytes are a particular form of large hepatocytes; they may be found histologically in chronic hepatitis B infection (occurring in cells containing hepatitis B surface antigen), but are not found in hepatitis E.

Lymphoid aggregates
Lymphoid aggregates is incorrect. Hepatitis C infection is associated histologically with both lymphoid aggregates and a marked increase in the activation of sinusoidal lining cells, although neither of these is feature of hepatitis E infection.

Marked increase in the activation of sinusoidal lining cells
Marked increase in the activation of sinusoidal lining cells is incorrect. Hepatitis C infection is associated histologically with both lymphoid aggregates and a marked increase in the activation of sinusoidal lining cells, although neither of these is a feature of hepatitis E infection.

Microvesicular steatosis
Microvesicular steatosis is incorrect. Microvesicular steatosis is a well-recognised liver biopsy feature of hepatitis D infection, but is not seen in hepatitis E infection.

stem: A 72-year-old man with a history of Parkinson’s disease comes to the Gastroenterology Clinic with his relatives for review. They describe episodes of bloating and abdominal distension accompanied by vomiting which occurs intermittently, once every 2-3 weeks, and can last for a number of hours before resolving spontaneously. Abdominal examination in the clinic is unremarkable. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Intestinal pseudo-obstruction
Intestinal pseudo-obstruction is a common feature of advanced Parkinson’s disease, and results in symptoms of intermittent abdominal bloating and vomiting. Prokinetics are an option, although agents such as metoclopramide may actually worsen the underlying movement disorder.

Coeliac disease
Coeliac disease is incorrect. We are not given any evidence of diarrhoea or weight loss to suggest underlying coeliac disease although the two could theoretically co-exist in this patient.

Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease
Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease would more usually be associated with symptoms of epigastric pain and water brash, rather than the marked abdominal distension seen here.

Peptic ulcer disease
Peptic ulcer disease in the absence of symptoms of indigestion would be unusual as the underlying diagnosis. Bowel Obstruction

Small bowel lymphoma
Small bowel lymphoma is very rare and usually develops after a number of years of symptoms of coeliac disease.

stem: Which of the following is the most likely causative pathogen?
explanation:
Streptococcus bovis
S. bovis is a bacterium that is found among the normal flora of the human gastrointestinal tract in 5–16% of adults. There have been studies that have demonstrated an increased risk of concurrent colorectal cancer in the presence of S. bovis endocarditis. This patient’s symptoms of weight loss, change in bowel habit and evidence of microcytic anaemia make the possibility of an underlying colorectal malignancy more likely.

Coxiella burnetii
C. burnetii is an obligate intracellular bacterium that causes ‘Q fever’. It is an uncommon cause of infective endocarditis but often will cause culture-negative infective endocarditis. Additional symptoms of this disease include malaise, pyrexia of unknown origin and atypical pneumonia. Microcytic anaemia, change in bowel habit and weight loss are not features and suggest an alternative diagnosis.

Staphylococcus aureus
S. aureus is the most common cause of infective endocarditis. Given the history of constipation, weight loss and the presence of anaemia, however, it is likely that this patient has an underlying diagnosis of colorectal cancer, making S. bovis a more likely answer.

Staphylococcus epidermidis
S. epidermidis is a coagulase-negative staphylococcus that is commonly a skin commensal organism. It is a less likely cause of infective endocarditis in this patient.

Streptococcus mitis
S. mitis is a member of the viridans family and is linked to poor dental hygiene or dental procedures. It does not explain the weight loss, constipation or anaemia.

stem: Which of the following medications is most likely to be effective for her?
explanation:
Cholestyramine
There is no evidence that the diarrhoea is due to active Crohn’s disease (normal inflammatory markers, inactive disease on imaging). Given the history of surgery for ileocaecal disease, bile acid malabsorption is very likely. Bile acids are usually reabsorbed in the terminal ileum, but if not, they reach the colon where they increase motility, reduce colonic transit time and are deconjugated by bacteria to produce end products that stimulate water and electrolyte secretion. Cholestyramine is a bile acid sequestrant that can significantly reduce symptoms of bile acid diarrhoea.

Codeine phosphate
Codeine phosphate is incorrect. Where symptoms continue, addition of codeine may be of value, but this is not the first-line treatment.

Loperamide
Loperamide is incorrect. Loperamide can also be used to increase stool bulk but, again, is not first-line therapy.

Mesalazine
Mesalazine is incorrect. There is a very limited role for mesalazine in inducing remission in mild Crohn’s disease, but even so, this patient does not have any objective evidence of active disease.

Prednisolone
Prednisolone is incorrect. Given the absence of active markers of disease, a course of steroids is not appropriate here. Crohn’s Disease A 25-year-old woman presented with weight loss, abdominal pain and diarrhoea. Her anti-endomysial antibody was positive, and a duodenal biopsy confirmed subtotal villous atrophy and intraepithelial lymphocytes.

stem: A 25-year-old woman presented with weight loss, abdominal pain and diarrhoea. Her anti-endomysial antibody was positive, and a duodenal biopsy confirmed subtotal villous atrophy and intraepithelial lymphocytes. Which of the following is a well recognised feature of coeliac disease?
explanation:
Splenic atrophy
Splenic atrophy is well recognised as a potential complication of coeliac disease, being identified in approximately 50% of affected patients. The identification of Howell–Jolly bodies on blood film microscopy may be a useful indicator of underlying hyposplenism. Splenic atrophy responds poorly to gluten withdrawal.

Colonic ulceration
Colonic ulceration is incorrect. Although ulcers in the colon are clearly associated with ulcerative colitis, there is no strong association with coeliac disease.

PR bleeding
PR bleeding is incorrect. If PR bleeding is present, other aetiologies would be sought.

Erythema nodosum
Erythema nodosum is incorrect. Erythema nodosum has a number of associations, which include inflammatory bowel disease; however, it is not associated with coeliac disease.

Hypersplenism
Hypersplenism is incorrect. Coeliac disease is associated with hypo- rather than hypersplenism.

stem: Which of the following would be most useful next diagnostic step?
explanation:
CT abdomen
The symptoms of epigastric pain radiating to the back in association with weight loss and signs of biliary obstruction are suggestive of an underlying pancreatic carcinoma. Non-invasive imaging with CT is the appropriate next step.

CA 19-9
CA 19-9 is incorrect. CA19-9 is a tumour marker for pancreatic cancer but has a limited role in screening for cancer, and is used for detection of recurrence after resection.

Gastroscopy
Gastroscopy is incorrect. Gastroscopy would be useful if the patient had new upper GI symptoms such as dyspepsia or reflux, but the epigastric pain radiating to the back suggests retroperitoneal pathology, which a gastroscopy would not be able to access.

Endoscopic ultrasound
Endoscopic ultrasound is incorrect. An endoscopic ultrasound to get biopsies or brushings can be considered but only once a diagnosis is made by CT.

US abdomen
US abdomen is incorrect. An ultrasound can image pancreatic pathology but is less sensitive than CT.

stem: A 26-year-old nurse was reviewed in clinic to investigate a raised ALT level. She had sustained a needle-stick injury 8 months ago, after which she did not present immediately to occupational health, and only attended her general practitioner when she later began to feel tired and lethargic. Blood tests revealed positive anti-HBs antibodies and anti-HCV antibodies, and low levels of HCV RNA were detected. Liver biopsy demonstrated early inflammatory change. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Chronic hepatitis C infection
The combination of positive anti-HCV antibodies and detectable HCV RNA is most consistent with ongoing viral replication, i.e. chronic hepatitis C infection. Although a small proportion of people exposed to hepatitis C spontaneously clear the virus, this woman still has detectable HCV RNA even 8 months after exposure; this, together with the raised ALT/inflammatory change of her liver without another obvious explanation, makes resolving hepatitis C infection a less likely explanation.

Autoimmune hepatitis
Autoimmune hepatitis is incorrect. This woman’s HCV antibody and RNA results mean that this is the most likely cause of her raised ALT/biopsy findings. Furthermore, no autoantibody results are given that might support the diagnosis of autoimmune hepatitis.

Chronic hepatitis B infection
Chronic hepatitis B infection is incorrect. The positive anti-HBs antibodies imply that this woman is immune to hepatitis B, probably as a result of previous vaccination.

Functional symptoms
Functional symptoms is incorrect. This woman’s raised ALT, antibody results and liver biopsy findings all mean that her tiredness/fatigue is unlikely to be functional, and much more likely to be explained by hepatitis C infection. Viral Hepatitis A 31-year-old man presented with microcytic anaemia. He described a change in his bowel habit over the past few months.
