His past medical history included hyperpigmented retinal pigment epithelium, noted when he attended the optician; he had also had some teeth removed for overcrowding during his teenage years, and had suffered from a number of troublesome lipomas. His father had died at the age of 41 years from colonic carcinoma. Colonoscopy revealed a number of dysplastic polyps and a right-sided colonic carcinoma.

Resolved hepatitis C infection
Resolved hepatitis C infection is incorrect. The combination of positive anti-HCV antibodies and detectable HCV RNA is most consistent with ongoing viral replication, i.e. chronic hepatitis C infection. Although a small proportion of people exposed to hepatitis C spontaneously clear the virus, this woman still has detectable HCV RNA even 8 months after exposure; this, together with the raised ALT/inflammatory change of her liver without another obvious explanation, makes resolving hepatitis C infection a less likely explanation.

stem: A 31-year-old man presented with microcytic anaemia. He described a change in his bowel habit over the past few months. His past medical history included hyperpigmented retinal pigment epithelium, noted when he attended the optician; he had also had some teeth removed for overcrowding during his teenage years, and had suffered from a number of troublesome lipomas. His father had died at the age of 41 years from colonic carcinoma. Colonoscopy revealed a number of dysplastic polyps and a right-sided colonic carcinoma. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Gardner syndrome
This scenario describes typical clinical features of Gardner syndrome. Gardner syndrome has an autosomal dominant mode of inheritance and is characterised by multiple adenomatous intestinal polyps, osteomas and soft-tissue tumours, including lipomas, fibromas and epidermoid cysts. Congenital hypertrophy of the retinal pigment epithelium is also a feature. It is caused by a mutation on the adenomatous polyposis coli gene (APC) on chromosome 5q21. Polyps occur at a mean age of 16 years, and may be found anywhere throughout the gastrointestinal tract. Colonic carcinoma develops in 7% of affected individuals by the age of 21, in 50% by age 39 and in 90% by age 45, and the average age of presentation with colonic carcinoma in unscreened people with Gardner syndrome is 35 years. Total colectomy is the treatment of choice after the appearance of colonic polyps.

Juvenile polyposis
Juvenile polyposis is incorrect. Juvenile polyposis is an autosomal dominant condition that presents first in childhood (rather than young adulthood), and is characterised by multiple hamartomatous polyps throughout the GI tract.

Neurofibromatosis
Neurofibromatosis is incorrect. Neurofibromatosis-1 is associated with an increased risk of GI stromal tumours, but the syndrome is not otherwise associated with GI polyps or malignancies; furthermore, none of the typical dermatological manifestations of neurofibromatosis (including neurofibromas, café-au-lait macules, and so on) is described in this scenario.

Peutz–Jeghers syndrome
Peutz–Jeghers syndrome is incorrect. Peutz–Jeghers syndrome is an autosomal dominantly inherited condition that is associated with intestinal hamartomas as well as peri-oral pigmented macules – however, it is not associated with any of the extra-intestinal features found in Gardner syndrome.

Sporadic colonic carcinoma
Sporadic colonic carcinoma is incorrect. Sporadic colonic carcinoma more usually presents with a tumour in the left colon than on the right, and would be very unusual in a patient as young as this.

stem: A 77-year-old woman complains of abdominal pain, nausea, anorexia and weight loss of 4 months’ duration. The pain is dull, boring and radiates through to her back. Examination reveals mild epigastric tenderness but there are no palpable masses. Gamma GT and alkaline phosphatase are both above the upper limit of normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Carcinoma of the pancreas
In a woman of this age with this history and constellation of physical findings, carcinoma of the body or tail of the pancreas would seem to be the most likely diagnosis. Unlike carcinoma of the head of the pancreas, obstructive jaundice does not typically occur with tumours in the body or tail (unless tumours are very large/advanced). However, an increase in cholestatic liver enzymes (gamma GT and alkaline phosphatase) is frequently seen.

Cholangiocarcinoma
The commonest presentation of cholangiocarcinoma (cancer of the biliary tree) is with obstructive jaundice, often without significant abdominal discomfort; the absence of overt jaundice here makes it less likely to be the underlying diagnosis.

Gastric carcinoma
The description of a dull, boring pain that radiates through to the back is highly suggestive of pancreatic disease, making gastric carcinoma less likely. Furthermore, it would be unusual for these gastric carcinomas to cause abnormal liver enzymes (although this may be found in the case of gastric carcinoma that has metastasised to the liver).

Peptic ulcer disease
The description of a dull, boring pain that radiates through to the back is highly suggestive of pancreatic disease, making peptic ulcer disease less likely.

Zollinger–Ellison syndrome
Zollinger–Ellison syndrome occurs in association with pancreatic gastrinomas; these are very rare tumours (most pancreatic tumours are adenocarcinomas), and tend to present with recurrent peptic ulceration and diarrhoea, and this is unlikely to be the case here.

stem: A 62-year-old paediatrician presents to her GP with intermittent abdominal pain, weight loss, anaemia, diarrhoea and intermittent facial flushing. He refers her to the gastroenterologist as he suspects a carcinoid tumour. She is keen to know more about her condition. Which one of the following statements regarding carcinoid tumours is true?
options: Aortic stenosis is the most common valve disease in advanced carcinoid tumour
Diagnosis is made by measuring serum 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid levels
Carcinoid tumours are often fast- growing
The carcinoid syndrome is caused by release of serotonin and prostaglandins
It is most commonly found in the colon
explanation:
The carcinoid syndrome is caused by release of serotonin and prostaglandins
Carcinoid syndrome usually occurs when a carcinoid tumour has metastasised to the liver. The symptoms of flushing, wheeze and diarrhoea occurs as serotonin and prostaglandins secreted from the tumour, are released into the circulation via the hepatic vein and bypass the portal vein (and therefore metabolism by the liver).

Aortic stenosis is the most common valve disease in advanced carcinoid tumour
Aortic stenosis is the most common valve disease in advanced carcinoid tumour is incorrect.

Diagnosis is made by measuring serum 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid levels
Diagnosis is made by measuring serum 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid levels is incorrect. Diagnosis is made my measuring 24-hour urine 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid levels (5-HIAA). 5-HIAA is the end-product of serotonin metabolism.

Carcinoid tumours are often fast- growing
Carcinoid tumours are often fast- growing is incorrect. Carcinoid tumours are very often slow growing.

It is most commonly found in the colon
It is most commonly found in the colon is incorrect. Carcinoid tumours are most commonly located in the small bowel and appendix. Neuroendocrine Tumours A 27-year-old man who works as a bond trader comes to the Emergency Department complaining of recurrent abdominal pain and bloody diarrhoea. He has griping pains in his lower abdomen and passes bloody diarrhoea 5-6 times per day. He has not had any weight loss. He is a smoker, drinks occasional alcohol and uses cocaine up to 4-5 times per week. He has not had any foreign travel in the last year. On examination his BP is 135/88 mmHg, with pulse 98/min and regular. Temperature is normal. His BMI is 25 and the abdomen is soft, although there is left-sided tenderness on palpation. A faecal calprotectin is borderline. The remainder of the investigations show.

stem: Which of the following is the most important next investigation?
explanation:
Abdominal X-ray
An abdominal X-ray is crucial for this patient to rule out toxic megacolon, a severe complication of ulcerative colitis. Toxic megacolon is characterised by significant bowel dilatation, loss of haustral markings and thumbprinting, which can be identified on an X-ray. Given the patient's worsening abdominal distension, fever and elevated inflammatory markers, immediate identification and intervention are essential. Early detection of toxic megacolon can prevent further complications such as perforation, sepsis and death.

CT abdomen
A CT abdomen is not typically required in the initial evaluation of acute UC unless there is a strong suspicion of perforation. While a CT scan provides detailed imaging, it is more invasive and time-consuming compared to an abdominal X-ray. In this patient’s acute setting, an X-ray is quicker and sufficient to identify toxic megacolon. CT scans are reserved for cases where other complications or differential diagnoses are suspected after initial assessment with an X-ray.

Faecal calprotectin
Faecal calprotectin is a marker of intestinal inflammation and can support the diagnosis of inflammatory bowel disease. However, it is not the most immediate concern in this acute scenario. This test is more useful for monitoring disease activity and response to treatment over time rather than diagnosing acute complications. Given the patient’s severe symptoms and risk of toxic megacolon, an abdominal X-ray takes precedence to quickly identify life-threatening conditions.

Sigmoidoscopy
While sigmoidoscopy is useful for obtaining biopsy specimens and confirming active inflammation, it is not appropriate as the first investigation in this situation. Performing a sigmoidoscopy in a patient with suspected toxic megacolon poses a high risk of bowel perforation. It should be considered only after ruling out toxic megacolon with an abdominal X-ray. The patient's immediate safety and the need to identify any critical complications make the X-ray the priority. Ulcerative Colitis

Stool culture
Stool cultures are important for ruling out infectious causes of diarrhoea, such as Clostridium difficile, which can co-exist with ulcerative colitis. However, in the acute setting of potential toxic megacolon, stool cultures are not the most urgent investigation. The results take time to process and will not immediately aid in the identification of life-threatening complications. An abdominal X-ray provides rapid information that is critical for immediate management, making it the priority over stool cultures.

stem: A 35-year-old man presents with recent-onset dysphagia. This had been initially to liquids, but then, 2 months later, to solids. His weight has been stable. In the past week he has woken up coughing during the night. An upper gastrointestinal endoscopy performed at the onset of his symptoms was reported as being normal. What is the most useful diagnostic test?
explanation:
Oesophageal pull-through manometry
The history described is the classic one for achalasia, ie an abrupt-onset dysphagia, often without weight loss. Achalasia is a condition associated with failure of relaxation of the lower oesophageal sphincter, and where the sphincter actually is often hypertensive resulting in dysphagia. The oesophagus dilates and loses the normal pattern of peristaltic waves; these are often replaced by simultaneous contraction of the oesophageal body or loss of all activity. It is important to recognise symptoms of regurgitation and aspiration – a night-time cough or recurrent sore throats in the morning could be suggestive of this. Investigation consists of upper gastrointestinal endoscopy (to rule out pseudo-achalasia due to a carcinoma), barium swallow (which classically shows the ‘rat’s tail’ appearance of the lower sphincter), and pull-through manometry. Pull-through manometry is the most specific diagnostic test, and will demonstrate the hypertensive sphincter and motility disorder.

13
C urea breath test 13 C urea breath test is incorrect. A C urea breath test may be used to assess for the presence of Helicobacter pylori in the upper gastrointestinal tract, but would not add any useful information here. 13 13

24-hour oesophageal pH study
24-hour oesophageal pH study is incorrect. A 24-hour oesophageal pH study is useful in the diagnosis of gastro-oesophageal reflux disease, but is not a useful test for suspected achalasia.

Barium follow-through
Barium follow-through is incorrect. As already described, a barium swallow may be suggestive of the condition, but extending a contrast study as far as a follow-through is unlikely to be of any additional benefit. Achalasia

Repeat upper gastrointestinal endoscopy
Repeat upper gastrointestinal endoscopy is incorrect. Assuming the first endoscopy had good views, it is unlikely that a repeat gastroscopy would provide any further useful information (furthermore, upper gastrointestinal malignancy is clearly very unlikely in a man of this age).

stem: Which of the following is the next investigation of choice?
explanation:
Colonoscopy +/- rectal biopsy
The lower GI symptoms coupled with anaemia and raised ESR in this age group point to possible inflammatory bowel disease limited to the distal portion of the colon / rectum. As such colonoscopy +/- rectal biopsy is the next investigation of choice. Abdominal imaging with ultrasound or CT may also be of value, although they are less useful in the initial stages of investigation versus direct imaging. Oral amino salicylates are the initial therapy of choice for many patients, with rectal steroids also an option for patients with predominantly distal disease.

Bone marrow examination
Bone marrow examination is incorrect. In this case, with gastrointestinal symptoms as a potential cause for the patient’s anaemia, GI investigations are the most important next step.

CT abdomen with contrast
CT abdomen with contrast is incorrect. CT abdomen with contrast is less effective in imaging colonic inflammation versus colonoscopy; hence it is usually reserved for individuals who are unfit or unwilling to undergo colonoscopy.

Haemoglobin electrophoresis
Haemoglobin electrophoresis is incorrect. There is no indication for haemoglobin electrophoresis until a GI cause for blood loss has been excluded. Ulcerative Colitis

Ultrasound abdomen
Ultrasound abdomen is incorrect. Abdominal ultrasound is most useful for excluding other GI pathology such as hepatobiliary disease.

stem: A 32-year-old man was referred with gastro-oesophageal reflux disease and commenced on a proton-pump inhibitor. Which of the following is true of the gastric K+/H+-ATPase proton pump?
options: It also occurs in other tissues
It is an acute antigen in pernicious anaemia
It is made up of alpha-, beta- and gamma-subunits
It is situated in chief cells
explanation:
Omeprazole binds to it irreversibly
It is the alpha-subunit of the proton-pump that catalyses the enzymatic activity, and which forms an irreversible covalent complex with omeprazole. However, as the half-life of the pump is 24–36 hours, the duration of the effect of proton-pump inhibitors is limited by the degradation of these pumps.

It also occurs in other tissues
It also occurs in other tissues is incorrect. The proton pump is only contained in the tubulovesicles of the parietal cell.

It is an acute antigen in pernicious anaemia
It is an acute antigen in pernicious anaemia is incorrect. Pernicious anaemia is associated with chronic autoantibody production (IgG) against the gastric K +/H +-ATPase proton pump, but it is not an acute antigen.

It is made up of alpha-, beta- and gamma-subunits
It is made up of alpha-, beta- and gamma-subunits is incorrect. The proton pump has only alpha and beta subunits.

It is situated in chief cells
It is situated in chief cells is incorrect. The proton pump is only contained in the tubulovesicles of the parietal cell. Gastro-oesophageal.

stem: A 65-year-old vegetarian woman – who ate a diet rich in a wide range of different fruits and vegetables – presented to the clinic complaining of facial flushing and diarrhoea. The flushing episodes could last from a few minutes to a few hours, and the diarrhoea was often accompanied by a feeling of peristaltic rushing. Her general practitioner was worried that she may have an enlarged liver and sent off for a 24-h urinary 5hydroxyindoleacetic acid (5-HIAA) test to assess for carcinoid syndrome. The 5-HIAA result came back above the normal range. What would be the most appropriate next step?
options: Arrange an echocardiogram to rule out right-sided cardiac disease
Proceed to computed tomography of the abdomen
Repeat the 5-HIAA test after dietary restriction
Try subcutaneous somatostatin for symptomatic relief
explanation:
Repeat the 5-HIAA test after dietary restriction
The clinical features described – together with the raised 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid (5-HIAA) result – could be consistent with carcinoid syndrome. However, this woman is a vegetarian; bananas, aubergines, avocados, pineapples and walnuts may all lead to a falsely elevated urinary 5-HIAA level. As such, the most appropriate next step is to repeat the 5-HIAA assay after removal of dietary factors that may falsely elevate it. Should the test still be positive when repeated after dietary restriction, appropriate tests to identify and characterise the carcinoid tumour include computed tomography, radiolabelled octreotide scanning, and echocardiography (with the latter particularly to assess for the valvular heart disease associated with the condition). However, none of these tests would be appropriate at this stage.

Arrange an echocardiogram to rule out right-sided cardiac disease
Arrange an echocardiogram to rule out right-sided cardiac disease is incorrect. This would not be an appropriate next step at this stage. It is important to first rule out a dietary cause for the raised urinary 5-HIAA.

Proceed to computed tomography of the abdomen
Proceed to computed tomography of the abdomen is incorrect. This would not be an appropriate next step at this stage. It is important to first rule out a dietary cause for the raised urinary 5-HIAA.

Scan with radiolabelled octreotide
Scan with radiolabelled octreotide is incorrect. This would not be an appropriate next step at this stage. It is important to first rule out a dietary cause for the raised urinary 5-HIAA. Neuroendocrine Tumours

Try subcutaneous somatostatin for symptomatic relief
Try subcutaneous somatostatin for symptomatic relief is incorrect. Somatostatin and its analogues are recognised to provide symptomatic relief in the carcinoid syndrome, but would not be initiated without a confirmed diagnosis, meaning this option may be excluded.

stem: A 62-year-old woman complains of diarrhoea, weight loss and abdominal pain, with malaise and fever. She has oral ulcers, red, itchy eyes and tender nodules on her shins. She has tenderness in the right iliac fossa and a vague right iliac fossa mass. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Crohn’s disease
The most likely diagnosis is Crohn’s disease. Although this condition often first presents in people somewhat younger than this patient, it is not unusual for the condition to first present in women over 60 years of age. The intestinal features of the condition are the most well recognised, but Crohn’s disease also has a huge number of extra-intestinal manifestations, including episcleritis, uveitis, erythema nodosum, pyoderma gangrenosum, vasculitis, gallstones, kidney stones or abnormal liver enzymes.

Appendicular abscess
Appendicular abscess is incorrect. Appendicular abscess could certainly explain some of the abdominal symptoms described, but would not explain the eye and skin features of this woman’s illness.

Ileocaecal tuberculosis
Ileocaecal tuberculosis is incorrect. Ileocaecal tuberculosis may present with very similar symptoms to ileocaecal Crohn’s disease; both conditions may also look similar endoscopically and demonstrate granulomas on histology, and the differentiation of the two conditions can therefore be difficult. However, no risk factors for tuberculosis are given in the question, making it less likely to be the diagnosis.

Ovarian mass
Ovarian mass is incorrect. Ovarian mass could certainly explain some of the abdominal symptoms described, but would not explain the eye and skin features of this woman’s illness. Crohn’s Disease

Ulcerative colitis
Ulcerative colitis is incorrect. Given that the intestinal symptoms described are so suggestive of terminal ileitis (with no description given of the urgency and tenesmus that may characterise proctitis), Crohn’s disease is much more likely than ulcerative colitis.

stem: A 21-year-old woman is seen in the Gastroenterology Clinic for follow-up. She has a diagnosis of familial adenomatous polyposis. Which of the following tumours is most associated with familial adenomatous polyposis?
explanation:
Medulloblastoma
Mutations in the APC gene are more commonly associated with medulloblastoma. This is one of the forms of Turcot syndrome (polyps and a primary brain tumour), with glioblastoma associated with hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer being another.

Endometrial cancer
Endometrial cancers are more common in association with hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer. This is a different form of familial polyposis.

Glioblastoma
Hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer is more commonly associated with glioblastoma. Mutations in the APC gene (ie in familial adenomatous polyposis) are more commonly associated with medulloblastoma.

Lung cancer
Lung cancer is unusual as a tumour presentation in familial adenomatous polyposis.

Ovarian cancer
Ovarian cancer is more commonly associated with hereditary non-polyposis colorectal cancer.

stem: A 65-year-old woman has recent-onset diarrhoea, a temperature of 37.6 °C and intermittent abdominal cramps. She had a chest infection 3 weeks ago and was prescribed antibiotics. What is the most likely cause of her diarrhoea?
explanation:
Clostridium difficile infection
This woman most probably has Clostridium difficile infection. The clue is in the information that she has recently had antibiotics – antibiotics disrupt the normal healthy gut flora (which helps to protect against GI infection), leaving the gut vulnerable to infection with spore-forming bacteria such as C. difficile. The conventional means of diagnosis include ELISA of the toxins (A and B) produced by the organism, or by PCR. Culture of C. difficile is not diagnostic because it is carried by approximately 5% of normal healthy adults. The main treatments for a first episode of disease include vancomycin or metronidazole. For recurrent C. difficile infection, there is an increasingly recognised role for faecal microbiota transplantation, ie generation of a liquidised bacterial suspension from the stool of healthy people, and delivery of this suspension into the gut of affected people in order to restore the normal gut flora. Although any of the other organisms listed may cause acute diarrhoeal disease, none of them has a particular association with recent antibiotic use, in contrast to C. difficile infection.

Enterotoxigenic Escherichia co-infection
Enterotoxigenic Escherichia co-infection is incorrect. For the reasons already described.

Salmonella infection
Salmonella infection is incorrect. For the reasons already described.

Staphylococcus aureus infection
Staphylococcus aureus infection is incorrect. For the reasons already described C.difficile and Pseudomembranous Colitis

Viral infection
Viral infection is incorrect. For the reasons already described.

stem: A 21-year-old student presents to the Emergency Department with an extremely painful perianal swelling. She has had three milder episodes in the last 18 months that resolved with antibiotics. On further questioning she admits to recurrent mouth ulceration and 4 kg of unintentional weight loss in the last 6 months. On examination her temperature is 38C, BP 118/80 mmHg, HR 98 bpm, and abdomen soft and non-tender. Examination of the perianal area shows a discharging sinus surrounded by erythematous tender skin. The registrar suspects underlying Crohn’s disease. What is the next best investigation to guide initial management?
explanation:
Immediate MRI pelvis
This patient has a perianal abscess, which is likely due to underlying Crohn’s disease. The priority is to delineate the extent of the abscess and potential fistula by an urgent pelvis MRI before draining it via EUA.

Flexible sigmoidoscopy and biopsy
Flexible sigmoidoscopy and biopsy is incorrect. There is no role for flexible sigmoidoscopy in the management of perianal abscess.

Examination under anaesthesia (EUA)
Examination under anaesthesia (EUA) is incorrect. If there are delays in obtaining an MRI, the patient should get an immediate CT, which is the next best imaging modality in this context. If this is not possible, then the patient should proceed for EUA, as a perianal abscess can destroy the anal sphincter.

Immediate MRI small bowel
Immediate MRI small bowel is incorrect. Small bowel MRI is useful for characterising pathology in the terminal ileum and small bowel, but is not the priority at present. Crohn’s Disease

Immediate CT abdomen and pelvis
A CT is incorrect. A CT is inferior to MRI in detecting perianal pathology due to its decreased contrast resolution and poorer definition of the anal sphincter complex.

stem: A 30-year-old business executive presented complaining of heartburn for the past 6 months. It was suspected that he was suffering from gastro-oesophageal reflux disease. What is the most important physiological mechanism that prevents reflux?
options: Formation of an anatomical sphincter by the lower circular smooth-muscle fibres of the oesophagus
Increased intrathoracic compared with intra-abdominal pressure
Parasympathetic stimulation of the lower circular smooth-muscle fibres of the oesophagus
Valve-like mechanism of the short portion of the oesophagus
explanation:
Parasympathetic stimulation of the lower circular smooth-muscle fibres of the oesophagus
The lower circular smooth-muscle fibres of the oesophagus are under neural control. The parasympathetic efferent fibres passing through the vagus nerve contain vagal excitatory fibres (VEF) and vagal inhibitory fibres (VIF). When VEF are stimulated, the muscle fibres contract, and this is the major physiological mechanism to avoid gastro-oesophageal reflux. Options A, C and E are all additional physiological anti-gastro-oesophageal reflux mechanisms, but have a much smaller contribution than option D, making them all incorrect options here.

Diaphragmatic muscle surrounding the oesophagus
Diaphragmatic muscle surrounding the oesophagus is incorrect. This is an additional physiological anti-gastrooesophageal reflux mechanism, but has a much smaller contribution than parasympathetic stimulation of the lower circular smooth-muscle fibres of the oesophagus.

Formation of an anatomical sphincter by the lower circular smooth-muscle fibres of the oesophagus
Formation of an anatomical sphincter by the lower circular smooth-muscle fibres of the oesophagus is incorrect. The lower oesophageal muscle fibres do not form a true anatomical sphincter.

Increased intrathoracic compared with intra-abdominal pressure
Increased intrathoracic compared with intra-abdominal pressure is incorrect. This is an additional physiological anti-gastro-oesophageal reflux mechanism, but has a much smaller contribution than parasympathetic stimulation of the lower circular smooth-muscle fibres of the oesophagus. Gastro-oesophageal

Valve-like mechanism of the short portion of the oesophagus
Valve-like mechanism of the short portion of the oesophagus is incorrect. This is an additional physiological anti-gastro-oesophageal reflux mechanism, but has a much smaller contribution than parasympathetic stimulation of the lower circular smooth-muscle fibres of the oesophagus.

stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step for him?
explanation:
Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy
The combination of dysphagia, epigastric pain and weight loss – especially in someone with a history of smoking and alcohol excess – is highly suggestive of significant oesophagogastric pathology, including possibly malignancy. The most sensitive test for assessing for such pathologies is upper gastrointestinal (GI) endoscopy; this will also allow biopsies to be taken.

Abdominal ultrasound scan
Abdominal ultrasound scan is incorrect. The combination of dysphagia, epigastric pain and weight loss is highly suggestive of oesophagogastric disease, including malignancies. An abdominal ultrasound may be useful for looking at the liver, biliary tree and possibly pancreas, but would be unlikely to accurately visualise the stomach and/or oesophagus.

Barium swallow
Barium swallow is incorrect. The combination of dysphagia, epigastric pain and weight loss is highly suggestive of oesophagogastric disease, including malignancies. A barium swallow is useful for visualising the upper GI tract (and may suggest malignancies, achalasia, etc), but is not as sensitive as upper GI endoscopy for detecting pathology – especially early tumours. Furthermore, upper GI endoscopy allows biopsies to be taken of any pathology, unlike barium studies.

Gastrin levels
Gastrin levels is incorrect. Assessment of gastrin levels would be appropriate where there was strong suspicion of a gastrinoma (i.e. recurrent peptic ulceration with unexplained diarrhoea). However, this man has a combination of dysphagia, epigastric pain and weight loss, which is highly suggestive of oesophagogastric disease; gastrinomas are predominantly located in the duodenum and pancreas, and this is therefore very unlikely to be the explanation here.

Helicobacter pylori screen
Helicobacter pylori screen is incorrect. Helicobacter pylori could certainly explain epigastric pain. However, the combination of dysphagia, epigastric pain and weight loss – particularly in someone who has a smoking and alcohol history – is suggestive of more sinister pathology, including oesophagogastric malignancies. Upper GI endoscopy will allow assessment for oesophagogastric malignancies, as well as allowing biopsy/Campylobacter-like organism (CLO) testing for H. pylori.

stem: Which of the following statements is true?
options: A liver biopsy is required to distinguish between alcoholic liver disease and non- alcoholic fatty liver
An ALT: AST ratio of >2 suggests that NAFLD is more likely than alcoholic liver disease
An ALT: AST ratio of >2 suggests that alcoholic liver disease is more likely than NAFLD
An abdominal ultrasound would be able to differentiate between alcoholic liver disease and NAFLD
A raised GGT would confirm that this was alcoholic liver disease
explanation:
An ALT: AST ratio of >2 suggests that NAFLD is more likely than alcoholic liver disease
NAFLD is an umbrella term comprising simple steatosis, non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH) and resultant liver cirrhosis. Typically, the ALT is greater than the AST.

A liver biopsy is required to distinguish between alcoholic liver disease and non- alcoholic fatty liver
A liver biopsy is required to distinguish between alcoholic liver disease and non- alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) A liver biopsy is required to distinguish between alcoholic liver disease and non- alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) is incorrect. Even on liver biopsy, it can be difficult to differentiate between NAFLD and alcoholic liver disease. Generally, a liver biopsy would be performed to stage the degree of fibrosis if significant liver damage is suspected.

An ALT: AST ratio of >2 suggests that alcoholic liver disease is more likely than NAFLD
An ALT: AST ratio of >2 suggests that alcoholic liver disease is more likely than NAFLD is incorrect. In alcoholic liver disease, the AST: ALT ratio is typically more than 2. The relatively low ALT is partly related to dietary deficiency of vitamin B6.

An abdominal ultrasound would be able to differentiate between alcoholic liver disease and NAFLD
An abdominal ultrasound would be able to differentiate between alcoholic liver disease and NAFLD is incorrect. An abdominal ultrasound will not be able to differentiate between NAFLD and alcoholic liver disease- both would have similar features of a fatty looking liver in the early stages, and a diffusely irregular cirrhotic liver in the later stages. Non-alcoholic

A raised GGT would confirm that this was alcoholic liver disease
A raised GGT would confirm that this was alcoholic liver disease is incorrect. A raised GGT may be suggestive of alcoholic liver disease but is not specific and GGT is raised in many other conditions.

stem: A 76-year-old man underwent investigation for abdominal pain. A liver ultrasound demonstrated the presence of multiple hepatic lesions. Further tests revealed an elevated urinary 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid level. Which of the following statements about carcinoid tumours is true?
options: Fibrosis of the heart valves is a recognised feature
Fifty percent of patients die within 2 months of diagnosis
Octreotide is not useful at controlling the diarrhoea
They most commonly involve the colon
explanation:
Fibrosis of the heart valves is a recognised feature
Carcinoid tumours may arise from either the gastrointestinal (GI) tract or from the bronchi. Of those arising from the GI tract, the majority originate in the jejunum and ileum (rather than the colon). These are neuroendocrine tumours that secrete a variety of vasoactive agents, including serotonin. The carcinoid syndrome typically occurs when these tumours spread, and a high burden of liver metastasis becomes established; at this stage, so much normal liver parenchyma has been replaced by tumour that the ability of the remaining healthy liver to catabolise these vasoactive agents is exceeded, and they may then enter the central circulation and cause systemic effects. This can be detected via a number of means, including a urinary test for 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid (5-HIAA), a breakdown product of serotonin. Carcinoid syndrome is also characterised by a number of other clinical features which relate to the vasoactive agents released by the tumour. These include flushing, bronchospasm and fibrous depositions on heart valves. It is the valves of the right side of the heart that are most frequently affected, as inactivation of vasoactive agents by the lungs causes relative sparing of the left side of the heart. This is the reasoning behind the the correct answer here.

Fifty percent of patients die within 2 months of diagnosis
Fifty percent of patients die within 2 months of diagnosis is incorrect. These tumours are usually slow-growing, with a 3-year survival rate of 50%.

Octreotide is not useful at controlling the diarrhoea
Octreotide is not useful at controlling the diarrhoea is incorrect. Somatostatin analogues (such as octreotide) may be useful for treating the diarrhoea associated with carcinoid syndrome.

Presentation only occurs after metastasis
Presentation only occurs after metastasis is incorrect. Presentation of these tumours does not only occur with metastasis; tumours may also present because of mass effect (eg intestinal obstruction), as appendicitis, or with a pellagra syndrome (ie ‘dermatitis, dementia and diarrhoea’, due to niacin deficiency). Neuroendocrine Tumours

They most commonly involve the colon
They most commonly involve the colon is incorrect. As outlined, the majority of carcinoid tumours originate in the jejunum and ileum.

stem: A 79-year-old woman has been seen twice by her general practitioner during the past 8 months complaining of dull abdominal pain radiating through to her back. The general practitioner had diagnosed probable degenerative spinal disease and prescribed analgesics, although these had not helped greatly. The pain was partially relieved by sitting forwards. Her daughter, who said that she had ‘not been eating for weeks’, had brought her to the Emergency Department. On examination, the woman was cachetic. Blood tests revealed a normochromic normocytic anaemia, while liver function tests demonstrated mildly elevated transaminases and grossly elevated bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase levels. An ultrasound scan revealed common bile duct obstruction with suspicion of a mass in the epigastrum. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Pancreatic carcinoma
The most likely diagnosis is carcinoma of the pancreas. Pancreatic carcinoma has an incidence of nine per 100 000, with the peak incidence occurring above 60 years of age. There is a 3:2 male preponderance. Typical symptoms include epigastric pain radiating to the back (which is classically partially relieved by sitting forwards), and jaundice (occurring late, and often the presenting feature). Pancreatic carcinoma is also associated with thrombophlebitis migrans, and some patients may present with thromboembolic phenomena. Where pancreatic tumours involve the head of the pancreas, biliary obstruction is common; ultrasound is useful for demonstrating a dilated biliary tree proximal to an obstruction, but often visualises the pancreas itself poorly, and further imaging is usually required to confirm the diagnosis. Spiral computed tomography, magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) and endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) can be useful adjuncts to investigations where the diagnosis is unclear. The CA-19.9 tumour marker does not have very high specificity and sensitivity, but may still be useful. The majority of these tumours are unsuitable for resection and the survival rate at 5 years is only 2%. About 20% of patients have a technically resectable tumour, but surgical resection is sometimes impossible due to comorbidities.

Cholecystitis
Cholecystitis is incorrect. Cholecystitis may be complicated by gallstones within the common bile duct, which could explain cholestatic liver enzymes and the description of biliary tract obstruction on ultrasound. However, the long duration and nature of the pain described – along with the presence of anaemia – would not be typical features of cholecystitis, and are much more consistent with pancreatic disease.

Gastric carcinoma with local spread
Gastric carcinoma with local spread is incorrect. Gastric carcinoma may manifest with a very variable pattern of upper gastrointestinal symptoms and normocytic anaemia; however, it would not be a typical cause of biliary tract obstruction (unlike pancreatic malignancy) and is therefore unlikely to be the diagnosis here.

Gastrointestinal lymphoma with bile-duct obstruction
Gastrointestinal lymphoma with bile-duct obstruction is incorrect. A gastrointestinal lymphoma could potentially be associated with a large malignant lymph node that extrinisically compressed the biliary tree, although this would be unusual; however, this is unlikely to be the diagnosis here, as the description of epigastric pain radiating to the back that is relieved by sitting forwards is much more suggestive of primary pancreatic disease.

Hepatocellular carcinoma
Hepatocellular carcinoma is incorrect. Hepatocellular carcinoma tends not to produce significant abdominal pain until very advanced, and would typically appear on ultrasound as a hepatic mass rather than with biliary tract obstruction; as such, it may also be ruled out.

stem: A 24-year-old female farm worker presented to her general practitioner with abdominal swelling. She remembered an episode of abdominal pain a few months earlier, but nothing else of note. Her medications included the oral contraceptive pill. She was single and did not drink alcohol. She tells you that her mother takes anticoagulation for a previous deep vein thrombosis at a young age. Liver function testing revealed elevated alanine aminotransferase (ALT) and bilirubin levels. Examination of the abdomen demonstrated mild ascites and splenomegaly. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Budd–Chiari syndrome
This scenario is suggestive of Budd–Chiari syndrome. This rare condition usually presents chronically, with evidence of ascites ± splenomegaly ± hepatomegaly ± other signs of liver disease on examination. Acute and fulminant forms of Budd–Chiairi syndrome are also recognised, and tend to present with acute abdominal pain and hepatomegaly; however, these are much less common. Budd–Chiari syndrome is caused by obstruction of hepatic venous flow. This is frequently caused by thrombosis, but external compression of the vessels may also be a cause. The condition occurs more commonly in people with a hypercoagulable state, eg those with myeloproliferative disorders, those with protein C, antithrombin III or protein S deficiency, or patients taking the oral contraceptive pill. Treatment includes venous shunting and anti-coagulation, although some patients progress and require liver transplantation.

Alcohol-related cirrhosis
Alcohol-related cirrhosis is incorrect. This can be ruled out in the absence of an alcohol history.

Hydatid disease
Hydatid disease is incorrect. Hydatid disease would be expected to follow a longer time course, with symptoms related to cyst enlargement, coupled with an obstructive picture of liver enzymes.

Organophosphate toxicity
Organophosphate toxicity is incorrect. The information that this woman works on a farm may increase suspicion for organophosphate poisoning, but this typically manifests with neurological symptoms rather than features of liver disease. Portal Hypertension A 28-year-old woman visits her GP some 10 days after returning from honeymoon in Mauritius. During the trip she admits to eating food from local street stalls, and now complains of symptoms consistent with an irritable bowel type picture, with alternating constipation and diarrhoea, coupled with abdominal bloating. She is given a course of tinidazole but returns some 2 weeks later with the diarrhoea.

Viral hepatitis
Viral hepatitis is incorrect. No risk factors for viral hepatitis are described in the scenario, and viral hepatitis does not typically cause abdominal pain, making it unlikely.

stem: What is the most likely cause of the haematemesis?
explanation:
Gastric erosions
Gastric erosions are the most likely cause of haematemesis in this patient. He has a history of aspirin use, which can damage the gastric mucosa and lead to superficial erosions. These erosions can cause minor bleeding, leading to one episode of haematemesis without significant physiological compromise or anaemia, which matches the patient's presentation. The absence of any abdominal pain or tenderness, coupled with the patient's normal vital signs and a normal haemoglobin level, supports the diagnosis of gastric erosions.

Duodenal ulcer
Duodenal ulcers are incorrect because they typically present with abdominal pain, often epigastric or right upper quadrant pain that is relieved by eating or antacids. This patient denies any abdominal pain, making a duodenal ulcer less likely. Furthermore, duodenal ulcers tend to cause more significant GI bleeding than a single episode of haematemesis without any signs of ongoing bleeding or anaemia. The patient's normal haemoglobin also suggests that he has not experienced a considerable loss of blood, which would be more characteristic of a duodenal ulcer.

Mallory–Weiss tear
Mallory-Weiss tear is incorrect because it is usually preceded by repeated episodes of vomiting or retching, which leads to tears in the mucosa at the gastro-oesophageal junction. This patient's history does not include prior vomiting, which makes this diagnosis unlikely. Additionally, Mallory-Weiss tears tend to present with more significant bleeding than just one episode of haematemesis. His haemoglobin level is normal, indicating that he has not suffered substantial blood loss, which further argues against a Mallory-Weiss tear.

Oesophageal varices
Oesophageal varices are incorrect as there is no indication of chronic liver disease or portal hypertension in this patient's history. Typically, oesophageal varices are associated with conditions like cirrhosis, which can cause symptoms like jaundice, ascites or a history of heavy alcohol use. This patient drinks alcohol moderately and has normal liver function test results, which makes oesophageal varices unlikely. Additionally, bleeding from oesophageal varices often leads to significant haemodynamic instability, which is not observed in this patient, who has normal vital signs and haemoglobin levels.

Helicobacter pylori gastritis
Helicobacter pylori gastritis is incorrect because, while it can cause gastritis and ulcers, the patient's recent use of aspirin more strongly suggests gastric erosions as the cause of his symptoms. The history of aspirin use is a significant factor in mucosal damage, making this a more plausible explanation for the haematemesis than H. pylori gastritis. Additionally, H. pylori infection often leads to chronic gastritis, which may present with intermittent epigastric discomfort, but aspirin-induced erosions can cause acute bleeding episodes more consistently. Lastly, the patient's normal haemoglobin and other examination findings are not distinctively indicative of H. pylori-related conditions.

stem: A slim 39-year-old deputy head teacher has a 3-month history of dyspepsia, particularly at night. He had a trial of a proton pump inhibitor 1 month ago and his symptoms have returned. He has not had melaena or weight loss. He is a regular smoker and occasionally drinks alcohol. He reports that his symptoms of abdominal pain are often relieved by drinking a glass of milk, On examination, there is some mild epigastric tenderness and no evidence of any masses or lymphadenopathy. The most useful next management step would be?
options: 13C urea breath test and eradicate if positive
Course of H2 antagonists/proton pump inhibitors
Stool antigen enzyme immunoassay and eradication therapy if positive
explanation:
13C urea breath test and eradicate if positive
NICE defines dyspepsia broadly to include people with recurrent epigastric pain, heartburn or acid regurgitation, with or without bloating, nausea or vomiting. This patient has symptoms of dyspepsia and has had a one-month trial of PPI therapy. The next step in managment would therefore be to test for Helicobacter pylori (H pylori) infection and then treat if the results are positive (leaving a two-week washout period after PPI before testing for infection. One of the most reliable noninvasive screening tests that is both sensitive and specific is the 13C urea breath test. This involves ingesting a drink that is labelled with 13C urea. If H. pylori is present, its urease enzyme will convert the urea to ammonia and 13C-labelled CO 2, which will be detected in the expired air. H. pylori is strongly associated with gastritis, gastric and duodenal ulceration, gastric cancer and MALT lymphoma. Spontaneous eradication is rare. Treatment involves two antibiotics and a PPI for one week, and reinfection is uncommon. Retesting is usually not appropriate unless there are severe recurrent symptoms, complicated peptic ulcer disease or mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT) lymphoma. Other potential screening tests include serological tests that detect IgG antibodies to H. pylori, but these cannot distinguish between current and past infection.

Course of H2 antagonists/proton pump inhibitors
Course of H2 antagonists/proton pump inhibitors is incorrect. This patient has had recurring symptoms of dyspepsia despite a trial of acid suppression with PPIs; therefore, another trial with acid suppression alone is unlikely to be successful.

H. Pylori eradication therapy
H. Pylori eradication therapy is incorrect. Helicobacter pylori is a common cause of dyspepsia, and as such needs to be diagnosed formally before it is eradicated in the ‘test and treat’ approach. His symptoms of abdominal pain relieved by milk (an alkaline product), suggests the possibility of a duodenal ulcer.

Stool antigen enzyme immunoassay and eradication therapy if positive
Stool antigen enzyme immunoassay and eradication therapy if positive is incorrect. Stool antigen enzyme immunoassay can also be used as a screening tool but is less sensitive and specific than the 13C urea breath test, and tends to be used in young children that cannot comply with the breath test.

Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy
Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy is incorrect. He has no ALARM symptoms (anaemia, weight loss, anorexia, recent onset of progressive symptoms age > 50 years, melaena/haematemesis, dysphagia), and so there is no indication for an oesophagogastroduodenoscopy (OGD). Gastro-oesophageal.

stem: Endomysial and gliadin antibodies are negative. A jejunal biopsy shows abnormal villi with an inflammatory cell infiltrate of lymphocytes, plasma cells and eosinophils. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Tropical sprue
The jejunal biopsy can be abnormal in all the conditions listed, but it is the combination of time in the tropics, malabsorption and the resulting deficits, plus the acute inflammatory epithelial infiltrate that makes tropical sprue the diagnosis here. Tropical sprue is mostly seen in residents or long-stay travellers (> 6 months) in southern and South East Asia, the Caribbean and central South America. Diagnosis requires demonstration of partial villous atrophy, exclusion of other causes of diarrhoea, and the presence of fat (steathorroea) and B 12 malabsorption (macrocytic anaemia). Hypocalcaemia can also be a feature. Treatment is with tetracycline and folic acid.

Coeliac disease
Coeliac disease is incorrect. The main differential is coeliac disease, but the travel history and negative coeliac serology makes tropical sprue more likely.

Crohn's disease
Crohn’s disease is incorrect. Crohn's disease would be associated with more severe symptoms of diarrhoea, and other signs such as aphthous ulceration and abdominal pain. Histology typically includes granulomas and deep ulcers in addition to an inflammatory infiltrate.

Giardia lamblia infection
Giardia lamblia infection is incorrect. Giardia lamblia infection is a protozoal infection typically seen in travellers, but is commonly associated with foul- smelling stools, bloating, excessive flatulence and belching. On biopsy, the parasite is commonly seen in the majority of cases, and villous abnormalities are not typical features.

Whipple's disease
Whippie's disease is incorrect. Although diarrhoea is associated with Whipple’s disease, there are no other features to support this diagnosis – such as a migratory seronegative large joint arthropathy, skin pigmentation, finger clubbing and fevers. Furthermore, jejunal biopsy characteristically shows ‘foamy’ macrophages which stain positive with periodic acid–Schiff (PAS).

stem: Which vitamin/mineral deficiency is most likely to account for his symptoms?
explanation:
B1
B 1 (thiamine) deficiency can occur within 2 weeks of poor intake. Causes include chronic alcohol excess (the most common cause), malnutrition and persistent vomiting. Symptoms are peripheral neuropathy, psychosis and ophthalmoplegia, all of which are displayed here. Korsakoff’s psychosis is characterised by coherent, fluent speech, but with ‘confabulations’ and very poor memory recall. Treatment is initiated with parenteral thiamine. Magnesium is required for activation of thiamine, so it is important to treat coexistent hypomagnesaemia.

B2
B 2 is incorrect. B 2 deficiency presents with stomatitis, anaemia, ataxia and mucosal fissures.

B6
B 6 is incorrect. B 6 deficiency presents with peripheral neuropathy and sideroblastic anaemia. Although this patient had anaemia and peripheral neuropathy, B 6 deficiency does not account for the cognitive impairment or ophthalmoplegia.

B12
B 12 is incorrect. B 12 deficiency is also a reasonable option as it presents with macrocytic anaemia and peripheral neuropathy, but again does not account for the cognitive impairment or ophthalmoplegia. B 12 deficiency can also be associated with subacute cord degeneration, which would have neurological signs of weakness and spastic paraparesis.

Folate
Folate is incorrect. Folate deficiency manifests as macrocytic anaemia and is common in chronic alcoholic use; however, again, it does not account for all the symptoms described.

stem: Which of the following is the most likely cause of his presentation?
explanation:
Alcohol dependence
This patient has significant consumption of alcohol, (28 pints of beer per week), plus potentially other alcohol use that he may not be admitting to. This is, therefore, the most likely cause of his presentation with pancreatitis. Note also that the patient has a macrocytosis, of which alchol misuse is a common cause.

Hypertriglyceridaemia
Hypertriglyceridaemia is incorrect. Baseline triglycerides of 10 or more are most associated with increased risk of acute pancreatitis.

Liraglutide
Liraglutide is incorrect. Although there are case reports of pancreatitis associated with use of GLP-1 agonists, recent evidence has not supported any increased risk of pancreatitis associated with their use.

Metformin
Metformin is incorrect. Metformin is associated with cases of pancreatitis, case reports suggest this risk is increased in patients with renal impairment.

Type 2 diabetes
Type 2 diabetes is incorrect. Although type diabetes is associated with increased background risk of pancreatitis, in this case it’s consumption of alcohol which is likely to have been the larger contributor to risk.

stem: A 62-year-old man was admitted after an episode of haematemesis thought to be related to varices. Which of the following statements about acute upper gastrointestinal haemorrhage is correct?
options: Intravenous nitrates reduce the risk of re-bleeding
Intravenous ranitidine reduces the risk of re-bleeding
Intravenous somatostatin analogues reduce the risk of re-bleeding
Oral omeprazole reduces the risk of re-bleeding
Oral tranexamic acid reduces the risk of re-bleeding
explanation:
Intravenous somatostatin analogues reduce the risk of re-bleeding
The modern treatment for upper gastrointestinal (GI) bleeding is: Active fluid resuscitation via adequate venous access. Endoscopic identification of the lesion within 24 hours, and therapeutic intervention if appropriate. This includes direct intervention (with heat, clips, drugs (adrenaline) or haemostatic powder), or specific therapy for oesophageal varices (typically variceal banding). Radiological intervention (ie embolisation of bleeding vessel) and/or surgical intervention have an important role in cases of upper gastrointestinal bleeding that cannot be controlled by endoscopy. Acid suppression prior to endoscopy has not consistently been shown to have a role in reducing the risk of rebleeding. However, intravenous proton pump inhibitor does appear to reduce re-bleeding after endoscopy if a patient is at high risk of a re-bleed. As such, the intravenous nitrates and intravenous ranitidine options are incorrect. Somatostatin, a naturally occurring peptide, displays a wide range of biological actions, mainly inhibitory ones, leading to its use in the treatment of a variety of digestive diseases. Octreotide is the most extensively investigated of these. The marked effect of somatostatin on splanchnic haemodynamics – together with its inhibitory action on acid-peptic and pancreatic exocrine secretions – represents the rationale for its use in upper gastrointestinal bleeding. As well as its haemodynamic effects, the peptide also increases lower oesophageal sphincter pressure, thereby reducing the inflow of blood into the submucous venous plexus of the oesophagus and hence into oesophageal varices. Through its inhibitory action on acid-peptic secretion, somatostatin may also inhibit peptic digestion of any blood clots at the site of haemostasis on a varix itself. In addition, the natural peptide has been shown to enhance human platelet aggregation in vitro, whose stimulation can activate the haemostatic process. The drug can be given by intravenous infusion.

Intravenous nitrates reduce the risk of re-bleeding
Intravenous nitrates reduce the risk of re-bleeding is incorrect. Intravenous nitrates have no role in the management of acute GI bleeding.

Intravenous ranitidine reduces the risk of re-bleeding
Intravenous ranitidine reduces the risk of re-bleeding is incorrect. Acid suppression prior to endoscopy has not consistently been shown to have a role in reducing the risk of re-bleeding.

Oral omeprazole reduces the risk of re-bleeding
Oral omeprazole reduces the risk of re-bleeding is incorrect. Acid suppression prior to endoscopy has not consistently been shown to have a role in reducing the risk of re-bleeding. Portal Hypertension

Oral tranexamic acid reduces the risk of re-bleeding
Oral tranexamic acid reduces the risk of re-bleeding is incorrect. Further studies are ongoing about the possible role for intravenous tranexamic acid in reducing re-bleed risk in GI bleeds, but there is no consistent evidence for oral tranexamic acid being of any benefit in this situation.

stem: A 55-year-old man complains of intermittent epigastric pain, diarrhoea and steatorrhoea. He has mild iron deficiency anaemia and raised calcium and parathyroid hormone levels. An upper gastrointestinal endoscopy has shown peptic ulcers in the stomach, duodenum and jejunum. Which of the following tests is most likely to help in diagnosis?
explanation:
Serum gastrin level
The presence of multiple ulcers and hyperparathyroidism suggests Zollinger–Ellison syndrome. This syndrome is caused by a pancreatic tumour that secretes gastrin, and for this reason serum gastrin levels are a helpful test in trying to make the diagnosis. Gastrinoma may occur as part of the multiple endocrine neoplasia-1 (MEN-1) syndrome, which is associated with parathyroid and pituitary adenomas; the presence of raised parathyroid and calcium levels here is clearly suggestive of parathyroid disease. If this man’s diarrhoea was thought to be attributable to malabsorption, there would be a potential role for small-bowel follow-through (to look for features of small intestinal Crohn’s disease), stool fat (to assess for fat malabsorption) and for duodenal biopsy (to examine for coeliac disease); however, his diarrhoea seems much more likely to be caused by a gastrinoma, and none of these tests is therefore likely to be of use.

Duodenal biopsy
Duodenal biopsy is incorrect for the reasons described.

Plain X-ray of the abdomen
Plain X-ray of the abdomen is incorrect. Plain X-ray of the abdomen is useful to look for dilated loops of bowel in suspected intestinal obstruction, but appears unlikely to be helpful in this scenario.

Small-bowel follow-through
Small-bowel follow-through is incorrect for the reasons described.

Stool fat content
Stool fat content is incorrect for the reasons described.

stem: A 23-year-old woman is reviewed in the Gastroenterology Clinic. She presents with diarrhoea, weight loss and an intensely itchy rash affecting her buttocks and the tops of both legs. An endoscopy with small bowel biopsy reveals villous atrophy. Which of the following is the most important intervention to manage her underlying condition?
explanation:
Gluten-free diet
This patient’s symptoms are consistent with coeliac disease and dermatitis herpetiformis. Avoidance of gluten is crucial to the resolution of symptoms. Over time, non-avoidance of gluten is associated with persistence of the rash, and diarrhoea and may increase risks of small bowel lymphoma. Where symptoms are refractory to gluten avoidance, a short course of corticosteroids may be helpful.

Lactose-free diet
Many patients with coeliac disease also have lactose intolerance, although avoidance of lactose without avoidance of gluten will not lead to a resolution of symptoms. Avoidance of gluten is the most important step in treating coeliac disease.

Oral cyclophosphamide
Cyclophosphamide does not have a role in treating coeliac disease. It may be deployed as part of a combination regimen for the treatment of gastrointestinal lymphoma related to longstanding coeliac disease.

Oral mesalamine
Oral mesalamine is used to treat inflammatory bowel disease including Crohn’s and ulcerative colitis; it does not have a role in the treatment of coeliac disease. Mesalamine also has a role delivered rectally for the treatment of patients with limited distal ulcerative colitis.

Oral prednisolone
Prednisolone has a role in patients with coeliac disease who have refractory symptoms despite following a gluten-free diet. In the initial period, gluten avoidance is the most important intervention. It is used as an acute intervention for patients with an exacerbation of inflammatory bowel disease.

stem: A 17-year-old girl was admitted to the Emergency Department after being found drowsy at home. Her parents had been to a party and found her lying on the sofa with an empty bottle of vodka and empty packets of paracetamol around her when they returned home. They mentioned that she had a row with her boyfriend the previous evening. Her blood tests on admission to the Emergency Department revealed a paracetamol level of 70 mg/kg (nomogram with treatment range not available) and an international normalised ratio (INR) of 2.1 (<1.0). What is the appropriate management in this case?
options: Begin immediate N-acetylcysteine and arrange for her to be closely monitored on the medical ward
Continue observation as her paracetamol level is below the treatment line
Give her oral methionine when she is awake enough to take it
Give her vitamin K and continue observation
Refer her immediately to a liver unit
explanation:
Begin immediate N-acetylcysteine and arrange for her to be closely monitored on the medical ward
Since it is unclear when she took a paracetamol overdose, caution should be exercised and intravenous Nacetylcysteine begun immediately. Her international normalised ratio (INR) of 2.1 suggests that the overdose probably occurred the previous evening and that some liver necrosis has already begun to develop. After optimal resuscitation (ie with intravenous fluids), she should be very closely monitored for the development of adverse prognostic features, including hepatic encephalopathy, worsening acidosis, progressive kidney disease, rise in bilirubin and prolongation of the INR. The paracetamol level itself and liver enzyme values are not prognostic. Should these adverse features continue to progress despite intravenous N-acetylcysteine and resuscitation, there should be a low threshold to refer her to a liver unit in case she develops acute liver failure requiring emergency liver transplantation. N-acetylcysteine works as an -SH group donator, so prevents some of the liver damage caused by abnormal paracetamol metabolism via an alternative oxidative pathway that results in the production of NAPQI (N-acetylp-benzoquinone imine), a highly toxic metabolite. There is some evidence that continued N-acetylcysteine infusion may have positive effects on mortality and morbidity in patients who already have established liver failure.

Continue observation as her paracetamol level is below the treatment line
Continue observation as her paracetamol level is below the treatment line is incorrect. The lack of clarity about when the overdose was taken, the implied intake of other potential hepatotoxins at the same time (including alcohol), and the raised INR all imply that this is a high-risk paracetamol overdose, regardless of where the paracetamol level falls on the nomogram; N-acetylcysteine should be started immediately.

Give her oral methionine when she is awake enough to take it
Give her oral methionine when she is awake enough to take it is incorrect. Methionine appears to be a less effective antedote to paracetamol overdose than N-acetylcysteine, and cannot be administered until the patient is less obtunded.

Give her vitamin K and continue observation
Give her vitamin K and continue observation is incorrect. It is possible that part of the reason for her prolonged INR is nutritional deficiency of vitamin K; however, this is clearly too high-risk an overdose for this to be a safe and appropriate course of management.

Refer her immediately to a liver unit
Refer her immediately to a liver unit is incorrect. As described, there is no indication at present that she requires liver transplantation, but there should be a low threshold to discuss her case with a specialist centre should she develop progressive adverse prognostic factors despite optimal medical management with fluids and Nacetylcysteine. Drug-Induced.

stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate course of action?
explanation:
Change omeprazole to lansoprazole
It is important to be aware of the drug interaction between omeprazole and clopidogrel, which has been reported to reduce the anti-platelet effect of the latter. No significant interaction is seen between clopidogrel and lansoprazole.

Add ranitidine
Add ranitidine is incorrect. This has little additional effect on top of omeprazole in reducing gastric acid secretion, and does not affect the interaction between omeprazole and clopidogrel.

Increase omeprazole dose to 60 mg
Increase omeprazole dose to 60 mg is incorrect. This may negatively impair the anti-platelet function of clopidogrel further.

Stop clopidogrel after 4 weeks
Stop clopidogrel after 4 weeks is incorrect. This increases the risk of re-stenosis and is not an option. Restenosis rates are very high during the first 60 days. Peptic Ulcer Disease and Gastritis A 75-year-old nun presented to her general practitioner with gradual-onset abdominal swelling over some months and generalised abdominal tenderness, perhaps worse in her right flank. On examination, there was inguinal lymphadenopathy. Blood tests revealed a normochromic, normocytic anaemia, decreased serum albumin level and an elevated creatinine of 180 μmol/l. Her CA-125 level was raised.

Stop clopidogrel after 3 months
Stop clopidogrel after 3 months is incorrect. Clopidogrel should be continued, preferably for at least 1 year.

stem: A 75-year-old nun presented to her general practitioner with gradual-onset abdominal swelling over some months and generalised abdominal tenderness, perhaps worse in her right flank. On examination, there was inguinal lymphadenopathy. Blood tests revealed a normochromic, normocytic anaemia, decreased serum albumin level and an elevated creatinine of 180 μmol/l. Her CA-125 level was raised. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Ovarian carcinoma
This scenario is very suggestive of ovarian carcinoma. Ovarian carcinoma has an annual incidence of around 12.9–15.1/100 000 women per year, but the incidence rises with increasing age: the median age of presentation is 61, with the peak occurring between the ages of 75 and 79 years. There is an increased genetic predisposition to the condition in carriers of the BRCA1 gene (breast–ovarian carcinoma syndrome). Low parity, delayed childbearing, obesity and subfertility all appear to be risk factors for the condition. CA-125 has reasonable sensitivity and specificity for ovarian carcinoma, although levels may also be raised in certain benign gynaecological conditions (eg endometriosis), or non-gynaecological conditions (eg cirrhosis, ascites, breast cancer, and so on). Cross-sectional imaging is helpful in confirming the diagnosis and staging the disease, with ultrasound, CT and MRI all being of use. This woman’s creatinine may be raised because of urinary tract obstruction from the malignancy, either from the mass of the primary tumour, or because of spread of the cancer into the omentum. It would be typical for people with ovarian carcinoma to have a normochromic, normocytic anaemia and a low albumin level (although any ascitic fluid is likely to be protein-rich). The initial treatment of choice in this scenario would be to drain the ascites (to relieve symptoms), and to consider stenting of the ureters if they are being extrinsically compressed by tumour mass. Chemotherapy (either with or without surgery) might be appropriate in younger patients, but many patients present with very advanced disease, which has a 5% 5-year survival rate.

Cervical carcinoma
Cervical carcinoma is incorrect. Cervical carcinoma tends to occur in younger women than this patient; furthermore, major risk factors include early onset of sexual activity, multiple sexual partners and sexually transmitted infections, which are all clearly unlikely here. In addition, the typical presenting symptom of cervical carcinoma is with heavy/irregular vaginal bleeding, which has not been described.

Cirrhosis of the liver
Cirrhosis of the liver is incorrect. Although this woman’s abdominal swelling may suggest ascites, the absence of any obvious risk factors for or clinical features of chronic liver disease make it very unlikely that the diagnosis is cirrhosis.

Haemochromatosis
Haemochromatosis is incorrect. Although haemochromatosis may cause cirrhosis with subsequent ascites formation there is no specific information such as joint problems, diabetes and skin discoloration to suggest this diagnosis.

Wilson’s disease
Wilson’s disease is incorrect. Although Wilson’s disease may cause cirrhosis with subsequent ascites formation there is no specific information such as neuropsychiatric disease to suggest this diagnosis.

stem: A 51-year-old patient is awaiting surgery for a left nephrectomy secondary to renal cell carcinoma. Which of the following organs is in direct contact (and not separated by peritoneum) with the anterior surface of the left kidney?
explanation:
Pancreas
The kidneys are retroperitoneal structures located between T12-L3 vertebrae, with the left kidney placed slightly more superiorly than the right kidney. Only the pancreas and the left suprarenal gland make direct contact with the left kidney, with no intervening peritoneum. The left kidney is in contact with the spleen, stomach, jejunum and left colonic flexure, but with intervening peritoneum.

Duodenum
Duodenum is incorrect. The duodenum makes contact with the right kidney.

Jejunum
Jejunum is incorrect. The small bowel becomes intraperitoneal again at the duodenojejunal flexure at L2, hence the jejunum is intraperitoneal and is not in contact with the kidney.

Spleen
Spleen is incorrect. The spleen does contain a renal impression where it abuts the left kidney, but there is peritoneum between.

Stomach
Stomach is incorrect. The anterior surface of stomach is related to the left lobe of the liver, the anterior abdominal wall, and the distal transverse colon. The posterior surface of the stomach is related to the left hemidiaphragm, the spleen, the left kidney (although there is peritoneum between the two structures), and the pancreas (stomach bed).

stem: A 49-year-old bar owner who now lives in Southern Spain comes to the gastroenterology clinic for review. He has type 2 diabetes, osteoarthritis of both knees and early cirrhosis, (although he claims to drink only minimal amounts of alcohol). On examination his BP is 152/88, a pulse of 75 and regular. He is tanned and has a number of spider naevi over the upper body. His BMI is 31. Blood testing reveals elevated transaminases, ferritin, and transferrin saturation. Which of the following is likely to be present?
explanation:
C282Y mutation
The clinical picture here with cirrhosis, Type 2 diabetes, probable chondrocalcinosis of the knees, and hyperpigmentation, is consistent with a diagnosis of haemochromatosis. C282Y is responsible for the majority of cases of haemochromatosis.

H63D mutation
H63D is incorrect. The H63D mutation is responsible for a smaller number of cases of haemochromatosis, and can precipitate symptoms in patients who are H63D/C282Y compound heterozygotes.

Delta-F508
Delta-F508 is incorrect. This is the commonest mutation responsible for cystic fibrosis in Northern Europeans.

SLC4A1 mutation
SLC4A1 is incorrect. This is the mutation responsible for hereditary spherocytosis type 4. Hereditary Haemochromatosis A 58-year-old office manager presents with a single episode of haematemesis and melaena. On examination he is alert, BP 130/80 mmHg, HR 80 bpm, RR 20 breaths per minute, temperature 37.5 oC. He has multiple spider naevi on the upper chest and Dupuytren’s contracture on the left hand. There is no abdominal tenderness. Gastroscopy shows small grade 1 oesophageal varices that were not bleeding, and multiple bleeding areas in the stomach associated with a friable mucosa.

W1282X
W1282X is incorrect. This is the mutation responsible for cases of cystic fibrosis in the Ashkenazi Jewish population.

stem: A 58-year-old office manager presents with a single episode of haematemesis and melaena. On examination he is alert, BP 130/80 mmHg, HR 80 bpm, RR 20 breaths per minute, temperature 37.5 oC. He has multiple spider naevi on the upper chest and Dupuytren’s contracture on the left hand. There is no abdominal tenderness. Gastroscopy shows small grade 1 oesophageal varices that were not bleeding, and multiple bleeding areas in the stomach associated with a friable mucosa. What is the most appropriate management to reduce long-term risk of bleeding?
explanation:
Oral propranolol
This patient has signs of chronic liver disease and is likely to have portal hypertension. Endoscopy showed small non-bleeding varices, and the evidence of multiple areas of haemorrhage in the stomach associated with a friable mucosa points to portal hypertensive gastropathy (PHG) as the cause of gastrointestinal (GI) bleed. Bleeding secondary to PHG tends to be less severe than bleeding from oesophageal varices. Oral propranolol (a non-cardioselective beta blocker) in a dose sufficient to reduce the resting pulse rate by 25% has been shown to decrease portal pressure and reduce bleeding from portal hypertensive gastropathy as well as frequency of variceal bleeds.

Adrenaline (epinephrine) injection
Adrenaline (epinephrine) injection is incorrect. Adrenaline has no role in the long-term management of Tutor bleeding in PHG. It is mainly used in the endoscopic treatment of non-variceal upper GI bleeding.

Intravenous ethanolamine
Intravenous ethanolamine is incorrect. Ethanolamine is occasionally used to treat bleeding varices.

Intravenous octreotide
Intravenous octreotride is incorrect. Intravenous octreotride (a somatostatin analogue) is used in the management of acute haemorrhage from oesophageal varices as it reduces portal venous pressure. It is mainly used when terlipressin is not available. Portal Hypertension A 61-year-old man presented with a 1-year history of intermittent difficulty with swallowing and halitosis; he also felt like there was a fullness in his neck, and occasionally even regurgitated undigested food. He was diabetic and was currently taking metformin. Other past history of note included recurrent bouts of pneumonia (two in the past 3 years) and asthma, which had been recently diagnosed by his general practitioner. On examination he looked well and his body mass index (BMI) was 32 kg/m 2. Investigations:

Variceal banding
Variceal banding is incorrect. Variceal banding has no role in the treatment of PHG. It is used as primary prophylaxis of Grade 2 or 3 oesophageal varices, or for the treatment of bleeding oesophageal varices.

stem: A 23-year-old woman was referred with abnormal liver biochemistry in the third trimester of pregnancy. Which feature would be most consistent with pregnancy-related cholestasis as the underlying diagnosis?
explanation:
Elevated serum bile acids
A number of pregnancy-related liver disorders are well recognised. These include: Pregnancy-related cholestasis results in elevated serum bile acids, normal urate and fat-soluble vitamin malabsorption (prolonging the prothrombin time). Acute fatty liver of pregnancy is much more serious and is associated with pre-eclampsia (hypertension, proteinuria) and a high urate level. Immediate delivery is mandatory if other features of toxaemia exist. Hyperemesis gravidarum can result in abnormal liver enzymes. HELLP (Haemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes and Low Platelets) is a potentially life-threatening condition (a microangiopathic process associated with hypertension in some cases, with risk of haemorrhage and stroke), and again merits consideration for immediate delivery. Elevated serum bile acids are a typical feature of pregnancy-related cholestasis. The other options given may be associated with other pregnancy-related liver diseases (eg thrombocytopenia and HELLP) but not cholestasis, making elevated serum bile acids the correct answer here.

Elevated urate
Elevated urate is incorrect. As described, elevated urate is not associated with cholestasis.

Hypoalbuminaemia
Hypoalbuminaemia is incorrect. As described, hypoalbuminaemia is not associated with cholestasis.

Macrocytosis
Macrocytosis is incorrect. As described, macrocytosis is not associated with cholestasis. Pregnancy-related Liver DiseaseA 42-year-old woman undergoes a bowel resection for a Dukes’ C colon carcinoma. She is recommended to have chemotherapy, and you plan to discuss the relative merits of capecitabine versus 5-fluorouracil (5-FU) with her.

Thrombocytopenia
Thrombocytopenia is incorrect. As described, thrombocytopenia is not associated with cholestasis.

stem: A 52-year-old woman presented for review. She had been complaining of tiredness and lethargy for some months, but her general practitioner had initially attributed this to the menopause. There was a past history of pernicious anaemia, which had been adequately treated. Her weight was normal. Blood tests demonstrated elevated transaminases, with alkaline phosphatase and bilirubin levels just above the upper limit of normal. An autoimmune profile showed raised antinuclear and anti-smooth muscle antibodies. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Type I autoimmune hepatitis
The features described in this scenario are most consistent with type I autoimmune hepatitis. This condition tends to occur in association with other autoimmune diseases (e.g. pernicious anaemia, thyroiditis), and antinuclear and anti-smooth muscle autoantibodies are often detectable. Liver biopsy usually shows a necroinflammatory process, which untreated may progress to significant fibrosis and cirrhosis; approximately onethird of patients have cirrhosis at the time of presentation. The typical starting treatment is with oral prednisolone 30 mg daily for 2 weeks, followed by a slow reduction. Corticosteroid induction treatment is often accompanied by a steroid-sparing agent, such as azathioprine. Remission occurs in up to 80% of cases. Liver transplantation may be offered in advanced disease where medical therapy has failed, but the disease may recur in the transplanted liver.

Hepatitis A infection
Hepatitis A infection is incorrect. Hepatitis A is spread faeco-orally; no obvious risk factors are described in this scenario. While hepatitis A may cause an illness characterised by raised transaminases, it is not associated with positive liver auto-antibodies, and as such hepatitis A is unlikely.

Hepatitis B infection
Hepatitis B infection is incorrect. Hepatitis B is spread sexually or through blood-to-blood transmission; no obvious risk factors are described in this scenario. While hepatitis B may cause an illness characterised by raised transaminases, it is not associated with positive liver auto-antibodies, and as such hepatitis B is unlikely.

Non-alcoholic steatohepatitis
