Non-alcoholic steatohepatitis is incorrect. Major risk factors for non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH) include type 2 diabetes mellitus and other features of the metabolic syndrome, none of which it appears that this woman has; in addition, NASH is not associated with positive liver auto-antibodies. Autoimmune Hepatitis A 31-year-old patient who had previously quiescent ileal Crohn’s disease, has had 2 relapses in the last 12 months that necessitated hospital admission. He is now feeling relatively well and denies any abdominal pain, diarrhoea or weight loss. MR small bowel has not demonstrated any strictures or fistulae. Which treatment option should now be considered for maintenance therapy?

Type II autoimmune hepatitis
Type II autoimmune hepatitis is incorrect. Type II autoimmune hepatitis tends to occur in women more than men, but typically in women somewhat younger than the person in this scenario. This condition is associated with anti-liver/kidney microsomal antibodies (in contrast to the antinuclear and anti-smooth muscle antibodies that tend to be found in those with type I disease).

stem: A 31-year-old patient who had previously quiescent ileal Crohn’s disease, has had 2 relapses in the last 12 months that necessitated hospital admission. He is now feeling relatively well and denies any abdominal pain, diarrhoea or weight loss. MR small bowel has not demonstrated any strictures or fistulae. Which treatment option should now be considered for maintenance therapy?
explanation:
Azathioprine
Azathioprine (or its metabolite mercaptopurine) should be started if a patient has more than one relapse requiring corticosteroids in the last 12 months. The general approach is to withdraw azathioprine after 5 years of therapy, depending on the course of the disease. Azathioprine is associated with an approximately 4-fold increased risk of developing lymphoma.

Mesalamine
Mesalamine is incorrect. The main role for 5-aminosalicylic acid (5-ASA), such as sulfasalazine and mesalamine, is in maintenance of remission in ulcerative colitis but azathioprine is favoured first line.

Infliximab
Infliximab is incorrect. While the anti-tumour necrosis factor (TNF) agents infliximab and adalimumab are reasonable options for maintenance therapy, azathioprine is usually tried first, or in combination with anti-TNF. If this patient had severe disease on imaging or endoscopy, or continued to be unwell, then biological therapy would have been a good first choice for maintenance, as azathioprine takes a few weeks to reach therapeutic levels. Given this patient is treatment-naive and had reassuring imaging findings, azathioprine is the best choice.

Corticosteroids
Corticosteroids is incorrect. Corticosteroids are used to induce remission during an acute flare, but due to their long-term side-effects, are not used for maintenance therapy. Crohn’s Disease

Adalimumab
Adalimumab is incorrect. While the anti-tumour necrosis factor (TNF) agents infliximab and adalimumab are reasonable options for maintenance therapy, azathioprine is usually tried first, or in combination with anti-TNF. If this patient had severe disease on imaging or endoscopy, or continued to be unwell, then biological therapy would have been a good first choice for maintenance, as azathioprine takes a few weeks to reach therapeutic levels. Given this patient is treatment-naive and had reassuring imaging findings, azathioprine is the best choice.

stem: A 48-year-old patient has a history of worsening heartburn and nocturnal cough. He feels otherwise well and has no other relevant past medical history. Gastroscopy showed Barrett's oesophagus (3 cm segment) with biopsies revealing no dysplastic change. What should be the next step in management?
options: Acid suppression and subsequent surveillance gastroscopy
explanation:
Acid suppression and subsequent surveillance gastroscopy
Barrett’s oesophagus is an endoscopic or pathological diagnosis defined as metaplasia of oesophageal mucosa from squamous to columnar epithelium. It is a premalignant condition that incurs a 10% lifetime risk of developing oesophageal adenocarcinoma. Initial management includes acid suppressive therapy to reduce the symptoms (although this does not induce regression of Barrett’s oesophagus) and surveillance gastroscopy. Mild dysplasia can be managed with radiofrequency ablation but there is little evidence for this where there is no dysplasia.

Acid suppression and lifestyle modification
Acid suppression and lifestyle modification is incorrect. Anti-reflux suppression with pharmacotherapy does not stop progression of Barrett’s oesophagus.

Fundoplication
Fundoplication is incorrect. Anti-reflux suppression with surgery with fundoplication does not stop progression of Barrett’s oesophagus.

Oesophagectomy
Oesophagectomy is incorrect. Oesophagectomy can be considered in some cases of high-grade dysplasia, as around 40% are found to have a cancer present at resection. However, this is not applicable in this case where no dysplasia was found. Oesophageal Tumours A 60-year-old man presented with alternating constipation and diarrhoea, anorexia and weight loss. Colonoscopy revealed a mass in the sigmoid colon and a biopsy from this confirmed colorectal cancer.

Multidisciplinary team (MDT) discussion
Multidisciplinary team (MDT) discussion is incorrect. MDT discussion is not necessary at this point, and would be more useful for the management of complex cases or high-grade dysplasia, or if oesophageal cancer were present.

stem: A 60-year-old man presented with alternating constipation and diarrhoea, anorexia and weight loss. Colonoscopy revealed a mass in the sigmoid colon and a biopsy from this confirmed colorectal cancer. Which of the following would most strongly indicate the presence of metastases at the time of surgery?
options: Depth of penetration of the bowel wall
Location of tumour in the colon
explanation:
Carcinoembryonic antigen levels
Carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) is a tumour marker for gastrointestinal malignancies and particularly for colorectal carcinoma. Although the sensitivity and specificity of CEA is overall not high enough for it to be useful as a diagnostic tool for colorectal cancer, significantly elevated levels of CEA are highly correlated with tumour recurrence and the presence of metastases. Preoperative CEA is indicated for all newly diagnosed colon cancer and higher preoperative CEA levels have been identified as an independent predictor of both overall and disease-free survival rates.

Depth of penetration of the bowel wall
Depth of tumour penetration of the bowel wall at surgery is a useful indicator of tumour prognosis, but not specifically predictive for metastases. Colorectal cancer begins as intramucosal epithelial lesions, usually arising in adenomatous polyps or glands. As the cancer grows, it becomes invasive, penetrates the muscularis mucosae of the bowel and invades lymphatic and vascular channels to involve regional lymph nodes, adjacent structures and distant sites.

Location of tumour in the colon
The location of the tumour in the colon does not indicate the risk of metastases. Right-sided colorectal cancer has a worse prognosis than left-sided colorectal cancer, as the right side location is associated with several negative prognostic factors, including older age, advanced stage and mucinous histology, which can influence prognosis and response to treatment.

Proportion of bowel circumference involved
The proportion of bowel circumference involved is a useful indicator of tumour prognosis, but not specifically predictive for metastases. The circumferential extent of a tumour is one factor that represents the amount and invasion area of a rectal cancer. Circular growth of the tumour was found to be associated with more advanced T stage and positive lymph node status and patients with circular tumours were found to be more likely to receive preoperative adjuvant radiation.

Size of the tumour
The size of the tumour is a useful indicator of tumour prognosis, but not specifically predictive for metastases. The prognostic significance of tumour size/horizontal growth of most solid tumours in TNM staging is reflected by its major role in determining prognosis, recurrence, survival and clinical management.

stem: A 50-year-old woman presented with a 1-year history of recurrent episodes of right upper abdominal pain. She has now had jaundice and fever for the past 4 days. On examination she had a temperature of 38.4 oC, was hypotensive and tachycardic. Abdominal ultrasonography demonstrated calculi in the common bile duct. What is the next best step once she has been stabilised?
explanation:
Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP)
This patient has cholangitis, and has the full set of classic features of Charcot’s triad – fever, pain and jaundice. Her hypotension and tachycardia suggest significant sepsis; her ultrasound result suggests that gallstones blocking the common bile duct are the source of her cholangitis, for which the definitive management is to relieve the pressure in the obstructed biliary system. Endoscopic bile duct clearance is the preferred technique, with ERCP being the typical route by which this is achieved.

Laparoscopic cholecystectomy
Laparoscopic cholecystectomy is incorrect. Cholecystectomy is indicated in people with recurrent problems related to gallstone disease (i.e. recurrent episodes of acute cholecystitis), but is not safe to perform at the time of cholangitis, when there is a great deal of inflammation present.

Laparotomy and stone extraction
Laparotomy and stone extraction is incorrect. Laparotomy for acute presentations related to gallstones/cholecystitis is rarely performed.

Lithotripsy
Lithotripsy is incorrect. Extracorporeal shock-wave lithotripsy (ESWL) is not useful for gallstone disease as – in contrast to ureteric calculi – these stones tend to contain very little calcium. JaundiceA 55-year-old man who has had Type I diabetes for 40 years and autoimmune hypothyroidism comes to the clinic for review. Over the past few months he has suffered increasing problems with reflux, bloating, nausea and unpredictable vomiting. He has found it more difficult to predict his mealtime insulin requirements, and has had some very high and some very low blood sugars. On examination his BP is 135/80 mmHg with a postural drop of 15 mmHg; his BMI is 23 kg/m2. There is bilateral diabetic neuropathy with numbness to the mid-shin on both sides. A gastroscopy could not be completed due to the presence of food in the stomach. Investigations show:

Open cholecystectomy
Open cholecystectomy is incorrect. The typical means of cholecystectomy is via laparoscopy, although an open procedure may be used in difficult cases.

stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate initial therapy?
explanation:
Domperidone
This patient is suffering from diabetic gastroparesis – an autonomic neuropathy characterised by delayed gastric emptying in the absence of a mechanical cause of obstruction – that can cause poor glycaemic control, malnutrition and poor quality of life. He has postural hypotension, which is also a sign of autonomic neuropathy and helps to point to the diagnosis. The presence of food in the stomach of a patient who has fasted for an endoscopy is also suggestive of gastroparesis, although the standard method for measuring gastric emptying is scintigraphy. Initial therapy includes a prokinetic anti-emetic, such as domperidone. In severe cases a gastric pacemaker can be considered.

Gaviscon
Gaviscon can reduce symptoms associated with acid reflux but does not increase the rate of gastric emptying.

Omeprazole
Omeprazole can also reduce symptoms associated with acid reflux but, again, does not increase the rate of gastric emptying.

Ondansetron
Ondansetron can reduce nausea but their role in gastroparesis has not been established.

Ranitidine
Ranitidine can be useful in suppressing acid reflux but does not alter the course of the disease.

stem: A 52-year-old man attends the Gastroenterology Clinic for review. He complains that his breasts appear to have enlarged slightly over the past few years. What is the cause of gynaecomastia in cirrhosis?
explanation:
Altered oestrogen metabolism
Whilst the causes of gynaecomastia in cirrhosis are complex, the most likely cause is disordered metabolism of sex steroids, which leads to excess levels of oestrogens. Often there is associated testicular atrophy and loss of body hair.

Furosemide prescription
Furosemide prescription is incorrect. Whilst gynaecomastia may occur in cirrhosis secondary to the use of spironolactone (an aldosterone antagonist), there is no association with furosemide.

Excess levels of corticosteroids
Excess levels of corticosteroids is incorrect. It is excessive levels of oestrogen (rather than corticosteroids) which appear to be the major driving factor towards gynaecomastia in cirrhosis.

Excess energy intake from alcohol
Excess energy intake from alcohol is incorrect. Patients with alcohol-related cirrhosis often suffer nutritional deficiency, but although they obtain a large intake of calories from alcohol they tend to substitute alcohol in place of food, so the overall energy intake is often increased only marginally. Cirrhosis and

Excess levels of testosterone
Excess levels of testosterone is incorrect. It is excessive levels of oestrogen (rather than testosterone) which appear to be the major driving factor towards gynaecomastia in cirrhosis.

stem: A 55-year-old man presents to the General Practitioner with a recurrent bluish-red rash on his neck, wheeze, abdominal pain and watery diarrhoea. He has facial telangiectasia, mild pedal oedema, an elevated jugular venous pressure (JVP), a pansystolic murmur and moderate hepatomegaly. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Carcinoma of the pancreas with liver metastases
explanation:
Carcinoid syndrome
Carcinoid syndrome occurs in only 5% of patients with carcinoid tumours, when there are liver metastases. Although serotonin (and other vasoactive molecules) produced by these neuroendocrine tumours is normally degraded by the liver, infiltration of the liver by metastases means that there is a lack of normal liver parenchyma to perform this role, such that these molecules enter the systemic circulation where they cause their effects. Carcinoid syndrome manifests as bluish-red flushing (mainly on the neck and face), bronchospasm, abdominal pain and recurrent watery diarrhoea. Cardiac abnormalities develop in 50% of patients and consist of tricuspid regurgitation or pulmonary stenosis.

Carcinoma of the pancreas with liver metastases
Carcinoid tumours may occur throughout the gastrointestinal tract (including the pancreas), although the vast majority of pancreatic cancers are non-secretory adenocarcinomas (approximately 90%) that would not give the sort of symptoms described here. Approximately 1–2% of pancreatic tumours are neuroendocrine. Risk factors for pancreatic cancer include smoking, obesity and diabetes.

Intestinal tuberculosis (TB)
Intestinal TB may present with any of a wide range of gastrointestinal symptoms, including diarrhoea and abdominal pain; however, this option is incorrect, as rash, wheeze and cardiac failure would not be explained by TB. Gastrointestinal TB accounts for 1–3% of TB cases in the world. The commonest site affected in the gastrointestinal tract is the ileocaecal region.

Lymphoma
Although lymphoma may present with a wide range of symptoms (including diarrhoea and abdominal pain, in the case of intestinal lymphoma), the constellation of rash, wheeze and heart failure would not be explained by lymphoma. The sandwich sign, or hamburger sign, is a computed tomography (CT) finding of lymphadenopathy on both sides of the mesenteric vasculature, thereby sandwiching the vasculature between the lymphadenopathy.

Tropical sprue
Tropical sprue is a condition of presumed infectious aetiology that affects the small intestine; although it may present with diarrhoea/malabsorption, none of the other symptoms described here would be typical. Tropical sprue is typically seen in temperate regions. Diarrhoea is often pale and malodorous. Other symptoms include weight loss, fatigue, generalised weakness, sore tongue and night blindness. Neuroendocrine Tumours A 58-year-old woman with dyspepsia was referred for endoscopy.

stem: A 58-year-old woman with dyspepsia was referred for endoscopy. Which of the following is not a risk factor for gastric adenocarcinoma?
explanation:
Aspirin use
Aspirin in fact appears to reduce the risk of oesophageal, gastric and colorectal carcinoma, probably by inhibition of cyclooxygenase 2 (COX-2) and several other malignancy-related pathways. The risk factors for gastric cancer include: Helicobacter pylori Low dietary vitamin C Family history High dietary salt Racial origin (Japan > UK > Sweden) Gastric surgery (with the risk particularly increased with biliary diversion to the stomach) Pernicious anaemia Smoking

Helicobacter pylori
Helicobacter pylori is incorrect. H. pylori is a risk factor for gastric adenocarcinoma.

Low dietary Vitamin C
Low dietary vitamin C is incorrect. Low dietary vitamin C is a risk factor for gastric adenocarcinoma.

Partial Gastrectomy
Partial gastrectomy is incorrect. Partial gastrectomy is a risk factor for gastric adenocarcinoma.

Pernicious anaemia
Pernicious anaemia is incorrect. Pernicious anaemia is a risk factor for gastric adenocarcinoma.

stem: A 26-year-old woman was referred by her general practitioner. She had recently returned from her honeymoon in Africa. While she was there, she ate food bought from a number of roadside stalls. She described a history of abdominal cramps, bloating and diarrhoea. Examination of three stool specimens revealed cysts in two out of the three specimens. The condition responded to a course of metronidazole. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Giardiasis
Giardiasis is caused by the protozoal parasite Giardia lamblia, and is spread by faeco-oral transmission, particularly in areas with poor sanitation. Up to one-third of the population may have been previously exposed to Giardia in certain African countries, and many animals may also be hosts for the infection. Risk factors for the infection include close contact with affected people/animals, drinking fresh water in countries where the infection is prevalent, certain forms of immunodeficiency (particularly X-linked agammaglobulinaemia), and men who have sex with men. About 70% of infected patients have one or more intestinal symptoms (diarrhoea, flatulence, cramps, bloating, nausea), but fever occurs in fewer than 20%. Malaise, anorexia, chronic diarrhoea, malabsorption and weight loss can occur in chronic sufferers. Between 20% and 25% are asymptomatic. The conventional means of diagnosis has been via microscopy of stool, looking for trophozoites or cysts, with microscopy of at least three stool specimens having a sensitivity of ~90%. However, molecular assays are now available that have even higher sensitivity, including tests for Giardia antigens in stool specimens, or ELISA. Treatment is typically with a 1-week course of metronidazole.

Cryptosporidium
Cryptosporidium is incorrect. A scenario that describes gastrointestinal (GI) symptoms after travel in Africa and cysts in stool would certainly make Cryptosporidium a possibility; however, this infection does not respond to metronidazole, making it less likely to be the diagnosis than giardiasis.

Salmonella infection
Salmonella infection is incorrect. The description given of cysts in the stool means that this illness cannot be explained by a bacterial infection, and Salmonella can therefore be discounted.

Tapeworm infection
Tapeworm infection is incorrect. A scenario that describes GI symptoms after travel in Africa and cysts in stool would certainly make tapeworm infection a possibility; however, this infection does not respond to metronidazole, making it less likely to be the diagnosis than giardiasis. GastroenteritisTyphoid fever
Typhoid fever is incorrect. The description given of cysts in the stool means that this illness cannot be explained by a bacterial infection, and typhoid fever can therefore be discounted.

stem: A 22-year-old woman with a history of Lynch syndrome comes to the clinic for review. Her father died of colon cancer at the age of 39. She is aware that medical therapy may reduce her risk of colon cancer rather than committing immediately to surgical intervention. Which of the following medications is known to impact on her risk of colon cancer?
explanation:
Aspirin
Lynch syndrome is also known as hereditary non-polyposis colon cancer syndrome, and is recognised as a major cause of heritable colon cancer. The underlying pathophysiology is thought to be carriage of pathological DNA mismatch repair variants. In a study specifically examining the effect of aspirin in this population, 861 participants were randomised to aspirin or placebo. The study showed a 37% reduction in progression to colorectal cancer for aspirin versus placebo.

Dietary starch
Dietary starch is incorrect. Eating resistant starch may reduce expression of oncogenic RNAs, but there is little randomised controlled trial (RCT) evidence to suggest that this translates into reduced risk of colon cancer.

Oil of evening primrose
Oil of evening primrose is incorrect. There is no evidence that oil of evening primrose oil impacts on bowel cancer, although it can be of value in alleviating symptoms of the menopause and treatments for breast cancer.

Omega 3 fatty acids
Omega 3 fatty acids is incorrect. Evidence supports the use of omega 3 fatty acids to survival in patients diagnosed with bowel cancer, but primary prevention evidence is not as strong as that for use of aspirin.

Vitamin C
Vitamin C is incorrect. High dose vitamin C has animal evidence to support an anti-colon cancer effect, although this isn’t available in humans.

stem: You suspect acute cholecystitis related to gallstones. What is the most likely composition of her gallstones?
explanation:
Black pigment
Bile contains a number of substances including cholesterol, bile pigments from metabolised haemoglobin, and phospholipids. According to differences in aetiology, different gallstones are seen. Black pigment stones are small, friable, irregular and radiolucent and are comprised largely of bile pigments. Risk factors include haemolysis (i.e. sickle cell anaemia, hereditary spherocytosis, thalassaemia) and cirrhosis.

Brown pigment
Brown pigment is incorrect. Brown pigment stones are very rarely seen in the UK, and form as a result of stasis and infection within the biliary system, usually in the presence of E. coli and/or Klebsiella.

Calcium
Calcium is incorrect. Gallstones do not ever contain just calcium salts, unlike renal stones which can be made up of calcium oxalate.

Cholesterol
Cholesterol is incorrect. Cholesterol stones make up 80% of all GB stones in the UK, being large, often solitary and radiolucent. They are seen in association with hypertriglyceridaemia.

Mixed
Mixed is incorrect. Mixed stones are faceted stones and are comprised of calcium salts, bile pigment and cholesterol; 10% of these are radiopaque and may therefore be seen on plain x-ray.

stem: A 45-year-old man comes to your clinic complaining of having epigastric pain for 2 months. His GP prescribed him H2 blockers 3 weeks ago, which have produced only partial relief of his symptoms. His weight is stable. His physical examination is normal. An upper gastrointestinal endoscopy reveals a 1 cm duodenal ulcer. Which of the following risk factors are associated with the development of ulcer disease?
explanation:
Cigarette smoking
Cigarette smoking doubles the risk of developing duodenal ulcers. Other risk factors include: Regular non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) and corticosteroid use Gastric infection with Helicobacter pylori increases risk about 5–7-fold At least 90% of patients with Zollinger–Ellison syndrome (gastrin-secreting tumours) have a duodenal ulcer Physical stress – intensive care unit admission, burns, major surgery, etc

Spicy foods
Spicy foods is incorrect. There is no evidence that spicy food (or any other dietary factors) predispose to peptic ulcer development.

Emotional stress
Emotional stress is incorrect. Although considered a risk factor in the past, several studies have shown that emotional stress is not a risk factor for the development of duodenal ulcer.

Regular use of paracetamol
Regular use of paracetamol is incorrect. Paracetamol is not a risk factor for peptic ulcer disease. Peptic Ulcer Disease and Gastritis A 25-year-old cook applied for a job at a cafeteria. He gave a history of having had enteric fever 2 years ago. Which of the following investigations is most likely to indicate a chronic carrier status?

Moderate alcohol intake
Moderate alcohol intake is incorrect. Excess alcohol intake is a risk factor, but moderate intake does not predispose to ulcer development.

stem: A 60-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes complains of blood-stained diarrhoea and cramping abdominal pain of several months’ duration. She underwent a hysterectomy and radiotherapy 8 months ago for endometrial carcinoma and her diarrhoea began a short period after this. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Chronic radiation enteritis
The clear relationship time-wise between this woman receiving radiotherapy and development of abdominal pain and blood-stained diarrhoea is very suggestive of radiation enteritis.

Irritable bowel syndrome
Irritable bowel syndrome is incorrect. Irritable bowel syndrome may cause chronic abdominal pain and diarrhoea, but certainly cannot account for bleeding from the gastrointestinal tract, and therefore cannot be the diagnosis here.

Lymphoma
Lymphoma is incorrect. Lymphoma may present with a wide range of gastrointestinal and systemic symptoms, but the absence of either features suggestive of ‘B’ symptoms or the presence of lymphadenopathy makes this unlikely.

Pseudomembranous colitis
Pseudomembranous colitis is incorrect. Pseudomembranous colitis is colonic inflammation occurring in association with Clostridium difficile infection. The major risk factor for C. difficile infection is recent use of antibiotics; no history of recent antibiotic use is given, making this diagnosis unlikely. In addition, pseudomembranous colitis tends to give such marked symptoms that affected patients would typically present to medical services and be diagnosed much earlier than after several months of symptoms.

Ulcerative colitis
Ulcerative colitis is incorrect. Ulcerative colitis (UC) may occur at any age, but tends to first present at a somewhat younger age than this woman is. In addition, UC often gives symptoms relating to rectal involvement (including urgency and tenesmus), and untreated ulcerative colitis tends to give symptoms that relapse and remit over the course of months to years; this does not fit with the scenario described here.

stem: A 24-year-old patient presents with a 7-week history of colicky abdominal pain, fevers and diarrhoea 2–3 times per day on most days without blood. Over the past year he has lost 6 kg in weight and has felt more fatigued. He has not had any recent foreign travel. He is a non-smoker and occasionally drinks alcohol. On examination, his BMI is 19, pulse is 110 bpm, temperature is 37.6 °C, and he has a tender diffuse mass in the right iliac fossa. PR shows soft stool, and an anal tag. His haemoglobin is 115 g/l, white cell count 12.6 × 10 9/l, platelets 566 × 10 9/l and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) 48 mm in 1 hour. Stool culture is negative for infection. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Crohn's disease
This patient has the typical symptoms of abdominal pain, fevers, diarrhoea, a right iliac fossa mass (inflammatory mass) and weight loss. The anal tag suggests perianal disease involvement. An iron deficiency anemia is very common in Crohn’s. Further investigations include a colonoscopy with biopsies of the terminal ileum, and small bowel MRI imaging.

Ileocaecal tuberculosis
Ileocaecal tuberculosis is incorrect. Although ileocaecal TB can present with abdominal pain, a RIF mass, weight loss and fevers there is nothing in the history such as foreign travel or belonging to a high-risk group, to suggest TB.

Small bowel lymphoma
Small bowel lymphoma is incorrect. Primary malignant lymphomas of the small bowel account for less than 2% of GI malignancies. Symptoms include weight loss, colicky abdominal pain, nausea, but rarely diarrhoea (however, immunoproliferative small intestinal disease (IPSID) does present with diarrhoea). Furthermore, the presence of the anal tag makes Crohn’s disease more likely.

Ulcerative colitis
Ulcerative colitis is incorrect. Ulcerative colitis does not present with a mass, and typically the diarrhea is bloody. Crohn’s Disease

Yersiniosis
Yersiniosis is incorrect. Yersinia enterocolitica is an infectious bacterium that can cause diarrhea and abdominal pain. However it tends to be a self-limiting illness that resolves within a month, mostly seen in under-5s. Other associated symptoms include vomiting and erythema nodosum.

stem: Which of the following would be the next appropriate investigation?
explanation:
Anti-smooth muscle antibody
A raised anti-smooth antibody level is suggestive of autoimmune hepatitis (in particular, type I disease). Antinuclear antibodies may also be positive. More women than men are affected – 78% of patients are women. About 41% of people with type I autoimmune hepatitis have coexisting autoimmune pathology. This patient’s raised ESR level and deranged liver function tests are also supportive of this. The disease is highly steroidresponsive, although about 45% of patients will progress to cirrhosis.

Creatine kinase (CK)
Creatine kinase is incorrect. CK is found in skeletal and myocardial muscle. It is raised in rhabdomyolysis, myositis, myocardial infarction, myocarditis, malignant hyperthermia and neuroleptic malignant syndrome. It is not raised in autoimmune hepatitis, which is the diagnosis in this case. Specific CK molecules can be measured, such as CK-MB, which can be a useful biochemical marker for secondary myocardial infarction, when the troponin level remains high immediately after a primary myocardial infarction.

Hepatic ultrasound scan
Hepatic ultrasound scan is incorrect. Autoimmune hepatitis causes a huge spectrum of liver disease, ranging from minor liver inflammation through to acute liver failure and cirrhosis; the liver may appear completely normal on ultrasound. As such, while liver ultrasound is reasonable to consider, it would not help to determine the underlying cause of hepatic injury in this case. The most appropriate next step would be to assess for the presence of anti-smooth muscle antibodies.

Short Synacthen ® test
Short Synacthen ® test is incorrect. People with type I diabetes mellitus are at increased risk of other autoimmune conditions, including Addison’s disease. However, this woman is not described as having any of the typical clinical features (eg postural hypotension, buccal pigmentation) or laboratory features (hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, hypoglycaemia, etc.) that might suggest Addison’s disease. Furthermore, Addison’s disease is associated with the presence of anti-adrenal antibody. Autoimmune Hepatitis

Thyroid function testing
Thyroid function testing is incorrect. People with type I diabetes mellitus are at increased risk of other autoimmune conditions, including thyroid disease. However, none of this patient’s current symptoms are suggestive of thyroid dysfunction. Furthermore, autoimmune thyroid disease is associated with the presence of antibodies such as antithyroid peroxidase.

stem: A 49-year-old woman presents to the clinic for review, referred by her GP with a diagnosis of irritable bowel syndrome. She has had increasing difficulty managing her symptoms over the past 6 months. On examination her BP is 144/82 mmHg, pulse 80 bpm and BMI 23 kg/m 2. On reviewing her symptoms, which of the following raises suspicion of a diagnosis other than IBS?
explanation:
Pain not relieved by defecation
All of the other options are recognised to be associated with irritable bowel syndrome. NICE have developed diagnostic criteria for irritable bowel syndrome that include at least a 6-month history of either: abdominal pain or discomfort bloating change in bowel habit Consider positively diagnosing IBS only if abdominal pain is either relieved by defecation, or associated with altered bowel frequency or stool form, and at least two of the following are present: altered passage of stool (straining, urgency, incomplete evacuation) abdominal bloating (women > men), distension, tension or hardness symptoms aggravated by eating passage of mucus rectally

Abdominal pain
Abdominal pain is incorrect. Abdominal pain or discomfort for at least 6 months is a criterion recognised by NICE for IBS.

Alternating diarrhoea and constipation
Alternating diarrhoea and constipation is incorrect. NICE's diagnostic criteria for IBS include at least a 6-month history of a change in bowel habit.

Mucus in the stool
Mucus in the stool is incorrect. The passage of mucus rectally is one of the criteria for positively diagnosing IBS, when in combination with other symptoms. Functional Bowel DiseaseA 59-year-old, otherwise fit man undergoes endoscopic follow-up for Barrett’s disease of the oesophagus. His latest biopsy shows poorly differentiated cells.

Symptoms aggravated by eating
Symptoms aggravated by eating is incorrect. The aggravation of symptoms by eating is one of the criteria for positively diagnosing IBS, when in combination with other symptoms.

stem: A 56-year-old man presents with a long history of intermittent abdominal pain and steatorrhoea. He has also recently been diagnosed with diabetes mellitus. His past medical history includes hypertension and gout. He consumes an average of 35 units of alcohol a week and smokes one pack of cigarettes a day. A CT abdomen shows calcification and atrophy of the pancreas. Given the likely diagnosis, which one of the following statements regarding his condition is true?
options: Faecal calprotectin levels can be used to confirm malabsorption
If he had a pancreatic pseudocyst, this would require urgent immediate drainage
Proton pump inhibitor therapy used with pancreatic supplements can the efficacy of the
He is not an increased risk for pancreatic malignancy
Abstinence from alcohol would not reduce the rate of pancreatic damage
explanation:
Proton pump inhibitor therapy used with pancreatic supplements can the efficacy of the
Proton pump inhibitor therapy used with pancreatic supplements can the efficacy of the pancreatic supplements This patient has classic signs of chronic pancreatitis (secondary to alcohol excess) as evidenced by the symptoms of recurrent abdominal pain, steatorrhoea (exocrine insufficiency) and diabetes (endocrine insufficiency). The CT findings confirm the diagnosis. PPI therapy is useful as an adjunct as they can help to prevent the acid breakdown of the pancreatic supplements.

Faecal calprotectin levels can be used to confirm malabsorption
Faecal calprotectin levels can be used to confirm malabsorption is incorrect. Steatorrhoea is defined as faecal fat>7g/day but faecal fat measurement is rarely used. Low faecal elastase levels can be used to confirm exocrine insufficiency. Faecal calprotectin is a marker of intestinal inflammation and is sometimes used to differentiate between IBD and IBS.

If he had a pancreatic pseudocyst, this would require urgent immediate drainage
If he had a pancreatic pseudocyst, this would urgent immediate drainage is incorrect. Not all pancreatic pseudocysts need urgent drainage, the majority are managed conservatively.

He is not an increased risk for pancreatic malignancy
He is not an increased risk for pancreatic malignancy is incorrect. Chronic pancreatitis increases the risk of pancreatic malignancy particularly in smokers. Chronic Pancreatitis A social worker had been diagnosed with hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection. Which test will conclusively establish the presence of this infection?

Abstinence from alcohol would not reduce the rate of pancreatic damage
Abstinence from alcohol would not reduce the rate of pancreatic damage is incorrect. Abstinence from alcohol can slow down disease progression.

stem: A social worker had been diagnosed with hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection. Which test will conclusively establish the presence of this infection?
explanation:
HCV RNA
The answer is HCV RNA (Option D). Hepatitis C (HCV) RNA is the most sensitive test for detection of hepatitis C infection. It may be detected within 1–2 weeks of infection. As such, option D is the correct answer.

Anti-HCV
Anti-HCV (Option A) is incorrect. Anti-HCV is usually positive from about 6 weeks following infection (and certainly later than HCV RNA would be expected to be positive). Furthermore, a positive anti-HCV antibody is not the same as active hepatitis C infection; a proportion of people exposed to hepatitis C clear the infection spontaneously, but will still of course be anti-HCV antibody positive.

ELISA-3
ELISA-3 (Option B) is incorrect. Antigens from the nucleocapsid regions have been used to develop enzymelinked immunosorbent assays (ELISA), but such assays are only used in research settings rather than clinical practice at the moment, ruling this option out.

HBV DNA
HBV DNA (Option C) is incorrect. HBV is a useful test for assessing for infection with hepatitis B, but is not a test that gives any information about the presence of absence of hepatitis C infection; as such, it may be ruled out. Viral Hepatitis

IgM anti-HAV
IgM anti-HAV (Option E) is incorrect. IgM anti-HAV is a useful test for assessing for infection with hepatitis A, but is not a test that gives any information about the presence or absence of hepatitis C infection; as such, it may be ruled out.

stem: A 76-year-old man presents with worsening jaundice, intermittent abdominal pain and weight loss. He is jaundiced, cachectic and has a non-tender mass in the right upper quadrant. Which of the following would be the next appropriate investigation?
options: Computed tomography scan of the abdomen
explanation:
Computed tomography scan of the abdomen
The combination of jaundice, a non-tender right upper abdominal mass and weight loss in a man of this age is most likely to be explained by carcinoma of the pancreas. Other differential diagnoses would include biliary tumours (such as cholangiocarcinoma, or ampullary cancer) and liver masses (including primary tumours and liver metastasis). Computed tomography of the abdomen is the most appropriate test for confirming the diagnosis, and will also help in staging disease if cancer is present too.

Alpha-fetoprotein level
Alpha-fetoprotein level is incorrect. Alpha-fetoprotein (α-FP) is a biomarker that forms part of the assessment for hepatocellular carcinoma; however, it is not a biomarker for pancreatic cancer, so is unlikely to be of any benefit in this scenario.

Liver biopsy
Liver biopsy is incorrect. A liver biopsy may eventually be required to definitively confirm the diagnosis (eg where a CT scan is suggestive of a tumour with liver metastasis, and where histology is required before considering chemotherapy), but would not be performed without imaging first, so is not the appropriate next investigation here.

Serum gastrin level
Serum gastrin level is incorrect. Serum gastrin levels are a useful test in suspected cases of gastrinoma/Zollinger–Ellison syndrome (a neuroendocrine tumour associated with overproduction of gastrin, often manifesting clinically with recurrent peptic ulceration and diarrhoea). However, there is nothing from the scenario given to strongly suggest that this is the underlying diagnosis.

Sweat test
Sweat test is incorrect. A sweat test is useful to perform in cases of suspected cystic fibrosis, but this is unlikely to be the diagnosis here.

stem: A 44-year-old woman presents with a 4-month history of jaundice and progressively worsening liver function tests. She does not report any abdominal pain or weight loss. Her past medical history includes hypertension, high cholesterol and diabetes mellitus. A liver screen is negative and imaging does not show any abnormalities so she is sent for a percutaneous liver biopsy. Which of the following, if present, would be a contraindication for liver biopsy?
explanation:
Platelet count 40 x10 9/l
Contraindications to percutaneous liver biopsy include: Increased prothrombin time, international normalized ratio (INR) greater than 1.5 Thrombocytopenia, (platelet count less than 50 x10 9/l) Severe ascites Difficult body habitus Suspected haemangioma Suspected echinococcal infection Uncooperative patient In this case the platelet count of 40 x10 9/l, is the most important factor. Transfusion with platelets just before or during the procedure would be necessary. The level at which thrombocytopaenia becomes a contraindication to percutaneous liver biopsy is uncertain from published data, but most centres expect a minimum platelet count of 50 x 10 9/l.

BMI 28
BMI 28 is incorrect. Large BMI’s can make percutaneous biopsies very challenging, although there is no agreed cut-off. A BMI of 28 should not be a contraindication.

INR 1.3
INR 1.3 is incorrect. An INR of more than 1.5 is a contraindication, and would need to be corrected prior to the procedure if this was the case. Otherwise if correction of coagulation is not possible, a liver biopsy is more safely obtained from the transjugular route.

Mild ascites
Mild ascites is incorrect. Tense ascites, and not mild ascites, is a contraindication for percutaneous liver biopsy. The reasons for this vary from the high likelihood of not obtaining a biopsy specimen because of the distance between the abdominal wall and the liver to, the risk of uncontrollable bleeding into the ascites. Thrombocytopenia

Suspected Wilson’s disease
Suspected Wilson’s disease is incorrect. Wilson’s disease is normally diagnosed well before age 44 because of elevated transaminases, chorea or the presence of Kaiser Fleischer rings on ophthalmic examination. It is no more associated with bleeding risk than other causes of cirrhosis.

stem: A 62-year-old woman is sent to the Gastroenterology Clinic for review. Her medical history of note includes ulcerative colitis and prolonged use of oral ketoconazole for recurrent nail-bed infections. On examination in the clinic she is jaundiced and has two-finger-breadth hepatomegaly. Biochemistry results show: bilirubin 260 μmol/l (normal range 1–22 μmol/), alanine aminotransferase (ALT) of 410 U/l (5–35 U/l) and a non-specific increase in globulin levels. You note that her LFTs were normal 1 year earlier. Autoantibody screen reveals antiLKM2 antibodies. What diagnosis fits best with this clinical picture?
explanation:
Drug-induced hepatitis
While autoimmune hepatitis may be associated with anti-LKM positivity, this antibody may also be positive in drug-induced hepatitis. The short history of liver injury – coupled with the information regarding recent exposure to ketoconazole, a classical cause of drug-induced liver injury – makes it more likely that this woman has drug-induced hepatitis than autoimmune hepatitis. Nevertheless, it is not possible to fully differentiate the two on the basis of this information alone, and a liver biopsy is likely to be required. Drug-induced chronic hepatitis is more common in women than men, and presents with jaundice, hepatomegaly, raised transaminases and elevated bilirubin. Liver function may after drug withdrawal, although relapses are also possible. Other drugs that may cause a chronic hepatitis include: Methyldopa Isoniazid Nitrofurantoin

Autoimmune hepatitis
Autoimmune hepatitis is incorrect. Anti-LKM antibody may be positive in both autoimmune hepatitis and drug induced hepatitis. However as ketoconazole is known to cause liver injury along with thte short history of duration, drug-induced liver injury seems the most likely diagnosis. For an absolute diagnosis a liver biopsy would be required to differentiate between the two likely causes.

Primary biliary cholangitis (PBC)
Primary biliary cholangitis (PBC) is incorrect. Primary biliary cholangitis (PBC; formerly called ‘primary biliary cirrhosis’) is a cholestatic liver disease, so typically associated with raised alkaline phosphatase but relatively normal transaminase levels. PBC is associated with positive anti-mitochondrial antibody (AMA), but would not explain positive anti-LKM antibody.

Primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC)
Primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC) is incorrect. Primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC) may certainly be found in people with a history of inflammatory bowel disease, and could explain a raised bilirubin; however, this is a cholestatic liver condition, so is associated with a raised alkaline phosphatase but only modest elevations in transaminases. PSC has an association with a positive anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA), but is not an explanation for a positive anti-LKM antibody. Drug-induced hepatitis Drugs that can result in this clinical picture include: Methyldopa Isoniazid Ketoconazole (an antifungal) Nitrofurantoin Drug-induced chronic hepatitis is commoner in women and presents with jaundice and hepatomegaly, with deranged transaminases and elevated bilirubin. It is associated with anti-LKM2 autoantibodies. While autoimmune hepatitis may also be associated with anti-LKM positivity, the short history and ketoconazole exposure make drug-induced hepatitis more likely here. Liver function can after drug withdrawal but relapses are possible. Other causes of chronic hepatitis include: Hepatitis B Hepatitis C Autoimmune hepatitis Alpha 1-antitrypsin deficiency Wilson’s disease Inflammatory bowel disease Drug-Induced Liver InjuryA 55-year-old geography teacher was referred for management of obesity. He had a body mass index (BMI) of 36 kg/m 2 and investigations showed: cholesterol, 7.7 mmol/l; fasting triglycerides, 3.1 mmol/l; ALT, 150 U/l. He denied alcohol excess. What is the significance of his raised liver enzymes?

Gallstones
Gallstones is incorrect. First, it is very unlikely that gallstone disease would cause such marked abnormalities in her bilirubin and transaminases, especially in the apparent absence of abdominal pain. Second, gallstone disease has no association with anti-LKM antibody.

stem: A 45 year old patient who has just moved to the UK from Cambodia, has chronic kidney disease secondary to diabetes mellitus and is on dialysis. She is asymptomatic. Her last blood results showed an ALT of 120 u/l and AST 200 u/l. Further investigations show hepatitis C antibody: negative, hepatitis B surface antigen: negative, hepatitis B surface antibody positive, CMV IgG positive, EBV negative, anti-mitochondrial antibody negative, ferritin normal, caeruloplasmin normal. What is the next most appropriate step in investigating the cause of her raised ALT and AST?
options: Perform a liver biopsy to exclude auto-immune hepatitis
Perform a liver biopsy to exclude steatohepatitis
explanation:
Order Hepatitis C PCR
Patients who are immunocompromised or on haemodialysis may have Hepatitis C but can have negative Hepatitis C antibodies. Therefore they require virological testing by PCR in order to detect the virus. Furthermore anti-HCV antibodies may also miss patients who have not yet developed the antibodies. This patient has had dialysis abroad, which makes her risk for having Hepatitis C even higher.

Perform a liver biopsy to exclude auto-immune hepatitis
Perform a liver biopsy to exclude auto-immune hepatitis is incorrect. A liver biopsy to exclude auto immune hepatitis is not appropriate at this time, especially given that ANA had not been tested for.

Order HBV DNA levels
Order HBV DNA levels is incorrect. This patient has positive hepatitis B antibodies and negative hepatitis surface antigen, therefore she has either been exposed to hep B in the past and cleared the infection naturally, or has been vaccinated. She does not have a current infection, so HBV DNA levels would be of no value.

Order a HIV test
Order a HIV test is incorrect. A HIV test may be appropriate to order before starting dialysis in the UK, but a positive test would not account for the deranged liver function tests. Hepatitis C is more likely in this case. Viral Hepatitis A 51-year-old man presented to his general practitioner complaining of tiredness. He had no history of alcohol excess and took no medication. There had been a history of intermittent bloody diarrhoea over the past few years. His general practitioner noticed that his alkaline phosphatase level was raised, and that his antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA) was positive. He was then referred for a gastroenterological opinion.

Perform a liver biopsy to exclude steatohepatitis
Perform a liver biopsy to exclude steatohepatitis is incorrect. A liver biopsy to exclude steatohepatitis is not appropriate given that other causes have not been excluded. A liver biopsy will almost certainly show fatty liver changes in patients with long standing diabetes mellitus and as such performing a liver biopsy specifically to exclude steatohepatitis would be of limited value.

stem: A 55-year-old geography teacher was referred for management of obesity. He had a body mass index (BMI) of 36 kg/m 2 and investigations showed: cholesterol, 7.7 mmol/l; fasting triglycerides, 3.1 mmol/l; ALT, 150 U/l. He denied alcohol excess. What is the significance of his raised liver enzymes?
options: Low significance – should be monitored, but will with weight reduction
explanation:
Consistent with non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH)
Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) is rapidly becoming one of the most common causes of chronic liver disease in the world. It is often found in association with other features of the metabolic syndrome, ie hypertension, dyslipidaemia, obesity and diabetes mellitus. It represents a spectrum of liver disease, ranging from simple fatty liver to NASH (non-alcoholic steatohepatitis; which usually occurs with liver fibrosis, but not necessarily) to cirrhosis. It is now recognised that NAFLD-related cirrhosis is probably the major cause of what was previously termed ‘cryptogenic cirrhosis’. This man’s very raised BMI and markedly abnormal lipid profile mean it is very likely that he has the metabolic syndrome, and put him at high risk of advanced liver disease related to NAFLD (ie NASH with significant hepatic fibrosis), making option E the correct answer. However, it can only be said that his results are consistent with/suggestive of NASH from the information given, since NASH may only be definitely diagnosed on a liver biopsy.

Highly significant - has cirrhosis
Highly significant - has cirrhosis is incorrect. Whether a person with NAFLD has cirrhosis may not be predicted from clinical or biochemical features (including the degree of derangement of liver enzymes).

Likely autoimmune hepatitis
Likely autoimmune hepatitis is incorrect. This man’s marked obesity and dyslipidaemia make it very likely that the cause of his abnormal liver enzymes is NAFLD; furthermore, no positive liver autoantibody results are described that might suggest autoimmune hepatitis.

Low significance – should be monitored, but will with weight reduction
Low significance - should be monitored, but will with weight reduction is incorrect. People with NAFLD with more severe features of metabolic syndrome are most likely to have advanced liver disease – this man’s very abnormal BMI and lipid results clearly put him at particularly high risk of severe liver disease related to NAFLD.

Negligible - he can be reassured
Negligible - he can be reassured is incorrect. People with NAFLD with more severe features of metabolic syndrome are most likely to have advanced liver disease – this man’s very abnormal BMI and lipid results clearly put him at particularly high risk of severe liver disease related to NAFLD. Non-alcoholic.

stem: A 37-year-old man who is known to have ulcerative colitis is admitted from the gastroenterology clinic with severe disease. He is opening his bowels eight to ten times per day with profuse bloody diarrhoea despite taking maximal mesalazine, steroid enemas and prednisolone 40 mg/day. He is commenced on therapy with IV steroids, fluids, nutritional support and prophylactic heparin. At day 3, which of the following features is most associated with progression to colectomy?
explanation:
Stool frequency >8 per day
Acute severe UC affects about 15% of patients at some point in their disease and is associated with a high mortality. Stool frequency >8 per day is associated with progression to surgery

Colon diameter >4.0 cm
Colon diameter >4.0 cm is incorrect. A colon diameter >5.5cm is an indication for urgent surgical referral but its presence on day 3 has not been correlated with outcomes.

CRP >30 mg/l
CRP >30 mg/l is incorrect. A CRP more than 45 is associated with progression to colectomy (in the presence of 3-8 stools/day).

Hb >140 g/l
Hb >140 g/l is incorrect. Haemaglobin is not a marker for progression to colectomy, but is used as part of the definition for an acute UC flare.

WCC > 11.0 ×< 10 9/l
WCC > 11.0 ×9/l is incorrect. White cell count is not correlated with progression to colectomy, CRP, is a more useful sign.

stem: A 45-year-old man presented for review at the gastroenterology clinic. His past history of note included hypertension, treated with amlodipine. He had mild ankle oedema, which had been attributed to the amlodipine. Over the past few months, he had suffered intermittent epigastric pain. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy revealed enlarged gastric folds in the body and fundus of his stomach. Biopsy demonstrated hyperplasia of the gastric pits, gland atrophy and an increase in mucosal thickness. A CLO (Campylobacter-like organism) test was negative. The full blood count was normal, and an autoantibody screen was negative; serum albumin was reduced at 28 g/l (NR 37–49 g/l). What diagnosis fits best with this clinical picture?
explanation:
Menetrier's disease
This scenario describes a typical case of Menetrier’s disease. This is a rare condition associated with giant gastric folds, predominantly in the fundus and body of the stomach. Histologically, there is hyperplasia of the gastric pits, gland atrophy and an increase in overall mucosal thickness. Hypochlorhydria is usually present, sometimes with no gastric acid production seen at all in advanced cases. Clinically, affected people often complain of epigastric pain, whilst protein loss from the gastric mucosa can result in mild hypoalbuminemia. The treatment and time course of the disease is unclear: some patients spontaneously, whereas in others this can be a premalignant state. Antisecretory drugs such as proton pump inhibitors may be tried for symptom relief.

Autoimmune gastritis
Autoimmune gastritis is incorrect as the negative autoantibody screen is negative, which makes this diagnosis unlikely. Furthermore, autoimmune gastritis is typically associated with histology showing widespread atrophic gastritis, which is not what is found here.

Bacterial overgrowth syndrome
Bacterial overgrowth syndrome is incorrect as this man has no obvious risk factors for bacterial overgrowth, and his symptoms would be very atypical. No breath test results are given that might support this diagnosis.

Duodenal reflux
Duodenal reflux is incorrect as duodenal reflux (also called ‘biliary reflux’) may certainly cause upper abdominal pain, but would not be consistent with either the low albumin levels or the gastric histology findings identified here.

Helicobacter pylori
Helicobacter pylori is incorrect as this man has a negative CLO test, and there is no sign of bacterial organisms on his gastric histology. As such, Helicobacter pylori infection is very unlikely.

stem: A 61-year-old man was referred for further investigation of malabsorption and villous atrophy found on duodenal biopsy. His coeliac serology was negative and his symptoms failed to on a gluten-free diet. He was investigated for possible Whipple’s disease. Which of the following statements about Whipple’s disease is correct?
options: Neurologic involvement always responds to antibiotic treatment
Periodic acid–Schiff-staining granules are seen in the macrophages
The causative organism is a Gram-negative coccus
explanation:
Periodic acid–Schiff-staining granules are seen in the macrophages
Whipple’s disease is an infective disease that may involve multiple organ systems, but which particularly affects the gastrointestinal tract. It is caused by Tropheryma whipplei; this bacterium has an equivocal Gram stain result on staining and has a bacillus-like morphology. The clinical features that may occur are diverse, and include depression, ophthalmoplegia, arthropathy, encephalitis, arthritis, and cardiac, cerebral and lung involvement. Most lesions (except cerebral lesions) are reversible on prolonged antibiotic therapy, but lifelong follow-up is mandatory as relapses do occur. The typical gastrointestinal features of the condition include bloating, abdominal discomfort, weight loss and diarrhoea. These are caused by small-bowel malabsorption related to infection of the small bowel by the causative bacterium. Diagnosis may be made by endoscopy and biopsy from the duodenum or jejunum; villous atrophy is a typical appearance, along with macrophages full of PAS-positive (periodic acid–Schiff) material.

Neurologic involvement always responds to antibiotic treatment
Most lesions (except cerebral lesions) are reversible on prolonged antibiotic therapy. Central nervous system symptoms can be irreversible.

It typically affects middle-aged women
It typically affects middle-aged women is incorrect. It most typically affects middle-aged white men.

Recurrence after treatment is rare
Recurrence after treatment is rare is incorrect. Lifelong follow-up is mandatory as relapses do occur as outlined. Whipple’s Disease A 34-year-old man, originally from Pakistan, was admitted with ascites and weight loss. The protein level on ascitic tap was 18 g/l.

The causative organism is a Gram-negative coccus
The causative organism is a Gram-negative coccus is incorrect. As described T. whipplei has a bacillus-like morphology.

stem: Which of the following is the investigation most likely to reveal the underlying cause of his symptoms?
explanation:
Ferritin
This patient has signs and symptoms consistent with haemachromatosis. This includes the raised glucose, subtle signs of chronic liver disease (palmar erythema, spider naevi, raised ALT), joint pains, possibly indicating chondrocalcinosis, and loss of libido consistent with decreased testosterone. Haemachromatosis can also affect the heart. The initial test to perform is a ferritin, with subsequent tests to confirm the diagnosis including a transferrin and genetic analysis to identify the HFE gene.

Dexamethasone suppression test
A dexamethasone suppression test is used to identify Cushing's disease, in which there is an excess of cortisol. This condition can account for the diabetic symptoms but not the joint pain or liver cirrhosis and thus is not the unifying diagnosis.

Fasting blood glucose
A fasting blood glucose can confirm the presence of diabetes which this patient is likely to have because of haemachromatosis, but it cannot account for his other symptom.

Caeruloplasmin
A reduced caeruloplasmin can be found in Wilson’s disease, a rare autosomal recessive disorder characterised by the accumulation of copper in the liver, basal ganglia, eyes and other organs. Symptoms can include neurological dysfunction, symptoms related to liver cirrhosis and kayser fleischer rings in the eyes.

Parathyroid hormone
Parathyroid hormone (PTH) regulates serum calcium and phosphate. This patient has a normal calcium so PTH would not be a useful test here Hereditary Haemochromatosis A 57-year-old man presented with a history of persistent heartburn. He had seen his general practitioner about this on several occasions and had now been referred to the gastroenterology clinic for further evaluation. A trial of low-dose proton-pump inhibitor (PPI) and lifestyle measures had failed to alleviate his symptoms. Screening blood test results were unremarkable, with no evidence of anaemia. He subsequently underwent an upper gastrointestinal endoscopy; this revealed an abnormally high junction between the columnar epithelium of the stomach and the oesophageal squamous epithelium, with fronds of columnar epithelium extending up into the oesophagus, consistent with Barrett’s oesophagus.

stem: A 57-year-old man presented with a history of persistent heartburn. He had seen his general practitioner about this on several occasions and had now been referred to the gastroenterology clinic for further evaluation. A trial of low-dose proton-pump inhibitor (PPI) and lifestyle measures had failed to alleviate his symptoms. Screening blood test results were unremarkable, with no evidence of anaemia. He subsequently underwent an upper gastrointestinal endoscopy; this revealed an abnormally high junction between the columnar epithelium of the stomach and the oesophageal squamous epithelium, with fronds of columnar epithelium extending up into the oesophagus, consistent with Barrett’s oesophagus. Which of the following is correct about this man?
options: Continuous low-dose PPI therapy would be appropriate in this case
He has a 30–50 times increased risk of adenocarcinoma of the oesophagus compared with someone
He has a 30–50 times increased risk of carcinoma of the stomach
He has a 30–50 times increased risk of squamous-cell carcinoma of the oesophagus compared with
He has no increased risk of carcinoma
explanation:
He has a 30–50 times increased risk of adenocarcinoma of the oesophagus compared with someone
He has a 30–50 times increased risk of adenocarcinoma of the oesophagus compared with someone without Barrett’s oesophagus Barrett’s oesophagus is attributable to columnar metaplasia of the oesophageal epithelium and is associated with a greatly increased risk of oesophageal adenocarcinoma. It is thought to develop as a result of chronic severe reflux disease. There is a 4:1 male to female ratio, with peak presentation at 55–60 years. The condition occurs more frequently in white populations, and has on average a prevalence of 9.6% in patients undergoing endoscopy. Barrett’s oesophagus may be asymptomatic, or can be discovered during investigations for chest pain, heartburn or occasional dysphagia to solids. The differential diagnosis includes uncomplicated gastrooesophageal reflux disease (GORD), gastritis, hiatus hernia, benign oesophageal stricture and malignancy. All affected patients should be on long-term, high-dose proton-pump inhibitors (PPIs), as these may prevent progression to malignancy. Endoscopic treatment of Barrett’s (such as with radiofrequency ablation, or with endomucosal resection) may be indicated where dysplasia occurs. Regular endoscopic surveillance of Barrett’s is required, with the frequency of surveillance dependent upon the degree of dysplasia on histology. In total, around 500 new oesophageal adenocarcinomas per year develop per 100 000 patients with Barrett’s oesophagus.

Continuous low-dose PPI therapy would be appropriate in this case
Continuous low-dose PPI therapy would be appropriate in this case is incorrect. High-dose (rather than lowdose) PPI is preferred as the treatment for people with Barrett’s oesphagus.

He has a 30–50 times increased risk of carcinoma of the stomach
He has a 30–50 times increased risk of carcinoma of the stomach is incorrect. Barrett’s oesophagus has no significant association with gastric cancer.

He has a 30–50 times increased risk of squamous-cell carcinoma of the oesophagus compared with
He has a 30–50 times increased risk of squamous-cell carcinoma of the oesophagus compared with someone without Barrett’s oesophagus He has a 30–50 times increased risk of squamous-cell carcinoma of the oesophagus compared with someone without Barrett’s oesophagus is incorrect. Barrett’s oesophagus has no significant association with squamouscell carcinoma of the oesophagus.

He has no increased risk of carcinoma
He has no increased risk of carcinoma is incorrect. This option is clearly incorrect because of the increased risk of oesophageal adenocarcinoma. Oesophageal Tumours A 56-year-old man with polycythaemia rubra vera is admitted with acute abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting and abdominal distension. He is apyrexial, with tender hepatomegaly and ascites. An ascitic tap reveals fluid with a high serum ascites albumin gradient (SAAG) and no organisms.

stem: A 56-year-old man with polycythaemia rubra vera is admitted with acute abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting and abdominal distension. He is apyrexial, with tender hepatomegaly and ascites. An ascitic tap reveals fluid with a high serum ascites albumin gradient (SAAG) and no organisms. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Budd–Chiari syndrome
Budd–Chiari syndrome occurs following obstruction to the venous outflow system of the liver due to occlusion of the hepatic vein. In approximately one-third of patients with the condition, the cause is unknown. Patients with hypercoagulable states (such as polycythaemia or leukaemia) and women taking the oral contraceptive pill are at increased risk. The syndrome may present as either an acute or chronic form. Typical symptoms in the acute form include abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, tender hepatomegaly and ascites. Liver histology shows centrilobular congestion with hepatocyte atrophy. The chronic form presents with hepatomegaly, mild jaundice, ascites and splenomegaly with portal hypertension.

Haemochromatosis
Haemochromatosis is incorrect. Haemochromatosis (as well as other infiltrative diseases) may explain hepatomegaly, although this would not typically be associated with the other symptoms described. It is recognised that haemochromatosis may cause chronic liver disease, but one would expect other symptoms such as tanned skin and diabetes.

Malignant liver disease
Malignant liver disease is incorrect. Malignant liver disease may explain ascites with a high protein count, but it is unlikely to present as such an acute syndrome until very late in the disease process. In addition, no information is given regarding a cancer that may have metastasised to the liver, or of risk factors for chronic liver disease that may cause a hepatocellular carcinoma.

Mesenteric artery occlusion
Mesenteric artery occlusion is incorrect. Mesenteric ischaemia can present with acute abdominal pain and vomiting, but the constellation of tender hepatomegaly and ascites is much more suggestive of venous outflow obstruction than arterial insufficiency. Portal Hypertension

Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis
Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis is incorrect. Although the symptoms described and the presence of ascites with a high protein count are consistent with spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP), other features in the scenario do not fit with this diagnosis. Specifically, a high neutrophil count (> 250 neutrophils/mm3) and organisms on ascitic fluid culture would be expected (and sometimes a fever), but none of these is described here. In addition, tender hepatomegaly is not a typical feature of SBP.

stem: A 34-year-old man, originally from Pakistan, was admitted with ascites and weight loss. The protein level on ascitic tap was 18 g/l. What is the most likely cause of the ascites?
explanation:
Hepatic cirrhosis
Of the options given, only cirrhosis is associated with transudative ascites. All of the other options given typically cause exudates. Although the exact cut-off of ascitic fluid protein level used to define an exudate or transudate is influenced by the patient’s plasma albumin level, this man’s ascitic fluid protein level is so low that a transudate seems extremely likely. Causes of a transudate (protein < 30 g/l, assuming a normal albumin level): Hepatic cirrhosis Right-sided cardiac failure Hypoalbuminaemia (nephrotic syndrome) Acute nephritis Budd–Chiari syndrome Causes of an exudate (protein > 30 g/l): Infection (tuberculosis, spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, etc) Inflammation (vasculitis, pancreatitis, etc) Malignancy

Intra-abdominal malignancy
Intra-abdominal malignancy is incorrect. As described this would typically cause exudates.

Liver metastases
Liver metastases is incorrect. As described this would typically cause exudates.

Peritoneal lymphoma
Peritoneal lymphoma is incorrect. As described this would typically cause exudates. Ascites

Tuberculous peritonitis
Tuberculous peritonitis is incorrect. As described this would typically cause exudates.

stem: A 47-year-old man presents to the General Practitioner, complaining of unquenchable thirst and a need to empty his bladder more frequently at night. He has no significant past medical history of note. His random blood glucose is 11.7 mmol/L. Given the likely diagnosis, which of the following foods should be avoided as far as possible to help manage symptoms?
explanation:
Cornflakes
This patient has type II diabetes. The glycaemic index is a measure of a food’s ability to raise blood sugar levels. Indexing is achieved by comparing a food’s digestion rate with that of glucose (which has a glycaemic index of 100); the higher the glycaemic index, the faster the food will enter the bloodstream and raise the blood glucose level. Of the options given, cornflakes have the highest glycaemic index (84); the other foods listed as options all have a somewhat lower glycaemic index: banana, 50; carrot, 49; yoghurt, 33; and peanuts 14.

Banana
This patient has a likely diagnosis of type II diabetes based on his age and current symptoms. He appears to be hyperglycaemic and needs to control his blood sugar. Bananas have a glycaemic index score of 50, whereas cornflakes have a score of 84.

Carrots
Carrots have a moderate glycaemic index score of 49, whereas cornflakes have a score of 84. Patients with type II diabetes are able to control symptoms with a healthy diet and are encourages to each a wide range of foods including fruit and vegetables.

Peanuts
Peanuts have a relatively low glycaemic index score of 14, so do not need to be actively avoided. Peanuts should be consumed in moderation, especially if they are flavoured. Diabetes - Type II

Natural unsweetened yoghurt
Natural unsweetened yoghurt has a glycaemic score of 33 which is considered low, whereas cornflakes have a score of 84.

stem: A 60-year-old man with coronary artery disease was found to have gallstones on routine abdominal ultrasonography. He had no history of biliary colic or jaundice. What is the best treatment for this patient?
explanation:
No treatment
The answer is No treatment (Option D). Therapeutic intervention is not required for a patient with asymptomatic cholelithiasis. Less than 25% of patients with asymptomatic cholelithiasis will develop symptoms that require intervention over a 5-year followup period.

Endoscopic removal of stones
Endoscopic removal of stones (such as via endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography [ERCP]) (Option A) is incorrect. Endoscopic removal of gallstones is indicated for acute complications of stone disease, specifically cholangitis and/or pancreatitis related to stones in the biliary tree; however, ERCP is not indicated for people with gallbladder stones without complications.

Laparoscopic cholecystectomy
Cholecystectomy (Option B) is indicated for people with frequent gallstone-related problems, such as recurrent biliary colic or cholecystitis. It is typically performed laparoscopically, although open procedures may still be required in complex cases. However, cholecystectomy is not appropriate for people without any gallstonerelated complications.

Lithotripsy
Lithotripsy (Option C) is not useful for gallstone disease, because gallstones (in contrast to ureteric calculi) contain very little calcium, so are not fragmented by this technique. Gallstones and

Open cholecystectomy
Cholecystectomy (Option E) is indicated for people with frequent gallstone-related problems, such as recurrent biliary colic or cholecystitis. It is typically performed laparoscopically, although open procedures may still be required in complex cases. However, cholecystectomy is not appropriate for people without any gallstonerelated complications.

stem: Which of the following is the investigation most useful in determining the diagnosis?
explanation:
Unconjugated bilirubin
The most likely diagnosis here is Gilbert’s syndrome, caused by reduced glucuronyltransferase activity. This leads to elevated unconjugated bilirubin. Mild jaundice can be precipitated by stress, a period of fasting, or acute infection, (as here). The patient should be encouraged to begin eating again if possible, jaundice resolves without the need for intervention.

Hepatitis serology
Hepatitis serology is incorrect. Given that transaminases and alkaline phosphatase are in the normal range, viral hepatitis is very unlikely.

Liver biopsy
Liver biopsy is incorrect. The two previous episodes of jaundice, coupled with normal liver function tests (LFTs) apart from bilirubin, count much more towards a diagnosis of Gilbert’s syndrome, for which liver biopsy isn’t indicated.

MRI liver
MRI liver is incorrect. Liver architecture remains normal in Gilbert’s syndrome, there is therefore no indication to progress to MRI. Gilbert SyndromeA 44-year-old alcoholic man is admitted to the Emergency Department with increased abdominal distension, confusion and drowsiness. He continues to drink 4-6 pints of strong lager per day and is poorly compliant with his medication. On examination his GCS is 12. BP is 95/60 mmHg, pulse is 85/min and irregular and his temperature is 38.2 °C. There are signs of chronic liver disease, including significant ascites. An ascitic tap reveals 550 cells/microlitre.

Reticulocytes
Reticulocytes is incorrect. Haemoglobin is in the normal range, which counts against significant haemolysis taking place.

stem: A 65-year-old woman was referred with dysphagia. Which of the following findings would be most useful in supporting a diagnosis of a connective tissue disorder?
explanation:
Raynaud’s phenomenon
The occurrence of dysphagia together with Raynaud’s phenomenon is very suggestive of an underlying connective tissue disorder, and particularly CREST syndrome (Calcinosis cutis, Raynaud’s phenomenon, oEsophageal hypomotility, Sclerodactyly and Telangiectasia) or progressive systemic sclerosis. None of the other options given would strongly suggest underlying connective tissue disorders.

Cerebellar ataxia
Cerebellar ataxia is incorrect. Cerebellar disease may be associated with dysarthria, but not with dysphagia.

Cogwheel tremor
Cogwheel tremor is incorrect. Cogwheel tremor would be consistent with Parkinson’s disease. Parkinson’s is often associated with impaired bulbar function causing speech and respiratory dysfunction (dysphonia, stridor, sleep apnoea etc), but not typically dysphagia.

Iron-deficiency anaemia
Iron-deficiency anaemia is incorrect. Iron-deficiency anaemia together with dysphagia often merits gastroscopy to assess for serious structural causes of dysphagia (eg oesophageal carcinoma). One rare explanation could be Plummer–Vinson syndrome, a condition of unclear aetiology that is characterised by the the combination of iron-deficiency anaemia and oesophageal web; this occurs particularly in middle-aged women.

Left hemiparesis
Left hemiparesis is incorrect. Hemiparesis may represent previous stroke and is often associated with impaired bulbar function causing speech and respiratory dysfunction (dysphonia, stridor, sleep apnoea, etc), but not typically dysphagia.

stem: A 45-year-old woman with ulcerative colitis is admitted with a history of jaundice, pruritus and intermittent abdominal pain. Examination shows hepatosplenomegaly and mild ascites. Blood tests confirm an obstructive jaundice, and anti-mitochondrial antibodies are not detected. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Sclerosing cholangitis
This patient has inflammatory bowel disease and is therefore at risk of developing sclerosing cholangitis. This results from inflammation and fibrosis of the bile ducts, which leads to the formation of multiple areas of narrowing throughout the biliary system. Patients with HIV with low CD4 counts may also develop sclerosing cholangitis. Affected patients can be asymptomatic or can present with jaundice, pruritus and intermittent abdominal pain. The alkaline phosphatase level will be raised and anti-mitochondrial antibody is not detectable (in contrast to primary biliary cholangitis (PBC)). Liver biopsy will show fibrous obliterative cholangitis with loss of interlobular and adjacent septal bile ducts. Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) will demonstrate the multiple strictures. Affected patients require close surveillance for the development of cholangiocarcinoma and colonic carcinoma, along with surveillance for hepatocellular carcinoma if chronic liver disease develops. There are no specific medical therapies; liver transplantation may be required in the most severe cases.

Chronic active hepatitis
Chronic active hepatitis is incorrect. This patient’s blood tests show an obstructive picture with no mention of raised transaminases, so chronic active hepatitis is not the most likely diagnosis.

Liver cirrhosis
Liver cirrhosis is incorrect. Although early chronic liver disease may be associated with hepatomegaly, cirrhosis is often associated with a shrunken liver, meaning it is unlikely to be the diagnosis here.

Metastatic carcinoma
Metastatic carcinoma is incorrect. Metastatic carcinoma with malignant infiltration of the liver may cause hepatomegaly, cholestatic liver enzymes, abdominal pain and ascites, but the description of splenomegaly would not be typically consistent with this diagnosis.

Pancreatic carcinoma
Pancreatic carcinoma is incorrect. On a similar note, although a cancer of the head of the pancreas may present with obstructive jaundice (often painlessly, with tumours more distally in the pancreas often first presenting with abdominal pain), pancreatic carcinomas are not a typical cause of hepatosplenomegaly.

stem: A 77-year-old man presents with facial flushing, diarrhoea, weight loss and leg oedema. He reports a recent gradual worsening in his breathing. On examination, he has a bilateral wheeze and a palpable liver. Ultrasound shows multiple lesions within the liver. What test is most likely to reveal the cause of his symptoms?
options: Computed tomography scan of the abdomen
explanation:
Urinary 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid
The features described within this scenario are very suggestive of this man having carcinoid syndrome. Carcinoid tumours are found in 1–2% of resected appendixes and in ~25% of individuals at postmortem. However, they typically only present clinically in the following scenarios: Metastasis to the liver – replacement of the normal liver parenchyma with metastatic lesions means that there is no first-pass metabolism of 5-hydroxytryptamine (5-HT, serotonin), bradykinins and histamine, the chemicals responsible for causing the features of the carcinoid syndrome as they enter the systemic circulation. Acute appendicitis – due to obstruction of the lumen by the carcinoid tumour.
