Pellagra syndrome (the ‘three Ds’ – diarrhoea, dermatitis and dementia) – due to nicotinic acid deficiency (carcinoid tumours utilise tryptophan, a nicotinamide precursor). Carcinoid tumours may also cause right-sided cardiac valve lesions, which lead to peripheral oedema. Other symptoms associated with carcinoids include wheeze, flushing, diarrhoea and weight loss. Urinary 5-hyroxyindoleacetic acid (5-HIAA) levels are typically very elevated in carcinoid syndrome, so this is the best test here.

Colonoscopy
Colonoscopy is incorrect. Most gastrointestinal tract carcinoid tumours are within the small bowel, so a normal colonoscopy would not be helpful for ruling out the presence of a GI carcinoid tumour.

Computed tomography scan of the abdomen
Computed tomography scan of the abdomen is incorrect. Carcinoid tumours may be variable in size and location (with approximately 30% of them occurring within the lungs), so a CT scan of the abdomen would not necessarily demonstrate the tumour.

Fasting serum gastrin
Fasting serum gastrin is incorrect. Fasting serum gastrin levels may be very elevated in people with gastrinoma (another form of neuroendocrine tumour), but not in carcinoid syndrome.

Urinary catecholamines
Urinary catecholamines is incorrect. Urinary catecholamines are a useful test in people with suspected phaeochromocytoma and paraganglionoma, but levels would not be expected to be raised in those with carcinoid syndrome.

stem: A 24-year-old student presented with bloody diarrhoea. She described passing up to 12 motions per day for the past 2–3 weeks, but had now attended the Emergency Department after also developing abdominal pain and distension. On examination, she was dehydrated, with a clearly distended, tender abdomen. Blood test results showed anaemia with raised plasma viscosity, potassium that was mildly decreased at 3.2 mmol/l, and a raised urea in keeping with the dehydration. Liver function testing revealed a decreased albumin level. An autoantibody screen was positive for perinuclear antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (pANCA). Sigmoidoscopy demonstrated a friable mucosa with a uniform pattern of inflammation and loss of normal mucosa. Stool culture was negative. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Ulcerative colitis
The scenario given is typical for a first presentation of ulcerative colitis (UC). Although GI symptoms tend to predominate, extra-intestinal manifestations of UC may also occur, such as arthropathy, uveitis and pyoderma gangrenosum. The annual incidence of ulcerative colitis is 50–150 cases/100 000 of the population, with the most common age at presentation being between 14 and 38 years. Perinuclear antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (pANCA) is positive in 45% of cases. General management of acute severe ulcerative colitis includes correction of dehydration and subcutaneous heparin, given the increased risk of venous thromboembolism. The mainstay of medical management in this scenario is intravenous hydrocortisone, with 5-aminosalicylic acid compounds (such as mesalazine) often used as an ‘add-on’ therapy. For patients with acute severe ulcerative colitis not responding sufficiently to intravenous steroids, other options for medical therapy include intravenous ciclosporin or intravenous infliximab; however, between 15 and 20% of patients with the condition fail to respond to any medical therapy, and eventually require colectomy.

Coeliac disease
Coeliac disease is incorrect. Coeliac disease is certainly on the list of differential diagnoses of a young patient with diarrhoea, but would not result in an acute illness such as this. Furthermore, the information from the sigmoidoscopy that this woman has colitis means that this is much more likely to be the cause of her symptoms than a small bowel malabsorptive condition like coeliac disease.

Crohn’s disease
Crohn’s disease is incorrect. Crohn’s disease may affect anywhere in the entire GI tract, and is associated with skip lesions; the sigmoidoscopy findings of a uniform pattern of inflammation within the distal colon are much more typical of ulcerative colitis. In addition, a positive pANCA tends to be found more consistently in UC than Crohn’s disease.

Diverticulitis
Diverticulitis is incorrect. Diverticulitis may present as an acute illness with similar symptoms to that described, but much more commonly occurs in middle-aged and older people than in people of this age. Furthermore, diverticular disease has no association with pANCA, again making it unlikely to be the diagnosis here.

Ischaemic colitis
Ischaemic colitis is incorrect. Although the symptoms described might fit with ischaemic colitis, this condition typically occurs in older people with clear risk factors for/previous vascular disease, including atrial fibrillation (which increases the risk of thromboembolism), hypertension, dyslipidaemia, previous ischaemic heart disease or stroke, and so on. The absence of such any such relevant history and this woman’s young age both mean that ischaemic colitis is unlikely. Ulcerative Colitis A 24-year-old man presented to his general practitioner with a nodular rash over his shins, which was dusky blue in appearance at first but had later faded to a bruise-like appearance. His past history included intermittent diarrhoea, occasionally with blood. There was no other past history of note. On examination, there was minor tenderness on the left side of his abdomen, and proctoscopy demonstrated moderate inflammation of the rectum. Blood test results revealed a raised C-reactive protein (CRP) and a normochromic normocytic anaemia.

stem: A 24-year-old man presented to his general practitioner with a nodular rash over his shins, which was dusky blue in appearance at first but had later faded to a bruise-like appearance. His past history included intermittent diarrhoea, occasionally with blood. There was no other past history of note. On examination, there was minor tenderness on the left side of his abdomen, and proctoscopy demonstrated moderate inflammation of the rectum. Blood test results revealed a raised C-reactive protein (CRP) and a normochromic normocytic anaemia. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Ulcerative colitis
The combination in a young person of intermittent bloody diarrhoea, proctitis and a rash that is very suggestive of erythema nodosum is together very suggestive of ulcerative colitis. Ulcerative colitis has an annual incidence of 50–150/100 000 of the population, and a peak age of incidence of 14–38 years. The typical clinical presentation is with abdominal tenderness and bloody diarrhoea, and possibly with extra-intestinal manifestations of the condition (such as back pain, uveitis or small joint polyarthritis).

Crohn’s disease
Crohn’s disease is incorrect. Crohn’s disease is the other form of inflammatory bowel disease, and could potentially explain all the features described. However, although Crohn’s disease may affect any part of the gastrointestinal tract, the most common manifestation is with disease of the ileo-caecal region, and proctitis is much more commonly a feature of ulcerative colitis than Crohn’s.

Mycoplasma infection
Mycoplasma infection is incorrect. Mycoplasma has – rarely – been associated with erythema nodosum, but would be more likely to give a clinical presentation with pneumonia than with any of the features described.

Sarcoidosis
Sarcoidosis is incorrect. Although sarcoidosis is well established as a condition associated with erythema nodosum, the symptoms described in this scenario are not characteristic of sarcoidosis, with the lack of typical features of the condition (in particular, the lack of respiratory symptoms) making this option unlikely.

Tuberculosis
Tuberculosis is incorrect. Although tuberculosis is well established as a condition associated with erythema nodosum, the symptoms described in this scenario are not characteristic of tuberculosis, with the lack of typical features of the condition (in particular, the lack of respiratory symptoms) making this option unlikely. Ulcerative Colitis A 32-year-old woman with known protein C deficiency presented to the Emergency Department with a history of diarrhoea, steatorrhoea and weight loss. She suffered a Colles’ fracture some years ago. On examination, there is an old, healed, midline abdominal scar. Blood tests demonstrate anaemia with an increased red cell distribution width, a serum calcium level just below the lower limit of normal, and a normal CRP.

stem: A 27-year-old woman attended for review. She had a past history of perianal abscess but nothing else of note. During the past few months, she had twice presented to the Emergency Department complaining of abdominal pain. In addition, she had experienced intermittent episodes of bloody diarrhoea. Blood tests revealed microcytic anaemia and mild hypokalaemia. Her albumin level was reduced, but other liver function tests were unremarkable. Barium imaging demonstrated a small-bowel stricture with evidence of mucosal ulceration extending into the colon, interspersed with normal-looking mucosa. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Crohn’s disease
This scenario is highly suggestive of active Crohn’s disease. Crohn’s disease has a prevalence of around 1 in 1000, and is most commonly seen in people of white European or Jewish descent. Although the intestinal features of the condition are the most recognisable, extra-intestinal manifestations that may be present at diagnosis include small-joint seronegative polyarthritis, erythema nodosum, clubbing and sacroiliitis. Crohn’s disease may affect anywhere within the GI tract, and can result in gut inflammation, strictures and fistulae. The disease is characterised by ‘skip lesions’, that is, inflamed areas interspersed by areas that are apparently completely unaffected. Endoscopic features of Crohn’s include asymmetric disease, deep longitudinal fissuring, a cobblestone appearance and the presence of strictures. Histologically, there is involvement of the full thickness of the intestinal wall; in addition, crypt distortion is common, and granulomas are sometimes seen.

Coeliac disease
Coeliac disease is incorrect. Coeliac disease causes malabsorption from the proximal small bowel; as such, it could explain diarrhoea and anaemia, but not any of the other clinical findings described.

Small-bowel lymphoma
Small-bowel lymphoma is incorrect. A small-bowel lymphoma may cause a very variable spectrum of GI symptoms, and could result in an intestinal mass that may narrow or obstruct the gut lumen. However, it would not be typical of a small-bowel lymphoma to cause a small bowel stricture and mucosal ulceration, making this unlikely to be the diagnosis here.

Tropical sprue
Tropical sprue is incorrect. Tropical sprue is a small-bowel malabsorptive disease that is contracted in particular regions of the world; this woman has no obvious relevant travel history, and intestinal strictures are not a feature of the condition, making this also unlikely to be the diagnosis. Crohn’s Disease Which one of these statements about irritable bowel syndrome is correct?

Ulcerative colitis
Ulcerative colitis is incorrect. Although the symptoms and laboratory tests findings described could potentially be explained in a young woman by a diagnosis of ulcerative colitis, the presence of a small-bowel stricture rules this out as a possibility. More specifically, ulcerative colitis only affects the colon (unlike Crohn’s, which affects the whole GI tract), and is not associated with intestinal structuring (again, in contrast to Crohn’s disease).

stem: An 18-year-old student – who had just returned from a gap-year trip to India – presented to the Emergency Department. He reported profound tiredness and a lack of appetite for the last week of his travels, and had noticed that he had developed jaundice just before he was due to return home. He had previously also felt feverish, but this appeared to have subsided once the jaundice appeared. He denied any sexual contacts while abroad. He did not have a blood transfusion or any tattoos during his trip, and denied ever using recreational drugs. Blood tests revealed an alanine aminotransferase (ALT) of 950 U/l, bilirubin of 240 μmol/l and an elevated alkaline phosphatase that was just outside the upper limit of normal. White blood cell count, albumin level and prothrombin time were all normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Hepatitis A
This young man’s history is highly suggestive of hepatitis A, with typical features of fever, anorexia and malaise that subside at the onset of jaundice. The incubation period of hepatitis A is approximately 14–28 days, and the infection is very prevalent in India. Anti-hepatitis A IgM antibody will confirm the diagnosis (IgG antibody would suggest a previous hepatitis A infection, or another underlying cause such as hepatitis E). Treatment is conservative. Cholestasis is only prolonged in rare cases, and fatal fulminant hepatitis is thought to occur in less than 0.1% of patients.

Cytomegalovirus
Cytomegalovirus is incorrect. Cytomegalovirus (CMV)-associated hepatitis is rare in people who are immunocompetent, and certainly would be much less likely to be the diagnosis than hepatitis A in this scenario.

Hepatitis B
Hepatitis B is incorrect. Hepatitis B is spread through blood contact, and is also sexually transmitted; this man has no obvious risk factors for either infection route.

Hepatitis C
Hepatitis C is incorrect. Hepatitis C is spread through blood contact; this man has no obvious risk factors for infection. Viral Hepatitis

Leptospirosis
Leptospirosis is incorrect. Leptospirosis usually occurs with a history of exposure to rat-infested water, which does not seem to be likely in this scenario.

stem: A 32-year-old man presents with abdominal pain, bloating and nausea after meals. He says that he has lost 10 kg in weight over the last 3 months and also has had some non-blood-stained diarrhoea. He smokes 30 cigarettes per day but does not drink alcohol. His plain abdominal X-ray demonstrates dilated loops of small bowel. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Crohn’s disease
The features described are suggestive of a small-bowel stricture. This, together with the diarrhoea, supports a diagnosis of inflammatory bowel disease; ulcerative colitis only affects the large bowel, but this scenario would fit well with small-bowel Crohn’s disease. In addition, Crohn’s disease is more common and severe in smokers (in contrast to ulcerative colitis, which is less common in smokers).

Coeliac disease
Coeliac disease is incorrect. Uncomplicated coeliac disease does not cause strictures, but may be associated with ulcerating jejunitis or small bowel lymphoma, which could present in this way; however, these are uncommon complications of coeliac disease, and are not the most likely cause of the symptoms described here.

Giardiasis
Giardiasis is incorrect. Giardiasis may cause diarrhoea, some weight loss, and occasional bloating and abdominal pain, but could not explain dilated loops of small bowel.

Pancreatic insufficiency
Pancreatic insufficiency is incorrect. Chronic pancreatitis and pancreatic insufficiency could explain some of the symptoms outlined here, but would not be a cause of small-bowel obstruction. Crohn’s Disease A 72-year-old patient had hepatocellular carcinoma.

Small-bowel adenocarcinoma
Small-bowel adenocarcinoma is incorrect. Small-bowel adenocarcinoma would be a differential diagnosis in this scenario, but is much rarer than Crohn’s disease.

stem: A 44-year-old publican was admitted from the Emergency Department. His wife said that he had been confused for around 24–48 h. On examination, there were obvious signs of chronic liver disease, as well as nystagmus and cerebellar ataxia. He was clearly confused and disorientated. Investigations showed an abnormal alanine aminotransferase (ALT), mildly raised bilirubin levels and an alkaline phosphatase level just above the upper limit of normal. His full blood count and glucose were normal. Which diagnosis fits best with this clinical picture?
explanation:
Wernicke’s encephalopathy
The combination of ophthalmoplegia, ataxia and confusion in someone who seems likely to have alcoholrelated chronic liver disease – but who lacks any specific localising neurological signs – is very suggestive of Wernicke’s encephalopathy. Only ~10% of people with Wernicke’s encephalopathy demonstrate the full ‘classic triad’ of ophthalmoplegia, ataxia and confusion, with a much larger range of neuro-psychiatric features (including visual and hearing disturbance, changes in cognition, and seizures) also occurring as part of the syndrome. Given that the condition is caused by depletion of B vitamins, it is unsurprising that the treatment of choice is thiamine supplementation; this is often initially intravenous, followed by oral supplements. Untreated, the condition may become chronic, and Korsakoff syndrome may develop.

Acute alcohol poisoning
Acute alcohol poisoning is incorrect. The history of confusion for up to 48 h would not fit with this episode being caused by acute alcohol poisoning, and this option may be ruled out.

Drug abuse
Drug abuse is incorrect. It is unlikely that any drug overdose would give the particular pattern of neurological defect described.

Subdural haematoma
Subdural haematoma is incorrect. If a history of head injury had been given, then subdural haematoma would have been an alternative diagnosis; computed tomography imaging of the brain often reveals evidence of cerebral atrophy secondary to chronic alcohol excess in patients with Wernicke’s encephalopathy.

Urinary sepsis
Urinary sepsis is incorrect. Although delirium is a well-recognised complication of urinary sepsis and could potentially explain this man’s confusion, none of the other neurological features of his illness could be explained by delirium. The lack of any description of lower urinary tract symptoms, fever or raised inflammatory markers also means that urinary sepsis is very unlikely.

stem: A 42-year-old man presents to the Gastroenterology Clinic. He complains of abdominal pain and rectal bleeding. He has a colonoscopy, at which two polyps are found and biopsied. Which of the following is most concerning for development of colon cancer?
explanation:
Serrated polyp
Serrated polyps have been recognised in the last decade as important premalignant lesions, accounting for between 15% and 30% of colorectal cancers.

Inflammatory polyp
Inflammatory polyps are benign and generally do not carry the risk of developing into colon cancer.

Hyperplastic polyps
Hyperplastic polyps are a common type of polyp in the colon and rectum. Often numerous, particularly within the rectum, they are usually small (5 mm or less) and associated with no significant risk of malignant progression.

Pedunculated polyps
The main characteristic feature of this type of polyps is their mushroom-like shape. Usually, 13% of colon polyps are pedunculated. More importantly, pedunculated polyps are easy to diagnose as they are raised out from the surface. Also, they are easy to remove in one piece from their stalk. Therefore, the risk of these becoming cancerous is low.

Tubular architecture
Polyps with histology showing a villous architecture have a higher risk of malignant transformation than those with a tubular architecture. Other histological features that suggest a high risk of malignant change include severe dysplasia and/or squamous metaplasia.

stem: A 48-year-old man comes to the hepatology clinic for review. He presents with features of cirrhosis and portal hypertension and is found to be hepatitis C-positive on further investigation with genotype 1. He has a medical history of hyperlipidaemia and alcohol abuse. On examination his BP is 122/72 mmHg, with pulse 73/min and regular. He has a number of spider naevi over his upper body and is mildly tender in the right upper quadrant. There is moderate ascites. He asks about the possibility of liver transplantation. Which of the following is a contraindication to liver transplantation?
options: Acute liver failure secondary to paracetamol toxicity
explanation:
Co-existent HIV infection with AIDS
Absolute contraindications to liver transplantation include untreated HIV, severe irreversible pulmonary disease, ongoing alcohol abuse and extrahepatic malignancy,. Relative contraindications include inadequate social support, smoking and BMI >40 kg/m 2. Some relative and absolute contraindications can be transient and/or treatable.

Previous history of alcohol abuse
Previous history of alcohol abuse is incorrect. Active alcohol abuse, and not previous alcohol abuse, is a relative contraindication.

Primary sclerosing cholangitis
Primary sclerosing cholangitis is incorrect. End-stage primary sclerosing cholangitis is an indication for liver transplant. It is the only effective treatment at present.

Hepatocellular carcinoma
Hepatocellular carcinoma is incorrect. Small hepatocellular carcinomas (with no local or extrahepatic disease) are an indication for liver transplant.

stem: A 72-year-old patient had hepatocellular carcinoma. Which of the following is the most significant feature in the epidemiology of this condition?
options: Over 80% of tumours are surgically resectable
Primary biliary cholangitis is associated with a higher incidence of hepatocellular carcinoma than
The highest incidence of the condition in the world is in Europe
The most common aetiological factor is alcohol-related cirrhosis
The risk of hepatocellular carcinoma is increased in patients with chronic hepatitis B who are e
explanation:
The risk of hepatocellular carcinoma is increased in patients with chronic hepatitis B who are e
The risk of hepatocellular carcinoma is increased in patients with chronic hepatitis B who are e antigen-positive The major risk factors for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) include all of those for chronic liver disease, including hepatitis B and C viral infection (HBV/HCV), alcohol, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) and metabolic liver disorders (including haemochromatosis). The development of HCC in people with chronic viral hepatitis is related to the integration of viral DNA into the genome of the host hepatocyte. HCC may also occur in people with chronic HBV infection without chronic liver disease, although the majority of people with HBV who develop HCC are cirrhotic. People with chronic HBV infection who are e antigen-positive have a higher probability of development of HCC than those who are e antigen-negative.

Over 80% of tumours are surgically resectable
Over 80% of tumours are surgically resectable is incorrect. Only 15–20% of cases of HCC are surgically resectable; this reflects the multicentricity, bilobar involvement, portal vein involvement and/or lymphatic infiltration that are found in many cases of the condition at the time of diagnosis.

Primary biliary cholangitis is associated with a higher incidence of hepatocellular carcinoma than
Primary biliary cholangitis is associated with a higher incidence of hepatocellular carcinoma than haemochromatosis Primary biliary cholangitis is associated with a higher incidence of hepatocellular carcinoma than haemochromatosis is incorrect since up to 30% of patients with cirrhosis due to haemochromatosis will develop primary HCC, while only a very small proportion of people with primary biliary cholangitis (PBC; previously called ‘primary biliary cirrhosis’) will have this complication. Men are affected more than women, which might account for the high incidence seen in haemochromatosis and low incidence in primary biliary cholangitis.

The highest incidence of the condition in the world is in Europe
The highest incidence of the condition in the world is in Europe is incorrect. Globally, the incidence of HCC is at its highest in East Africa and South East Asia, with disease occurrence overall much lower in Europe. This is particularly due to of the very high prevalence of chronic viral hepatitis in countries within these regions.

The most common aetiological factor is alcohol-related cirrhosis
The most common aetiological factor is alcohol-related cirrhosis is incorrect. At present, chronic HCV infection is the most common aetiological cause of HCC in many Western countries, while chronic HBV is the most common aetiological agent in developing countries; HCC in people with alcohol-related cirrhosis is seen less commonly than in people with HBV- or HCV-related chronic liver disease.

stem: A 60-year-old male civil servant reports a one year history of regular upper abdominal pain related to meals. His past medical history includes rheumatoid arthritis for which he is taking naproxen for on most days. On endoscopy, he was found to have three duodenal ulcers and a 2-cm ulcer in the fundus of the stomach. A CLO test was negative. Abdominal computed tomography shows a 4-cm mass in the head of the pancreas. Which one of the following is the most probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Gastrinoma
This patient has multiple peptic ulcers and a pancreatic mass which is likely to be a tumour, therefore the most likely diagnosis is a gastrinoma. Gastrinomas may also arise in the duodenum or gastric antrum. 60% are malignant and 25% are associated with MEN 1. The Zollinger Ellison syndrome describes the association of gastrin-producing tumours, gastric hypersecretion and severe peptic ulcer disease.

Glucagonoma
Glucagonoma is incorrect. A glucagonoma is a rare neuroendocrine tumour that develop from alpha cells of the pancreas resulting in overproduction of glucagon. Symptoms include diabetes mellitus, weight loss and anaemia. Peptic ulceration is not a recognised feature of the disorder.

H. pylori-induced peptic ulcers
H. pylori-induced peptic ulcers is incorrect. H. pylori does not tend to cause multiple ulcers, and cannot explain the pancreatic mass. The negative CLO test (which detects H.pylori) further steers us away from H.pylori as the cause.

NSAID-induced peptic ulcers
NSAID-induced peptic ulcers is incorrect. NSAIDS can induce peptic ulceration but again they do not tend to cause multiple ulcers and does not account for the presence of the pancreatic mass.

Pancreatic lymphoma
Pancreatic lymphoma is incorrect. Primary pancreatic lymphomas are very rare and make up less than 0.5% of pancreatic tumours. Presenting symptoms can include, abdominal pain, pancreatitis, nausea, weight loss and jaundice. They are not typically associated with multiple peptic ulcers.

stem: Which of the following would be the investigation of choice?
explanation:
Transferrin saturation
This man has haemochromatosis and diabetes (causing polydipsia and polyuria), pseudogout (causing joint pain), skin pigmentation, hypogonadism (with sparse body hair) and liver disease (causing spider naevi). Haemochromatosis used to be known as “bronzed diabetes”, where iron overload leads to cirrhosis, chondrocalcinosis, and diabetes mellitus. Hypogonadism also occurs, primarily due to pituitary iron deposition. Mutation screening for the two commonest mutations which cause haemochromatosis exists, and is available at a number of UK centres. Management of haemochromatosis centres on venesection.

Blood glucose
Blood glucose is incorrect because although blood glucose is likely to be elevated, it is not diagnostic and therefore the best option to diagnose the underlying condition is transferrin saturation.

Caeruloplasmin
Caeruloplasmin is incorrect. Lower than normal levels of caeruloplasmin may be a feature of Wilson’s disease.

Serum ferritin
Serum ferritin is incorrect because transferrin saturation is the diagnostic blood test of choice, as serum ferritin may be raised in alcoholic cirrhosis, and a number of inflammatory conditions. Hereditary Haemochromatosis

Urinary copper excretion
Urinary copper excretion is incorrect. Urinary copper excretion is usually increased in patients with Wilson’s disease.

stem: The GP arranges for a liver ultrasound and a liver screen. Which of the following is suggestive of Wilson's disease?
explanation:
Decreased serum caeruloplasmin
This patient has signs of chronic liver disease as suggested by the palmar erythema and deranged liver function tests. Wilson’s disease is a rare autosomal recessive disorder of copper metabolism. The process of incorporating copper into its carrier protein, caeruloplasmin, is impaired, as well as the process of copper excretion via bile. This leads to accumulation within the liver and eventually to copper deposition in various organs including the liver, brain, kidneys and cornea. Clinical features include neurological abnormalities (tremor, dysarthria, involuntary movements and eventually dementia) and either ‘fulminant’ Wilson’s disease with a presentation of acute hepatitis or a more chronic liver disease picture. A specific sign is the Kayser–Fleischer ring, which is caused by copper deposition in Descemet’s membrane in the cornea. The mainstay of treatment is with chelating agents such as D-penicillamine and trientine. Caeruloplasmin, which carries 95% of copper, is reduced in Wilson’s disease.

Increased serum copper
Increased serum copper is incorrect. The reduced caeruloplasmin means there is reduced serum copper (with the excess copper being deposited in tissues).

Polycythaemia
Polycythaemia is incorrect. Wilson’s disease is associated with anaemia and haemolysis rather than polycythaemia. This can be seen in the more advanced stages of disease.

Reduced liver copper content
Reduced liver copper content is incorrect. There is increased copper content within the liver on biopsy; the liver being one of the main organs where the copper is deposited.

Reduced urinary copper
Reduced urinary copper is incorrect. Urinary copper excretion is increased in Wilson’s. Other conditions causing elevated urinary copper levels include autoimmune hepatitis and cholestasis. Wilson’s Disease A patient with symptoms of heart-burn wants to modify his diet to reduce his symptoms. He believes he can do this by reducing secretion of gastrin.

stem: An 82-year-old woman was admitted from a nursing home with profuse diarrhoea. She had been discharged 2 weeks earlier from the orthopaedic ward, where she had had surgery for a fractured neck of femur. There was some evidence of osteomyelitis during that admission, and she was treated with clindamycin and discharged on tablets. On examination, she was drowsy and dehydrated, with lower abdominal tenderness. She soiled the bed with watery diarrhoea during the examination. Blood test results confirmed acute kidney injury. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Pseudomembranous colitis
Pseudomembranous colitis may occur in up to 10% of patients who have received a course of clindamycin. In addition, it is thought that many nursing-home residents show chronic carriage of Clostridium difficile, the causative pathogen. Sigmoidoscopy will usually reveal raised, white-yellow, exudative plaques adherent to the colonic mucosa (the pseudomembrane). The diagnosis is made either by confirming the presence of clostridium toxin in the stool, or through Clostridium difficile PCR. First-line treatment is with oral metronidazole or vancomycin for 10–14 days, accompanied by appropriate rehydration therapy; refractory/recurrent cases may be treated either by alternative antibiotics (eg fidaxomicin), or by faecal microbiota transplantation. The mortality rate is as high as 10% in the elderly.

Colonic malignancy
Colonic malignancy is incorrect. Although colonic malignancy could be a cause of diarrhoea in an elderly person, it is unlikely that this would cause such an acute and severe presentation.

Enteric parasitic infection
Enteric parasitic infection is incorrect. Although enteric parasitic infection may certainly cause severe gastroenteritis, it is unlikely that a nursing home resident would have been exposed to such a parasite.

Salmonellosis
Salmonellosis is incorrect. Salmonellosis would not be impossible here, but the osteomyelitis associated with this tends to affect the long bones, and typically occurs in patients with sickle cell disease. C.difficile and Pseudomembranous Colitis A 65-year-old publican with a history of cirrhosis was admitted in a drowsy, unkempt state from home. On examination he appeared confused. In terms of the severity of his liver disease, which of the following additional clinical features would score three points in the Child–Pugh classification?

Ulcerative colitis
Ulcerative colitis is incorrect. It would be very unusual for a first episode of ulcerative colitis to occur in a woman of this age, and other clinical features (including tenesmus and rectal bleeding) might also be expected should this be the diagnosis here.

stem: A 65-year-old publican with a history of cirrhosis was admitted in a drowsy, unkempt state from home. On examination he appeared confused. In terms of the severity of his liver disease, which of the following additional clinical features would score three points in the Child–Pugh classification?
options: Prothrombin time 4 seconds above the normal range
explanation:
Encephalopathy grade 3
The Child–Pugh classification is a method used for scoring the severity of liver disease in patients with cirrhosis (although it is not applicable to patients with primary biliary cholangitis or sclerosing cholangitis). Three points are scored for each of: encephalopathy grade 3 or 4, moderate–severe ascites, bilirubin > 50 μmol/l (NR 1–22 μmol/l), albumin < 28 g/l (NR 37–49 g/l), and prothrombin time > 6 seconds above the normal range. Two points are scored for each of: encephalopathy grade 1 or 2, mild ascites, bilirubin 34–50 μmol/l, albumin 28–35 g/l, and prothrombin time 4–6 seconds above the normal range. One point is scored for each of: no encephalopathy, absent ascites, bilirubin < 34 μmol/l, albumin > 35 g/l, and prothrombin time 1–4 seconds above the normal range. The amalgamated points score then enables patients to be grouped into Child–Pugh grade A (< 6 points), B (7–9 points) or C (> 10 points). Child–Pugh grade C classification is most highly predictive of a poor prognosis.

Albumin 29 g/l (NR 37–49 g/l)
Albumin 29 g/l (NR 37–49 g/l) is incorrect as this scores two points in the Child–Pugh classification.

Bilirubin 48 μmol/l (NR 1–22 μmol/l)
Bilirubin 48 μmol/l (NR 1–22 μmol/l) is incorrect as this scores two points in the Child–Pugh classification.

Mild ascites
Mild ascites is incorrect as this scores two points in the Child-Pugh classification. Alcoholic Liver Disease and Alcoholism

Prothrombin time 4 seconds above the normal range
Prothrombin time 4 seconds above the normal range is incorrect as this scores two points in the Child–Pugh classification.

stem: A 17-year-old man presents to the Allergy Clinic for review. He has suffered from two episodes over the past 6 months where he has presented with facial swelling and shortness of breath, without urticaria, and one episode of severe vomiting associated with abdominal pain. Examination in the clinic is entirely unremarkable. Deficiency of what protein is most likely to be responsible for his condition?
explanation:
C1 esterase inhibitorComplement C3
Complement C3 is incorrect. Increased complement activation is associated with active inflammatory conditions such as SLE.

Interferon-gamma
Interferon-gamma is incorrect. Interferon-gamma is a pro-inflammatory cytokine responsible for the innate and adaptive immune responses to viral, bacterial and protozoal infections.

Interleukin-1
Interleukin-1 is incorrect. Interleukin-1 is a pro-inflammatory cytokine most strongly associated with acute episodes of gout, and it may also be associated with accelerated cardiovascular disease.Interleukin-6
Interleukin-6 is incorrect. Interleukin-6 is a pro-inflammatory cytokine strongly associated with rheumatoid arthritis.

stem: A 26-year-old woman complains of tiredness, abdominal pain and intermittent diarrhoea with a 10-kg weight loss over a period of 6 months. She is pale and has an itchy vesicular rash on her elbows and knees. She has a microcytic, hypochromic anaemia and low ferritin and folate levels, a low serum albumin and normal free T 4, but a slightly raised thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) level. Which of the following investigations is most appropriate?
explanation:
Duodenal biopsy
This woman has symptoms, signs and a biochemical picture of malabsorption. The description of an itchy vesicular rash over extensor areas suggests dermatitis herpetiformis and this, combined with her malabsorption, are together highly suggestive of coeliac disease. Coeliac serology should be performed, although a distal duodenal biopsy is required to confirm the diagnosis definitively. She should be managed with a gluten-free diet and her iron and folate stores replenished. Coeliac disease is associated with a number of other conditions. This woman also has subclinical hypothyroidism and her thyroid antibodies should be checked. Insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus, hypothyroidism, chronic liver disease and fibrosing alveolitis are all more commonly seen in patients with coeliac disease.

Bone marrow examination
Bone marrow examination is incorrect. Although bone marrow examination may be a useful investigation for anaemia of uncertain aetiology, the clinical scenario given is much more suggestive of her anaemia representing iron malabsorption rather than primary bone marrow failure.

Colonoscopy
Colonoscopy is incorrect. Although this woman’s chronic diarrhoea might suggest that colonoscopy is appropriate, her blood tests are very suggestive of malabsorption. Malabsorption does not occur through primary large bowel disease, so a colonoscopy is unlikely to be helpful.

Schilling test
The Schilling test is incorrect. The Schilling test has been one of the classical tests used to evaluate whether vitamin B12 deficiency is caused by pernicious anaemia. However, it is performed in only very few centres now that antibody testing for anti-intrinsic factor antibodies has become so widely available. No mention is given of B12 deficiency here, so the test is unlikely to be useful.

Small-bowel follow-through
A small bowel follow-through is incorrect. Small bowel follow-through remains a useful means of looking for small bowel disease (including narrowing of the lumen in inflammation), and would be particularly useful if this woman had suspected small bowel Crohn’s disease as the cause of her diarrhoea and malabsorption. However, the typical description of dermatitis herpetiformis given here makes coeliac disease much more likely to be the diagnosis, and jejunal biopsy would therefore be the better first-line test.

stem: What is the most appropriate initial treatment plan?
options: Plain abdominal film, stool culture and intravenous antibiotics
Plain abdominal film, stool culture, sigmoidoscopy and biopsy, coonsideration of intravenous
Plain abdominal film, stool culture, sigmoidoscopy and intravenous antibiotics
explanation:
Plain abdominal film, stool culture, sigmoidoscopy and biopsy, coonsideration of intravenous
Plain abdominal film, stool culture, sigmoidoscopy and biopsy, coonsideration of intravenous corticosteroid therapy This woman presents with symptoms of an acute colitis. The major differential diagnosis is between an infective aetiology (particularly given her recent travels), or inflammatory bowel disease – most likely ulcerative colitis (UC). There are clues given that the latter is the case here. First, there is the description of a rash that sounds consistent with erythema nodosum, which is associated with UC. Second, she has had episodes of bloody diarrhoea previously, which again is consistent with a relapsing–remitting condition such as UC. A plain abdominal film is needed to rule out a toxic megacolon. Stool culture is indicated to rule out an infective cause. Sigmoidoscopy is useful to confirm the type of colitis present and to assess the severity of it however caution should be taken in acute flares for the risk of perforation. Given that intravenous corticosteroids are the mainstay of treatment of acute severe colitis, the plan that has intravenous corticosteroids in it is the best choice here. The other options are all less appropriate initial management plans, since they do not include the use of intravenous corticosteroids. Although there is an argument to be made for the administration of empirical antibiotics pending the result of a stool culture, the scenario given is more suggestive of UC than infective colitis, and withholding corticosteroids could allow a severe flare of ulcerative colitis to progress.

Oral antibiotics
Oral antibiotics alone are not sufficient for this patient. This option does not address the need for diagnostic imaging to rule out complications such as toxic megacolon. It also overlooks the necessity of stool culture to identify a possible infective cause. Furthermore, this scenario is more suggestive of a UC flare-up, which requires intravenous corticosteroids for effective management. Without these additional investigations and treatments, the patient's condition could deteriorate.

Oral antibiotics and stool culture
While this option includes stool culture to rule out an infective cause, it is still incomplete. It does not address the need for a plain abdominal film to rule out toxic megacolon, which is critical in acute colitis. Moreover, oral antibiotics alone are insufficient for treating a severe flare-up of UC. The patient requires intravenous corticosteroids to manage the acute symptoms effectively and prevent further complications.

Plain abdominal film, stool culture and intravenous antibiotics
This option includes appropriate measures such as a plain abdominal film to rule out toxic megacolon and stool culture to identify any infective cause. However, it falls short by not including sigmoidoscopy, which is important for confirming the type of colitis and assessing its severity. Additionally, intravenous antibiotics might be considered if an infection is suspected, but in the context of UC, intravenous corticosteroids are crucial for managing acute severe colitis. Without corticosteroids, the patient’s condition might worsen despite the other interventions. Ulcerative Colitis

Plain abdominal film, stool culture, sigmoidoscopy and intravenous antibiotics
This option covers several important diagnostic steps, including a plain abdominal film to rule out toxic megacolon, stool culture to check for infections and sigmoidoscopy to confirm the type and severity of colitis. However, it omits the use of intravenous corticosteroids, which are essential in treating acute severe colitis. Intravenous antibiotics are not the mainstay treatment for UC and their use without corticosteroids would not adequately address the inflammatory component of the disease. The omission of corticosteroids makes this option less appropriate for managing the patient’s condition effectively.

stem: Barium swallow showed a dilated oesophagus with a tapering ‘bird’s beak’ appearance at the distal end. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Achalasia
The constellation of mixed dysphagia to both liquids and solids, regurgitation and the barium swallow result described is very typical of achalasia. Further details supportive of this diagnosis are the normal blood results picture and preserved body mass. Achalasia is a condition characterised by a hypertensive lower oesophageal sphincter that fails to relax, accompanied with a lack of peristalsis in the oesophagus and subsequent progressive oesophageal dilatation. The major options for definitively treating the condition are endoscopic pneumatic dilatation or a surgical cardiomyotomy. Other options that may be considered in less fit patients who are unable to undergo these options include botulinum toxin injection or treatment with a dihydropyridine calcium antagonist.

Barrett’s oesophagus
Barrett’s oesophagus is incorrect. Barrett’s oesophagus is associated with a range of upper gastrointestinal symptoms, but they tend to be much less marked than those described here (or may be completely asymptomatic). Furthermore, Barrett’s oesophagus in itself is unlikely to cause any mechanical obstruction of the oesophagus (even when associated with a nodule), so would not be expected to result in any abnormalities on a barium swallow.

Hiatus hernia
Hiatus hernia is incorrect. Hiatus hernia may cause chest pain and reflux, but would not typically explain dysphagia to solids and liquids. Furthermore, a barium study in those with hiatus hernia would be expected to demonstrate the tissue that is herniating through the diaphragm, but could not explain any of the features seen on the barium swallow here.

Oesophageal carcinoma
Oesophageal carcinoma is incorrect. Oesophageal carcinoma is associated with progressive dysphagia, first to solids and later to liquids; simultaneous dysphagia to both solids and liquids is much more consistent with functional oesophageal disease, such as achalasia. Weight loss is also an early prominent feature of oesophageal carcinoma, again making it less likely to be the diagnosis here. Barium swallows in those with oesophageal carcinoma will typically demonstrate an irregular lesion disrupting the oesophageal lumen. The ‘bird’s beak’ pattern described in the barium study is much more consistent with achalasia than the mechanical oesophageal obstruction that occurs with oesophageal tumours.

Severe oesophageal reflux
Severe oesophageal reflux is incorrect. Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GORD) does not typically cause dysphagia; however, in severe cases, a reflux-related benign inflammatory stricture of the lower oesophagus may occur, which could cause this symptom. Even then, it would be more typical for the dysphagia to be principally to solids, rather than to solids and liquids at the same time. Furthermore, the barium swallow result described is very typical of achalasia; in those with GORD, reflux of barium alone would be expected to be seen.

stem: A 63-year-old man presents to his GP complaining of lethargy. Blood testing reveals: Haemoglobin 101 g/l, MCV 78 f/l, hypochromic cells on blood film, low ferritin, and negative coeliac screen. He has had no symptoms of indigestion or change in bowel habit and is on no medication of note. He follows a normal diet. PR examination is normal. Which of the following would be the next most appropriate step to take in this patient?
options: Supplement with iron tablets and review hameoglobin in 6 months
explanation:
Colonoscopy
According to the BSG guidelines, upper and lower GI investigations should be considered in all postmenopausal female and all male patients where iron deficiency anaemia (IDA) has been confirmed, unless there is a history of significant overt non GI blood loss. This is done via endoscopy, and from the options presented colonoscopy would be the best choice. Ideally a patient receives a gastroscopy and colonoscopy in the same session. Colonoscopy allows for biopsy of lesions, treatment of adenomas, and identification of superficial pathology such as NSAID damage- unlike radiological investigations.

Barium enema
Barium enema is incorrect. A barium enema is not appropriate in the investigation of IDA.

CT colonography (CT ‘pneumocolon’)
CT colonography (CT ‘pneumocolon’) is incorrect. A CT colonography is not the first choice, but can be used if a patient does not tolerate the colonoscopy or cannot have sedation.

Flexible sigmoidoscopy
Flexible sigmoidoscopy is incorrect. A flexible sigmoidoscopy would miss potential lesions in the transverse colon and ascending colon. Expanded Explanation Overview Clinical Presentation Differential Diagnosis Diagnosis / Investigation Management A 43-year-old executive with right -sided abdominal pain was suspected of having gallstones.

Supplement with iron tablets and review hameoglobin in 6 months
Supplement with iron tablets and review haemoglobin in 6 months is incorrect. Establishing the underlying cause of IDA is an important step to take, before treating with iron tablets and delaying investigations.

stem: A 67-year-old man presented to the Emergency Department with epigastric and left upper quadrant pain for the third time in a year. He had suffered from diarrhoea for around 18 months, and claimed that his weight had decreased by 12.7 kg (2 stones). The paramedics who visited his accommodation noticed empty whisky bottles by the rubbish bin. His serum amylase was within the normal range. What diagnosis fits best with this clinical picture?
explanation:
Chronic pancreatitis
This scenario describes a typical description of chronic pancreatitis. Alcohol excess is the most common cause seen in practice, with other causes including pancreatic duct obstruction, malnutrition, hyperparathyroidism and certain genetic mutations (including those found in cystic fibrosis). The male to female ratio is 5:1. Typical symptoms include: Left upper quadrant and epigastric pain Significant weight loss Bulky, foul-smelling, fatty stools Epigastric mass (in 10% of patients) Jaundice (in 5–10%) In terms of investigations, serum amylase and lipase levels may be elevated, but the amylase can also be normal. Abnormal glucose tolerance or diabetes can also occur. A reduced level of fecal elastase is a useful diagnostic test. Imaging studies of the pancreas area also useful in making the diagnosis, and may include plain radiography (may reveal calcification), ultrasound, computed tomography (CT) scan, MRCP, or – rarely – ERCP. Chronic pancreatitis is a risk factor for pancreatic cancer, and the two may sometimes be difficult to differentiate on imaging; in such cases, endoscopic ultrasound (EUS) (to visualize the pancreas and to obtain histology) is particularly useful. The mainstay of management of the condition is to remove any trigger that will exacerbate the condition (i.e. alcohol). Pancreatic enzyme supplements will diarrhoea and help to treat malabsorption. Endoscopic stenting of the pancreatic duct may also have a role in treatment.

Cirrhosis
Cirrhosis is incorrect. Alcohol excess is clearly an established risk factor for cirrhosis, but would not explain this man’s abdominal pain, weight loss and diarrhoea.

Acute pancreatitis
Acute pancreatitis is incorrect. Acute pancreatitis may be caused by alcohol and may give abdominal pain in a similar area to that described in this scenario. However, this man’s normal amylase level is inconsistent with acute pancreatitis, and the chronicity of his abdominal pain, weight loss and diarrhoea are much more consistent with chronic pancreatitis.

Peptic ulcer disease
Peptic ulcer disease is incorrect. Peptic ulcer disease may cause chronic upper abdominal pain and weight loss, but would not explain this man’s diarrhoea.

Coeliac disease
Coeliac disease is incorrect. Coeliac disease may cause weight loss and diarrhoea, but is not associated with abdominal pain as described.

stem: Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy shows mild oesophagitis. Which of the following is the next most appropriate investigation?
explanation:
Computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen
The history of epigastric pain radiating to the back, which is associated with nausea and vomiting, suggests pancreatic pathology. The main differential diagnoses would be chronic pancreatitis, which is likely given the alcohol history, or pancreatic malignancy. From the options given, CT is the best modality for assessing pancreatic disease: radiological signs of chronic pancreatitis include pancreatic calcification, pancreatic duct dilatation, pancreatic atrophy and pseudocysts.

24-hour pH monitoring
24-hour pH monitoring is incorrect. 24-hour pH monitoring is used to quantify the severity of reflux disease and is not appropriate in this scenario. Even though the patient has signs of increased acid release (oesophagitis), this does not account for his abdominal symptoms and weight loss.

Colonoscopy
Colonoscopy is incorrect. There is no role for colonoscopy in assessing pancreatic disease.

Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP)
Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) is incorrect. ERCP does play a role in the management of acute gallstone pancreatitis, where obstructing gallstones may be removed. However, this is appropriate only after pancreatitis and obstructing gallstones are confirmed by means of imaging (ultrasound [US] is the best modality for detecting gallstones).

Repeat endoscopy following acid suppression
Repeat endoscopy following acid suppression is incorrect. Oesophagitis would not account for the weight loss and epigastric pain radiating to the back, and so repeating the endoscopy following acid suppression would not be useful.

stem: A 45-year-old woman is referred to the gastroenterology clinic after her GP noted her transaminases to be three times the upper limit of normal. Which of the following underlying diagnoses is most associated with progression of liver disease to hepatocellular carcinoma?
explanation:
Hepatitis C
The risk of developing hepatocellular carcinoma in a patient with active hepatitis C and cirrhosis is between 2 and 6% per year. In general hepatocellular carcinoma develops after approximately 20 years of exposure to the virus.

Hepatitis A
Hepatitis A is incorrect. Hepatitis A is a self-limiting viral infection and does not lead to chronic viraemia or increased risk of hepatocellular carcinoma.

Hepatitis E
Hepatitis E is incorrect. Like hepatitis A, hepatitis E is self limiting and does not result in increased risk of cirrhosis or hepatocellular carcinoma.

Hepatic steatosis
Hepatic steatosis is incorrect. Hepatic steatosis without fibrosis is not associated with increased risk of hepatocellular carcinoma. Patients with steatosis who develop inflammation, (steatohepatitis), may eventually develop a hepatocellular carcinoma.

Wilson’s disease
Wilson’s disease is incorrect. Wilson’s disease usually presents early and intervention with copper chelating agents significantly reduces progression to cirrhosis and thus the long term risk of hepatocellular carcinoma.

stem: A 49-year-old man is referred to the Emergency Department by his General Practitioner with a six hour history of severe abdominal pain and vomiting. His previous medical history includes an appendectomy 20 years ago. On examination, he has a distended abdomen, generalised tenderness with no features of peritonism and tinkling bowel sounds. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial investigation?
options: Computed tomography of the abdomen with constrast
explanation:
Abdominal X-ray
This patient likely has a bowel obstruction which can be confirmed with abdominal X-rays. An abdominal X-ray is quick and straightforward to obtain within the Emergency Department and will demonstrate characteristic features (including dilated bowel loops) if an intestinal obstruction is present. Features of bowel obstruction on abdominal X-ray include dilated bowel loops, gas–fluid levels, predominantly central dilated loops and valvulae conniventes being visible.

Abdominal ultrasound
Abdominal ultrasound may be difficult to visualise the intestines by ultrasound (ie because of bowel gas), so this is not a useful modality for diagnosing obstruction. Ultrasound is used more reliably to image the hepatobiliary and renal systems. Small bowel obstruction can sometimes be visualised with dilation of small bowel loops, ineffective peristalsis with the whirling appearance of intraluminal contents and the prominence of the valvulae connivances.

C-reactive protein
While C-reactive protein is a sensitive marker for inflammation/infection, it is not sensitive or specific for the diagnosis of intestinal obstruction. C-reactive protein tends to rise after 6–8 hours and peaks after 72 hours, meaning it is unlikely to be significantly raised here. C-reactive protein is an acute-phase reaction protein that is synthesised in the liver.

Computed tomography of the abdomen with constrast
Although abdominal CT is a very useful test for helping to define the cause of intestinal obstruction, it is a test with a considerable radiation load and requires administration of contrast that may cause acute kidney injury. As such, abdominal X-ray should be the initial test performed in people suspected of having intestinal obstruction, with abdominal CT reserved to provide further information for those in whom obstruction is thought highly likely.

Exploratory surgery
Exploratory surgery as a test for intestinal obstruction would clearly only be reserved for instances where other investigational modalities have been exhausted and where the diagnosis is still unclear. An exploratory laparoscopy may be the initial method, converting to a laparotomy if pathology is identified.

stem: Which of the following tests is the most appropriate next investigation?
explanation:
Anti-tissue transglutaminase antibody testing
This lady has undiagnosed coeliac disease, an autoimmune disease affecting the small bowel. It is recognised that a peak of new cases of coeliac disease occurs in pregnancy or during the post-partum period. This may reflect changes in the immune system which are associated with pregnancy. It is also increasingly recognised that occult coeliac disease is an important cause of anaemia in patients of this age group. This is because the inflammatory process causes villous atrophy, disrupting the structure and function of the small bowel, resulting in malabsorption of multiple nutrients, minerals and fat soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K). The cause of coeliac disease is thought to be multi-factorial with a strong genetic susceptibility; 95% of patients have either the HLA-DQ2 or HLA-DQ8 protein present. The symptoms of coeliac disease are very varied; common complaints are fatigue, anaemia, large volume loose stool or steatorrhoea, abdominal pain and bloating, and weight loss. Some patients also report mouth ulcers. The gastrointestinal symptoms of coeliac disease can be incorrectly labelled as irritable bowel syndrome (as in this patient). The evidence of iron deficiency anaemia in someone with this history should therefore alert you to the possible diagnosis of coeliac disease, and this should be investigated. Her vitamin B 12 and folate levels are within the lower level of normal range due to their site of absorption being affected in coeliac disease; again, this should alert you to an underlying small intestine pathology that requires further investigation. Anti-TTG antibody screening is seen as the initial screening investigation of choice for patients with possible coeliac disease. Total serum immunoglobulin A (IgA) levels should be checked in parallel as 2% of people have IgA deficiency resulting in a false negative result. In these patients, IgG-TTG should be checked. The only effective treatment for coeliac disease is a gluten free diet, which must be strictly adhered to. If untreated, it can increase the risk of intestinal lymphoma. Coeliac disease is associated with other autoimmune conditions such as type one diabetes, vitiligo, hypothyroidism and dermatitis herpetiformis; NICE recommends screening in these patients, as well in firstdegree relatives of those with confirmed coeliac disease, patients with newly diagnosed chronic fatigue syndrome and irritable bowel syndrome.

Abdominal ultrasound scan
Abdominal ultrasound scan is incorrect. Nothing in her history suggests the need for an ultrasound scan at this stage. Typically, an abdominal ultrasound is used in patients who present with focal symptoms such as right upper quadrant or right iliac fossa pain, in those with organomegaly or in patients with abnormal liver function tests.

Small bowel follow through
Small bowel follow through is incorrect. This involves the ingestion of contrast medium (normally barium or Gastrografin if there are concerns regarding possible perforation) with a series of x-rays taken at specific time periods in order to assess the gastrointestinal tract for abnormalities. Conditions where a small barium follow through may be indicated include investigation of dysphagia, pharyngeal pouch, pyloric stenosis, bowel obstruction, volvulus and diverticula. It can also be used to detect foreign bodies.

Thyroid function testing
Thyroid function tests is incorrect, although post-partum thyroiditis and autoimmune hypothyroidism are the most likely differentials. However, given there is no change in weight or other signs of hypothyroidism, this as a cause of her symptoms is much less likely.

Upper GI endoscopy
Upper GI endoscopy is incorrect. While this may be done with small bowel sampling to confirm the diagnosis, serological testing is the first line investigation for coeliac disease. It is important to note that multiple (4–8) biopsy sites are needed for confirming coeliac disease as not all areas may be equally affected. Multiple sites reduce the risk of false positives. Useful external weblinks NICE guidelines: coeliac disease www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng20/resources/coeliac-disease-recognition-assessment-and-management1837325178565.

stem: A 26-year-old schoolteacher had been diagnosed with hepatitis B infection 2 years earlier. She was now worried about whether the infection was still active. Which of the following test results is most sensitive at confirming continued viral replication?
explanation:
HBV DNA
Hepatitis B (HBV) DNA is the most sensitive index of viral replication. In people with chronic hepatitis B, HBV DNA titres may be high even if HBeAg (the traditional serological marker of high infectivity) is negative, because the patient may be infected with a hepatitis B ‘pre core’ mutant that does not produce HBeAg but which may cause severe disease.

Anti-HBe
Anti-HBe is incorrect. Anti-HBe is a marker of reduced infectivity, so does not give any information regarding viral replication.

Anti-HBs
Anti-HBs is incorrect. Anti-HBs is a serological marker of immunity against hepatitis B.

HBeAg
HBeAg is incorrect. HBeAg is a useful serological marker in people with chronic hepatitis B, and is consistent with a more highly infective state; however, it is not a sensitive marker of viral replication, unlike HBV DNA. Viral Hepatitis A 45-year-old woman presented with night sweats, right upper-quadrant abdominal pain, weight loss and anorexia. A scan revealed a liver abscess consistent with bacterial infection. Her past history of note included Crohn’s disease, which may have been a possible contributing cause. She was known to be allergic to penicillin, describing that she developed diarrhoea as a child after taking amoxicillin. Which of the following intravenous antibiotic regimens would be most appropriate as an empirical regimen?

IgM anti-HBc
IgM anti-HBc is incorrect. IgM anti-HBc is a serological test that is useful for confirming acute hepatitis B infection, but does not in any way reflect on viral replication.

stem: A 55-year-old Vietnamese businessman relocated to the UK and presented with several months of diarrhoea, anorexia and weight loss. On examination, he had some non-specific abdominal tenderness and distension. He also had a little increased pigmentation, and glossitis was noted on examining his oropharynx. Rectal examination revealed steatorrhoea. Blood tests demonstrated megaloblastic anaemia, with vitamin B12 and folate deficiencies. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Tropical sprue
The clue to the diagnosis here is that this man is a Vietnamese expatriate; South America, India and Vietnam are common areas from which tropical sprue originates. Tropical sprue may present several months after people native to tropical areas emigrate to a temperate climate. The exact aetiology is unknown, but it is thought to be infective. Clinically, the typical presentation is with diarrhoea; this represents malabsorption, and may manifest as steatorrhoea in the worst cases. Up to 50% of affected people have megaloblastic anaemia with associated vitamin B12 and folate deficiencies. Treatment usually consists of 4–6 weeks of treatment with ampicillin or tetracycline.

Chronic pancreatitis
Chronic pancreatitis is incorrect. No risk factors for chronic pancreatitis are described (e.g. alcohol excess), and there is no mention of the sort of epigastric pain that typically defines the condition.

Coeliac disease
Coeliac disease is incorrect. Although the clinical features described would fit with coeliac disease, the information that this man was originally from Vietnam makes tropical sprue more likely.

Small-bowel lymphoma
Small-bowel lymphoma is incorrect. Small-bowel lymphomas may present with a wide variety of GI features, but often cause significant abdominal pain; as no mention is made of abdominal pain, this is less likely to be the diagnosis here.

Ulcerative colitis
Ulcerative colitis is incorrect. Ulcerative colitis typically presents with bloody diarrhoea; it does not present with malabsorption (since it affects only the colon rather than the small bowel), so is not the diagnosis here. You are asked to review a 53-year-old diabetic man who has diarrhoea. He is currently taking metformin at total daily dose of 2 g/day. The diarrhoea appears to worsen with increased metformin dose.

stem: You are asked to review a 53-year-old diabetic man who has diarrhoea. He is currently taking metformin at total daily dose of 2 g/day. The diarrhoea appears to worsen with increased metformin dose. What is the most likely cause of his diarrhoea?
explanation:
Bile acid malabsorption
Biguanide medications (such as metformin) are one cause of bile acid malabsorption. Bile salts cause diarrhoea by reducing the absorption of water and electrolytes in the colon; in higher concentrations, they lead to secretion of water into the colon, and may stimulate colonic motility. Other causes of bile acid malabsorption include: Medications – ie colchicine Ileal resection/terminal ileal disease (eg Crohn’s disease) – this disrupts the enterohepatic circulation, causing excessive bile salts to enter the colon Cholecystectomy – since the gallbladder functions to concentrate bile, patients who have undergone cholecystectomy experience large quantities of bile salts entering into the small intestine, which may exceed the resorptive capacity of the terminal ileum Treatment in this case would be substitution from metformin to another drug for managing his diabetes. In other cases, cholestyramine is useful for binding to and inactivation of bile acids.

Autonomic neuropathy related to diabetes
Autonomic neuropathy related to diabetes is incorrect. Diabetic autonomic neuropathy may be a contributory factor to his diarrhoea, but the close temporal association between using metformin and the onset of his symptoms means that this is much more likely to be the major causative factor.

Osmotic diarrhoea related to ‘diabetic foods’
Osmotic diarrhoea related to ‘diabetic foods’ is incorrect. Osmotic diarrhoea may occur in diabetics who ingest too much sorbitol (a common substitute for glucose in so-called ‘diabetic foods’) and this may be a contributory factor to his diarrhoea. However, the association between commencing metformin and the onset of diarrhoea suggests that this is likely to be the cause,

Secretory diarrhoea
Secretory diarrhoea is incorrect. Secretory diarrhoea most commonly occurs in response to endotoxin-producing bacteria, (eg cholera or Escherichia coli); the chronicity of his diarrhoea makes this very unlikely to be the diagnosis.

Steatorrhoea
Steatorrhoea is incorrect. Steatorrhoea represents malabsorption (ie occurs secondary to conditions such as chronic pancreatitis, Crohn’s disease, obstructed biliary flow, coeliac disease, etc), but is not caused by Type 2 diabetes mellitus in itself, making it unlikely to be the diagnosis here.

stem: A 47-year-old publican underwent investigation because of the finding of abnormal liver function tests. Which of the following would be most suggestive of a diagnosis of chronic ongoing hepatitis?
options: A past history of hepatitis A infection
explanation:
Positive smooth muscle antibodies
The answer is Positive smooth muscle antibodies (Option D). Chronic active hepatitis has four major causes: Chronic hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection Chronic hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection Autoimmune Drugs (e.g. methyldopa, isoniazid) In autoimmune hepatitis there is a characteristic elevation of serum antibodies – including smooth muscle antibodies (SMA) (70%), anti-nuclear factor (ANF) antibodies (70%), and anti-mitochondrial antibodies (AMA) (35%). If this man had abnormal liver enzymes and positive smooth muscle antibodies, it would be very suggestive of ongoing chronic active autoimmune hepatitis; as such, option D is the correct answer here.

A past history of hepatitis A infection
Hepatitis A (Option A) is incorrect. Hepatitis A causes an acute hepatitis, varying in severity from subclinical infection right up to acute liver failure; however, it is not associated with chronic hepatitis, and option A is therefore incorrect.

Minimal alcohol ingestion
Minimal alcohol ingestion (Option B) is incorrect. Those who use alcohol excessively may experience chronic liver injury, but this man has minimal alcohol ingestion, ruling out.

On concurrent methyldopa
On concurrent methyldopa (Option C) is incorrect. Methyldopa (along with a number of other medications) is recognised as a cause of chronic active hepatitis; however, the vast majority of people who use this medication will experience no liver disease at all. Autoimmune Hepatitis A 29-year-old patient with severe ileo-colonic Crohn’s disease comes for a routine clinical review. She has had 20cm of her ileum resected one year ago and is currently on infliximab infusions. She reports a 2-month history of watery diarrhoea, up to 6 times a day. She denies any abdominal pain, vomiting or fevers. Her weight has been stable. Her last foreign travel was to Amsterdam last year and she has not had any recent antibiotic use. On examination, her abdomen is soft and non-tender. Investigations reveal:

Pruritus
Pruritus (Option E) is incorrect. Pruritus is associated with cholestatic liver disease, but is not a sensitive or specific marker for chronic active hepatitis.

stem: A 54-year-old man presented with dysphagia and a normal upper gastrointestinal endoscopy. A barium swallow demonstrated achalasia. Which of the following statements about achalasia is correct?
options: Difficulty in swallowing liquids but not solids
Failure of relaxation of lower oesophageal sphincter
explanation:
Failure of relaxation of lower oesophageal sphincter
Achalasia is characterised by failure of relaxation of the lower oesophageal sphincter and abnormal oesophageal body motility (simultaneous contractions).

Decreased risk of oesophageal adenocarcinoma
Decreased risk of oesophageal adenocarcinoma is incorrect. Oesophageal squamous-cell carcinoma develops in 1–2% of patients with achalasia, and there also appears to be a small increased risk of adenocarcinoma.

Difficulty in swallowing liquids but not solids
Difficulty in swallowing liquids but not solids is incorrect. Dysphagia is usually intermittent, of long duration, and for both liquids and solids.

Increased incidence of coeliac disease
Increased incidence of coeliac disease is incorrect. Achalasia has no association with coeliac disease. Achalasia A 22-year-old woman presented to her general practitioner after a Mediterranean holiday. Her family often ate out during their holiday, particularly eating shellfish. She presented with malaise, lack of appetite, jaundice and dark urine. She had a fever initially, but this subsided once the jaundice appeared. On examination, she had hepatomegaly, as well as tenderness in the right upper quadrant of her abdomen. Her alanine aminotransferase (ALT) and aspartate aminotransferase (AST) levels were ten times the upper limit of the normal range; the bilirubin was six times the upper limit of normal; and alkaline phosphatase was only mildly elevated.

Small-bowel dysmotility
Small-bowel dysmotility is incorrect. Achalasia is not associated with dysmotility in the gastrointestinal tract anywhere other than the oesophagus/gastro-oesophageal junction.

stem: A 22-year-old woman presented to her general practitioner after a Mediterranean holiday. Her family often ate out during their holiday, particularly eating shellfish. She presented with malaise, lack of appetite, jaundice and dark urine. She had a fever initially, but this subsided once the jaundice appeared. On examination, she had hepatomegaly, as well as tenderness in the right upper quadrant of her abdomen. Her alanine aminotransferase (ALT) and aspartate aminotransferase (AST) levels were ten times the upper limit of the normal range; the bilirubin was six times the upper limit of normal; and alkaline phosphatase was only mildly elevated. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Hepatitis A
This scenario is very suggestive of hepatitis A infection, with the clue to the diagnosis here being her holiday to the Mediterranean and her eating shellfish while she was there. Hepatitis A is now relatively rare, but tends to occur in outbreaks; in the UK and USA, there are currently approximately 9–45 cases/100 000 per year. The virus is transmitted via undercooked food that has been subject to faecal contamination with hepatitis A (shellfish is a common source of transmission), and poor standards of faecal–oral hygiene are likely to have played a part in this case. The acute disease is usually self-limiting and lasts less than 6 weeks, but it can occasionally persist for up to 5 months. Infection may be sub-clinical, or manifest as an acute hepatitic illness of variable severity; in less than 0.1% of cases, hepatitis A can cause fulminant liver failure. The diagnosis is made on the basis of the patient’s history and the presence of hepatitis A virus antibodies.

Gallstones
Gallstones is incorrect. Although biliary obstruction with associated cholangitis (from gallstones within the common bile duct) may present with fever, jaundice and right upper quadrant pain, this condition is typically associated with a significant rise in alkaline phosphatase and only a relatively modest increase in transaminases, ruling this out.

Hepatitis B
Hepatitis B is incorrect. Acute hepatitis B may present with an acute hepatitic illness; however, hepatitis B infection is spread through blood or sexual transfer rather than faeco-orally (as is strongly implied to be the case here).

Pancreatic carcinoma
Pancreatic carcinoma is incorrect. Although biliary obstruction with associated cholangitis (from extrinsic compression of the duct from pancreatic carcinoma) may present with fever, jaundice and right upper quadrant pain, this condition is typically associated with a significant rise in alkaline phosphatase and only a relatively modest increase in transaminases, ruling this out. Viral Hepatitis A 45-year-old man with a 20-year history of ulcerative colitis (but who had been lost to follow-up) was reviewed. He was found to have had a change in bowel habit for 4 months, with increasing diarrhoea up to 3-4 times per day.

Salmonella
Salmonella is incorrect. Salmonella infection is faeco-orally spread, but is not typically associated with significant hepatitis.

stem: A 42-year-old man comes to the clinic for review. He reports a 1-year history of retrosternal discomfort and burning pain, which comes on after eating. He also reports an occasional sour taste at the back of his mouth, particularly when he lies flat in bed. He has found Gaviscon to be helpful. He drinks 15 units of alcohol per week and smokes one cigar per day. He has not had any weight loss or dysphagia. Clinical examination is unremarkable. His BMI is 29. What is the next best step?
explanation:
Start omeprazole
This patient has typical symptoms of oesophageal reflux, including retrosternal discomfort precipitated by meals and water brash (regurgitation of acid into the throat). The absence of red flag symptoms and the age of onset (<55 years of age) make an endoscopy unnecessary as the risk of malignancy is extremely low. The next best step is to start treatment with a proton pump inhibitor such as omeprazole.

Upper GI endoscopy
Upper GI endoscopy is incorrect. An endoscopy would be indicated in patients over 55 years with new-onset upper GI symptoms.

Oesophageal manometry
Oesophageal manometry is incorrect. This is used to diagnose motility disorders such as achalasia or diffuse oesophageal spasm, which present with dysphagia.

Urea breath test
Urea breath test is incorrect. This is more useful in excluding Helicobacter pylori as a cause of dyspepsia (upper abdominal pain) rather than reflux, for which H. pylori is not implicated. Gastro-oesophageal

Start ranitidine
Start ranitidine is incorrect. This can be a useful adjunct in managing reflux, but PPI therapy is first line.

stem: A 48-year-old man presents to the Gastroenterology Clinic. He has been suffering from heartburn for some time and has noticed occasional regurgitation of his morning toast. Endoscopy reveals a gastric-looking mucosa spreading up into the oesophagus, with areas of columnar metaplasia found on biopsy. What diagnosis fits best with this clinical picture?
explanation:
Barrett’s oesophagus
This question gives a very typical description of Barrett’s oesophagus. Barrett’s oesophagus is defined as the endoscopic appearance of gastric-type mucosa within the oesophagus (which usually has a characteristic ‘velvet-like’ appearance), with histology of these regions showing columnar metaplasia. It is thought to be caused by chronic gastro-oesophageal reflux disease. The male to female ratio for Barrett’s is 4:1, with a mean age at onset of 40 years. People with Barrett’s oesophagus may have no symptoms (with the condition discovered incidentally), or may be diagnosed during investigations for dyspepsia, reflux or chest pain. Physical findings range from a normal examination to epigastric tenderness. Therapy with high-dose proton-pump inhibitors is the mainstay of drug therapy. Endoscopic surveillance is recommended in Barrett’s oesophagus, as progression from metaplasia, to dysplasia, to oesophageal adenocarcinoma may occur. The exact interval of surveillance depends upon a number of factors, including the histology from previous biopsies. The risk of adenocarcinoma is 30–50 times the risk in people with Barrett’s oesophagus versus those without, which corresponds to around 500 cases per 100,000 patients with Barrett’s oesophagus per year.

Achalasia
Achalasia is incorrect. Achalasia is a dysmotility disorder of the oesophagus, principally associated with a hypertensive lower oesophageal sphincter. This diagnosis could not account for the endoscopic and histological findings described here.

Erosive oesophagitis
Erosive oesophagitis is incorrect. Erosive oesophagitis may present with these symptoms, and can certainly cause mucosal changes to the lower oesophagus. However, the mucosal changes seen on endoscopy in those with erosive oesophagitis are of breaks in the oesophageal mucosa (rather than gastric-type mucosa); furthermore, histology would show inflammatory changes only rather than columnar change.

Gastritis
Gastritis is incorrect. Gastritis may only be diagnosed when an area of the stomach itself demonstrates inflammation endoscopically and histologically. Gastric-type mucosa in sites other than the stomach (whether inflamed or not) may not be defined as gastritis. Oesophageal Tumours

Hiatus hernia
