Computed tomography (CT) scan of the brain is incorrect. A CT of the brain is appropriate to consider (eg to look for subdural haematoma, a pathology that is common in this patient group), but again would not supersede checking blood glucose.

Red cell folate
Red cell folate is incorrect. Folate deficiency may manifest as confusion and drowsiness, but again would not be the first test performed. Alcoholic Liver Disease and Alcoholism

Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy
Upper GI endoscopy is incorrect. Gastroscopy would be appropriate to consider if there were features of gastrointestinal haemorrhage, but none is described here.

stem: A 45-year-old man is referred by the GP to the endoscopy clinic. He has no weight loss but has been suffering from severe reflux symptoms refractory to high-dose PPI, has stopping smoking and has reduced his alcohol consumption over the past six months. He is otherwise completely well. The GP is concerned about possible malignancy. Endoscopy reveals Barrett’s changes with high-grade dysplasia. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
options: Referral for upper GI multi-disciplinary team
explanation:
Referral for upper GI multi-disciplinary team
High-grade dysplasia (HGD) is associated with one or more areas of invasive adenocarcinoma in 30–40% of patients. Treatment for HGD involves endoscopic (endoscopic resection) or surgical (oesophagectomy) management. Either way, this patient would need to be discussed in a multi-disciplinary team where the age, comorbidities, nutritional status and staging of the disease would be put into context.

Add Metoclopramide
Add metoclopramide is incorrect. Metoclopramide has no role in the management of HGD in Barretts. Metoclopramide can be used in gastroparesis.

Continue high dose PPI
Continue high-dose PPI is incorrect. Although high-dose PPI should be continued for symptomatic relief, this does not have a role in inducing regression of dysplasia. HGD is associated with a high risk of invasive malignancy and should be referred to an upper GI multi-disciplinary team for further management.

Photodynamic therapy
Photodynamic therapy is incorrect. This appears to be effective in downgrading when used for high-grade dysplasia, but its efficacy in preventing the progression of Barrett’s oesophagus to invasive cancer is not clear. It involves the administration of a photosensitising agent by intravenous injection, which is then activated by the application of light to the selected area. This produces high-energy oxygen molecules, leading to necrosis of the tumour.

Repeat endoscopy in 2 years
Repeat endoscopy in 2 years is incorrect. Surveillance endoscopy is considered for patients with either nondysplastic (OGD every 3–5 years if maximum length <3 cm, and every 2–3 years if maximum length >3 cm) or low-grade dysplasia (every 6 months until two consecutive evidences of non-dysplastic Barrett’s oesophagus.

stem: A 52-year-old man presents with an acute upper gastrointestinal haemorrhage but he has no further bleeding after the initial episode. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy reveals a suspicious ulcer, which is biopsied. This reveals the presence of mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue and Helicobacter pylori. What is the most appropriate initial treatment in this case?
explanation:
Helicobacter pylori eradication therapy
Where there is localised mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT) co-existent with Helicobacter pylori infection, there is evidence that eradication of H. pylori can result in resolution of the MALT. However, for larger areas of lymphoid tissue or where the patient is H. pylori negative, eradication therapy is much less effective.

High-dose proton-pump inhibitor therapy
High-dose proton-pump inhibitor therapy is incorrect. High-dose proton-pump inhibitor may help to partially resolve the ulcer, but this will not by itself make any difference to the natural history of the MALT lymphoma.

Chemotherapy for lymphoma
Chemotherapy for lymphoma is incorrect. Chemotherapy is certainly a potential option for treating the MALT lymphoma, depending upon staging. However, given that Helicobacter pylori eradication therapy may completely resolve those MALT lymphomas at their earliest stages, this is the most appropriate initial therapy pending formal staging.

Surveillance endoscopy in 3 months
Surveillance endoscopy in three months is incorrect. The MALT lymphoma may continue to grow without any intervention. Peptic Ulcer Disease and Gastritis A 56-year-old man underwent an upper gastrointestinal endoscopy for iron deficiency anaemia. Biopsies of a mass in the stomach are reported as showing a mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT) lymphoma.

Referral for surgery
Referral for surgery is incorrect. Surgery is usually reserved for those patients with gastric MALT lymphoma who have very severe complications, including refractory gastrointestinal bleeding, gastric perforation or obstruction.

stem: A 56-year-old man underwent an upper gastrointestinal endoscopy for iron deficiency anaemia. Biopsies of a mass in the stomach are reported as showing a mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT) lymphoma. Which of the following is true of MALT lymphomas?
options: Metastatic spread to the liver is common
The stomach is the only site of origin
explanation:
Paraproteins may be a feature
Gastric mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT) lymphomas are understood to arise principally as a result of Helicobacter pylori infection in the stomach. Paraprotein formation and pseudohyponatraemia are recognised complications.

40% regress with Helicobacter pylori eradication
40% regress with Helicobacter pylori eradication is incorrect. In non-metastatic tumours, H. pylori eradication results in complete remission in ~80% of cases (rather than 40%, hence option A is incorrect). Where metastasis has occurred, standard B-cell lymphoma regimens are usually effective.

Metastatic spread to the liver is common
Metastatic spread to the liver is common is incorrect. Metastasis of MALTomas is rare, but if it does occur then it may make treatment much more difficult.

The stomach is the only site of origin
The stomach is the only site of origin is incorrect. They may arise from any mucosal surface (rather than just the stomach).

They are a T-lymphocyte clone
They are a T-lymphocyte clone is incorrect. These lymphomas originate from B cells rather than T cells.

stem: A 63-year-old patient presents to the GP with a history of 1 stone weight loss in the last 3 months and some non-specific right upper quadrant discomfort. He is found to be anaemic and have a raised ALT and AST on blood tests and so an abdominal ultrasound is arranged. It is reported as being suspicious of a hepatocellular carcinoma. Which of the following conditions is associated with the greatest increased risk of developing hepatocellular carcinoma?
explanation:
α1-antitrypsin deficiency
Hepatocellular carcinoma usually complicates chronic liver disease secondary to chronic alcoholism or viral hepatitis. Metabolic disorders that may be complicated by hepatocellular carcinomas include hereditary haemochromatosis and α 1-antitrypsin deficiency. Α1-antitrypsin is a protease inhibitor predominantly produced by the liver that controls tissue degradation. Α1-antitrypsin deficiency can cause liver cirrhosis and lung injury in the form of emphysema.

Diabetes mellitus
Diabetes mellitus is incorrect. Diabetes mellitus has a milder increased risk for HCC.

Secondary haemochromatosis
Secondary haemochromatosis is incorrect. Primary /hereditary haemachromatosis and not secondary haemochromatosis, is a risk factor for HCC.

Aspergillus infection
Aspergillus infection is incorrect. Aspergillus infection itself is not a risk factor for HCC however aflatoxin exposure, which are naturally occurring toxins produced by a few Aspergillus species, is a risk factor. Hepatobiliary Tumours

Hepatitis E
Hepatitis E is incorrect. Hepatitis E is an RNA virus that is transmitted by the faecal-oral route and usually only causes a self-limiting illness. It does not cause liver cirrhosis, and therefore is not a risk factor for HCC.

stem: A 37-year-old man presented complaining of severe epigastric pain that was becoming increasingly constant. A screening test for Helicobacter pylori was positive. Which condition is most strongly associated with this infection?
explanation:
Gastric B-cell lymphoma
Over 70% of patients with gastric B-cell lymphomas (mucosal-associated lymphoid tissue lymphoma, or MALT lymphoma/MALToma) have Helicobacter pylori infection. H. pylori gastritis has been shown to contain the clonal B-cell that eventually gives rise to the MALT lymphoma. Some low-grade tumours regress with H. pylori eradication alone.

Autoimmune gastritis
Autoimmune gastritis is incorrect. Autoimmune gastritis is characterised by an atrophic gastritis with loss of parietal cells. As the name implies, it is an autoimmune condition, with H. pylori having no contribution to its pathogenesis.

Erosive gastropathy
Erosive gastropathy is incorrect. Erosive gastropathy is a term used to describe the situation where there is gastric mucosal damage, but little or no accompanying inflammation; the most common causes are the use of aspirin/non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) and alcohol. In contrast, H. pylori typically more often causes an inflammatory gastritis rather than a gastropathy.

Gastric stromal tumour
Gastric stromal tumour is incorrect. While MALTomas are strongly associated with H. pylori, gastric stromal tumours have no association with this infection at all.

Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease
Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease is incorrect. Far from H. pylori causing gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GORD), there is actually a growing body of evidence that it is eradication of H. pylori that worsens GORD, via a possible mechanism of increased acid secretion following H. pylori elimination.

stem: A 28-year-old patient has had a recent diagnosis of ulcerative colitis following presentation with abdominal pain and bloody diarrhoea. She is now in remission after starting Mesalazine. She has done some reading on the internet about the extra intestinal manifestations of inflammatory bowel disease and had some questions. Which extra intestinal manifestation runs a course independent of IBD activity?
explanation:
Primary sclerosing cholangitis
Extra-intestinal manifestations commonly occur in IBD (around 40% of patients) and involve the skin, eyes, biliary tree, axial and peripheral locomotor system. Some occur in the absence of active luminal disease including PSC, ankylosing spondylitis and small joint arthritis. Up to 4% of IBD patients develop PSC.

Erythema nodosum
Erythema nodosum is incorrect. Erythema nodosum is the most common cutaneous manifestation of IBD, affecting women more than men. Lesions are typically found in the pre-tibial area and look like warm raised tender nodules. Flares of erythema nodosum typically occur with intestinal flares.

Episcleritis
Episcleritis is incorrect. Episcleritis is the most common ocular manifestation and presents with ocular irritation and superficial erythema with or without pain. Visual acuity and pupillary reflexes are normal. It typically flares at the same time as a gut flare up.

Sweet Syndrome
Sweet syndrome presents as tender papules, plaques, and/or nodules, mostly seen around the face and upper limbs. It is associated with active inflammatory bowel disease and most of the time it runs a parallel course. Ulcerative Colitis

Large joint arthritis
Large joint arthritis is incorrect. Large joint arthritis presents as a migratory non-deforming and non-erosive large-joint arthropathy involving less than 5 joints which are clinically inflamed. It is typically associated with an IBD flare.

stem: A 48-year-old man with a 2-year history of ulcerative colitis had been receiving parenteral nutrition for 4 months. He developed a dermatitis and had noticed some loss of hair. Serum biochemistry showed a marginally raised glucose concentration and a reduction in alkaline phosphatase activity. What is the most likely explanation?
explanation:
Zinc deficiency
Dermatitis and alopecia are typical of zinc deficiency. Patients with inflammatory bowel disease may lose considerable quantities of zinc from the gut and therefore will be more prone to both conditions.

Chromium deficiency
Chromium deficiency is incorrect. The most consistent feature of chromium deficiency is glucose intolerance, although this deficiency is very rarely seen in clinical practice.

Copper deficiency
Copper deficiency is incorrect. The most consistent features of copper deficiency include cardiac dysrhythmias and altered lipoprotein metabolism, although this deficiency is very rarely seen in clinical practice.

Magnesium deficiency
Magnesium deficiency is incorrect. The most consistent features of hypomagnesaemia are hypocalcaemia and neuromuscular excitability.

Selenium deficiency
Selenium deficiency is incorrect. Selenium deficiency is particularly associated with a cardiomyopathy. This is seen as Keshan disease in areas where soil has a low selenium content.

stem: A 43-year-old man was referred after he was found to have abnormal liver biochemistry. Investigations showed he had an alanine aminotransferase (ALT) of 98 U/l and he was hepatitis B surface antigen positive. Which of the following statements about chronic active hepatitis owing to the hepatitis B virus is correct?
options: It carries an increased risk of subsequent hepatocellular carcinoma
It causes marked elevation of serum transaminases
It is usually associated with positive hepatitis D serology
It is more common in women than in men
explanation:
It carries an increased risk of subsequent hepatocellular carcinoma
Chronic hepatitis B is well recognised as being a carcinogen, with hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) being the result. Although many cases of HCC in those with chronic hepatitis B occur in those who have developed cirrhosis, there are particular groups of people with chronic hepatitis B even without cirrhosis who merit surveillance for HCC because they are at higher risk (ie based on ethnicity and/or family history).

It causes marked elevation of serum transaminases
It causes marked elevation of serum transaminases is incorrect. Liver enzymes may be almost completely normal in the condition, ruling out this option.

It is usually associated with positive hepatitis D serology
It is associated with positive hepatitis D serology is incorrect. Hepatitis D infection can only occur in people who already have hepatitis B infection, but hepatitis B is not directly associated with positive hepatitis D serology, ruling this option out. According to studies hepatitis D coinfection is found in between 10-25% of patients with hepatitis B.

It is more common in women than in men
It is more common in women than in men is incorrect. Chronic hepatitis B is just as common in men as in women. Viral Hepatitis

It responds well to corticosteroids
It responds well to corticosteroids is incorrect. Several different treatments are available to treat chronic hepatitis B, but corticosteroids are certainly not an effective treatment.

stem: A 75-year-old woman was referred to clinic by her general practitioner because of progressive unintentional weight loss, early satiety and increasing anorexia. She described two or three episodes of vomiting blood. Her past history included excess consumption of alcohol, and a 30 pack-year smoking history. On examination, there was an epigastric mass. Blood tests revealed a microcytic anaemia and abnormal liver enzymes. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Gastric carcinoma
The clinical features and blood test findings described – in a woman of this age, with a history of heavy alcohol and tobacco use – is together very suggestive of gastric carcinoma. The annual incidence of gastric carcinoma in the Western world is around 7/100 000. In Japan, the incidence is much higher at around 80/100 000, and it is thought to be diet-related; other risk factors for gastric carcinoma include chronic Helicobacter pylori infection, smoking, alcohol excess and chronic atrophic gastritis. Most gastric cancers (35%) occur in the antrum. There is a slight male preponderance (3:2) and the disease is more common in the over-65 age group. Metastasis at presentation of gastric carcinoma is common, with the liver the most common site of metastasis. The 5-year survival rate is poor at 12% overall; however, early gastric carcinoma detected prior to metastasis might be associated with higher rates of survival (35% in one case series).

Benign gastric ulcers
Benign gastric ulcers is incorrect. Benign gastric ulcers may present with haematemesis, but the other symptoms described in this scenario (in particular, progressive weight loss) are more typical of malignant than benign gastric disease; furthermore, an epigastric mass and the blood test results described are also clearly more suggestive of malignant disease.

Gastric lymphoma
Gastric lymphoma is incorrect. Gastric lymphomas represent only ~5% of gastric tumours; it is very unusual for a gastric lymphoma to result in haematemesis or melaena (in contrast to gastric adenocarcinoma), making it unlikely to be the diagnosis here.

Helicobacter gastritis
Helicobacter gastritis is incorrect. Although Helicobacter gastritis may cause marked dyspepsia, it does not typically cause such marked constitutional symptoms as those described, and would not explain this woman’s epigastric mass.

Pancreatic carcinoma
Pancreatic carcinoma is incorrect. Pancreatic cancer could produce a broadly similar clinical picture to that described here – however, the presence of haematemesis points much more towards gastic cancer.

stem: A 45-year-old patient was referred with itching and abnormal liver biochemistry. Which of the following is a feature of primary biliary cholangitis?
explanation:
Anti-mitochondrial antibodies
Primary biliary cholangitis (PBC), previously known as primary biliary cirrhosis, is a condition associated with positive anti-mitochondrial (M2) antibodies and elevated serum IgM levels. PBC is also associated with an increased level of copper in the liver; however, this increased copper occurs as a complication of cholestasis and is not necessarily related to any difference in plasma levels, meaning that the increased serum copper level option is incorrect. Given how sensitive and specific anti-mitochondrial antibodies are for confirming the diagnosis, a liver biopsy is not a necessity to confirm the diagnosis; however, a biopsy may still be helpful in assessing for hepatic fibrosis/ severity of liver disease. Typical biopsy findings include inflammatory duct destruction and patchy fibrosis, with cirrhosis occurring in those most greatly affected. PBC usually affects middle-aged women, therefore the middle-aged male option is not correct. The progression of the condition is variable, with a small number of affected people developing sufficiently severe liver disease to merit liver transplantation. Treatment with ursodeoxycholic acid improves liver biochemistry, but probably does not the prognosis. Cholestyramine may be used as a symptomatic treatment for pruritus, one of the most common symptoms in those affected with the condition.

Histological piecemeal necrosis
Histological piecemeal necrosis is incorrect. Piecemeal necrosis is well described in the histology of chronic active hepatitis, but is not part of the histology of PBC.

Increased serum copper level
Increased serum copper level is incorrect. As described, PBC is associated with increased levels of copper in the liver.

Increased serum IgA
Increased serum IgA is incorrect. Serum IgA is not typically raised in the condition, ruling out this option. Primary Biliary Cholangitis A 52-year-old man with a long history of ulcerative colitis was found by his general practitioner to have abnormal liver function tests, with a raised alkaline phosphatase. He did not drink alcohol, and took no regular medications. On examination, there were no features of chronic liver disease. What are the most appropriate next investigations to confirm the diagnosis?

Middle-aged male patients
Middle-aged male patients is incorrect. PBC usually affects middle-aged women, as outlined.

stem: A 32-year-old woman was referred for endoscopy and found to have a duodenal ulcer and a positive urease test. She was given lansoprazole, amoxicillin and clarithromycin for seven days. She says that she does not really have time to attend for an appointment with her GP or at the hospital. Which of the following is the most appropriate way of determining the successful eradication of Helicobacter pylori once treatment has been completed?
explanation:
13
C urea breath test 13 NICE consider this the only reliable option for re-testing after eradication therapy.

Blood serology testing
Blood serology testing is incorrect. Serological testing for H. pylori remains positive for at least 6–12 months after successful eradication of the infection, so would not be helpful here.

Endoscopy and antral histology
Endoscopy and antral histology is incorrect. Endoscopy with histology is invasive; such tests also have a high risk of giving false-negative results after eradication therapy.

Endoscopy and CLO test
Endoscopy and CLO test is incorrect. Endoscopy with CLO testing is invasive; such tests also have a high risk of giving false-negative results after eradication therapy. Peptic Ulcer Disease and Gastritis

Faecal antigen testing
Faecal antigen testing is incorrect. Faecal antigen has now largely replaced the 14C urea breath, although NICE do not consider it reliable enough to determine eradication yet.

stem: USS liver - Evidence of fatty infiltration Which of the following is the most effective intervention?
explanation:
Weight loss
The primary therapy for NAFLD is weight loss. It is recommended in all patients who have a BMI of more than 25. Weight loss also helps in improving liver biochemical tests, liver histology improves insulin response and quality of life.

Metformin
Metformin is incorrect. Although metformin reduces hepatic glucose output, it does not have a significant impact on fatty liver disease.

Pioglitazone
Pioglitazone is incorrect. Glitazones do reduce intra-hepatic fat, but the adverse effects of glitazones including weight gain and reduced bone mineral density preclude their use in this situation for the majority of patients.

Simvastatin
Simvastatin is incorrect. Although Simvastatin reduces LDL cholesterol, it doesn’t significantly impact on liver fat. Non-alcoholic

Vitamin E
Vitamin is incorrect. Although vitamin E is used in the treatment of fatty liver disease, it doesn’t significantly reduce liver fat versus other options such as GLP-1 agonists.

stem: A 35-year-old man presents with abdominal pain, joint pains, fever and weight loss. He gives a history of passing bulky, malodorous stools over the past month that are difficult to flush away. A biopsy of the small bowel shows stunted villi with PAS- (Periodic acid–Schiff-) positive macrophages. What is the most likely characteristic finding in this condition?
options: Bony erosions and subluxation of joints on X-ray of affected joints
Mesenteric thickening with lymph node enlargement on CT scan
The presence of bacilli within macrophages on electron microscopy
explanation:
The presence of bacilli within macrophages on electron microscopy
This patient has Whipple’s disease, which usually occurs in males. Peripheral arthritis occurs in 15% of patients. The disease is associated with steatorrhoea and abdominal pain. Stunted villi with PAS (Periodic acid–Schiff-) positive macrophages are seen in this condition and Transverse ulceration seen on a barium meal followthrough.

Bony erosions and subluxation of joints on X-ray of affected joints
Bony erosions and subluxation of joints on X-ray of affected joints is incorrect. Bony erosions and subluxations are a feature of rheumatoid arthritis.

Mesenteric thickening with lymph node enlargement on CT scan
Mesenteric thickening with lymph node enlargement on CT scan is incorrect. Mesenteric thickening with lymph node enlargement are characteristic of intestinal tuberculosis.

Occult blood in stools
Occult blood in stools is incorrect. Faecal occult blood is not seen in Whipple’s.

Positive HLA-B27
Positive HLA-B27 is incorrect. Although there is slight evidence of HLA-B27 association with Whipple’s disease this is not a characteristic finding.

stem: A 19-year-old patient comes to the gastroenterology clinic complaining of bloating, weight loss and diarrhoea. She has no other significant medical history. Her symptoms are partially eased when she goes on a gluten-free diet. Her coeliac screen was borderline. She is very reluctant to consume gluten for the purposes of a gastroscopy and duodenal biopsy, because she is worried about coping with her symptoms during work. Which of the following tests can exclude coeliac disease and thus avoid the need for an unnecessary gastroscopy?
explanation:
HLA DQ2 and HLA DQ8
HLA DQ2 and/or HLA DQ8 are associated with coeliac disease. Absence of these makes coeliac disease extremely unlikely.

HLA B27
HLA B27 is incorrect. This is associated with IBD, psoriasis, ankylosing spondylitis and reactive arthritis.

NOD2 gene mutations
NOD2 gene mutations is incorrect. These have been associated with Crohn’s disease.

HLA DR3 and HLA DR4
HLA DR3 and HLA DR4 is incorrect. These are associated with type 1 diabetes.

HFE gene mutations
HFE gene mutations is incorrect. Mutations in the HFE gene are associated with hereditary haemachromatosis.

stem: A 42-year-old chronic alcoholic who has had three episodes of pancreatitis over the past 18 months comes to the clinic for routine follow up. You review his routine bloods but it is apparent that his lipid profile was uninterpretable due to a lipaemic sample. Elevation of which of the following components of the lipid profile is likely to be responsible for the lipaemic sample?
explanation:
Chylomicrons
Lipaemia is the result of the accumulation of lipoprotein particles. Lipoproteins are made up of chylomicrons, high density lipoproteins (HDL), intermediate density lipoproteins (IDL), low density lipoproteins (LDL) and very low density lipoproteins (VLDL). Lipoproteins are hydrophilic structures, required for the transportation of hydrophobic lipids, which are mostly insoluble in the blood. Chylomicrons are the largest particles, typically 70–1000 nm, and therefore have the highest potential to cause lipaemia of the sample. Typically, HDL (6–12 nm), LDL (20–25 nm), IDL (25–35 nm) and VLDL (25–60 nm) do not cause lipaemic samples. The most common cause of lipaemic samples is inadequate time between meals and blood sampling. Pathological conditions causing lipaemic samples include diabetes mellitus, multiple myeloma, kidney disease and acute pancreatitis, as in this case. Chylomicrons are made up of largely of triglycerides, with the remaining small proportion coming from phospholipids, cholesterol and proteins. Chylomicrons are formed in the small intestine and are used to transport lipids absorbed in the small intestine to adipose, cardiac and skeletal muscle tissue. Here, the triglyceride component is hydrolysed by lipoprotein lipase, forming free fatty acids which are taken up by the tissues. The chylomicron remnants are then taken up by the liver where they are further metabolised. Alcoholism is thought to lead to increased intestinal production of chylomicrons and therefore raised levels of triglycerides. Increased production of chylomicrons therefore will increase the chance that the blood sample will be lipaemic.

HDL
HDL is incorrect. These are produced in the small intestine and liver and are the smallest of the lipoproteins and therefore do not cause lipaemic blood samples. Their metabolism is complex but ultimately they remove fat from cells (unlike the other lipoproteins, which deliver fat to cells) and deliver the metabolites to the liver, where they are excreted in bile into the intestine or to the adrenals, ovaries and testes. The delivery of HDL cholesterol to these organs is important for the synthesis of steroid hormones. HDL is associated with reduced risk of atherosclerosis. Firstly, it is able to transport cholesterol from foam cells (lipid-laden macrophages) in the atherosclerotic arteries, to the liver for excretion into the bile. It is also able to inhibit oxidation, inflammation and platelet aggregation, all of which help to protect from atherosclerosis. High HDL levels correlate with improved cardiovascular health although specifically increasing HDL levels with medication has not been shown to necessarily health. Certain lifestyle and diet modifications such as increased aerobic exercise, smoking cessation, magnesium supplements and reduced simple carbohydrates have been associated with high HDL levels. Consumption of modest amounts of alcohol also results in elevated HDL, with a much smaller rise in triglycerides.

IDL
IDL is incorrect. IDL are formed by the breakdown of VLDL. They are involved in the transportation of fats and cholesterol around the body via the bloodstream, where they are cleared from the plasma into the liver by receptor-mediated endocytosis or further hydrolysed in the blood stream to form LDL. Elevated levels, like LDL, result in the formation of atheroma. However, due to IDL small size, they do not usually cause lipaemic blood samples, and therefore is not the correct answer.

LDL
LDL is incorrect. LDL are the most cholesterol rich of the lipoproteins and are the products of VLDL and IDL metabolism. However, their small size is unlikely to cause lipaemic blood samples. High LDL levels are associated with an increased risk of cardiovascular disease. LDL is cleared by the liver via hepatic LDL receptors or by non-hepatic LDL (scavenger) receptors, most commonly found on macrophages. Elevated levels of dietary saturated fat or cholesterol delivery to the liver results in down regulation of the hepatic LDL receptors, thus increasing LDL levels. The reverse is true with decreased dietary fat and cholesterol. LDL not taken up by hepatic LDL receptors binds to the scavenger receptors on the macrophages. These ultimately migrate to the subendothelial space in the arteries, undergo further oxidation and form foam cells resulting in atherosclerotic plaques. Familial hypercholesterolaemia is a genetic disorder, inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern, causing raised LDL. It results in early onset cardiovascular disease, which is less responsive to conventional treatment such as dietary modification and medications. Genetic mutations most commonly affect the LDL receptor protein, which removes LDL from the circulation into the liver, or the apolipoprotein B which is part of LDL and is needed for receptor binding. Heterozygous patients typically have early onset cardiovascular disease, which is usually managed with medications including statins and bile acid sequestrants. Homozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia is much rarer and does not respond to lifestyle modification or medical management. LDL apheresis may be used, and in severe cases, liver transplant is required. Chronic Pancreatitis A 78-year-old woman returned for her third visit in 3 months to the Emergency Department, complaining of extremely severe dull epigastric pain that radiated to her back. On the previous 2 occasions her bloods were unremarkable and she was discharged. On this occasion a haemoglobin of 104 g/l and elevated alkaline phosphatase is noted.

VLDL
VLDL is incorrect. Its relative small size is unlikely to cause lipaemic blood samples. VLDL are made in the liver and transport endogenous cholesterol and triglycerides to peripheral tissues. Its synthesis increases with increased intrahepatic free fatty acids which may be see in high fat diets as well as obesity and uncontrolled diabetes. High levels of VLDL ultimately result in high LDL and IDL, resulting in increased risk of atheroma and cardiovascular disease.

stem: A 78-year-old woman returned for her third visit in 3 months to the Emergency Department, complaining of extremely severe dull epigastric pain that radiated to her back. On the previous 2 occasions her bloods were unremarkable and she was discharged. On this occasion a haemoglobin of 104 g/l and elevated alkaline phosphatase is noted. What is the most appropriate initial management plan?
options: Arrange an upper gastrointestinal endoscopy in the first instance
Discharge home for a trial of proton-pump inhibitor therapy
explanation:
Arrange an abdominal ultrasound scan
The combination of epigastric pain, anaemia and raised alkaline phosphatase in a woman of this age is most likely to be explained by pancreatic carcinoma. Pain arising from the pancreas is often partially relieved by sitting forwards. Bile duct obstruction with jaundice is a late feature of the condition. A mass might be palpable if the carcinoma occurs in the head of the pancreas, but this would be more unusual if the tumour is in the body or tail. The most appropriate next step is an abdominal ultrasound scan; ultrasound is very good at imaging the biliary tree, so is useful at demonstrating biliary dilatation if there is extrinsic compression/internal obstruction because of malignancy. Ultrasound does not always image the normal pancreas (because of bowel in the way), but would be able to detect a large pancreatic mass. As such, arranging an abdominal ultrasound is correct here.

Arrange an upper gastrointestinal endoscopy in the first instance
Arrange an upper gastrointestinal endoscopy in the first instance is incorrect. Severe epigastric pain and anaemia could be explained by an upper gastrointestinal tract malignancy; however, pain radiating to the back and a raised alkaline phosphatase are much more suggestive of primary pancreatic pathology. As such, upper GI endoscopy should not be considered before an abdominal ultrasound.

Check her CA-19.9 level
Check her CA-19.9 level is incorrect. CA-19.9 (CA, carbohydrate antigen) might be useful as a marker of disease progression in pancreatic carcinoma, but cannot be used for diagnosis as there is a high false-positive rate.

Check her serum ferritin level
Check her serum ferritin level is incorrect. Although checking her serum ferritin may be helpful (as a low level would confirm iron-deficiency anaemia), this does not in itself help to identify the unifying diagnosis.

Discharge home for a trial of proton-pump inhibitor therapy
Discharge home for a trial of proton-pump inhibitor therapy is incorrect. Severe epigastric pain and anaemia could be explained by an upper gastrointestinal tract malignancy; however, pain radiating to the back and a raised alkaline phosphatase are much more suggestive of primary pancreatic pathology. As such, trial of protonpump inhibitor therapy should not be considered before an abdominal ultrasound.

stem: A 56-year-old woman with type I diabetes mellitus and hypothyroidism was referred for investigation of a megaloblastic anaemia. Her BP is 122/72, pulse is 70 and regular. Her BMI is 22. Which of the following is most likely to be the cause?
explanation:
Pernicious anaemia
The list of causes of vitamin B12 deficiency is long, and includes: Gastric causes – pernicious anaemia, chronic severe atrophic gastritis Pancreatic – any cause of pancreatic insufficiency Small-bowel bacterial overgrowth (since bacteria utilise vitamin B12), terminal ileal resection, severe terminal ileal disease (ie Crohn’s disease) Tuberculosis Metformin therapy Zollinger–Ellison syndrome Although all of the options listed can cause vitamin B12 malabsorption, the information provided here that this woman has other autoimmune disease makes pernicious anaemia the most likely explanation. Pernicious anaemia results from anti-parietal and anti-intrinsic factor antibodies, together resulting in reduced intrinsic factor production, reduced intrinsic factor activity, and consequently reduced B12 absorption. Salivary R-binders bind to vitamin B12, and these protect the vitamin from gastric acid denaturation. Intrinsic factor, synthesised in the stomach, cannot bind to vitamin B12 until the R-binder has been split off by pancreatic trypsin. Once the vitamin B12–intrinsic factor complex is formed, it is actively absorbed in the terminal ileum.

Crohn's disease
Crohn’s disease is incorrect. No history is given that would particularly suggest Crohn’s disease (such as diarrhoea, abdominal pain and/or weight loss).

Metformin therapy
Metformin therapy is incorrect. This woman may be using metformin if she had type 2 diabetes mellitus, but this is not a licensed treatment for Type 1 diabetes, (although it may be used in overweight / obese patients with T1DM).

Pancreatic insufficiency
Pancreatic insufficiency is incorrect. This woman has pancreatic endocrine failure because of diabetes, but there is no information to suggest her having pancreatic exocrine failure too.

Small-bowel bacterial overgrowth
Small-bowel bacterial overgrowth is incorrect. Although small-bowel bacterial overgrowth occurs at higher rates in diabetics than in people without the condition, there is no description of diarrhoea, abdominal bloating, or any other features that may suggest this condition.

stem: A 55-year-old man is referred to the Gastroenterology Clinic due to difficulty in tolerating oral intake. He first noticed the symptoms six months ago with regurgitation of liquids. He has now noticed that he is regurgitating some solid food. He describes interrupted sleep secondary to coughing at night, which has improved now that he sleeps on four pillows. He is a current smoker. He has lost 1 kg in weight over the last six months. He undergoes a barium swallow which shows a bird beak appearance. On examination, his blood pressure is 147/87 mmHg, heart rate 75 bpm and regular, height 180 cm and weight 104 kg. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Achalasia
Achalasia is a disorder of motility of the oesophagus which may be autoimmune in aetiology. The presence of dysphagia to both liquids and solids in a patient with preserved weight is highly suggestive of an oesophageal motility disorder. Barium swallow with a bird beak appearance is indicative.

Barrett’s oesophagus
Barrett’s oesophagus would not, in itself, typically be expected to cause dysphagia. Barrett’s oesophagus is a pre-cancerous condition.

Benign oesophageal stricture
Obstructive oesophageal disorders (including oesophageal carcinoma and benign oesophageal strictures) typically first present with dysphagia to solids and progress with time to dysphagia to liquids with an associated degree of weight loss. The patient first noted dysphagia to liquids and has a relatively small weight loss. Average body weight loss at the time of diagnosis of oesophageal cancer is 5%, whereas the patient in this case has only lost 1 kg.

Carcinoma of the oesophagus
In carcinoma of the oesophagus, 57–85% of patients present with weight loss, which, on average, is weight loss of approximately 5% of their total body weight one year before this. Achalasia

Schatzki’s rings
Schatzki’s rings are mucosal rings within the lower oesophagus that cause episodic symptoms of regurgitation and dysphagia. This patient has progressive and persistent symptoms. Symptoms of Schatzki’s rings are more likely when food is not properly chewed.

stem: A 36-year-old man with ulcerative colitis was admitted with abdominal pain and an amylase level of 1433 U/l. Which medication is most likely to be a cause of his symptoms?
explanation:
Azathioprine
In the maintenance treatments used for ulcerative colitis, azathioprine is effective but associated with a number of potentially serious side effects. These include: Pancreatitis – acute pancreatitis is well recognised as a potential complication of azathioprine use. The presence of acute abdominal pain and a raised amylase clearly makes this the likely diagnosis here. Hypersensitivity reactions – a variety of symptoms are possible, including malaise, dizziness, vomiting, diarrhoea, fever, rigors, myalgia, arthralgia and rash. Interstitial nephritis – rare, but calls for immediate withdrawal. Bone marrow suppression – this effect is dose related. Leucopenia can result in increased susceptibility to infection, particularly in people also receiving corticosteroids. Liver disease – a liver injury that may present with cholestatic liver enzymes. Causes of acute pancreatitis include: ‘GET SMASHED’: Gallstone disease Ethanol, ie alcohol excess Trauma/ surgery Steroids Mumps, and other infections, including Coxsackievirus, Salmonella, Campylobacter, Mycoplasma Autoimmune, eg SLE, polyarteritis nodosa Scorpion venom Hypothermia, hypercalcaemia, hyperlipidaemia, hereditary ERCP Drugs – including oestrogens (plus other causes – pregnancy, idiopathic, pancreatitc tumours, etc).

Aspirin
Aspirin is incorrect. Aspirin is not a recognised cause of pancreatitis.

Budesonide
Budesonide is incorrect. Although budesonide is a steroid, it is an unlikely cause of pancreatitis as it is used in dose forms in inflammatory bowel disease that allow local delivery of steroid and reduce systemic exposure.

Paracetamol
Paracetamol is incorrect. Paracetamol is not recognised as causing pancreatitis.

Sulfasalazine
Sulfasalazine is incorrect. Mesalazine may rarely cause pancreatitis, but this is much less likely with sulfasalazine.

stem: A 48-year-old man presented with symptoms of indigestion and regurgitation of food. In addition, he had a painful epigastric mass on palpation of the abdomen. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy revealed a gastric mass and biopsy revealed it to be a gastrointestinal stromal tumour. He was commenced on treatment with imatinib. Which of the following options fits best with the mode of action of imatinib?
explanation:
Inhibition of tyrosine kinase
Imatinib is licensed for the treatment of chronic myeloid leukaemia and gastrointestinal stromal tumours. It is a tyrosine kinase inhibitor, specifically the tyrosine kinase domain in Abl (the Abelson proto-oncogene), c-kit and the platelet-derived growth factor receptor. It might have other potential additional uses, including in the treatment of systemic mastocytosis and some sarcomas. Imatinib is generally well tolerated, although severe congestive cardiac failure is recognised as an uncommon side-effect in some patients.

Inhibition of mitogen-activated protein (MAP) kinase
Inhibition of mitogen-activated protein (MAP) kinase is incorrect. Inhibition of mitogen-activated protein is a useful pharmacological approach in the treatment of leukaemia. Imatinib works via another route (more specifically, it is a tyrosine kinase inhibitor).

Inhibition of p53 production
Inhibition of p53 production is incorrect. TP53 plays an important role in cell division, damage of this gene causes a potential for uncontrolled cell division and therefore tumours. Imatinib works via another route (more specifically, it is a tyrosine kinase inhibitor).

Stimulation of guanylate cyclase
Stimulation of guanylate cyclase is incorrect. Guanylate cyclase is an important cell messenger, upregulation has been associated with parkinson's disease. Imatinib works via another route (more specifically, it is a tyrosine kinase inhibitor).

Stimulation of p53 production
Stimulation of p53 production is incorrect. TP53 plays an important role in cell division, damage of this gene causes a potential for uncontrolled cell division and therefore tumours. Imatinib works via another route (more specifically, it is a tyrosine kinase inhibitor).

stem: A 20-year-old patient with coeliac disease presents with a bleeding abnormality. She has noticed an increased susceptibility to bleeding which is difficult to stop. Which one of the following is the most likely cause?
explanation:
Vitamin K deficiency
Vitamin K is a fat-soluble vitamin, and malabsorption of fat-soluble vitamins by bowel disorders such as coeliac or inflammatory bowel disease can cause vitamin K deficiency. Vitamin K is required for the production of the vitamin K coagulation factors, II, VII, IX and X.

Disseminated intravascular coagulation
Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) is incorrect. There is no suggestion of another predisposing factor to DIC and this would not link in with the underlying coeliac disease.

Folate deficiency
Folate deficiency is incorrect. Folate deficiency will not, of course, have any impact on the blood coagulation.

Iron deficiency
Iron deficiency anaemia is incorrect. Iron deficiency again will not have any impact on the blood coagulation.

Vitamin A deficiency
Vitamin A deficiency is incorrect. Vitamin A deficiency will not have any effect on blood coagulation either.

stem: What is the most appropriate first-line investigation if coeliac disease is suspected?
explanation:
Anti-tissue transglutaminase (TTG) antibodies
IgA antibodies to tissue transglutaminase are the first-line screening test. In the presence of IgA deficiency, the IgG anti-gliadin antibody test is the next screening. This patient has a likely diagnosis of coeliac disease, as evidenced by the symptoms of weight loss, lethargy (secondary to iron deficiency anaemia) and diarrhoea. Iron deficiency anaemia in a woman that cannot be explained by menstruation or diet, warrants investigation for coeliac disease. Other deficiencies include B 12, folate and vitamin D, as they are all absorbed in the proximal small bowel. The pruritic rash is dermatitis herpetiformitis, an intensely itchy rash typically found on the extensor surfaces, which is associated with the disease. Coeliac disease can also be associated with raised transaminases, which usually resolve on following a gluten-free diet.

Anti-enterocyte antibodies
Anti-enterocyte antibodies is incorrect. Anti-enterocyte antibodies are used as a marker for T-cell lymphoma.

Anti-gluten antibodies
An anti-gluten antibody test is incorrect. Anti-gluten antibodies is not the most appropriate first-line investigation.

Anti-reticulin antibodies
Anti-reticulin antibodies is incorrect. Anti-reticulin antibodies have good specificity but poor sensitivity for detecting coeliac disease, and are not routinely used for screening.

Small bowel biopsy
Small bowel biopsy is incorrect. Small bowel biopsy the gold standard for diagnosis, this is not the first-line screening test, as it is an invasive procedure. Typical features seen on biopsy include villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia and intraepithelial lymphocytosis.

stem: A 56-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with a very large, upper gastrointestinal haemorrhage. He is known to drink up to three-quarters of a bottle of whisky per day and 2–3 pints of beer and has previously been diagnosed with alcoholism. On examination, he is hypotensive at 85/60 mmHg and his heart rate is 110 bpm. There is blood around his mouth and he has a further 150 ml haematemesis in the department. An emergency endoscopy is arranged and intravenous bolus of terlipressin is given. Which of the following is most appropriate for reducing mortality rate?
explanation:
Antibiotics
Intravenous cephalosporins and oral fluoroquinolones have shown a significant short-term survival improvement. This leads to one life saved in every 22 patients treated and an infection prevented in every four patients. Twenty per cent of variceal bleed patients exhibit signs of infection within 48 hours of admission.

Octreotide
Data from randomised trials on octreotide vs placebo show no difference in failure to control bleeding, transfusion volume or mortality.

Somatostatin
Somatostatin causes splanchnic vasoconstriction and reduces portal venous pressure. It has been shown to reduce the risk of failure to control bleeding, with a lower side-effect profile, compared to terlipressin. This has, however, been disputed in other trials.

Terlipressin
Terlipressin can be regarded as a circulating depot of lysine vasopressin. Following intravenous injection, three glycyl moieties are cleaved from the N-terminus to release lysine vasopressin. Vasopressin then reduces blood flow in the splanchnic circulation, thereby helping to reduce portal hypertension and reduce the risk of bleeding oesophageal varices. Side-effects include abdominal cramps, headache and raised blood pressure. Terlipressin has shown improvement in controlling bleeding, in comparison to placebo, but without an improvement in mortality. Terlipressin has several systemic side-effects, including increased peripheral venous resistance and reduction in cardiac output, heart rate and coronary blood flow. A 56 year old watercress farmer is admitted for worsening jaundice, pruritis and some right upper quadrant discomfort. He has dark urine and pale stools. There is no history of alcohol or IVDU use and no recent foreign travel. He occasionally takes NSAIDS for headaches, and St John's wort for depression. On examination he is afebrile, icteric, has some tenderness in the RUQ and hepatomegaly. US abdomen shows no gallstones, although intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts are dilated. What does the differential diagnosis include?

Tranexamic acid
The HALT-IT trial showed no reduction in mortality when using tranexamic acid in upper and lower gastrointestinal bleeds. This may be due to relatively low pressures of venous bleeding seen in most gastrointestinal bleeds or due to the delay in symptoms from the point of initiation of bleeding. Further research is required to provide a more detailed explanation for this result.

stem: Which of the features described is most indicative of advanced portal hypertension?
explanation:
Caput medusae
Caput medusae represents recanalisation of the paraumbilical veins, which normally close shortly after birth. This only occurs when there is marked portal hypertension, making it the correct answer here. Strict avoidance of alcohol, and treatment with propranolol and spironolactone are the key points of medical management in this case, but even these measures may be unlikely to have a very great effect on his long-term prognosis.

Ascites
Ascites is incorrect. While ascites may certainly be a manifestation of portal hypertension, it may also have other causes (e.g. development of hepatocellular carcinoma). In contrast, caput medusae always represents portal hypertension.

Decreased albumin
Decreased albumin is incorrect. Decreased albumin is consistent with chronic liver failure, but it is not a manifestation of portal hypertension.

Peripheral oedema
Peripheral oedema is incorrect. Peripheral oedema is commonly found in those with chronic liver failure, but it is not a manifestation of portal hypertension. Portal Hypertension You are asked to review a 42-year-old man with a history of Crohn’s disease, who has been admitted to the surgical ward for a partial small bowel resection. The dietician is asking about the usual requirements for potassium replacement each day. He weighs 80 kg.

Raised bilirubin
Raised bilirubin is incorrect. Raised bilirubin is consistent with chronic liver failure, but it is not a manifestation of portal hypertension.

stem: You are asked to review a 42-year-old man with a history of Crohn’s disease, who has been admitted to the surgical ward for a partial small bowel resection. The dietician is asking about the usual requirements for potassium replacement each day. He weighs 80 kg. Which of the following is a reasonable total daily potassium replacement?
explanation:
120 mmol
Studies suggest that average potassium replacement should be set at approximately 90-120 mmol/day according to WHO criteria. 120mmol is set at the higher end of the normal range to account for GI fluid loss. NICE guidelines recommend a daily replacement for potassium of 1 mmol/kg/day as a minimum which for this patient is 80 mmol. However, given the background of Crohn’s disease and the planned small bowel resection, he is likely to have increased GI losses of potassium and hence, a slightly higher daily replacement is appropriate. The WHO criteria for potassium replacement recommend anywhere from 90-120 mmol per day and hence, 120 mmol would be considered appropriate in this case.

20 mmol
20 mmol is incorrect. This is too little and may risk muscle weakness and potential exacerbation of any ileus.

40 mmol
40 mmol is incorrect. This is also too little.

60 mmol
60 mmol is incorrect. This level may be about right for a child’s requirement but is inadequate to meet an adult’s needs. Crohn’s Disease

170 mmol
170 mmol is incorrect. This level may be too much, unless there is evidence of excessive potassium loss, for example from a high-output stoma.

stem: A 28-year-old patient is admitted with severe exacerbation of his ulcerative colitis, opening his bowels 10 or more times per day with copious blood stained diarrhoea. He has been maintained on prednisolone 40mg daily and maximised mesalazine by his GP with little effect. Initial management in hospital includes IV corticosteroids, s/c heparin, IV fluids, and an abdominal film shows mucosal oedema but not toxic megacolon. You assess him 48hrs later. His BP is 110/60 mmHg, pulse is 92/min and regular. His abdominal tenderness has reduced and he has active bowel sounds. His Hb has fallen from 108 g/l on admission to 91 g/l and he is opening his bowels some 12 times /day. Which of the following is the correct next investigation?
explanation:
Flexible sigmoidoscopy
BSG guidelines are clear in recommending flexible sigmoidoscopy in confirming a flare of acute severe UC. Biopsies should be available within 72 h (ideally within 24 h), and a histological diagnosis within 5 days to confirm diagnosis and exclude cytomegalovirus (CMV). If CMV is confirmed, then it is associated with a very poor response to treatment and high relapse rate. Patients with UC are believed to have an increased risk for the colonic reactivation of CMV infection due to a combination of inherent and iatrogenic factors.

Colonoscopy
Colonoscopy is incorrect. A colonoscopy is not an appropriate investigation in the context of severe acute UC where there is a higher risk of perforation associated with the bowel prep as well as the longer procedure. The main aim is to confirm the diagnosis which can be achieved by visualizing the distal colon alone.

Repeat abdominal x-ray
Repeat abdominal x-ray is incorrect. A repeat abdominal X-ray will not provide any additional information, especially given it had been performed earlier. If the patient had significant pain and tenderness, a repeat abdominal X-ray may be appropriate to exclude toxic megacolon.

Barium enema
Barium enema is incorrect. Barium enema is contraindicated in acute severe UC. Ulcerative Colitis A 62-year-old patient with a history of type 2 diabetes is referred to the gastroenterology clinic with significant unintentional weight loss and epigastric pain radiating to her back. She has lost 8 kg in weight over the past three months. The epigastric pain is becoming more severe and radiates to her back. There is no history of water brash, dysphagia or regurgitation. Her medical history includes type 2 diabetes and hypertension. Cardiovascular and respiratory system examination is unremarkable. She is tender to palpation in the epigastrium. Investigations show:

Stool culture
Stool culture is incorrect. Stool cultures should be taken on admission to exclude an infectious cause of colitis. In this scenario, taking stool cultures will not provide information quickly enough especially as there is evidence that the patient is deteriorating. A flexible sigmoidoscopy should be performed urgently to confirm the diagnosis and obtain biopsies.

stem: A barium swallow shows evidence of severe oesophageal dysmotility and a gastroscopy shows a hiatus hernia and mild oesophagitis, with normal duodenal biopsies. Given the likely diagnosis, which of the following would be the most appropriate intervention?
explanation:
Metronidazole
The history described here is suggestive of bacterial overgrowth syndrome, which is known to be associated with systemic sclerosis, particularly where there is demonstrable dysmotility, as seen here. The best management strategy is unclear, but initial attempts at eradication of bacterial overgrowth with metronidazole, ciprofloxacin or co-amoxiclav is appropriate.

Doxycycline
Doxycycline is incorrect. Doxycycline has no role in the management of small bowel bacterial overgrowth.

Gluten-free diet
Gluten-free diet is incorrect. A gluten-free diet is unlikely to alleviate her symptoms given that the normal duodenal biopsy effectively excludes coeliac disease.

Metoclopramide
Metoclopramide is incorrect. Metoclopramide is a prokinetic drug that can be used to manage gastroparesis, which is associated with systemic sclerosis, but the history of loose stool and constipation does not support this diagnosis. Small Intestinal Bacterial Overgrowth (SIBO) A 57-year-old bar owner returns from the summer season in Tenerife. He visits the GP because he is having increasing relationship difficulties, and is unable to maintain his erection when attempting sexual intercourse with his partner. He admits to drinking a little too much, around 40 units of alcohol per week, and has a history of arthritis in his knees, for which he takes occasional diclofenac. On examination his BP is 155/92 mmHg, his pulse is 87 bpm and regular. He looks rather tanned, and has signs of chronic liver disease. His secondary sexual hair seems a little sparse. Investigations:

Ranitidine
Ranitidine is incorrect. Ranitidine can be used as additional acid suppression therapy, but given that this patient’s symptoms are not related to acid reflux, this is not the best intervention at present.

stem: A 64-year-old man, with a history of diabetes mellitus, returns from India after a two-week trip and presents with abdominal pain, fever, nausea and sweats. Examination reveals an enlarged tender liver. On ultrasound, several abscesses are visualised. An aspirate is taken from one of the abscesses. Which of the following organisms is most likely to be grown from the aspirate?
explanation:
Staphylococcus aureus
The most common causes of a pyogenic abscess are enterococci, Staphylococcus aureus and Escherichia coli, making S. aureus the correct answer here. Klebsiella histolytica is not a true bacterial organism; the other options given may all cause pyogenic abscess, but only very rarely. Patients with pyogenic abscesses typically present with pain, fever, shock and weight loss. Management is by ultrasound-guided drainage and antibiotics targeted to the cultured organism. Assessment for other gastrointestinal pathology sometimes reveals an underlying cause for loss of the normal bowel wall barrier to infections. Amoebic abscess tends to present later, unless the abscesses burst. These are caused by infection with Entamoeba histolytica. Again, they are managed with aspiration and appropriate antibiotics. Hydatid liver abscesses have a typical ultrasound appearance and should not be aspirated because of the risk of seeding and peritoneal spread.

Clostridium perfringens
Clostridium perfringens is incorrect. As outlined, C. perfringens only rarely causes pyogenic abscess.

Klebsiella histolytica
Klebsiella histolytica is incorrect. As described, K. histolytica is not a true bacterial organism.

Pseudomonas aeruginosa
Pseudomonas aeruginosa is incorrect. As outlined, P. aeruginosa only rarely causes pyogenic abscess. Liver AbscessEntamoeba histolytica
Entamoeba histolytica is incorrect. This anaerobic parasitic amoebozoan is a cause of non-pyogenic liver abscess, which is a less likely diagnosis here. Amoebic abscess tends to present later, unless the abscesses burst. An amoebic abscess is also more likely to solitary.

stem: A patient with a long history of rheumatoid arthritis and restrictive cardiomyopathy thought to be due to amyloidosis comes to the Gastroenterology Clinic. She has suffered from increasing episodes of diarrhoea over the past few months, and now has peripheral pitting oedema of both lower limbs. Her albumin is 22 g/l. You suspect her of having a protein-losing enteropathy. Measurement of which of the following in a sample of faeces would be most appropriate to confirm the diagnosis?
explanation:
α1-Antitrypsin
Albumin is degraded by proteases in the gut; however, α1-antitrypsin is a plasma protein that is resistant to degradation by proteases (it is a protease inhibitor) and its measurement can indicate leakage of plasma proteins into the gut. It is therefore the preferred investigation in patient suspected of having protein losing enteropathy.

Albumin
Albumin is incorrect. Albumin is degraded by proteases in the gut and is therefore not a reliable indicator of protein-losing enteropathy.

Calmodulin
Calmodulin is incorrect. Calmodulin is an intracellular calcium-binding protein.

Calprotectin
Calprotectin is incorrect. Faecal calprotectin is increased in inflammatory bowel disease; elevation of calprotectin would not therefore be expected in patients with amyloidosis.

Elastase
Elastase is incorrect. Faecal elastase is used as a measure of pancreatic insufficiencyand is therefore not useful here.

stem: A 56-year-old man complains of diarrhoea, abdominal pain, weight loss and joint pains, with two or three pale, bulky stools daily. A duodenal biopsy shows stunted villi and stains macrophages positively with PAS stain, and electron microscopy shows bacilli within the macrophages. What is the best treatment?
explanation:
IV ceftriaxone
This patient has Whipple’s disease. The causative organism is the Gram-positive bacillus Tropheryma whipplei. Diarrhoea and arthropathy are typical presenting features of the condition. The best test for the condition is a duodenal biopsy, with subtotal villous atrophy, PAS staining of macrophages and the presence of bacilli within macrophages confirming the diagnosis. Although Whipple’s disease most typically involves the gastrointestinal tract, involvement of the heart, brain and lungs is well recognised too. In Whipple's disease, without central nervous system involvement, the initial therapy is either ceftriaxone or penicillin intravenously for at least two weeks. This is followed by TMP-SMX for one-year.

Anti-tuberculosis treatment
Anti-tuberculosis treatment is incorrect. Whipple’s disease is caused by bacteria rather than mycobacteria, so anti-tuberculosis treatment will be of no benefit.

Gluten-free diet
Gluten-free diet is incorrect. Although the combination of diarrhoea and stunted villi on duodenal biopsy may suggest coeliac disease, coeliac disease would not explain the staining of macrophages with PAS stain or the presence of bacilli within macrophages. A gluten-free diet would be the right choice of treatment for coeliac disease, but will not be effective here.

Low-fat diet
A low-fat diet is incorrect. A low-fat diet may reduce some of this man’s diarrhoea, but it does not provide any specific treatment for his condition, so is not the correct choice here. Whipple’s Disease

Metronidazole
Metronidazole is incorrect. Metronidazole is not recognised as an antibiotic that is effective against the condition.

stem: A 76-year-old man is admitted with jaundice and weight loss. He has no history of abdominal pain or fevers. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Pancreatic adenocarcinoma
The combination of painless jaundice and weight loss in a person of this age is very suggestive of malignant obstruction of the biliary tree. Adenocarcinoma of the head of the pancreas would be the most likely cause of this, although other malignancies (including cholangiocarcinoma and ampullary tumours) would also be possibilities.

Choledocho-duodenal fistula
Choledocho-duodenal fistula is incorrect. Choledocho-duodenal fistulae typically cause abdominal pain and peritonism – and often an ileus – so this is also unlikely to be the diagnosis.

Chronic pancreatitis
Chronic pancreatitis is incorrect. Chronic pancreatitis typically presents with a long history of typical epigastric pancreatitic pain and weight loss; the lack of any prior abdominal pain here (or any risk factors for chronic pancreatitis, such as alcohol excess) means that this is unlikely to be the diagnosis here.

Gallstone obstruction
Gallstone obstruction is incorrect. Gallstone impaction within the common bile duct may result in jaundice, but weight loss would not be explained by this. Similarly, it would be unusual for a man of this age to have gallstone disease without other symptoms suggestive of biliary colic or cholecystitis in the past.

Mirizzi syndrome
Mirizzi syndrome is incorrect. Mirizzi syndrome is impaction of a gallstone in the cystic duct, so is unlikely to result in a presentation similar to that described here.

stem: A 37-year-old man presents to his GP with long-standing dyspeptic symptoms. He tests positive for Helicobacter pylori, which is treated with omeprazole 20 mg, amoxicillin 1 g and clarithromycin 500 mg all twice a day for 1 week. Two months later his symptoms return. His weight is stable and there is no history of gastrointestinal bleeding or non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) use. What would be the most appropriate way of confirming eradication of H. pylori in this man?
options: Endoscopy and biopsy for H. pylori sensitivities
explanation:
[13C] urea breath test
Confirmation of H.pylori eradication should occur at least 4 weeks after completion of antibiotics and whilst off PPIs for at least 2 weeks. Non-invasive tests should be used unless the patient has complex peptic ulcer disease or MALT lymphoma. The 13C urea breath testing is the most specific and sensitive non- invasive test. This involves ingesting a drink that is labelled with 13C urea. If H.pylori is present, its urease enzyme will convert the urea to ammonia and 13C labelled C02, which will be detected in the expired air. The breath test is the only currently validated method for assessing eradication in primary care

Endoscopy and biopsy for H. pylori sensitivities
Endoscopy and biopsy for H. pylori sensitivities is incorrect. Endoscopy and culture of H. pylori is only successful in 30–40% of positive biopsies and is an invasive test that is not indicated from the history.

Endoscopy and urease test
Endoscopy and urease test is incorrect. Endoscopy and urease testing is an invasive test that is not indicated in this context.

Faecal H.pylori antigen
Faecal H.pylori antigen is incorrect. Faecal H.pylori antigen is less sensitive and specific than the 13C urea breath test.

H.pylori serology
H.pylori serology is incorrect. H. pylori serology is an IgG test and cannot distinguish between current and past. H.pylori is strongly associated with gastritis, gastric and duodenal ulceration, gastric cancer and MALT lymphoma. Spontaneous eradication is rare. Treatment involves two antibiotics and a PPI for one week. Treatment failure is usually due to poor compliance or antibiotic resistance.

stem: A 57-year-old publican was referred by his general practitioner with chronic central upper abdominal pain. He admitted to drinking three or four pints of beer most evenings in the pub. Over the past 18 months, he had lost about 12.5 kg (2 stones) in weight, and his wife described that he preferred alcohol to food. He also had intermittent diarrhoea, which he reported as being occasionally oily and difficult to flush away. Examination revealed a thin man with tenderness to deep palpation in the epigastrium. Blood tests revealed a mild normochromic normocytic anaemia and a raised alanine aminotransferase (ALT) level to twice the upper limit of normal. Amylase level was normal, and anti-gliadin antibodies were not detected. Upper abdominal ultrasound was performed, which demonstrated diffuse pancreatic calcification but nothing else of note. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Chronic pancreatitis
Chronic pancreatitis The combination of chronic epigastric pain, steatorrhoea, weight loss and pancreatic calcification in a person with alcohol excess is together very suggestive of underlying chronic pancreatitis. Excess alcohol consumption is the most common cause for this condition, accounting for up to 80% of cases in the developed world. At least one way in which alcohol is believed to contribute to the condition is through alteration of the balance of trypsinogen in the pancreas. Other causes of chronic pancreatitis include structural abnormalities of the pancreatic duct, genetic causes (e.g. cystic fibrosis transmembrane regulator gene mutations), and autoimmune disease. The most frequent clinical manifestation of chronic pancreatitis is with epigastric pain, with other clinical features including those of exocrine pancreatic failure (weight loss, steatorrhoea) and endocrine failure (impaired glucose tolerance/diabetes mellitus). The diagnosis is made through a combination of tests of the function of the pancreas (with faecal elastase having largely replaced other functional tests), and imaging of the pancreas (usually via CT and/or MRCP). Since pancreatic carcinoma is well recognised as a potential complication of chronic pancreatitis, - but that distinguishing one diagnosis from the other may be difficult on imaging - then endoscopic ultrasound may also be very useful. The mainstay of treatment is removal of any precipitating factor (i.e. abstinence from alcohol), with other important therapies including pain relief and supplementation of pancreatic enzymes.

Acute pancreatitis
Acute pancreatitis is incorrect. The normal amylase level makes acute pancreatitis unlikely, while the presence of pancreatic calcification is much more consistent with chronic pancreatitic disease rather than acute.

Coeliac disease
Coeliac disease is incorrect. Weight loss and malabsorptive diarrhoea may make coeliac disease seem a possibility, but the abdominal pain described would be very atypical for this diagnosis; furthermore, negative anti-gliadin antibodies also make this unlikely.

Gastric carcinoma
Gastric carcinoma is incorrect. Gastric carcinoma could fit with most of the symptoms described, but would not explain this man’s steatorrhoea; in addition, pancreatic calcification would not be consistent with gastric disease. Chronic Pancreatitis Which condition is most strongly associated with gastric acid hypersecretion?

Recurrent cholecystitis
Recurrent cholecystitis is incorrect. Although chronic cholecystitis could result in abdominal pain and abnormal liver enzymes, it would not typically cause steatorrhoea, and would also not explain the pancreatic calcification described.

stem: Which condition is most strongly associated with gastric acid hypersecretion?
explanation:
Systemic mastocytosis
Several hormones in the small intestine inhibit gastrin and gastric acid secretion in vivo; resection of the small bowel leads to the removal of this inhibition, and gastric acid hypersecretion results. Systemic mastocytosis is associated with increased histamine production, and consequently increased gastric acid secretion.

Cushing syndrome
Cushing syndrome is incorrect. Corticosteroid therapy and Cushing syndrome have both been associated with peptic ulcer disease; however, it has not been demonstrated that this relationship is due to gastric acid hypersecretion.

Large-bowel resection
Large-bowel resection is incorrect. In contrast to the case with the small intestine, there is no evidence that large-bowel resection has any effect on gastric acid secretion.

Pernicious anaemia
Pernicious anaemia is incorrect. In pernicious anaemia, gastrin levels are elevated in the presence of mucosal atrophy in the body of the stomach, and acid production is therefore reduced.

Vasoactive intestinal polypeptide- (VIP-)secreting tumour
Vasoactive intestinal polypeptide- (VIP-)secreting tumour is incorrect. VIP inhibits gastric acid secretion, and achlorhydria is a feature of VIP-secreting tumours; this option therefore can be ruled out.

stem: Which of the following tests is required before confirming irritable bowel syndrome?
explanation:
Coeliac Serology
In the presence of a normal haematology and biochemistry screen, and normal physical examination makes irritable bowel syndrome the most likely diagnosis. Coeliac disease may however be a possibility and should be excluded, particularly as it can mimic symptoms of IBS. If it proves to be positive, following a gluten-free diet may significantly impact on his symptoms.

Barium enema
Barium enema is incorrect. There is no indication of underlying GI blood loss and no evidence of raised ESR suggestive of malignancy or inflammatory bowel disease.

CT abdomen
CT abdomen is incorrect. CT abdomen is not indicated given the very low risk of significant intra-abdominal pathology in this patient.

Sigmoidoscopy
Sigmoidoscopy is incorrect. Although sigmoidoscopy may be considered for reassurance, it’s invasive. A sequence of investigations where lactose intolerance is ruled out first is more appropriate.

Upper GI endoscopy with biopsy
Upper GI endoscopy with biopsy is incorrect. There is no indication of peptic ulcer disease, and although coeliac disease cannot be ruled out, serology has a high sensitivity and specificity for the underlying diagnosis.

stem: A 56-year-old homeless patient attends the emergency department as he has been feeling very dizzy and weak. He reports a 3-day history of diarrhoea and vomiting. On examination, he is pale. His BMI is 18 and he has dry skin, ridged nails, peripheral neuropathy, and angular stomatitis. His blood tests show that he is anaemic with a raised MCV, and has several dietary deficiencies. Which of the following vitamin deficiencies is most likely to be present?
explanation:
Vitamin B12
B12 deficiency is associated with peripheral neuropathy and angular stomatitis, which fits well with the symptoms here, especially as a homeless patient may well have an alcohol concern coupled with nutritional deficiency.

Chromium
Chromium is incorrect. Chromium deficiency is rare, and can occasionally occur after long term after total parenteral nutrition. Chromium deficiency can result in impaired glucose metabolism and glucose intolerance.

Copper
Copper is incorrect. Copper deficiency is rare, as daily requirements are very low. Deficiency can cause neurological symptoms of peripheral neuropathy and optic neuropathy as well as haematological manifestations of anaemia and neutropenia.

Selenium
Selenium is incorrect. Selenium is involved in the conversion of thyroxine (T4) into its active counterpart triiodothyronine (T3). Deficiency is rare and occurs usually in the context of patients on TPN without selenium supplementation, or in Keshan disease which is an endemic form of dilated cardiomyopathy found in some areas of China.

Vitamin C
Vitamin C is incorrect. Vitamin C is associated with symptoms of scurvy, not seen here.

stem: A 43-year-old man presented with bloody diarrhoea and weight loss. Which one of the following findings would favour a diagnosis of Crohn’s disease on rectal biopsy?
explanation:
Patchy inflammation
Crohn’s disease is characterised histologically by transmural (full-thickness) inflammation, in contrast to ulcerative colitis. The inflammation is patchy with ‘skip lesions’. Non-caseating granulomas are present in 20– 40% of cases. In ulcerative colitis, inflammation is confined to the mucosa and submucosa only. The inflammation is confluent and histological changes to the crypts are common, including crypt distortion, neutrophilic crypt distraction and crypt abscesses.

Crypt abscesses
Crypt abscesses is incorrect. Crypt abscesses are found much less commonly in Crohn’s disease than in ulcerative colitis.

Crypt distortion
Crypt distortion is incorrect. Crypt distortion is found much less commonly in Crohn’s disease than in ulcerative colitis.

Inflammatory infiltrates
Inflammatory infiltrates is incorrect. Inflammatory infiltrates are found in both conditions, and are therefore not helpful in distinguishing one condition from the other. Crohn’s Disease A 40-year-old man, who has Crohn's disease confined to the colon, is reviewed in clinic. He has been suffering from diarrhoea > 6 times/day, which has been unresponsive to corticosteroids and mesalazine (which he has been taking for 3 weeks). He had also had an exacerbation earlier in the year that required a weaning dose of corticosteroids. Investigations:

Superficial ulceration
Superficial ulceration is incorrect. As described, Crohn’s is characterised by transmural inflammation.

stem: A 34-year-old man presented with symptoms of reflux oesophagitis. He was started on lansoprazole because he has already made appropriate lifestyle changes without complete resolution of the reflux symptoms. What is the mode of action of lansoprazole?
options: It binds to the histamine H1 receptor
It binds to the histamine H2 receptor
It inhibits the hydrogen–calcium-ATP proton pump
It inhibits the hydrogen–potassium-ATP proton pump
It inhibits the hydrogen–sodium-ATP proton pump
explanation:
It inhibits the hydrogen–potassium-ATP proton pump
Lansoprazole is a commonly prescribed proton-pump inhibitor. Like all the drugs within this class, it functions by blocking the hydrogen–potassium-ATP pump that allows the gastric parietal cells to secrete acid. These drugs are indicated for acid suppression to treat a range of conditions, including peptic ulceration, oesophagitis, and for Helicobacter pylori eradication as part of a triple-therapy regime.

It binds to the histamine H1 receptor
It binds to the histamine H 1 receptor is incorrect. Histamine H1-receptor antagonists are those medications used to treat allergic reactions, including cetirizine and loratidine; however, such medications do not have a significant effect on acid suppression.

It binds to the histamine H2 receptor
It binds to the histamine H2 receptor is incorrect. Histamine H2-receptor blocking drugs (such as ranitidine) act directly upon the GI tract to reduce gastric acid secretion; however, lansoprazole is not a member of this family, and has a different mechanism of action.

It inhibits the hydrogen–calcium-ATP proton pump
It inhibits the hydrogen–calcium-ATP proton pump is incorrect. Lansoprazole and related medications function via inhibition of hydrogen–potassium-ATP proton pumps, but not via interaction with hydrogen–calcium-ATP proton pumps.

It inhibits the hydrogen–sodium-ATP proton pump
It inhibits the hydrogen–sodium-ATP proton pump is incorrect. Lansoprazole and related medications function via inhibition of hydrogen–potassium-ATP proton pumps, but not via interaction with hydrogen–sodium-ATP proton pumps.

stem: A 46-year-old woman was referred with profuse watery diarrhoea and dehydration. Investigations showed an average daily stool weight of 4353 g/24 hours and a serum vasoactive intestinal polypeptide (VIP) level of > 400 pg/ml (normal range < 20 pg/ml). What is the most likely mechanism of her diarrhoea?
options: Osmotic secondary to high oral water intake
explanation:
Secretory due to enterocyte stimulation
The diagnosis is VIPoma, a gut hormone-secreting tumour that is typically found in the pancreas or small bowel (VIP stands for vasoactive intestinal polypeptide). The diarrhoea is secretory (due to VIP causing general cellular secretion), with the result being massive, watery diarrhoea and electrolytes deficiencies (particularly hypokalaemia). The normal daily stool weight is 250–300 g, so the figures given here are significantly elevated.

Infective due to small-bowel overgrowth
