Epidemiology  Fifty per cent of liver cirrhosis patients will develop ascites in < 10 years.  Approximately 75% of patients presenting with ascites have underlying cirrhosis. Aetiology  The most common cause of ascites is related to portal hypertension from cirrhosis (75%).  Other causes can be subdivided into vascular, low albumin, peritoneal disease and miscellaneous:  vascular – aside from liver disease with portal hypertension, other potential vascular causes include:  Budd–Chiari syndrome – thrombosis or obstruction of the hepatic vein due to:  tumour  haematological disease  the oral contraceptive pill.  congestive cardiac failure  constrictive pericarditis.  low albumin:  nephrotic syndrome  protein-losing enteropathy.  peritoneal disease – including:  Meigs syndrome (pleural effusion, ascites and benign ovarian tumour)  infectious peritonitis such as tuberculosis or fungal disease  malignancy (especially ovarian and gastrointestinal).  other causes include:  pancreatic leak  chylous ascites  peritoneal dialysis-related ascites  occasionally occurs in advanced hypothyroidism.  Most common risk factors for cirrhosis in the United Kingdom and Europe:  alcohol misuse  hepatitis B and C infection  obesity or type II diabetes – at risk of developing nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) which progresses to cirrhosis.  Less common causes of cirrhosis:  autoimmune liver disease (autoimmune hepatitis, primary biliary cholangitis, primary sclerosing cholangitis)  genetic conditions (eg haemochromatosis, Wilson’s disease, alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency, cystic fibrosis)  medication use over a long period of time, eg methotrexate  Budd–Chiari syndrome or veno-occlusive disease  sarcoidosis  glycogen storage disease.  Causes of liver failure: G

Pathophysiology  Ascites is the accumulation of free fluid within the peritoneal cavity.  In cases caused by portal hypertension, hypertension in the portal system causes a transudative ascitic fluid as the increased portal pressure forces fluid into the extracellular space.  Clinical Presentation  Patients may present with:  visible abdominal distention  weight gain  abdominal discomfort  abdominal pain (more typical of malignancy-related causes)  nausea and vomiting  in cases of large volumes of ascites, patients may present with dyspnoea due to impaired expansion of the lungs  patients may also present with symptoms related to the understanding cause. General examination  Examination of the patient would include a full examination for all stigmata of chronic liver disease in addition to clues regarding the underlying cause.  Inspection:  stand at the end of the bed, note the presence or absence of pigmentation, jaundice and malnourishment  check for abdominal scars, fistulae and signs of glucose testing  the patient may be dyspnoeic from diaphragmatic splinting  in the hands, check for clinical signs of cirrhosis:  Dupuytren's contracture  palmar erythema  leukonychia  asterixis.  spider naevi are found in the distribution of the superior vena cava in cirrhosis  check the eyes for corneal arcus, xanthelasma, jaundice and anaemia  in the mouth, check for angular stomatitis and ulcers  while the patient is sitting forward, the neck should be checked for lymphadenopathy, including Troisier’s sign.  Check the axilla and chest for:  acanthosis nigricans  spider naevi

Examination of the abdomen  Look for scars, fullness in flanks, descending masses and distended veins (eg caput medusae).  An umbilical nodule could suggest a malignant aetiology.  When palpating, palpate all nine quadrants (superficially, then deeply).  Then palpate the:  liver edge  spleen edge  kidneys.  Then examine for ascites.  Percuss for ascites:  percuss away from you and while keeping your finger horizontal, ask the patient to roll towards you and assess whether there is shifting dullness.  Auscultation, check for bowel sounds and renal bruits.  Examine for peripheral oedema. Examination for ascites  Examine for shifting dullness:  percuss the patient's abdomen from the level of the umbilicus and repeat, moving laterally towards one side:  when the sound becomes dull, keep fingers at this spot and ask the patient to move onto their opposite side  wait briefly for the fluid to move and percuss again  if it is now resonant to percussion, this is a positive test  percuss down until dullness is reached again  repeat on the other side.  Large ascites can be detected by a 'fluid thrill':  two examiners are required; the first places the side of the palm of one hand firmly on the centre of the abdomen, with the fingers pointing towards the groin  the second examiner places the palm of one hand on one flank and then flicks the other flank  a positive test is when palpable fluid thrill can be felt by the palm resting on the opposite flank.  Differential Diagnosis  Differentials for ascites may include:  flatus (bowel distention or obstruction)  fetus (pregnancy)  obesity  tumour  haematoperitoneum.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Diagnosis of ascites involves a detailed history including past medical history, followed by an examination to confirm the presence of ascites as well as a full examination for all stigmata of G

Autoimmune Hepatitis  Autoimmune hepatitis is an inflammatory liver disease of unknown cause.  Overview Key Facts  Autoimmune hepatitis (AIH) is an inflammatory liver disease of unknown cause.  Autoimmune hepatitis is associated with concurrent autoimmune disorders in roughly 40% of patients, including:  pernicious anaemia  ulcerative colitis  glomerulonephritis  autoimmune thyroiditis  autoimmune haemolysis  diabetes mellitus  primary sclerosing cholangitis  coeliac disease  rheumatoid arthritis.  Treatment depends on severity and may include one or more of the following:  regular monitoring  immunosuppressant therapy  transplantation.  The outcome for treated patients is very good.  Complications include hyperviscosity syndrome and hepatocellular carcinoma. Epidemiology  Commonly affects young or middle-aged women.  Bimodal ages affected:  10–30 years old, or  > 40 years old.  The greatest prevalence is among people of Northern-European descent who have a high frequency of human leukocyte antigen (HLA)-DR3 and HLA-DR4. Aetiology  The aetiology is unknown.

Benign Neck Lumps and Swellings  Benign neck lumps and swelling can be either congenital or acquired, and can arise from a number of anatomical structures in the neck. G

JAM  Overview Key Facts  Benign neck lumps and swelling can be either congenital or acquired, and can arise from a number of anatomical structures in the neck.  The most common benign soft tissue tumours found in the neck are lipomas, which usually present as asymptomatic, soft, poorlydefined masses deep to the skin.  Other benign neck lumps include:  cystic hygroma  thyroglossal cyst  branchial cyst  ranula  laryngocele  sialadenitis/sialithiasis (covered separately)  pharyngeal pouch (covered separately).  Occasionally what a patient might identify as a lump is actually part of their normal anatomy, eg structures such as:  transverse process of C1 vertebra  hyoid bone  thyroid or cricoid cartilage.  If the diagnosis is uncertain, referral should not be delayed by undertaking investigations in primary care, particularly in high-risk individuals. Epidemiology Cystic hygroma  Cystic hygromas occur in approximately one per cent of children with no particular gender or ethnic preponderance. Thyroglossal cyst  Occurs in around 7% of the population and most commonly presents in childhood. Branchial cyst  The most common cause of congenital neck masses, the majority present in childhood.  Occasionally they may present later in life, usually by early adulthood. Ranula  Ranulas usually present in childhood or early adulthood. Laryngocele  The condition is rare, and believed to be more frequent in wind instrument players and glassblowers. Aetiology  Congenital:  thyroglossal cyst  branchial cyst  cystic hygroma.  Most common acquired benign neck masses are:

Pathophysiology Thyroglossal cyst  Persistent connection between the caecum of the tongue and the pyramidal lobe of the thyroid gland causing a mass in the midline. Branchial cyst  Congenital epithelial cysts occurring lateral from the midline, thought to be due to failure of obliteration of the second branchial cleft in embryonic development. Cystic hygroma  A cystic lymphatic lesion that occurs in the posterior triangle of the neck.  Most present at birth or before the age of two years. Ranula  A type of mucocele in the floor of the mouth originating from the sublingual glands.  The two principal causes are:  a blocked duct causing a swelling  a ruptured cyst that leads to extravasation of mucin. Laryngocele  An air pocket that arises from the deepest point of the laryngeal ventricle.  Clinical Presentation Thyroglossal cyst  Midline cystic lump that is near the hyoid bone and moves upwards when the individual swallows or protrudes their tongue. Branchial cyst  painless, slow-growing, smooth, fluctuant swellings in the lateral neck. Cystic hygroma  Can be seen on antenatal ultrasound scans in pregnancy, commonly found in neck and axillae, soft painless swellings, sometimes translucent. Ranula  Clear/bluish cysts usually contained within the floor of the mouth (mylohyoid) but can push through. Laryngocele  An air-filled cyst can bulge internally into the larynx, externally into the neck or be combined (where the connection is through the thyrohyoid membrane).  They usually present with an intermittent neck swelling, which becomes palpable when the the valsalva manoeuvre is performed.  Differential Diagnosis  Thyroid lump/swelling – may be nodular or diffuse  Inflammatory lymphadenopathy  Malignant lesions  Normal anatomical structures. Budd-Chiari and Veno-occlusive Disease  Budd-Chiari syndrome is a disorder affecting the liver and blood vessels, where blood flowing into the liver has difficulty in being able to flow out.  Overview Key Facts  Budd–Chiari syndrome (BCS) is a rare condition.  BCS involves hepatic venous outflow obstruction at any level from the small hepatic veins to the junction of the inferior vena cava (IVC) and the right atrium.  Patients present with acute, subacute or chronic liver failure.  Diagnosis of BCS can usually be established non-invasively using a Doppler ultrasonography.  An underlying diagnosis can be found in 80% of patients with BCS, so it is necessary to also perform investigations for these predisposing conditions.  Veno-occlusive disease (VOD), also known as sinusoidal obstruction syndrome (SOS), most commonly occurs in patients undergoing haematopoietic cell transplantation.  VOD/SOS clinically resembles BCS; however, venous outflow obstruction in VOD is due to occlusion of terminal hepatic venules and sinusoids rather than hepatic veins and the IVC. Epidemiology  BCS is rare but potentially life-threatening.  1/100 000 of general population worldwide are affected by BCS.  BCS is more common in women in their third or fourth decade of life. G

DR. JAM Aetiology  BCS:  myeloproliferative disorders occurring in 50% of cases  polycythaemia vera is most common  essential thrombocythemia  hypercoaguable disorders, such as:  factor V Leiden  protein C and S deficiency  antithrombin III deficiency  paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria  antiphospholipid syndrome.  Bechet syndrome  systemic lupus erythematosus  mixed connective tissue disease  Sjögren’s syndrome  irritable bowel disease  sarcoidosis  minimal change nephrotic syndrome  alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency.  pregnancy and the immediate post-partum period are related to hormonal changes and IVC compression which predispose to BCS, as well as oral contraceptives  secondary BCS may be due to external compression or invasion of the venous lumen by abscess, tumours (10%), trauma or cysts  idiopathic forms (20%) are common in South Asia.  Venous-occlusive disease:  haematopoietic cell transplantation  chemotherapy, eg oxaliplatin  pyrrolizidine alkaloids (Jamaican bush tea)  high-dose radiation therapy to liver  post-liver transplantation. Pathophysiology  BCS:  obstruction leads to increased portal vein and hepatic sinusoid pressures as blood flow stagnates  decreased portal perfusion, leading to compensatory increase in arterial perfusion  increased sinusoidal pressure and decreased sinusoidal blood flow can lead to portal hypertension  resulting venous congestion causes ischaemic damage and necrosis of adjacent hepatocytes  hypoxia stimulates sinusoidal lining cells to release free radicals, contributing further to oxidative hepatocyte injury.  Veno-occlusive disease:  toxic injury to the liver sinusoids causes endothelial cells to slough, leading to embolisation of hepatic venules, causing fibrosis of the venules leading to hepatic congestion and post-sinusoidal portal hypertension.

C.difficile and Pseudomembranous Colitis  Pseudomembranous colitis is an acute exudative colitis that is most commonly associated with toxins produced by the overgrowth of Clostridium difficile.  Overview Key Facts  Pseudomembranous colitis is an acute exudative colitis that is most commonly associated with toxins produced by the overgrowth of Clostridium difficile (C.difficile).  The condition is precipitated by broad spectrum antibiotic use disrupting normal gut flora, and is more common in elderly or chronically ill patients in hospital.  The condition is a major healthcare problem and accounts for up to 25% of all hospital acquired diarrhoea cases associated with antibiotic use.  The most common causative agents include:  ampicillin G

DR. JAM  cephalosporins  clindamycin  carbapenems  fluroquinolones.  Patient-to-patient spread in hospital is common through the faecaloral route.  Signs and symptoms of C.difficile infection vary depending on severity, ranging from asymptomatic carrier status to severe pseudomembranous colitis which may be associated with severe and copious diarrhoea which may be bloody, with associated fever and abdominal pain.  Treatment depends on severity of C.difficile infection and may include rehydration and replacement of electrolytes, removal or change of antibiotics, oral vancomycin or metronidazole, and in severe cases may require surgical intervention.  Pseudomembranous colitis is associated with significant morbidity and mortality levels; appropriate and limited antibiotic prescribing as well as rapid detection and management of the condition as it develops plays a significant role in reducing this. Epidemiology  The condition is a major healthcare problem and accounts for up to 25% of all hospital acquired diarrhoea cases associated with antibiotic use.  The mortality rate of C.difficile infection in the elderly is up to 25%. Aetiology  Overgrowth of Clostridium difficile, which is precipitated by broad spectrum antibiotics.  Broad-spectrum antibiotics disrupt the normal bowel flora.  Most common causative agents are:  ampicillin  cephalosporins  clindamycin  carbapenems  fluroquinolones.  Patient-to-patient spread in hospital is common through the faecaloral route  Risk factors for developing the condition include:  increasing age  long duration of hospital care/long-term care facilities  immunocompromise  prolong antibiotic courses  presence of co-morbidities. Pathophysiology  Clostridium difficile is a gram-positive, anaerobic, sporeforming rod that produces toxin A and B.  Toxin A and B cause an inflammatory response in the large intestine leading to vascular permeability and pseudomembrane formation.

Chronic Kidney Disease  Chronic Kidney Disease is defined as evidence of kidney damage (eg urinary abnormality such as haematuria or proteinuria; abnormal structure of the kidney) or estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) < 60 ml/min for at least 3 months.  Overview Key Facts  Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD) is defined as evidence of kidney damage (eg urinary abnormality such as haematuria or proteinuria; abnormal structure of the kidney) or estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) < 60 ml/min for at least 3 months.  End stage renal disease (ESRD) is defined as eGFR < 15 ml/min/1.72 m2, or need for renal replacement therapy or dialysis.  There are numerous causes including hypertension, diabetes, acute kidney injury (AKI), and cardiovascular disease.  Ageing is a major risk factor for CKD/ESRD, prevalence is greatest in the elderly population (more than 90% off all cases occur in patients aged over 60). Epidemiology  Ageing is one of the major risk factors for CKD/ESRD.  Prevalence is greatest in the elderly population (more than 90% off all cases occur in patients aged over 60 with less than 0.5% occurring in patients under 40).  The age-standardised prevalence of CKD stages 3–5 is estimated by NICE to be 8.5% (10.6% in women, and 5.8% in men).  ESRD patients joining RRT programmes in the UK is about 125/million each year.  The prevalence of patients on UK RRT programmes is 800/million. Aetiology  The most common causes of ESRD in the UK are:  diabetic nephropathy (17%)  chronic glomerulonephritis (including: focal segmental glomerulus’s, IgA nephropathy and lupus nephritis) (15%)  hypertension and renal artery stenosis (15%)  chronic pyelonephritis (10%) – most often due to reflux nephropathy, but also renal calculi (nephrolithiasis) with infection  polycystic kidney disease (8%)  obstructive uropathy (including: renal stones and benign prostatic hyperplasia) (5%)  post-acute kidney injury (5%)  chronic tubulointerstitial nephritis (4%), eg sarcoidosis, lithium toxicity, and myeloma  amyloidosis (1%).  Rarer causes of CKD include:  analgesic nephropathy  other hereditary disorders, eg Alport syndrome  toxic nephropathy  after nephrectomy for renal tumours.  In 15% of cases of ESRD the aetiology remains unknown as patients present with small kidneys where biopsy would be unhelpful. They are most likely a result of hypertension, chronic glomerulonephritis, pyelonephritis, or dysplastic kidneys.  Patients with the following conditions are considered to be at high risk of developing CKD and should be assessed for CKD:  diabetes  hypertensive

Pathophysiology  Although most cases of advanced CKD are slowly progressive towards ESRD, patients with particular pathologies (eg postobstructive atrophy and hypertension – when controlled) may manifest stable CKD for many years.  Progression is multifactorial. It is thought that the reninangiotensin (RAA) system plays a major role:  vasoactive mediators angiotensin and aldosterone exacerbate the intraglomerular hypertension seen in remaining nephrons increasing proteinuria, which itself directly damages tubular cells  RAA system upregulation also provokes increased inflammation and oxidative stress, and stimulates fibrosis within the tubulointerstitium (See figure below). JAM  dehydration  tachypnoea  uraemic frost – precipitation of urea on the skin  oedema  palpable bilateral flank masses  hepatomegaly  distended bladder  hypertension  peripheral oedema  peripheral neuropathy  frothy urine.  Differential Diagnosis  Many cases of CKD progress so slowly that very abnormal biochemistry is relatively well tolerated by the patient:  However, 15–20% of ESRD patients initially present as uraemic emergencies (two-fold worse prognosis). The key parameters that differentiate CKD from AKI are:  small kidneys at imaging  anaemia – normocytic  CKD related mineral bone disorder  clinical tolerance of very severe uraemia.  Diagnosis/Investigation  There are several recognised stages of CKD (see table below):  Stage 1: renal function is normal (eGFR > 90 ml/min): urinary or structural abnormalities (eg type I diabetes and microalbuminuria).  Stage 2: eGFR 60–89 ml/min and urinary/renal structural abnormalities also require follow-up.  Note CKD stages 1 and 2:  will not have renal-related anaemia – if present, another cause should be sought  will not have CKD–mineral and bone disorder (see other relevant information)  may have hypertension.  Stage 3: Largest proportion (eg 6% of the UK adult population). Over 95% will not be at risk of future progression as their eGFR is simply reduced from ageing and thus is divided into two stages:  Stage 3a patients (eGFR 45–59 ml/min) being considered at low risk (unless they have associated proteinuria)  a high proportion of stage 3 patients will be hypertensive, because this too is associated with ageing  renal-related anaemia and secondary hyperparathyroidism may begin during stage 3b CKD, because it is at this level of renal function that perturbations in erythropoietin production and vitamin D metabolism start to occur (phosphate remains normal).  Stage 4: most patients will be hypertensive, and many are anaemic. Cirrhosis and Liver Failure  Cirrhosis is the irreversible distortion and nodules and surrounding fibrosis of the normal smooth liver architecture.

GIT & LIVER part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Overview Key Facts  Cirrhosis is the irreversible distortion and nodules and surrounding fibrosis of the normal smooth liver architecture.  The condition develops progressively, usually over years as a result of repeated damage.  Cirrhosis affects the liver’s synthetic, metabolic and excretory actions.  Cirrhosis can be divided into:  compensated cirrhosis: liver can still function effectively; with no, or few, noticeable clinical symptoms  decompensated cirrhosis: liver becomes damaged to the point when it cannot function adequately and clinical complications eg jaundice, ascites, variceal haemorrhage, and hepatic encephalopathy.  Liver failure may be recognised by the development of coagulopathy and encephalopathy. Epidemiology  The true prevalence of cirrhosis can become difficult to assess as the initial stages of it are often asymptomatic.  Liver disease affects 600 000 people, of those 60 000 have cirrhosis.  Between 2005–2015 there was a 49% increase in the number of admissions with a diagnosis of cirrhosis in England.  Six in 1 million people between 1992 and 2009 were affected by acute liver failure – the most common cause being overdose of paracetamol. Aetiology  Most common risk factors for cirrhosis in the United Kingdom (UK) and Europe:  alcohol misuse  hepatitis B and C infection  obesity or type II diabetes: at risk of developing nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) which progress to cirrhosis.  Less common causes of cirrhosis:  autoimmune liver disease (autoimmune hepatitis, primary biliary cholangitis, primary sclerosing cholangitis)  genetic conditions (eg haemochromatosis, Wilson’s disease, alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency, cystic fibrosis)  medication use over a long period of time eg methotrexate  Budd-Chiari syndrome or veno-occlusive disease  Sarcoidosis  glycogen storage disease.  Causes of liver failure:  infections: viral hepatitis (B,C,CMV), yellow fever  drugs: most commonly paracetamol overdose  vascular: Budd-Chiari syndrome or veno-occlusive disease G

Coeliac Disease  Coeliac disease is an autoimmune condition in which gluten (dietary protein found in barley, wheat and rye) activates an abnormal mucosal response causing characteristic damage and chronic inflammation to the lining of the small intestine.  Overview Key Facts  Coeliac disease is an autoimmune condition in which gluten (dietary protein found in barley, wheat and rye) activates an abnormal mucosal response causing characteristic damage and chronic inflammation to the lining of the small intestine.  Coeliac disease is also known as:  gluten-sensitive enteropathy  coeliac sprue  non-tropical sprue.  Refractory coeliac disease is the recurrence of malabsorptive clinical signs and symptoms associated with villous atrophy in coeliac patients who have, for more than 12 months, adhered to a gluten-free diet.  Coeliac disease commonly affects the proximal part of small intestine.  Treatment is largely adhering to a gluten-free diet.  Prognosis is generally good, with recovery from symptoms in up to 90% of patients with gluten avoidance. Epidemiology  There is a rise in patients being diagnosed with coeliac disease worldwide; the prevalence globally is estimated to be 1%.  Incidence of coeliac disease in the United Kingdom is 1 in 100 people.  Coeliac disease is twice as common in women than men.  It is prevalent in any age, but peaks in childhood and 50–60 years old. Aetiology  Gluten peptides are found in barley, wheat and rye.

GIT & LIVER part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  There is an increased immunological response to ingested gluten; the reason for this is unknown, but there are predisposing factors:  genetic predisposition:  association to HLA antigens  presence of HLA-DQ2 in 95%, the rest are DQ8.  immunological factors:  patients with autoimmune conditions, eg type I diabetes mellitus and autoimmune thyroid disease have an increased risk of developing coeliac disease.  The prevalence of coeliac disease also correlates with a high wheat consumption.  First-degree relatives of patients with coeliac disease have a 10– 15% risk of coeliac disease themselves. Pathophysiology  Symptoms are due to a genetically predisposed individual developing an immunological response to gluten peptide antigens which are derived from prolamins in wheat (gliadin), rye (secalin), barley (hordein), and related grains.  In coeliac disease, these gluten peptides are resistant to human proteases, enabling them to persist in the small intestinal lumen.  these peptides trigger immune activation in the intestinal submucosa – mediated by T helper cells.  Tissue transglutaminase is released in response of gluten consumption and modifies gluten peptides into a form that stimulates the immune system more effectively.  Epithelium of small intestine is damaged, causing:  loss of brush border  villous atrophy  crypt hyperplasia.  Resorption of nutrients in the small intestine is impaired, leading to malabsorptive symptoms.  Clinical Presentation  Clinical presentations for coeliac disease include:  diarrhoea: either chronic or intermittent  bloating  abdominal pain/discomfort: recurrent abdominal pain, distention or cramping  failure to thrive (children)  weight loss  fatigue  iron-deficiency causing a microcytic anaemia  vitamin B12/folate deficiency causing a macrocytic anaemia  osteopenia/osteoporosis.  Associated conditions include:  dermatitis herpetiformis (intensively itchy and widespread rash)  Down syndrome  selective immunoglobulin A (IgA) deficiency G

GIT & LIVER part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Overview Key Facts  Colorectal cancer (CRC) refers to malignant tumours of the distal gastrointestinal (GI) tract – the colon or the rectum.  Most CRCs are adenocarcinomas, arising from cells of epithelial origin:  less commonly, they can be carcinoid tumours, gastrointestinal stromal tumours (GIST) or lymphomas.  75% occur beyond the splenic flexure, so detection is possible with flexible sigmoidoscopy; however, colon cancer can only be excluded by a full colonoscopy, computed tomography (CT) colonography or barium enema with rigid sigmoidoscopy.  barium enemas are no longer routine practice in the United Kingdom (UK).  Staging was historically by Dukes’ staging, though this has now largely been replaced by tumour node metastasis (TNM) staging.  CRC can become complicated by:  obstruction  perforation  fistulation  bleeding.  Principles of surgery include:  pre-op preparation  in curable elective cases, aim for wide resection of tumour with regional lymphatics  in obstructed emergency cases, aim for primary relief of the obstruction followed by elective surgery if necessary  in incurable cases, aim to relieve present or potential obstruction and alleviate symptoms  post-op care is vital.  Of all colonic cancers, 70–80% are amenable to resection.  20–30% of patients have disseminated disease at presentation.  The postoperative 5-year survival rate is 50–70% overall. Epidemiology  CRC is the second most common cause of death from malignancy in the UK (after lung cancer).  Third commonest cancer in the western world.  More common in western Europe and North America than in developing countries.  Less than 5% of patients are aged < 40.  Peak incidence is in people aged 70–80 years.  F > M (marginally). Aetiology  The exact cause of CRC is unclear, though there are likely contributions from both genetic and environmental factors (mostly dietary).  Dietary factors include: G

GIT & LIVER part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  constipation and obstruction  abdominal colic and perforation  more overt bleeding and mucous per rectum  25–30% of patients with left colon tumours present as an emergency – usually obstruction of perforation.  rectal tumours:  bleeding is the presenting complaint in 60% of patients  change in bowel habit (including mucus)  tenesmus  palpable prolapsing mass  symptoms worse in the morning.  Examination findings in CRC:  presence of a mass (either per abdomen or per rectum)  evidence of intestinal obstruction  evidence of spread (hepatomegaly, ascites, jaundice, supraclavicular lymph nodes)  general effects of malignancy (weight loss, anaemia).  Differential Diagnosis  Benign anal disease.  Bowel ischaemia.  Diverticular disease.  Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS).  Inflammatory bowel disease – ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease.  Benign polyps.  Colonic vascular malformations.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Sigmoidoscopy:  most rectal tumours should be detectable on rigid sigmoidoscopy and most CRCs are within reach of the flexible sigmoidoscope. Biopsies should be taken  the rest of the large bowel must be investigated in order to exclude adenomas or synchronous tumours.  Colonoscopy:  complete investigation of the large bowel  biopsies may be taken  gold standard of large-bowel investigation for primary surgical pathology  may not be possible to do a complete colonoscopy to the caecum, in which case computed tomography (CT) colonography is needed to complete the investigation  patients who are considered to be at high risk of colon cancer (inflammatory bowel disease, previous cancer, HNPCC/strong family history) may be offered surveillance colonoscopy.  CT colonography (CTC): G

JAM  an alternative to colonoscopy or barium enema which gives good bowel definition unlike standard CT  in addition, gives information about local spread and the presence or otherwise of distant metastases  negatives are that biopsies cannot be taken.  Double-contrast barium enema:  useful for visualising the right side of the large bowel  lesion is shown as a filling defect or ‘apple core’ stricture. Biopsies are not possible and small lesions may be missed  now rarely performed.  Ultrasonography:  good for characterising metastases in the liver pre- and postoperatively  transanal ultrasonography can be used in staging rectal tumours, especially early ones being considered for local excision.  Spiral CT scan:  elective colorectal cancer patients usually have a staging chest, abdominal and pelvic CT scan to exclude distal metastases and give information about local tumour spread.  Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI):  used for preoperative staging of rectal cancer  especially useful for identifying local lymph nodes and the mesorectum to identify patients with a potentially involved circumferential resection margin (CRM)  also used to characterise suspected liver metastases and assess liver resectability.  Screening programmes:  the NHS bowel cancer screening programme aims to detect asymptomatic individuals at early stages of disease, this is carried out in patients aged 60–74 via home faecal testing kits every two years  patients with positive tests are invited to colonoscopy.  Management Non-pharmacological  Radiotherapy is used for rectal cancer rather than colonic cancer for two reasons:  there is a defined anatomical location  there is less risk of small-bowel injury.  Radiotherapy reduces local recurrence (by 40%) but does not affect distant metastases; it may lead to a 6% improvement in 5-year survival in those patients going on to have curative resection.  Recent research has shown that preoperative radiotherapy should be used, unless the operating surgeon can demonstrate low baseline local recurrence rates (they show a smaller benefit). Debate continues about the timing, delivery and use of radiotherapy and chemo-radiotherapy.  Postoperative radiotherapy should be reserved for patients who are judged after surgery to be at high risk of recurrence.

GIT & LIVER part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Palliative radiotherapy may be suitable for patients who are unfit for surgery and symptomatic (eg with pain, imminent obstruction, bleeding, or mucous from a low rectal tumour).  Side-effects of radiotherapy include local effects (delayed wound healing, urinary and bowel dysfunction, nerve damage) and systemic effects (increased cardiovascular mortality).  All decisions are taken through a structured multidisciplinary team (MDT) process. Pharmacological  Adjuvant chemotherapy is indicated in TNM stage III CRC, but not in TNM stage I.  The benefit in TNM stage II cancer is not clear yet and often depends on the position of the tumour, grade of tumour, assessment of poor prognostic factors, surgery performed, and fitness of the patient.  Patients are discussed in an MDT on a case-by- case basis.  TNM stage III:  current UK guidelines suggest that fit patients with TNM stage III CRC should be offered either:  6-month course of 5-fluorouracil (5-FU) and folinic acid (FUFA), or  1-week course of 5-FU by continuous portal vein infusion.  this gives a 5-year survival benefit of around 6%.  TNM stage II:  the place of chemotherapy in the treatment of patients with TNM stage II cancer must be a matter for discussion between patients and oncologists  patients should be encouraged to become part of nationally coordinated randomised controlled trials.  TNM stage I:  chemotherapy is not recommended. Surgical  Preoperative preparation:  optimise fitness: the patient’s general condition influences choice of procedure; liaise with medical/anaesthetic staff. Respiratory function and nutritional status are especially important  define extent of tumour: the presence of distant metastases influences choice of surgical procedure:  patients should have a staging CT scan and any pathology, radiology, endoscopy results and clinical features should be discussed at an MDT meeting before surgery to decide on optimal treatment, including pre- or post-operative adjuvant therapy.  imaging: of the rest of the colon by actual or virtual colonoscopy or barium enema (essential to exclude synchronous pathology); of the lung and liver by spiral CT or MRI; of local anatomy (especially in rectal tumours) by MRI or endorectal ultrasonography (to assess local involvement). Neoadjuvant therapy (eg short-course radiotherapy or longcourse chemoradiation) is often indicated depending on the local staging G

DR. JAM  bowel preparation: bowel lumen bacteria are thought to be the chief source of sepsis in bowel surgery. In elective cases, one day of liquid-only diet and two sachets of sodium picosulfate before surgery are a common regimen. In emergency obstructed cases, on-table lavage can be performed  prophylactic antibiotics: metronidazole and cephalosporin at induction and for at least three doses postoperatively  counselling and consent: diagnosis, results of investigations, planned procedures, possible outcomes, complications, and risks of mortality are made clear to patients and, if they agree, their relatives. The chance of a stoma should always be explained.  Surgery with curative intent:  surgical management depends on the site of the tumour, and the presence of obstruction  non-obstructed cancer of the right colon:  treated by right hemicolectomy and primary anastomosis sparing the middle colic arteries.  non-obstructed cancer of the transverse colon or splenic flexure:  treated by an extended right hemicolectomy taking the middle colic arteries.  non-obstructed cancer of the sigmoid colon, middle or upper rectum:  treated by an anterior resection taking the inferior mesenteric artery and its sigmoid and superior rectal branches.  operable low rectal and anorectal tumours:  treated by abdominoperineal excision and end colostomy taking the inferior mesenteric artery  selected tumours may be treated by transanal excision  the rectum, anus, sphincter, and levator muscles are taken en bloc in an extralevator abdominoperineal excision of the rectum (ELAPE) which necessitates pelvic floor reconstruction with a mesh or myocutaneous flap.  In the case of obstruction, there should be primary relief of the obstruction with a primary excision of the cancer, if this is not possible, then there may be a role for elective resection after emergency obstruction relief.  This is done in one of several ways:  three-stage approach:  1 – primary decompression with a proximal-loop colostomy  2 – resection of tumour at a later date leaving the colostomy to protect the anastomosis  3 – closure of the colostomy  this has the advantage of a simple initial life-saving operation, allowing the patient to recover before the more extensive resection, which can be undertaken by a senior surgeon on an elective list  unfortunately, cumulative mortality rate is about 20%, and 50% of patients never have their colostomy closed.  Hartmann’s procedure: primary resection with an endcolostomy:

GIT & LIVER part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  this approach achieves the dual objectives of relieving the obstruction and resecting the tumour while avoiding the potential complications of an anastomosis under suboptimal conditions  reversal of Hartmann’s procedure has a high complication rate and 10% mortality rate, so many patients end up with a permanent colostomy. Primary resection and formation of a mucous fistula or doublebarrelled colostomy (Paul Mikulicz’s procedure) can simplify the second operation.  primary resection and anastomosis: this approach ensures that the definitive operation is done at the first laparotomy but the anastomosis is done in suboptimal conditions:  on-table lavage and subtotal colectomy can reduce the incidence of sepsis and discrepancy between dilated proximal bowel end and collapsed distal bowel end  a defunctioning loop ileostomy can give the anastomosis time to heal and involves a relatively simple procedure to reverse it.  Obstructing rectal tumours are comparatively rare and may not be as curable, so primary decompression with a colostomy or endoluminal stent is often most appropriate until the tumour can be assessed and a management plan decided on.  In very advanced or even recurrent tumours an aggressive approach by an MDT of several specialties (eg colorectal surgeon, urologist, gynaecologist, orthopaedic surgeon) can result in up to 25% longterm salvage.  Surgery with palliative intent:  in the incurable case one should aim to relieve present or potential obstruction and alleviate symptoms:  resection of the primary tumour offers the best palliation. It relieves obstruction, reduces the risk of future obstruction and reduces future metastatic spread  a bypass procedure may be appropriate if the primary tumour is not resectable  defunctioning colostomy is less traumatic and relieves obstruction in frail patients  radiotherapy and chemotherapy may give temporary alleviation. Radiotherapy is particularly useful in rectal tumours  stenting is becoming more widely practised in incurable obstructing lesions  local techniques for rectal cancer include electrocoagulation, contact irradiation, local excision, or transanal resection of tumour with a cutting loop diathermy and laser treatment.  Post-operative care after colonic or rectal resection is important:  hydration and monitoring of electrolytes:  intravenous (IV) fluids needed until normal oral intake has resumed; hypokalaemia due to diarrhoea or high stoma output should be avoided to minimise ileus.  prophylactic antibiotics:  three postoperative doses of cefuroxime and metronidazole are often given.  analgesia:  patient-controlled analgesia, and epidural or regular opiates are important to minimise post-operative pain. JAM Post-operative epidurals have been shown to reduce many major complications after abdominal surgery.  catheterisation:  to monitor urine output and avoid urinary retention in the post-operative period.  careful nursing and dressing of wound:  patients should be nursed in a low sitting position, except for after an abdomino-perineal resection, in which case they are nursed on the side. The wound should be carefully observed and kept clean and dry. Abdominal skin sutures or staples usually can be removed at days 10–14.  physiotherapy:  chest physiotherapy to prevent atelectasis; early mobilisation to prevent urinary retention and deep vein thrombosis.  early enteral feeding:  has shown significant benefit – the ‘nil by mouth for ten days’ adage is outdated.  deep vein thrombosis (DVT) prophylaxis:  subcutaneous heparin and anti-thromboembolic stockings.  care of colostomy:  initially an ileostomy drainable bag over the colostomy; stoma therapist must be involved to fit a permanent device; patients are taught how to care for their stoma before being discharged.  counselling and informing patients:  histology of specimen, what was done during the operation, plans for future surgery and prognosis should be explained to the patient and relative. Appropriate follow-up (+/- chemotherapy) should be arranged.  Post-operative complications of colorectal cancer:  general complications:  cardiorespiratory problems  DVT  pulmonary embolism  post-operative renal failure.  specific complications:  anastomotic leak:  typically occurs 7–10 days post-operatively  along with cardiorespiratory problems, this is a major cause of postoperative mortality  risk is higher in low anastomoses  the surgeon, male patient, preoperative radiotherapy, and surgical technique are other major factors  the results of anastomotic leak or dehiscence are pelvic abscess, peritonitis, fistulation, or death.  anastomotic stricture:  caused by recurrence, fibrosis or ischaemia  tends to present later on

GIT & LIVER part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  may be amenable to endoscopic dilations.  wound infection and dehiscence:  as with any laparotomy, the wound is less likely to heal if the patient is elderly with comorbidity and unwell at the time of surgery  risk of wound infection is higher in colorectal surgery and is minimised by preoperative optimisation of the patient, prophylactic antibiotics and meticulous technique  perineal wounds are especially prone to infection, abscess, pressure necrosis, and primary or secondary haemorrhage, especially after radiotherapy.  intestinal obstruction:  herniation of small bowel through a defect left in the mesentery following resection of bowel  adherence of bowel to wound closure  adhesions between loops of bowel  oedema or stricture of colostomy  anastomotic stricture.  urinary retention:  post-operative pain  prostatic obstruction  denervation of bladder.  injury of urinary tract:  ureteric injury leading to hydronephrosis, pyonephrosis, urinary fistula  bladder injury during anterior dissection  urethral injury during perineal dissection may lead to fistula or stricture.  sexual dysfunction:  erectile dysfunction due to injury of nervi erigentes, which is more common after abdomino-perineal excision than after anterior resection  failure of ejaculation due to damage to the presacral nerves  dyspareunia in females due to fibrosis around the vagina.  'phantom' rectum:  after abdominoperineal resection, this distressing sensation of an uncomfortable rectum occurs in up to 50% of patients.  colostomy complications:  bleeding  prolapse  retraction  stenosis  skin excoriation  parastomal hernia.  altered bowel function: G

JAM  bowel frequency and incontinence are more likely with a lower colorectal anastomosis  seventy percent of patients with a colo-anal anastomosis have normal continence  function tends to improve with time, up to one year after the operation.  Follow-up after surgery for colorectal cancer:  short-term aims:  check for post-operative complications  give emotional and practical support  assist with stoma management  ensure that patients who did not have preoperative colonoscopy or barium enema get one within six months of discharge  arrange appropriate adjuvant therapy  general practice follow-up has been found to be as effective as a hospital follow-up.  long-term aims:  follow-up to identify recurrence or metastatic disease  detect metachronous tumours  re-colonoscopy within three years of removing a benign adenoma is the current recommendation  it is essential to do a postoperative large-bowel investigation within six months of discharge if one was not performed preoperatively.  Prognosis  Of all colonic cancers, 70–80% are amenable to resection; 20–30% of patients have disseminated disease at presentation.  The post-operative 5-year survival rate is 50–70% overall (but this varies depending on several factors).  A worse prognosis is expected in the following:  high Dukes'/TNM stage  emergency presentation (especially perforation)  young patients  short history of disease  development of complications  low rectal tumours  anaplastic tumours.  Recurrence:  local recurrence is thought to be due to:  lateral spread beyond the excision margin  spread into the mesorectum  residual cancer in regional lymph nodes  high Dukes'/TNM stage  low rectal tumours.  of local recurrence, 80% occurs within two years post-op, typically presenting as follows:  pelvic pain  leg pain  urinary symptoms  changes in bowel habit  seen as follow-up endoscopy or follow-up CT imaging.  Complications:

GIT & LIVER part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  obstruction:  more common in left colonic tumours, which tend to be annular and constricting  luminal contents are more solid than on the right, predisposing to absolute constipation  tumour may obstruct by acting as the apex for volvulus or intussusception  patients present with colicky, central lower abdominal pain, distension, and absolute constipation.  perforation:  may occur through a carcinoma or proximal to it  caecum is the most common area of perforation, especially in the presence of a competent ileocaecal valve due to the formation of a closed loop obstruction  perforation may result in generalised faecal peritonitis or localised abscess  mortality is high and long-term surgical cure is much less likely in a perforated carcinoma.  fistula formation:  direct invasion of a colorectal tumour into a neighbouring organ (eg bladder or vagina) can cause a fistula  vesicocolic fistulas present with pneumaturia and recurrent urinary tract infections (UTIs)  rectovaginal fistulas present with faecal vaginal discharge  fistulae of the transverse colon and the stomach or duodenum may present with faecal vomiting  fistulae caused by colorectal cancer can be difficult to distinguish from those caused by diverticular disease.  other complications:  haemorrhage  appendicitis (secondary to caecal carcinoma)  colo-colic intussusception (carcinoma causes 50% of all adult intussusceptions)  invasion into adjacent organs. Other  Management of liver metastases:  some 15 000 patients die after colorectal cancer surgery every year  in 20% of patients, the liver is the first or only site of recurrence  in recent years, the trend has been to treat liver metastases more aggressively  studies have shown that patients with solitary resectable lesions survive longer if treated and 25% can be cured  multiple metastases in multiple segments of the liver are considered for resection so should be discussed with the liver surgeon if the patient is fit and willing  chemotherapy is also used in these patients.  Preoperative assessment of metastatic liver resection:  ultrasonography  CT  MRI  hepatic angiography  laparoscopy  laparoscopic ultrasonography.  Difficulties are presented by:  extensive adhesions  lesions close to the diaphragm G

Patients do better if:  primary was at an early stage  they had a long disease-free interval  there were fewer metastases  metastases were < 8 cm (and low percentage of hepatic replacement).  The following are other prognostic factors:  extrahepatic disease  distribution of metastases  symptoms  sex (male)  age  resection margins and histological differentiation.  Results of resection:  60–70% of patients develop recurrence after liver metastasis resection  there are 25–30% long-term (5-year) survivors  surgery extends median survival by 14–20 months  post-operative mortality rates are < 5%  adequate resection should improve long-term survival in at least 20% of patients.  Other treatment modalities for liver metastases:  cryotherapy (can be used to treat the margins of irresectable lesions intra-operatively)  radiofrequency ablation (one small study has demonstrated 46% 3-year survival rate)  laser interstitial therapy  microwave treatment. Constipation  Constipation is a defined as a symptom-based disorder involving unsatisfactory defecation due to infrequent stools, difficulty passing stools, or sensation of incomplete emptying.  Overview Key Facts  Constipation is a defined as a symptom-based disorder involving unsatisfactory defecation due to infrequent stools, difficulty passing stools, or sensation of incomplete emptying.  The Rome IV diagnostic criteria define constipation as spontaneous bowel movements occurring less than three times a week.  Stools are usually dry, hard or lumpy. They may be abnormally large or small.  Chronic constipation describes symptoms present for at least three months in the preceding six months. Epidemiology  Constipation is a common problem that can occur at any age.  In the United Kingdom in 2009, 12.8 per 1 000 people had General Practitioner-diagnosed constipation.  Worldwide, the prevalence is roughly 14%.

GIT & LIVER part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Constipation is more common as age increases.  Constipation is more common in women than in men.  Constipation is more common during pregnancy and may be due to physiological, biochemical and dietary changes during pregnancy. Aetiology Functional (Primary or Idiopathic) Constipation Secondary (Organic) Constipation Chronic constipation without a known cause There are three types: normal transit: most common subgroup. Constipation with no time delay in stool passage through the colon slow transit: prolonged delay in stool passage through the colon obstructed defecation: can be caused by pelvic floor dyssynergia Constipation caused by medication or an underlying medical condition Organic Causes of Constipation  Lifestyle:  not eating enough fibre, eg fruits and vegetables  not drinking enough fluids  being less active; lack of exercise, not moving enough, sedentary.  Drugs:  iron and calcium supplements  analgesics, eg opiates and non-steroidal antiinflammatory drugs (NSAIDs)  antimuscarinics, eg procyclidine and oxybutynin  antidepressants such as tricyclic antidepressants  antipsychotics such as clozapine or quetiapine  antiepileptics, eg carbamazepine, gabapentin, phenytoin  antihistamines, eg hydroxyzine  antispasmodics, eg hyoscine  calcium channel blockers  diuretics.  Endocrine and metabolic diseases:  diabetes mellitus (with autonomic neuropathy)  hypercalcaemia and hyperparathyroidism  hypothyroidism  uraemia  hypermagnesaemia  hyperkalaemia.  Myopathic conditions:  amyloidosis  myotonic dystrophy  scleroderma.  Neurological conditions:  autonomic neuropathy  cerebrovascular disease  Hirschsprung’s disease  multiple sclerosis  Parkinson’s disease  spinal cord injury. JAM  Management Non-pharmacological  Treatment of any identified underlying cause.  Important to consider possible secondary causes, eg colorectal cancer.  Eating a healthy, balanced diet and having regular meals.  Diet should contain whole grains, fruits and vegetables.  Gradually increase fibre intake (minimise bloating and flatulence).  Drinking an adequate fluid intake.  Increasing activity and exercise levels.  Toileting routines:  regular, unhurried toilet routine  respond immediately to the sensation of needing to defecate  patients with limited mobility should have appropriate help to access toilet. Pharmacological  Medication-induced constipation treatment is to withdraw the medication if possible.  Offer a bulk-forming laxative first-line, such as ispaghula.  If stool remains hard/difficult to pass then add or switch to an osmotic laxative, such as macrogol.  If stools are soft but difficult to pass, or there is an inadequate emptying sensation, then add a stimulant laxative.  If a patient has opioid-induced constipation:  avoid bulk-forming laxative  offer an osmotic and a stimulant laxative or docusate.

GIT & LIVER part 2 MIL ALRAJHI Surgical  Surgical management, such as subtotal colectomy with ileorectal anastomosis, is considered rarely in people with slow transit constipation if all treatment options have been ineffective.  If colorectal cancer is suspected, seek specialist advice or arrange referral to a Gastroenterologist or Colorectal Surgeon.  Prognosis  Medical therapy is fairly effective in reliving constipation symptoms.  Complications of long-term constipation are:  anal fissure  haemorrhoids  faecal impaction. Crohn’s Disease  Crohn's disease is a chronic inflammatory bowel disease that can affect any part of the digestive tract, from the mouth to the anus, causing inflammation in patches of the intestinal wall, leading to symptoms like diarrhoea, abdominal pain and malnutrition.  Overview Key Facts  Crohn’s disease and Ulcerative Colitis are collectively called ‘inflammatory bowel disease’.  Both Crohn’s disease and Ulcerative colitis are chronic, relapsingremitting, non-infectious inflammatory diseases of the gastrointestinal tract.  Crohn’s disease is characterised by:  inflammation involving discrete parts of the gastrointestinal tract, from between the mouth to the anus – named skip lesions’ as there are normal areas in between  full-thickness inflammation  terminal ileum involvement (70%).  The condition may occur at any age, but commonly first presents in adolescence and early adulthood.  Management may require both primary and secondary care input, and includes pharmacological and surgical options depending upon the severity of gastrointestinal symptoms and response to treatment.  Extra intestinal symptoms may require input from the appropriate specialists (eg dermatology or rheumatology). Epidemiology  Crohn’s and Ulcerative Colitis affects men and women at approximately equal rates. G

DR. JAM  Incidence of Crohn’s disease in the UK is about 83 per million people per year, and 5.2 per 100 000 children per year.  Crohn’s disease commonly occurs in adolescence and early adulthood, but may occur in any age. Aetiology  Cause of Crohn’s disease remains unclear.  It is a condition that is caused by environmental triggering events in genetically susceptible people.  Several genetic susceptibility loci have been identified.  A positive family history of Crohn’s disease.  Smoking increases the risk of Crohn’s disease.  Other environmental factors include: oral contraceptive pill, diet high in refined sugar, infectious agents such as measles virus, NSAIDs use, and episodes of infectious gastroenteritis. Pathophysiology  Initial lesion begins as an inflammatory infiltrate, which develops into ulceration of the superficial mucosa.  Inflammation involves the deeper layers and forms non-caseating granulomas.  Deep ulcers located transversely and longitudinally, creating a cobblestone appearance.  Acute transmural inflammation leads to bowel obstruction due to mucosal oedema.  Chronic transmural inflammation leads to bowel wall thickening, leading to scarring, luminal narrowing, and stricture formation. This may lead to fistulisation, sinus tract formation, perforation, and/or abscess formation.  Granulomas seen in Crohn’s disease:

Cytomegalovirus  Cytomegalovirus is a common worldwide infection with high levels of seropositivity.  Overview Key Facts  Cytomegalovirus (CMV) is a common worldwide infection with high levels of seropositivity.  It causes severe illness in the immunocompromised and neonates, but mostly asymptomatic or mild ‘infectious mononucleosis’ type illness in the immunocompetent.  May lead to severe illness in most bodily systems.  Congenital infection risks hearing, neurological and cognitive function.  In the immunocompromised, it may lead to morbidity and mortality.  Treatment and prevention are possible with antivirals. Antivirals needed for all those with immunocompromise or severe congenital infection.  CMV infection is self-limiting and mild in the immunocompetent.  Congenital infection can cause sensorineural deafness, learning disability, sight problems and developmental delay. Epidemiology  High rates of seropositivity worldwide.  The most common cause of non-genetic sensorineural hearing loss in children.

GIT & LIVER part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Seropositivity common, studies quote 30–98% positive in the worldwide population, with the higher rates in developing countries (eg high figures in Brazil, lower in Germany).  Two peaks of primary infection – under age 3 and in adolescents (the latter peak thought to be due to sexual activity).  Approximately 1% of all neonates in developed countries have CMV infection, with approximately 5–10% of these being symptomatic.  In developing countries, the occurrence of CMV in live births is approximately 6%. Aetiology  Transmission, via body fluids/tissues:  blood, blood product transfusion  transplantation from CMV-positive to CMV-seronegative recipient  sexual contact  saliva  transplacental (vertical transmission following maternal latent reactivation or primary infection; congenital infection more likely in primary infection).  Vulnerable groups for severe infection – neonates and the immunocompromised.  Transplant recipients are especially at risk as they may contract CMV from the received material and develop a severe infection due to the immunosuppressants needed to counteract rejection.  Those with HIV are most at risk if CD4+ count is less than 50. Pathophysiology  Human CMV is a β-herpes virus (human β-herpes virus type 5).  Following primary infection, the virus develops latency.  Latency sites – endothelial cells of arterial walls, T cells.  Reactivation in the immunocompetent is normally asymptomatic with active viral shedding at this point.  In the immunocompromised, primary infection or reactivation may cause disseminated and thus severe infection.  Due to the variety of CMV strains that exist, someone can be reinfected, producing a secondary primary infection, but these tend to be milder.  Severe infection is mostly associated with immunocompromised states impacting on CD4 count (eg transplant recipients, HIV, older age).  Clinical Presentation In the immunocompetent  Majority asymptomatic:  possible, ‘infectious-mononucleosis type syndrome’ with – tiredness, pyrexia, lymphadenopathy, mild hepatitis, nontypical lymphocytosis  associated with Guillain–Barré syndrome. JAM Non-pharmacological  Supportive in mild infection in the immunocompetent, eg analgesia, adequate hydration.  When hospitalised, isolation needed from other patients with infection control measures utilised.  In neonates, antiviral therapy tends to be used in severe cases only. Prevention  CMV-status assessment in all transplant donors and recipients.  Only giving CMV-negative material to CMV-negative recipients.  Prophylaxis with antivirals if a CMV-positive transplant is given to a CMV-negative recipient.  Barrier contraception.  Handwashing, especially before and after eating and toileting.  Stringent hygiene in the pregnant.  In HIV patients – regular monitoring of immune status (aiming CD4+ > 100), medication selection and adherence. Occasionally antivirals are given to those with CD4+ < 50 to prevent CMV infection. Pharmacological  Antivirals needed for all those with immunocompromise or severe congenital infection.  Antivirals are the standard treatment of choice; this can reduce infection severity, further deterioration of affected sites and viral load.  Common antivirals of choice are valganciclovir PO or ganciclovir IV; these are given for approximately 1 month.  Route of delivery (PO or IV) dependent on clinical status.  Retinitis – intravitreal antivirals if sight-threatening.  In AIDs – maintenance antiviral therapy may be needed.  Immunoglobulins may be used in combination with antivirals.  Prognosis  Infection self-limiting and mild in the immunocompetent.  CMV-induced hepatitis is normally mild with most recovering fully.  Severe infection may lead to mortality; most deaths from CMV pneumonia.  Congenital infection has the possibility of sensorineural deafness, learning disability, sight problems and developmental delay.  Side-effects of long-term antivirals may contribute to morbidity (eg ganciclovir/valganciclovir can cause bone marrow suppression).

GIT & LIVER part 2 MIL ALRAJHI Diverticular Disease  Diverticular disease is the umbrella term for diverticulosis and diverticulitis. Diverticulosis is the presence of diverticulae in the wall of the bowel.  Overview Key Facts  Diverticular disease is the umbrella term for diverticulosis and diverticulitis.  diverticulosis is the presence of diverticulae in the wall of the bowel  diverticulitis is the infection and inflammation of these diverticulae.  A diverticulum is a sac or pouch formed at a weakness in the gastrointestinal tract (GIT) wall.  They may be congenital (rare) or acquired:  congenital diverticula involve all layers of the colon wall  acquired diverticula involve areas of mucosa that herniate through the muscular wall.  May be asymptomatic, or may become inflamed resulting in diverticulitis.  Presents as:  left Iliac fossa (LIF) pain  altered bowel habit.  per rectal (PR) bleeding.  Acutely management consist of:  analgesia  antibiotics  fluids.  Complicated cases may require surgery. Epidemiology  It is common in developed countries (with low-fibre diets).  Incidence is increasing.  Incidence increases with age.  Ten percent of all people aged 40 are affected.  60–70% of people aged 80 have diverticulosis. Aetiology  Lack of dietary fibre leads to high intraluminal pressures, longstanding constipation, increased segmentation and muscular hypertrophy in the colonic wall.  Acquired diverticula occur at the site of weakness in the now noncompliant colonic wall.  The main sites of weakness are where the mesenteric blood vessels penetrate the bowel wall. Drug-Induced Liver Injury  Drug-induced liver injury (DILI) can cause acute and chronic liver disease.  Overview Key Facts  Drug-induced liver injury (DILI) can cause acute and chronic liver disease.  DILI can be idiosyncratic (not predictable) or intrinsic (predictable dose-related hepatoxicity, eg paracetamol overdose).  Early diagnosis of DILI and removal of the offending agent is essential for the prevention of chronic liver disease or liver failure.  Pre-existing liver disorder and family history of liver disorder act as major risk factors in drug DILI.  Side-effects associated with drugs also cause DILI and may require discontinuation after recognition.  The most common hepatotoxic drug is paracetamol. Epidemiology  Women are more susceptible to developing liver disorders such as hepatitis and are more prone to acute liver failure than males.  The most common hepatotoxicity is due to paracetamol overdose, ie 57%. G

DR. JAM  In the United Kingdom (UK) the frequency is 2.3–2.4 per 100 000. Aetiology  Acetaminophen.  Halothane-induced DILI usually occurs after multiple exposures (anaesthetic agent).  Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs).  Isoniazid (antibacterial-drug-induced liver damage).  Penicillins and cephalosporins.  Sulfonamide.  Ketoconazole (antifungal).  Thiazolidinedione (oral hypoglycaemic).  Ezetimibe (lipid-lowering drug).  Herbal medicines (Kava root, antidepressant). Pathophysiology  DILI may be the result of direct toxic effect from the administered drug or its metabolite.  Injury may result from immune-mediated mechanisms.  A number of drugs are lipid-soluble and are processed in the liver and are excreted in bile or urine.  The first step of drug metabolism is:  phase I reaction and is catalysed by enzymes of the hepatic cytochrome p450 cytochrome system  intermediate bioactive agents produced in this step interact with cellular organelles (eg mitochondria) leading to hepatocyte damage and dysfunction.  DILI may result due from drug-induced inhibition of the mitochondrial respiratory system, which results in the proliferation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) and depletion of ATP.  ROS proliferation, ATP depletion and the above-mentioned mitochondrial damage contribute a major part to induce hepatotoxicity.  Clinical Presentation  Lethargy, malaise and nausea.  Lack of appetite.  Pruritus, in advanced liver damage.  Jaundice.  Abdominal pain, similar in nature to acute cholecystitis.  Increased levels of alanine aminotransferase (ALT) and aspartate aminotransferase (AST), which reflect hepatocyte destruction.  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses may include:  jaundice  acute cholecystitis  acute viral hepatitis  liver cancer  liver abscess  fatty liver  Wilson’s disease  hepatic cirrhosis.

GIT & LIVER part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Diagnosis/Investigation  History regarding drug administration and the start of symptoms.  Drugs that are known to have liver toxicity usually evoke clinical features within hours to a few days.  Immune-mediated toxic effects may take weeks to manifest the toxic effects.  Ultrasound abdomen for liver texture and to exclude acute cholecystitis.  Alanine transaminase (ALT), aspartate transaminase (AST), alkaline phosphatase (ALP) and gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase (GGT) are measured by performing liver function tests.  Very high levels of paracetamol can elevate liver enzymes above 20 000–25 000 IU/l.  Computed tomography (CT) scan to exclude liver cancer, only if indicated on ultrasound.  Management Non-pharmacological  Monitoring in pre-existing cases of liver disorders.  The majority of cases of DILI are acute illnesses.  The majority of cases do not require hospitalisation; cessation of hepatotoxic agent relieves the symptoms and the liver heals within a few weeks.  Patient education. Surgical  Very severe cases that lead to acute liver failure may require hepatic transplant.  Prognosis  Prognosis is generally very good if DILI is identified and the causative agent is stopped. Functional Bowel Disease  Functional bowel disorders comprise irritable bowel disease, functional bloating, functional constipation and functional diarrhoea.  Overview Key Facts  Functional bowel disorders comprise irritable bowel disease (IBS), functional bloating, functional constipation and functional diarrhoea.  The condition primarily affects younger people in their 20s and 30s, with women far more commonly affected than men. G

DR. JAM  Prevalence decreases with age.  To separate these chronic conditions from transient symptoms, they must have occurred for the first time ≥ six months before patient presents, and their presence on ≥ three days a month during the last three months.  Organic causes of symptoms should be considered and excluded as appropriate.  Treatment involves:  providing reassurance  patient information, lifestyle and diet advice  identifying and managing triggers  pharmacological intervention with antispasmodics or loperamide.  Antidepressants can be considered if abdominal pain symptoms continue to persist. Epidemiology  IBS commonly affects young people aged 20–30 years old, and prevalence decreases with increasing age.  IBS affects up to 10% of population, with a ratio of 5 : 1, woman : man. Aetiology  An exact underlying cause of IBS is unknown, and is likely to be an interplay of environmental and genetic factors.  Possible mechanisms:  visceral hypersensitivity  abnormal gastrointestinal immune function  changes in colonic microbiota  abnormal autonomic activity  abnormal central pain processing of afferent gut signals  abnormal gastrointestinal motility.  Risk factors for IBS:  genetic  enteric infection ⇢ causing damage to neuroenteric innervation  gastrointestinal inflammation, eg inflammatory bowel disease (IBD)  dietary factors: alcohol, caffeine, spicy, fatty foods (90% report food triggers symptoms)  psychosocial: anxiety, stress and/or depression influences the physiological functioning of the gastrointestinal tract via the brain-gut axis.  Causes of functional abdominal bloating:  intra-abdominal gas  fluid within the lumen of the gut  faeces  low or inappropriately contracted diaphragm  exaggerated lumbar lordosis  intra-abdominal fat

GIT & LIVER part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  weak or inappropriately relaxed abdominal muscles  psychiatric problems.  Causes of functional constipation:  normal transit constipation  slow transit constipation  evacuation disorders.  Causes of functional diarrhoea:  IBD. Pathophysiology  IBS:  altered gut reactivity (motility and secretion) in response to various stimuli, eg environmental (abuse, personal life stresses) or luminal (certain foods, inflammation)  altered reactivity can lead to pain as well as constipation or diarrhoea  increased gut hypersensitivity, enhanced perception of visceral type pain and sensations.  Clinical Presentation  The clinical presentation for IBS can involve any of the following symptoms for at least six months:  abdominal pain  bloating  change in bowel habit. Diagnostic Criteria  Abdominal pain, either:  relieved by defecation and/or  associated with altered stool frequency (increased or decreased), and/or  associated with altered stool appearance (hard, lumpy, loose, or watery); and at least two of the following:  altered stool passage (straining, urgency, or incomplete evacuation)  abdominal bloating  symptoms worsened by eating  passage of rectal mucus.  Other functional symptoms that may support the diagnosis include:  non-cardiac chest pain  higher prevalence of fibromyalgia  lethargy  nausea  tension headaches  backaches  bladder symptoms (such as nocturia, urgency, and incomplete emptying)  dyspareunia,  faecal incontinence. JAM  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses for functional bowel disease include:  Crohn’s disease  ulcerative colitis  coeliac disease  colon cancer  bowel infections  diverticular disease  non-coeliac gluten intolerance  somatisation disorders.  Diagnosis/Investigation  A clinical diagnosis of IBS requires the fulfilment of symptombased diagnostic criteria and a limited evaluation to exclude organic disease.  The following tests are recommended:  full blood count  erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein  antibody testing for coeliac disease (tissue transglutaminase or epithelial membrane antigen).  The following tests are not necessary to confirm diagnosis in people who meet IBS diagnostic criteria, but may be useful in a case-to-case basis:  ultrasound  thyroid function tests  faecal calprotectin (excludes inflammatory bowel disease)  hydrogen breath test (for lactose intolerance and bacterial overgrowth)  stool studies  rigid/flexible sigmoidoscopy (exclude inflammatory bowel disease, polyps, carcinoma)  colonoscopy (exclude inflammatory bowel disease)/barium enema.  Management Non-pharmacological  Offer sources of information and support.  National Health Service patient leaflet  information regarding the IBS network.  Encourage the person to identify any associated stress/depression/anxiety.  Diet modification:  eat regular meals, healthy balanced diet  eat according to The Eatwell Guide  for predominant symptoms of diarrhoea and/or bloating:  reduce intake of insoluble fibre, eg brown rice, highfibre food

GIT & LIVER part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  consider reducing foods that may exacerbate symptoms, eg caffeine, alcohol, carbonated drinks, and gas-producing foods.  for predominant symptoms of constipation:  take fibre supplements, eg ispaghula, high-soluble fibre such as oats  gradually increase fibre intake to minimise flatulence and to minimise bloating.  adequate fluid intake  dietician referral  consider a trial of a low fermentable oligo-, di-, monosaccharides and polyols (FODMAP) diet.  Regular physical activity to encourage weight loss. Pharmacological  Symptoms of constipation persist, prescribe bulk-forming laxative, such as:  ispaghula husk  methylcellulose.  If symptoms of diarrhoea persist, prescribe loperamide.  If there are ongoing symptoms of abdominal pain/spasm, prescribe an antispasmodic drug, such as:  mebeverine hydrochloride  peppermint oil.  If symptoms of abdominal pain persist, prescribe a tricyclic antidepressant (TCA), such as amitriptyline.  If the TCA is ineffective, consider a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor, eg:  fluoxetine  citalopram.  Prognosis  Symptoms of IBS may fluctuate over years.  Poorer prognosis is associated with:  a longer duration of symptoms  previous history of surgery  higher somatic scores  co-morbid anxiety and depression. Gallstones and Gallbladder Disease  A gallstone is a solid precipitation of bile constituents (often mainly cholesterol) formed in the gallbladder. G

DR. JAM  Overview Key Facts  A gallstone, also known as a cholelith (whence the name cholelithiasis), is a solid precipitation of bile constituents (often mainly cholesterol) formed in the gallbladder.  Gallstones are common (found in up to 15% of adults in the United Kingdom (UK)), they are often asymptomatic, and remain so lifelong.  Gallstones disease is where gallstones in the gallbladder or biliary tree causing symptoms and complications.  Complications of gallstones include biliary colic (most common), acute cholecystitis and pancreatitis.  Gallstone disease often presents with right hypochondrial or epigastric pain and cholestatic liver function tests.  Gallstones are one of the commonest causes of jaundice.  Imaging to aid diagnosis is via ultrasound, magnetic resonance cholangio-pancreatography (MRCP) or endoscopic ultrasound.  Treatment is dependent on complication and severity:  no treatment is required for asymptomatic gallstones in a normal gallbladder and normal biliary tree  urgent referral for investigation should be arranged in patients with known gallstones and jaundice, or if biliary obstruction is suspected  endoscopic retrograde cholangio-pancreatography (ERCP) can be used to relieve bile duct obstruction either by directly removing the stone or performing a sphincterotomy  patients who are systemically unwell with a suspected gallstone disease related condition require emergency admission  all other patients with symptoms should be referred to upper gastrointestinal (GI) surgery for assessment for laparoscopic cholecystectomy; the definitive treatment of symptomatic gallstones. Epidemiology  Stones are found in 10–20% of the population but are asymptomatic in the majority of patients.  More common in women, those with raised body mass index (BMI), and those > 40 years old. Aetiology  Risk factors include:  female sex:  progesterone reduces gall bladder mobility  oestrogen increased the crystallisation of bile.  high parity (both progesterone and oestrogen are raised in pregnancy)  drugs  oral contraceptive pill (again ore oestrogen and progesterone)  clofibrate.

GIT & LIVER part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Crohn’s disease (terminal ileum)  increasing age  short-bowel syndrome  haemolysis (pigment stones)  diet  diabetes mellitus  non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD)  obesity  prolonged fasting/weight loss  hormonal replacement therapy (HRT). Pathophysiology  The gallbladder stores and concentrates bile until it is stimulated for release by Cholecystokinin (CCK) released by the duodenum when food enters it.  Alterations to bile chemical composition results in deposits that form stones within the gallbladder.  They are categorised by the main constituent present:  70–90% of gallstones are a mixture of mainly cholesterol with bile pigment  10% are pure cholesterol  pigmented stones are made of bilirubin and calcium salts  pure pigment stones are rare except with chronic haemolysis, eg sickle cell disease, spherocytosis.  Stones can aggravate the gallbladder or block the biliary ducts resulting in symptoms and potentially serious complications.  Clinical Presentation  Biliary colic.  severe intermittent right hypochondrial or epigastric pain that lasts less than eight hours.  Acute/chronic cholecystitis.  constant, severe pain, abdominal tenderness  fever  the patient may present with a septic picture.  Cholestatic jaundice if duct obstruction is present:  pale stools due to lack of stercobilinogen  dark urine due to increased conjugated bilirubin in urine.  Pancreatitis.  constant epigastric pain radiating to back, in severe cases this can be fatal so patients may present with systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS) and be acutely unwell.  Cholangitis.  fever  jaundice  right upper quadrant pain (Charcot’s triad).  Other presentations may include indigestion and intolerance to fatty food or an incidental finding.
