It is useful when non-invasive investigations fail to demonstrate a cause for biliary dilatation  ERCP is no longer used as a diagnostic test in obstructive jaundice due to the risk of complications. It should always be interventional.

GIT & LIVER part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Remember Courvoisier’s law:  a palpable gall bladder in the presence of painless jaundice is unlikely to be caused by gallstones.  Management Non-pharmacological  Asymptomatic gallbladder stones (cholecystolithasis):  watch and wait for symptoms to develop before treatment.  Avoidance of food and drink that trigger symptoms, such as fatty foods. Pharmacological  Ursodeoxycholic acid can be used to dissolve cholesterol stones.  this is a slow process and usually reserved for those unfit for other treatment.  Pain relief.  diclofenac  intramuscular opioid for severe pain. Surgical  Definitive treatment is by cholecystectomy indicated for:  symptomatic gallbladder stones  acute cholecystitis  the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) recommend within one week of diagnosis.  symptomatic or asymptomatic bile duct stones (choledocholithiasis):  also, clearance of the bile duct either surgically at time of cholecystectomy or with ERCP prior to cholecystectomy  treatment is recommended for bile duct stones regardless of whether they are symptomatic or not, due to a high risk of complications.  in severe pancreatitis due to gallstones where jaundice and cholangitis are present, early ERCP to achieve duct compression and cholecystectomy once acute symptoms settle  ERCP relieves obstruction by sphinterectomy, stone retrieval or stenting.  Prognosis  80% of patients with gallstones will remain asymptomatic.  2–4% of patients with asymptomatic gallstones develop symptoms or complications annually.  Once symptoms occur, these patients are at an increased risk of recurrence until cholecystectomy.  The most common complication is biliary colic, which although is associated with morbilidy, mortality due to the condition is rare.  First presentation acute pancreatitis has a mortality of 3–20%. Gastric Cancer  The majority of gastric cancers are adenocarcinomas.  Overview Key Facts  The majority of gastric cancers are adenocarcinomas.  Cancer can arise in any portion of the stomach but 50% occur in the cardia region.  Risk factors include hypochlorhydia, diet, gastric polyps and H.pylori infection.  Diagnosed using endoscopy with biopsy and staged with endoscopic ultrasound and computed tomography (CT) scan.  In the United Kingdom (UK), the cancer has often spread locally at time of diagnosis.  Treatment depends on staging and can include surgical resection, gastrectomy, and chemotherapy. Epidemiology  Incidence is decreasing in the Western world but remains one of the commonest causes of cancer deaths.  Seven thousand new cases are diagnosed in the UK each year. Aetiology  Risk factors:  Japanese ethnicity G

DR. JAM  H.pylori infection (associated with 1 in 3 gastric tumours)  hypochlorhydia  pernicious anaemia  chronic atrophic gastritis  partial gastrectomy.  family history of gastric cancer/familial syndromes, eg familial adenomatous polyposis  male sex  age  dietary factors  high salt and nitrates/processed foods  gastric polyps.  rare and usually benign. Pathophysiology  Usually takes the form of an adenocarcinoma arising from the glandular epithelium.  Incidence in cardia region is rising and it is now responsible for 50% of all gastric cancers.  Very little early detection in the UK and most patients have local spread at time of diagnosis. Clinical Presentation  Dyspepsia.  Dysphagia.  Epigastric pain.  Anorexia and weight loss.  Early satiety.  Iron-deficiency anaemia.  Haematemesis/melaena.  Nausea and vomiting.  Virchow’s node.  a palpable lymph node in the left supraclavicular fossa, which indicates spread of upper gastrointestinal malignancy.  Differential Diagnosis  Peptic/duodenal ulcer.  Oesophageal stricture.  Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GORD).  Achalasia.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Endoscopy and biopsy:  the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) recommends the following:  suspected cancer pathway referral within two weeks for people with abdominal mass consistent with stomach cancer

GIT & LIVER part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  urgent endoscopy within two weeks in people with dysphagia or aged = 55 with weight loss and upper abdominal pain/reflux/dyspepsia.  endoscopic ultrasound and CT scan of abdomen and thorax to determine resectability  offer human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2) testing to those with metastatic adenocarcinoma.  Classification of gastric cancer:  Lauren classification divides adenocarcinomas into diffuse and intestinal:  diffuse type tumours are poorly differentiated, disbursed throughout the stomach, and can be aggressive. Diffuse type malignancies metastasise at a faster rate than their more benign intestinal counterparts and there is no gender difference in their incidence  intestinal type tumours are, in contrast, well differentiated and slow growing. They are more common in men and slow to metastasise.  the Japanese Gastroenterological Endoscopy Society (JGES) classify according to whether tumour is polypoid, flat, or ulcerated.  Management Non-pharmacological  Multidisciplinary team (MDT) discussion. Pharmacological  Adjuvant chemotherapy may improve prognosis for advanced disease.  NICE recommend Trastuzumab for HER2 positive metastatic adenocarcinoma.  Triple therapy to eradicate H.Pylori.  PPIs for Gastric ulcers. Gastroenteritis  Gastroenteritis is a transient disorder due to enteric infection with viruses, bacteria, or parasites.  Overview Key Facts  Gastroenteritis is a transient disorder due to enteric infection with viruses, bacteria, or parasites.  Characterised by the sudden onset of diarrhoea, with or without vomiting. Associated symptoms may include fever, blood in stools and lethargy.  Gastroenteritis affects up to 20% of the United Kingdom (UK) population annually, but only one in six seek medical attention.  The most common cause is viral.  In most people, the condition is self-limiting and may be managed at home with adequate fluid hydration; however, there is a risk of complications such as dehydration which may require hospital admission.  Mortality is rare in developed countries, but the risk is greatest in young children, the elderly, those with co-morbidities and those who are immunocompromised. Epidemiology  Around 20% of the UK population develops infectious intestinal disease each year.  Of those infected, only one in six presents to a General Practitioner. G

DR. JAM  Of those who present, only a small proportion will have a stool specimen sent for investigation.  Viral gastroenteritis is the most common.  Norovirus infections are increasing. Can be transmitted by contact with an infected person, consumption of contaminated food or water, or contact with contaminated surfaces or objects Bacteria Campylobacter Two species of Campylobacter account for the majority of infections: C.jejuni and C.coli Consumption of undercooked meat (especially poultry), unpasteurised milk, or untreated water, the source of infection is often not found Escherichia coli Gram-negative, rod-shaped bacterium

JAM Gastrointestinal Disease in Advanced HIV  Gastrointestinal disorders are a major cause of morbidity and mortality in advanced HIV disease and fall into four major categories based on clinical presentation.  Overview Key Facts  Gastrointestinal disorders are a major cause of morbidity and mortality in advanced HIV disease and fall into four major categories based on clinical presentation:  oral/oesophageal disease – candidiasis, periodontal disease (gingivitis), oral herpes simplex, Kaposi’s sarcoma, aphthous ulcers, and oral hairy leukoplakia  diarrhoea – opportunistic infection with atypical Mycobacteria, Cryptosporidium and Microsporidia; CMV colitis; Giardia lamblia infection; and bacterial dysentery  biliary and pancreatic disease – cholangiopathy and pancreatitis  anorectal diseases (proctitis and anal warts) – HSV, CMV, Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Chlamydia proctitis and HPV.  Chronic diarrhoea in advanced HIV is associated with HAART treatment failure, and may lead to severe malnutrition, further impairment of immunity, and resultant cyclical infection.  Diarrhoea is also a side effect of protease inhibitors, especially lopinavir. Epidemiology  Up to 90% of untreated HIV positive patients in Africa will develop chronic diarrhoea. Aetiology  Bacterial infections such as non-typhi Salmonella, Shigella, Campylobacter and E. coli account for 20% cases of diarrhoea in advanced HIV.  Mycobacterial infection – notably atypical Mycobacteria – account for 10-15% cases.  40% of cases are due to protozoal infection e.g. Cryptosporidiosis and Microsporidiosis.  Viruses such as CMV account for 20% of cases of diarrhoea in advanced HIV. Pathophysiology  The low CD4 count in advanced/untreated HIV places patients at high risk of infection by ‘professional’ and ‘opportunistic’ pathogens.

GIT & LIVER part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Clinical Presentation  Dysphagia and odynophagia are commonly caused by oesophageal candidiasis.  Discrete mouth lesions:  painful ulceration is seen with aphthous ulcers and HSV infection  adherent white plaques are seen in oral hairy leukoplakia and oral candidiasis. The former is unaffected by tooth-brushing, whereas the white surface material rubs away in Candida to leave a raw bleeding surface beneath.  Diarrhoea may be watery (cryptosporidium, microsporidia) or bloody (salmonella, CMV).  Biliary disease presents with jaundice, steatorrhoea, and dark urine; patients may also develop pancreatitis which manifests as severe abdominal pain, nausea and vomiting.  Anorectal disorders typically present with anal discharge (often purulent), tenesmus (feeling of incomplete emptying), perianal itch, bleeding, and diarrhoea.  Differential Diagnosis  Oral/oesophageal disorders:  discrete lesions within the mouth – aphthous ulcers, oral hairy leukoplakia, oral candidiasis, Kaposi’s sarcoma  HSV – perioral cold sores.  Diarrhoea:  ‘professional’ pathogens – Salmonella, Shigella, Giardia, CMV  opportunistic infections – MAI complex, Isospora, Cryptosporidium, Microsporidia  Anorectal disorders:  anal warts and ulceration – HPV (common warts), HSV, anal cancer  proctitis – rectal gonorrhoea, Chlamydia, lymphogranuloma venereum, syphilis.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Oral disorders are often diagnosed clinically. However, useful investigations include:  viral and fungal swabs for suspected HSV or Candida infection  biopsy and microscopy of suspected oral hairy leukoplakia.  Diarrhoea requires extensive investigation:  full blood count (FBC), urea and electrolytes (U&E), liver function tests (LFTs), c-reative protein (CRP) – look for signs of dehydration from severe diarrhoea  blood cultures (salmonellosis)  stool culture – microscopy, culture and sensitivity and ova, cysts and parasites  sigmoidoscopy or colonoscopy with tissue biopsy:  CMV colitis – ‘owl’s eye’ sign due to inclusion bodies in colonic mucosa. Gastrointestinal Tuberculosis  Tuberculosis is a bacterial infection that can affect any part of the body but usually affects the lungs.

GIT & LIVER part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Overview Key Facts  Tuberculosis is a bacterial infection that can affect any part of the body but usually affects the lungs.  Gastrointestinal tuberculosis is a form of extra-pulmonary tuberculosis that is caused by the bacteria Mycobacterium tuberculosis.  It is defined as an infection of the peritoneum, abdominal organs and abdominal lymph nodes with the M.tuberculosis organism and may include involvement of any of the following sites:  peritoneum  oesophagus  stomach  intestinal tract  hepatobiliary tree  pancreas  perianal area  lymph nodes.  The condition is more common in developing countries and relatively rare in developed countries.  At-risk groups in developed countries include immigrants, the homeless and those in institutions such as prison or long term care facilities.  Infection often occurs secondary to pulmonary tuberculosis (TB) due to swallowing infected sputum or by haematogenous spread (the patient may not have signs of pulmonary TB).  Presenting symptoms include fever, anorexia, weight loss, abdominal pain, diarrhoea, nausea and vomiting.  As symptoms may be non-specific, diagnosis is often delayed.  Ultrasound or computed tomography (CT) may suggest a diagnosis, but biopsy either laparoscopically or endoscopically is confirmative.  Treatment of gastrointestinal TB is the same as that of pulmonary TB and involves a combination of antibiotic therapy, most commonly consisting of rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide and ethambutol. Epidemiology  Tuberculosis is common in developing countries but less common in developed countries.  Groups most at risk in developed countries include:  those on low incomes  homeless people  people with alcohol problems  HIV-positive individuals  immigrants from countries with a high incidence of TB  patients with diabetes. G

DR. JAM Aetiology  The causative organism is the bacteria Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Pathophysiology  Infection may occur secondary to pulmonary TB due to swallowing infected sputum or by haematogenous spread.  Clinical Presentation  Patients may present with non-specific signs and symptoms such as:  malaise  persistent fever  anorexia  weight loss  diarrhoea  abdominal pain.  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses include:  Crohn’s disease  Ulcerative colitis  Primary intestinal lymphoma  Gastroenteritis  Malignancy  Peptic ulcer disease  Anorexia nervosa  Chronic pancreatitis.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Ultrasound or CT may suggest diagnosis.  Biopsy, either laparoscopically or endoscopically is confirmative.  Management  Note that TB is a notifiable disease.  A clinician (usually a TB specialist) should notify a new culture-confirmed case of TB, or where TB is suspected and a decision has been made to treat the person, within three working days. Conventional anti-tuberculous therapy  Management of active TB is delivered in a combination of four drugs:  rifampicin  isoniazid  pyrazinamide  ethambutol.

GIT & LIVER part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Short courses of treatment for six months are now standard. All drugs are given for two months and isoniazid and rifampicin are continued for a further four months.  If pyrazinamide has to be discontinued due to side-effects, a 9month regimen is necessary.  Second-line agents (eg ethionamide, propionamide, streptomycin, cycloserine) may be needed.  Compliance can pose major problems and directly observed therapy (DOT – larger doses of drugs administered three times per week) is used when poor compliance is anticipated.  Side-effects from these drugs are common. They include:  hepatitis due to rifampicin, isoniazid and pyrazinamide. There is an increased risk of hepatotoxicity from antituberculous chemotherapy with age  optic neuritis: may be caused by ethambutol; visual acuity should be checked before treatment is initiated. May also cause yellowing of vision  peripheral neuropathy: may be due to isoniazid; 10 mg pyridoxine daily is given in those at particular risk of this complication (eg people with alcohol problems, diabetes and patients with renal failure)  urinary discolouration (red/orange colour) – rifampicin. Surgical  Surgical management may be required either to:  bypass damaged segments of bowl  remove diseased areas  manage complications such as stricture formation or perforation. Prognosis  The condition may cause significant morbidity and mortality, especially as non-specific symptoms can delay diagnosis.  The need for prolonged regimes of treatment leading to poor compliance, as well as the emergence of multi-drug resistant forms, complicates treatment further. Gastro-oesophageal Reflux Disease  Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease is a common chronic condition caused by reflux of acidic stomach juices going back up into the oesophagus or beyond (eg oral cavity, larynx, lung) causing symptoms of heartburn and acid regurgitation and associated complications.  Overview Key Facts  Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GORD) is a common chronic condition caused by reflux of acidic stomach juices going back up into the oesophagus or beyond (eg oral cavity, larynx, lung) causing symptoms of heartburn and acid regurgitation and associated complications. G

DR. JAM  Diagnosis is clinical, but endoscopy can be useful in evaluating for complications.  Proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) can serve as both diagnosis and initial treatment.  Relapse rate is high if treatment is stopped.  Complications include:  stricture  Barrett’s oesophagus  oesophageal carcinoma. Epidemiology  Between 10–20% of the adult population has GORD symptoms at some stage of their lives. Aetiology  The lower oesophageal sphincter is located at the gastrooesophageal junction.  During oesophageal peristalsis, the lower oesophageal sphincter relaxes to allow food to enter the stomach.  At rest, the sphincter prevents reflux of stomach contents into the oesophagus.  The lower oesophageal sphincter contains intrinsic smooth muscle and skeletal muscle.  In GORD, transient lower oesophageal sphincter relaxation occurs more frequently.  Risk factors of GORD include:  hiatus hernia  heavy alcohol use  smoking  stress and anxiety  pregnancy  obesity  certain foods:  chocolate  coffee (can relax the lower oesophageal sphincter)  fatty meals (delay gastric emptying)  carbonated drinks  citrus and spicy foods.  medications, such as:  tricyclic antidepressants  nitrates  calcium channel blockers  anticholinergics.  gastric acid hypersecretion, eg Zollinger–Ellison syndrome  delayed gastric emptying  oesophageal dysmotility, eg systemic sclerosis  family history.

GIT & LIVER part 2 MIL ALRAJHI Pathophysiology  Laryngo-pharyngeal symptoms may be caused by pharyngeal reflux.  This mostly occurs at night when the tone of the upper oesophageal sphincter relaxes.  Acid may stimulate the vagus nerve causing chronic coughing and throat clearing.  Severity of mucosal damage is dependent on:  duration of contact with stomach contents (number of reflux episodes)  characteristics of stomach content  how resistant the epithelium is to damage.  Clinical Presentation  Oesophageal:  heartburn (burning and retrosternal discomfort after meals, lying, bending over, straining – relieved by antacids)  belching  acid regurgitation (sour/bitter taste, mainly after meals)  waterbrash (increased salivation in mouth)  odynophagia (painful swallowing due to oesophagitis or ulceration)  enamel erosion  halitosis.  Extra-oesophageal:  nocturnal asthma  chronic cough  laryngitis  sinusitis.  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses include:  coronary artery disease  function oesophageal disorder/functional heartburn  achalasia  peptic ulcer disease  malignancy  Zollinger–Ellison syndrome.  consider in patients with lack of response to treatment.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Diagnosis is clinical, supported by testing when appropriate.  PPI trial  endoscopy should be performed in cases of:  dysphagia  > 55 years old with ALARM symptoms: G

JAM  anaemia, iron deficiency  loss of weight > 10 kg in six months  anorexia  recent onset of progressive symptoms  melaena/haematemesis.  treatment refractory dyspepsia.  24-hour oesophageal pH monitoring for patients with persistent symptoms on PPI therapy and unrevealing endoscopy.  it can show abnormal exposure to oesophageal acid without having oesophagitis.  Manometry evaluates oesophageal contractions and lower oesophageal sphincter function.  Management Non-pharmacological  Lifestyle modification:  weight loss  smoking cessation  small, regular meals  avoid eating < three hours before sleeping  raise the bed head  reduce:  caffeine  chocolate  spicy foods  citrus foods  alcohol  hot drinks  fizzy drinks. Pharmacological  Antacids or alginates reduce symptoms.  Add a PPI, the mainstay therapy for GORD.  For refractory symptoms, add a H2 blocker or increase dose/frequency of PPI.  Avoid drugs affecting oesophageal dysmotility:  nitrates  anticholinergics  calcium channel blockers  tricyclic antidepressants.  Avoid drugs that damage mucosa, eg bisphosphonates and NSAIDs.  When symptoms abate, treatment can be titrated down to the minimum dose that maintains remission, eg:  reducing dose of PPI  giving PPI intermittently

Surgical  A laparoscopic Nissen fundoplication involves mobilisation of the fundus of the stomach which is then wrapped around the lower oesophagus.  Magnetic sphincter augmentation with beads.  Surgery aims to increase resting lower oesophageal sphincter pressure.  consider it in patients who have a good response to PPIs who do not wish to undertake long-term medical treatment.  Prognosis  Most patients respond well to PPI treatment.  It is common for patients to relapse when their PPI therapy is stopped.  Complications of GORD include:  oesophageal ulcer, haemorrhage or perforation  oesophageal stricture  Barrett’s oesophagus  adenocarcinoma of the oesophagus. Other  If endoscopy demonstrates erosive, ulcerative, strictures or Barrett’s oesophagus, then maintain PPI.  Endoscopy showing multiple linear oesophageal ulcers:  Barrett’s oesophagus: G

JAM Gilbert Syndrome  Gilbert syndrome is a benign, inherited metabolic condition resulting in temporarily high and isolated unconjugated levels of bilirubin.  Overview Key Facts  Gilbert syndrome is a benign, inherited metabolic condition resulting in temporarily high and isolated unconjugated levels of bilirubin.  One in three patients are asymptomatic; the rest develop mild jaundice. It is often an incidental diagnosis following liver function tests.  Diagnosis is based on increased levels of unconjugated bilirubin in the absence of liver disease.  No treatment is required. Management is based on patient information and education. Epidemiology  There is an estimated prevalence of 5–10% in Western Europe, with many cases undetected. Aetiology  Genetic – autosomal recessive (gene mutation UGT-1A1).

GIT & LIVER part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  It can be triggered by other illnesses, eg viral infection.  Potential triggers of jaundice – fasting and/or dieting, surgery, heavy physical exertion, dehydration, alcohol, infection and lack of sleep. Pathophysiology  Bilirubin is formed from red-cell breakdown; in hepatic conjugation, it is bound to UDP-glucuronic acid and then secreted into bile.  In Gilbert syndrome, there is a reduction in the conjugation enzyme (UDP-glucuronyl transferase) which reduces conjugation by about two-thirds leading to an increase in unconjugated bilirubin.  Clinical Presentation  One of three patients is asymptomatic.  Gilbert’s is often found incidentally on blood tests or with mild jaundice* on examination.  Examination signs – mild jaundice, no hepatomegaly, no other signs of liver disease.  Patients may report a provoking factor, eg lack of sleep, infection.  *Jaundice = yellowing of the skin, sclera and mucous membranes.  Differential Diagnosis  Can be split into differential for conjugated and unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia: Conjugated raised bilirubin Unconjugated raised bilirubin Gallstones Steatohepatitis Infection, eg viral hepatitis, Epstein–Barr virus, cytomegalovirus Some drugs, eg paracetamol, alcoholic hepatitis, erythromycin, oestrogens, corticosteroids Metabolic, eg Wilson's disease, ischaemic hepatitis, haemochromatosis Autoimmune, eg 1° biliary cirrhosis, 1° sclerosing cholangitis, autoimmune hepatitis Malignancy, eg cholangiocarcinoma, extrinsic compression, metastases, renal carcinoma Infiltration, eg tuberculosis, lymphoma, amyloid, sarcoid Drugs, eg methyldopa and sulfasalazine (causing haemolysis) and rifampicin (impaired liver bilirubin clearance) Other genetic, eg Crigler–Najjar syndrome Physiological neonatal jaundice With haemolysis: thalassaemia sickle cell disease prosthetic heart valve autoimmune haemolytic anaemia hereditary spherocytosis G

DR. JAM  Diagnosis/Investigation  Diagnosis is based on: Presence of unconjugated bilirubinaemia + absence of: liver enzyme abnormality haemolysis evidence of liver disease  Diagnosis should also include the assessment of potential precipitating factors and exclude other diagnoses.  Clinical history should include asking about abdominal pain, pruritis, pale stools and darkness of urine. Signs that indicate liver disease (but not Gilbert syndrome) General Hepatosplenomegaly, palmar erythema, spider naevi (>5 in women), finger clubbing, leukonychia, Dupuytren’s contracture, gynaecomastia, Murphy’s sign, widespread abdominal tenderness, caput medusae, ascites In liver failure Reduced neuromuscular function, eg in hepatic encephalopathy (ataxia, nystagmus, asterixis) Altered mental state, eg drowsiness, confusion Bruising, purpura and petechiae  Investigations include:  Bloods:  raised serum bilirubin (but not > 68–85 μmol/l)  ask for unconjugated/conjugated breakdown (in Gilbert syndrome, the conjugated levels are normal or < 20% of total); other LFTs normal  full blood count (FBC), including blood film and reticulocyte count (to exclude haemolysis).  Following referral – liver biopsy, bilirubin levels following fasting or nicotinic acid; genetic testing is very rarely used.  Management  No treatment is necessary.  Referral to gastroenterology/hepatology is only needed if diagnosis is uncertain. Non-pharmacological  Patient information, especially that it is benign, not contagious and self-limiting. Pharmacological  Note:  increased risk of drug toxicity with gemfibrozil (a fibrate) and/or statin  some have a higher risk of toxicity from paracetamol overdose.

GIT & LIVER part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Prognosis  Prognosis is good and life expectancy is normal. Haemorrhoids  Haemorrhoids are abnormal enlargements of the normal arteriovenous anal cushions of the anal canal.  Overview Key Facts  Haemorrhoids are abnormal enlargements of the normal arteriovenous anal cushions of the anal canal.  Classified as first, second, or third degree.  Associated with typically painless bright red postrectal (PR) bleeding that is not mixed in with the stool.  May thrombose, which can cause a painful perianal swelling.  Diagnosis is mostly clinical; assess for/exclude pathological causes of rectal bleeding.  Can be managed conservatively (lifestyle advice/analgesia and topical therapy) or with secondary care intervention (haemorrhoid banding/ligation/haemorrhoidectomy). Epidemiology  Affects approximately 4.4% of the general worldwide population.  No sex predominance.  Incidence peaks at 45–65 years. Aetiology  Commonly idiopathic, but may be predisposed by:  pregnancy  cardiac failure  excessive use of purgatives  chronic constipation  portal hypertension. Pathophysiology  Enlargement and distal displacement of the normal arteriovenous anal cushions, which may prolapse through the anal canal.  Even in a person with no haemorrhoids, three anal vascular cushions are found in the 3-, 7- and 11-O’clock positions, consisting of rectal mucosa, arterioles, venules and their anastomoses.  They are supported by elastic connective tissue and smooth muscle. They engorge during increased abdominal pressure, and theoretically assist the sphincter in maintaining watertight closure of the canal. G

DR. JAM  Haemorrhoids occur when these vascular cushions enlarge and eventually prolapse through the anus.  Clinical Presentation  Symptoms of haemorrhoids:  bleeding:  painless fresh blood  on paper or splashes into pan  blood is seen around the stool motion - not intermixed.  symptoms of anaemia  haemorrhoids may lead to anaemia, but this is rare – other causes of anaemia should be excluded.  mucous discharge  pruritus  patients may complain of prolapse on defecation or exercise.  Haemorrhoids may also become thrombosed. This can cause bleeding and severe pain.  Signs of haemorrhoids  skin tags may be present around the anus  prolapsed haemorrhoids, or haemorrhoids prolapsing on straining:  prolapsed haemorrhoids are usually at the 3-, 7- and 11-o’clock lithotomy positions  they often include tissue from above and below the dentate line and are usually dark-red or purple.  on proctoscopy, dark haemorrhoidal tissue is seen.  Classification  haemorrhoids may be classified as either internal and external haemorrhoids, or as first to fourth degree. Both classifications are used by the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE).  internal vs. external  internal haemorrhoids originate above the dentate line, while external haemorrhoids originate below this line.  classification by degrees:  first degree – confined to the anal canal, may bleed but do not prolapse  second degree – prolapse on defecation/straining, with spontaneous reduction  third degree – may prolapse spontaneously or with defecation and remain persistently prolapsed outside the anal margin unless digitally reduced  fourth degree – irreducible prolapse.  Differential Diagnosis  Fissure in anus.  Perianal haematoma due to trauma.  Perianal or ischiorectal abscess.  Tumour of the anal margin.

GIT & LIVER part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Prolapsing rectal polyp.  Rectal prolapse.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Mostly clinical, but:  exclude other causes of anaemia and rectal bleeding.  this may involve sigmoidoscopy, colonoscopy, gastroscopy, or contrast studies.  The abdomen should also be examined for pelvic mass or an enlarged liver:  this helps to eliminate predisposing causes such as liver disease-causing portal hypertension, or a pelvic cancer increasing intrabdominal pressure.  Proctoscopy may also be of use in diagnosis.  Management Non-pharmacological  If asymptomatic, the haemorrhoids should not be treated.  If symptomatic, NICE recommends conservative measures such as ensuring stools are soft and easy to pass, with good fibre and fluid intake.  Further conservative measures include good anal hygiene (ensuring the anal region is clean and dry), and not withholding stool. Pharmacological  Simple analgesia with paracetamol is effective for pain relief:  avoid opioids as these can cause and worsen constipation  avoid non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) if rectal bleeding is present.  Topical preparations are also of benefit, these may include:  creams/ointments etc which contain an astringent and an emollient (eg Anusol®)  those that contain a local anaesthetic and an astringent (eg Germoloids®).  NICE CKS has full recommendations for topical treatments.  Secondary care pharmacological approaches may be indicated if conservative measures fail or there is recurrence:  injection sclerotherapy – obliterates blood supply to the haemorrhoid, causing atrophy  infrared coagulation/photocoagulation – fixes the haemorrhoid and reduces the tendency to prolapse.  Injecting and banding haemorrhoids:  banding or injection of a sclerosant via a proctoscope can be done as an outpatient in clinic on unprepared bowel.  Indications:  symptomatic first- or second-degree haemorrhoids that have persisted despite medical intervention (asymptomatic haemorrhoids should not be treated) G

DR. JAM  third- or fourth-degree haemorrhoids or above may be banded or injected in a patient reluctant or unfit to undergo surgery but the results will not be as effective  banding is more effective than injections, but has more complications, such as pain or bleeding.  Pre-procedure:  the procedure and its risks and complications should be described to the patient  a PR examination and rigid sigmoidoscopy should be performed to exclude any other pathology that might cause anal canal-type bleeding  the patient lies in the left lateral position  this is not a sterile procedure, but gloves should be worn  the assistant drawing up the phenol should also wear gloves because it is highly irritant, and the injector should wear goggles.  do not inject phenol in almond oil if the patient is allergic to nuts  do not band or inject if the patient is on warfarin, has a clotting disorder, or is immunosuppressed.  Procedure:  a lubricated, illuminated proctoscope is inserted, the obturator is removed and the proctoscope slowly withdrawn to visualise the haemorrhoids  the position and size of the haemorrhoids is noted as clockfaced numbers, as if the patients were in lithotromy (ie anterior is 12-o'clock lithotomy, posterior is 6-o'clock lithotomy, right lateral is 9-o'clock lithotromy, left lateral is 3-o'clock lithotomy)  the proctoscope is then re-inserted with the obturator to above the dentate line.  if injecting, a 3–4-ml aliquot of sclerosant (usually 5% phenol in almond oil) is injected submucosally (forming a thin-walled ‘ballooning’ of the mucosa immediately) above the dentate line in the position correlating with the most prominent haemorrhoids  a long-procedures aimed to produce mucosal adherence and prevent prolapse and bleeding include infrared photocoagulation, cryotherapy, bipolar diathermy, laser photocoagulation and direct-current electrotherapy  gabriel or spinal needle is used for this because it is long enough to traverse the proctoscope. Do not inject anteriorly  if banding, the mucosa is suctioned or grasped into the bander above the dentate line in the position correlating to the most prominent haemorrhoids and the band applied.  No more than three haemorrhoids should be banded or injected at a single sitting.  Between the applications, the proctoscope should be re-inserted, ensuring that another bit of mucosa is visualised, and that the proctoscope is again position high above the dentate line.  If the patient feels sharp pain on insertion of the needle or grasping or suctioning the mucosa, the proctoscope should be repositioned before sclerosant is injected or the bands applied.  Intraprocedural hazards:

GIT & LIVER part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  not applying the bands or injecting the sclerosant high enough: often haemorrhoids prolapse below the dentate line into the perianal sensate area and so the procedure should be performed above the engorged, haemorrhoidal tissue into fairly normal-looking mucosa  if mucosa/skin below the dentate line is banded, the patient will feel immediate intense pain that will not be relievedunless the band is removed.  injecting sclerosant too deeply: if the thin-walled mucosa does not immediately balloon out while injecting, pull back the needle. Deep injections anteriorly affect the adjacent prostate, urethra or vagina (see ‘Complications’ below)  spilling sclerosant: phenol is highly irritant and, if it is spilled or injected into the anal canal and runs out onto the perianal skin, it will cause pruritusand ulceration.  Postoperative management:  review in Outpatients in six weeks  may need further treatment  if heavy bleeds persist despite treatment or any worrying symptoms emerge, investigate the large bowel for other causes of bleeding  if haemorrhoids do not regress and are still symptomatic, consider surgical options for treatment.  Complications of banding and injection of haemorrhoids:  recurrence of haemorrhoids: avoid constipation. Repeating treatment may be necessary  pain: the procedure should be painless unless the band or sclerosant has been applied too low  bleeding: this is more likely with banding and can be torrential, requiring hospital admission. Advise the patient that some spotting is normal but to seek medical advice if it becomes heavy. Secondary haemorrhage may occur at ten days after banding (when the bands slough off)  deep injections of sclerosant: can cause perirectal fibrosis, urethritis, vaginal or rectal oleogranulomas, pain, ulcers, haematospermia or impotence. Surgical  Surgical treatment options for haemorrhoids include haemorrhoidectomy, stapled haemorrhoidectomy, and haemorrhoidal artery ligation  Rubber band ligation is used to ‘tie off’ haemorrhoids. With reduced blood supply, the haemorrhoid becomes necrotic and drops off.  Haemorrhoidectomy – surgical removal of the haemorrhoid.  Indications:  symptomatic haemorrhoids that have not responded to conservative or local management or are unsuitable for banding or injection of sclerosants. These are usually third- or fourth-degree haemorrhoids, haemorrhoids straddling the dentate line or long-standing haemorrhoids associated with anal skin tags  a formal haemorrhoidectomy can also be performed for acutely thrombosed haemorrhoids as an alternative to conservative management, but complications are more likely. DR. JAM  Preoperative preparation:  the patient is fully consented and warned about the outcome, hazards and complications  the rectum is emptied by means of glycerine suppositories or a phosphate enema  the procedure is under general, regional or even local anaesthesia, and the patient is in the lithotomy position.  Procedure:  sigmoidoscopy is performed to exclude other causes of anal canal-type bleeding  the perineum is prepped with antiseptic solution and the patient is draped  the haemorrhoids are injected with 1% lidocaine plus adrenaline 1 in 200 000 to define tissue planes, reduce bleeding and assist analgesia during this short but painful operation, making the general anaesthesia easier  lace three Dunhill forceps on the junction between each of the haemorrhoids and the perianal skin (ie just distal to the haemorrhoidal cushion) including any tags. Traction on these will prolapse the haemorrhoids into view  place three Burkitt’s forceps on the junction between each of the haemorrhoids and the normal anal mucosa (ie just proximal to the haemorrhoidal cushion)  starting with the lowest haemorrhoid to avoid blood in the surgical field, hold the other haemorrhoids out of the way and excise them one at a time  to excise the haemorrhoid, place a forefinger into the anal canal under the prolapsed haemorrhoid and incise just the skin and mucosa with diathermy in an ellipse around the haemorrhoid (including any skin tag). Identify the white fibres of the anal sphincter before deepening the incision  the aim of dissection is to dissect the disc of prolapsed mucosa of the haemorrhoid off the sphincter, staying in a plane between the two. The pedicle will become evident and will need to be suture-ligated with a 2.0 Vicryl suture  before starting dissection on the remaining haemorrhoids, ensure that an adequate skin bridge can be left between the incisions, thus avoiding anal stenosis. If it looks difficult, just excise the two most prominent haemorrhoids  the final result should resemble a three-leafed clover, with triangular-shaped skin bridges between each excised pile  the wounds can be left open or sutured with undyed Vicryl. They are dressed with Kaltostat that is tucked into the anal canal and folded out over the wounds.  Intraoperative hazards:  damage to the anal sphincter  incorporating the sphincter into the transfixion ligature (causing severe post-op pain).  Post-op:  patient is sent home on metronidazole, lactulose and analgesia for seven days  dressings are soaked off in the bath.  Complications:  bleeding: may be reactionary within 24 hours of the operation. Secondary bleeding, often due to infection, typically occurs on post-op day ten.

GIT & LIVER part 2 MIL ALRAJHI Bleeding may not be apparent externally if blood fills the rectum. The patient may need transfusion, examination under anaesthesia or packing of the anal canal  acute retention of urine: due to post-op pain  constipation: avoided by post-op analgesia and laxatives  stricture: occurs if the surgeon has failed to leave a bridge of epithelium between each excised haemorrhoid  anal fissures: due to poor healing. Other  Anatomy of the rectum  the anal canal is the last 4 cm of the alimentary tract  there are two layers of circular muscle making up the wall, an internal anal sphincter of smooth muscle, and an external anal sphincter of skeletal muscle  the intersphincteric groove is the area between the external and internal sphincters  the anorectal junction is at a 90° angle at the pelvic floor, where the puborectalis muscle forms a sling around the bowel and is continuous with the external sphincter  the mucous membrane in the anal canal forms horizontal folds called ‘anal valves’ above which submucosal anal glands secrete mucus  infection in these glands produces anal abscesses and fistulas.  The dentate line:  the pectinate (dentate) line is just above the level of the anal valves, some way above the intersphincteric groove  the colorectum is lined with columnar epithelium as far as the dentate line in the middle of the anal canal, where sensitive squamous epithelium takes over  the pecten is the area between the dentate line and the intersphincteric groove, where the epithelium is transitional.  Anatomy of the anal canal: G

JAM HELLP Syndrome  HELLP syndrome is a serious pregnancy complication characterised by haemolysis, elevated liver enzymes and low platelet count, which can lead to serious maternal and fetal complications and requires prompt medical intervention.  Overview Key Facts  Considered as a severe form of pre-eclampsia occurring between 27 and 37 weeks gestation.  Characterised by:  H – haemolysis  EL – elevated liver enzymes  LP – low platelets.  Symptoms include hypertension, proteinuria, epigastric/right upper quadrant pain, nausea, vomiting, headache and malaise.  Treated with intravenous (IV) magnesium sulphate, IV dexamethasone, control of blood pressure, replacement of blood products as needed and definitively by delivery of fetus and placenta.

GIT & LIVER part 2 MIL ALRAJHI Epidemiology  Occurs in 1–8 per 1000 pregnancies.  Usually presents between 27 and 37 weeks gestation but can also present postpartum (15–30% of cases).  Risk factors include advanced maternal age, European ethnicity, obesity, comorbidities (eg diabetes, hypertension), abnormal placentation and previous pregnancies with pre-eclampsia. Aetiology  Aetiology is unclear but factors thought to contribute to HELLP syndrome include:  abnormal trophoblast invasion of the spiral arteries  inadequate placental vascular remodelling in early pregnancy  an inappropriate maternal systemic inflammatory response  placental release of anti-angiogenic factors  genetic predisposition  immunological intolerance. Pathophysiology  Features include vasospasm, endothelial dysfunction, hepatic ischaemic damage, micro-angiopathic haemolytic anaemia and thrombocytopenia.  The liver is often affected by vascular changes resulting in reduced hepatic perfusion. This damage can lead to intra-parenchymal haemorrhage and/or subcapsular hepatic haematomas.  Hepatocyte dysfunction and apoptosis result in periportal necrosis – variation in this is likely in relation to the volume of placentalderived humoral, anti-angiogenic and inflammatory factors.  Hypotheses about pathophysiology include:  maternal immune system coming into contact with fetal antigens causing acute rejection reactions  liver injury mediated by CD-95 ligand found in the placenta  systemic inflammatory response syndrome.  Clinical Presentation Criteria  Haemolysis:  elevated LDH > 600 IU/l  elevated bilirubin > 1.2 mg/dl  low serum haptoglobin.  Elevated liver transaminases – AST and/or ALT > 70 IU/l.  Thrombocytopenia – platelets <100 000/μl. Symptoms/signs  Common:  nausea/vomiting  hypertension  brisk tendon reflexes  right upper quadrant pain G

DR. JAM  malaise  headache  oedema.  Uncommon/rare:  visual loss/disturbances  jaundice  bleeding, eg haematuria.  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses include:  acute fatty liver of pregnancy – hypoglycaemia, leukocytosis and higher levels of increased total bilirubin help to distinguish from HELLP syndrome  thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura – thrombocytopenia is more severe than in HELLP syndrome and requires transfusion  haemolytic uraemic syndrome – more significant microvascular injury affecting renal function compared to HELLP syndrome  systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and/or catastrophic antiphospholipid antibody syndrome – more likely in patients with a pre-existing history of either condition.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Investigations to order:  full blood count (FBC) – reduced Hb, low/normal haematocrit, thrombocytopenia  peripheral blood smear – schistocytes, burr cells, polychromasia  liver function tests – elevated AST and ALT  bilirubin – elevated  serum LDH – elevated  uric acid – elevated  urinalysis + protein : creatinine ratio – proteinuria and elevated ratio  PT/PTT – prolonged  fibrinogen – reduced  fetal ultrasound scan (USS) – fetal growth restriction.  Investigations to consider:  serum glucose – hypoglycaemia  urea and electrolytes (U&Es) – may be raised creatinine and electrolyte abnormalities  antithrombin - decreased  haptoglobin – decreased  maternal upper abdomen USS, CT or MRI – rule out liver bleeding  LDH to AST ratio < 22 in HELLP syndrome.

GIT & LIVER part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Management Suspected  First-line – seizure prophylaxis, ie continuous infusion of IV magnesium sulfate + IV dexamethasone.  If blood pressure is > 160/105 mmHg, antihypertensive treatment – IV labetalol or nicardipine or hydralazine. Confirmed  First-line – delivery of baby + IV dexamethasone + seizure prophylaxis (IV magnesium sulfate).  If blood pressure is > 160/105 mmHg, antihypertensive treatment – IV labetalol or nicardipine or hydralazine.  If the platelet count is < 25 × 109/l or < 30 × 109/l in cases of bleeding, surgery or massive transfusions – platelet transfusion and/or anti-D immunoglobin.  If fibrinogen < 2.94 μmol/l – fresh frozen plasma or cryoprecipitate.  If haematocrit < 25% – blood transfusion.  Prognosis  The maternal mortality rate is 1–2%.  The recurrence rate is 2–6%. Other  Complications:  disseminated intravascular coagulation  placental abruption  acute renal failure  pulmonary oedema  liver haematoma  hypoglycaemia  ascites. Hepatic Encephalopathy  Hepatic encephalopathy is a neuropsychiatric syndrome that may complicate acute or chronic liver disease.  Overview Key Facts  Hepatic encephalopathy is a neuropsychiatric syndrome that may complicate acute or chronic liver disease.  Underlying mechanisms are complex, but the absorption of toxins (such as ammonia) from bacterial breakdown of proteins in the gut is thought to play a major part.  Portosystemic shunting of blood occurs, toxins, therefore, bypass the liver and cross the blood–brain barrier G

DR. JAM  Common causes of acute hepatic encephalopathy are fulminant viral hepatitis and paracetamol toxicity, which are potentially fully reversible.  Indications of poor prognosis in acute cases are:  worsening acidosis  rising prothrombin time  falling Glasgow Coma Scale score.  These patients should be referred to a specialist centre as they may need transplantation.  Chronic hepatic encephalopathy may supervene in chronic liver disease of any type.  It is often precipitated by:  alcohol  drugs  GI haemorrhage  infections  constipation.  Symptoms may vary depending on severity, but mild cases may only be demonstrated by personality and degrees of intellectual impairment, with more severe changes leading to a ﬂapping tremor, decreased consciousness level and constructional apraxia.  Diagnosis is based on reported neurological deficits combined with laboratory abnormalities showing severe liver dysfunction.  Treatment includes lactulose, a high protein diet and treating precipitating causes.  Acute kidney injury may often supervene; the chance of recovery from hepatorenal failure is extremely poor. Epidemiology  Fifty per cent of liver cirrhosis patients will develop hepatic encephalopathy. Aetiology  Cirrhosis due to any cause. Pathophysiology  Underlying mechanisms are complex, but the absorption of toxins (such as ammonia) from bacterial breakdown of proteins in the gut is thought to play a major part in the development of the condition.  Portosystemic shunting of blood occurs, toxins, therefore, bypass the liver and cross the blood–brain barrier leading to symptomatology.  Clinical Presentation  Presentation of hepatic encephalopathy may include:  personality changes  intellectual impairment  confusion  reduced level of consciousness  vomiting

GIT & LIVER part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  seizures  hyperventilation  flapping tremor  constructional apraxia.  Hepatic encephalopathy is graded using the Conn score, higher grades indicated higher severity:  Grade 0: No personality or behavioural abnormality detected.  Grade 1: lack of awareness, euphoria or anxiety, shortened attention span, impaired performance of addition.  Grade 2: lethargy or apathy, minimal disorientation for time or place, subtle personality change, inappropriate behaviour, impaired performance of subtraction.  Grade 3: somnolence to semi stupor but responsive to verbal stimuli, confusion, gross disorientation.  Grade 4: coma.  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses include:  delirium due to other causes, ie infection, hypoglycaemia  brain tumour  stroke  meningitis  uraemia  Wernicke’s encephalopathy.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Diagnosis is based on reported neurological deficits alongside history and examination findings, combined with laboratory abnormalities showing severe liver dysfunction.  Arterial or serum ammonia levels will be raised, also check liver function tests, clotting, urea and electrolytes.  Psychometric tests may be useful for diagnosis in mild cases.  Electroencephalogram (EEG): may show high-amplitude lowfrequency waves and triphasic waves (not specific to hepatic encephalopathy.  Magnetic resonance imagining/computed tomography scanning should be carried out, especially on first presentations, to exclude other causes of altered mental function such as intracranial masses, bleeding or signs of infection.  Management  Management includes treating or removing precipitants, bowel cleansing, and supportive care.  ITU admission may be required in severe cases.  screen for and treat sepsis aggressively  if ascites is present, consider bacterial peritonitis and perform a diagnostic ascitic tap  there should be a low threshold for prescribing antibiotics. JAM  strict ﬂuid and electrolyte balance  low protein diet  laxatives (lactulose) to clear the gut and thus reduce toxin absorption  neomycin is now less commonly used  rifaxamin, a semi-synthetic antibiotic that decreases intestinal production and absorption of ammonia  in severe cases due to acute fulminant hepatic failure, transplantation may be required.  Prognosis  The prognosis is variable and depends on numerous factors including:  degree of hepatic failure  precipitating cause  co-existing conditions  time to initiation of treatment  presence of cirrhosis.  The development of hepatic encephalopathy in patients with cirrhosis is associated with a worse prognosis and is also more likely to be associated with relapses which tend to be severe.  Mortality rates are especially high if there is also renal impairments, where mortality exceeds 50%. Hepatobiliary Tumours  Hepatocellular carcinoma is the most common liver cancer – typically due to cirrhosis.  Overview Key Facts  Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is the most common liver cancer – typically due to cirrhosis.  Cholangiocarcinoma is an uncommon adenocarcinoma arising from the biliary epithelium.  Gallbladder carcinoma are tumours developing from the gallbladder.  Other liver cancers include:  fibrolamellar carcinoma  angiosarcoma  hepatoblastoma.  The liver is also a common site of cancer metastasis; these malignancies are considered to be secondary liver cancers as opposed the cancers which originate within the liver (primary malignancies).  85% of carcinomas of the gallbladder are adenocarcinomas.

GIT & LIVER part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Diagnosis is confirmed with ultrasound and biopsy.  Serum alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) is a tumour marker for HCC.  These cancers often present late and therefore the prognoses are poor. Epidemiology  Hepatic cancer:  primary hepatic malignancy are rare with only 4 000 new cases per year in the United Kingdom (UK)  secondary tumours are common, typically metastasising from the stomach, colon, breast and lung  hepatocellular carcinoma is rare in the UK (1–2 per 100 000):  incidence is increased 20–30 times in Africa, Asia, and Japan.  Cholangiosarcoma:  incidence is increasing  high incidence is reported in Thailand, South America, and Northern Japan.  Carcinoma of the gallbladder:  occurs in the elderly, but is uncommon  700 new cases diagnosed in UK per year  Woman : Man ratio 2 : 1. Aetiology Risk Factors  Hepatocellular carcinoma:  hepatitis B and C virus  alcohol consumption  haemochromatosis  cirrhosis  long-term oral contraceptive use  aflatoxin- carcinogen from the mould Aspergillus flavus which may contaminate food  smoking.  Cholangiocarcinoma:  sclerosing cholangitis  choledochal cyst or other biliary tract abnormality  liver fluke infection  Caroli’s disease (dilatation of the intrahepatic bile ducts predisposing to infection and stone formation)  smoking.  Carcinoma of the gallbladder:  ulcerative colitis  primary sclerosing cholangitis  gallstones  gallbladder polyps  smoking. JAM  Liver transplant:  very few patients are suitable – they should have single tumours smaller than 5 cm with no vascular or metastatic spread  AFP must be less than <1000iu/mL  5-year survival 90%.  Chemotherapy/ethanol injection into tumour/embolisation:  palliative with little survival benefit.  Targeted cancer therapies and biologics are available for use in advanced hepatocellular cancer (Sorafenib, Regorafenib) Cholangiocarcinoma  Treatment of cholangiocarcinoma will depend on the position and size of the cancer and whether it has spread beyond the bile duct, as well as on the individual patient's general health  Surgery (resection or transplant) is the only definitive cure but fewer than 20% of patients are suitable  transplant is offered if unresectable at presentation  few patients are suitable, but this gives the best prognosis  Chemotherapy  There are now a number of chemotherapies used for those with cholangiocarcinoma.  Gemcitabine and Cisplatin (Gem/Cis) is first line standard of care chemotherapy treatment for those with inoperable cholangiocarcinoma  Capecitabine is now offered to patients following surgical resection for their cholangiocarcinoma.  Folinic acid, fluorouracil and oxaliplatin (FOLFOX) may be offered to those patients with advanced or metastatic cholangiocarcinoma who have already received first line treatment  Radiotherapy, is not routinely used to treat cholangiocarcinoma, although there may be occasions when it is used palliatively.  Palliative stenting:  relieves jaundice and improves quality of life. Gallbladder cancer  Radical cholecystectomy is the mainstay of treatment and can be curative:  only suitable for localised early disease  5-year survival up to 5%.  Adjuvant treatments include radiotherapy and chemotherapy, and may follow regimes that are similar to those used in cholangiocarcinoma.  Prognosis  Hepatocellular carcinoma:  5-year survival for symptomatic patients is up to 10%  5-year survival post liver transplant is 70%.  Cholangiocarcinoma:  5-year survival rate following surgical resection between 20%–43%

Hereditary Haemochromatosis  Hereditary haemochromatosis is an inherited liver condition causing iron overload, that, over time, leads to chronic liver disease.  Overview Key Facts  Hereditary haemochromatosis is an inherited liver condition causing iron overload, that, over time, leads to chronic liver disease.  The condition is inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern with variable penetrance.  The mutation is of the HFE gene, which causes increased intestinal iron absorption, leading to iron deposition in joints, liver, heart, pancreas, pituitary, adrenals, and skin.  The condition is often asymptomatic until late stages of disease; patients may present with lethargy, arthralgia, skin pigmentation, hepatomegaly, and signs of chronic liver disease. Epidemiology  Clinical disease more common in men (3 : 1).  Women tend to present later in life: this may be due to the protective effect of menstruation causing iron loss.  One of the commonest inherited conditions in people of Northern European descent (especially Celtic) – with prevalence of around 1 in 400. DR. JAM Aetiology  The gene responsible for heredity haemochromatosis is HFE. The 2 commonest HFE mutations are:  C282Y (most common in Caucasians)  H63D.  Autosomal recessive pattern of inheritance.  Penetrance is variable. Pathophysiology  Hepatic hepcidin gene expression is inappropriately low, causing ongoing duodenal absorption of iron.  During low-hepcidin conditions, macrophages continually release iron.  There is increased intestinal iron absorption, leading to iron deposition in joints, liver, heart, pancreas, pituitary, adrenals, and skin.  The iron, stored as ferritin, is deposited in organs as haemosiderin, which is toxic to the tissue.  Clinical Presentation  The condition is usually asymptomatic until late stages of disease. Presenting signs and symptoms include:  tiredness  arthralgia  loss of libido  hypogonadism  skin pigmentation: bronzing of skin resulting in grey/brown skin  signs of chronic liver disease  hepatomegaly.  Generalised skin hyperpigmentation:

Hereditary Non-Polyposis Colorectal Cancer  Hereditary non-polyposis colorectal cancer also known as Lynch syndrome, is an inherited condition associated with an increased risk of developing colorectal cancer.  Overview Key Facts  Hereditary non-polyposis colorectal cancer (HNPCC) – also known as Lynch syndrome is an inherited condition associated with an increased risk of developing colorectal cancer, as well as an increased risk in developing numerous other GI and non-GI cancers.  In affected women, there is also an increased risk of endometrial and ovarian cancer.  The condition is inherited in an autosomal dominant fashion and is associated with mutations in mismatch repair genes, which can lead to uncontrolled cell growth and ultimately cancer.

GIT & LIVER part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  The condition may be suspected in patients who develop colorectal cancer at a young age, have a strong family history of colorectal cancer or cancers associated with HNPCC or if they have a personal history of other associated cancers.  The diagnosis can be confirmed with genetic testing.  Management involves colorectal screening with colectomy when the number of polyps present makes prophylactic colectomy advisable.  Family members of patients diagnosed with the condition should also be screened for the condition and then managed with surveillance.  Surveillance and early detection or prophylactic removal of sections of affected bowel can significantly reduce the risk of developing cancer.  Female patients may wish to have the uterus and ovaries surgically removed after having children to decrease the risk of cancer further. Epidemiology  There are approximately 40 000 new colorectal cancers diagnosed each year in the United Kingdom (UK), a quarter of these following screening.  Colorectal cancer is the second most common cause of cancer death in the UK.  Hereditary non-polyposis colorectal cancer (HNPCC) accounts for 2-5% of all colorectal carcinomas. Aetiology  HNPCC is an autosomal dominant inherited disorder of DNA mismatch repair genes, located on chromosomes 2 and 3. Pathophysiology  Mutation in one of the DNA mismatch repair (MMR) genes, MMR genes normally produce proteins that correct mismatch sequences that can occur during DNA replication.  In HNPCC, a mutation inactivates an MMR gene leading to accumulation of cell mutations which greatly increase the likelihood of malignant transformation.  Normal colonic epithelium is transformed into adenomatous polyp to invasive colorectal cancer.  Clinical Presentation  Signs and symptoms at presentation may include:  Colonic manifestations:  gastrointestinal bleeding  abdominal pain  change in bowel habit.  Extracolonic manifestations:  endometrial cancer signs and symptoms eg post-menopausal bleeding, abdominal pain  ovarian cancer symptoms eg change in bowel habit, bowel distention, bloating, abdominal pain. G

JAM  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses include:  Peutz-Jeghers syndrome  Sporadic colorectal cancer  Familial adenomatous polyposis  Hyperplastic polyposis.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Features that may raise clinical suspicion of HNPCC include:  age less than 50 years at diagnosis of colorectal cancer or endometrial cancer  developing colorectal cancer with a history of other cancers associated with HNPCC  family history of associated cancers in one or more first-degree relative or two more second-degree relatives  a formal diagnosis is based on genetic testing (blood test) as well as analysis of tumour tissue if applicable.  General tests for all patients with suspected colorectal cancer may include:  bloods: FBC, liver biochemistry, renal function  colonoscopy plus biopsy of lesions  double-contrast barium enema  CT colonography  CT scan of thorax, abdomen, and pelvis (staging).  Management  Genetic counselling of patients/relatives.  Surveillance colonoscopy every 18 months to two years from the age of 25 until the number of polyps present make prophylactic colectomy advisable.  From the age of 50, patients will also require 2-yearly upper GI endoscopy.  Women with the condition should receive an annual pelvic examination and/or ultrasound/endometrial biopsy; consider hysterectomy and oophorectomy after they have had children.  Treatment of any malignancy found should follow that as recommended by NICE.  NICE also recommends consideration of daily aspirin, to be taken for more than 2 years, to reduce the risk of colorectal cancer in people with Lynch syndrome.  Prognosis  Lifetime risk of cancer in patients with HNPCC:  colorectal cancer – up to 80%  pancreatic cancer – up to 6%  gastric cancer up to 13%  intestinal cancer up to 6%

Jaundice  Jaundice is a yellowing of the skin and whites of the eyes that occurs when there's too much bilirubin in the blood.  Overview Key Facts  Jaundice is also known as icterus.  It is caused by raised plasma bilirubin, leading to yellow pigmentation of the skin, sclera and mucous membranes.  Normal plasma bilirubin levels are between 5–19 μmol/l.  Jaundice may not be apparent until serum bilirubin is greater than 51 μmol/l.  Causes can be classified as pre-hepatic, hepatic or post-hepatic.  Management and prognosis depends on underlying cause. Epidemiology  There are no literature reports about the incidence of patients presenting with jaundice in primary care.  One study in South-West Wales looked at obvious jaundice (bilirubin more than 120 μmol/l) and found that the incidence, annually, of jaundice was 56 per 100 000.  Gallstone disease, alcohol misuse, and malignancy are common causes of jaundice in the United Kingdom. Aetiology  The causes of jaundice can be split into pre-hepatic, hepatic, posthepatic causes. Pre-hepatic Hepatic Post-hepatic Haemolytic anaemia Viral infection Gallstones Drugs Alcohol Extra-hepatic malignancy Malaria Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease Pancreatitis Gilbert’s syndrome Autoimmune liver disorders Crigler–Najjar syndrome Metabolic causes Drugs Malignancy of the biliary system Pre-hepatic Jaundice G

JAM  Haemolytic anaemias occur due to increased abnormal red blood cell haemolysis as a result of:  homozygous sickle cell disease and thalassemia major  inherited disorders that produces abnormalities in the structure of haemoglobin.  hereditary spherocytosis:  defects in the membrane structure.  glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency:  enzyme abnormalities.  vitamin B12 deficiency:  can cause ineffective erythropoiesis in the bone marrow.  Malaria:  intravascular haemolysis  disseminated intravascular coagulation.  Gilbert syndrome:  3% of the population have this inherited metabolic disorder  it causes excess unconjugated bilirubin due to a defect in the hepatic enzymes responsible for bilirubin conjugation  common presentation is an incidental finding on blood tests, where serum bilirubin levels are slightly raised, while other liver function tests are normal  in this syndrome, plasma bilirubin levels rise during illness, stress, fasting  no treatment is required.  Crigler–Najjar syndrome.  There are defects in the hepatic bilirubin conjugating enzyme leading to unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia.  There are two types:  type I: progressive jaundice in neonates within the first few days of life; left untreated, it can lead to bilirubin encephalopathy and maybe death  type II is less severe and brain damage does not occur. Pathophysiology  Causes of jaundice can vary from benign causes, eg Gilbert syndrome, to life-threatening conditions, eg pancreatic cancer.  Bilirubin is produced due to the breakdown of haemoglobin within the red blood cells.  Bilirubin metabolism occurs in three stages:  pre-hepatic  hepatic  post-hepatic.  Dysfunction at any of these stages may lead to jaundice. JAM Prehepatic Haemoglobin molecules are broken down in macrophages into biliverden and then bilirubin This mainly occurs in the spleen and liver Bilirubin is then released from the macrophages and is then bound to plasma albumin and transported to the liver where it becomes conjugated Hepatic In the liver, hepatocytes selectively remove unconjugated bilirubin from the blood Within the hepatocytes, glucuronic acid is attached to the bilirubin and it becomes conjugated bilirubin Posthepatic Conjugated bilirubin is then transported through the liver, then the cystic ducts and then stored in the gallbladder In the intestine, some bilirubin is passed into the stool and the rest is converted into urobilogens via the gut flora and reabsorbed and excreted via the kidneys  Clinical Presentation  Yellowing of the skin, sclera, and mucous membranes.  Symptoms and signs accompanying jaundice depends on the underlying cause of jaundice.  To work out the underlying cause of jaundice, take a history and examine.  Jaundiced skin:  Jaundiced sclera:

Leishmaniasis  Leishmaniasis describes a spectrum of disease which may affect the skin, mucous membranes and organs (visceral leishmaniasis or kala-azar).  Overview Key Facts  Leishmaniasis describes a spectrum of disease which may affect the skin, mucous membranes and organs (visceral leishmaniasis or kala-azar).  Leishmaniasis is a catch-all term referring to distinct clinical syndromes (cutaneous, mucocutaneous and visceral) caused by unicellular parasites transmitted by sandflies.  Cutaneous leishmaniasis is a common tropical illness endemic in South Asia and South America. It presents with a spectrum of chronic skin lesions – typically ulcerated plaques:  differential diagnosis includes lymphomatous leprosy, impetigo, and skin cancer  the investigation of choice is skin biopsy – microscopy is performed to detect amastigote parasites, and organisms are cultured where possible  treatment of choice is sodium stilbogluconate.  Mucocutaneous leishmaniasis typically arises at the mucocutaneous junction of the nose and may be complicated by secondary bacterial infection:  investigation of choice is biopsy and microscopy  treatment of choice is sodium stilbogluconate.  Visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar) is a relatively rare disease affecting around 500 000 people each year. It is endemic in Bangladesh, India, North East Africa, and Brazil:

JAM Liver Abscess  Liver abscesses occur when pus forms a collection within the liver which has spread from an infective source.  Overview Key Facts  Liver abscesses occur when pus forms a collection within the liver which has spread from an infective source.  Pyogenic abscesses most commonly occur following intraabdominal sepsis.  Most common organism isolated is E.coli, a common bowel commensal.  Amoebic abscesses are caused by Entamoeba histolytica which spreads from the gut via the portal system to the liver.  Fungal abscess secondary to Candida spp. represent < 10% of cases.  Patients may present with swinging pyrexia, weight loss, right upper-quadrant pain, and anorexia.  Diagnosis is confirmed by liver ultrasound, which is also used to guide aspiration or drain insertion.  Broad-spectrum antibiotics are given until sensitivities are available.  Abscesses represent a caseated infection (an infection with a defined border) hence antibiotics may be unable to penetrate the abscess, therefore drainage and surgery may be required.

GIT & LIVER part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Untreated pyogenic liver abscesses are fatal; death may be secondary to sepsis/organ failure.  Prognosis is dependent on numerous factors, including: causative organism (amoebic abscess confers a poor prognosis), underlying comorbidities, and malignancies, and time to diagnosis. Epidemiology  Incidence in United Kingdom (UK) is 3.6 per 100 000.  Amoebic abscesses occur mainly in Central and South America, Africa and Asia. Aetiology  Occur following intra-abdominal sepsis.  Can occur spontaneously.  Most commonly caused by bacteria – the most common organism isolated is E.coli, but Streptococcus, Klebsilla, Enterococcus, Proteus, Staphylococcus aureus and anaerobes are recognised.  Less common causes are Candida (around 10%) and amoebic abscess - Entamoeba histolytica (10%).  Risk factors include:  male sex  advancing age  diabetes mellitus  cancer  cirrhosis  liver transplant  cardiopulmonary disease  immunocompromise  biliary tract infection  appendicitis  diverticulitis  pancreatitis. Pathophysiology  Pus forms a collection within the liver which has spread from a source, most commonly the biliary tract.  Other forms of spread include the portal and hepatic veins or penetrating trauma.  Underlying pathophysiology is dependent on the cause.  Clinical Presentation  Swinging fever secondary to bacterial showers released by the abscess into the systemic circulation.  Weight loss.  Pyrexia.  Right upper-quadrant pain and tenderness.  Right should tip pain.  Anorexia. Liver Transplant  Liver transplantation may be indicated in patients with irreversible liver damage where all other forms of treatment have failed.  Overview Key Facts  Liver transplantation may be indicated in patients with irreversible liver damage where all other forms of treatment have failed.  The most common indications for liver transplant in the United Kingdom (UK) are cirrhosis viral hepatitis, autoimmune/idiopathic liver disease, and paracetamol poisoning.  There are approximately 1 000 liver transplants carried out annually in the UK; the majority are from donors after brain death.  Although there is no age cut-off, patients over 70 are less likely to be be suitable.  Post-transplant, lifelong immunosuppressive drugs are given to reduce the risk of graft rejection.  Patients need to be monitored for drug side-effects and signs of infection and rejection.  The 5-year survival rate after liver transplant is approximately 80%. Epidemiology  In 2016–2017, there were 980 total liver transplants in the UK, with the majority of transplants from donors after brain death. Aetiology  Conditions which may be amenable to hepatic transplantation:  fulminant hepatic failure due to hepatitis C or paracetamol poisoning  primary biliary cirrhosis  Wilson’s disease G

Pathophysiology  Pathophysiology depends on the indication for liver transplant.  In the development of end-stage liver disease damage to liver cells results in fibrosis and eventually cirrhosis that can restrict blood flow through the liver, damage cells and develop into hepatocellular carcinoma.  The liver function deteriorates to such a level that it is life threatening.  Reduction in blood flow through the liver secondary to cirrhosis, regardless of the cause, manifests with the classical signs and symptoms of liver disease secondary to portal hypertension.  This results in elevated pressure within the stomach, lower oesophagus, intestine and spleen.  Clinical Presentation  Symptoms that may be present are reflective of end-stage liver failure and may include:  jaundice  scleral icterus – bilirubin deposition within the sclera  ascites due to reduced albumin production within the liver, leading to reduced intravascular oncotic pressure and leaking of fluid into the third space/abdominal cavity  hepatic encephalopathy  variceal bleeding due to distension and engorgement of the veins in the oesophagus from portal hypertension  hepato-splenomegaly secondary to either:  primary pathology to the liver, eg a malignancy  portal hypertension secondary to this pathology which ‘backs up’ to the spleen, causing splenomegaly.  Diagnosis/Investigation Assessment and Waiting List  Diagnose the cause and assess the severity with blood tests and imaging, eg virology for hepatitis B or C.  Assess liver damage and function – see table below – LFTs, bilirubin, albumin, INR.  Patients placed on a waiting list determined by an assessment and ranking is aided using tools such as the Model for End Stage Liver Disease (MELD) to indicate those with higher priority.

Meckel’s Diverticulum  Meckel’s diverticulum is defined as a congenital malformation of the small intestine, commonly the ileum.  Overview Key Facts  Meckel’s diverticulum is defined as a congenital malformation of the small intestine, commonly the ileum:  occurs in 2% of people  occurs two feet (60 cm) from the caecum  is two inches (5 cm) long  (and… all of this is true two-thirds of the time).  It contains all layers of the intestinal wall.  It is caused by a failure of closure of the vitelline duct (connects yolk sac to the gut tube).

JAM Neuroendocrine Tumours  Neuroendocrine tumours describe a wide range of tumours that originate in cells of the diffuse neuroendocrine system.  Overview Key Facts  Neuroendocrine tumours (NETs) describe a wide range of tumours that originate in cells of the diffuse neuroendocrine system.  Neuroendocrine cells receive neuronal input and subsequently release hormones.  NETs can be cancerous (malignant) or non-cancerous (benign).  NETs can arise in various areas of the body, this includes the digestive system (stomach and intestines), pancreas and respiratory system.  The most common primary location of NETs is in the gastrointestinal system.  Functionally active neuroendocrine tumours produce excessive hormones from the tumour cell eg insulinoma, gastrinoma, carcinoid, glucagonoma.  Functionally inactive tumours may be diagnosed:  by chance eg during a routine ultrasound;  large tumours of the pancreatic head may cause extra-hepatic jaundice  due to tumour symptoms eg gastrointestinal bleeding.  Except for insulinoma, the majority of neuroendocrine tumours are malignant.  Malignant neuroendocrine tumours tend to grow slowly.  Signs and symptoms are dependent on the location of the tumour and the hormone it produces.  Treatment is dependant on the tumour type, location, stage at diagnosis and general health of the patient.  Treatment options include somatostatin analogues, chemotherapy, radiotherapy and surgical excision.  Surgery is often curative in patients with limited disease. Epidemiology  The most common primary location of neuroendocrine tumours is within the gastrointestinal system.  NETs are the second most prevalent gastrointestinal tumour after the colon.  The incidence of neuroendocrine tumours is around 10 per 100 000 population. Aetiology  There is a significantly increased risk of developing a NET in patients with the following conditions:  Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 (MEN1):  autosomal dominant disorder

GIT & LIVER part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  family history  MEN1 gene mutation  associated cancers: pituitary, parathyroid, pancreatic, pheochromocytoma, medullary thyroid cancer.  Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 (MEN2):  RET proto-oncogene mutation  autosomal dominant  associated cancers: parathyroid adenoma, pheochromocytoma, medullary thyroid carcinoma.  Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1):  NF1 gene mutation  tumours grow along the nervous system anywhere in the body eg in skin, brain  autosomal dominant.  Von-Hippel-Lindau (VHL).  Tuberculous sclerosis (TSC). Pathophysiology  Tumours that develop from specialised cells called neuroendocrine cells.  NETs can be classified as foregut, midgut, or hindgut depending on their embryonic origin:  foregut: respiratory tract, thymus, stomach, duodenum, and pancreas  midgut: small bowel, appendix, and ascending colon  hindgut: transverse colon, descending colon or rectum.  Neuroendocrine cells receive neuronal input and subsequently release hormones.  Functionally active neuroendocrine tumours produce excessive hormones from the tumour cell eg insulinoma, gastrinoma, carcinoid, glucagonoma.  Functionally inactive tumours are diagnosed: by chance eg during routine USS, large tumours of the pancreatic head causing extrahepatic jaundice, tumour symptoms eg gastrointestinal bleeding.  Except for insulinoma, the majority of neuroendocrine tumours are malignant.  Malignant neuroendocrine tumours grow slowly.  Clinical Presentation Gastrinomas Tumours produce excess levels of gastrin which can cause stomach ulcers. Symptoms include: pain nausea loss of appetite bleeding, leading to anaemia (fatigue, short of breath) severe bleeding can cause stool to become black and tarry G
