Non-alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease  Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease is defined as an accumulation of excess fat (triglyceride) in the liver (steatosis) with hepatocytes containing more than 5% of triglycerides which is not the result of excessive alcohol consumption or other secondary causes.

GIT & LIVER part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Overview Key Facts  Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) is defined as:  an accumulation of excess fat (triglyceride) in the liver (steatosis) with hepatocytes containing more than 5% of triglycerides which is not the result of excessive alcohol consumption or other secondary causes.  NAFLD encompasses a spectrum of disease from hepatic steatosis to non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH).  It is the most common cause of liver disease in Western countries due to the rise in the prevalence of obesity.  Patients are often asymptomatic and the condition is found after mild abnormality in liver function tests (LFTs), elevation of alkaline phosphatase, aminotransferases, or bilirubin is noted during work-up for other conditions such as hypertension.  If symptomatic, symptoms may include pruritus, fatigue, malaise, and right upper quadrant discomfort, hepatomegaly may be found on physical examination.  Management includes lifestyle modification:  diet  exercise  weight loss  drinking in moderation.  This is in addition to optimal management of existing comorbidities.  Transplantation may be considered if cirrhosis or carcinoma of the liver develops. Epidemiology  NAFLD is now the most common cause of abnormal LFT results in the United Kingdom.  It is the most common cause of liver disease in Western countries.  A rise in NAFLD likely due to rapid rise in obesity prevalence.  The prevalence of NAFLD increases with increasing age.  it is highest in men aged 40–65 years old.  In Europe, the prevalence of NAFLD (as assessed by ultrasound scan) is estimated to be 20–30%. Aetiology  The exact cause of NAFLD is unknown.  NAFLD is linked with insulin resistance, obesity and metabolic syndrome.  Risk factors for NAFLD include:  central obesity (body mass index (BMI) > 30 kg/m2)  impaired glucose regulation or type II diabetes mellitus  hypertension  hyperlipidaemia (hypertriglyceridemia and/or low highdensity lipoproteins).  Other risk factors: G

JAM Non-Hodgkin’s Lymphoma  Non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma is a haematological malignancy that may arise from the B cells (85%), T cells or natural killer cells.  Overview Key Facts  Non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma (NHL) is a haematological malignancy that may arise from the B cells (85%), T cells or natural killer cells.  The condition is differentiated from Hodgkin’s lymphoma due to the absence of Reed–Sternberg cells at biopsy.  Non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma is five times more common than Hodgkin’s lymphoma.  Incidence increases with age; the median age at presentation is above 50.  Aetiology is not clearly understood; however, there are numerous associations including genetics, certain infections such as Epstein– Barr virus, immunodeficiency and chemical exposure.  The most common symptom of non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma is asymmetric painless lymphadenopathy.  Other systemic symptoms may include night sweats, fever and weight loss.  Patients may also present with symptoms of anaemia, organomegaly, oropharyngeal, central nervous system (CNS) skin involvement, or infection due to cytopenia.  There are four stages of the disease, classified based on the Ann Arbor clinical staging of lymphomas.  Patients with signs or symptoms suggestive of NHL should be referred under the 2-week wait rule (adults) or consider assessment within 48 hours in children and young people.  Diagnosis is confirmed by lymph node biopsy (excisional/core needle biopsy) – Reed–Sternberg cells are absent.  Treatment is chemotherapy +/- radiotherapy. Epidemiology  There are 13 000 new diagnoses of NHL annually in the United Kingdom.  NHL is five times more common than Hodgkin’s lymphoma.  Can affect all age groups but incidence increases with age – median age at presentation is above 50.  Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma is the most common type of lymphoma. Aetiology  The exact cause is unknown.  Genetic factors may play a role, hence family history is relevant.  Increased risk is associated with:  viral and bacterial infection, eg Epstein–Barr virus, H. pylori  autoimmune disorders  chronic inflammation

GIT & LIVER part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  primary or secondary immunodeficiency  exposure to chemicals. Pathophysiology  Genetic mutations occurring at any stage of lymphoid cell development resulting in heterogenous clonal lymphoid tumours.  85% arise from the B lymphocytes, the remainder arise from T lymphocytes and natural killer cells.  Characterised by an irregular pattern of spread.  Extra nodal disease is common.  Clinical Presentation  There is a spectrum of presentation, and may vary depending on severity and type of lymphoma.  Superficial lymphadenopathy: the most common symptom is asymmetric enlarged painless peripheral lymph nodes.  Associated systemic symptoms (B-symptoms):  persistent fever  unexplained splenomegaly  night sweats  shortness of breath  weight loss.  Oropharyngeal involvement affecting the oropharyngeal lymphoid structures present as sore throat or noisy/abnormal/obstructed breathing.  Cytopenia secondary to the involvement of the bone marrow may present with anaemia related symptoms or infections.  Abdominal organs involvement in advanced disease: hepato/splenomegaly and related symptoms or with acute abdomen symptoms. This is the second most common extra-nodal site affected after the bone marrow.  CNS involvement.  Skin involvement presenting as dry patches/scaly with associated pruritus.  Lymphocytosis +/- physical symptoms (asymptomatic).  Differential Diagnosis  Hodgkin’s lymphoma.  Acute lymphocytic leukaemia.  Other leukaemias.  Infectious mononucleosis.  Hepatitis – especially Hepatitis C.  Cytomegalovirus.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Detailed history and examination.  Diagnosis can be made by lymph node biopsy (excisional/core needle biopsy). Non-pharmacological  In low-grade NHL in patients who are asymptomatic, a watch-andwait approach may be used.  To reduce risk of overwhelming bacterial infection, patients with NHL should be vaccinated against Meningococcus group C and Haemophilus influenzae group B. Low > 94% 1–2 Low–Intermediate 79% 3–5 Intermediate–High 53% Nutrition and Malnutrition  Nutrition and malnutrition refer to the balance between the intake of nutrients and the body's requirements, with malnutrition indicating deficiencies or imbalances that can impact health.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Overview Key Facts  The maintenance of adequate nutrition requires three main criteria to be fulfilled:  intact gastrointestinal (GI) tract:  this may be compromised by resections resulting in a short-bowel syndrome, or by ﬁstulae such that segments of the bowel are bypassed  as different nutrients are absorbed from different parts of the gut, a variety of clinical sequelae may occur depending on the segment of bowel affected (eg vitamin B12 deﬁciency after terminal ileal resection, iron deﬁciency after partial gastrectomy).  ability to absorb nutrients:

GIT & LIVER part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  impairment of absorptive function may be caused by mucosal damage as occurs in Crohn’s or coeliac disease, or after radiation damage  motility problems resulting in accelerated transit times may reduce absorption.  adequate intake:  this depends on both the motivation to maintain an adequate oral intake, often lacking in sick and older patients and on the composition of the diet.  An inability to maintain nutrition is an indication to provide supplementation by one of three routes (underlying disease will determine which is appropriate):  oral:  the most simple form but relies on a conscious patient with an intact swallowing mechanism  high-protein or carbohydrate drinks may be used to provide good nutritional intake in a small volume.  enteral:  useful when swallowing impaired (eg in neurological disease) or when high-volume intake is needed  may take the form of a simple nasogastric tube, or a percutaneous gastrostomy (PEG) or jejunostomy, which can be inserted endoscopically, radiologically or surgically  can be used for long- and short-term nutrition.  parenteral:  this is intravenous (IV) feeding, either to supplement enteral nutrition or to provide total support in the case of complete intestinal failure. Malabsorption  Malabsorption is deﬁned as a failure to absorb sufﬁcient exogenous nutrients or to reabsorb endogenous substances such as bile salts.  It may be caused by several factors because normal absorption depends on gut structure, motility and secretion of hormones and enzymes.  Malabsorption usually results in diarrhoea.  Clinical presentation depends on the type and site of the defect and includes weight loss and general ill health, osteomalacia, or speciﬁc nutritional deﬁciencies such as of B12 and folate. Refeeding syndrome  When re-establishing feeding (orally, enterally or parenterally) in malnourished patients with inadequate oral intake for more than five days, it is important to recognise the high risk of refeeding syndrome.  Over-enthusiastic feeding of these patients can precipitate surges in insulin levels, which in turn provoke large intracellular shifts in potassium, phosphate and magnesium, leading to low plasma levels of these ions.  Potential serious adverse clinical consequences of these preventable electrolyte deﬁciencies include:  cardiac instability/arrhythmias and sudden death  seizures  delirium  paraesthesiae G

JAM  myopathy  haemolysis  paralysis  oedema  respiratory and cardiac failure.  A cautious approach to refeeding is therefore paramount, gradually increasing calorie intake and correcting electrolyte deﬁciencies.  It is mandatory to monitor serum electrolytes (including potassium, phosphate, magnesium and calcium) daily in this situation.  Also, during refeeding, there is increased consumption of thiamine by cells.  At-risk patients should also receive thiamine replacement before starting nutritional support (oral, enteral or parenteral) as prophylaxis for Wernicke’s encephalopathy.  Diagnosis/Investigation Assessment of nutritional status  Nutritional assessment should be based on a pragmatic approach using a combination of history, examination and blood tests to identify speciﬁc nutrient deﬁciencies.  The following assessments help evaluate nutritional status and risk:  reported recent weight loss  dietary assessment – food diary  behavioural patterns to food intake  body mass index (BMI) – weight in kilograms/(height in metres)2  biochemical markers:  renal proﬁle  electrolytes (magnesium, phosphate and potassium)  albumin (unreliable – often normal in severe malnutrition and affected by inﬂammation and synthetic liver function)  C-reactive protein (CRP)  glucose  HbA1c (glycated haemoglobin).  Given that around a third of hospitalised patients are at risk of malnutrition and provision of good nutritional status improves clinical outcomes, the National Institute of Health and Care Excellence (NICE) recommends that all patients admitted to hospital should be screened for risk of malnutrition using a validated screening tool.  The British Association of Parenteral and Enteral Nutrition (BAPEN) has developed the Malnutrition Universal Screening Tool (MUST) which is widely used for this purpose.  Using this tool, the overall risk of malnutrition is calculated based on the BMI, the percentage of unintentional weight loss over a 3- to 6-month period and whether the patient has had, or is likely to have had, no nutritional intake for more than five days.

JAM  Overview Key Facts  Rupture of the oesophagus is a tear occurring through all layers of the oesophageal wall.  Rupture of the oesophagus can occur due to iatrogenic, traumatic or spontaneous causes.  Clinically, patients experience severe, tearing chest pain, and there may be subcutaneous emphysema over the thorax or in the neck. Patients may also present with sepsis.  Chest X-ray typically shows mediastinal gas; pneumothorax/pleural effusion may also be present.  Computed tomography (CT) of the chest will often provide a definitive diagnosis; water-soluble contrast swallow can more accurately delineate a tear.  Patients may require surgical repair or endoscopic stenting.  Mortality rates are high due to delayed diagnosis, difficult surgical access of the oesophagus and high risk of sepsis.  Early diagnosis and subsequent management of oesophageal perforation reduces the risks of complications and mortality. Epidemiology  A relatively rare presentation; in 2005–2006, oesophageal rupture was responsible for 340 admissions in England. Aetiology  Spontaneous rupture:  usually results in a torn left posterior aspect of the oesophagus, just above the cardia.  Boerhaave syndrome:  spontaneous oesophageal rupture that occurs due to a sudden increase in intraoesophageal pressure combined with a decrease in intrathoracic pressure, ie following vigorous vomiting/straining  patients often present with severe chest or abdominal pain after an episode of vomiting, often associated with alcohol intake.  Latrogenic:  there are five typical sites of perforation during endoscopy; the clinical picture may be less acute and dramatic than with spontaneous rupture; however, mediastinitis usually develops  this is because patients are usually starved prior to endoscopy and the diagnosis is immediate.  Swallowed foreign bodies and oesophageal cancer can also cause oesophageal rupture.  Penetrating injury:  rare, as the oesophagus is smaller than other vital intrathoracic organs, there is likely to also be trauma to surrounding structures  resection may be needed.  Typical sites of perforation during endoscopy:

JAM  Overview Key Facts  The two main types of oesophageal cancer are adenocarcinoma and squamous cell carcinoma (SCC).  Rarer types of oesophageal cancers include melanoma, lymphoma and sarcomas.  Approximately 8 000 cases are diagnosed in the United Kingdom (UK) annually.  SCCs arise in the mid-thoracic portion and adenocarcinomas arise in the lower portion of the oesophagus.  This is due to squamous cells lining the upper third of the oesophagus, and more glandular cells lining the lower third; the middle third is a transitional zone.  Risk factors include:  gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GORD)  smoking  alcohol intake  obesity  oesophageal motility disorders.  Patients are often asymptomatic until a late stage, in which the patient may experience worsening dysphagia due to obstruction.  Urgent endoscopy (within two weeks) is required for diagnosis and biopsy of patients with dysphagia or those over 55 with weight loss and any of the following:  upper abdominal pain  reflux  dyspepsia.  Management options include resection with oesophagectomy, palliative oesophageal stenting, radiotherapy and chemotherapy; this will depend on the type, stage and grade.  Prognosis is dependent on the stage of the condition at diagnosis; the 5-year survival is estimated to be around 15%. Epidemiology  8 000 new diagnoses are made in the UK each year.  Adenocarcinomas account for 65% of oesophageal cancers in the UK.  More males than females are affected by the disease (3 M : 1 F).  Rare in people aged under 40.  Increased incidence in Asia, South Africa and Kenya. Aetiology  Risk factors include:  advancing age  achalasia  Plummer–Vinson syndrome  Chinese or Russian ethnicity  tylosis (autosomal dominant palmar and plantar keratosis) – represents a very high risk

GIT & LIVER part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  low intake of fresh vegetables and fruit.  Adenocarcinoma:  Barrett’s oesophagus (the incidence of adenocarcinoma in patients with Barrett’s oesophagus is 1% per year, which represents a 40–80-fold increase in risk)  obesity  GORD (independent of Barrett’s oesophagus).  SCC:  smoking  high alcohol intake. Pathophysiology  Can be squamous or adenocarcinoma.  SCCs arise in the mid-thoracic portion of the oesophagus; pathogenesis may be due to inflammation of the epithelium, causing dysplasia and malignant transformation.  Adenocarcinomas arise in the lower oesophagus and a predisposing factor is GORD, which can lead to Barrett’s oesophagus.  In Barrett’s oesophagus, the extension of columnar gastric epithelium into the oesophagus to replace normal squamous epithelium increases the risk of malignant change.  Clinical Presentation  Clinical presentations for oesophageal cancer include:  asymptomatic patients until a late stage  pain on swallowing (odynophagia)  dysphagia (difficulty swallowing)  dyspepsia (reflux/heartburn)  weight loss  progressive dysphagia for solids then liquids  hoarseness  vomiting  anorexia  haematemesis  upper abdominal pain  anaemia.  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses for oesophageal cancer include:  benign stricture  achalasia  Barrett’s oesophagus  gastric cancer.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Endoscopy allows biopsy and histological confirmation. NICE Recommendation  Endoscopic mucosal resection for T1 and radical resection for T1b adenocarcinoma.  Definitive chemoradiotherapy or surgical resection for T1bN0 squamous cell carcinoma.  Consider oesophagectomy.  Prognosis  Late diagnosis results in poor survival figures.  Survival rates are also dependent on the patient’s existing condition and co-morbidities.  Survival at stage 1 is approximately 55% at five years, reducing to 15% at stage 3.  Overall survival rate at five years is estimated at 15%. Pancreatic Cancer  Pancreatic tumours are predominantly adenocarcinomas and have a high incidence between the ages of 65 and 75 years.  Overview Key Facts  Pancreatic tumours are predominantly adenocarcinomas and have a high incidence between the ages of 65 and 75 years.  Smoking increases the risk of developing pancreatic cancer two- to threefold.  Diabetes is also associated with increased risk of pancreatic cancer; it has been suggested that diabetes may be an early symptom.  Tumours may invade the common bile duct and duodenum.  Surgical resection is curative; however, disease is often diagnosed at a late stage and 5-year survival is less than 1%. Epidemiology  9 000 new diagnoses of pancreatic cancer occur each year in the United Kingdom (UK).  The incidence of pancreatic carcinoma is 110–120 per million.  Incidence increases to 800–1 000 per million in those over the age of 75 years.  70–80% of pancreatic carcinoma arise in the head of the pancreas. Carcinomas in the tail often present at an advanced stage.  More than 6 000 deaths per year are attributed to pancreatic cancer in the UK.

GIT & LIVER part 2 MIL ALRAJHI Aetiology  Risk is increased two- to threefold in smokers and there is a higher risk in those with diabetes.  it has been suggested that diabetes is an early symptom of pancreatic carcinoma rather than a risk factor  5–10% of all pancreatic cancer patients have an inherited component.  Pancreatic cancer can be associated with these inherited cancer syndromes:  hereditary pancreatitis  Peutz–Jeghers syndrome  familial atypical multiple mole melanoma  familial breast cancer syndrome  hereditary non-polyposis colorectal cancer syndrome. Pathophysiology  70–80% arise in the head of the pancreas, where there is maximal pancreatic tissue.  Those in the tail are often silent in the early stages and present at an advanced stage.  10% are multifocal.  > 60% of the tumour mass consists of strong desmoplastic stroma.  Pancreatic carcinoma may invade the common bile duct, causing obstructive jaundice.  Tumours can also invade the duodenum, leading to small-bowel obstruction.  Lymph node metastases are common, as well as perineural and vascular invasion.  Distant metastases are usually found in liver, lungs, skin and brain.  Progression from normal epithelium to invasive carcinoma is due to accumulation of genetic alterations involving mutations in the oncogene and inactivation of tumour suppressor genes.  Diagram depicting the functions of the cells in the pancreas: G

GIT & LIVER part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Diagnosis/Investigation  Ultrasound and pancreas computed tomography (CT) protocol are used to assess the pancreas.  a normal ultrasound does not exclude pancreatic cancer.  CT chest, abdomen and pelvis are used to stage the disease for distant metastases.  Endoscopic ultrasound, locoregional staging and histological diagnosis via fine-needle aspiration are also important investigations.  Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatogram (ERCP) brushings taken for histological diagnosis or invasion into the common bile duct may show ‘double duct sign’; it is possible to perform bile duct stenting to relieve jaundice and pruritus either as a palliative measure or prior to curative resection.  Liver function tests to investigate the degree of obstructive jaundice; they cannot distinguish between any cause of obstructive jaundice or liver metastases.  Carbohydrate antigen-19-9 (CA-19-9) is released from exocrine pancreatic cancer cells; baseline levels may guide treatment and follow-up and provide significant prognostic information.  Accurate staging to determine resectability is critical. National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) Recommendations  Refer for 2-week wait if the patient is > 40 years old with jaundice.  Consider urgent CT/ultrasound in patients > 60 years old with weight loss and:  diarrhoea  back pain  nausea  vomiting  constipation  new-onset diabetes.  CT image showing pancreatic adenocarcinoma in the head of the pancreas: G

Pharmacological  Pain management (endoscopic ultrasound-guided or image-guided percutaneous neurolytic coeliac plexus block).  Enteric-coated pancreatin.  Neoadjuvant therapy for people with borderline resectable pancreatic cancer.  Adjuvant therapy after surgery (six cycles of chemotherapy plus adjuvant gemcitabine and capecitabine).  Supportive, palliative and end-of-life care.  Offer combination chemotherapy to people with locally advanced pancreatic cancer.  Offer Folfirinox® to patients with metastatic pancreatic cancer and an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) performance status of 0–1. Second line is oxiplatin-based chemotherapy. Surgical  Surgical resection  10–20% suitable for surgery, the only curative treatment currently available

Other Endocrine Tumours  These are very rare, with an annual incidence of 4 : 1 000 000, but they are incidentally detected at post-mortem.  They can occur independently or as part of multiple endocrine neoplasia (MEN-1) syndrome. MEN-1 is characterised by inherited endocrine tumours, often causing parathyroid tumours and resulting in hyperparathyroidism and high calcium. MEN-1 is also associated with pituitary and pancreatic tumours (gastrinomas, insulinomas, prolactinomas and carcinoid tumours).  The more important lesions include:  insulinoma  gastrinoma (Zollinger–Ellison syndrome)  glucagonoma  vipoma  somatostatinoma.  Insulinomas arise from the islets of Langerhans and often present with unusual symptoms:  visual disturbances  irritability  abnormal behaviour  confusion  amnesia  paraesthesiae and drowsiness after an overnight fast or before meals, as a result of hypoglycaemia.  Patients often discover that glucose is helpful and may go for years without diagnosis.  Glucagonoma  these tumours arise from the alpha-cells of the pancreas  they present clinically with a characteristic rash (migratory necrolytic erythema), weight loss, glucose intolerance or frank diabetes and anaemia  tumours are often very large at diagnosis and are usually malignant.  Vipoma  excessive vasoactive intestinal polypeptide (VIP) produces an extreme secretory diarrhoea (usually > 3 litres per day)  results in hypochlorhydria and hypokalaemia.  Somatostatinoma  rare tumour  produces a syndrome of diabetes mellitus, diarrhoea, gallbladder disease, weight loss, steatorrhoea and hypochlorhydria  inhibition of insulin and pancreatic enzymes.

GIT & LIVER part 2 MIL ALRAJHI Parasitic Infections  A parasite is an organism that lives on, or in, a host, and causes harm to a different host organism.  Overview Key Facts  A parasite is an organism that lives on, or in, a host, and causes harm to a different host organism.  Parasites commonly cause disease in humans.  Many parasites are types of helminth worms which:  can be grouped based on morphological characteristics  are rarely fatal  can be associated with significant morbidity and disability, particularly in low and middle income countries.  Patients may be asymptomatic with disease only detected after further investigation after a finding of isolated eosinophilia. This is seen in schistosomiasis, strongyloides and filariasis. Epidemiology  Global prevalence of helminth infection is estimated at 1.5 billion.  Morbidity correlates with the burden of disease – highest in hyperendemic regions.  Important consequences in children include:  poor nutrition and anaemia  direct disease complications such as intestinal obstruction  poor school performance.  Neurocysticercosis is thought to be the major cause of epilepsy worldwide.  Schistosomiasis is an important cause of morbidity and mortality in sub-Saharan Africa (notably around Lake Malawi), South America and South East Asia.  S. mansoni; endemic in South America and Africa – associated with liver/GI disease  S. haematobium; endemic in sub-Saharan Africa – chronic infection associated with bladder cancer.  Lymphatic filariasis is a mosquito-borne parasitic infection common throughout the tropics.  Roundworm (ascaris lumriocoides) is one of the most common intestinal worm infections worldwide.  The most common parasitic worm infection in the UK is threadworms (enterobius vermicularis) which infests the gut. Aetiology  Most helminth infections are transmitted via faecal-oral route or direct inoculation of skin through the soil.  Important examples of parasitic worm infections include:  threadworm (enterobius vemicularis)  tapeworms – cysticercosis, hydatid disease (echinococcus) G

JAM  roundworms (nematodes) – lymphatic filariasis, loiasis, onchocerciasis and ascariasis  flatworms – schistosomiasis and liver fluke.  Several parasitic worm diseases are ‘zoonoses’ – they can be transmitted to humans from animals, such as:  hydatid (sheep and goats)  cysticercosis (pigs)  schistosomiasis (freshwater snails). Pathophysiology  Clinical disease can result from several different mechanisms:  direct impact of adult worm within tissues (eg ‘worm bolus’) causing intestinal obstruction in ascariasis.  deposition of immature parasite ‘daughter cells’ within tissues (eg onchocerciasis)  dissemination of disease through generation of cystic structures (eg neurocysticercosis and hydatid disease).  Stronglyoides infection is unusual in that the parasite can complete the full life cycle within the human host – illness can persist for many years after initial infection.  Hydatid is an unusual disease caused by propagating cysts formed by echinococcus granulosis. Cysts can develop within the liver and rarely in the lungs.  Clinical Presentation  Clinical presentation varies with parasite type and with route of transmission.  Threadworm presents with intense perianal itching which is worse at night.  Hookworm commonly presents with symptomatic anaemia – reduced exercise tolerance, shortness of breath and fatigue.  Onchocerciasis presents with skin lesions and progressive eye disease with eventual blindness.  Neurocysticercosis presents with new onset epilepsy – frequently in teenagers.  Lymphatic filariasis presents with profound (often unilateral) lower limb swelling.  Strongyloides infection usually presents with diarrhoea and associated skin changes (larva currens rash) although hyperinfection (disseminated strongyloidiasis) in immunosuppressed presents as a Gram negative sepsis and organ failure.  Schistosomiasis can present with wide variety of symptoms at different time points:  acute cercarial dermatitis (‘swimmer’s itch’) - self-limiting, intensely pruritic erythematous papular rash within 24 hours of freshwater exposure  katayama fever (acute schistosomiasis) – fever, urticaria, diarrhoea, hepatosplenomegaly, wheeze and cough at 4-8 weeks post-infection  chronic disease manifestations vary with site of high worm burden:

GIT & LIVER part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  urinary tract – terminal haematuria, fibrosis and calcification  bowel and liver – bloody diarrhoea, splenomegaly, ascites and GI bleeding (due to periportal fibrosis and resultant portal hypertension).  Hydatid disease has a range of clinical presentations, depending on the site of hydatid cysts:  liver cysts – abdominal pain and distension  breathlessness – lung and cardiac involvement  early morning headaches, nausea and focal neurology – brain involvement  anaphylactoid-reaction due to rupture of abdominal or lung cysts. This is seen in around 2% of patients who experience cyst rupture.  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnosis varies with region and clinical presentation.  Diarrhoea – strongyloides, hookworm, ascariasis and inflammatory bowel disease.  Liver lesion – hydatid disease, amoebic liver abscess, bacterial liver abscess, haematoma, simple cyst and malignancy.  Multiple brain lesions – neurocysticercosis, hydatid disease, toxoplasmosis and malignancy.  Asymptomatic eosinophilia – any parasitic infection, ChurgStrauss and drug reaction.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Blood tests:  full blood count (FBC) for eosinophilia  liver function and renal function.  Stool for multiple chemical sensitivity (MCS) and OCP (ova, cysts and parasites) – particularly useful in suspected strongyloides and hookworm infection.  Terminal urine (sample taken at end of urination) for OCP for suspected schistosomiasi  Specific investigations vary with suspected disease:  onchocerciasis – skin snips to detect microfilariae  neurocysticercosis – serology, computed tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scanning  hydatid disease - echinococcus serology, ultrasound imaging  lymphatic filariasis – night-time blood for microscopy and serology.  Management Non-pharmacological  Patients with neurocysticercosis are at significant risk of further seizures and require standard epilepsy advice – avoid driving, safety measures at home and around water. JAM Pharmacological  Isolated hydatid cysts are often managed with prolonged (several weeks or months) courses of albendazole or praziquantel.  Lympatic filariasis – diethylcarbamazine (DEC).  Onchocerciasis – single dose ivermectin.  Hookworm – mebendazole.  Strongyloides – ivermectin or albendazole.  Schistosomiasis – praziquantel.  Threadworm – mebendazole.  Roundworm – mebendazole. Surgical  Some hydatid cysts are managed using the PAIR (percutaneous aspiration, injection and reaspiration) procedure with appropriate steroid and antihelminth cover. Cysts are aspirated and injected with hypertonic saline to kill the daughter cysts within.  Extensive abdominal hydatid disease and any hydatid pulmonary or cardiac involvement usually require surgical removal – must be performed by expert surgeon to minimize risk of spilling cyst contents within abdominal cavity and further seeding.  Lymphatic filariasis involving the scrotum and causing severe hydrocoele may require surgical repair.  Prognosis  Prognosis varies with parasite sub-type and access to treatment.  Despite antibiotic treatment, many patients with lymphatic filariasis will have residual deformity and oedema requiring surgical management. Pemphigus  Pemphigus is a group of rare, autoimmune, superficial blistering disorders affecting the skin and/or mucosa.  Overview Key Facts  Pemphigus is a group of rare, autoimmune, superficial blistering disorders affecting the skin and/or mucosa.  The three main conditions include pemphigus vulgaris, pemphigus foliaceus and paraneoplastic pemphigus.  The conditions have a relapsing and remitting nature with potential triggers.  Clinical features include epidermal loss and blistering (skin and/or mucosa).  Treatment aims to induce remission: analgesia + disease suppression.

GIT & LIVER part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Pemphigus vulgaris and foliaceus have a good prognosis if the disease is adequately controlled; paraneoplastic pemphigus has a poor prognosis (mortality up to 90%). Epidemiology  All forms of pemphigus are rare.  Around 70% of pemphigus cases are due to pemphigus vulgaris, which affects < 1 in 100 000 per annum.  Incidence increases with age and is more common in women.  Ethnicity: more cases are seen in Asian and Ashkenazi Jew populations. Aetiology  Due to autoimmunity  Aetiology of autoimmunity is unknown; it is linked to loss of 'selftolerance', genetic predisposition (eg HLA), infection, hormones (women > men) and other factors. HLA Allele Links Paraneoplastic pemphigus HLA-DR4 (relative risk 14) a Pemphigus vulgaris HLA-DRB1  Pemphigus is also linked to myasthenia gravis.  Triggers of autoimmune ‘flare-ups’ may include: burns, stress, pregnancy, vaccination, sun/UV light and drugs (eg rifampicin, penicillamine).  Paraneoplastic pemphigus is linked to underlying cancers, especially B-cell lymphoproliferation (eg non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma). Pathophysiology  ‘Pemphigus’ is a name given to conditions that produce blisters confined to the epidermis (directly intraepidermal). As they are relatively superficial, they rupture easily and secondary infections at the sites are common.  Autoantibody processes causing damage:  IgG autoantibodies bind to transmembrane desmosome proteins in keratinocytes at the intracellular junctions, which makes the cells unable to adhere to each other (aka acantholysis); as a result, blisters form  HLA are crucial to MHC class II molecules in the adaptive and innate immune system via their T-cell interactions.  Clinical Presentation  Blisters that:  are poorly defined, varying in size, irregular  are easily burst, ‘flaccid’  may have turbid fluid within  may cause ‘weeping ulcers’ that crust if on the skin  on the oral mucosa, are rarely intact  heal slowly. Peptic Ulcer Disease and Gastritis  Peptic ulcer disease describes a breach of the epithelium mucosa to the submucosa/muscularis mucosa layers and involves gastric or duodenal ulcers which are confirmed via endoscopy.  Overview Key Facts  Peptic ulcer disease describes a breach of the epithelium mucosa to the submucosa/muscularis mucosa layers and involves gastric or duodenal ulcers which are confirmed via endoscopy.  The primary causes are Helicobacter pylori infection, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) and aspirin.  Patients with ‘sinister’ symptoms (weight loss, iron deficiency, dysphagia, haematemesis/melaena or an abdominal mass) require urgent endoscopy to exclude gastric and oesophageal malignancy.  With confirmed peptic ulcer disease, management is a combination of:  lifestyle modification  medication review to stop/reduce any ulcer-inducing drugs  full dose proton pump inhibitor (PPI) for up to two months  testing for H. pylori and treatment with eradication therapy if positive  follow-up with repeat endoscopy to confirm healing and H. pylori retesting if appropriate.

GIT & LIVER part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  For acute bleeding peptic ulcers, endoscopy is required to locate and stop bleeding using adrenaline injection, cauterisation or clips; if these actions fail, surgery or embolisation are required.  The overall mortality rate for peptic ulcer disease is up to 8%. Epidemiology  Incidence rates are approximated at 0.1–0.3%.  Recurrence rates have reduced drastically due to widespread use of acid suppression and H. pylori eradication.  The ratio of duodenal to gastric ulceration is 4 : 1.  Duodenal ulcers are twice as common in men peaks at approximately 45–64 years of age.  Incidence of gastric ulcers increases with age and affects men and women in equal numbers. Aetiology Risk factors include:  H. pylori colonisation (cause of 95% of duodenal and up to 80% of gastric ulcers)  high alcohol intake  NSAID and aspirin use  severe stress  high-dose steroids when combined with NSAIDs  male sex  smoking (increases acid, decreases protective prostaglandins)  Zollinger–Ellison syndrome (gastrinoma) – rare. H. pylori  Gram-negative spiral bacillus.  Primary cause of peptic ulcer disease.  Infection rates increase with age; more than half of those > 50 years are colonised in the gastric antral mucosa.  Detected in 70% of patients with gastric ulcer and > 90% of patients with duodenal ulcer, compared with 50% of control subjects. Pathophysiology  The mucosa is injured due to the action of insults such as acid, H. pylori and NSAIDs, as well as inadequate mucosal protective factors, such as mucus or reduced blood supply.  H. pylori can either increase or decrease the release of gastric acid, both of which can cause ulceration. In the latter, gastric ulcers result from atrophic gastritis and there is also an associated increase in gastric cancer. In the duodenum, H. pylori increases gastric acid production.  Clinical Presentation  Clinical presentations for peptic ulcer disease and gastritis include:  epigastric pain (sometimes radiating to the back if a posterior duodenal ulcer is present)  vomiting G

If this is negative, but clinical suspicion remains high, an urgent computed tomography (CT) abdomen/pelvis should be organised to rule out perforation.  Serology stays positive after treatment and is not useful for confirming eradication. H. pylori Detection (test-and-treat)  In patients > 55 years of age without alarm symptoms, noninvasive urea breath tests and stool antigen tests are appropriate.  Urea breath test:  urea breath test sensitivity 88–95% and specificity 95–100%  patient ingests urea labelled with carbon-13 (13C), carbon dioxide (CO2) produced by urease is detected in the exhaled breath.  Stool antigen testing:  stool antigen test sensitivity 94% and specificity 92%  detection of H. pylori antigen by enzyme immunoassay  least invasive and cost-effective.  do not perform test if taken proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) in the last two weeks or antibiotics in the last four weeks.  In patients requiring endoscopy:  antral biopsy at endoscopy with haematoxylin/eosin or Giemsa stain  urease testing (CLO): the bacillus secretes a urease enzyme which splits urea to release ammonia. A biopsy sample is put into a jelly containing urea and a pH indicator; this will change colour if H. pylori is present

JAM  Management Non-pharmacological  Lifestyle modification:  weight loss  avoid aggravating foods  smaller meals  avoid eating just before bed  smoking cessation  reduce alcohol intake.  Relaxation techniques for stress management.  Treat depression and anxiety.  Review and stop exacerbating drugs such as NSAIDs, bisphosphonates, steroids, selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs). Pharmacological  National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guidance suggests the following:  full-dose PPI therapy or H2 receptor antagonist therapy for eight weeks  if positive for H. pylori, then all symptomatic patients found to be positive should undergo eradication therapy (test-andtreat).  Eradication regimes vary, but usually involve triple therapy:  PPI for two months + two antibiotics (amoxicillin and clarithromycin) for seven days  metronidazole resistance is a problem in some areas  if using NSAIDs, provide eradication following PPI therapy of eight weeks. Monitoring Treatment Success  Effective H. pylori eradication should be assessed by stool testing or repeat biopsies/breath testing in patients with complications and persistent symptoms.  NICE recommend testing to confirm eradication should be performed 6–8 weeks after beginning treatment  for diagnosed gastric ulcers – repeat endoscopy 6–8 weeks after initiation of treatment is recommended  if symptoms persist following treatment, offer low-dose PPI or H2 receptor antagonist. Surgical  For acute upper GI bleeds relating to ulcers, endoscopy is required to locate and stop bleeding using adrenaline injection, cauterisation or clips; if these actions fail, surgery or embolisation are required.  NICE recommend laparoscopic fundoplication for those with acid reflux who either cannot tolerate or do not desire to remain on long-term therapy.

GIT & LIVER part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Prognosis  Relapse of peptic ulcer disease after H. pylori eradication is less than 5% per year, compared with more than 60% in patients without eradication therapy.  The mortality rate for peptic ulcer disease is up to 8%.  The mortality rate for bleeding peptic ulcer is 10%.  The mortality rate for perforated peptic ulcer is 25%. Complications  Haemorrhage:  acute haemorrhage – duodenal ulcers are the most common cause of GI haemorrhage; posterior duodenal ulcers can penetrate into the gastroduodenal artery.  Perforation and consequent peritonitis:  if suspected, broad-spectrum antibiotics should be started.  Strictures and scarring may progress to gastric outlet obstruction.  Gastric cancer from H. pylori infection. Peutz-Jeghers Syndrome  Peutz-Jeghers syndrome is a rare inherited syndrome with an autosomal dominant pattern of inheritance.  Overview Key Facts  Peutz-Jeghers syndrome is a rare inherited syndrome with an autosomal dominant pattern of inheritance.  Characteristic features of the condition are peri-oral and mucosal pigmentation alongside multiple gastrointestinal hamartomatous polyps.  The condition is associated with an increased risk of numerous malignancies, including those of the GI tract, as well as those of the pancreas, lung, breast, thyroid, uterus, ovaries and testes.  Patients suspected to have the condition should be referred to a genetic centre for genetic testing and counselling.  Endoscopy is used as part of diagnosis and management – colonoscopy and upper GI endoscopy.  Polyps may be removed via endoscopic polypectomy; surgical excision may also be required.  Large bowel screening via colonoscopy is recommended for all patients aged over 25 with the condition, and should be carried out every 2 years; polypectomy (via the endoscopic route if possible) should be carried out if polyps are identified.  Family members of an affected patient with an identified gene should also be referred for genetic counselling and genetic testing. JAM Epidemiology  The condition is relatively rare.  Reported incidence is between 1 in 50 000 to 1 in 200 000 live births.  Men and women are equally affected as the inheritance of the condition is autosomal dominant and not sex-linked. Aetiology  Autosomal dominant condition – an individual with only one copy of the affected gene will have the condition, and has a 50% chance of passing the affected gene and hence the condition on to any offspring. Pathophysiology  A gene known as STK11 is a tumour suppressor gene that is on chromosome 19 is inactivated, this is the most common associated mutation.  Clinical Presentation  Patients may be asymptomatic and present with a request for screening due to a positive family history.  Other presentations may be varied and include:  anaemia  rectal bleeding  rectal prolapse  diarrhoea  rectal mucous discharge  abdominal discomfort and distention  abdominal pain – patients may present acutely with signs and symptoms of obstruction.  Patients may also present with signs and symptoms of a related malignancy.  Signs include:  mucocutaneous pigmentation  perioral freckles  rectal polyp/mass  signs associated with extra-GI malignancy ie – thyroid mass.  Differential Diagnosis  Cowden's disease.  Juvenile polyposis.  Cronkhite-Canada syndrome.  Other causes of acute abdomen.

GIT & LIVER part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Diagnosis/Investigation  Endoscopy – colonoscopy is the investigation of choice, with polyp biopsy and histology.  STK11 genetic testing.  Dental examination and imaging along with skull imaging.  Further investigations may be relevant as per patients presenting signs and symptoms ie if there is suspicion of malignancy.  Management  Genetic counselling for patients with the condition, as well as family members of patients who are diagnosed.  Initial surveillance endoscopy (colorectal and upper GI) plus polyp excision (which may be via the endoscopic route or via surgical excision if endoscopic removal is not possible).  Ongoing gastrointestinal surveillance and/or polyp excision is required every 2 years from 25 years of age.  Prognosis  There is no cure for the condition, management is based on surveillance and symptom management.  There is an increased risk of malignancy, including colorectal, stomach, pancreas and oesophageal cancer as well as increased risk of breast, lung, uterine, ovarian and testicular cancers. Pharyngeal Pouch  A pharyngeal pouch (also known as Zenker’s diverticulum) is an acquired diverticulum caused by protrusion of the mucosa through muscle layers of the wall of the pharynx.  Overview Key Facts  A pharyngeal pouch (also known as Zenker’s diverticulum) is an acquired diverticulum caused by protrusion of the mucosa through muscle layers of the wall of the pharynx.  The diverticulum occurs through Killian’s dehiscence between the thyropharyngeus and the cricopharyngeus parts of the inferior constrictor muscle.  The condition tends to occur in patients aged over 50 and may present with dysphagia, cough, weight loss, aspiration and regurgitation.  It is important to exclude other causes of dysphagia, such as oesophageal carcinoma.  Laryngoscopy and barium swallow will confirm the diagnosis.  Management is generally surgical; without treatment, pouches will continue to enlarge and patients generally notice an increase in severity of symptoms. G

DR. JAM Epidemiology  Incidence is 5 per million.  It tends to occur in people aged > 50 years.  Sex ratio is 2 : 1 (men : women). Aetiology  The true aetiology is unknown, but it may involve increased cricopharyngeal tonicity due to gastro-oesophageal reflux. Neuromuscular inco-ordination may also play a part. Pathophysiology  There are two types of diverticulum: pulsion and traction  a pulsion diverticulum is one that is formed by internal luminal pressure forcing the mucosa outward  a traction diverticulum is one where external scarring (eg by tubercular lymphadenopathy in the mediastinum) ‘pulls’ the mucosa outward. A pharyngeal pouch is a pulsion diverticulum.  Clinical Presentation  Clinical features of pharyngeal pouch:  dysphagia  regurgitation  weight loss  hoarseness  aspiration pneumonia  swelling on the left side of the neck, which gurgles on palpation (Boyce’s sign)  halitosis  recurrent sore throat  lung abscesses  Eventually, these may lead to a malnourished patient with weight loss.  The Lahey classification of pharyngeal pouches is as follows:  type I: small mucosal protrusion  type II: definite pouch (the oesophagus and hypopharynx are in line on barium swallow examination)  type III: large pouch (the hypopharynx and pouch are in line in the lateral view on barium swallow; the oesophagus is pushed forward).  Differential Diagnosis  Oesophageal carcinoma  Oesophageal web  Oesophageal stricture  Oesophageal ring  Reflux oesophagitis  Achalasia.

GIT & LIVER part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Diagnosis/Investigation  Full blood count  Plain neck radiograph (there may be a triangular lucency in the prevertebral tissue and/or fluid level)  Barium swallow  Careful endoscopy.  Management  Management is dependent on the size of the pouch.  Pouches can be excised endoscopically or externally.  Open excision of the pharyngeal pouch.  Endoscopic stapling/diathermy: endoscopic resection is much less invasive – it avoids many of the post-operative complications seen with an external excision  it is often the only option in elderly high-risk patients  opponents of the endoscopic method claim an increased rate of recurrence, compared to that with external excision (6– 7%) and the chance of missing a malignancy in the pouch which cannot be sent for histology.  External approach: this is best done by one-stage diverticulectomy. Indications  Symptomatic pharyngeal pouch. Preoperatively  Starve the patient overnight preoperatively.  Beware of inhalation during induction of general anaesthesia (Mendelson syndrome).  Examine the pouch transorally and pack the pouch with proflavine ribbon for easy identification.  Pass a nasogastric tube after intubation, if not possible preoperatively. Incision  Make an incision at the level of the cricoid at the anterior border of the left sternomastoid. Procedure  Retract the sternomastoid and carotid sheath laterally to expose the packed pouch.  Remove the pack via the mouth.  Excise or invert the pouch, then oversew or staple.  Perform cricopharyngeal myotomy (to try to prevent recurrence).  Send the pouch for histological examination (1% risk of carcinoma in a pouch). Post-operatively  Keep the patient nil by mouth and feed via the nasogastric tube. Complications G

Porphyria Cutanea Tarda  Porphyria cutanea tarda is the most common of the porphyrias.  Overview Key Facts  Porphyria cutanea tarda (PCT) is the most common of the porphyrias.  PCT is a disorder of porphyrin metabolism where there is an acquired deficiency in uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase (UROD).  Clinical features include:  hyperpigmentation and scarring  blistering and crusted skin lesions on the back of hands and other areas of the body that are prone to sun exposure  hypertrichosis  dark or reddish urine.  Investigation findings include substantial increases in porphyrins in plasma or urine.  The underlying cause of PCT cannot be cured, but symptoms can be controlled by avoiding exacerbating factors, repeated phlebotomies/low-dose hydroxychloroquine.

GIT & LIVER part 2 MIL ALRAJHI Epidemiology  A disease of adults.  Men and women are equally susceptible.  The annual incidence in the United Kingdom (UK) is estimated to be 2–5 per million. Aetiology  PCT is caused by a deficiency or reduced activity of uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase (UROD) in the haem-synthesis pathway.  Less than 20% of the normal activity of UROD is required to cause the clinical manifestation of PCT.  Specific environmental factors and infectious agents can increase susceptibility by increasing oxidative stress in the liver for example:  iron overload  myelofibrosis  end-stage renal disease. Pathophysiology  Impairment of the haem-synthesis pathway due to deficiency of uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase (UROD).  This leads to the accumulation of highly carboxylated porphyrinogens in the liver, which are oxidised to the corresponding porphyrins, enter the plasma and are subsequently excreted in the urine.  These photosensitive porphyrins are transported to the skin and cause photodamage on exposure to light with a wavelength near 400 nm.  Photons are released that activate oxygen which mediates damage to proteins, lipids and basement membrane.  This results in dermo-epidermal separation and blister formation.  Excess porphyrins in plasma are excreted in the urine, causing urine to become reddish or dark.  Clinical Presentation  Blistering skin lesions on sun-exposed areas of the body:  most commonly on the back of the hands, forearms, face, ears, neck and feet  blisters contain serous or serosanguinous fluid  increased susceptibility to infection  rupturing leads to scarring with hypo- or hyperpigmentation  in some cases scarring can be associated with calcification, leading to ‘pseudoscleroderma’ due to its resemblance to the cutaneous scarring seen in scleroderma.  Hypertrichosis, especially on the cheeks and forearm, is troublesome for women.  Scarring alopecia.  Red urine due to large concentrations of porphyrins.  Following minor injuries, there may be slow-to-heal crusted erosions. JAM  Post-inflammatory pigmentation and cysts/tiny white raised spots (milia).  Fragile skin.  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses include:  variegate porphyria  hereditary coproporphyria (HCP)  congenital erythropoietic porphyria (CEP)  pseudoporphyria  hepatoerythropoietic porphyria  homozygous forms of acute porphyrias.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Mildly elevated liver transaminases (aspartate transaminase (AST) and alanine aminotransferase (ALT)) and iron overload.  Elevated plasma and urine total porphyrins are the first-line investigations:  normal levels exclude all porphyrias that cause blistering skin lesions.  Second-line tests to exclude other causes of blistering lesions include:  faecal porphyrins  erythrocyte total porphyrins  plasma fluorescence emission.  Each of the samples of blood, urine and faeces must be collected into a special darkened container (which excludes light).  Management Non-pharmacological  Avoid exacerbating factors, eg sunlight exposure, excess alcohol intake, stopping the combined contraceptive pill, smoking, oestrogen use.  Repeated phlebotomy:  preferred over low-dose hydroxychloroquine if serum ferritin > 600 ng/ml or homozygosity or compound heterozygosity for HFE mutations  performed every 2 weeks, guided by the serum ferritin and porphyrin levels.  Chronic renal failure/end-stage renal failure on haemodialysis – erythropoietin and low-volume phlebotomy. Pharmacological  Reflectant sunscreens (containing titanium dioxide or zinc oxide) – cover UVA, UVB and visible light.  Low-dose hydroxychloroquine:  works by mobilising the excess porphyrin from the liver, so that it is excreted as urine

DR. JAM  Overview Key Facts  Portal hypertension occurs due to increased resistance to portal venous flow.  Pressure in the portal vein is pathological when > 12 mmHg.  Complications are the development of varices, hepatic encephalopathy and ascites.  The most serious complication is acute and often catastrophic oesophageal varices bleeding.  As a result of the rising portal pressure, the spleen enlarges and anastomoses may open between the portal and systemic circulation.  Some of the collaterals, which most commonly occur at the oesophagogastric junction, umbilicus and rectum may become very large (varices).  Complications are the development of varices, hepatic encephalopathy and ascites.  The most serious complication is acute and often catastrophic oesophageal varices rupture leading to massive gastrointestinal (GI) bleeding.  Hepatic encephalopathy is a neuropsychiatric syndrome due to elevated ammonia as a consequence of reduced toxin eradication via the liver.  Ascites is defined as the accumulation of free fluid within the peritoneal cavity.  A variety of conditions may cause portal hypertension; in the United Kingdom, the single most common cause is cirrhosis secondary to alcohol.  All patients with cirrhosis of the liver should have upper GI endoscopy to determine the presence or absence of oesophageal varices.  Prophylactic treatment with non-selective beta-blockers +/- nitrates is given to those with large varices with no history of haemorrhage.  Active oesophageal variceal bleeding can be life threatening and is therefore a medical emergency. Treatment involves:  rapid resuscitation with volume support and blood products  vasoactive drugs  prophylactic antibiotics  balloon tamponade (temporary measure) and early gastroscopy with band ligation/glue injection. Epidemiology  50% of liver cirrhosis patients have gastro-oesophageal varices at initial diagnosis.  30% of patients with varices will bleed at some point.  50% of liver cirrhosis patients will develop hepatic encephalopathy.  50% of liver cirrhosis patients will develop ascites in < 10 years. Aetiology  Cirrhosis due to any cause.

GIT & LIVER part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Portal vein thrombosis:  congenital malformation  pancreatitis  tumour.  Budd–Chiari syndrome – thrombosis or obstruction of hepatic vein due to:  tumour  haematological disease  the oral contraceptive pill.  Intrahepatic tumours, such as:  cholangiocarcinoma  hepatocellular carcinoma.  Constrictive pericarditis.  Right heart failure.  Splenic vein thrombosis (segmental portal hypertension). Pathophysiology  The rise in portal vein pressure causes the spleen to enlarge and anastomoses may open between the portal and systemic circulation.  Collaterals most commonly occur at the oesophagogastric junction, umbilicus and rectum.  Collaterals may become very large (varices); these can bleed.  Bleeding is often catastrophic in addition many patients also have a coagulopathy as a result of their underlying liver disease.  Portosystemic shunting of blood occurs, toxins thus bypass the liver and cross the blood-brain barrier causing hepatic encephalopathy.  Ascites is the accumulation of free fluid within the peritoneal cavity, portal hypertension causes a transudative ascetic fluid as the increased portal pressure forces fluid into the extracellular space.  Clinical Presentation  Clinical presentations for portal hypertension include:  splenomegaly  ascites resulting in a distended abdomen  abdominal pain and fever (spontaneous bacterial peritonitis)  haematemesis/melaena from oesophageal varices or portal gastropathy  caput medusae (dilated veins around the umbilicus)  visible rectal varices/haemorrhoids  hepatic encephalopathy:  confusion  reduced level of consciousness  vomiting  seizures  hyperventilation  flapping tremor G

GIT & LIVER part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  All patients with cirrhosis of the liver should have upper GI endoscopy to determine the presence or absence of oesophageal varices.  Management Non-pharmacological  If there are no varices, or only very small varices, no treatment is required except regular endoscopic review. The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) recommends review every three years. Pharmacological  Larger varices in patients with no history of variceal haemorrhage should be treated with prophylactic, non-selective beta-blockers (propranolol or carvedilol) alone or in combination with a nitrate.  This reduces portal pressure and thus the risk of haemorrhage. Surgical  Patients intolerant of beta-blockers and who are at high risk of bleeding may be considered for endoscopic variceal ligation.  NICE recommends offering band ligation as primary prevention of bleeding in those with cirrhosis and medium to large oesophageal varices. Emergency treatment of variceal haemorrhage:  Resuscitation (ABC) – IV access, volume expansion and blood products  Nil by mouth  Correction of coagulopathy and thrombocytopenia  Vasoactive drugs – terlipressin concomitantly with prophylactic antibiotics at presentation  Early gastroscopy with band ligation of oesophageal varices and injection sclerotherapy using N-butyl-2-cyanoacrylate for gastric varices  Temporary balloon tamponade (Sengstaken–Blakemore tube) if endoscopy not immediately available or bleeding cannot be stopped.  Bleeding that does not respond to these measures or recurrent haemorrhage is an indication for emergency transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunting (TIPSS). TIPSS Procedure Placement of a shunt under radiological screening which decompresses the portal venous system. Anatomically, the shunt connects the portal vein (high pressure) to the hepatic vein (low pressure). It is less invasive than surgery and is a rescue procedure for patients with recurrent or resistant haemorrhage not fit for surgery. It may precipitate hepatic encephalopathy which occurs in up to 24%. If there is a shunt blockage, a second shunt may be ‘piggybacked’ across the first. G

JAM  Secondary prevention of haemorrhage:  patients should undergo repeated band ligation until varices are eradicated  beta-blockers should be given as this reduces the risk of rebleeding by up to 40%.  Treatment of hepatic encephalopathy:  screen for and treat sepsis  fluid and electrolyte balance  high protein diet  laxatives (lactulose) to clear the gut and thus reduce toxin absorption  rifaximin, a semi-synthetic antibiotic which decreases intestinal production and absorption of ammonia  remove or treat precipitants.  Treatment for ascites:  fluid restriction  low sodium intake and diuretic therapy  paracentesis (may be used for ascites not responding to diuretics).  Paracentesis may result in a further shift of fluid from the intravascular space into the peritoneal cavity with the risk of circulatory collapse; reduce by supporting circulation using intravenous albumin.  Remove drain at earliest opportunity due to risk of infection.  Prognosis  Mortality rate after first presentation of bleeding varices is 50%.  The majority of survivors will re-bleed, with a mortality of 30%.  60% of varices rebleed within one year.  Mortality six weeks after a variceal bleed is 10%.  Hepatic encephalopathy mortality is high, especially if renal failure supervenes and when the mortality exceeds 50%. Other  Hepatic encephalopathy:  neuropsychiatric syndrome which may complicate acute or chronic liver disease from any cause  acute kidney injury may often supervene; the chance of recovery from hepatorenal failure is extremely poor  the underlying mechanisms are complex, but the absorption of toxins (such as ammonia) from bacterial breakdown of proteins in the gut is thought to play a major part  common causes of acute hepatic encephalopathy are fulminant viral hepatitis and paracetamol toxicity  chronic hepatic encephalopathy may supervene in chronic liver disease of any type, often precipitated by alcohol, drugs, GI haemorrhage, infections or constipation.

GIT & LIVER part 2 MIL ALRAJHI Pregnancy-related Liver Disease  Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy presents with pruritis and elevated bile acids in the second/third trimester of pregnancy.  Overview Key Facts  Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy (ICP) presents with pruritis and elevated bile acids in the second/third trimester of pregnancy.  Acute fatty liver of pregnancy (AFLP) presents with maternal liver dysfunction of variable severity in the third trimester of pregnancy.  In ICP, elevated oestrogen and progesterone results in biliary stasis and decreased excretion of bile salts.  In AFLP, abnormal maternal-fetal fatty acid metabolism results in microvesicular fatty infiltration of hepatocytes.  Diagnosis of ICP is made by clinical presentation and elevated serum bile acid levels, above 10 μmol/l.  Diagnosis of AFLP is made by clinical presentation and supported by laboratory findings of deranged liver function tests (LFTs), hypoglycaemia and thrombocytopenia.  Complications of ICP include intra-uterine fetal demise, preterm delivery, meconium-stained amniotic fluid and neonatal respiratory distress syndrome (NRDS).  Complications of AFLP include maternal liver failure and severe coagulopathy along with fetal demise.  Management of ICP includes ursodeoxycholic acid and delivery.  Management of AFLP includes prompt delivery and supportive management for liver dysfunction.  Prognosis of both ICP and AFLP is good if there is prompt diagnosis and management. Epidemiology  Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy (ICP):  most common liver condition in pregnancy  affects 0.5–1.5% of pregnancies around the world  more common in women aged over 35 years.  Acute fatty liver of pregnancy (AFLP):  rare, but life-threatening  affects 1 in 7000–20 000 pregnancies. Aetiology  ICP:  mutations in the phospholipid export pump MDR3 may contribute to the disease  elevated oestrogen and progesterone levels cause hepatobiliary tract stasis which results in decreased bile excretion  family history in 50% of women, associated with HLA-B8 and HLA-BW16 mutations. G

DR. JAM  AFLP:  mutations in mitochondrial fatty acid oxidation resulting in fetal long-chain 3-hydroxyacyl CoA dehydrogenase (LCHAD) deficiency. Risk factors ICP AFLP Prior ICP or family history of ICP Maternal age ≥ 35 Multiple gestation Hepatitis C virus Prior AFLP or fam Multiple gestation Male sex of fetus Pre-eclampsia or H Low BMI, < 20 Pathophysiology ICP  Fetus unable to remove bile acids from the blood.  Bile acids have vasoconstrictive effects on human placental chorionic veins which can cause sudden asphyxia and subsequent anoxia.  Increased bile acids can also cause fetal distress and stillbirth which may be due to bile acid-mediated oxytocin receptor expression. AFLP  Third-trimester nausea, vomiting, malaise, jaundice.  RUQ or epigastric pain.  Liver failure ranging from mild to fulminant.  Extrahepatic manifestations ⇢ ascites, AKI, hypoglycaemia, encephalopathy, coagulopathy.  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses include:

JAM  Overview Key Facts  Primary biliary cholangitis (PBC), previously known as primary biliary cirrhosis, is an autoimmune condition of the liver.  PBC causes small-bile-duct obliteration and build-up of toxins which can no longer be excreted as efficiently.  PBC is more common in women.  Alkaline phosphatase (ALP) is raised. ALP is released by the cells of the biliary tree and bile ducts; therefore damage to these cells results in leakage of ALP.  Antimitochondrial antibodies (AMA) are the hallmark of PBC.  Treatment involves management of symptoms such as pruritus and delaying progression of the condition.  Liver transplantation and subsequent immunosuppression is the definitive treatment, which is usually reserved for end stage disease or intractable pruritus. Epidemiology  Ninety per cent of patients are women, often middle age.  It is more commonly seen in those of South Americana and African descent.  PBC accounts for 5% of deaths due to liver cirrhosis. Aetiology  The cause is unknown.  Environmental, genetic factors and autoimmune aetiology are suggested.  PBC is an autoimmune mediated condition.  Strongly associated with other autoimmune disease such as rheumatoid, arthritis, Sjörgen syndrome and CREST syndrome. Pathophysiology  Progressive inflammation and destruction of small intrahepatic ducts leads to eventual cirrhosis. The four stages are as follows:  Destruction of interlobular ducts.  Small-duct proliferation.  Fibrosis.  Cirrhosis.  Clinical Presentation  Patients may be symptomatic and the condition may be diagnosed after an incidental finding of raised ALP.  Other presentations include:  pruritus  cholestatic jaundice  diarrhoea  lethargy  xanthelasmata due to hypercholesterolaemia

GIT & LIVER part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  skin pigmentation  clubbing  hepatosplenomegaly  portal hypertension varices  osteoporosis and osteomalacia.  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnosis fro PBC includes:  chronic hepatitis B/C/D  hepatitis due to other viruses  chronic drug induced hepatitis  haemochromatosis  alpha1-antitrypsin deficiency  Wilson’s disease.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Antimitochondrial (M2) antibody present in 95% of cases.  Raised alkaline phosphatase (ALP) – often in advance of symptoms/signs.  Raised IgM.  A liver biopsy may be required to confirm a diagnosis.  Management Non-pharmacological  Regular monitoring with liver function tests and ultrasound scans. Pharmacological  Cholestyramine relieves pruritus.  Ursodeoxycholic acid – however it is doubtful if improves prognosis or delays time to liver transplantation.  The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence recommend the use of obeticholic acid, either as a monotherapy or in combination with ursodeoxycholic acid if ursodeoxycholic acid is not tolerated or no response.  Obeticholic acid acts to reduce circulating bile acid. Surgical  Liver transplantation is the only hope of a cure and assessment should be made at an appropriate stage in disease process.  Indications include intractable pruritus and end stage disease. Pyoderma Gangrenosum  Pyoderma gangrenosum is a rare skin condition that is classed as a neutrophilic dermatosis.  Overview Key Facts  Pyoderma gangrenosum is a rare skin condition that is classed as a neutrophilic dermatosis.  Around half of all cases are associated with underlying medical disorders; for example, it is the second most common skin manifestation in inflammatory bowel disease.  The condition typically affects the legs (shins) or trunk in classical pyoderma gangrenousum.  Other types of pyoderma gangrenosum include pustular pyoderma gangrenosum, genital pyoderma gangrenosum, parastomal gangrenosum and bullous gangrenosum.  Typical presentation of the classical form is with red pustules that quickly enlarge to form full-thickness ulcerating lesions which excrete fluid.  These ulcerated lesions are often extremely painful.  The initial and new lesions often appear after minor trauma to the affected area.  Treatment usually involves arresting progression and encouraging healing and may involve analgesia, wound care and bandaging, topical therapies, oral prednisolone and ciclosporin and surgical reconstruction of skin.  Without treatment, prognosis is variable:  some ulcers heal slowly, some persist and some continue to enlarge. Epidemiology  The condition more commonly affects those aged over 50, but can affect any age or sex.

GIT & LIVER part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  allergic reaction  malnutrition  infection  tuberculosis (TB)  HIV.  vasculitis  vasospastic conditions:  rheumatoid arthritis  systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE)  polyarteritis nodosa  systemic sclerosis  Raynaud syndrome.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Diagnosis is usually clinical, due to the characteristic appearance of lesions and history of intense pain.  A skin prick test (pathergy test) will be positive – the skin prick will cause a papule, pustule or ulceration.  Biopsy may be indicated if there is diagnostic uncertainty – the ulcer edge must show a neutrophilic infiltrate for diagnosis via biopsy.  Wound swabs should also be taken to identify any superimposing infection.  Management  Management should be initiated and monitored by a dermatologist.  Treatment often depends on the size of the ulcer.  Treatment usually involves arresting progression and encouraging healing and may involve analgesia, wound care and bandaging, topical therapies, immunosuppression and surgical reconstruction of skin.  Treating any underlying conditions may also help healing and stop further ulcers forming.  Smaller ulcers may heal with topical therapies including potent steroids, including steroid injection into the ulcer margins, tacrolimus and ciclosporin solution, as well as wound care and dressings.  Larger ulcers may require high-dose oral or in severe cases IV corticosteroid therapy. Oral immunosuppression with ciclosporin if steroids fail or cannot be used.  Other systemic treatments that can be considered include:  immunosuppressants such as:  azathioprine, cyclophosphamide, tacrolimus, mycophenolate mofetil, 6-mercaptopurine, methotrexate and chlorambucil.  sulfa drugs such as:  dapsone.  biologics such as:  infliximab and etanercept.  colchicine G

Small Intestinal Bacterial Overgrowth (SIBO)  Small intestinal bacterial overgrowth (SIBO) is characterised by excessive colonisation of the normal gut flora.  Overview Key Facts  Small intestinal bacterial overgrowth (SIBO) is characterised by excessive colonisation of the normal gut flora.  SIBO is thought to develop due to a failure of normal mechanisms that control bacterial growth within the small gut.  In particular, decreased gastric acid secretion and factors that affect (and slow) gut motility are important; as are some immunodeficiency syndromes/conditions.  Any structural defect can have an effect on gut motility:  classically, procedures that create a blind loop (such as Roux-en-Y) predispose patients  however, any intestinal surgery predisposes to diverticular formation or stricture formation, both of which will lead to increased risk of SIBO.  There is limited data on its prevalence, though it is known to be common in conditions where there is intestinal stasis/formation of a blind loop.  SIBO is a common cause of malabsorption (possibly the second most common after coeliac disease in the Western world).  The condition may lead to steatorrhoea and megaloblastic anaemia (due to vitamin B12 malabsorption), as well as raised folate due to increased folate synthesis by intestinal bacteria.

GIT & LIVER part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  In SIBO, the two main malabsorptions are vitamin B12 and fat:  vitamin B12 deficiency is due to its utilisation by the bacteria  fat malabsorption is due to deconjugation of bile acids by intestinal bacteria  this also causes deficiency of fat-soluble vitamins  as vitamin K is produced by bacteria, deficiency of this vitamin is rare.  SIBO remains a poorly understood condition which can be treated with antibiotic therapy and supportive measure, but is often associated with frequent relapses. Epidemiology  There is limited data on prevalence, though it is known to be common in conditions where there is intestinal stasis/formation of a blind loop.  Increased prevalence of small bowel bacterial overgrowth is also noted among patients with inflammatory bowel disease compared with other individuals.  SIBO is a common cause of malabsorption (possibly the second most common after coeliac disease in the Western world). Aetiology  Disorders of protective antibacterial mechanisms:  immunodeficiency syndromes  pancreatic exocrine insufficiency.  Anatomical abnormalities:  small intestinal obstruction  diverticula  fistulae  previous ileo-caecal resections/GI surgery.  Motility disorders:  scleroderma  autonomic neuropathy in diabetes mellitus  post-radiation enteropathy. Pathophysiology  Decreased gastric acid secretion and small intestine dysmotility.  Disturbances in gut immune function and anatomical abnormalities of the GI tract.  Bacterial overgrowth causes an inflammatory response in the intestinal mucosa.  Clinical Presentation  Clinical presentations include:  abdominal pain  aelching  bloating  diarrhoea  distension G

JAM  flatulence  indigestion.  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses include:  irritable bowel syndrome  functional bloating  coeliac disease  chronic pancreatitis.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Hydrogen breath testing and jejunal biopsy may be used.  The gold standard for diagnosis of SIBO is culture of small intestinal fluid aspirate.  Duodenal aspirate is often sufficient, although aspiration from more distal small intestine regions is advocated by some.  If culture of a duodenal aspirate shows > 105 CFU/ml, it is considered a sensitive marker for SIBO.  Management Non-pharmacological  Low FODMAP (fermentable oligosaccharides, disaccharides, monosaccharides, and polyiols) diet.  Dietician consultation. Pharmacological  Bacterial overgrowth responds to antibiotic therapy.  many antibiotics are effective in SIBO, including metronidazole, ciprofloxacin, co-amoxiclav and rifaximin  the aim is to reduce rather than eliminate gut flora.  A 2-week course of antibiotics may be tried initially.  In many patients, especially those with a motility disorder and/or anatomical abnormalities, long-term antibiotic therapy may be needed.  Prucalopride increases gut motility and is used as an adjunct therapy to antibiotics.  Prognosis  The prognosis of SIBO is generally good, however the condition is associated with frequent relapses and symptom-free periods.

GIT & LIVER part 2 MIL ALRAJHI Systemic Sclerosis  Systemic sclerosis is a connective tissue disorder characterised by thickening and ?brosis of the skin (scleroderma) with distinctive involvement of internal organs and vascular damage.  Overview Key Facts  Systemic sclerosis is a connective tissue disorder characterised by thickening and ﬁbrosis of the skin (scleroderma) with distinctive involvement of internal organs and vascular damage.  Fibrosis may occur in:  skin tissues  the gastrointestinal (GI) tract  the heart and lungs and other vital organs.  Vascular damage may lead to:  secondary Raynaud's phenomenon  ischaemia of extremities  pulmonary arterial hypertension  renal disease.  Systemic sclerosis can be divided into two types depending on the extent of skin involvement – limited or diffuse scleroderma.  It is a rare condition, occurring in all racial groups, with an incidence of 4–12 per million per year.  It is more common in women (women : men ratio 4 : 1) and may start at any age.  Management focuses on managing symptoms and preventing complications:  this may include immunosuppressants, corticosteroids and supportive therapies.  Mortality rates in people with the condition are up to eight times higher than in people without it. Epidemiology  Systemic sclerosis is a rare condition, occurring in all racial groups.  Incidence is estimated to be between 4–12 cases per million per year.  It is more common in women (women : men ratio 4 : 1) and may start at any age. Aetiology  The cause is not clearly understood.  Genetic, infectious and environmental factors all appear to play a role.  Some cases may be due to or triggered by exposure to substances such as vinyl chloride.
