Tapeworm  A parasite is an organism that lives on or in a host and causes harm to a different host organism.  Overview Key Facts  A parasite is an organism that lives on or in a host and causes harm to a different host organism.  Parasites commonly cause disease in humans.  Many parasites are types of helminth worms which:  can be grouped based on morphological characteristics  are rarely fatal  can be associated with significant morbidity and disability, particularly in low- and middle-income countries.  Tapeworms are a type of worm that can infect the gut and include the beef tapeworm Taenia saginata and the pork tapeworm Taenia solium.  Most people are infected by eating undercooked meat or drinking water contaminated with tapeworm larvae.  Tapeworm infection is rare in the United Kingdom (UK) and is more commonly associated with tropical climates and developing countries.  Gastrointestinal (GI) infection may be asymptomatic or cause nausea, diarrhoea, abdominal pain, weight loss and malnutrition.  Certain tapeworm larvae (T. solium) can migrate away from the GI system and form larval cysts in body tissues and organs (cysticercosis):  this migration can lead to cysts of the CNS (neurocysticercosis) or muscles.  Signs and symptoms of cysticercosis may include headache, seizures and spinal symptoms for CNS infection.  Hydatid disease is an unusual condition caused by propagating cysts formed by the hydatid tapeworm Echinococcus granulosus:  the infection is present in sheep and goats, but is usually transmitted to humans via domesticated dogs

GIT & LIVER part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  cysts can develop within the liver and rarely in the lungs.  Diagnosis is made by imaging techniques alongside serology for cysticercosis or stool microscopy for intestinal tapeworm infection.  Treatment depends on the type of tapeworm and the area infected.  For intestinal tapeworm, infection treatment is with albendazole or other anthelmintic drugs. For more invasive disease, prolonged courses of anthelmintics or surgical intervention may be required. Epidemiology  Tapeworm infection is more commonly associated with tropical climates and developing countries. Aetiology  Transmission is often by eating undercooked or raw meat that is contaminated with the tapeworm larvae.  Transmission can also occur by drinking contaminated water and via the faecal–oral route.  Clinical Presentation  Clinical presentation varies with parasite type and with the route of transmission.  GI infection may be asymptomatic or cause nausea, diarrhoea, abdominal pain, weight loss and malnutrition.  Hydatid disease has a range of clinical presentations, depending on the site of hydatid cysts:  liver cysts – abdominal pain and distension  breathlessness – lung and cardiac involvement  early morning headaches, nausea and focal neurology – brain involvement  anaphylactoid reaction due to rupture of abdominal or lung cysts; this is seen in around 2% of patients who experience cyst rupture.  Neurocysticercosis can present with headache, spinal symptoms and may present with new-onset epilepsy – frequently in teenagers.  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnosis varies with region and clinical presentation.  Diarrhoea – Strongyloides, hookworm, ascariasis and inflammatory bowel disease.  Liver lesion – hydatid disease, amoebic liver abscess, bacterial liver abscess, haematoma, simple cyst and malignancy.  Multiple brain lesions – neurocysticercosis, hydatid disease, toxoplasmosis and malignancy.  Asymptomatic eosinophilia – any parasitic infection, Churg– Strauss syndrome and drug reaction.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Blood tests:  full blood count (FBC) for eosinophilia  liver function and renal function G

DR. JAM  serology for cysticercosis and echinococcus serology for hydatid disease.  Stool for microbiology, culture and sensitivity (MCS) and OCP (ova, cysts and parasites).  Specific investigations vary with suspected disease:  neurocysticercosis – computed tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scanning  hydatid disease – ultrasound imaging  calcified lesions may be visible in muscles with cysticercosis affecting the muscle tissue.  Management Non-pharmacological  Patients with neurocysticercosis are at significant risk of further seizures and require standard epilepsy advice – avoid driving, safety measures at home and around water. Pharmacological  Isolated hydatid cysts are often managed with prolonged (several weeks or months) courses of albendazole or praziquantel.  Treatment for intestinal tapeworm infection is with albendazole or other anthelmintic drugs.  Neurocysticercosis may require treatment with steroids and anticonvulsants before the infection can be cleared with anthelmintics. Surgical  Some hydatid cysts are managed using the PAIR (percutaneous aspiration, injection and re-aspiration) procedure with appropriate steroid and anthelmintic cover. Cysts are aspirated and injected with hypertonic saline to kill the daughter cysts within.  Extensive abdominal hydatid disease and any hydatid pulmonary or cardiac involvement usually require surgical removal – must be performed by an expert surgeon to minimise the risk of spilling cyst contents within the abdominal cavity and further seeding.  Prognosis  Treated intestinal tapeworm has an excellent prognosis.  The prognosis of cystic tapeworm conditions depends on the location of the disease and promptness of identification and treatment initiation.  Neurocysticercosis is thought to be a major cause of epilepsy worldwide.

GIT & LIVER part 2 MIL ALRAJHI Ulcerative Colitis  Ulcerative colitis is a chronic inflammatory bowel disease where the lining of the large intestine becomes inflamed, leading to the development of sores that can bleed and cause diarrhoea, often accompanied by blood and mucus in stool.  Overview Key Facts  Crohn’s disease and ulcerative colitis are collectively called ‘inflammatory bowel disease’ (IBD) – in 10% of cases it may not be possible to clearly differentiate between the two conditions.  Both Crohn’s disease and Ulcerative colitis are chronic, relapsingremitting, non-infectious inflammatory diseases of the gastrointestinal tract.  Ulcerative colitis (UC) is characterised by:  diffuse, continuous, superficial inflammation of the large bowel limited to the intestinal mucosa  usually affects the rectum with a variable length of colon affected proximally  ulcerative proctitis is inflammation limited to the rectum; left-sided colitis is inflammation that does not extend beyond the splenic flexure  extension proximally beyond splenic flexure is known as extensive colitis  treatment depends on the acuteness and severity of symptoms as well as response to medical management  surgery with colectomy is curative and should be considered with cases that are severe, resistant to medical management or in cases of toxic megacolon  there is an increased risk of developing colorectal cancer and therefore patients with Ulcerative colitis should be followed up with screening colonoscopy. Epidemiology  Ulcerative colitis is the most common form of IBD and affects men and women equally.  Peak incidence of ulcerative colitis occurs in late adolescence and early adulthood during the second to fourth decades of life.  15-20% of ulcerative colitis cases are paediatric. Aetiology  Cause of ulcerative colitis remains unclear.  It is a condition that is caused by environmentally triggering events in genetically susceptible people.  It is an immune-mediated condition resulting in impaired epithelial barrier function and chronic inflammation.  Risk increases in: positive family history, not smoking (risk of ulcerative colitis is decreased in smokers, however smoking cessation increases the risk of developing ulcerative colitis). G

DR. JAM Pathophysiology  Most cases of ulcerative colitis occur in the rectum.  Ulcerative colitis usually involves only the mucosa, formation of crypt abscesses, and depletion of goblet cells.  Ulcerated areas are covered by granulation tissue. The undermining of mucosa and granulation tissue excess results in pseudopolyps.  Early disease causes bleeding, petechial haemorrhages, and haemorrhagic inflammation. Oedema is present.  Acute severe colitis can lead to toxic megacolon.  Chronic and sever cases can exhibit areas of precancerous changes.  Biopsy sample showing lymphocytic infiltration of the intestinal mucosa , architectural distortion of the crypts: Endoscopic appearance of diffuse inflammatory polyposis in a patient with ulcerative colitis:  Clinical Presentation  Persistent bloody diarrhoea for more than six weeks.  Faecal urgency and/or incontinence.  Pre-defecation pain, which is relieved by passage of stool.  Nocturnal defecation.  Tenesmus.  Abdominal pain.  Non-specific symptoms: fatigue, malaise, anorexia, or fever.  Weight loss, delayed growth.  On examination:

GIT & LIVER part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  pallor, clubbing, or aphthous mouth ulcers  abdominal distension, tenderness, or mass: eg in the left lower quadrant  signs of malnutrition/malabsorption.  Extra-intestinal manifestations.  Pauci-articular arthritis/Axial arthritis/Polyarticular arthritis.  Erythema nodosum.  Aphthous mouth ulcers.  Episcleritis.  Metabolic bone disease.  Pyoderma gangrenosum.  Uveitis.  Primary sclerosing cholangitis.  Aphthous ulcer: Erythema nodosum: G

DR. JAM  Differential Diagnosis  The main differential to consider is Crohn’s disease.  Crohn’s disease versus Ulcerative colitis: Crohn’s disease Ulcerative colitis Pathology Transmural inflammation Mucosal ulcers Fissuring ulcers Neutrophils infiltrates Mucosa and submucosa only involved Inflammatory cell infiltrate Crypt abscesses Clinical Abdominal pain prominent Frequent fever Diarrhoea, blood per rectum Anal/perianal/oral lesions Stricturing common, leading to obstructive symptoms Diarrhoea, often with blood and mucus Abdominal pain less prominent Associations Increased incidence in smokers Skin disorders: erythema nodosum, pyoderma gangrenosum Iritis/ uveitis Arthritis Clubbing Decreased incidence in smokers Increased incidence of primary sclerosing cholangitis Other systemic manifestations occur but less common than in Crohn’s disease

GIT & LIVER part 2 MIL ALRAJHI Complications Fistulae: enteroenteral, enterovesical, enterovaginal, perianal Carcinoma B12 deficiency Iron deficiency anaemia Abscess formation Fistulae don’t develop Toxic megacolon Increased carcinoma risk Iron-deficiency anaemia  Other differentials to consider include:  infectious colitis  pseudomembranous colitis  ischaemic colitis  radiation colitis  colorectal cancer  diverticular disease  irritable bowel syndrome  coeliac disease.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Serum full blood count: anaemia which may be due to blood loss, malabsorption.  Increased platelet count suggests active inflammation.  Raised inflammatory markers such as C-reactive protein (CRP) and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) during active inflammation or an infectious complication.  Serum urea and electrolytes: assess for dehydration and signs of electrolyte disturbance.  Serum liver function tests: low serum albumin shows protein losing enteropathy.  Serum ferritin, vitamin B12, folate, and vitamin D levels.  Coeliac serology: excludes coeliac disease.  Stool microscopy and culture (including C.difficile toxin) to exclude infective gastroenteritis or pseudomembranous colitis.  Faecal calprotectin (raised suggests active inflammation, normal suggests irritable bowel syndrome).  Colonoscopy. Findings may show: discontinuous colonic or ileal inflammation, and rectal sparing.  Upper intestinal endoscopy for children & young people: if there are upper gastrointestinal tract symptoms.  CT to stage ulcerative colitis, looking for extraluminal complications eg abscesses and fistulas.  Plain abdominal X-rays identifies colonic dilation, indicates complications eg bowel obstruction and toxic megacolon.  Management Non-pharmacological:  Arrange emergency hospital admission if the patient is systemically unwell with symptoms of bloody diarrhoea, fever, tachycardia, or hypotension. G

DR. JAM  If no hospital admission is required, then arrange a secondary care referral to a paediatric gastroenterologist or gastroenterologist for adults.  Refer to appropriate specialist (eg rheumatology, dermatology, or ophthalmology) if suspected extra-intestinal manifestations cannot be managed in primary care.  Assess the impact of symptoms on daily functioning such as home, work, school, and leisure activities. Assess for associated anxiety and/or depression.  Provide advice on Crohn’s disease and offer sources of information and support eg Crohn’s and Colitis UK.  Smoking cessation.  Assess risk of osteoporosis.  Monitor serum ferritin, vitamin B12, folate, calcium and vitamin D levels and arrange supplementation accordingly. Pharmacological:  Aminosalicylates eg mesalazine and sulfasalazine:  can be used for both exacerbation and to maintain remission.  Corticosteroids:  for acute phase - not for maintenance therapy.  Calcineurin inhibitors eg tacrolimus or ciclosporin:  can be used in place of, or as an adjunct to, corticosteroids.  Immunosuppressive drugs eg thiopurines such as azathioprine, mercaptopurine, or methotrexate (second-line):  to maintain remission if frequent exacerbations, or if remission cannot be maintained by aminosalicylates.  Biologic therapy eg infliximab, adalimumab, and golimumab:  effective at inducing remission in people with severe disease which has not responded to conventional therapy. Also effective at maintaining remission. Surgical:  Colectomy offers a cure to patients with ulcerative colitis.  Indications for surgery: severe colitis, toxic megacolon, intolerable medication side-effects, medically intractable symptoms.  Prognosis  The condition may have a significant psychosocial impact on the patient.  The condition is associated with significant morbidity, with an increased risk of mortality when compared to the general population.  Most common cause of death for patients with ulcerative colitis is toxic megacolon.  3% to 5% of patients develop colonic adenocarcinoma.  Lifetime risk for surgery is 20-30% for people with ulcerative colitis.  Factors which may suggest a poor prognosis for patients with ulcerative colitis are:  sever symptoms at presentation

GIT & LIVER part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  extensive disease  raised inflammatory markers  age less than 50 years, and particularly childhood disease  poor compliance with drug treatment.  Risk of inflammatory bowel disease associated carcinoma is increased if:  onset of IBD occurred at less than 15 years old  disease duration has been greater than 10 years  there is widespread disease eg total colitis  compliance with treatment and follow-up is poor.  Patients with both Crohn’s disease and ulcerative colitis are recommended to have surveillance colonoscopy 8-10 years after onset of symptoms. Vascular Lesions of the Colon  Vascular malformations fall into two categories within the colon: Angiodysplasia – abnormal, dilated blood vessels in the colon that can cause gastrointestinal bleeding and congenital vascular malformations – rare, often present from birth, and may involve larger, malformed blood vessels leading to chronic bleeding or other complications.  Overview Key Facts  Vascular malformations fall into two categories within the colon:  angiodysplasia  haemangiomas.  Angiodysplasia:  colonic angiodysplasia consists of small, submucosal arteriovenous malformations of unknown aetiology and unclear histology  they may occur sporadically, or in association with hereditary telangiectasia of the skin and mouth in Osler– Weber–Rendu disease  more common in the elderly  may present with rectal bleeding.  haemangioma:  these are usually cavernous or giant haemangiomas and involve the whole thickness of the bowel wall.  they commonly occur in the rectum and present with bleeding per rectum. Epidemiology  Colonic vascular lesions accounts for the second highest number of lower gastrointestinal (GI) bleeds (LGIBs) in patients < 60 years old: G

DR. JAM  uncommon in general population with 0.83% prevalence  responsible for 6% of all LGIBs. Aetiology  Cause unknown. Pathophysiology  Mostly found in the proximal colon, comprises mostly veins that are prone to bleeding.  Further pathophysiology remains unclear.  Clinical Presentation  Presents as:  painless per rectum (PR) bleeding  positive faecal occult blood test  recurrent small lower GI bleeding, resulting in anaemia  large acute bleed requiring emergency admission.  Differential Diagnosis  Other causes of lower GI bleed:  malignancy  diverticular disease  haemorrhoids  polyps in the colon  inflammatory bowel disease  bowel ischaemia.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Diagnosis is by colonoscopy showing spider naevi-like lesions, or haemangiomas.  Management Surgical  Depends on the lesion identified:  angiodysplasia – coagulation via colonoscopy may be curative for small lesions. Extensive troublesome areas of angiodysplasia may need resection  haemangiomas – electrocoagulation or sclerotherapy may control symptoms. Surgery may be required for more extensive lesions  in catastrophic PR bleeding – interventional radiology may be required, or, failing that, emergency laparotomy and excision of the bleeding segment.

GIT & LIVER part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Prognosis  10% of all patients with malformation will eventually bleed. The risk of re-bleeding is unknown, but may be up to 50%.  Mortality of bleeds associated with a malformation is approximately 10%.  Poorer prognosis is seen with emergency surgery, and shock at presentation. Viral Hepatitis  Hepatitis is inflammation of the liver that can be caused by a number of different aetiologies.  Overview Key Facts  Hepatitis is inflammation of the liver that can be caused by a number of different aetiologies, including:  viruses  autoimmunity  ischaemia  alcohol  genetics.  Some people have no symptoms, while others can develop:  jaundice  poor appetite  lethargy  abdominal pain  diarrhoea.  Viral hepatitis is the most common cause of hepatitis globally.  There are five major hepatitis viruses:  hepatitis A:  spread via the faecal–oral route  virus – ribonucleic acid (RNA)  no chronic state.  hepatitis B:  spread – blood-borne, sexual transmission, vertical transmission  virus – DNA  can progress to cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma.  hepatitis C:  spread – blood-borne, sexual transmission, vertical transmission  virus – RNA G

DR. JAM  can progress to chronic hepatitis, cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma.  hepatitis D:  spread – blood-borne (dependent on concurrent hepatitis B infection for replication)  virus – incomplete  chronicity – those with chronic hepatitis B have an increased incidence of cirrhosis.  hepatitis E:  spread – faecal–oral, vertical transmission  virus – RNA  chronicity – only in those severely immunocompromised.  Hepatitis can be acute or chronic and rarely results in acute liver failure.  Management is often supportive and dependent on the type, which can be self-limiting.  Hepatitis B and C can progress to chronic hepatitis which can progress to cirrhosis and liver cancer.  Liver transplantation is the treatment of choice for patients with end-stage liver disease/decompensated cirrhosis. Epidemiology  Viral hepatitis is the most common type of hepatitis globally.  Hepatitis A is endemic in Africa and South America.  Hepatitis B is endemic in the Far East, Africa and the Mediterranean.  Risk groups for hepatitis B:  people born or bought up in a country where the infection is common  intravenous (IV) drug users  health workers  commercial sex workers  men who have sex with men  people who have had multiple sexual partners. Aetiology  There are five major hepatitis viruses.  Hepatitis A:  spread via the faecal–oral route  virus – ribonucleic acid (RNA)  chronicity – no chronic state.  Hepatitis B:  spread – blood-borne, sexual transmission, vertical transmission  virus – DNA  chronicity – can progress to cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma.  Hepatitis C:

GIT & LIVER part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  spread – blood-borne, sexual transmission, vertical transmission  virus – RNA  chronicity – can progress to chronic hepatitis, cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma.  Hepatitis D:  spread – blood-borne (dependent on concurrent hepatitis B infection for replication)  virus – incomplete  chronicity – those with chronic hepatitis B have increased incidence of cirrhosis.  Hepatitis E:  spread – faecal–oral, vertical transmission  virus – RNA  chronicity – only in those severely immunocompromised.  Other viral infections can cause hepatitis:  Epstein–Barr virus  yellow fever  cytomegalovirus  rubella  herpes simplex. Pathophysiology  Hepatitis virus replicates in hepatocytes, interfering with cell function and causing liver inflammation, injury and wound healing.  Over time (for some viruses) this process may lead to fibrosis.  Clinical Presentation  Viral hepatitis infection may be asymptomatic, present acutely with fulminant liver failure or present after slow insidious progression to chronic hepatitis:  acute:  right upper quadrant pain, myalgia, fatigue, nausea and vomiting, diarrhoea  usually self-limiting, but a proportion of patients may develop fulminant liver failure with jaundice and confusion (hepatic encephalopathy).  chronic infection (hepatitis B and C):  several years after initial infection, patients develop signs of chronic liver disease, eg itch, abdominal swelling, spider naevi.  Hepatitis A:  fever  malaise  anorexia  nausea  arthralgia  jaundice.  Hepatitis B: G

DR. JAM  most people are asymptomatic  some may present with complications, eg:  cirrhosis  hepatocellular carcinoma  liver failure.  often resembles hepatitis A, although arthralgia and urticaria are much more common (prodromal illness).  Hepatitis C:  less severe than A or B  often asymptomatic  people who are chronically infected will experience nonspecific symptoms including malaise, weakness and anorexia.  Hepatitis E:  presentation similar to hepatitis A  self-limiting illness  however, acute hepatic failure is common in those who are pregnant.  Yellow discolouration of the sclera in a jaundiced patient:  Differential Diagnosis  Hepatitis caused by a number of different aetiologies, including:  autoimmunity  ischaemia  alcohol  genetics  other infections:  viruses:

GIT & LIVER part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Epstein–Barr virus (EBV)  yellow fever  cytomegalovirus  rubella  herpes simplex.  malaria  toxoplasmosis  brucellosis  leptospirosis.  Diagnosis/Investigation  In patients with suspected hepatitis, blood tests can be performed to exclude organ damage:  full blood count (FBC) – non-specific findings, eg neutrophilia, lymphocytosis, lymphopenia  LFTs – transaminitis seen in acute/chronic hepatitis and EBV infection  coagulation screen  serological testing is important in patients presenting with acute or chronic liver disease, as hepatitis B and C can progress to chronic infection and cancer and are widely treatable.  Further tests for individual diagnoses are listed below.  Hepatitis A:  hepatitis A serology:  checks for hepatitis A virus immunoglobulin M (HAVIgM) and hepatitis A virus immunoglobulin G (HAVIgG)  positive HAV-IgM and HAV-IgG means acute hepatitis A is likely  positive HAV-IgG and negative HAV-IgM indicates past hepatitis A or immunity from previous vaccination.  check liver function tests – alanine aminotransferase (ALT) and aspartate aminotransferase (AST) may be significantly increased (>1000 IU/l).  Hepatitis B:  hepatitis B serology:  hepatitis surface antigen (HBsAg) rises in current hepatitis B infection  after HBsAg is detected, hepatitis B e-antigen (HBeAg) and hepatitis B virus DNA (HBV-DNA) are detectable around the same time.  presence of HBsAg, HBeAg and HBV-DNA indicates progression to chronic hepatitis B  IgM anti-HBc indicates infection within the last 6 months  IgG anti-HBc persists for life and indicates past infection  anti-HBs without anti-HBc is a marker of immunisation.  Hepatitis C:  anti-HCV antibodies confirm exposure G

DR. JAM  HCV-PCR confirms ongoing infection.  Management Pharmacological and conservative management  Hepatitis A:  symptomatic supportive care for nausea, pain or itch  rest  if pain relief required suggest paracetamol/ibuprofen/weak opioid, eg codeine if mild liver impairment  nausea – metoclopramide or cyclizine  itch – maintain cool, well-ventilated environment, wear loose-clothing, avoid hot baths or showers or chlorphenamine  notify the Health Protection Unit for surveillance and contract tracing  avoid alcohol.  Hepatitis B:  symptomatic care as above  notify the Health Protection Unit  avoid alcohol  antivirals – pegylated interferon alpha-2a  or nucleotide analogues, eg tenofovir – not usually indicated for acute hepatitis B except in cases of fulminant hepatitis.  Hepatitis C:  notify Health Protection team  lifestyle advice:  stop alcohol consumption  stop smoking  maintain healthy body weight and diet.  acute hepatitis C  up to 45 percent of acute cases spontaneously clear without treatment within 6 months  if treatment is required, this should be the same regime as with chronic hepatitis C.  chronic hepatitis C:  antiviral therapy –direct-acting antivirals (DAAs) are now considered first-line treatment  the type will depend on the genotype of the infection  usually a once daily, oral tablet regimen for either 8 or 12 weeks  The goal of treatment is to eradicate the virus, achieve a sustained virological response (SVR) and prevent disease progression.  SVR (undetectable HCV RNA in the blood 12 weeks after treatment completion) is considered to be equivalent to a cure.  Hepatitis E:  no specific treatment

GIT & LIVER part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  self-limiting disease. Surgical management  Hepatitis may progress to end-stage liver disease.  Liver transplantation is the treatment of choice for patients with end-stage liver disease/decompensated cirrhosis.  Prognosis  Hepatitis A is usually self-limiting:  chronicity does not occur and < 1% of patients develop fulminant hepatitis.  In hepatitis B, there is a risk of extra-hepatic manifestations, eg:  glomerulonephritis  vasculitis  polyarteritis.  15–20% of chronic hepatitis B patients will develop cirrhosis.  In hepatitis C, 20–50% will clear the virus spontaneously without treatment.  50–80% will develop chronic hepatitis C. Whipple’s Disease  Whipple’s disease is a rare, chronic multisystem condition thought to be caused by a combination of infection with the gram-positive actinobacteria, Tropheryma whippelei, alongside an abnormal response of cell-mediated immunity.  Overview Key Facts  Whipple’s disease is a rare, chronic multisystem condition thought to be caused by a combination of infection with the gram-positive actinobacteria, Tropheryma whippelei, alongside an abnormal response of cell-mediated immunity.  Gastrointestinal symptoms include abdominal pain and distention, diarrhoea and steatorrea, anorexia, and weight loss.  Other associated symptoms include generalised lymphadenopathy, arthropathy, cough, and intermittent pyrexia.  As the condition progresses, there may be cardiac, respiratory, and central nervous system involvement.  Treatment is based on long term antibiotic therapy and should be guided by specialist advice.  Prognosis with treatment is good, however up to 40% of patients may relapse following initial successful treatment.  Untreated the condition is associated with insidious progression and eventual death. G

DR. JAM Epidemiology  It is a very uncommon condition, when it does occur it most often affects middle-aged and older men. Aetiology  Whipple’s disease is caused by an infection with the gram-positive actinobacteria, Tropheryma whippelei.  Infections can occur in family clusters which suggests an immunogenetic link.  There is an association with the HLA-B27 antigen.  A risk factor is agricultural working and those who work within sewage plants. Pathophysiology  Jejunal biopsy shows deposition of macrophages containing PASpositive granules within villi.  Deposition of macrophages from a duodenal biopsy in Whipple’s disease:  Clinical Presentation  Clinical presentations include:  abdominal pain  weight loss  diarrhoea  abdominal distention  steatorrhea and malabsorption  arthropathy – may be episodic  low grade and intermittent fever

GIT & LIVER part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  chronic cough  hyperpigmentation  generalised lymphadenopathy  endocarditis.  As the condition progresses, there may be:  anaemia  pleural effusions  cardiac involvement (valve disease, pericarditis)  central nervous system (CNS) involvement:  cognitive function abnormalities  oculomasticatory and oculofascioskeletal myorhythmia (rhythmic movement of masticatory and other skeletal muscles synchronised with ocular movements).  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnosis includes:  rheumatoid arthritis  sarcoidosis  coeliac disease  tropical sprue  HIV/AIDS  familial Mediterranean fever.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Gastroscopy to obtain small bowel biopsies.  Look for PAS-positive macrophages on histology.  Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) to identify bacterial DNA.  Immunohistochemistry: antibodies against Trophyma whipplei to detect antigens.  Management  The mainstay of management is antibiotic therapy which requires expert supervision.  An initial regimen may be:  14 days of ceftriaxone or benzylpenicillin  followed by a year of maintenance therapy with trimethoprim/ sulfamethoxazole.  Prognosis  Whipple’s disease usually resolves with treatment although consequences such as CNS and joint damage may be irreversible.  Relapse can occur in up to 40% of cases following initial successful treatment.  Without treatment, the condition will continue to progress and cause eventual death. G

DR. JAM Wilson’s Disease  Wilson’s disease is an inherited condition that is inherited in an autosomal-recessive fashion.  Overview Key Facts  Wilson’s disease is an inherited condition that is inherited in an autosomal-recessive fashion.  It is a rare inherited disorder, affecting 1 in 30 000 births.  The condition is caused by a mutation in the ATP7B gene which impairs copper incorporation into caeruloplasmina and copper excretion.  High levels of free copper, via oxidant damage, causes inflammation and cell injury resulting in hepatitis.  Continued exposure leads to fibrosis which can cause end-stage liver disease and hepatic failure.  Copper can also accumulate in basal ganglia causing central nervous system (CNS) signs and symptoms, and the iris (manifesting as Kayser-Fleischer rings).  Management involves lifelong avoidance of copper containing foods, as well as copper chelation with lifelongs penacillamine. End stage hepatic disease requires transplantation.  Untreated, the condition is progressive and fatal.  Siblings should be screened for the condition once the diagnosis is confirmed. Aetiology  Autosomal-recessive disease caused by mutations in the ATP7B gene.  Copper is incorporated into caeruloplasmin in the liver.  The gene product of ATP7B is involved in excess copper excretion in the bile.  In Wilson’s disease, copper incorporation into caeruloplasmin and excretion of copper into bile is impaired. Pathophysiology  Excess copper is initially stored in the liver.  High levels of free copper, via oxidant damage, causes inflammation and cell injury resulting in hepatitis.  Continued exposure leads to fibrosis, which progresses to endstage liver disease and hepatic failure.  Copper can also accumulate in basal ganglia and iris.  Clinical Presentation  Children typically present with hepatic features  hepatitis  chirosis  liver failure.

GIT & LIVER part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Adults more often present with:  CNS signs:  tremor  dysarthria  dysphagia  dementia  parkinsonism  ataxia/clumsiness.  Mood symptoms:  depression/mania  loss of libido  personality change.  Cognition defects:  decreased memory.  slow to solve problems.  decreased IQ.  Kayser-Fleischer rings: Copper deposition in iris.  Kayser-Fleischer ring:  Differential Diagnosis  Alpha-1 Antitrypsin deficiency.  Hemochromatosis.  Viral hepatitis B.  Viral hepatitis C.  Autoimmune hepatitis.  Steatohepatitis. G

DR. JAM  Alcoholic cirrhosis.  Essential tremor.  Parkinson disease.  Psychiatric diseases.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Liver function tests.  24 hour urine copper - increased.  Slit-lamp exam – shows sunflower cataracts.  Blood ceruloplasmin - reduced.  Management  Avoid high copper containing foods eg liver, chocolate, nuts, mushrooms.  Lifelong penicillamine is the mainstay of treatment.  Liver transplantation may be indicated with severe hepatic disease.  Siblings should also be screened for the condition.  Prognosis  Early, and then lifelong treatment has better prognosis.  Pre-cirrhotic liver disease is reversible.  Neurologic symptoms improve about 5-6 months’ post-treatment.  If untreated, Wilson’s is progressive and invariably fatal. 

stem: A 43-year-old man was referred to the Gastroenterology Clinic by his general practitioner. He complained of a long history of arthralgia, but more recently had begun to complain of diarrhoea, with up to eight semi-formed oily stools per day. He also described excessive abdominal cramps and bloating, accompanied by a general loss of appetite. Examination demonstrated signs of weight loss and anaemia, mild oedema and ascites, along with a pericardial rub heard on auscultation. A 72-h faecal fat collection revealed 10 g fat/ 24 h. Blood tests revealed a mixedpicture anaemia, along with hypocalcaemia, hypokalaemia and decreased serum albumin. Anti-gliadin and antiendomysial antibodies were negative. A small bowel follow-through study showed evidence of mucosal oedema. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Whipple’s disease
The diagnosis here is likely to be Whipple’s disease. This is an uncommon condition, but one that occurs slightly more commonly in men, peaking between the ages of 30 and 60 years. Whipple’s disease is now understood to be an infectious condition, with the causative organism being the bacterium Tropheryma whipplei. The condition typically generates symptoms in a number of organ systems, but particularly in the gastrointestinal (GI) tract, including malabsorptive diarrhoea; extra-intestinal manifesations of the condition include fever, arthralgia, serositis and neurological impairment (including ophthalmoplegia and cognitive changes). Diagnosis of the condition is based on biopsy of the small-intestinal lamina propria, which reveals infiltration by periodic acid– Schiff- (PAS-)positive macrophages containing Gram-positive bacilli. Standard therapy involves a prolonged period of treatment (typically several months) with co-trimoxazole, or a penicillin-, streptomycin- or tetracycline-based regimen.

Coeliac disease
Coeliac disease is incorrect. Coeliac disease could explain this man’s GI symptoms, but not the extra-intestinal features found on examination; furthermore, the negative anti-gliadin and anti-endomysial antibodies make this very unlikely.

Giardiasis
Giardiasis is incorrect. Giardiasis could explain this man’s diarrhoea, but not any of the other features of this man’s illness.

Laxative abuse
Laxative abuse is incorrect. The blood tests and small bowel follow-through study are very indicative of malabsorption; laxative abuse is not associated with these findings.

Ulcerative colitis.

stem: Which of the following are associated with this patient’s condition?
explanation:
Episcleritis
This patient has symptoms and investigations consistent with ulcerative colitis, an extra-intestinal feature of which is episcleritis, occurring in up to 4% of cases. Episcleritis causes redness and burning pain in the eye.

Addison’s disease
Addison’s disease is incorrect. This patient has symptoms and investigations consistent with ulcerative colitis; there is no known association between Addison’s disease and ulcerative colitis. However, a known extraintestinal complication of ulcerative colitis is episcleritis.

Erythema migrans
Erythema migrans is incorrect. Erythema migrans is a rash seen in the early stages of Lyme disease. This patient has symptoms and investigations consistent with ulcerative colitis, which is not associated with erythema migrans. Cutaneous associations of ulcerative colitis include pyoderma gangrenosum and erythema nodosum. Other extra-intestinal manifestations include episcleritis.

Gallstones
Gallstones is incorrect. This patient has symptoms and investigations consistent with ulcerative colitis. Only Crohn’s disease is associated with an increased risk of gallstones. Ulcerative colitis is associated with primary sclerosing cholangitis and cholangiocarcinoma. Other extra-intestinal associations include episcleritis.

stem: A 42-year-old man with chronic hepatitis C infection was being assessed in the liver clinic. Liver biopsy showed significant chronic inflammation with fibrotic change. He was being considered for combination therapy, including ribavirin, and underwent a baseline full blood count. Which of the haematological side-effects of ribavirin would be most likely to occur if he was on this treatment?
explanation:
Haemolytic anaemia
Haemolytic anaemia is a well-recognised potential side-effect of oral ribavirin, and is the correct answer here. Ribavirin inhibits the activity of a wide range of DNA and RNA viruses. It is currently licensed in inhaled form for the treatment of severe bronchiolitis caused by respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), and in oral form, in combination with interferon-alpha/novel direct-acting antivirals, for the treatment of hepatitis C infection. Aside from haemolytic anaemia, potential side-effects of ribavirin include nausea, vomiting, dry mouth and stomatitis. Other specific cautions and contraindications relating to its use include: Pregnancy – avoid treatment during pregnancy and for 6 months after delivery, and counsel men to use barrier contraception Cardiac disease Haemoglobinopathies Severe liver dysfunction Other cautions – autoimmune disease, previous psychiatric history Extensive monitoring (including renal function, liver function testing and full blood count) is recommended at weeks 2 and 4 of treatment. Treatment may need to be continued for 6–12 months (although a much shorter use). course of treatment is possible now that direct-acting antivirals against hepatitis C have more widespread

Microcytic anaemia
Microcytic anaemia is incorrect as haemolytic anaemia is by far the most common potential haematological complication with the use of oral ribavirin.

Neutrophilia
Neutrophilia is incorrect as haemolytic anaemia is by far the most common potential haematological complication with the use of oral ribavirin.

Thrombocythaemia
Thrombocythaemia is incorrect as haemolytic anaemia is by far the most common potential haematological complication with the use of oral ribavirin.

stem: Abdominal ultrasound reveals gallstones but no biliary duct dilatation. What is the most likely cause of his jaundice?
explanation:
Co-amoxiclav
Cholestatic/ mixed cholestatic and hepatitis liver injury can develop during co-amoxiclav therapy or shortly afterwards. Epidemiological studies put the risk of acute liver toxicity at about six times higher with coamoxiclav compared to amoxicillin therapy alone. Cholestatic liver injury occurs more commonly in patients aged over 65 years and it is more common in men; these reactions are rarer in children. The jaundice is usually self-limiting and is rarely fatal. The duration of co-amoxiclav therapy should be appropriate to the indication and not exceed 14 days on the advice of the Committee on Safety of Medicines. Rarer side-effects of co-amoxiclav include erythema multiforme, toxic epidermal necrolysis and exfoliative dermatitis.

Paracetamol
Paracetamol is incorrect. Used at the prescribed dose in the absence of hepatic disease, paracetamol is unlikely to cause significant hepatic dysfunction. This is in contrast to acute overdose.

Hepatitis B infection
Hepatitis B infection is incorrect. No risk factors are described for this man acquiring hepatitis B infection. Furthermore, hepatitis B causes a hepatitic liver injury, and would not explain why his alkaline phosphatase level was raised.

Hepatitis C infection
Hepatitis C infection is incorrect. No risk factors are described for this man acquiring hepatitis C infection. Furthermore, hepatitis C causes a hepatitic liver injury, and would not explain why his alkaline phosphatase level was raised.

stem: Which of the following conditions is associated with protein-losing enteropathy?
explanation:
Sarcoidosis
Sarcoidosis is another potential cause of protein losing enteropathy. Other causes include inflammatory bowel disease, pseudomembranous colitis, Cytomegalovirus (CMV) colitis, tuberculosis, and connective tissue diseases.

Amoebiasis
Amoebiasis is incorrect. Amoebiasis can be asymptomatic, or can cause bloody diarrhoea with mucus. However, it is not associated with a protein-losing enteropathy. Causes of protein-losing enteropathy include connective tissue diseases, pseudomembranous colitis, inflammatory bowel disease, tuberculosis, and sarcoidosis.

Cholera
Cholera is incorrect. Cholera causes a severe watery diarrhoea, but does not cause a protein-losing enteropathy. Causes of protein-losing enteropathy include connective tissue diseases, pseudomembranous colitis, inflammatory bowel disease, tuberculosis, and sarcoidosis.

Colonic carcinoid tumour
Colonic carcinoid tumour is incorrect. Carcinoid tumours can cause carcinoid syndrome, resulting in flushing, diarrhoea and wheezing. They are not associated with protein-losing enteropathy. Causes of protein-losing enteropathy include connective tissue diseases, pseudomembranous colitis, inflammatory bowel disease, tuberculosis, and sarcoidosis.

stem: A 56-year-old retired primary schoolteacher gave a 5-month history of pruritus and lethargy. She had a past medical history of Hashimoto’s thyroiditis. On examination she was jaundiced, had a palpable liver and a justpalpable spleen. She admitted to drinking two units of alcohol per day. Twenty-four hours after admission, she had haematemesis and her haemoglobin count dropped to 88 g/l. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy revealed oesophageal varices. Anti-mitochondrial antibodies were positive. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Primary biliary cholangitis
The answer is Primary biliary cholangitis (Option E). The presence of jaundice, splenomegaly and oesophageal varices is very suggestive of this woman having cirrhosis and portal hypertension. Anti-mitochondrial antibodies are a sensitive and specific test for primary biliary cholangitis (PBC; formerly known as primary biliary cirrhosis), making this the correct answer. PBC most typically occurs in middle-aged women, with pruritus and lethargy being the typical symptoms experienced by affected people. There is an association between PBC and a range of autoimmune disorders, including thyroid disease, sicca syndrome and certain rheumatological conditions (including systemic sclerosis).

Alcohol-related cirrhosis
Alcohol-related cirrhosis (Option A) is incorrect. This woman’s alcohol intake is within recommended safe limits, making alcohol-related cirrhosis unlikely to be correct.

Primary sclerosing cholangitis
Primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC) (Option B) is incorrect. PSC particularly occurs in people with a background of inflammatory bowel disease, which this woman does not appear to have. Furthermore, PSC is not associated with anti-mitochondrial antibodies; as such, PSC is unlikely to be the diagnosis.

Non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH)-related cirrhosis
Non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH)-related cirrhosis (Option C) is incorrect. NASH particularly occurs in people with other features of metabolic syndrome, including diabetes, obesity, dyslipidaemia and hypertension. This woman is not described as having any of these conditions, making this very unlikely to be the diagnosis.

stem: A 62-year-old man with a 7-year history of type 2 diabetes comes to the Gastroenterology Clinic for review following severe diarrhoea. He is taking a number of medications for diabetes, hypertension and cardiovascular protection. Investigations have revealed normal faecal fat excretion, but a selenium ( acid taurine (SeHCAT) test is positive. Routine bloods are unremarkable. Which of the following medications is the most likely cause this?
explanation:
Metformin
SeHCAT is the usual name for 23-seleno-25-homo-tauro-cholic acid (selenium homocholic acid taurine or tauroselcholic acid). The key here is in recognising that SeHCAT is a test for bile acid malabsorption, and that metformin can lead to increased bile acid excretion. This appears to be dose dependent, and patients are more likely to complain of diarrhea when the dose of metformin is increased too rapidly. Slow release preparations of metformin, versus the IR formulation may be associated with less diarrhoea.

Amlodipine
Amlodipine is incorrect. Diarrhoea is reported uncommonly in conjunction with amlodipine therapy and this is not associated with bile salt malabsorption.

Aspirin
Aspirin is incorrect. Non-steroidals such as aspirin may be associated with lymphocytic colitis.

Indapamide
Indapamide is incorrect. Diarrhoea was not seen with increased frequency in the indapamide clinical trial program.

stem: TPMT level was within normal limits. What is the most appropriate next treatment?
explanation:
Azathioprine
For people with Crohn’s disease who have had at least two exacerbations within 12 months requiring corticosteroids, the next most appropriate drug treatment from the options given is azathioprine. Azathioprine is a member of the thiopurine class of medications, with the other major member of this group being 6 mercaptopurine. Patients taking thiopurines need close monitoring for the potential complications associated with these medications, including myelosuppression, abnormal liver enzymes and/or pancreatitis. Before thiopurines may be commenced, assessment of the patient’s level of TPMT is required (thiopurine methyltransferase, ie an enzyme that metabolises the medication); patients that lack TPMT should not be given thiopurines, while those with low levels should be started on reduced doses. Although not listed here, another potential therapeutic option would be anti-TNF (tumour necrosis factor) therapy (i.e. infliximab or adalimumab). However, most clinicians would still only start anti-TNF therapy should the patient still be experiencing active Crohn’s disease despite use of a thiopurine and/or methotrexate. An exception to this would be fistulating Crohn’s disease, where anti-TNF therapy is often commenced early (i.e. following antibiotics and/or surgical drainage where appropriate).

Cyclophosphamide
Cyclophosphamide is incorrect. Cyclophosphamide has no role in the treatment of active Crohn’s disease.

Enteral nutrition
Enteral nutrition is incorrect. While enteral nutrition may be considered as an alternative to corticosteroids for the induction of remission in children and adults, it would not typically be considered for an exacerbation refractory to corticosteroids in adults.

Methotrexate
Methotrexate is incorrect. Methotrexate does have a role for treating active Crohn’s disease in adults that is refractory to corticosteroids, but is probably less effective than thiopurine medications. As such, most clinicians would only start methotrexate in those patients who had failed to respond to azathioprine or 6-mercaptopurine.

stem: Given the likely diagnosis, which of the following risk factors is the strongest predictor for the risk of progression to cirrhosis?

HBV DNA titre
This patient has jaundice and deranged liver function secondary to hepatitis B. HBV DNA viral load is the most important factor in determining the risk of progression to liver cirrhosis. The higher the viral load, the higher the risk of cirrhosis

Age at diagnosis
Age at diagnosis is incorrect. The age at diagnosis is irrelevant in determining the risk of progression to liver cirrhosis.

Genotype
Genotype is incorrect. HBV is divided into 8 genotypes’ (A-H). The genotype predicts response to treatment as well as the clinical course, but overall the viral load is a stronger predictor to progression to cirrhosis than genotype.

ALT level
ALT level is incorrect. The risk of liver cirrhosis is independent of the ALT level.

HBeAg status

stem: A 35-year-old office worker presented with a 5-month history of intermittent right-sided abdominal pain, watery but not bloody diarrhoea, intermittent vomiting and weight loss of 1 stone. On examination she had clubbing of the digits. Abdominal examination confirmed right-sided tenderness, and rectal examination was unremarkable. Her Hb was 111 g/l, WCC 9.8 × 10 9/l and CRP 15 mg/l (NR 0–10 mg/l). What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Small bowel Crohn's disease
The combination of abdominal pain, diarrhoea, significant weight loss and finger clubbing are together very suggestive of inflammatory bowel disease, particularly Crohn’s disease. Vomiting and right-sided abdominal pain are more suggestive of small bowel disease, with the absence of features of colonic disease (rectal bleeding, etc) implying that there is no large bowel involvement. In addition, finger clubbing is a wellrecognised feature of active small bowel Crohn’s disease.

Irritable bowel syndrome
Irritable bowel syndrome is incorrect. The combination of abdominal pain, diarrhoea, vomiting, significant weight loss and finger clubbing are together very suggestive of inflammatory bowel disease. Such significant weight loss and finger clubbing would not be found in irritable bowel syndrome.

Large bowel Crohn's disease
Large bowel Crohn's disease is incorrect. The combination of abdominal pain, diarrhoea, significant weight loss and finger clubbing are together very suggestive of inflammatory bowel disease, particularly Crohn’s disease. Vomiting and right-sided abdominal pain are more suggestive of small bowel disease, with the absence of features of colonic disease (rectal bleeding, etc) implying that there is no large bowel involvement. In addition, finger clubbing is a well-recognised feature of active small bowel Crohn’s disease.

Subacute appendicitis
Subacute appendicitis is incorrect. Even if appendicitis is subacute, this woman has had abdominal pain for much longer and experienced much more weight loss than would likely be expected were this the underlying diagnosis. Furthermore, appendicitis has no association with finger clubbing.

Ulcerative colitis
Ulcerative colitis is incorrect. If this woman had ulcerative colitis, it would be expected that she would have features of rectal disease, such as tenesmus and rectal bleeding. In the absence of these, ulcerative colitis is unlikely. Crohn’s.

stem: A 42-year-old man presents to the GP with indigestion and is sent for a breath test for Helicobacter which is found to be positive. Which of the following pathologies is most associated with H pylori infection?
explanation:
Duodenal ulcer
Case series suggest that almost all cases of duodenal ulceration are associated with Helicobacter pylori infection, (90%).

Gastric carcinoma
While H. pylori is associated with gastric carcinoma, it is less strongly associated with carcinoma than with duodenal or gastric ulceration.

Gastric ulcer
Although gastric ulceration is associated with H pylori, case series suggest that slightly less, (at around 80%), are associated with the bacterium.

Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GORD)
GORD is much more strongly linked to factors such as obesity, smoking and alcohol consumption.

Non-ulcer dyspepsia
The cause of non-ulcer dyspepsia is unclear; it is a functional disorder and may be related to disorders of gastric emptying or gastric accommodation. stem: A 43-year-old executive with right -sided abdominal pain was suspected of having gallstones. Which of the following is the strongest risk factor for gallstone disease?
options: A past history of a right hemicolectomy and ileal resection for Crohn's disease
Raised aspartate aminotransferase (AST) and alanine aminotransferase (ALT) levels
explanation:
A past history of a right hemicolectomy and ileal resection for Crohn's disease
The answer is A past history of a right hemicolectomy for Crohn’s disease (Option A). Cholesterol gallstones are thought to arise as a result of a triple defect: Supersaturation of gallbladder bile (high in cholesterol, low in bile salts) Increased rate of cholesterol nucleation in the gallbladder Reduction in gallbladder contractility Predisposing factors to gallstone formation include: Older age Female sex (related to the action of oestrogens) Oral contraceptive use (again, related to the action of oestrogens) Cirrhosis (associated with bile pigment stones rather than cholesterol stones) Ileal resection (by reducing enterohepatic circulation and increasing bile salt loss) Clofibrate (by increasing biliary supersaturation) Colestyramine (by binding bile salts) Crohn’s disease Although an increase in dietary cholesterol is a risk factor for gallstone disease, this is a much weaker risk factor than the combination of Crohn’s disease and previous ileal resection. As such, option A is the best answer here, and option B should be ruled out.

An increase in dietary cholesterol
An increase in dietary cholesterol (Option B) is incorrect. Although an increase in dietary cholesterol is a risk factor for gallstone disease, this is a much weaker risk factor than the combination of Crohn’s disease and previous ileal resection.

Irritable bowel syndrome
Irritable bowel syndrome (Option C) is incorrect. This is not recognised as a risk factor for gallstone disease.

Raised aspartate aminotransferase (AST) and alanine aminotransferase (ALT) levels
Raised aspartate aminotransferase (AST) and alanine aminotransferase (ALT) levels (Option D) is incorrect. There are many causes of raised transaminases, of which gallstone disease is just one option.

Thyrotoxicosis
Thyrotoxicosis (Option E) is incorrect. This is not recognised as a risk factor for gallstone disease and is therefore incorrect. Gallstones and.

stem: A 55-year-old mechanic presented with a 4-week history of tenesmus and rectal bleeding. His bowel habit had not changed significantly. Rectal examination revealed a granular mucosa and a sigmoidoscopy revealed touch bleeding on a background of diffuse erythema. Above 10 cm, the mucosa appeared to be normal. Rectal biopsies showed generalised mucosal inflammation with crypt abscesses. What would the most appropriate initial therapy be?
explanation:
Rectal mesalazine
The clinical, endoscopic and histological findings presented make it very likely that this man has the distal proctitis form of ulcerative colitis. The most appropriate initial medical therapy would be topical 5aminosalicylate (5-ASA) compounds, such as rectal mesalamine.

Oral mesalamine
Oral mesalamine is incorrect. The clinical, endoscopic and histological findings presented make it very likely that this man has the distal proctitis form of ulcerative colitis. While 5-aminosalicylate (5-ASA) compounds are the appropriate initial medications, these are more likely to be effective for proctitis when used topically rather than orally.

Oral prednisolone
Oral prednisolone is incorrect. The clinical, endoscopic and histological findings presented make it very likely that this man has the distal proctitis form of ulcerative colitis. Oral prednisolone is effective in treating this condition, but does not typically have as much efficacy as topical 5-aminosalicylate (5-ASA) compounds.

Oral sulfasalazine
Oral sulfasalazine is incorrect. The clinical, endoscopic and histological findings presented make it very likely that this man has the distal proctitis form of ulcerative colitis. Oral sulfasalazine does have efficacy in treating this, but not as much as its metabolite, 5-aminosalicylate (5-ASA). As such, 5-ASA compounds are preferred to sulfasalazine in this scenario.

Rectal steroids
Rectal steroids is incorrect. The clinical, endoscopic and histological findings presented make it very likely that this man has the distal proctitis form of ulcerative colitis. Rectal steroids are effective in treating this condition, but are typically not as effective as topical 5-aminosalicylate (5-ASA) compounds. stem: Which of the following represents the most likely site of obstruction?
explanation:
Distal common bile duct
The key to solving this question is the fact that both liver enzymes and amylase are elevated. This suggests any obstruction has occurred after the pancreatic duct joins the common bile duct, in other words in the distal portion of the duct. The most likely cause in an obese woman presenting with fever is a gall stone. Given the raised white count and fever she should be treated with antibiotics to cover cholangitis, and listed for endoscopic retrograde cholangio-pancreatography (ERCP), where it may well be possible to remove any stone during the procedure.

Cystic duct
Cystic duct is incorrect. The cystic duct joins the common bile duct before it is joined by the pancreatic duct, the fact that both amylase and LFTs are abnormal means the obstruction must be below the junction with the pancreatic duct.

Hepatic duct
Hepatic duct is incorrect. The hepatic joins the cystic duct to form the common bile duct, an obstruction of the hepatic duct would therefore only be expected to lead to abnormal liver function tests.

Pancreatic duct
Pancreatic duct is incorrect. Pancreatic duct obstruction leads to elevated amylase, but a marked elevation in liver function tests (LFTs) like that seen here wouldn’t be expected.

Proximal common bile duct
Proximal common bile duct is incorrect. Proximal common bile duct obstruction leads to abnormal liver function tests without a significant rise in amylase. Gallstones and.

stem: A 23-year-old woman developed severe watery diarrhoea 10 days after receiving both a quinolone and a cephalosporin following childbirth complicated by infection. She was unwell, with a temperature of 38 °C and pulse of 105 bpm, and she was very thirsty. On examination, there was widespread non-specific abdominal tenderness. A plain abdominal X-ray revealed gas throughout a non-dilated left-sided colon. Proctoscopy revealed an inflamed rectum. Stool cultures and histology were awaited. She was given intravenous fluids, but was still tachycardic and unwell. What would be the next most appropriate management step?
explanation:
Start vancomycin
The abnormal rectal mucosa seen on proctoscopy – together with the recent complicated childbirth, where antibiotics were prescribed – make Clostridioides difficile (pseudomembranous) colitis the most likely diagnosis. Vancomycin is the first-line treatment of choice for this condition.

Await further results
Await further results is incorrect because this woman is clearly unwell and merits empirical treatment for the presumed diagnosis.

Blood transfusion
Blood transfusion is incorrect. This woman’s fever, X-ray findings and proctoscopy all suggest that her tachycardia is caused principally through colitis, and a blood transfusion is unlikely to provide much benefit for this.

Start ciprofloxacin
Start ciprofloxacin is incorrect. It is unusual for bacterial causes of colitis other than C. difficile to cause a proctitis, and it is therefore unlikely that ciprofloxacin will provide much benefit.

Start hydrocortisone
Start hydrocortisone is incorrect. Although hydrocortisone would be the treatment of choice should the woman be having a flare of ulcerative colitis, the lack of any history of inflammatory bowel disease and/or any rectal bleeding makes it unlikely that this is the underlying diagnosis. stem: Which of the following is the most likely level of obstruction?
explanation:
Ampulla of Vater
The pancreatic duct joins the common bile duct at the level of the ampulla of Vater, and as such the elevated amylase is consistent with obstruction at this level. In this case the most appropriate option is progression to endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP), with sphincterotomy to allow for stone removal; otherwise there is increasing risk of biliary sepsis and acute pancreatitis.

Common bile duct
Common bile duct is incorrect. Obstruction within the common bile duct or higher would cause jaundice but not usually result in elevated amylase The common bile duct is formed from the union of the common hepatic cystic ducts.

Common hepatic duct
Common hepatic duct is incorrect. Obstruction in the common hepatic duct would not cause a raised amylase either, although it would cause jaundice. The common hepatic duct is formed by the convergence between the right and left hepatic ducts.

Cystic duct
Cystic duct is incorrect. The cystic duct joins the gallbladder to the common bile duct. Obstruction at this level would not cause a raised amylase.

Right hepatic duct
Right hepatic duct is incorrect. The right hepatic duct drains bile from the right side of the liver. Like the other options, it is not located close enough to the pancreas for the pancreatic amylase levels to be elevated in the event of an obstruction. Gallstones and.

stem: A 42-year-old woman was referred to the liver clinic by her general practitioner. She had undergone blood tests as part of a medical assessment at work, and these had shown a raised alanine aminotransferase (ALT) at 160 U/l (NR 5–35 U/l), but normal alkaline phosphatase (ALP), bilirubin, platelet count and prothrombin time. Her past history of note included obesity and gestational diabetes. She denied drinking any alcohol. The woman had had an admission with cholecystitis 2 years ago, although had not had any abdominal pain since. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD)
This question describes a typical scenario for non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD). NAFLD is believed to affect ~25% of the population of Western countries. The major risk factors are those of the metabolic syndrome, ie obesity, diabetes mellitus, hypertension and dyslipidaemia. The condition causes a range in severity of liver disease, ranging from simple steatosis alone to non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH) up to advanced liver fibrosis or even cirrhosis. The majority of people with the condition are asymptomatic; many are diagnosed after undergoing further investigation following the incidental finding of abnormal liver enzymes.

Autoimmune hepatitis
Autoimmune hepatitis is incorrect. Autoimmune hepatitis is a relatively rare condition, while NAFLD is understood to affect ~25% of the population. Her background of obesity and gestational diabetes means that she has two very strong risk factors for NAFLD. There is no positive autoantibody data that might support a diagnosis of autoimmune hepatitis; as such, this diagnosis is unlikely.

Primary biliary cholangitis (PBC)
Primary biliary cholangitis (PBC) is incorrect. Primary biliary cholangitis (PBC; formerly called ‘primary biliary cirrhosis’) is a cholestatic liver disease, so is associated with raised ALP but relatively normal ALT levels. Typical symptoms include lethargy and pruritus, while it appears that this woman is asymptomatic. Anti-mitochondrial antibody (AMA) is a sensitive and specific test for this condition.

Gallstones
Gallstones is incorrect. This woman has had cholecystitis in the past, she has not experienced abdominal pain since. As such, it is highly unlikely that her raised ALT is explained by gallstone disease.

Cirrhosis
Cirrhosis is incorrect. This woman would be unlikely to have a normal bilirubin, platelet count and prothrombin time if she had cirrhosis. Although her ALT is raised, liver enzymes are not a useful marker for the presence of advanced liver fibrosis/cirrhosis. Non-alcoholic.

stem: Which of the following medications is most useful with respect to prophylaxis against further GI bleeding?
explanation:
Propranolol
Propranolol is effective in reducing portal hypertension and is likely to impact significantly on risk of cirrhosis progression and hence also on risk of further variceal haemorrhage. Dose can be uptitrated to the maximum tolerated with respect to blood pressure, heart rate or sensation of pre-syncope.

Indapamide
Indapamide is incorrect. Thiazide like diuretics have much less impact on portal blood pressure than nonselective beta blockers, and so are not optimal here.

Omeprazole
Omeprazole is incorrect. Although omeprazole is effective for gastro-oesophageal reflux disease and peptic ulcer disease, it is has little effect on risk of bleeding from varices.

Ranitidine
Ranitidine is incorrect. Ranitidine is less effective than omeprazole even for managing peptic ulcer disease and is not an option here.

Spironolactone
Spironolactone is incorrect. Spironolactone is a useful intervention to reduce ascites, and is usually used in combination with propranolol. stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate antibiotic treatment for him?
explanation:
Intravenous ceftriaxone
Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP) is the development of a monomicrobial infection of ascites in the absence of a contiguous source of infection. The most common organisms that have been isolated include Escherichia coli, Gram-positive cocci (mainly Streptococcus species) and Enterococcus. This man has relatively severe bacterial peritonitis, with a raised systemic white cell count, pyrexia, renal impairment and significantly abnormal LFTs, and as such intravenous therapy with cefotaxime, ceftriaxone or ciprofloxacin (IV rather than oral) would be indicated.

Intravenous amoxicillin
Intravenous amoxicillin is incorrect. There is no role for amoxicillin in the management of SBP.

Oral ciprofloxacin
Oral ciprofloxacin is incorrect. Oral ciprofloxacin is reasonable to use in SBP when the patient is asymptomatic and well, which is not the case here.

Oral co-amoxiclav
Oral co-amoxiclav is incorrect. Oral co-amoxiclav is also an option when patients are asymptomatic and well.

Intravenous metronidazole
Intravenous metronidazole is incorrect. There is no role for metronidazole in the management of SBP. stem: A nursing-home resident was brought by his carers to the Emergency Department because they were concerned that he was finding it difficult to eat. His past history of note included the use of a corticosteroid inhaler for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. On examination of his oropharynx, there were several areas of erythema, and a number of white plaques accompanied by some white, curd-like material. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Oropharyngeal candidiasis
This man is in a nursing home and is using a corticosteroid inhaler for his chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. The likely explanation for his problems is that the combination of the use of a corticosteroid inhaler together with inadequate oral hygiene has allowed a Candida infection to take hold, making this option correct. The best treatment is to encourage mouth-swilling after using the inhaler, along with use of a nystatin mouthwash to get rid of the acute infection. It is worth noting that dentures can harbour Candida spp., so they should be soaked overnight in a dilute nystatin solution. Resistant infections can be treated with a short course of fluconazole.

Darier’s disease
Darier’s disease is incorrect. Darier’s disease is an uncommon inherited condition, in which small, pruritic, brown, wart-like lesions can develop over large areas of the skin; its presentation does not fit with that of this scenario.

Hairy leukoplakia
Hairy leukoplakia is incorrect. Hairy leukoplakia is caused by Epstein–Barr virus infection, and manifests as a white patch on the side of the tongue with a ‘hairy’ appearance that is difficult to remove; it Chat is particularly found with in people with severe immunodeficiency/immunosuppression, such as people with severe HIV infection/AIDS. The description of several different areas of white plaque with associated erythema is much more consistent with Candida than hairy leukoplakia.

Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection
Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection is incorrect. The description of several different areas of white plaque with associated erythema is much more consistent with Candida, while the lack of obvious risk factors for, or any clinical features specific for HIV infection helps to exclude this option.

Leukoedema
Leukoedema is incorrect. Leukoedema is a milky-coloured discoloration of the buccal mucosa that is completely benign, and does not generate plaques or erythema. stem: Which of the following other electrolyte abnormalities is likely to be present?
explanation:
Hypomagnesemia
This is the most common electrolyte abnormality seen in chronic alcoholism and occurs as a result of both malnutrition and alcohol-related diuresis. Alcoholics may often experience diarrhoea or steatorrhoea which can further exacerbate gastrointestinal (GI) losses. Hypomagnesaemia causes transient hypoparathyroidism, as magnesium is required for parathyroid hormone secretion. The reduction in circulating parathyroid hormone enhances renal excretion of magnesium. As a result of the transient hypoparathyroidism, hypomagnesaemia leads to abnormalities in calcium metabolism, ultimately resulting in hypocalcaemia. This normally resolves with adequate magnesium replacement. Magnesium also plays an important role in potassium regulation in the kidney, inhibiting channel efflux. Therefore, hypomagnesaemia will result in increased potassium excretion in the kidney, causing hypokalaemia. This is why in refractory hypokalaemia, magnesium should be checked and adequately replaced. Severe hypomagnesaemia requires IV replacement with magnesium salts. However, in most patients, oral replacement and avoidance of alcohol is adequate. Oral replacement is usually required for a period of time.

Hyperchloraemia
Hyperchloraemia is incorrect. Chloride is not typically affected by alcoholism.

Hyperphosphataemia
Hyperphosphataemia is incorrect. Hypophosphataemia is the second most common electrolyte abnormality seen in alcoholic patients after hypomagnesaemia. This is partly due to poor intake, as well as impaired phosphate reabsorption. This is a result of proximal tubular dysfunction.

Hypochloraemia
Hypochloraemia is incorrect. Chloride is not typically affected by alcoholism.

Hypouricaemia
Hypouricaemia is incorrect. Typically, hyperuricaemia is seen in alcoholism. Ethanol results in increased uric acid production and decreased excretion as a result of dehydration. She had a history of rheumatoid arthritis, which was managed with low-dose prednisolone, diclofenac and codeine phosphate. On examination in the Emergency Department, her blood pressure was 90/60 mmHg and her pulse 100 bpm; after fluid resuscitation, her blood pressure improved to 115/80 mmHg, with a pulse of 80 bpm.
