stem: A 29-year-old man is admitted with jaundice, drowsiness and ascites. On arrival in the Emergency Department his BP is 95/60 mmHg, with pulse 92/min and regular. His GCS is 13 and he is deeply jaundiced. His relatives report that he was found slumped in his flat, with three empty packets of paracetamol in his bedroom. Which of the following markers is used for prognosticating mortality in acute liver failure secondary to paracetamol overdose?
explanation:
Creatinine >300
The Kings College criteria are the most widely accepted tool for prognosticating patients that present with acute liver failure (ALF). Fulfilment of the criteria suggests a high mortality and a need for listing in the superurgent liver transplant list. They are not as reliable in the paediatric population. The criteria for ALF secondary to paracetamol overdose are: pH <7.3 or INR >6.5 and creatinine >300 and at least grade 3 hepatic encephalopathy. From the options above, the presence of a creatinine >300 is the most reliable predictor of mortality.

pH <7.35
pH <7.35 is incorrect. pH <7.3 and not <7.35 predicts poor outcome.

ALT >1000
ALT >1000 is incorrect. ALT levels are not used to predict outcomes in ALF.

INR >2.8
INR >2.8 is incorrect. INR >6.5 (and not >2.8) is used to prognosticate mortality in ALF.

Platelet count <20
Platelet count <20 is incorrect. Platelet levels are not used to predict outcomes in ALF. Drug-Induced.

stem: You review a 24-year-old woman who is noted to be markedly underweight. You suspect that she may have a protein malabsorption syndrome and contemplate trying her on an elemental diet. When thinking about dietary protein, which of the following best describes the site of amino acid absorption?
explanation:
The jejunum
Most absorption occurs in the jejunum after degradation in the duodenum by pancreatic proteases.

The caecum
The caecum is incorrect. The caecum is primarily the site for absorption of water, it is also the site of bacterial metabolism of free fatty acids, which may in turn have an impact on insulin receptors.

The proximal stomach
The proximal stomach is incorrect. Dietary protein is digested into polypeptides in the stomach by the acid environment and pepsin activity.

The distal stomach
The distal stomach is incorrect. The distal stomach is responsible for further digestion of dietary protein by stomach acid and pepsin activity.

The duodenum
The duodenum is incorrect. Polypeptides pass into the duodenum where they are degraded by pancreatic proteases but this is not the major site of absorption. Nutritional Assessment,.

stem: An 18-year-old man presented with acute hepatitis, nausea, jaundice, elevated transaminases and a prolonged prothrombin time. On examination, there were signs of chronic liver disease, and a brown-green ring at the periphery of the iris in both eyes. His serum copper level was low. What other laboratory findings would be expected?
options: High serum caeruloplasmin level and low urinary copper excretion
High serum uric acid level and high urinary copper excretion
High serum uric acid and low serum caeruloplasmin levels
Low serum caeruloplasmin level and low urinary copper excretion
Low serum uric acid level and high urinary copper excretion
explanation:
Low serum uric acid level and high urinary copper excretion
The diagnosis here is Wilson’s disease. This is a disorder of copper transport, caused through an autosomal recessive inheritance of a mutation in the ATP7B gene, which results in a defect in the incorporation of copper into caeruloplasmin. Pathologically, the condition is characterised by inadequate biliary copper excretion, leading to accumulation of copper in the liver, brain, kidneys and cornea. Clinically, the liver manifestations of the condition may present very variably, ranging from acute hepatitis/ acute liver failure through to cirrhosis. The description of a brown-green ring at the periphery of the iris is consistent with Kayser–Fleischer rings, which are copper deposits that occur in Descemet’s membrane in the cornea in people with the condition. Laboratory findings in Wilson’s disease include raised aspartate aminotransferase (AST), low caeruloplasmin, low serum copper, raised urinary copper excretion and low serum uric acid (also owing to increased urinary excretion). As such, this is the only option given that may be consistent with a diagnosis of Wilson’s disease. Aminoaciduria, glycosuria and calciuria also occur, with poor acidification of urine. The exact reason for these renal changes is unclear; although the Wilson’s gene is expressed in renal tissue, typically no specific histologic abnormalities are seen, and the renal problem appears to be functional.

High serum caeruloplasmin level and low urinary copper excretion
High serum caeruloplasmin level and low urinary copper excretion is incorrect. These findings are not consistent with the expected laboratory findings for Wilson’s disease.

High serum uric acid level and high urinary copper excretion
High serum uric acid level and high urinary copper excretion is incorrect. These findings are not consistent with the expected laboratory findings for Wilson’s disease.

High serum uric acid and low serum caeruloplasmin levels
High serum uric acid and low serum caeruloplasmin levels is incorrect. These findings are not consistent with the expected laboratory findings for Wilson’s disease.

Low serum caeruloplasmin level and low urinary copper excretion
Low serum caeruloplasmin level and low urinary copper excretion is incorrect. These findings are not consistent with the expected laboratory findings for Wilson’s disease. Wilson’s.

stem: Which treatment is most likely to help these patients’ symptoms?
explanation:
Cholestyramine
Moderate ileal resection can lead to bile salt malabsorption which commonly presents with watery diarrhoea. The diagnosis can be confirmed with a SEHCAT scan. Cholestyramine is the mainstay of treatment, and works by acting as a bile acid sequestrant. The absence of any abdominal pain or signs of inflammation count against active Crohn’s disease being the cause of her symptoms.

Oral steroids
Oral steroids is incorrect. Oral steroids would be of value if there was evidence of a moderate or severe relapse. However, the normal faecal calprotectin and inflammatory markers as well as absence of abdominal pain or systemic disturbance make this very unlikely.

Loperamide
Loperamide is incorrect. Loperamide is useful in reducing intestinal output/secretions secondary to a short bowel syndrome.

Metronidazole
Metronidazole is incorrect. Metronidazole is used in the management of small bowel bacterial overgrowth, which is a possibility here and can present with diarrhoea although other symptoms such as bloating and flatulence usually occur. Given the small bowel surgery, bile salt malabsorption remains the most likely cause.

Liquid or elemental diet
Liquid or elemental diet is incorrect. A liquid or elemental diet is used to downstage active small bowel disease in Crohn’s and has been shown to reduce inflammation. It is also used when there is severe stricturing disease that causes obstructive symptoms. Neither of these cases applies here. Crohn’s.

stem: A 58-year-old man complains of tiredness, fever, weight loss, arthralgia and diarrhoea. Jejunal biopsy reveals flattened mucosa that contains macrophages positive for periodic acid–Schiff (PAS). What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Whipple’s disease
This scenario is consistent with a diagnosis of Whipple’s disease. This is an uncommon disorder, caused by infection with is Tropheryma whipplei. It usually presents between 30-60 years of age, occurring more frequently in men. The condition may affect a number of different organ systems, causing features including gastrointestinal disease (e.g. malabsorptive diarrhoea), lymphadenopathy, arthritis, cardiac disease (e.g. pericarditis), ocular problems, and neurological complications (including dementia, ophthalmoplegia and myoclonus).

Coeliac disease
Coeliac disease is incorrect. The small bowel histology described is highly suggestive of Whipple’s disease; if this man had coeliac disease, it would be expected that histology from his small bowel would show partial villous atrophy and intraepithelial lymphocytes.

Tuberculosis
Tuberculosis is incorrect. Abdominal tuberculosis may cause a wide range of gastrointestinal and constitutional symptoms, so could be possible from the symptoms described. However, the histology described in this question is very typical of Whipple’s disease; if the diagnosis was tuberculosis, histology might be expected to show caseating granulomata and an inflammatory cell infiltrate.

Tropical sprue
Tropical sprue is incorrect. Tropical sprue may certainly cause chronic diarrhoea and weight loss, but extraintestinal symptoms (e.g. arthritis) are much less typical. There is no history given of travel to the tropics/ other regions where tropical sprue is commonly found. Small bowel histology in tropical sprue is very different from that described, typically demonstrating shortened villi, elongated crypts and a collection of different inflammatory cells.

Parasitic infection
Parasitic infection is incorrect. The histology of this man’s jejunal biopsy is very specific for Whipple’s disease, making it very unlikely that any other infection is responsible for his symptoms. Whipple’s.

stem: Colonoscopy with biopsies showed multiple areas of inflammation and punched-out ulcers; barium followthrough revealed evidence of severe small bowel inflammation. Given the likely diagnosis, which of the following is the biggest risk factor associated with the development of the disease?
explanation:
Smoking
The scenario described is very suggestive of Crohn’s disease, which appears to affect both the small and the large intestine. Smoking is a well-recognised risk factor for Crohn’s disease, and is thought to contribute by increasing the pro-inflammatory state of Crohn’s; Crohn’s disease may therefore after reducing/cessation of smoking.

Diet low in soluble fibre
Diet low in soluble fibre is incorrect. The scenario described is very suggestive of Crohn’s disease, which appears to affect both the small and the large intestine. While alteration in dietary fibre may affect the vulnerability to/severity of irritable bowel syndrome, it is not a risk factor for inflammatory bowel diseases such as Crohn’s disease.

Excess alcohol consumption
Excess alcohol consumption is incorrect. The scenario described is very suggestive of Crohn’s disease, which appears to affect both the small and the large intestine. Alcohol excess is not recognised as a risk factor for Crohn’s disease.

Increasing age
Increasing age is incorrect. The scenario described is very suggestive of Crohn’s disease, which appears to affect both the small and the large intestine. People with Crohn’s disease have a bimodal distribution, with peak ages of onset at 15–30 years and 60–80 years. However, the diagnosis can be made at any age, and only a small number of 23-year-olds have Crohn’s disease, so age is not a very strong risk factor.

Oral contraceptive use
Oral contraceptive use is incorrect. The scenario described is very suggestive of Crohn’s disease, which appears to affect both the small and the large intestine. The oral contraceptive pill is not recognised as a risk factor for Crohn’s disease. Crohn’s.

stem: A nurse was investigated following a needle-stick injury sustained while taking a blood sample from a patient infected with hepatitis B virus. The nurse’s vaccination record for hepatitis B was unknown. Which test would provide the earliest indication of acute hepatitis B infection in the nurse?
explanation:
HBsAg
HBsAg is the correct answer because it is the first virological marker detectable in the serum following hepatitis B infection. It typically becomes detectable approximately 4 weeks after exposure to the virus. The presence of HBsAg indicates an active hepatitis B infection, making it the earliest and most reliable marker for acute infection. Detecting HBsAg early allows for prompt medical intervention and monitoring, which is crucial for managing potential complications in the nurse.

Anti-HBe
Anti-HBe is a marker that appears later in the infection process. Anti-HBe is typically detected in serum several months after the initial exposure to hepatitis B. It indicates a lower level of viral replication and infectivity but is not useful for early detection of acute infection. Therefore, it would not provide the earliest indication of acute hepatitis B infection.

HBeAg
HBeAg is not the first marker to appear in serum following acute hepatitis B infection. HBeAg usually becomes detectable shortly after HBsAg but still later than HBsAg. This antigen indicates high levels of viral replication and infectivity, but its appearance is not early enough for the earliest detection. Hence, it is not the most suitable marker for early identification of acute infection.

IgG anti-HBc
IgG anti-HBc is not useful for early detection of acute hepatitis B infection. The presence of IgG anti-HBc usually indicates a past or resolved infection rather than an acute or recent one. This marker remains in the blood long after the initial infection has occurred, often persisting for life. Consequently, it does not provide timely information about a new acute infection.

IgM anti-HBc.

stem: A 19-year-old man is referred with tremors, difficulty speaking and forgetfulness. He is pale, mildly jaundiced, and has palmar erythema and telangiectasia on his anterior chest wall. He also has a postural tremor and dysarthria. What investigation is most likely to confirm the suspected diagnosis?
options: Computed tomography scan of the brain
Magnetic resonance imaging of the posterior cranial fossa
explanation:
Urinary copper level
This patient has a combination of liver disease and neurological signs. The diagnosis is Wilson’s disease. It is an autosomal recessive disorder and occurs worldwide. Wilson’s disease is characterised by abnormal copper metabolism, with the underlying metabolic problem being excessive tissue retention of copper. The urinary copper level is raised and the serum copper and caeruloplasmin levels are usually reduced. Diagnosis depends on measuring the amount of copper in the liver. A characteristic feature is the presence of corneal Kayser– Fleischer rings, which are due to copper deposition in Descemet’s membrane. Long-term treatment with penicillamine is effective in chelating copper.

Computed tomography scan of the brain
Computed tomography (CT) scan of the brain is incorrect. Abnormal brain imaging may be detected in those with Wilson’s disease, but none of these changes is sufficiently specific to help make the diagnosis of the condition.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the posterior cranial fossa
Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the posterior cranial fossa is incorrect. Abnormal brain imaging may be detected in those with Wilson’s disease, but none of these changes is sufficiently specific toChat helpwith make the diagnosis of the condition.

Serum α-fetoprotein assay
Serum α-fetoprotein assay is incorrect. Alpha-fetoprotein is a screen for hepatocellular carcinoma, an unlikely diagnosis in this 19-year-old man.

Serum iron studies
Serum iron studies is incorrect. Serum iron studies are an appropriate initial screen for people with suspected haemochromatosis, but are not helpful in the diagnosis of Wilson’s disease. Wilson’s.

stem: A 56-year-old man with severe exertional dyspnoea is admitted with jaundice and ascites. He has recently been diagnosed with COPD by his GP, although he insists that he only smokes occasional cigars. His father died of respiratory illness at 54 years of age. Bilirubin, aspartate transaminase (AST) and alkaline phosphatase levels are elevated and liver biopsy reveals the presence of periodic acid–Schiff- (PAS-) positive, diastaseresistant globules in periportal hepatocytes. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
α1-antitrypsin deficiency
The combination of liver disease, a COPD-like illness (despite a history of very light smoking), and a family history of lung disease together suggests a diagnosis of α1-antitrypsin deficiency. The liver biopsy appearance is also supportive of the diagnosis, with α1-antitrypsin deficiency pre-disposing to cirrhosis. Absolute avoidance of alcohol and cigarettes is crucial, and recombinant α1-antitrypsin may be considered for some patients.

Alcohol-related liver disease
Alcohol-related liver disease is incorrect. No history of alcohol consumption is described, and the liver histology is also inconsistent with alcohol-related liver disease.

Budd–Chiari syndrome
Budd–Chiari syndrome is incorrect. The absence of any description of hepatic venous outflow makes Budd– Chiari syndrome unlikely, and the personal and family history of lung disease would also not fit in with this diagnosis.

Cor pulmonale
Cor pulmonale is incorrect. Cor pulmonale may be associated with congestive liver disease and ascites, but the other details of this clinical scenario (along with liver histology results) do not fit with this as the diagnosis.

Haemochromatosis
Haemochromatosis is incorrect. Haemochromatosis similarly has no association with lung disease and is associated with liver histology demonstrating iron deposition. Alpha-1.

stem: A 26-year-old man was referred by his GP with episodic jaundice, but was otherwise well. He had no risk factors for viral hepatitis and no family history of liver disease. He drank 5–8 units of alcohol per week. Which feature would favour Gilbert syndrome as the cause?
explanation:
Unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia
Gilbert syndrome is a mild loss of glucuronosyltransferase activity, with an incidence of 5–7%. It shows an autosomal recessive inheritance pattern. The failure of conjugation results in an unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia. However, the bilirubin concentration is always less than 102 μmol/l. In itself, it has no significant sequelae. Episodes of jaundice are induced by fasting or by infection and are self-limiting. Crigler–Najjar syndrome is the second form of glucuronosyltransferase deficiency: Type I (autosomal recessive) results from the loss of both copies of the gene and causes death in early childhood if a transplant is not carried out. Type II (predeominantly autosomal recessive but can also be autosomal dominant) is the inherited loss of one gene, which causes a much milder illness with an unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia.

Abdominal pain
Abdominal pain is incorrect. Abdominal pain is not associated with Gilbert syndrome.

Clay-coloured stools
Clay-coloured stools is incorrect. Abdominal pain, clay-coloured stools and concomitant diabetes mellitus are not associated with Gilbert syndrome; abdominal pain and clay-coloured stools in combination with jaundice are suggestive of biliary obstruction, such as by gallstones.

Concomitant diabetes mellitus
Concomitant diabetes mellitus is incorrect. Concomitant diabetes mellitus is not associated with Gilbert syndrome.

Resolution of symptoms on fasting
Resolution of symptoms on fasting is incorrect. Fasting will precipitate jaundice rather than resolve it. JaundiceA 54-year-old man presented to the clinic with indigestion. He denied excessive alcohol intake, and was a nonsmoker. Past medical history of note included mild asthma, which was controlled with a low-dose Seretide® inhaler. On examination he looked well, his body mass index (BMI) was 31 kg/m 2 and his blood pressure was 142/80 mmHg; there was mild epigastric tenderness. Investigations.

stem: Which of the following statements about gastrin is true?
options: It is inhibited by pancreatic bicarbonate
It is produced from pancreatic A-cells
It is produced from pancreatic B-cells
It is secreted by the parietal cells in the stomach
Release is triggered by gastrointestinal luminal peptides
explanation:
Release is triggered by gastrointestinal luminal peptides
Gastrointestinal luminal peptides are a typical trigger of gastrin release. Other triggers to its release include stomach distension, vagal stimulation and hypercalcaemia.

It is inhibited by pancreatic bicarbonate
It is inhibited by pancreatic bicarbonate is incorrect. Gastrin’s role is to stimulate parietal cells in the stomach to secrete gastric acid and to stimulate the secretion of pepsinogen by chief cells; it is under negative feedback, so release is inhibited by increased acidity. Therefore, this option is incorrect, as acid (rather than alkali) inhibits gastrin release.

It is produced from pancreatic A-cells
It is produced from pancreatic A-cells is incorrect. Gastrin is produced by G-cells in the duodenum and in the pyloric antrum of the stomach.

It is produced from pancreatic B-cells
It is produced from pancreatic B-cells is incorrect. Gastrin is produced by G-cells in the duodenum and in the pyloric antrum of the stomach.

It is secreted by the parietal cells in the stomach
It is secreted by the parietal cells in the stomach is incorrect. Gastrin is produced by G-cells in the duodenum and in the pyloric antrum of the stomach. However, gastrin functions by stimulating parietal cells to secrete gastric acid. In a patient with recurrent duodenal ulceration, a finding of high levels of gastrin raises the possibility of Zollinger–Ellison syndrome (due to a gastrinoma). He has persistent left upper quadrant and epigastric pain, intermittent nausea and vomiting and a fever with temperatures up to 38.4 °C. His blood pressure is 123/82 mmHg; pulse is 90 bpm and regular. There is a mass in the epigastrium. Investigations.

stem: A 56-year-old man referred with abnormal blood biochemistry was found to be positive for hepatitis C virus (HCV) antibody. Which of the following treatment options is most likely to be beneficial?
explanation:
Simepravir and sofosbuvir
The next test would be required for this man would be a hepatitis C RNA level; this will help distinguish if he is one of the small number of people who spontaneously clear hepatitis C (who will have undetectable hepatitis C RNA levels), as opposed to the larger number who develop chronic infection. Before consideration of treatment, he will need further tests to establish which genotype of infection he has, and what degree of liver disease he has. Staging of liver disease was conventionally done with a liver biopsy, but non-invasive modalities are becoming increasingly available. Hepatitis C treatment has undergone an explosion in the past few years, with a huge range of very effective new direct-acting anti-virals arriving on the market. These are replacing/supplementing pegylated interferon and ribavirin, which were until recently the reference standard of therapy. Simepravir and sofosbuvir are examples of direct-acting anti-virals with activity against hepatitis C that may be used together as therapy for the condition.

Aciclovir and foscarnet
Aciclovir and foscarnet is incorrect. Aciclovir and foscarnet are used to treat herpesviruses, including CMV.

Emtricitabine and tenofovir
Emtricitabine and tenofovir of Tutor Emtricitabine and tenofovir is incorrect. Emtricitabine and tenofovir are used together as a component HIV therapy, with tenofovir also used as monotherapy, as a treatment of chronic hepatitis B.

Entecavir
Entecavir is incorrect. Similarly, entecavir may also be used as monotherapy for chronic hepatitis B.

Oseltamivir
Oseltamivir is incorrect. Oseltamivir is used to treat influenza. On examination his BP is 100/70 mmHg and pulse 105 bpm with atrial fibrillation. There is generalised abdominal distension and tenderness, with sluggish bowel sounds; an abdominal radiograph shows mildly dilated small bowel loops. Investigations show.

stem: A 51-year-old man presented to his general practitioner complaining of tiredness. He had no history of alcohol excess and took no medication. There had been a history of intermittent bloody diarrhoea over the past few years. His general practitioner noticed that his alkaline phosphatase level was raised, and that his antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA) was positive. He was then referred for a gastroenterological opinion. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Primary sclerosing cholangitis
The combination of a history of bloody diarrhoea, cholestatic liver enzymes and positive ANCA is collectively suggestive of underlying inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) complicated by primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC). PSC occurs more commonly in men, and IBD is strongly associated with the condition.

Alcohol-related cirrhosis
Alcohol-related cirrhosis is incorrect. In the absence of an alcohol history, alcohol-related cirrhosis is unlikely.

Familial hypercholesterolaemia
Familial hypercholesterolaemia is incorrect. Familial hypercholesterolaemia is not associated with any of the clinical features described in this scenario.

Haemochromatosis
Haemochromatosis is incorrect. Haemochromatosis may manifest with very variable liver enzymes but does not have an association with either IBD or a positive ANCA, making this unlikely.

Primary biliary cholangitis
Primary biliary cholangitis is incorrect. Primary biliary cholangitis is characterised by cholestatic liver enzymes but does not have an association with either IBD or a positive ANCA, making this unlikely. Primary Sclerosing Cholangitis An elderly man – who underwent an emergency partial gastrectomy 9 months ago – was referred by his general practitioner with symptoms of abdominal bloating, mild abdominal distension, flatulence and intermittent diarrhoea. On examination he looked pale, his blood pressure was 135/70 mmHg, and his pulse was 85 bpm and regular. General examination was unremarkable apart from a midline scar consistent with his partial gastrectomy. Investigations.

stem: A 35-year-old man presented with jaundice. The underlying cause was suspected to be acute hepatitis B infection. Which immunological test would most support the diagnosis of acute hepatitis B infection?
explanation:
IgM anti-HBc
A positive IgM anti-HBc result can only be explained by acute hepatitis B infection or with low levels in flares of chronic disease. It is among the earliest serological markers that may be detected after exposure to hepatitis B.

Anti-HBe
Anti-HBe is incorrect. Anti-HBe appears after the disappearance of HBeAg, with its presence consistent with reduced viral replication and decreased infectivity. Consequently, although anti-HBe is also a useful indicator of immunological control of chronic hepatitis B infection, it is not useful for assessing acute disease.

HBeAg
HBeAg is incorrect. HBeAg appears shortly after the appearance of HBsAg. Its principal clinical usefulness is as an indicator of relative infectivity, and its presence suggests viral replication. As such, HBeAg testing is useful during follow-up of chronic infection, but it is not a sensitive marker for acute infection.

HBsAg
HBsAg is incorrect. The presence of HBsAg indicates an infection with hepatitis B, but does not indicate the timeframe over which it has occurred; in fact, HBsAg that is detectable within blood for more than 6 months is the definition of chronic hepatitis B infection.

HBV DNA
HBV DNA is incorrect. Hepatitis B DNA levels are detectable soon after acute infection, but they are not a useful marker of stage of disease, as hepatitis B DNA is also detectable in chronic infection. She said that this was associated with retrosternal chest pain, and that she tended to regurgitate both liquids and solids. There had been gradual weight loss; otherwise, she felt well and had no significant past medical history. On examination she looked well: her blood pressure was 142/84 mmHg, she had no lymphadenopathy, abdominal examination was normal and her body mass index (BMI) was 27 kg/m 2. Investigations.

stem: A 59-year-old, otherwise fit man undergoes endoscopic follow-up for Barrett’s disease of the oesophagus. His latest biopsy shows poorly differentiated cells. Which of the following is the best management option?
options: Continue the maintenance dose of a proton-pump inhibitor and follow up every 3 months with
Give an increased dose of a proton-pump inhibitor and annual Barrett’s surveillance
explanation:
Repeat endoscopy and biopsies immediately
The major risk factor of Barrett's oesophagus is transformation to adenocarcinoma of the oesophagus. All patients with the condition must undergo regular endoscopies and biopsies to monitor dysplasia. Histology at biopsy Endoscopy frequency No dysplasia Every 2 - 5 years Low-grade dysplasia Every 6 months Repeat endoscopy with quadrantic biopsies every 1cm. High-grade dysplasia Every 3 months If a visible lesion is present,consider endoscopic ablation with mucosal resection (EMR) or radiofrequency ablation. Actions The most appropriate next step would be an immediate repeat endoscopy and biopsies. In cases of Barrett's oesophagus, which shows dysplasia, endoscopy should be repeated as soon as feasible if four-quadrant biopsy specimens were not obtained at 1 cm intervals or if there were any mucosal irregularities that were not removed with endoscopic resection. Endoscopic mucosal resection of mucosal irregularities is required to assess the grade of dysplasia accurately. Endoscopists who do not perform endoscopic mucosal resection should refer patients with Chat mucosal with irregularities to speciality centres for that procedure prior to proceeding with endoscopic eradication therapy. If biopsies again show poorly differentiated cells, then an evaluation for oesophagectomy would be required. This is because the presence of poorly differentiated cells is very suggestive of the presence of a possible oesophageal malignancy.

Continue the maintenance dose of a proton-pump inhibitor and follow up every 3 months with
Continue the maintenance dose of a proton-pump inhibitor and follow up every 3 months with focused biopsies Continue the maintenance dose of a PPI and follow up every 3 months with focused biopsies is incorrect. Although continuing the dose of PPI and close endoscopic surveillance may be appropriate if the histology from a repeat endoscopy/biopsy is negative, the presence of poorly differentiated cells should be sufficiently suspicious of possible malignancy to merit immediately repeating the endoscopy.

Give an increased dose of a proton-pump inhibitor and annual Barrett’s surveillance
Give an increased dose of a proton-pump inhibitor (PPI) and annual Barrett’s surveillance is incorrect. Although increasing the dose of PPI and close endoscopic surveillance may be appropriate if the histology from a repeat endoscopy/biopsy is negative, the presence of poorly differentiated cells should be sufficiently suspicious of possible malignancy to merit immediately repeating the endoscopy.

Refer for oesophagectomy
Refer for oesophagectomy is incorrect. Oesophagectomy is a major operation with significant associated morbidity and mortality, so would only be considered in people who unequivocally have histologically confirmed oesophageal cancer; thus it is an inappropriate option at this stage.

Refer for photodynamic therapy
Refer for photodynamic therapy is incorrect. Photodynamic therapy has a limited role in treating flat high-grade dysplasia of the oesophagus, but would require confirmatory histology before even being considered. stem: A 72-year-old man presents with left-sided lower abdominal pain. He describes a dislike of high-fibre foods, with a history of poor diet. The pain has been intermittent for the past couple of weeks and is partially relieved by defecation. He also suffers from intermittent diarrhoea. Blood testing demonstrates neutrophilia and microcytic anaemia. Barium enema shows multiple diverticulae, more marked on the left-hand side of the colon. He is otherwise fit and well and has no past medical history to note. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Diverticular disease
The combination of left-sided lower abdominal pain, raised inflammatory markers and microcytic anaemia in an older person with the imaging findings described together suggests diverticulosis complicated by diverticulitis as the underlying diagnosis. The incidence of diverticular disease in the general population is said to be as high as 35–50%. The condition is particularly common in Western countries, affecting more than 50% of the over-70 age group. The diagnosis of diverticular disease (and its complications) is via imaging, with endoscopy, contrast studies and cross-sectional imaging (i.e. computed tomography (CT) abdomen and pelvis with contrast) all having a potential contributory role. Management of the condition is as follows: For diverticulosis, an increased water and fibre intake is recommended to reduce intracolonic pressure, and therefore also the risk of further diverticulae developing. Acute diverticulitis is usually managed conservatively with intravenous antibiotics, such as ciprofloxacin, metronidazole, or co-amoxiclav. Only in the most severe cases – such as those where perforation has occurred – is surgical intervention appropriate (e.g. Hartmann’s procedure). Occasionally, a diverticular abscess forms, which usually requires radiological drainage and/ or surgical intervention. It has been reported that up to 30% of patients with diverticulitis will Chat eventually require with some form of surgical intervention.

Irritable bowel syndrome
Irritable bowel syndrome is incorrect. The features described of abdominal pain easing with defaecation and diarrhoea could both be found in irritable bowel syndrome; however, the neutrophilia and microcytic anaemia are not consistent with this diagnosis.

Ischaemic colitis
Ischaemic colitis is incorrect. Ischaemic colitis typically occurs in people with risk factors for cardiovascular disease, cardiac arrhythmia, or those who have been significantly hypotensive for a period of time and hypoperfused their colonic vasculature; none of those risk factors appears to apply here, making ischaemic colitis less likely than diverticular disease in this scenario.

Lactose intolerance
Lactose intolerance is incorrect. Abdominal discomfort and diarrhoea are both common features of lactose intolerance, but raised inflammatory markers and anaemia are not.

Ulcerative colitis
Ulcerative colitis is incorrect. Although this man’s symptoms and blood test results may fit with ulcerative colitis, he is somewhat older than people with ulcerative colitis typically first present, and would also be expected to have bloody diarrhoea were this the underlying diagnosis.

stem: A 22-year-old woman attends the Gastroenterology Clinic with her mother. She has apparently been starving herself over the past few months, and her family are deeply concerned that she is severely malnourished. She had on and off episodes of vomiting. She has no past medical history of note, although she tells you she has not had a period for approximately 5 months. On examination her BP is 95/60 mmHg; pulse is 70/min and regular. There is no postural drop. Her abdomen is soft and nontender; her BMI is signiﬁcantly reduced at 18.5. You notice an extensive covering of ﬁne hairs on her arms and legs. Which of the following is the most useful pointer towards malnutrition?
explanation: A Hypokalaemia Hypokalaemia is the most common electrolyte abnormality in anorexia nervosa. This may occur as a result of vomiting or laxative abuse. D Haemoglobin Haemoglobin is incorrect because poor nutrition per se may not lead to a fall in haemoglobin, a number of alternative causes including inﬂammation, haemolysis etc may be responsible. B ALT ALT, is incorrect because transaminases may be elevated for a number of reasons apart from malnutrition, including inﬂammation, infection and fatty inﬁltration (which is seen in states of excess rather than reduced nutrition). C Creatinine Creatinine, is incorrect because whilst creatinine level may be related muscle mass, levels can be altered by changes in renal function. E Urea Urea, is incorrect, it is signiﬁcantly altered by ﬂuid status and is therefore an unreliable marker of nutritional status versus albumin.

stem: A 27-year-old woman who had previously undergone a terminal ileal and limited right-colon resection for Crohn’s disease was seen in the clinic. She reported increased diarrhoea but was otherwise well. Investigations showed: C-reactive protein (CRP) < 5 μg/dl, haemoglobin 132 g/l, white cell count (WCC) 8.6 × 109/l, platelets 244 × 109/l. Repeat colonoscopy was normal to the neoterminal ileum; a barium follow-through showed a normal mucosa; and a lactose hydrogen breath test was normal. What is the most likely cause of her diarrhoea?
explanation:
Bile-salt malabsorption
This is a classic scenario for bile-salt malabsorption, which causes a secretory diarrhoea. This is because bilesalt metabolism is usually via the enterohepatic circulation, being reabsorbed in the terminal ileum. After resection of the terminal ileum, these bile salt salts will no longer be re-absorbed, so enter the colon where they irritate the mucosal lining (causing water secretion into the lumen) and affect gut motility, together resulting in diarrhoea. There is a theoretical risk of failure of absorption of fat-soluble vitamins, but this rarely becomes clinically significant. Treatment is with bile-salt sequestrants (binders), such as cholestyramine.

Collagenous colitis
Collagenous colitis is incorrect. Collagenous colitis is a cause of diarrhoea that is pathologically defined by a thickening of the subepithelial collagen band, and may occur in association with coeliac disease; thisAIisTutor diagnosed histologically, typically in people being investigated for diarrhoea with a macroscopically normal colonoscopy but who have had biopsies taken.

Mesalazine
Mesalazine is incorrect. Mesalazine may cause an increase in bowel frequency, but rarely causes true diarrhoea.

Primary sclerosing cholangitis
Primary sclerosing cholangitis is incorrect. No information is given on this woman’s liver blood tests or biliary tree imaging, so there is nothing to support her having primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC); furthermore, PSC is not associated with diarrhoea.

Small-bowel bacterial overgrowth
Small-bowel bacterial overgrowth is incorrect. Small-bowel bacterial overgrowth is rare but may occur after intestinal surgery (although the lack of an early peak on the breath test counts against this).

stem: A 27-year-old man was referred with a 10-week history of worsening diarrhoea. On review, he was opening his bowels 11 times per day and had blood mixed in with the stools. Full blood count showed Hb of 109 g/l. The problem had worsened over the past few days, and he was now suffering from severe abdominal pain and distension. He had a negative stool sample sent one month earlier. Which of the following is the first-line investigation to request?
options: Computed tomography of the abdomen and pelvis
explanation:
Computed tomography of the abdomen and pelvis
This man has acute severe colitis, which is characterised in the Truelove and Witts criteria by the following features: Fever of > 37.8 °C Bowels open more than six times per day, with blood Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) > 30 mm in 1 hour Pulse > 90 bpm. The key diagnosis to evaluate for complications of severe colitis including toxic megacolon, bowel perforation, and abscess formation. The information from this investigation will help inform the degree of involvement from the general surgeons. Causes of toxic megacolon include: Ulcerative colitis Crohn’s colitis Pseudomembranous colitis (Clostridium difficile infection). Chatspp.). with Dysenteric illnesses (ie enteroinvasive and enterohaemorrhagic Escherichia coli, Shigella

Barium Enema
Barium enema is incorrect. When barium enemas are used in people with chronic ulcerative colitis, a ‘lead pipe’ appearance is typically found (i.e. complete loss of haustral markings in the wall of the affected colon); however, it would not be safe to perform a barium enema with someone as acutely unwell as this man because of the risk of perforation.

Ultrasound scan of the abdomen
Whilst ultrasound can be useful for some differentials of the acute abdomen, namely acute appendicitis, cholecystitis and ascending cholangitis, it has no role in the investigation of acute severe colitis.

Flexible sigmoidoscopy
Flexible sigmoidoscopy is incorrect. Flexible sigmoidoscopy is useful for evaluating the degree of colitis and in obtaining histology to confirm the diagnosis. However, it must be performed with considerable care in severe colitis, as the bowel wall will be inflamed and friable and therefore at increased risk of perforation.

Stool microscopy
Stool microscopy is incorrect. Although stool microscopy is clearly warranted to assess for this man having an infective component to his colitis, the first-line intervention should still be to assess for the aforementioned complications, given the seriousness of this finding, if present.

stem: Biopsy of a suspicious area in the stomach showed a low-grade mucosal-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT) lymphoma with evidence of Helicobacter pylori. Which of the following is the most appropriate management for this patient?
explanation:
Helicobacter pylori eradication
More than 90% of gastric MALT lymphomas are associated with H. pylori infection, and H. pylori eradication is associated with regression of the lymphoma in up to 80% of cases. Genotyping to look for the Chatt(11;18) with (q21;q21) translocation can help predict response to therapy, with the presence of this translocation indicating a poorer response to H. pylori eradication.

Gastrectomy
Gastrectomy is incorrect. Gastrectomy is reserved for when gastric MALTomas are causing very severe complications, such as refractory gastrointestinal bleeding, gastrointestinal tract obstruction and/or perforation.

Long-term omeprazole therapy
Long-term omeprazole therapy is incorrect. Proton pump inhibitor may provide some symptomatic benefit, but it does not treat the MALToma specifically, and therefore will not stop it from potentially growing in size.

Oral imatinib
Oral imatinib is incorrect. More than 90% of gastric MALT lymphomas are associated with Helicobacter pylori infection, and H. pylori eradication is associated with regression of the lymphoma in up to 80% of cases; as such, this is the mainstay of management of small/early MALT lymphomas. However, imatinib may have a role in management of the condition. Specifically, where MALT lymphomas are large/later-stage, then combination chemotherapy, together with the addition of biological agents such as imatinib or rituximab, with or without limited radiotherapy, is often sufficient to achieve remission.

Partial gastrectomy
Partial gastrectomy is incorrect. Partial gastrectomy is reserved for where gastric MALTomas are causing very severe complications, such as refractory gastrointestinal bleeding, gastrointestinal tract obstruction and/or perforation.

stem: A 25-year-old man is admitted with cerebellar ataxia and abnormal liver biochemistry. He is suspected to have Wilson’s disease. Which finding is most typical of Wilson’s disease?
options: Onset of symptoms usually between 10 and 25 years
The absence of a Kayser–Fleischer ring
explanation:
Onset of symptoms usually between 10 and 25 years
Wilson’s disease has a genetic origin, occurring because of a mutation in the ATP7B gene (inherited in an autosomal recessive manner). The result is defective cellular transport of copper, and consequent copper deposition in organs throughout the body, including the liver and nervous system. The onset of symptoms is typically between 10 and 25 years, although clinical manifestations may first occur at any point between early childhood and late adulthood.

A poor prognosis with treatment
A poor prognosis with treatment is incorrect. Removal of copper from the body by a chelating agent such as penicillamine has greatly improved the prognosis of the condition, so patients now lead a normal lifeAIand expect Tutor a normal life expectancy. Alternatives to penicillamine include trientene and zinc acetate.

A raised serum copper level
A raised serum copper level is incorrect. The intracellular accumulation of copper in Wilson’s disease is associated with low serum concentrations of copper and of the copper-containing protein, caeruloplasmin; urinary excretion of the metal is high in most patients with the condition.

Bilateral upper motor neurone signs
Bilateral upper motor neurone signs is incorrect. Neurological signs in Wilson’s disease are most often owing to involvement of the cerebellar and basal ganglia. As such, movement disorders (eg tremor/Parkinsonism, ataxia) are common. Neurobehavioural manifestations (such as cognitive impairment) are also well recognised. However, pyramidal tract involvement is not typical, and bilateral upper motor neurone signs are not suggestive of Wilson’s. Wilson’s Disease

The absence of a Kayser–Fleischer ring
The absence of a Kayser–Fleischer ring is incorrect. Kayser–Fleischer rings are brown-/green-coloured depositions of copper within Descemet’s membrane in the cornea, and may be identified via slit lamp examination. These are found in > 90% of people with Wilson’s disease who have neurological involvement; given that this man has cerebellar ataxia, this makes the absence of a Kayser–Fleischer ring incorrect here. The liver manifestations of Wilson’s disease are very widely variable, ranging from asymptomatic abnormalities in liver enzmyes, to more severe manifestations including acute liver failure or advanced cirrhosis.

stem: A 24-year-old woman was referred with abdominal pain, diarrhoea and weight loss. On examination, she had an itchy blistering rash on both elbows. Investigations revealed haemoglobin of 103 g/l and mean corpuscular volume (MCV) 71 fl. What is the most appropriate diagnostic test?
explanation:
Endoscopy and duodenal biopsy
The history is that of coeliac disease and the description given of the rash is typical for dermatitis herpetiformis. Dermatitis herpetiformis is the skin manifestation of gluten sensitivity, and 70–80% of patients with dermatitis herpetiformis will have coexisting coeliac disease. In the UK, 1 in 300 patients have clinical evidence of the disease, with 1 in 200 having positive coeliac serology. Some 50% of patients are iron-deficient at presentation. Anti-endomysial IgA, anti-gliadin IgG, anti-reticulin IgM (or IgG) and anti-tissue transglutaminase IgG antibodies are used in the detection of coeliac disease. Of these, anti-endomysial IgA and tissue transglutamase are the most commonly used, as they are both sensitive and specific. However, 10% of patients with coeliac disease are IgA-deficient and therefore give a false-negative result. The definitive test is a duodenal biopsy; healing would be seen on biopsies taken after instigation of a gluten-free diet.

Barium meal and follow-through
Barium meal and follow-through is incorrect. A barium meal and follow-through would be aChat helpful test in with looking for features of suspected small bowel Crohn’s disease (eg strictures), but is unlikely to be useful here.

Crosbie capsule jejunal biopsy
Crosbie capsule jejunal biopsy is incorrect. Crosbie capsules are no longer used so would be an inappropriate choice here.

Skin biopsy of the rash
Skin biopsy of the rash is incorrect. A skin biopsy may help confirm the diagnosis of dermatitis herpetiformis, but confirmation of a diagnosis of coeliac disease requires a duodenal biopsy.

Ultrasound of the pancreas
Ultrasound of the pancreas is incorrect. Ultrasound of the pancreas may be useful if it was suspected that this woman’s diarrhoea and weight loss was caused by malabsorption secondary to pancreatic disease. However, no risk factors for pancreatic disease are given, and the description provided of dermatitis herpetiformis means that the diagnosis is much more likely to be coeliac disease than pancreatic insufficiency.

stem: The result of a hydrogen breath test off a proton pump inhibitor (PPI) is 10 parts per million (NR < 20 ppm). A gastroscopy had to be abandoned because of the presence of food in the stomach. Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
explanation:
Metoclopramide
Systemic sclerosis often leads to connective tissue proliferation in the gastrointestinal (GI) tract, in GI Chat resulting with manifestations in 80% of patients. This includes oesophageal disease (gastro-oesophageal reflux disease [GORD], strictures, intermittent dysphagia from a dysmotility), reduced gastric emptying and small bowel bacterial overgrowth secondary to the associated dysmotility. This patient appears to have gastroparesis, as evidenced by the presence of food in the stomach on endoscopy and her symptoms of bloating and early satiety, which can aggravate reflux. Management is symptomatic and by the use of prokinetic agents such as metoclopramide.

Ciprofloxacin
Ciprofloxacin is incorrect. The hydrogen breath test is negative, which effectively excludes bacterial overgrowth syndrome, and so ciprofloxacin is inappropriate.

Fundoplication
Fundoplication is incorrect. Fundoplication is used in severe reflux disease, but is not indicated here as the main issue relates to abdominal discomfort and early satiety. Furthermore, fundoplication would not be performed before acid reflux is formally quantified by pH studies.

Metronidazole
Metronidazole is incorrect. Metronidazole is not appropriate in the absence of small bowel bacterial overgrowth. Systemic Sclerosis A 27-year-old woman who is 28 weeks pregnant comes to the clinic with worsening abdominal pain and diarrhoea. She has a history of irritable bowel syndrome although her GP has never carried out formal investigations to rule out other diagnoses. On examination she looks pale. Her BP is 105/70 mmHg, pulse is 85/min and regular. Abdominal examination is consistent with a 28-week pregnancy. Investigations reveal:

Gaviscon
Gaviscon is incorrect. Gaviscon can be used as an adjunct to acid suppression therapy, but the main issue relates to gastroparesis and managing that may reduce acid reflux.

stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate way to confirm the underlying diagnosis?
explanation:
Clostridium difficile toxin testing
The clue is in the use of recent antibiotics required to treat the pneumonia and wound infection, thus predisposing to Cl. difficile, a Gram-positive anaerobe. Other risk factors include extremes ofChat age,with recent GI surgery, malignancy and prolonged hospital stay. Complications include the development of colitis (pseudomembranous colitis), which presents with fever, nausea, dehydration, abdominal pain and tenderness. The stool cytotoxin test has a high sensitivity (94-100%) and specificity (99%) for Cl. difficile and has become the standard screening test for this. Both metronidazole and vancomycin are potential treatment options.

Flexible sigmoidoscopy
Flexible sigmoidoscopy is incorrect. This is not used to diagnose Cl. difficile because it is an invasive test and there is a higher risk of perforation in acute colitis. Findings include characteristic yellow-white raised plaques. The rectum is spared in about 30% of cases.

CT abdomen
CT abdomen is incorrect. This can diagnose colitis or identify complications of colitis such as perforation, but cannot diagnose Cl. difficile as the underlying cause.

Stool culture
Stool culture is incorrect. Stool culture is less important than the demonstration of Cl. difficile toxin. C.difficile and Pseudomembranous Colitis A 65-year-old vegetarian woman – who ate a diet rich in a wide range of different fruits and vegetables – presented to the clinic complaining of facial flushing and diarrhoea. The flushing episodes could last from a few minutes to a few hours, and the diarrhoea was often accompanied by a feeling of peristaltic rushing. Her general practitioner was worried that she may have an enlarged liver and sent off for a 24-h urinary 5hydroxyindoleacetic acid (5-HIAA) test to assess for carcinoid syndrome. The 5-HIAA result came back above the normal range. What would be the most appropriate next step?

Abdominal X-ray
Abdominal X-ray is incorrect. This can show toxic megacolon with dilated bowel loops and mucosal oedema (‘thumb printing’) in cases of pseudomembranous colitis, but this is a non-specific finding in colitis and Cl. difficile cannot be diagnosed from an abdominal radiograph.

stem: A 42-year-old woman undergoes a bowel resection for a Dukes’ C colon carcinoma. She is recommended to have chemotherapy, and you plan to discuss the relative merits of capecitabine versus 5-fluorouracil (5-FU) with her. Which of the following is the major advantage of capecitabine over 5-FU?
options: Greatly reduced mortality compared with 5-FU in head-to-head trials
Superior progression-free survival compared with 5-FU in head-to-head trials
explanation:
Oral administration
Oral administration 5-fluorouracil (5-FU) is one of the most effective chemotherapeutic agents used in the treatment of advanced colorectal cancer, it is administered via IV infusion. Capecitabine is orally administered chemotherapy agent which is rapidly and almost completely absorbed by the gastrointestinal wall, it is then metabolised to 5-FU. Oral administration can achieve continuous exposure to 5-FU in a similar manner to infused 5-FU regimes without the need for central venous access, which is not only inconvenient to patients but increases the risk of infection and thrombosis.

Greatly reduced mortality compared with 5-FU in head-to-head trials
Greatly reduced mortality compared with 5-FU in head-to-head trials is incorrect. Capecitabine is an orally administered chemotherapy agent and is a prodrug of 5-FU. 5-FU inhibits the synthesis of thymidine monophosphate, which is required for DNA synthesis. Capecitabine is licensed for the treatment of a number of solid tumours, including breast, gastric and colon cancer. Studies of capecitabine versus 5-FU have shown broadly similar results with respect to mortality.

Lower rates of neutropenia
Lower rates of neutropenia is incorrect. Adverse events, including neutropenia, are broadly similar, as would be expected given that capecitabine is a prodrug of 5-FU itself.

No interaction with warfarin therapy
No interaction with warfarin therapy is incorrect. There is a significant pharmacokinetic interaction between capecitabine and warfarin, resulting in increased anticoagulant activity

Superior progression-free survival compared with 5-FU in head-to-head trials
Superior progression-free survival compared with 5-FU in head-to-head trials is incorrect. Studies of capecitabine versus 5-FU have shown similar results with respect to progression-free survival.

stem: A 50-year-old man with a long-standing history of alcohol abuse is admitted to hospital with increasing confusion over the past few days. He runs a pub and according to his wife has become angry and aggressive, followed by increasing drowsiness over the past 24 hours and is now largely confined to bed because he is unsteady on his feet. He is confused with a GCS of 14, and when you try to get him to walk there is clear ataxia. There is nystagmus and ophthalmoplegia on eye examination. You note a deficit in short-term memory. Deficiency of which vitamin is most likely to have caused his symptoms?
explanation:
Vitamin B1
A common cause of amnesic syndrome is Wernicke–Korsakoff syndrome resulting from thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency in association with chronic alcoholism or, occasionally, malnutrition or malabsorption. The Wernicke phase of this disorder is characterised by confusion, nystagmus, abducens and conjugate gaze palsies (ophthalmoplegia) as well as ataxia. These features are commonly accompanied by peripheral neuropathy. Prompt treatment with thiamine replacement is vital in order to avert a chronic and disabling amnesic disorder (Korsakoff syndrome).

Folic acid
Folic acid is incorrect. Sensory deficits are more likely to be seen in B12 deficiency, althoughChat similar withperipheral neuropathy symptoms may be seen, as may psychiatric disturbance including depression.

Vitamin A
Vitamin A is incorrect. Vitamin A deficiency does present with eye symptoms, but these include night blindness, keratomalacia and conjunctival dryness.

Vitamin B6
Vitamin B6 is incorrect. Vitamin B6 deficiency can be associated with confusion, although it is not associated with ophthalmoplegia. Wernickes Encephalopathy

Vitamin B12
Vitamin B12 is incorrect. Vitamin B12 deficiency can present with depression and confusion, but is also associated with sensory deficits including peripheral loss of vibration and position sense, and loss of peripheral reflexes.

stem: A 54-year-old man presents to the GP with altered bowel habit. For the past few weeks he has noticed intermittent bouts of mucous diarrhoea and occasionally this has been bloodstained. Faecal occult blood testing by his GP has confirmed the presence of blood in the stool. He undergoes colonoscopy and a suspicious polyp in the descending colon is removed and classified as a Dukes' A tumour. Which of the following best describes the appropriate time intervals for follow-up colonoscopy in this patient?
explanation:
Annually
Dukes' A colonic carcinoma carries an excellent prognosis, with 5-year survival now estimated at > 80%. It can be followed up using: Colonoscopy – indicated on an annual basis for the first 2 years, then this should be done 3-yearly Faecal occult blood – should be tested 6-monthly for the first 4 years and then once yearly Carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) – can be used to monitor for recurrence if it is elevated initially, although there is some controversy about the utility of CEA monitoring and it is not used universally

3-monthly
3-monthly is incorrect. 3 monthly follow up is likely only to add to anxiety, as it’s far too early to with detect growth Chat of any new potentially cancerous lesions.

6-monthly
6-monthly is incorrect. Although 6 monthly follow up may detect new early cancerous lesions, there is likely to be no impact on outcomes between 6 monthly and 1 year follow up, at the expense of increased resource utilisation and patient anxiety.

2-yearly
2-yearly is incorrect. 2 yearly colonoscopy follow up runs significant risk of tumour growth into the submucosa / muscle layer, by the time the lesion is identified.

3-yearly
3-yearly is incorrect. By the time 3 years have elapsed any new lesions may be subject to distant metastases.

stem: A 52-year-old man with recurrent episodes of pancreatitis related to alcoholism, and chronic central and left sided epigastric pain, comes to the clinic for review. Over the past few months he has developed chronic diarrhoea that is very difficult to flush away. He has lost 5kg in weight over the past 6 months although he attributes some of this to finally giving up alcohol. On examination his BP is 135/72 mmHg, pulse is 78/min and regular. There is mild epigastric tenderness on palpation of the abdomen, and his BMI is 20. Which of the following tests would be most useful in assessing whether pancreatic insufficiency is the cause of the diarrhoea seen here?
explanation:
Faecal elastase
This patient has signs of chronic pancreatitis, as evidenced by the history of recurrent pancreatitis and subsequent development of a malabsorptive diarrhoea as a consequence of loss of pancreatic exocrine function. Pancreatic elastase is excreted in the faeces unchanged, and therefore represents a useful tool for evaluation of pancreatic exocrine function. Values >200 mcg elastase/g of stool are said to represent normal pancreatic exocrine function.

Faecal calprotectin
Faecal calprotectin is incorrect. This is a marker of inflammation in the bowel and is commonly used to differentiate between IBS and IBD when there is any doubt in the history, and can avoid theChat needwith for colonoscopy. A raised faecal calprotectin can also occur in colorectal cancer or infectious colitis.

Serum albumin
Serum albumin is incorrect. While albumin level falls in significant malabsorption, it is a relatively insensitive marker of nutritional status and cannot be used to diagnose diarrhoea as a result of pancreatic insufficiency.

Serum amylase
Serum amylase is incorrect. Elevations are used as markers for assessment of acute pancreatitis. Serum amylase is often normal in pancreatic insufficiency and thus is not a reliable diagnostic marker. Chronic Pancreatitis

Serum lipase
Serum lipase is incorrect. This is also used as a marker for acute pancreatitis, rather than pancreatic insufficiency where it is commonly at a normal level.

stem: A 32-year-old woman with known protein C deficiency presented to the Emergency Department with a history of diarrhoea, steatorrhoea and weight loss. She suffered a Colles’ fracture some years ago. On examination, there is an old, healed, midline abdominal scar. Blood tests demonstrate anaemia with an increased red cell distribution width, a serum calcium level just below the lower limit of normal, and a normal CRP. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Short-bowel syndrome
The combination of protein C deficiency (ie a hypercoagulable state) with a previous laparotomy scar hints at previous small-bowel infarction and resection. Her Colles’ fracture is most likely to be due to osteoporosis/osteomalacia because of defective calcium and vitamin D absorption, and a slightly reduced serum calcium level would be consistent with this. The presence of anaemia with an increased red cell distribution width may be suggestive of deficiency of vitamin B12, folate and iron. The apparent severity of vitamin and electrolyte deficiency described suggests very extensive previous short-bowel resection with consequent short-bowel syndrome.

Active Crohn’s disease
Active Crohn’s disease is incorrect. Active small-bowel Crohn’s disease may cause malabsorptive disease, but the normal CRP level makes it unlikely that this is the case here.

Chronic pancreatitis
Chronic pancreatitis is incorrect. None of the risk factors for chronic pancreatitis (such as alcohol excess) is described, and there is no description of typical symptoms of the condition, such as abdominal Chatpain. with Coeliac disease
Coeliac disease is incorrect. Coeliac disease is more commonly associated with iron deficiency/microcytic anaemia than the mixed anaemia described here.

Ulcerative colitis
Ulcerative colitis is incorrect. As ulcerative colitis only affects the large bowel, it is not associated with features of significant malabsorption, and cannot be the correct diagnosis.

stem: A 45-year-old man with a 20-year history of ulcerative colitis (but who had been lost to follow-up) was reviewed. He was found to have had a change in bowel habit for 4 months, with increasing diarrhoea up to 3-4 times per day. What is the most appropriate next management step?
explanation:
Urgent colonoscopy
There is a stepwise increased risk of colonic adenocarcinoma that starts approximately 7–10 years after the onset of ulcerative colitis; as such, colonoscopy is the right answer here. The risk of cancer is proportional to the severity of the disease and its extent. Surveillance colonoscopy is offered to patients, starting at 10 years, with biopsies taken to assess for disease activity and for dysplasia. The 5-aminosalicylic acid (5-ASA) drugs (eg mesalazine) probably reduce this risk. A new change in bowel habit should always be investigated in a patient with long-standing disease.

Plain abdominal X-ray
Plain abdominal X-ray is incorrect. Although a plain abdominal X-ray is useful in acutely ill patients with ulcerative colitis to assess for complications (such as toxic megacolon), it is unlikely to be ofChat any with benefit here. Oral mesalazine
Oral mesalazine is incorrect. It is possible that his diarrhoea represents an increase in activity of his ulcerative colitis, and mesalazine would be an appropriate therapy were this the case; however, he clearly requires a colonoscopy to assess if his diarrhoea is caused by a malignancy.

Oral prednisolone
Oral prednisolone is incorrect. It is possible that his diarrhoea represents an increase in activity of his ulcerative colitis, and prednisolone would be appropriate therapy were this the case; however, he clearly requires a colonoscopy to assess whether his diarrhoea is caused by a malignancy. Ulcerative Colitis

Stool microscopy and culture
Stool microscopy and culture is incorrect. Although his symptoms could represent GI infection, they have been present longer than would typically be expected were this the case, and no other symptoms of infection (eg fever) are described; as such, although it is worth considering stool cultures, a colonoscopy would be the key investigation to arrange.

stem: A 54-year-old woman with systemic sclerosis was referred to the clinic with chronic diarrhoea. She had a previous history of chronic oesophageal reflux that had been managed with conservative measures, such as raising the head of the bed. Based on the most likely cause of this diarrhoea, what would be the best initial treatment option?
explanation:
Metronidazole therapy
Patients with systemic sclerosis have areas of stricture, dilatation and diverticulum formation within the small bowel. These changes, coupled with slow motility, means that they are vulnerable to problems with small intestinal bacterial overgrowth. The organisms that are usually responsible include Escherichia coli and Bacteroides spp., which are capable of unconjugating and hydrolysing bile salts. They are also capable of metabolising vitamin B 12 and interfering with intrinsic-factor binding, which can result in vitamin B 12 deficiency (although this is rarely severe enough to result in neurological deficit). Bacterial overgrowth is confirmed by the glucose-hydrogen breath test. In patients with small intestinal bacterial overgrowth, rotating antibiotics (eg metronidazole and ciprofloxacin) might be necessary to prevent the reoccurrence of symptoms.

Loperamide therapy
Loperamide therapy is incorrect. Although loperamide is a useful antidiarrhoeal agent, it willChat notwith specifically treat the small intestinal bacterial overgrowth that it is likely this woman has.

Cholestyramine therapy
Cholestyramine therapy is incorrect. Cholestyramine is a bile acid sequestrant, and is useful as a treatment for primary bile acid malabsorption/bile acid diarrhoea. However, it will not specifically treat the small intestinal bacterial overgrowth that it is likely this woman has.

Codeine phosphate therapy
Codeine phosphate therapy is incorrect. Although codeine phosphate has antidiarrhoeal effects, it will not address the likely small intestinal bacterial overgrowth present Small Intestinal Bacterial Overgrowth (SIBO)

Neomycin therapy
Neomycin therapy is incorrect. Neomycin is a non-absorbable antibiotic and although it may have efficacy in treating the small intestinal bacterial overgrowth that it is likely this woman has, its efficacy in this role is not as high as that of metronidazole; furthermore, neomycin also has higher rates of associated antibiotic resistance.

stem: Ultrasound and upper gastrointestinal (GI) endoscopy are both normal. An endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) shows calcification on the control film and irregularity of pancreatic side branches. Which one of the following would give him symptomatic relief from pain?
explanation:
Opiates
Chronic pancreatitis is characterised by continuous pancreatic inflammation and subsequent irreversible loss of endocrine and exocrine function. It may follow episodes of acute pancreatitis or may occur without an identifiable attack. Pancreatic calcification is diagnostic of chronic pancreatitis even in the absence of clinical symptoms, so for candidates who may not know this, other suggestive clues include the typical symptoms of with – the long-standing abdominal pain, weight loss, a normal upper GI endoscopy (excluding upper Chat GI malignancy main differential in this context) and normal serum amylase. Signs and symptoms relating to exocrine insufficiency may include steatorrhoea and protein catabolism secondary to protein malabsorption (from protease deficiency). Features of endocrine insufficiency include impaired glucose tolerance, and eventual diabetes mellitus. This question asks specifically about symptomatic relief of pain. Opiates are the most effective analgesia for chronic pancreatitis.

Creon®
Creon® is incorrect. Creon® contains pancreatic enzyme supplements, which can reduce steatorrhoea but there is limited evidence of its role in pain management.

Distal pancreatectomy
Distal pancreatectomy is incorrect. Distal pancreatectomy can be used to treat pain associated with chronic pancreatitis and has between a 50–80% success rate in relieving chronic pain; however, surgical treatment is the last resort.

Dietary supplements
Dietary supplements is incorrect. There is no evidence that dietary supplements relieve pain. Chronic Pancreatitis

Proton pump inhibitor (PPI)
Proton pump inhibitor (PPI) is incorrect. There is no evidence that PPIs relieve pain.

stem: A 38-year-old postman was admitted to hospital with a haematemesis. He had been drinking 'several' cans of cider a day for more than 10 years and on previous gastroscopy was noted to have varices. On examination he was deeply jaundiced but alert, with stigmata of chronic liver disease. Blood pressure was 95/50 mmHg and pulse 130 bpm. After appropriate resuscitation, his blood pressure increased to 125/70 mmHg and his pulse reduced to 100 bpm. He was still vomiting small amounts of fresh blood. What would be your next course of action?
explanation:
Intravenous terlipressin
Where haematemesis with haemorrhagic shock occurs in people with chronic liver disease, variceal bleed should be high on the list of differential diagnoses. Due to its associated high mortality, rapid recognition and intervention is required. Following resuscitation, the major priority is to administer vasoactive agents that decrease portal blood flow; early administration of these medications is associated with reduced mortality. Terlipressin is the typical medication used, although octreotide is also an appropriate option.

Endoscopy and banding
Endoscopy and banding is incorrect. Although this patient is likely to require an urgent gastroscopy (and to undergo endoscopic variceal band ligation if undergoing a variceal bleed), this should not occur before the patient has been adequately resuscitated and received terlipressin. Through its rapid actionChat in reducing portal with blood flow, administration of terlipressin prior to endoscopy means that the endoscopist is more likely to be able to accurately identify the point of variceal bleeding and place bands successfully; if terlipressin has not already been given, the endoscopist is likely to see just a field of blood and is unlikely to be able to perform banding successfully.

Give intravenous nitrates
Give intravenous nitrates is incorrect. Whilst oral nitrates have some role in secondary prevention of variceal bleeding, there is no role for a potent vasodilator like intravenous nitrates being used in the context of acute variceal bleeding.

Intravenous somatostatin
Intravenous somatostatic is incorrect. Whilst somatostatin does cause splanchnic vasoconstriction – with consequent reduction in portal blood flow – it has only a very short half-life; as such, terlipressin is used in preference. Portal Hypertension

Sengstaken–Blakemore tube
Sengstaken-Blakemore tube is incorrect. A Sengstaken–Blakemore tube is only indicated for variceal bleeding that is uncontrollable by endoscopic means, and despite maximum medical therapy.

stem: A 36-year-old man with diabetes is referred with abnormal liver biochemistry. Which blood test result is most suggestive of haemochromatosis?
explanation:
Transferrin saturation 78% (20–50)
Haemochromatosis is caused by a mutation in the gene HFE, which results in iron accumulation in different organs. The disease has an autosomal recessive inheritance pattern, with a gene frequency of 1:400 in the population. Iron accumulation within the liver leads to hepatitis and cirrhosis; in the pancreas, to diabetes; in the heart, to cardiomyopathy; in the pituitary, to hypogonadism; and in the skin, to discoloration. Women are relatively protected by menstrual blood loss. The following biochemical findings are suggestive of iron accumulation, and consistent with a diagnosis of haemochromatosis: Ferritin > 500 μg/l Serum iron > 30 μmol/l Transferrin saturation > 60% Total iron-binding capacity < 20 μmol/l. As such, Transferrin saturation 78% is the correct answer here, and the other options can be ruled out. A liver biopsy for iron accumulation and genotype testing are necessary for absolute confirmation of the diagnosis.

Alkaline phosphatase 178 U/l (45–105)
Alkaline phosphatase 178 U/l (45–105) is incorrect. Liver enzymes may be variable in people with the condition, but rises in transaminases are more typical than increases in alkaline phosphatase, ruling this option out.

Ferritin 324 μg/l (15–300)
Ferritin 324 μg/l (15–300) is incorrect. This result would not be suggestive of haemocrhomatosis.

Serum iron 25 μmol/l (12–30)
Serum iron 25 μmol/l (12–30) is incorrect. This result would not be suggestive of haemochromatosis.

Total iron-binding capacity (TIBC) 43 μmol/l (45–75).

stem: Electrocardiography (ECG) showed lateral ST depression, and upper gastrointestinal endoscopy revealed a large bleeding ulcer on the posterior aspect of the duodenum. The ulcer could not be easily reached with the endoscope, and it was decided to attempt embolisation. Which of the following arteries should be targeted for this procedure?
explanation:
Posterior superior pancreaticoduodenal artery
This woman is at great risk from her bleeding duodenal ulcer: she has lateral ST depressionChat thatwith is suggestive of myocardial ischaemia related to her fluid status. The ulcer cannot be easily reached with the endoscope, and her status would preclude surgery; the best option is therefore embolisation by a skilled interventional radiologist. The posterior aspect of the duodenum is supplied by the posterior superior pancreaticoduodenal artery.

Anterior superior pancreaticoduodenal artery
Anterior superior pancreaticoduodenal artery is incorrect. This artery supplies the anterior duodenum and head of pancreas.

Proximal gastroduodenal artery
Gastroduodenal artery is incorrect. This artery supplies the pylorus and proximal duodenum, before giving rise to several branches including the posterior superior pancreaticoduodenal artery. It is more likely that this woman’s bleed is from the posterior superior pancreaticoduodenal artery than from the proximal portion of the gastroduodenal artery.

Gastroepiploic artery
Gastroepiploic artery is incorrect. This artery primarily supplies the stomach. Peptic Ulcer Disease and Gastritis A 45 year old man is reviewed on the ward some 3 days after admission with a variceal haemorrhage. He claims that he has given up alcohol some 3 months earlier. On the ward his blood pressure is stable at 128/82, pulse is 72 and regular. There are spider naevi over the upper chest, and he is tender in the epigastrium. Investigations;

Splenic artery
Splenic artery is incorrect. This artery supplies the spleen.

stem: Which of the following investigations is most likely to help reach a diagnosis?
explanation:
Upper endoscopy with biopsy
This patient has gastric lymphoma, as suggested by the upper GI symptoms accompanied with the night sweats and enlarged lymph nodes and mass. Gastric lymphoma accounts for 10% of gastric malignancies in the developed world. Development of this tumour is thought to be linked to Helicobacter pylori infection in many patients, and H. pylori eradication can result in regression of small tumours. The tumour resemble Chatcan with superficially spreading carcinoma, linitis plastica or solitary adenocarcinoma. Diagnosis is best via gastroscopy with directed biopsy and brush cytology, to detect the tumour as well as confirm the presence of H. pylori.

Computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen
Computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen is incorrect. Although computed tomography can be useful to evaluate the extent of disease, it will not provide a specific diagnosis.

Exploratory laparotomy
Exploratory laparotomy is incorrect. Exploratory laparotomy is useful for staging and therapeutic resection where possible.

Peripheral blood smear
Peripheral blood smear is incorrect. There is no role for a blood film in the diagnosis of gastric lymphoma.

Upper gastrointestinal (GI) X-ray series
Upper gastrointestinal (GI) X-ray series is incorrect. There is no role for an upper GI X-ray series in the diagnosis of gastric lymphoma.

stem: A 66-year-old man presents to the Endoscopy Department for a flexible colonoscopy as part of investigation for iron deficiency anaemia. His previous medical history includes liver disease secondary to alcohol excess with a Child–Pugh score of C, hyperlipidaemia, hypertension, type II diabetes mellitus and gastro-oesophageal reflux disease. Due to ongoing alcohol consumption, he has been declined a liver transplant. On examination, four dysplastic polyps are identified and removed: 0.9 cm, 1.1 cm, 1.4 cm and 1.8 cm in diameter, respectively. With regard to surveillance colonoscopy, which of the following is the most appropriate?
explanation:
No further surveillance
The patient has a complex medical history. He has a Child–Pugh score of C and has not been listed for a liver transplant, which means he has a life expectancy of less than ten years. Due to the relative risk of malignant polyp development over ten years after this recent colonoscopy, guidelines recommend no surveillance colonoscopy in the following population: those with a life expectancy of less than ten years those aged over 75 years.

Repeat in two months
Following resection of large non-pedunculated polyps, a repeat colonoscopy should be completed in 2–6 months to check the site of resection. If this repeat colonoscopy is satisfactory, then the patient will require a third colonoscopy 12 months later.

Repeat in one year
Following curative resection of colorectal cancer, a follow-up colonoscopy should take place one year later.

Repeat in three years
A 3-year follow-up colonoscopy is recommended in patients with initial high-risk findings of: two or more premalignant polyps, including at least one advanced colorectal polyp five or more premalignant polyps. Patients without polyps can be discharged and advised to participate in bowel screening when invited.

Repeat in five years.

stem: Which is the next best step in management?
explanation:
Ascitic fluid analysis
This patient has signs and symptoms suggestive of spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP), which is defined by the presence of >250 polymorphonuclear cells (PMN)/mm 3 in ascites, in the absence of an intra-abdominal source of infection or malignancy. The next best step is to confirm the diagnosis with an ascitic tap before commencing antibiotics.

CT head
CT head is incorrect. This would be useful if suspecting confusion secondary to a subdural haematoma or intracranial event, but there is nothing in the history to suggest this. The patient’s confusion is probably hepatic encephalopathy due to decompensated liver disease precipitated by SBP.

CT abdomen and pelvis
