CT abdomen and pelvis is incorrect. This is not indicated here, given the likelihood of SBP which can be diagnosed by an ascitic tap alone. A CT may be appropriate if there were signs of perforation.

Abdominal ultrasound
Abdominal ultrasound is incorrect. This is not indicated here, but it would be useful if there were signs of cholecystitis.

Transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt.

stem: Blood cultures are positive for Streptococcus bovis and vegetations are visualised on the mitral valve on echocardiography. Which of the following is the most likely source of infection?
options: The continuous ambulatory peritoneal dialysis (CAPD) line
explanation:
Large bowel
S. bovis is a bacterium that is found among the normal flora of the human gastrointestinal (GI) tract in 5–16% of adults. There have been studies that have demonstrated an increased risk of concurrent colorectal cancer in the presence of S. bovis endocarditis. Streptococcus bovis endocarditis should raise alarm bells about possible underlying colonic carcinoma. Colonoscopy is recommended in all patients who present with S. bovis disease.

Biliary tree
Biliary tree is incorrect. There have been studies that show an association of S. bovis endocarditis, with S. bovis infections originating from the biliary tree, but the large bowel remains the most likely source of infection.

Dental abscess
Dental abscess is incorrect. S. bovis is not found in the oral cavity

Small bowel
Small bowel is incorrect. S. bovis is not found in the small bowel.

The continuous ambulatory peritoneal dialysis (CAPD) line.

stem: A 62-year-old man presents to the GP with itching and fatigue. He has no abdominal pain and is otherwise normally fit and well. He takes no regular medication and is a non-smoker. His blood tests show deranged liver function and he is referred to the gastroenterologists who suspect primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC). Which of the following statements regarding PSC is true?
options: PSC occurs most often in men>50 years of age
It is more commonly associated with Crohn’s disease than ulcerative colitis
It affects the extrahepatic bile ducts, and not the intrahepatic ducts
Cholangiocarcinoma complicates PSC in less than 5% of cases
Only liver transplantation is effective in late stage disease
explanation:
Only liver transplantation is effective in late stage disease
PSC is a chronic cholestatic syndrome characterised by fibrosing inflammation of the extra hepatic and intrahepatic ducts. Investigations show a cholestatic liver picture and p-ANCA is elevated in 65-85% of patients. MRCP can show dilated or structuring bile ducts. Whilst ursodeoxycholic acid is used for symptom management, it does not control the disease. The only option for treatment in late stage disease is liver transplantation.

PSC occurs most often in men>50 years of age
PSC occurs most often in men>50 years of age is incorrect. PSC has a male predominance and tends to occur most commonly in men under the age of 50 years.

It is more commonly associated with Crohn’s disease than ulcerative colitis
It is more commonly associated with Crohn’s disease than ulcerative colitis is incorrect. PSC is associated with ulcerative colitis more commonly than Crohn’s disease. In patients with PSC and UC annual surveillance colonoscopy is required because of the even greater risk of colorectal cancer.

It affects the extrahepatic bile ducts, and not the intrahepatic ducts
It affects the extrahepatic bile ducts, and not the intrahepatic ducts is incorrect. PSC affects both the intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts causing inflammation, fibrosis and strictiring.

Cholangiocarcinoma complicates PSC in less than 5% of cases.

stem: What is the most likely cause of his presentation?
explanation:
Ischaemic colitis
We are given multiple clues in this patient’s history, with atrial fibrillation, diabetes and a history of ischaemic heart disease all pointers to a diagnosis of ischaemic colitis. This is supported by the history of bloody diarrhoea, raised lactate and small but significant rise in amylase. Early diagnosis and intervention is the key to survival, with abdominal CT the investigation of choice.

Acute pancreatitis
Acute pancreatitis is incorrect. Acute pancreatitis would be suggested by abdominal pain radiating to the back and vomiting. The presentation with blood diarrhoea is not characteristic. A mildly elevated amylase is seen in other causes of an acute abdomen.

Clostridium difficile colitis
Clostridium difficile colitis is incorrect. C. difficile colitis can cause abdominal pain and bloody diarrhoea, and severe cases can cause a perforated colon. However, the absence of a history of recent antibiotic use, and of signs of large bowel dilatation on imaging, go against C. difficile colitis being the cause of the peritonism and raised lactate in this case.

Inflammatory bowel disease
Inflammatory bowel disease is incorrect. Acute ulcerative colitis can present with abdominal pain and bloody diarrhoea, with severe cases leading to peritonitis from a perforated colon. However, the age of this patient and the past medical history of AF make ischaemic colitis more likely.

Sigmoid volvulus.

stem: Which of the following represents the most appropriate management of this patient?
explanation:
Intravenous fluids and analgesia
In the first instance, this woman who has developed pancreatitis following endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (post-ERCP pancreatitis) should be managed medically/conservatively with intravenous rehydration, analgesia and antibiotics (if appropriate). ERCP is probably the third most common cause of pancreatitis after alcohol and biliary tract disease. It might be related to inadequate hydration at the time of the procedure, or to attempts to measure the pressure at the sphincter of Oddi.

Computed tomography-guided pancreatic aspiration
Computed tomography-guided pancreatic aspiration is incorrect. There is no information given to support this woman having a pancreatic collection, and hence no indication for aspiration. Even if a collection was present, initial management is typically conservative in the majority of cases.

Insert a percutaneous drain
Insert a percutaneous drain is incorrect. There is no information given to support this woman having a pancreatic collection, and hence no indication for drainage. Even if a collection was present, initial management is typically conservative in the majority of cases.

Proceed to cholecystectomy
Proceed to cholecystectomy is incorrect. Cholecystectomy would be very dangerous to perform on someone with severe abdominal inflammation related to pancreatitis. Although cholecystectomy will be appropriate for this woman at some point, it would be much safer to aim to perform this at least several weeks later, once all abdominal inflammation had entirely settled.

Proceed to further ERCP.

stem: A 44-year-old alcoholic man is admitted to the Emergency Department with increased abdominal distension, confusion and drowsiness. He continues to drink 4-6 pints of strong lager per day and is poorly compliant with his medication. On examination his GCS is 12. BP is 95/60 mmHg, pulse is 85/min and irregular and his temperature is 38.2 °C. There are signs of chronic liver disease, including significant ascites. An ascitic tap reveals 550 cells/microlitre. Which of the following is the most likely cause of his sepsis?
explanation:
Escherichia coli
Patients with decompensated cirrhosis have a high risk of developing spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP), as is the case in this vignette. SBP is diagnosed when neutrophils are > 250 cells/mm in ascitic fluid. E. coli is responsible for 50% of cases, with Gram-positive infections the next most common with the majority due to streptococci. Treatment includes antibiotics (cefotaxime or oral ciprofloxacin as per BSG guidelines). The outcome is very poor in patients with cirrhosis, mortality rates approaching 70%.

Salmonella typhi
Salmonella typhi is incorrect. This is a very rare and unusual cause of SBP and tends to commonly cause gastroenteritis.

Staphylococcus aureus
Staphylococcus aureus is incorrect. Staphylococcal infections occur with increased frequency in patients who are undergoing continuous ambulatory peritoneal dialysis (CAPD) renal replacement therapy rather than in SBP.

Streptococcus pneumoniae
Streptococcus pneumoniae is incorrect. This is a commensal of the respiratory tract but has been associated with SBP in cirrhotic patients, although much less commonly than the Gram-negative organisms and Streptococcus viridans.

Streptococcus viridans.

stem: A 21-year-old woman presented to the Emergency Department for review, having been referred by her general practitioner. She had been unwell for several weeks, with her main symptom being opening her bowels with bloody diarrhoea approximately eight times per day, including at night. She had a resting heart rate of 88 bpm. Her abdomen was bloated but non-tender, her albumin was 32 g/l (NR 37–49 g/l) and her Hb was 104 g/l (NR 11.5–16.5 g/dl). She also has a raised plasma viscosity. Abdominal X-ray revealed that her transverse colon had a diameter of 5 cm. Stool culture was negative. She has been using 4 g of paracetamol per day as analgesia. Which of her clinical features would fit best with severe ulcerative colitis?
options: Bowels opening eight times per day
Requiring 4 g of paracetamol per day as analgesia
explanation:
Bowels opening eight times per day
Defining features of an attack of acute severe colitis are (according to NICE, as adapted from Truelove and Witts’ severity index): At least six stools per day Visible blood in stools and at least one feature of systemic upset, i.e: 1. Temperature above 37.8°C 2. Pulse rate greater than 90 bpm 3. Anaemia 4. ESR above 30 mm/1 st hour

Albumin of 32 g/l
Albumin of 32 g/l is incorrect as albumin levels do not form part of the criteria for assessing for acute severe colitis.

Heart rate of 88 bpm
Heart rate of 88 bpm is incorrect as only a pulse > 90 bpm (in conjunction with other clinical/laboratory features suggestive of active disease) would suggest acute severe colitis.

Requiring 4 g of paracetamol per day as analgesia
Requiring 4 g of paracetamol per day as analgesia is incorrect as degree of analgesia use does not form part of the criteria for assessing for acute severe colitis.

Transverse colon diameter 5 cm.

stem: Which of the results qualify her to be listed for a super-urgent liver transplant?
explanation:
pH 7.28
This patient has acute liver failure secondary to paracetamol toxicity. Acute liver failure (ALF) is defined as a syndrome that occurs due to rapid cessation of normal liver function in individuals with previously normal livers. The rate of decline is taken as the time taken from the onset of jaundice until the onset of encephalopathy. Less than 7 days is considered ‘hyperacute liver failure’ (as applied to the case here). The Kings criteria are used to determine which patients would benefit the most from liver transplantation. For ALF secondary to paracetamol toxicity the following criteria apply: pH < 7.3 OR INR > 6.5 + Cr > 300 mcmol + grade 3/4 hepatic encephalopathy This patient has a pH lower than 7.3, and so qualifies for super-urgent listing.

Cr 230 and INR 2.8
Cr 230 and INR 2.8 is incorrect. Her Cr and INR alone are not enough to qualify for listing. Cr would need to be > 300 mcmol, INR > 6.5 and she would need to have at least grade 3 encephalopathy to be considered for transplant (if pH was more than 7.3).

ALT 1650 and AST 1800
ALT 1650 and AST 1800 is incorrect. The ALT and AST are not considered the best prognostic markers in liver failure as large rises can occur in patients with relatively well-preserved liver function.

Bilirubin 150
Bilirubin 150 is incorrect. Bilirubin levels are not part of the King’s criteria for determining need for liver transplant in the context of paracetamol toxicity.

Grade 1 encephalopathy.

stem: A 72-year-old man underwent investigation because of persistent tiredness. His General Practitioner noticed that he was jaundiced and suspected liver disease. He denied any gastrointestinal symptoms. Examination also revealed angular stomatitis. He had a history of steroid inhaler use for asthma, but nothing else of note. A blood film demonstrated features of a megaloblastic anaemia, with biochemistry tests normal aside from a raised serum bilirubin. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Pernicious anaemia
This scenario is very suggestive of pernicious anaemia. Pernicious anaemia is common in the elderly, occurring in ~1 in 8000 of the over-60 age group (there is also a raised incidence of gastric carcinoma in this age group of 1–3%). Increased bilirubin is a typical feature, and results from an increased turnover of immature red blood cells. The disease is usually insidious in onset, presenting with tiredness and lethargy. Very low serum levels of vitamin B 12 can result in a symmetrical peripheral polyneuropathy, progressively involving the posterior and then the lateral columns of the spinal cord (known as subacute combined degeneration of the cord). Anti-parietal cell antibodies are present in 90% of patients with pernicious anaemia, while anti-thyroid antibodies are present in up to 50% of affected people. Vitamin B 12 absorption can be measured using the Schilling test (although this is rarely performed in practice now antibody testing is so widely available). Treatment is with intramuscular injections of vitamin B 12.

Autoimmune hepatitis
Autoimmune hepatitis is incorrect. Although the information supplied that this man is jaundiced may suggest liver disease, the fact that the only blood test abnormality apart from his anaemia is his raised bilirubin with – Tutor no apparent abnormalities of his liver enzymes, or markers of liver synthetic function (e.g. prothrombin time) – is clearly inconsistent with significant liver disease like autoimmune hepatitis.

Chronic myeloid leukaemia
Chronic myeloid leukaemia is incorrect. If this man had chronic myeloid leukaemia (CML), it would be expected that his blood film would show members of the whole granulocytic cell lineage rather than just a megaloblastic anaemia; CML is therefore unlikely to be the diagnosis.

Crohn’s disease
Crohn’s disease is incorrect. This man is somewhat older than typical for a first presentation of Crohn’s disease; in addition, the absence of any specific GI symptoms and/or raised inflammatory markers also means that Crohn’s disease is very unlikely to be the diagnosis here.

Iron-deficiency anaemia.

stem: Which of the following describes the primary mechanism of action of lactulose in the gastrointestinal tract?
explanation:
Osmotic laxative
Lactulose is a synthetic sugar that is only able to be broken down by bacteria in the colon. The acidic metabolites produced in this process, have an osmotic effect which increases the water content and volume of the stools. An additional effect of the acidic metabolites, is the increased ionisation of the freely diffusible ammonia into ammonium which cannot diffuse back into the blood. Thus lactulose is also used in the treatment of hepatic encephalopathy.

Increased intestinal motility
Increased intestinal motility is incorrect. An example of a drug that increases intestinal motility is senna.

Chloride channel activator
Chloride channel activator is incorrect. Chloride channel activators have a laxative effect by activating chloride channels in the intestine which increases secretion of intestinal fluid. An example is Lubiprostone.

Stool softeners
Stool softeners is incorrect. Stool softeners such as sodium docusate work by enabling additional water and lipid to be coated on the stool, making it easier to move through the colon.

Bulk-forming agent.

stem: What is the most appropriate next intervention?
explanation:
IV hydrocortisone
This patient presents with a moderate to severe flare of Crohn’s disease, with bloody diarrhoea, systemic symptoms, and a markedly raised ESR. She is already on a weaning dose of oral prednisolone, and the lack of response indicates that outpatient steroid therapy has failed. According to current NICE and ECCO guidelines, the next step in such patients is escalation to inpatient intravenous corticosteroids, such as hydrocortisone, to induce remission. This provides a more potent anti-inflammatory effect and allows close monitoring for complications.

Azathioprine
Azathioprine is an immunomodulator used to maintain remission in Crohn’s disease, but it takes 6–12 weeks to exert clinical benefit. It is not appropriate for inducing remission during an acute flare. It may be introduced later as part of a steroid-sparing strategy once the patient is stabilised.

Infliximab
Infliximab is a biologic agent effective in moderate to severe Crohn’s disease, especially in patients refractory to corticosteroids or immunomodulators. However, it is not first-line for acute induction unless there is failure of intravenous steroids or contraindications. It may be introduced following inpatient management if the response to steroids is inadequate.

Metronidazole
Metronidazole has a role in perianal Crohn’s disease and certain complications, such as abscesses or bacterial overgrowth, but it is not effective as monotherapy for inducing remission in luminal Crohn’s disease and is not appropriate here.

Ileocaecal resection referal.

stem: An ultrasound (US) scan shows gallstones, a cirrhotic liver and intra- and extrahepatic bile duct dilatation. Which of the following is the most appropriate next investigation?
explanation:
Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP)
This man has painful jaundice of insidious onset, weight loss and signs of abdominal discomfort, while signs of liver cirrhosis are suggested by the US scan. There are no obvious pointers to the underlying cause of disease in the history, except that the presence of UC may indicate possible primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC). The finding of intra- and extrahepatic duct dilatation further supports possible PSC and subsequent cholangiocarcinoma.

Gastroscopy for variceal assessment
Gastroscopy for variceal assessment is incorrect. There is no role for a gastroscopy at this point. Oesophagogastroduodenoscopies (OGDs) are used for variceal assessment and surveillance in patients with chronic liver disease, but this is not the priority at present.

Autoimmune profile
Autoimmune profile is incorrect. Although useful it is not the most appropriate next investigation in this case.

Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP)
Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) is incorrect. ERCP has a role in managing stricturing disease in established PSC, but not in the initial investigations for bile duct obstruction. MRCP is superior to ERCP for investigating this initially, as it is non-invasive and permits tumour staging with assessment of hepatic involvement.

Liver biopsy.

stem: Which one of the following is the most appropriate initial screening test for the likely underlying diagnosis?
explanation:
Transferrin saturation
This man presents with features suggestive of hereditary haemochromatosis, including signs of chronic liver disease, increased skin pigmentation, elevated fasting glucose, and possible hypogonadism. The most appropriate initial screening test for detecting iron overload, which is characteristic of hereditary haemochromatosis, is transferrin saturation. Transferrin saturation is considered more reliable in this context because it is less likely to be affected by chronic liver disease or alcohol excess compared to serum ferritin, which may give false positives. A fasting transferrin saturation greater than 55% is indicative of iron overload and supports the diagnosis of hereditary haemochromatosis.

Serum copper
Serum copper is incorrect in this context. It is primarily used to diagnose conditions like Wilson's disease, where there is abnormal copper metabolism. This patient's clinical presentation does not align with the symptoms of Wilson's disease, which typically include neurological and psychiatric symptoms rather than signs of iron overload. Therefore, serum copper would not be a sensitive or relevant screen for hereditary haemochromatosis.

Serum ferritin
Serum ferritin is not the most appropriate initial screening test for hereditary haemochromatosis. Although serum ferritin levels can be elevated in cases of iron overload, they can also be raised due to chronic liver disease and excessive alcohol consumption, both of which are present in this patient. This can lead to false positives, making serum ferritin less reliable as a standalone screening test. Transferrin saturation is preferred as it more specifically indicates iron overload without being as influenced by liver disease or alcohol intake.

Serum iron
Serum iron alone is not a suitable screening test for hereditary haemochromatosis. Serum iron levels can fluctuate significantly due to various factors, including diet and time of day, leading to potential inaccuracies. While serum iron is a component in calculating transferrin saturation, it is not sufficient by itself to diagnose iron overload. Therefore, relying solely on serum iron would not provide a sensitive or specific assessment of the patient's condition.

Serum testosterone.

stem: A 45-year-old woman is referred to the Emergency Department by her General Practitioner. She presented with severe nausea and lethargy, and routine liver function testing has revealed a significant rise in transaminases and alkaline phosphatase. Which of the following accurately describes the evaluation of her liver function tests?
options: ALT is only released from hepatocytes
Clotting abnormalities are usually seen in mild hepatic dysfunction
Ferritin elevation is not always due to haemochromatosis
Gamma GT increases least in patients with obstructive jaundice
Hepatic synthesis of γ-globulin increases in chronic autoimmune liver disease
explanation:
Ferritin elevation is not always due to haemochromatosis
Ferritin is an acute phase protein produced by the liver in response to inflammation as well as in cases of iron overload.

ALT is only released from hepatocytes
ALT is only released from hepatocytes is incorrect. ALT is also present in muscle cells and levels are often elevated where there is muscle damage.

Clotting abnormalities are usually seen in mild hepatic dysfunction
Clotting abnormalities are usually seen in mild hepatic dysfunction is incorrect. Hepatic synthetic function, including the production of clotting factors, is only usually markedly deranged where there is a severe liver disease.

Gamma GT increases least in patients with obstructive jaundice
Gamma GT increases least in patients with obstructive jaundice is incorrect. Gamma GT is produced by hepatic ductal cells, and is often markedly increased in patients with obstructive jaundice.

Hepatic synthesis of γ-globulin increases in chronic autoimmune liver disease.

stem: A Norwegian woman who is living in England is reviewed in the Gastroenterology Clinic. She is 31 weeks pregnant with her ﬁrst child and has severe and uncontrollable itching. On examination, she looks relatively well, her BP is 105/60 mmHg, pulse 75/min, and her abdomen is consistent with a 31-week pregnancy. Investigation Result Normal value Haemglobin 109 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 5.4 × 109/l 4–11 × 109/l Platelets 195 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 139 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.3 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 90 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l ALT 320 IU/l 5–30 IU/l Alkaline phosphatase 420 IU/l 30–130 IU/l Bilirubin 67 µmol/l 2–17 µmol/l Which of the following is the most appropriate way to manage her?
explanation:
A Ursodeoxycholic acid The presentation with pruritus, raised ALP and ALT with only mildly elevated bilirubin is consistent with a diagnosis of cholestasis of pregnancy. The condition is characterised by pruritus (typically starting on the palms and soles of the feet) with raised fasting and post prandial serum bile acids. Total bilirubin is rarely raised (although it is in this instance). The condition occasionally presents with pale stool and dark urine. It typically occurs in the 3rd trimester and resolves up to 6 weeks post partum. Treatment is for pruritus with ursodeoxycholic acid and rifampicin. It is more common in Scandinavian women. B Urgent delivery of the fetus Cholestasis of pregnancy is associated with a slight increase in prematurity and post partum haemorrhage, however most pregnancies proceed to term without serious complications therefore urgent pre-term delivery is not indicated. C Anti-coagulation

Anticoagulation would be indicated in Budd-Chiari syndrome. However, this tends to present with abdominal pain and features of portal hypertension. Her ALT would probably be much higher representing hepatocyte ischaemia due to congestion. It is characterised by obstruction of the hepatic vein, sinusoidal congestion and portal hypertension. Pregnancy is a hypercoagulable state and risk of Budd Chiari is increased although remains rare. Most patients presenting with de novo occlusion tend to have an undiagnosed underlying thombophillia and should be investigated. D Oral corticosteroids There is no role for the use of steroids in cholestasis of pregnancy. Treatment is supportive aimed at reducing pruritus. E Observe Although the only treatment for cholestasis of pregnancy is delivery, use of ursodeoxycholic acid would reduce the severity of this patient’s symptoms therefore ursodeoxycholic acid is the most appropriate answer.

stem: A 17-year-old Turkish girl presented to the Emergency Department with a 4-h history of severe abdominal pain. the onset was rapid and without preceding symptoms. She described no change in her bowel habit or urinary symptoms. She had an appendectomy 6 months previously and an exploratory laparotomy 2 months ago for similar episodes. At neither operation was any abnormality found other than a small amount of peritoneal ﬂuid. On examination she is pyrexial at 39.2 °C and tachycardic at 105 bpm. Her abdomen is diffusely tender with guarding in the right upper quadrant. Bowel sounds are reduced. A painful erythematous rash was noted on the lower limbs. Investigation Result Normal Values Urinalysis blood + Hb 136 g/l 135 - 175 g/l MCV 85 ﬂ 80 - 100 ﬂ WCC 14.8 × 109/l 4.0 - 11.0 × 109/l PLT 387 × 109/l 150 - 400 × 109/l CRP 55 mg/l < 10 mg/l β-HCG Erect chest X-ray < 5 u/l normal < 5 u/l Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: B Familial Mediterranean fever Familial Mediterranean fever (FMF) presents typically (although not exclusively) in Turkish, Armenian, Arabic, Mediterranean and/ or Jewish people. It is an autosomal recessive disorder, with the site of the mutation being on chromosome 16. Approximately half of affected people have no family history of the condition. It typically presents at a young age, with only 5-10% presenting after the age of 20 years. FMF is characterised by recurrent episodes of fever with severe abdominal pain and signs of peritonitis, and so affected people often have a history of previous surgery, particular appendectomy. Other commonly-described symptoms include pleuritis, pericarditis, synovitis and an erysipeloid rash on the lower limbs. Attacks normally occur without warning, and typically last for 24-72 hours. Blood tests are consistent with an acute-phase response. FMF attacks can normally be prevented with Colchicine. Colchicine also prevents the development of amyloidosis, a recognised complication of the chronic inﬂammation that may occur if the condition is untreated. The diagnosis is principally made on clinical criteria (including response to Colchicine), although genetic testing is becoming more widely-available. However, a proportion of people with classical clinical features of FMF are found to have only one mutation or none at all, implying that there are more gene mutations causing the condition than are currently recognised. A Ectopic pregnancy Ectopic pregnancy is ruled out by the negative pregnancy test. C Acute intermittent porphyria Acute intermittent porphyria may present with acute severe abdominal pain but tends not to present with fever. D Pyelonephritis Although pyelonephritis presents with fever and abdominal pain, the multiple previous episodes and lack of ﬁndings on previous occasions, all count against pyelonephritis as the underlying diagnosis. E Abdominal angina Abdominal angina may present with acute severe abdominal pain but tends not to present with fever.

stem: A 54-year-old woman has chronic autoimmune hepatitis. She is managed on prednisolone and azathioprine. You review her in the clinic and notice that she has worsening of her jaundice with a rising bilirubin and increasing ascites. You admit her; the nurses call you to see her urgently the following morning as she has become increasingly drowsy. Her blood pressure is 100/50 mmHg, with pyrexia of 38.2 °C. Which investigation is most likely to conﬁrm the suspected diagnosis?
options: Peritoneal tap for microscopy and culture
explanation: E Peritoneal tap for microscopy and culture Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis occurs in around 8% of cirrhotic patients with ascites, infecting organisms probably gaining access to the peritoneum via haematological spread. Most frequent infecting organisms are Escherichia coli, Klebsiella and enterococci. Pain and pyrexia may frequently be absent. A raised neutrophil count alone in ascitic ﬂuid is enough to commence treatment. Mortality is high, at up to 25%, and recurs in 70% of patients within one year. Oral quinolones may be used as prophylaxis A Computed tomography (CT) head CT head would be a useful investigation in confusion during which an intracranial cause is suspected or needs to be excluded. This can be considered in, for example, subdural haematomas (worsening pain and confusion), subarachnoid haemorrhage (sudden occipital severe headache) or abscess (recent sinusitis or other infection, headache and fever). In this patient there is a clear cause for confusion – acute decompensation of the liver. B Electroencephalograpm (EEG) EEG can demonstrate encephalopathy, but it is unlikely to be of signiﬁcant aid in decision making as there is sufﬁcient evidence of liver decompensation clinically. C Blood culture Blood culture should be taken in this patient to help guide antibiotic therapy, but is unlikely to be very speciﬁc in making the diagnosis. It can demonstrate bowel organisms in this setting, but may not give much help regarding the exact origin, nor would it provide an answer in a timely fashion. D Lumbar puncture A lumbar puncture is a useful investigation in a confused patient with fever, but the clinical picture already suggests a clear cause of this. If he had symptoms of meningitis as well, such as photophobia or neck stiffness, then it would be a diagnostic investigation.

stem: A 42-year-old man who has a 20-year history of ulcerative colitis (UC) presents to the gastroenterology clinic for review. His UC is relatively quiescent, although most recently he has begun to suffer from tiredness, itching and vague right upper quadrant pain. On examination, you can feel two ﬁngers’-breadth hepatomegaly. His only medication is salazopyrine. Investigation Result Normal values Hb 121 g/l 135 - 175 g/l WCC 6.0 × 109/l 4.0 - 11.0 × 109/l PLT 320 × 109/l 150 - 400 × 109/l ALP 420 u/l 30 - 150 u/l ALT 74 u/l 7 - 55 u/l Which of the following is the most effective therapy for his underlying condition?
explanation:
C Liver transplantation Liver transplantation is the deﬁnitive treatment for patients with decompensated cirrhosis with a background of PSC. Increased levels of alkaline phosphatase and a positive history of ulcerative colitis make PSC a likely diagnosis. Complications of this condition include advanced-stage liver disease with hepatic decompensation. Around 70% of patients diagnosed with PSC are men, with an average age of around 40 years. Up to 90% of patients diagnosed with PSC have co-existent inﬂammatory bowel disease, normally ulcerative colitis.

Cholangiocarcinoma is also an established complication of PSC. Indications for liver transplantation in patients with PSC do not differ from those with other forms of chronic liver disease, which primarily relate to complications of portal hypertension, chronic liver failure and impaired quality of life. Moreover, patients with PSC have speciﬁc indications for liver transplant, which include recurrent bacterial cholangitis, intractable pruritis and cholangiocarcinoma. B Penicillamine As described in a systemic review by Klingenberg et al., there is insufﬁcient evidence to refute or support the use of penicillamine for patients with primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC). A Cholestyramine Cholestyramine, a bile acid sequestrant, is used to treat hyperlipidaemia and for the pruritus of biliary obstruction and chronic liver disease. D Prednisolone Corticosteroids, e.g. prednisolone, have not demonstrated any improvement in disease activity or outcome of PSC patients, as evident in a systemic review by Giljaca et al. E Azathioprine Many immunosuppressive agents are used in the management of patients with PSC, However, there no substantial evidence for its role in prognosis of patients with PSC is noted. A review study by Goode et al. mentioned controversial evidence underlying the usage of immunosuppressive therapy and other prospective agents that may bring new hope regarding the treatment of PSC in the 21st century.

stem: A 23-year-old woman from Vietnam presents with fever, abdominal pain and weight loss. There is no diarrhoea or rectal bleeding. Her mother has liver cirrhosis secondary to hepatitis
explanation: A 10-day course of metronidazole For larger liver abscesses aspiration is the intervention of choice, combined with antibiotic therapy. Liver abscesses due to amoebae mainly occur in endemic tropical countries. Clinical presentation can be indistinguishable from pyogenic abscesses. The collection is commonly single and conﬁned to the right lobe, but multiple leftsided abscesses may also occur. Speciﬁc anti-E. histolytica antibodies can be found in the sera of over 90% of patients with amoebic liver abscess. Management involves treatment with a 10-day course of metronidazole. A 2-week course of albendazole Albendazole is effective therapy for echinococcal or hydatid cysts rather than for amoebic liver abscess. B 10 day course of ciproﬂoxacin Ciproﬂoxacin is a potential intervention for liver abscess occurring as a result of biliary tract infection with potential Gram-negative pathogens. C 14 day course of co-amoxiclav Although co-amoxiclav is a potential option for Gram-negative liver abscess, quinolones are generally the preferred ﬁrst choice because of the risk of cholestatic jaundice associated with prolonged use of co-amoxiclav. E 2-week course of doxycycline Doxycycline is a standard intervention for the treatment of Chlamydia.

stem: A 56-year-old man is admitted to hospital having had a witnessed generalised tonic-clonic seizure in the street following which a bystander called an ambulance. He had a further seizure while in the ambulance on the way to hospital, terminated by PR diazepam. A third, brief seizure occurs on arrival at the A&E department. Relatives were contacted from patient’s mobile. His son gave history of previous admissions related to acute alcohol admission. He has no other signiﬁcant past medical history of note, and is not on any regular medications. He denies recreational drug use, and has not drunk any alcohol in the past 24 hours. Baseline observations are as follows: Investigation Result Temperature 36.5oC Pulse 88 bpm Blood Pressure 132/68 mmHg O2sats 97% air Blood glucose 5.4 mmol/l A computed tomography (CT) brain is performed which is normal. On return from the scanner, he suffers a further seizure which has lasted for around 2 minutes. What is the most appropriate short-term intervention?
options: Give intravenous (iv) lorazepam followed by long term sodium valproate
explanation:
C Give iv lorazepam Alcohol withdrawal seizures usually occur after an 8- to 24-hour alcohol-free period. If there is no known history of epilepsy, and no underlying structural brain lesion is identiﬁed, long-term antiepileptic treatment is not required. In the acute setting, iv lorazepam has been shown to reduce the risk of recurrent seizures. Patients are then managed according to a CIWA alcohol withdrawal protocol. D No intervention required Not treating with benzodiazepines in this situation runs the risk of further withdrawal seizures with associated mortality and morbidity. A Oral carbamazepine Oral carbamazepine is mainly used in the management of partial seizures, which may of course result from alcohol abuse, although here short-term prevention of further withdrawal seizures with lorazepam is most important.

B Give intravenous (iv) lorazepam followed by long term sodium valproate There is no indication for long-term sodium valproate unless generalised seizures are seen post alcohol withdrawal. E Start oral sodium valproate In this situation, iv benzodiazepines are the intervention of choice to prevent further withdrawal seizures. Anti- epileptics are not required unless seizures occur over the longer term.

stem: A 56-year-old man is brought to the hospital after collapsing in the street. On arrival, he is alert but disorientated and smells strongly of alcohol. He complains of a sore tongue. Examination reveals that he is unkempt and malnourished, with angular stomatitis and glossitis. A picture of his hands is shown below. Which vitamin deﬁciency is most likely to have resulted in the changes on his hands?
explanation: D Niacin The changes described are typical of pellagra, which is caused by niacin deﬁciency. Although pellagra is classically described as occurring with the triad of dementia, dermatitis and diarrhoea, not all of these changes are always present – in fact, it is not unusual for constipation to occur. The dermatitis predominantly affects sunexposed areas, and progresses from erythema (with dryness and cracking) through to more chronic changes (with thickening and pigmentation). Cognitive impairment is often a late effect, and is often preceded by apathy, depression and irritability. Pellagra is now rare, as niacin is found in many foods and is used to fortify breakfast cereals. However, people with severe malabsorptive disease, alcohol dependence or eating disorders are still amongst those at risk of niacin deﬁciency. Pyridoxine is needed for the synthesis of nicotinamide, and pyridoxine deﬁciency may therefore also cause pellagra. C Thiamine Thiamine deﬁciency in the UK is predominantly found in those with alcohol dependence, and normally presents as Wernicke's encephalopathy. Ataxia, nystagmus, ophthalmoplegia and confusion are the classic ﬁndings, and need treating promptly if more permanent cognitive impairment (Korsakoff' syndrome) is to be prevented. Wet beriberi (causing oedema) and dry beriberi (usually presenting with a polyneuropathy) tend not to be seen outside of South East Asia. A Vitamin B12 Vitamin B12 deﬁciency is rarely caused by inadequate intake, although this may occur in vegans. Typical features include a macrocytic anaemia, glossitis, and – over time – neurological changes. If left untreated, subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord may occur. B Vitamin C Vitamin C is particularly found in fresh fruit and vegetables. Deﬁciency initially causes non-speciﬁc symptoms, but features including corkscrew hair follicles, swollen gums, perifollicular haemorrhages, bruising and anaemia may develop as the deﬁciency progresses. Ascorbic acid supplementation and resumption of a normal diet will rapidly remove features of deﬁciency. E Riboﬂavin Riboﬂavin deﬁciency has a less clearly deﬁned deﬁciency syndrome, although angular stomatitis, glossitis and dermatitis may occur.

stem: A 23-year-old man presents to the Colorectal Clinic with two discrete episodes of haematochezia. He has had no fresh bleeding per rectum, nor has he been experiencing abdominal pain. He has a healthy lifestyle recently and denies unintentional weight loss. He has no medical history of note. His father died of colorectal cancer at the age of 54 and his paternal aunt has a current diagnosis of thyroid cancer. On examination, his observations are within normal limits. His abdomen is soft and non-tender and a digital rectal examination reveals no visible cause of his haematochezia. He is referred for a colonoscopy that shows 15 adenomatous polyps ranging from 3 mm to 1.5 mm. What is the most appropriate investigation to conﬁrm the likely diagnosis?
explanation: A Adenomatous polyposis coli genetic testing This patient has a likely diagnosis of familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP), given the young presentation of haematochezia and adenomatous polyps on colonoscopy. FAP is an autosomal-dominant condition caused by mutations in the adenomatous polyposis coli gene causing hundreds to thousands of adenomatous polyps throughout the colon. It comes with almost a 100% risk of colorectal cancer if not treated with a prophylactic pan-colectomy. The family history of colorectal cancer and associated malignancies with FAP (eg thyroid cancer) makes FAP an even more likely diagnosis. Colonoscopy and biopsy form the mainstay of investigation for the condition. However, genetic testing is recommended for patients with ten or more adenomatous polyps on a single colonoscopy, as it helps to aid the diagnosis and decision for surgical intervention. E Faecal immunochemical testing Faecal immunochemical testing is used in the investigation of colorectal cancer. It detects the presence of blood within the stool by using antibodies speciﬁc for haemoglobin. As this patient is presenting with haematochezia, this result is likely to be positive. However, it is much more likely that this patient has FAP rather than colorectal cancer or FAP that has already malignantly transformed into colorectal cancer. B Carcinoembryonic antigen testing Carcinoembryonic antigen testing is a tumour marker used in the assessment of colorectal cancer. Although FAP has a very high risk of becoming colorectal cancer, this is usually in later years (35–40 years). Furthermore, it would not aid in the speciﬁc diagnosis of FAP. Rather, if FAP had malignantly transformed into colorectal cancer. C CT abdomen Carcinoembryonic antigen testing is a tumour marker used in the assessment of colorectal cancer. Although FAP has a very high risk for becoming colorectal cancer, this is usually in later years (35–40 years). Furthermore, it would not aid in the speciﬁc diagnosis of FAP. Rather, if FAP had malignantly transformed into colorectal cancer. D Faecal calprotectin Faecal calprotectin is used in the investigation of inﬂammatory bowel disease (IBD), which is a useful differential diagnosis to consider given the onset of rectal bleeding at a young age. However, this typically presents with abdominal pain, diarrhoea and weight loss, and the absence of these features plus the family history of malignancy makes IBD less likely.

stem: A 62-year-old woman is referred to the clinic with worsening diarrhoea, intermittent wheeze and facial ﬂushing. There is a past medical history of hypertension, for which she takes ramipril, but nil else of note. On examination, her BP 149/88 mmHg, pulse is 88/min, her BMI is 21. Her abdomen is soft and only mildly tender with active bowel sounds. There is facial telangiectasia and evidence of tricuspid regurgitation. Routine bloods undertaken by her general practitioner reveal: Investigation Result Normal value Hb 108 g/l 135 - 175 g/l Sodium (Na+) 135 mmol/l 135 - 145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 3.2 mmol/l 3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l ALT 215 u/l 7 - 55 u/l Which of the following diagnoses ﬁts best with this clinical picture?
explanation: C Carcinoid syndrome Carcinoid syndrome presents with facial ﬂushing (75–90%), diarrhoea (>70%) and intermittent bronchospasm in 25% of patients. Associated clinical ﬁndings include facial telangiectasia and tricuspid regurgitation. It is caused by the action of serotonin, bradykinin and histamine produced by tumours arising from neuroendocrine cells. Diagnosis is by measuring an increase in urinary 5hydroxyindoleacetic acid, a metabolite of 5-HT (serotonin). It is likely that this patient’s abnormal alanine aminotransferase is due to the presence of liver metastases. Pellagra is nicotinic acid deﬁciency which can occur as a result of increased requirements for nicotinamide as a result of the carcinoid tumour. It is an important substrate in the metabolic formation of 5-HT, deﬁciency in nicotinic acid can lead to dementia in patients with extensive carcinoid metastases. B Thyrotoxicosis Although thyrotoxicosis may be associated with weight loss and diarrhoea, features such as telangiectasia, tricuspid regurgitation and elevated transaminases would be unexpected in the context of hyperthyroidism. A Phaeochromocytoma This is associated with marked hypertension and headaches, and maybe associated with hypokalaemia, but is not associated with signiﬁcant diarrhoea. D Cushing’s disease Cushing’s disease is associated with signiﬁcant weight gain, which doesn’t ﬁt with the diagnosis here. E Iron deﬁciency anaemia Iron deﬁciency alone is unlikely given the other symptoms including facial ﬂushing, diarrhoea, and evidence of tricuspid regurgitation, ﬁtting better with carcinoid.

stem: A 24-year-old woman is found to have the following blood results on routine preoperative blood tests. She presented due to yellowing of her skin following a short bout of ﬂu, from which she has now recovered. She has no past medical history of note and takes no regular medications. Examination reveals jaundice, but no other abnormalities. Investigation Result Normal value Bilirubin 36 µmol/l 2–17 µmol/l ALP 108 IU/l 30–130 IU/l ALT 20 IU/l 5–30 IU/l Urine dipstick Normal Given the likely diagnosis, which is the best course of action?
options: Complete viral screen for human immunodeﬁciency virus (HIV), infectious hepatitis, Epstein–Barr virus and cytomegalovirus
Ultrasound scan of the liver, including portal Doppler
explanation: B Complete full blood count This patient has asymptomatic jaundice following a recent viral infection. Gilbert syndrome is a common cause of unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia following fasting or physiological stress and is often diagnosed incidentally. It is characterised by mildly elevated bilirubin levels. In this patient who reveals no prior history of jaundice, it is important to rule out haemolysis as a cause of jaundice by also checking the patient’s full blood count. If this is abnormal, a blood ﬁlm, reticulocyte count, lactate dehydrogenase level and direct antigen test may also be requested. If these tests are negative, a presumptive diagnosis of Gilbert syndrome can be made. The diagnosis can be conﬁrmed by either an increase in bilirubin level provoked by fasting or by a slow rise in bilirubin level following administration of intravenous nicotinic acid. No treatment is necessary and the prognosis is excellent. A Complete viral screen for human immunodeﬁciency virus (HIV), infectious hepatitis, Epstein–Barr virus and cytomegalovirus Although this patient has had a recent viral illness, she has completely recovered and her liver function tests only reveal an abnormality in her bilirubin levels, pointing towards a diagnosis of Gilbert syndrome, which causes mild unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia. Viral screening for the above viruses would be necessary if she had evidence of acute liver disease on examination or her liver function tests. C Liver biopsy Liver biopsy is an invasive test and is not necessary to make a diagnosis of Gilbert syndrome in this patient who is otherwise well. A liver biopsy may be indicated if there is evidence of concomitant liver disease. D No further investigations necessary This patient likely has Gilbert syndrome which is a common cause of isolated unconjugated bilirubinaemia. However, given that this young patient reports no history of previous presentations with jaundice, it would be pertinent to rule out haemolysis (eg due to nonHodgkin’s lymphoma) as the cause of her bilirubinaemia and therefore, a full blood count of at least should be completed. If this reveals a low haemoglobin level, then further testing of reticulocyte count, blood ﬁlm, lactate dehydrogenase level and direct antigen test should be completed. E Ultrasound scan of the liver, including portal Doppler Although ultrasound scanning is a safe and non-invasive test, it is not necessary to make a diagnosis of Gilbert syndrome, especially in the absence of any evidence of liver disease on examination and normal transaminase levels on liver function testing.

stem: A 29-year-old sales assistant undergoes upper endoscopy for symptoms of dyspepsia. The OGD demonstrates a duodenal lesion and biopsies have returned showing a MALT lymphoma. What would be the best initial therapeutic strategy?
options: Test and treat for Helicobacter pylori
explanation: E Test and treat for Helicobacter pylori A MALT lymphoma is a B-cell tumour caused by an immune response to chronic H. pylori (HP) infection. The ﬁrst therapeutic strategy in treating a GI MALT lymphoma is to eradicate HP with a regimen of standard antibiotics and PPI, which leads to remission in 75% of cases. HP eradication regimens are usually given to all patients, due to the possibility of negative HP results. Patients should undergo a Carbon-13 urea breath test (UBT) approximately ≥6 weeks after eradication therapy and ≥2 weeks after PPI withdrawal, to conﬁrm eradication. The carbon-13 UBT is based on the detection of the products created when urea is split by the organism. Patients are asked to drink urea (usually with a beverage) labelled with a carbon isotope (carbon-13 or -14). After a certain duration, the concentration of the labelled carbon is measured on the breath. The concentration is high only when urease is present in the stomach. Because the human stomach does not produce urease, such a reaction is possible only with HP infection. Problems include negative results due to infection with coccoid forms of HP that do not produce as much urease; and intake of antibiotics, bismuth, histamine-2 (H2) blockers, or proton pump inhibitors. In the minority of patients who do not achieve lymphoma regression following antibiotic therapy, irradiation and systemic oncological therapies should be considered, depending on the stage of disease. A Duodenal stent insertion There is no suggestion from the history that the patient is suffering from symptoms of upper gastrointestinal tract or gastric outlet obstruction. B Radiotherapy In patients who do not achieve lymphoma regression following antibiotic therapy, radiotherapy with curative intent might be the preferred option for localised-stage disease. However, this is not an initial treatment strategy for this patient. C Chemotherapy In patients who do not achieve lymphoma regression following antibiotic therapy, chemo-immunotherapy with cyclophosphamide or chlorambucil may play a role in management, but this would not be an initial treatment strategy for this patient. D Laparoscopic resection Endoscopic mucosal resection and resectional surgery are rarely needed. In such instances, this would follow failure of initial medical therapies.

stem: A 38-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with nausea, vomiting and an upper GI haemorrhage. She admits that she went foraging for mushrooms some 3 days earlier and cooked some that she found in the forest, but no one else in the family wanted to take the risk of eating them. A sample of leftover mushrooms suggests they were Death Cap. On examination, her BP is 110/72 mmHg, with pulse 92/min and regular. She is tender in the epigastrium and right upper quadrant of her abdomen. There is dried blood around her lips and evidence of bruising on her arms and legs. Investigation Result Normal values Hb 91 g/l 135 - 175 g/l WCC 10.5 × 109/l 4.0 - 11.0 × 109/l PLT 121 × 109/l 150 - 400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 138 mmol/l 135 - 145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 5.2 mmol/l 3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 255 µmol/l 50 - 120 µmol/l Which of the following would be an indicator for transplant according to the King’s College Hospital criteria (nonparacetamol induced liver failure)?
explanation: D Bilirubin 320 µmol/l Bilirubin levels of >300 µmol/l is one of the prognostic indicators that determines referral for liver transplantation. Several factors are important in the prognosis of patients with acute liver failure. Several criteria have been developed to predict when liver transplantation is indicated, the most widely accepted being the King's College Hospital criteria: • INR >6.5; or, Three of the following ﬁve criteria: • Patient age <11 or >40; • Serum bilirubin >300 micromoles per litre; • Time from onset of jaundice to the development of coma >7 days; • INR >3.5; or • Drug toxicity, regardless of whether it was the cause of the acute liver failure. C Alkaline phosphatase 430 U/l ALP levels are not included in the King’s College Hospital criteria for predicting when to refer the patient for liver transplantation. A Age 34 Age of less than 11 years or more than 40 years is considered to be one of the prognostic indicator criteria for liver transplantation. B ALT 2300 U/l ALT level is not included in the King’s College Hospital criteria of prognostic indictors for liver transplantation. E INR 3.2 INR of >6.5 is considered one of the positive indicators that determines referral for liver transplantation.

stem: A 71-year-old woman with a background of previous non-ST elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI) and atrial ﬁbrillation presents with generalised abdominal pain. The pain is grumbling in character and has been worsening over the last 24 hours. She notes that she has had blood in her stool occasionally for the past few weeks. She is haemodynamically stable, and an inpatient colonoscopy is arranged. Her histology is shown below. Following the colonoscopy, she deteriorates rapidly, developing worsening abdominal pain and vomiting. Examination of her abdomen demonstrates guarding. Chest X-ray: normal Abdominal X-ray: no acute abnormality detected Lactate 6.2 mmol/l Normal Values 0.5 - 2.2 mmol/l What is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
explanation:
C Ischaemic colitis This patient has vascular risk factors and vague-sounding abdominal pain, with relatively rapid deterioration and a raised lactate level. These are all red ﬂags for ischaemic colitis. Moreover, the histology shows crypt loss with thickening of the mucosa and hyalinisation of the submucosa. There is also inﬂammatory cell inﬁltrate. Taken together these features indicate ischaemic colitis. D Perforation following colonoscopy While this history may well be suggestive of perforation following colonoscopy, the deterioration post- procedure, the lack of X-ray ﬁndings and the ischaemic changes on histology suggest that this condition was likely pre-existing before the colonoscopy and the deterioration was coincidental. However, it is important to note that colonoscopy can be a cause of ischaemic colitis, the diagnosis here. A Bowel cancer While malignancy must be suspected in patients with blood in the stool, this presentation is much too acute for bowel cancer, and an alternative diagnosis must be suspected.

B Infectious colitis Infectious colitis, eg caused by Escherichia coli, is an important differential. However, this is made less likely by the age of the patient and the fact that the history points to an ischaemic cause. These cases tend to present in epidemiological clusters. E Ulcerative colitis The patient’s age and the lack of change in bowel habit point away from ulcerative colitis, while the vascular risk factors are much more suggestive of an ischaemic cause.

stem: A 78-year-old retired banker was reviewed in the Outpatients Department after a recent admission with right lower lobe pneumonia. She has had two similar episodes, managed by her GP, over the last 2 years. She has mild angina for which she is taking Aspirin and Atenolol and problems swallowing that she has never addressed before. She is otherwise ﬁt and well. She smoked 15 cigarettes a day from the age of 20, and drinks 15 units of alcohol per week. Throughout her life, she has travelled widely in Africa and Asia. Examination revealed no abnormal signs and her blood tests were unremarkable. Her plain chest X-ray is shown below: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: C Achalasia A ﬂuid level is visible behind the heart and the oesophagus is dilated. This is suggestive of chronic oesophageal obstruction. From the scenario given and the radiological evidence supplied, achalasia is the most likely diagnosis. Achalasia can present at any age but is rare in childhood. Dysphagia is universal, and occurs for liquids and solids relatively early in the condition. Other typical symptoms may include regurgitation, weight loss, chest and abdominal pain, as well as possible aspiration pneumonitis (which may be the presenting complaint). Achalasia is caused by degeneration of the myenteric plexus, causing failure of relaxation of the lower oesophageal sphincter (LOS), and absent peristalsis in the body of the oesophagus. Diagnosis is conﬁrmed by oesophageal manometry, but prior upper gastrointestinal endoscopy is mandatory to exclude a tumour of the cardia. Tumours of the cardia may mimic achalasia, and chronic achalasia slightly increases the risk of oesophageal carcinoma. A number of treatment options are available. Pharmacological therapy includes calcium channel blockers (including Nifedipine) and nitrates, but tends to be only minimally effective. Injection of botulinum toxin into the LOS also produces variable degrees of success, but has a role in affected people who are unable to tolerate more invasive therapies. The major deﬁnitive choice of therapy, however, is between endoscopic dilatation (which carries the risk of perforation), or surgical intervention (Heller’s myotomy). There is also a growing role for an alternative combined surgical and endoscopic treatment called peroral endoscopic myotomy (POEM). D Chagas’ disease Chagas' disease can also mimic achlasia and is caused by Trypanosoma cruzi. Chagas’ disease, however, is conﬁned to South and Central America; this woman has travelled abroad but to Africa and Asia, meaning it is unlikely to be the diagnosis here. A Tracheo-oesophageal ﬁstula Outside of the paediatric setting, tracheo-oesophageal ﬁstula (TOF) is most associated with locally advanced oesophageal carcinoma, and/or as a complication of oesophageal carcinoma treated with radiotherapy or chemotherapy. This woman does not have a diagnosis of oesophageal carcinoma, making TOF unlikely. B Carcinoma of the lung The description of a signiﬁcant smoking history and recurrent pneumonia may make candidates think of carcinoma of the lung. However, an X-ray demonstrating oesophageal obstruction/ dilatation – without evidence of a lung lesion – makes achalasia and aspiration pneumonitis more likely as a diagnosis rather than primary lung carcinoma. E Pharyngeal pouch A pharyngeal pouch may cause recurrent aspiration pneumonitis, but is not associated with oesophageal obstruction.

stem: A 46-year-old man is admitted to hospital following a ﬁrst episode of syncope. It was witnessed by his wife, who said he suddenly went very pale and collapsed to the ﬂoor with loss of consciousness for a few seconds, and was immediately oriented on coming round. The patient described progressively worsening exertional dyspnoea and fatigue over the last few months. He had some pains in the small joints of his hands for the last few years, but more recently these had become more severe and had spread to involve other joints. He also reluctantly admitted to difﬁculties maintaining an erection recently, but put this down to being stressed at work. He was a solicitor, had never smoked, and drank approximately 16 units of alcohol per week. He had no signiﬁcant past medical history or family history and took no medications. On examination, he was dyspnoeic on minimal exertion. His pulse was irregularly irregular and his blood pressure was 110/60 mmHg. He had a raised jugular venous pressure, displaced apex beat, gallop rhythm and peripheral oedema. There were bilateral chest crepitations to the mid-zones. His abdomen was soft and not distended, with smooth, non-tender hepatomegaly but no palpable spleen. Neurological examination was normal. It was also noted that he had an absence of body hair, testicular atrophy and greyish skin pigmentation in his axillae and groins. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin (Hb) 140 g/l 135–175 g/l (WCC) 8.0 × 10 /l 9 4.0–11.0 × 10 /l9 Platelets (PLT) 250 × 10 /l 9 150–400 × 10 /l9 Sodium (Na ) + 136 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K ) + 3.8 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 120 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Urea 5.2 mmol/l 2.5–6.5 mmol/l Corrected calcium (Ca ) 2+ 2.20 mmol/l 2.20–2.60 mmol/l Bilirubin 14 μmol/l 2–17 µmol/l (ALP) 90 IU/l 30–130 IU/l (AST) 32 IU/l 10–40 IU/l (γGT) 48 IU/l 5–30 IU/l Albumin 38 g/l 35–55 g/l Cholesterol 5.2 mmol/l < 5.2 mmol/l Glucose (random) 15.2 mmol/l 3.5–5.5 mmol/l ECG Atrial fibrillation, widespread T-wave inversion CXR Cardiomegaly, pulmonary oedema Urinalysis Glucose +++ Echocardiogram (ECHO) Globally dilated and hypokinetic heart, no valvular lesions Which further investigation would be the most useful in conﬁrming the diagnosis?
options: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the pituitary fossa
explanation: A Genetic analysis The combination of pituitary dysfunction, arthralgia, diabetes mellitus, hepatomegaly (and cirrhosis) with normal liver function tests and cardiomyopathy points strongly towards a diagnosis of hereditary haemochromatosis (also known as ‘bronze diabetes’). This is an autosomal recessive disorder that is relatively common in Caucasians with approximately 1 in 300 people affected (homozygotes) and 10% of people carriers (heterozygotes). A genetic screen for the C282Y and H63D mutations exists. Haemochromatosis usually presents in men over the age of 40 years, and is much less common in women, presumably due to menstrual blood loss. It is due to excessive iron absorption from the small intestine and its subsequent deposition in cells of the liver, heart, pancreas and pituitary gland resulting in tissue damage and organ failure. The clinical features are as above. The abnormal skin pigmentation is due to melanin deposition, and the arthritis due to accumulation of calcium pyrophosphate in joints. If cirrhosis develops, there is an increased risk of hepatocellular carcinoma. The disease has an excellent prognosis if recognised and treated before complications develop. Diagnosis can be made by an elevated serum iron concentration, reduced total iron- binding capacity (TIBC) and increased transferrin saturation, although gene testing for haemochromatosis mutations is now also available and is the preferred way to conﬁrm the diagnosis. Liver biopsy may also be considered to demonstrate the extent of tissue damage and allow measurement of the hepatic iron concentration. Treatment with regular venesection or chelation therapy with desferrioxamine can result in a normal life expectancy. B Coronary angiography Although this patient has presented with symptoms of cardiac failure, given the constellation of symptoms and signs, the most likely cause is iron overload rather than coronary artery disease. C Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the pituitary fossa In this case pituitary dysfunction is related to iron overload rather than to a pituitary mass. MRI is therefore not indicated here. D Thyroid function tests Hypothyroidism is seen in association with haemochromatosis, related to pituitary dysfunction, although thyroid function testing wouldn’t conﬁrm the cause of the multiple endocrine deﬁciencies seen here. E 24 h ECG recording This may show evidence of arrhythmia, particularly atrial arrhythmias, although it won’t reveal the underlying cause of his presentation.

stem: A 64-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with abdominal pain and distension and a 2-day history of persistent vomiting. He has had intermittent abdominal pain for the last 5 weeks and diarrhoea for 3 days prior to the onset of vomiting. He has not passed a bowel motion since. His past medical history includes hypertension and coeliac disease, from which he has been asymptomatic for the past 10 years although he admits to being poorly compliant with his diet. He has lost 4 kg in weight over the past 5 months. Physical examination shows a distended abdomen. Bowel sounds are tinkling in nature. What is the most likely cause of this patient’s symptoms?
explanation: D Small bowel lymphoma Coeliac disease is a common and underdiagnosed condition, which may present at any age. It is a hypersensitivity to gluten found in wheat, rye and barley. The gliadin fraction of the protein provokes an inﬂammatory response causing subtotal or total villous atrophy of the small bowel, resulting in malabsorption. It classically presents with a history of diarrhoea, weight loss, lethargy and anaemia (folate, B12 or iron- deﬁcient). It is associated with an increased risk of developing small bowel lymphoma, which thankfully only occurs in a very small proportion of coeliac patients. It is the rapid deterioration seen here, with weight loss, which points us towards malignant transformation of the coeliac to small bowel lymphoma. E Small bowel carcinoma The history of coeliac disease makes small bowel lymphoma a more likely cause than carcinoma of the bowel, although carcinoma of the small bowel can also cause weight loss and small bowel obstruction. A Adhesions There is no previous history of bowel surgery or abdominal surgery to suggest that adhesions may be present to cause small bowel obstruction. B Carcinoma of the colon The history of coeliac disease makes small bowel lymphoma a more likely cause than carcinoma of the bowel, especially in the absence of lower GI symptoms before the presentation with acute abdomen. C Meckel’s diverticulum Meckel's diverticulum is the most common congenital anomaly of the gastrointestinal tract. It results from incomplete obliteration of the vitelline duct leading to the formation of a true diverticulum of the small intestine. Meckel's diverticulum is a true diverticulum, containing all layers of the small bowel wall. It arises from the anti- mesenteric surface of the middle-to-distal ileum. The diverticulum represents a persistent remnant of the omphalo-mesenteric duct, which connects the midgut to the yolk sac in the foetus. Meckel's diverticula are uncommon and often clinically silent, particularly in the adult. Asymptomatic Meckel's diverticulum may be discovered during abdominal exploration for the evaluation of unrelated pathology. Less commonly, it is found incidentally on diagnostic imaging. When symptomatic, Meckel's diverticulum may present with abdominal pain or symptoms of gastrointestinal bleeding or bowel obstruction. In this scenario, the past medical history of coeliac disease makes Meckel’s diverticulum a less likely diagnosis.

stem: A 40-year-old man attends clinic for investigation of heartburn symptoms. He has recently had an upper gastrointestinal (GI) endoscopy that has shown a shallow duodenal ulcer. The biopsies have shown the patient to be positive for Helicobacter pylori. He is currently only taking omeprazole and is allergic to penicillin. Which two antibiotics should be used for eradication therapy?
explanation: B Clarithromycin and metronidazole For patients who are penicillin allergic the recommended intervention for H. pylori eradication is a 1-week course of therapy with clarithromycin, metronidazole and a PPI. A post- treatment breath test may be used to conﬁrm eradication in the event that symptoms continue. Two weeks of therapy is considered when a MALT lymphoma has been identiﬁed. D Tetracycline and amoxicillin This is not a standard approach to eradication, and penicillin allergy precludes use of amoxicillin. A Ciproﬂoxacin and metronidazole Resistance rates of H. pylori are increasing to ciproﬂoxacin; this makes clarithromycin the preferred choice in patients who are penicillin allergic. Quinolone treatment is also no longer recommended wherever an effective alternative is available due to a small but signiﬁcant risk of debilitating adverse effects. C Tobramycin and ciproﬂoxacin Tobramycin is used in the ITU setting for gut decontamination of critically ill patients; it is not part of the standard approach to routine H. pylori eradication. E Chloramphenicol and metronidazole Chloramphenicol is reserved for life-threatening infections where resistance exists to other antibiotics, and is not used in routine practice for H. pylori eradication.

stem: A 42-year-old man presented to his GP complaining of lethargy, pruritus, right upper quadrant discomfort and dry mouth and eyes. Otherwise he was asymptomatic and had no previous history of note. He drank 24 units of alcohol per week. On examination, he had two-ﬁnger hepatomegaly and his spleen was just palpable. No signs of chronic liver disease were present. Investigation Result Normal Values Sodium (Na+) 132 mmol/l 135 - 145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.4 mmol/l 3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l Urea 2.4 mmol/l 2.5 - 6.5 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 70 µmol/l 50 - 120 µmol/l Albumin 3.4 g/dl 3.4 - 5.4 g/dl Bilirubin 25 µmol/l 1 - 22 µmol/l AST 44 u/l 10 - 40 u/l ALT 41 u/l 7 - 55 u/l ALP 556 u/l 30 - 150 u/l GGT 1021 u/l < 50 u/l (LDL) 3.22 mmol/l < 2.6 mmol/l (HDL) 5.56 mmol/l > 1 mmol/l Immunoglobulin M (IgM) 6.5 g/l 0.4 - 2.5 g/l What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
D Primary biliary cholangitis This man is most likely to have primary biliary cholangitis (PBC). This is a condition of unclear aetiology that is characterised by the destruction of the small and medium-sized bile ducts. There is a presumed autoimmune component to the pathogenesis of PBC, and other immunologically driven conditions (including Graves’ disease and pernicious anaemia) are found at higher rates in those with PBC than in the general population. PBC particularly affects women (female:male of 9: 1) and onset is usually between the ages of 30 and 60 years. The presenting symptoms are usually non-speciﬁc, with fatigue and pruritus being the most common complaints. Examination may be normal, although xanthelasmata are commonly found in association with PBC. Despite the name of the condition, there is actually a spectrum in the severity of liver disease associated with PBC; improvements in diagnostics mean that many people are diagnosed and ﬁrst treated whilst in an early phase of disease without signiﬁcant liver ﬁbrosis, although cirrhosis and portal hypertension may occur in advanced cases.

Investigation shows marked elevation of ALP and GGT, with lesser increases in the transaminases. Serum immunoglobulins (particularly IgM) are also often elevated. Positive antimitochondrial (M2) antibodies have a sensitivity and speciﬁcity of over 90%. Biopsy is not essential in making the diagnosis, although may help to conﬁrm the diagnosis and is useful for staging disease. Ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA) is the only speciﬁc treatment of any beneﬁt in PBC. For reasons that are not clear, not all affected people respond to UDCA. Treatment of the pruritus that occurs in PBC is often difﬁcult. Cholestyramine is the best treatment for pruritus, although it is often poorly tolerated; antihistamines, opiate antagonists and Rifampicin also have a role to play. Liver transplantation may be indicated for severe refractory pruritus, along with decompensated PBC cirrhosis. B Pancreatic carcinoma The history given in the scenario does not ﬁt with pancreatic carcinoma. A Gallstones The history given in the scenario does not ﬁt with gallstones. C Primary sclerosing cholangitis The elevated IgM and HDL cholesterol are consistent with PBC, but are not typical features of PSC. E Haemochromatosis Haemochromatosis tends to cause a hepatitic rather than a cholestatic illness.

stem: A 42-year-old woman comes to the Emergency Department complaining of severe epigastric pain, nausea and vomiting. You understand that she was recently started on medication for epilepsy. On examination, her blood pressure is 100/65 mmHg and her heart rate is 105 bpm regular. She is mildly pyrexial at 37.8 °C. Her epigastrium is very tender and she complains of severe pain on relatively minimal palpation. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal values Hb 121 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 13.1 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l PLT 130 × 109/l 150–400× 109/l Sodium (Na+) 138 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.5 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 142 μmol/l 50–120 μmol/l Corrected calcium (Ca2+) 2.14 mmol/l 2.2–2.7 mmol/l Amylase 1020 U/l 30–110 U/l Which of the following medications is most likely to be responsible?
explanation: D Valproate There is a good level of evidence to suggest valproate administration is associated with acute pancreatitis. Other medications associated with acute pancreatitis include, but are not limited to: azathioprine, 6- mercaptopurine, didanosine, codeine, isoniazid, 5-ASAs, metronidazole, pravastatin, procainamide, simvastatin, sulfamethoxazole, tetracycline, amiodarone, dexamethasone and lamivudine. B Phenytoin Phenytoin has not been reported to cause acute pancreatitis. A Gabapentin The woman has acute pancreatitis. Gabapentin has not been reported to induce acute pancreatitis. C Vigabatrin There is one case report of pancreatitis associated with vigabatrin and lamotrogine administration that has not been reproduced. E Lamotrigine There is minimal evidence to suggest lamotrigine administration is associated with acute pancreatitis. Reference Hung WY. Contemporary review of drug-induced pancreatitis: A different perspective. WJGP, 2014, 5, 405–

stem: A 50-year-old female Chinese patient who has recently moved to the UK presents with chronic diarrhoea. Her family report that she has worsening memory loss, depression and on direct questioning admits to insomnia. On examination, you ﬁnd dermatitis, tremor and ataxia. She has a normal full blood count, renal function, liver function and bone proﬁle in her blood results. You are concerned she may have a nu- tritional deﬁciency. Which vitamin is she most likely to be deﬁcient in?
explanation: E Nicotinic acid Deﬁciency in nicotinic acid (niacin) can cause pellagra, which presents with the triad of dermatitis, diarrhoea and dementia. It can also present with additional features of tremor, ataxia, insomnia, ﬁts and neuropathy. It most commonly presents in China and Africa and can be a side effect of tuberculosis (TB) treatment and carcinoid syndrome. C Vitamin B12 Vitamin B12 deﬁciency results in megaloblastic anaemia and can lead to neuropathy and neuropsychiatric problems. As the patient has a normal full blood count it is unlikely that her symptoms are related to B12 deﬁciency. A Vitamin A Vitamin A deﬁciency causes xerophthalmia, which is a major cause of blindness in the tropics. B Vitamin C Vitamin C can cause scurvy, which results in infections, anorexia, hyperkeratosis, bleeding tendency and halitosis. D Vitamin B1 Thiamine (vitamin B1) deﬁciency can cause wet beriberi (heart failure, peripheral oedema) or dry beriberi (neuropathy).

stem: A patient presents with easy fatigability, lethargy and intermittent diarrhoea. He is 28 years old and works as a solicitor. He has an uncle with type 1 diabetes and his mother has autoimmune hypothyroidism. On examination, he looks pale and tired. His BMI is 20 and he has an itchy rash on his arms and trunk. There is mild pitting oedema of both lower limbs. Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin 100 g/l 135–175 g/l MCV 118 ﬂ 76–98 ﬂ WCC 7.6 × 109/l 4–11 × 109/l Platelets 190 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 139 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.1 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 120 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Albumin 28 g/l 35–55 g/l ALT 56 IU/l 5–30 IU/l Glucose 4.8 mmol/l 3.5–5.5 mmol/l Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: A Coeliac disease The combination of diarrhoea, malabsorption and family history of two T-cell mediated autoimmune disorders, (Type 1 diabetes and Hashimoto’s disease) points towards coeliac disease or pernicious anaemia. However, pernicious anaemia does not usually present with intermittent diarrhoea. Although coeliac disease traditionally presents with iron deﬁciency anaemia, both folate and B12 deﬁciency are also commonly reported. The presence of an itchy rash on the arms and trunk is suggestive of dermatitis herpetiformis, which is strongly associated with coeliac disease and makes this the most likely answer. The next line of investigation would involve testing for coeliac antibodies (anti TTG or endomysial) followed by a duodenal biopsy, which should demonstrate increased intraepithelial lymphocytes and villous atrophy. B Crohn’s disease The history of diarrhoea and malabsorption mean this would be on the differential, particularly in the presence of classical terminal ileal involvement leading to B12 malabsorption. However, the description of dermatitis herpetiformis points towards coeliac as the more likely diagnosis. Cutaneous manifestations of Crohn’s include erythema nodosum and pyoderma gangrenosum. C Hypothyroidism Hypothyroidism would more commonly present with constipation and weight gain. Although hypothyroidism can cause a macrocytic anaemia, in this case it seems more likely to be secondary to malabsorption due to coeliac disease. D Pernicious anaemia Pernicious anaemia occurs as a result of intrinsic factor deﬁciency. Intrinsic factor is produced by the parietal cells in the stomach and pernicious anaemia is commonly seen in autoimmune and atrophic gastritis. Pernicious anaemia does not present with diarrhoea or dermatitis herpetiformis. E Blind loop syndrome More commonly referred to as small bowel intestinal overgrowth this can indeed lead to malabsorptive diarrhoea, vitamin B12 deﬁciency and unintentional weight loss. However, patients tend to have a predisposing reason for the overgrowth (for example previous bowel surgery, inﬂammatory bowel disease, small bowel diverticulae or scleroderma), none of which are reported in this case.

stem: A 27-year-old Zimbabwean woman presents to the Emergency Department following two episodes of haematemesis. She gives a 4-week history of increasing heartburn and dysphagia for both solids and liquids. She has been treated by her general practitioner (GP) with anti-reﬂux medication, with only partial relief of her symptoms. She has lost 2 kg in weight over the last 6 weeks. On examination, there is cervical lymphadenopathy and mild epigastric tenderness on palpation. Abdominal examination is otherwise unremarkable. She is admitted for investigation and undergoes a gastroscopy that reveals widespread shallow ulceration of the oesophagus with adherent white patches. What is the most likely cause for this patient's dysphagia?
explanation: C Candida oesophagitis This patient has developed candida oesophagitis as a complication of HIV infection. The appearance of the oesophagus at endoscopy is typical of candida infection.
