Approximately 90% of patients with HIV/AIDS will develop oral/oesophageal candidiasis. A Barrett’s oesophagus Barrett's is associated with prolonged, severe reﬂux disease. It is associated with increased risk of oesophageal malignancy. B Cytomegalovirus Infection with cytomegalovirus classically causes giant ulcers, although the symptom picture is similar to that seen here. D Gastro-oesophageal reﬂux GORD is likely to have a more pronounced improvement with antireﬂux medication and a more prolonged symptom course. On endoscopy the appearance is of distal ulceration/erythema, rather than the multiple adherent white patches seen here. E Oesophageal carcinoma Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) and adenocarcinoma account for >95% of oesophageal malignant tumours. Barium studies may suggest the presence of oesophageal cancer, but the diagnosis is established with endoscopic biopsy. Early oesophageal cancers appear endoscopically as superﬁcial plaques, nodules or ulcerations. Advanced lesions appear as strictures, ulcerated masses, circumferential masses or large ulcerations. The adherent white patches are not typical of oesophageal carcinoma.

stem: A 72-year-old heavy smoker presents with indigestion, which is now complicated by progressive dysphagia, ﬁrst to solids such as toast and now to liquids as well. Bloods taken by his general practitioner (GP) suggest iron deﬁciency anaemia and his viscosity is elevated. On examination, he has palpable lymph nodes in the left supraclavicular fossa, and wheeze throughout both lung ﬁelds. Which of the following would be the investigation of choice in this patient?
explanation: A Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy The presence of dysphagia and the enlarged left supraclavicular nodes raises the possibility of upper GI carcinoma, most likely oesophageal. As such, the investigation of choice would be upper GI endoscopy with biopsy. Carcinomas of the oesophagus may be squamous or adenocarcinomas; there is an association with smoking, alcohol consumption, ingestion of nitrate-containing foods, Plummer–Vinson syndrome, and chronic gastro-oesophageal reﬂux disease. Taking into account there is already lymph node enlargement, this patient is highly unlikely to be a candidate for oesophagectomy. Squamous cell carcinoma is more responsive than adenocarcinoma to radiotherapy, so this is at least an option for some patients. Unfortunately, 5 year survival for oesophageal carcinoma is very poor. D Bronchoscopy Given the predominant symptoms of indigestion and dysphagia, an endoscopy is likely to prove more useful in this situation. B Barium swallow Although barium swallow may demonstrate a stricture, it won’t conﬁrm the diagnosis or reveal a histological diagnosis. C Chest X-ray A chest x-ray is insensitive with respect to demonstrating an underlying oesophageal carcinoma, although it may show evidence of aspiration. E CT scan of the thorax Although a CT scan may demonstrate an oesophageal lesion and surrounding lymphadenopathy, it is unlikely to demonstrate a small cancer and won’t provide biopsy information.

stem: A 55-year-old man is admitted to the hospital with a 1-month history of dysphagia to solids. He has previously been ﬁt and well and, on direct questioning, denies previous episodes of dysphagia or reﬂux. On examination, he appears cachectic, although there are no palpable masses on abdominal examination. An upper endoscopy is performed, which reveals a lower oesophageal mass, not invading the gastro-oesophageal junction. Biopsy of this mass reveals an adenocarcinoma. Computed tomography (CT) scan of the patient’s chest, abdomen and pelvis is completed. After a multidisciplinary team (MDT) discussion, the tumour is staged as Tumour (T)3, Node (N)1, Metastasis (M)0. Which would be the most appropriate treatment for this patient?
options: External beam radiotherapy and oesophageal stenting
Neoadjuvant cisplatin, paclitaxel and radiotherapy followed by oesophagectomy
Neoadjuvant cisplatin and ﬂuorouracil followed by endoscopic mucosal resection
explanation: C Neoadjuvant cisplatin, paclitaxel and radiotherapy followed by oesophagectomy In T3–4, N1–3, M0 disease, the recommended treatment is neoadjuvant treatment, usually with cisplatin and paclitaxel plus radiotherapy followed by oesophagectomy. This is the standard regime based on the results of the Chemoradiotherapy for Oesophageal Cancer Followed by Surgery Study (CROSS) trial. This approach has been found to improve survival and resection rates, compared with surgery alone, in patients with oesophageal adenocarcinoma. Patients must be assessed for suitability for surgery. If unsuitable for surgery, they may be offered deﬁnitive chemoradiotherapy alone. This may be followed by nivolumab in patients who have residual pathological disease following neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy and surgery, particularly if there is lymph node involvement due to the high risk of disease recurrence. E Oesophagectomy Oesophagectomy alone is recommended for limited disease T1b or low-risk localised T2 disease in patients who are suitable for surgery. In high-risk T2 disease or above, neoadjuvant or deﬁnitive chemoradiotherapy is recommended. A Deﬁnitive chemoradiotherapy Deﬁnitive chemoradiotherapy would be an appropriate treatment for this patient if there were any indications that he was not suitable for surgery. Given that we are told he is usually ﬁt and well, with no indication of any past medical history, he is likely to beneﬁt from surgery and, therefore, this is not an appropriate treatment option. B External beam radiotherapy and oesophageal stenting External beam radiotherapy and oesophageal stenting may be offered to patients with metastatic disease (M1), in addition to palliative chemoradiotherapy, depending on the degree of dysphagia caused by the oesophageal tumour and its impact on nutrition, quality of life, performance status and prognosis. This treatment may also be considered for recurrent disease. D Neoadjuvant cisplatin and ﬂuorouracil followed by endoscopic mucosal resection Endoscopic therapy alone is recommended for patients with localised T1a disease. It is recommended over surgery, as those treated with endoscopic therapy have been shown to have improved cancerspeciﬁc survival and decreased morbidity. Endoscopic therapy is not usually recommended in combination with chemotherapy. It may be used as an alternative agent to chemoradiotherapy in T1b disease when patients are not suitable for surgery.

stem: A 22-year-old student teacher presents to the emergency general practitioner with severe, unremitting vomiting that has lasted for the past 13 h. There is associated fever, headache, diarrhoea and myalgia. He is unable even to keep water down. History of note is that six members of his class were absent today due to gastroenteritis, and it is currently November. Both the diarrhoea and vomiting were profuse and watery, with no sign of blood. Which one of the following is the most likely cause for this presentation?
explanation: C Norovirus The rapid presentation, coupled with a number of virtually simultaneous cases in his class of students, suggests a viral aetiology in this case. Norovirus belongs to the Calicivirus family, members of which may be responsible for a number of outbreaks of viral gastroenteritis, often during the winter months. Rotavirus is a member of the Reoviridae family and causes diarrhoea that may be dramatic in onset. Intravenous ﬂuid replacement is rarely required in adults presenting with these infections, and the majority can be managed as outpatients with oral rehydration therapy. E Shigella infection Shigella gastroenteritis can occur with any food and is spread by the faecal-oral route. It occurs after an incubation period of 2-3 days and causes bloody diarrhoea, abdominal pain and fever. The absence of abdominal pain and bloody diarrhoea makes this less likely. A Campylobacter infection Campylobacter gastroenteritis occurs following ingestion of contaminated milk, poultry or water. Following an incubation period of 2-5 days, there is bloody diarrhoea, abdominal pain, fever and sometimes peritonism. The absence of the above symptoms and rapid onset makes this an unlikely diagnosis. B Salmonella infection Salmonella gastroenteritis occurs following ingestion of contaminated poultry or eggs. Eggs are routinely screened in the UK, making this unusual infection. Infection occurs 12-48 h following exposure and presents with diarrhoea, vomiting, abdominal pain, fever and can progress to sepsis. Again the presentation does not match. D Cryptosporidium infection Cryptosporidium causes gastroenteritis in immunocompromised patients only after ingestion of water contaminated by cows. The absence of evidence of immunocompromise makes this less likely.

stem: A 52-year-old woman with a background of systemic sclerosis presents to the Gastroenterology Clinic with ﬂatulence, bloating and intermittent diarrhoea. She reports some abdominal pain and dyspepsia. Her current medications include nifedipine, omeprazole and senna. More recently, she has become fatigued and has noticed some new tingling in her hands and feet. Investigation: Investigation Result Normal value Hb 106 g/l 115–155 g/l MCV 106 ﬂ 76–98 ﬂ WCC 5.0 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l PLT 203 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 139 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.5 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 100 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Folate 10μg/l > 2.1 μg/l B12 80 ng/l > 150 ng/l Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
A Bacterial overgrowth syndrome This patient is presenting with symptoms of abdominal pain, ﬂatulence, diarrhoea and dyspepsia, alongside vitamin B12 deﬁciency. Given her past history of systemic sclerosis and her use of laxatives, it is likely that this patient has existing diverticular disease. Stasis of stool in small bowel diverticula can lead to bacterial overgrowth syndrome. This condition often results in malabsorption of fat, vitamin B12 and fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E and K). Animal models have demonstrated that there is competitive uptake of vitamin B12 by bacteria in the small intestine, which results in B12 deﬁciency. Folate levels become raised due to increased synthesis of folate by small bowel bacteria. Bacterial overgrowth syndrome can be diagnosed via the hydrogen breath test. Treatment involves empirical antibiotic treatment (eg metronidazole and tetracycline), as well as treatment of the underlying cause of the bacterial overgrowth. B Crohn’s disease Crohn’s disease is associated with vitamin B12 deﬁciency due to malabsorption in the terminal ileum. However, the key to diagnosis here is the patient’s background history of systemic sclerosis, putting her at risk of small bowel diverticulosis which can result in bacterial overgrowth syndrome. She also has an excess of folate, which is in keeping with bacterial overgrowth syndrome, rather than small bowel malabsorption due to Crohn’s disease. C Irritable bowel syndrome The abnormal investigation ﬁndings here, with macrocytic anaemia and vitamin B12 deﬁciency, essentially rule out irritable bowel syndrome as an underlying diagnosis. D Laxative misuse Laxative misuse may result in symptoms of diarrhoea and abdominal pain. However, this would be less likely to cause vitamin B12 deﬁciency and an excess of folate.

E Pernicious anaemia Although pernicious anaemia can result in vitamin B12 deﬁciency due to a lack of intrinsic factor, which helps the body to absorb vitamin B12, the key to diagnosis in this patient is the past history of systemic sclerosis. Furthermore, pernicious anaemia would not lead to folate excess. This has led to diverticular disease in the small bowel, which has resulted in bacterial overgrowth syndrome.

stem: You are asked to see an 18-year-old woman who is being treated with intravenous (IV) N-acetylcysteine for a paracetamol overdose. She is 20 minutes into the infusion and develops facial ﬂushing, severe itching and her blood pressure drops by 12 mmHg. The infusion has been stopped and the Foundation Year 1 (FY1) has given IV antihistamine. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
options: Restart the N-acetylcysteine infusion at the same rate
Re-start the N-acetylcysteine infusion at half rate
explanation: D Re-start the N-acetylcysteine infusion at half rate Patient on intravenous N-acetylcysteine can experience immediate or infusion-related side effects. Immediate side effects, including anaphylactoid or hypersensitivity-like reactions, have been reported in 0.3–3% of patients, in patients with low or absent paracetamol concentrations and in patients with liver cirrhosis. Infusion- related side effects occur due to rapid administration of the infusion, and are usually related to a higher incidence of hypersensitivity reactions. This patient was appropriately treated with antihistamine and N- acetylcysteine was stopped, which should be restarted at a slower rate after the adverse reaction has settled. E Switch to oral therapy Patients coming to the A&E with paracetamol overdose often have an associated history of alcohol intake and episodes of vomiting, which can affect the pharmacokinetics of oral medications. Thus, switching to oral therapy is therefore not the right option. A Do not restart N-acetylcysteine Paracetamol overdose can result in liver damage that may be fatal. Intravenous acetylcysteine is the antidote to treat paracetamol overdose, and is virtually 100% effective in preventing liver damage when given within 8 h of the overdose. Therefore, this option is wrong as N-acetylcysteine should restart after adverse effects have settled, but at a slower rate. B Give activated charcoal Activated charcoal is administered in patients who are clinically stable with patent airway, and if presented to the A&E within 1 h of paracetamol ingestion. C Restart the N-acetylcysteine infusion at the same rate This is an incorrect option as the infusion should be restarted at a slower rate to minimise the recurrence of adverse effects.

stem: A 27-year-old ofﬁce worker presents with a 3-year history of epigastric pain, especially 30 min after eating. This is associated with nausea and belching. She also describes constipation with occasional explosive diarrhoea. The stools are normally hard with mucus and she needs to strain with every motion. Abdominal pain is relieved after defecation but abdominal bloating persists. She wakes up an hour earlier each morning to ﬁnish her breakfast in order to prevent vomiting. She has missed work on a few occasions and feels that her weight has ﬂuctuated. Past medical history includes scarlet fever. She is not on any regular medications except intermittent laxatives over the counter. Abdominal examination is normal. Rectal examination reveals an anal ﬁssure. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Value Hb 131 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 6.0 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l PLT 180 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l MCV 87 ﬂ 76–98 ﬂ INR 1.0 < 1.1 ESR 1.1 mm/hour 1–20 mm/hour Sodium (Na+) 136 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 3.9 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Urea 3.7 mmol/l 2.5–6.5 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 70 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Albumin 39 g/l 35–55 g/l Liver function tests (LFTs) Normal Anti-endomysial antibody Negative Thyroid function tests (TFTs) Normal Gastroscopy Normal Flexible sigmoidoscopy and biopsy Normal Abdominal and pelvic ultrasound scan Normal What is the most likely diagnosis to account for her symptoms?
options: Overlap irritable bowel syndrome and functional dyspepsia
explanation:
A Overlap irritable bowel syndrome and functional dyspepsia This lady has signs of irritable bowel syndrome, especially in light of all the normal investigation results. It is the result of complex interactions between psychosocial factors, disordered bowel motility and altered intestinal sensations. This disorder is commonly associated with functional dyspepsia and patients are more likely to get chronic fatigue syndrome and globus hystericus. Diagnostic criteria have been developed, most notably the ‘Rome criteria’. These include symptoms of abdominal pain relieved by defecation that is associated with a change in stool frequency and consistency, abdominal bloating and passing mucus per rectum. B Diarrhoea pre-dominant irritable bowel syndrome Although she does report occasional diarrhoea, her more predominant symptom is constipation. C Sphincter of Oddi dysfunction The classical symptoms of Sphincter of Oddi dysfunction are of recurrent biliary-type epigastric / right upper quadrant pain, which last from 30 minutes to several hours, and is not relieved by bowel movements. It is not typically associated with diarrhoea, or a change in stool consistency. For diagnosis, the patient must have biliary pain, and imaging must reveal the absence of bile duct stones or other structural abnormalities, and elevated liver enzymes or dilated bile duct, but not both. D Malabsorption sydrome and non-ulcer dyspepsia There is no supporting evidence in the history of a malabsorption syndrome: no sustained weight loss, albumin is normal, and coeliac antibodies are negative. E Globus hystericus Globus sensation is a functional oesophageal disorder characterized by a sensation of a lump, retained food bolus, or tightness in the throat that is not due to an underlying structural lesion, gas-

troesophageal reﬂux disease, mucosal abnormality, or an esophageal motility disorder. This is not the presentation of this patient.

stem: A 62-year-old woman is referred to the Gastroenterology Clinic with worsening diarrhoea. She denies vomiting and fever, although she does describe intermittent facial ﬂushing. There is no past medical history of note. On examination, her blood pressure is 101/58 mmHg and her heart rate is 88 bpm. Her abdomen is soft and only mildly tender, with active bowel sounds. There is facial telangiectasia and evidence of tricuspid regurgitation. Her body mass index is 21 kg/m2. Routine bloods undertaken by her General Practitioner reveal: Investigation Result Normal values Hb 108 g/l 135 - 175 g/l Sodium (Na+) 135 mmol/l 135 - 145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 3.2 mmol/l 3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l Urea 5.5 mmol/l 2.5–6.5 mmol/l Creatinine 100 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l ALT 215 u/l 7 - 55 u/l What is the next best investigation to conﬁrm the diagnosis?
explanation: D Urinary 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid (5-HIAA) Urinary 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid (5-HIAA) is used in the diagnosis of carcinoid syndrome. Carcinoid syndrome presents with facial ﬂushing (75–90% of patients), diarrhoea (> 70%) and intermittent bronchospasm (25%). Associated clinical ﬁndings include facial telangiectasia and tricuspid regurgitation. It is caused by the action of serotonin, bradykinin and histamine produced by tumours arising from neuroendocrine cells. Diagnosis is by measuring an increase in the levels of urinary 5-HIAA, a metabolite of serotonin (5-HT). It is likely that this patient’s abnormal alanine aminotransferase level is due to the presence of liver metastases. Pellagra is a nicotinic acid deﬁciency that can occur as a result of increased requirements for nicotinamide due to the carcinoid tumour. It is an important substrate in the metabolic formation of 5-HT. Deﬁciency in nicotinic acid can lead to dementia in patients with extensive carcinoid metastases. E Urinary metanephrines Urinary metanephrines are used in the investigation of phaeochromocytoma. This is associated with marked hypertension and headaches and may be associated with hypokalaemia. However, it is not associated with signiﬁcant diarrhoea. A 0900 cortisol Cortisol measurement taken at 0900 is used in the diagnosis of Cushing’s disease. This disease is associated with signiﬁcant weight gain, which does not ﬁt with the diagnosis here. B Iron-binding studies Iron deﬁciency alone is unlikely, given the other symptoms, including facial ﬂushing, diarrhoea and evidence of tricuspid regurgitation— all of which ﬁt better with carcinoid. C Thyroid receptor antibodies Thyroid receptor antibodies are used in the diagnosis of autoimmune hyper- or hypothyroidism. Although thyrotoxicosis may be associated with weight loss and diarrhoea, features such as telangiectasia, tricuspid regurgitation and elevated transaminase levels would be unexpected in the context of hyperthyroidism.

stem: A 59-year-old woman presents to the Gastroenterology Clinic for review. She was referred by her General Practitioner with cramping abdominal pain and frequent episodes of diarrhoea. On further questioning, she denies indigestion. There is no signiﬁcant past medical history, apart from hypertension which is controlled with bendroﬂumethiazide. She drinks two bottles of wine per week. Examination reveals a blood pressure of 135/72 mmHg and a heart rate of 75 bpm and regular. She has pale conjunctivae. There are no abnormal ﬁndings, and her body mass index is 24 kg/m2. Investigations Results Normal value Hb 91 g/l 115–155 g/l MCV 78 ﬂ 76–98 ﬂ Ferritin 18 µg/l 10–120 µg/l WCC 8.1 × 109/l 4–11 × 109/l PLT 201 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 137 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.3 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 85 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Albumin 30 g/l 35–55 g/l ALT 44 IU/l 5–30 IU/l Amylase 50 U/l 70–300 U/l Which of the following is the most appropriate investigation?
explanation: D Tissue transglutaminase The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence guidelines recommend coeliac screening for any patient who presents with iron deﬁciency anaemia before beginning speciﬁc investigations. This is because of the recognition that underlying coeliac disease may present without the classical symptoms of abdominal bloating and diarrhoea. In this case, the low albumin level hints at chronic malabsorption, which may be due to an underlying small bowel disease. Following coeliac antibody testing, the patient should be referred for both upper and lower gastrointestinal investigations, with colonoscopy being a more deﬁnitive option (when preparation is adequate), compared to barium enema. A Ultrasound abdomen An abdominal ultrasound scan would be an appropriate ﬁrst-line investigation in patients with deranged liver function tests or abdominal pain. In this case, the patient importantly has no symptoms to suggest this and there are no data indicating signiﬁcantly deranged liver function tests. B Colonoscopy Colonoscopy is an important investigation to consider. However, importantly, in this case, there are no red ﬂag symptoms (eg weight loss or change in bowel habit). Therefore, it would be reasonable to screen the patient for coeliac disease before referring them for a colonoscopy. The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence guidelines state that all patients over the age of 60 with unexplained iron deﬁciency anaemia should be referred for a colonoscopy on the 2-week wait rule. C Faecal elastase Faecal elastase is a test of the exocrine function of the pancreas, particularly for patients with chronic pancreatitis. Chronic pancreatitis is commonly caused by alcohol excess and symptoms include abdominal pain and steatorrhoea. Amylase levels are often elevated, but not always. However, chronic pancreatitis does not explain this patient’s anaemia and the lack of a history of acute pancreatitis makes the diagnosis even less likely. E Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy This would be an investigation that could be considered if the patient had a normal colonoscopy and a normal coeliac screen.

stem: A 42-year-old former intravenous drug abuser presents to the Hepatology Clinic for review. He has just completed a 48-week course of Peg-interferon alpha-2a for hepatitis B infection. On examination, his observations are within normal limits. His abdomen is soft, with no obvious stigmata of liver disease. On review in the clinic, his results are as follows: Investigation Result HBsAg Positive HBeAg Positive Anti-HBc IgG Positive Anti-HBs IgG Negative Anti-HCV IgG Negative HCV RNA Negative Investigation Result Normal value Albumin 27 g/l 35–55 g/l ALT 122 u/l 7–55 u/l ALP 148 u/l 30–150 u/l Bilirubin 24 µmol/l 1–22 µmol/l Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
explanation:
B Switch to tenofovir This patient still shows signs of hepatitis B infection, given positive HBsAg and HBeAg. A positive anti-HBc IgG suggests chronic infectivity. Management of hepatitis B and C has been revolutionised

over recent years by the introduction of novel antiviral agents. In this situation, tenofovir is a logical next step and is recommended by the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE). Tenofovir is a nucleotide reverse transcriptase inhibitor which inhibits hepatitis B deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) replication. A Continue interferon Given that interferon has failed to achieve clearance of hepatitis B, alternative therapy is required. C Switch to lamivudine Lamivudine is less effective, compared to modern agents such as entecavir or tenofovir. It does, however, carry a lower acquisition cost, compared to more modern agents. D Reassurance and stop treatment This patient still shows signs of active infection with positive HBsAg and HBeAg. Therefore, additional treatment is needed. E Switch to ribavirin Ribavirin is used in combination with interferon for the treatment of hepatitis C. However, the combination is less effective than more modern agents, such as boceprevir, and has therefore been largely superseded.

stem: A young adult man is admitted to hospital after a seizure. He admits to drinking at least a bottle of vodka per day. He says he stopped drinking one day ago as he ran out of money. He previously had seizures after stopping drinking alcohol. He says he would like to stop forever and is admitted for a detoxiﬁcation regime and intravenous (iv) thiamine. Blood investigation showed AST 190 U/L and ALT-68 U/L. Which of the following results would you most expect to ﬁnd in his serum immunology screen?
explanation: A Markedly raised IgA Alcoholic hepatitis causes a markedly raised IgA, and it can also cause a mildly elevated IgG and IgM. Raised IgA can also be present in both chronic active hepatitis and IgA nephropathy. AST is often more than twice the ALT in alcoholic liver disease. If the ALT is >300 U/l, you may suspect an alternative cause for the deranged liver function results such as paracetamol overdose, an infective cause of the hepatitis, ischaemic hepatitis or autoimmune hepatitis. Hyperbilirubinaemia is often seen in alcoholic liver disease and can be up to 500 μmol/l. This usually reﬂects the severity of the disease. There will also usually be an elevated GGT and ALP. E Low IgM Selective IgM deﬁciency is a rare congenital immunodeﬁciency, with approximately 300 cases described, it is associated with severe bacterial infections with onset in childhood. B Low IgA Deﬁciency of IgA is associated with autoimmune disorders, chronic diarrhoea and respiratory infections. C Markedly raised IgM A raised IgM may be seen in primary biliary cholangitis, Waldenström’s macroglobulinaemia and as an acute response to infection. D Markedly raised IgE A markedly raised IgE would raise suspicion of non-liver-related diseases such as atopic dermatitis, psoriasis, asthma, allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA) and parasitic infection.

stem: A 78-year-old ex-medical secretary presents with a 6-month history of intermittent rectal bleeding, loose stool and weight loss. Her past medical history includes multi-nodular goitre and cervical carcinoma diagnosed 1 year ago. She received treatment at a different hospital. She takes carbimazole. On examination, she looks thin and pale. Abdominal examination is unremarkable. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Value Hb 89 g/l 115–155 g/l (WBC) 11.2 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l PLT 170 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l MCV 74 ﬂ 76–98 ﬂ Barium enema shows luminal narrowing of the distal sigmoid colon with some irregularity of the bowel wall, with no focal lesions. Colonoscopy is performed, the appearance of which is shown below: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
B Radiation enteritis Radiation injury to the rectum and sigmoid colon is commonly seen following treatment of cancers of the cervix, uterus, prostate and bladder. It often occurs 9–14 months following radiation exposure and results in a chronically ischaemic intestinal segment that may lead to stricture. Symptoms include diarrhoea, obstructed defaecation, bleeding, rectal pain or urgency. Diagnosis can be conﬁrmed with colonoscopy, and mucosal features consistent with radiation injury include pallor, friability and telangiectasias. Biopsy is not diagnostic but is helpful to exclude other causes. There have been no large controlled trials to evaluate the treatment of radiation proctitis, but a systemic review of available trials shows promising results for rectal sucralfate and metronidazole combined with topical anti-inﬂammatory treatment and heater probe. A Diverticulitis A diverticulum is an outpouching of the gut which usually occurs at the site of entry of perforating arteries. Diverticulitis is inﬂammation of a diverticulum. The presence of a diverticulum, termed diverticulosis, may cause altered bowel habits and left lower abdominal pain relieved by defaecation. In diverticulitis there would be added features of fever and peritonism, which can progress to haemorrhage or perforation. The history of chronic weight loss, chronic bleeding and narrowing sigmoid colon makes this an unlikely diagnosis. C Ulcerative colitis Ulcerative colitis (UC) is a type of inﬂammatory bowel disease. In

UC, gut involvement starts from the rectum and may spread to involve the entire colon. It causes episodic or chronic diarrhoea, which can include blood and mucus. There is commonly crampy abdominal pain with bowel frequency and urgency relating to severity. Patients also develop fever, malaise, anorexia and weight loss. The history would generally ﬁt, but the age of the patient is much higher than would be expected for UC, which normally presents between 15 and 30 years old. Also, the absence of abdominal signs makes it less likely. D Microscopic colitis Microscopic colitis is a chronic inﬂammatory disease of the colon characterised by chronic and watery diarrhoea, typically in a middle-aged female patient. It is not bloody, but can be associated with abdominal pain. The presence of anaemia and the late age of presentation, as well as the ﬁndings of sigmoid narrowing, makes this a less likely diagnosis. E Pseudomembranous colitis Pseudomembranous colitis is a complication of C. difﬁcile infection. The infection forms pseudomembranes on histology. It is associated with acute diarrhoea and abdominal pain following recent antibiotic use. The absence of antibiotics makes this less likely, and the history would be more acute in nature.

stem: You are asked to review a 56-year-old man who works in a smoked meats and ﬁsh factory. He receives free food from the factory every month. He complains of increasing indigestion and has lost a stone in weight over the past 2 months. He drinks 10 units per week. On examination, he has a mass in the epigastrium and a hard, palpable liver. Investigations reveal a microcytic anaemia; alanine aminotransferase and alkaline phosphatase are also both raised. Which of the following is the most likely underlying aetiological factor in his condition?
explanation: A Smoked foods This clinical picture is suggestive of gastric cancer. The patient has iron deﬁciency anaemia and a mass in the epigastrium. Aetiological risk factors include chronic H. pylori infection, tobacco abuse, alcohol consumption, food additives (nitrosamines), smoked foods, occupational exposure to heavy metals, rubber and asbestos. Although in a normal diet smoked foods only cause a very modest effect on risk of stomach cancer, in this case, regular consumption inis associated with elevated risk. Other associations with gastric cancer are gastritis with intestinal metaplasia, hypertrophic gastritis and pernicious anaemia. Unfortunately, few patients present early enough to be suitable for surgery. Whilst chemotherapy has not been proven to prolong survival, it may provide some degree of palliation. With the presence of metastases, gastrectomy is only considered in rare cases to prolong duration and quality of life. Five-year survival of gastric carcinoma is 12% overall, although survival for early carcinomas where resection is possible is much higher (>35%). Imatinib (Glivec) is an effective treatment for gastrointestinal stromal tumours (GIST) but is not useful in the management of gastric adenocarcinoma. D Chronic H. pylori infection H pylori does signiﬁcantly increase the risk of gastric cancer, although the weekly gifts of smoked foods are more likely here to be an aetiological factor. B Alcohol consumption This patient’s alcohol consumption is very modest and unlikely therefore to be a signiﬁcant contributor to risk of gastric cancer. C Genetics Hereditary gastric cancer syndromes such as hereditary diffuse gastric cancer do exist, but they are very rare, HDGC is autosomal dominant in its inheritance pattern. E Pernicious anaemia Pernicious anaemia is associated with a 2-4 fold increased risk of gastric cancer, less than may be expected with respect to the risk associated with excessive smoked foods consumption in this case.

stem: A 19-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with abdominal pain and vomiting. She has a long history of cramping abdominal pain, as does her younger brother. Her father has had two laparotomies. Examination and investigation reveals signs of small-bowel obstruction. A picture of her mouth is shown below: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
D Peutz-Jeghers syndrome The history of small bowel obstruction with the classic signs of perioral pigmentation ﬁts with Peutz-Jeghers syndrome. This disorder is inherited in an autosomal dominant fashion, with the defect being in a gene on chromosome 19 which encodes a serine threonine kinase. The characteristic pigmentation occurs circumorally, on the buccal mucosa, and may also occur on the hands and feet, and/ or around the anus. The pigmented areas may fade with age. Hamartomatous polyps typically develop in the small intestine, although they may occur in the stomach and colon too. Small intestinal intussusception may lead to small bowel obstruction requiring laparotomy. Accordingly, once diagnosed, screening for small intestinal polyps is undertaken; surgery has been the conventional means by which these are removed if present, but developments in enteroscopy mean that this is increasingly another option. Screening of the small bowel may be via radiological means, and/ or by capsule endoscopy. People with Peutz- Jeghers syndrome are also at increased risk of both other gastrointestinal (GI) tract malignancies, as well as non-GI malignancies (including breast and ovarian

cancer). C Familial adenomatous polyposis FAP is a familial bowel cancer syndrome, but is also not associated with perioral pigmentation. A Hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia HHT classically presents initially with epistaxis, occurring ﬁrst at a mean age of 12 years; by 21 years of age, over 90% of affected people are symptomatic. Telangiectasia (rather than pigmented spots) occurs on the lips, oral mucosa, tongue, face, conjunctivae, ears and ﬁngers. Upper gastrointestinal haemorrhage occurs frequently, causing anaemia which often requires transfusion. Other visceral angiodysplasias may also occur (including pulmonary AVMs), and vascular abnormalities in the liver may lead to cirrhosis. B Juvenile polyposis Juvenile polyposis may also cause small intestinal polyps, but not perioral pigmentation. E Cronkhite-Canada syndrome Cronkhite-Canada syndrome is a very rare disorder characterised by multiple intestinal polyps, alopecia, nail dystrophy and widespread skin pigmentation. It does not appear to have a familial tendency. The syndrome often ﬁrst presents with diarrhoea.

stem: A 41-year-old woman is referred with fatigue and general body itch- ing. She has a history of hypothyroidism and is on thyroxine as replacement therapy. Her clinical examination is normal. She drinks approximately 10 units of alcohol per week and is a non-smoker. On examination, her BP is 142/85 mmHg, pulse is 75/min and regular. Cardiovascular and respiratory examination is unremarkable. There are scratch marks on examination of her upper body, and spider naevi consistent with chronic liver disease. Bloods: Investigation Result Normal values Bilirubin 16 µmol/l 1 - 22 µmol/l ALP 321 u/l 30 - 150 u/l ALT 124 u/l 7 - 55 u/l Albumin 36 g/l 35 - 55 g/l Free Thyroxin (FT4) 17.5 pmol/l 10 - 22 pmol/l TSH 2.13 mu/l 0.4 - 5.0 mu/l WCC 8.2 × 109/l 4.0 - 11.0 × 109/l Hb 143 g/l 135 - 175 g/l PLT 345 × 109/l 150 - 400 × 109/l Renal function Normal Serum electrophoresis Increase in the IgM fraction Which investigation is most likely to be positive in this scenario?
explanation:
C Anti-mitochondrial antibodies Most likely diagnosis in this patient is Primary biliary cholangitis (PBC), which is a condition of gradual destruction of the intrahepatic bile ducts, leading to ﬁbrosis and cholestasis and ultimately hepatic cirrhosis, usually presented in middle-aged women. Pruritis, fatigue and elevated alkaline phosphatase are some of the characteristic features seen in PBC. Anti-mitochondrial antibodies test is speciﬁc to PBC, as these antibodies are present in more than 90 % of cases. A Myeloma screen Myeloma is a disease of older adults, characterized by bone pain, anaemia and kidney disease. Majority of patients with myeloma will have a monoclonal spike in the gamma or beta regions on protein electrophoresis, however, myeloma screening in this patient is less likely to be positive. B Smooth muscle autoantibodies Patients with clinical and histological picture of PBC but negative anti-mitochondrial antibodies are referred to as antibody –negative PBC or autoimmune cholangitis, which is associated with high levels of smooth muscle autoantibodies and antinuclear antibodies. D Anti-liver kidney microsomes (LKM) antibody

Anti-liver kidney microsomes (LKM) antibody also known as CYP2D6 antibody, is useful in diagnosis of autoimmune hepatitis. Patients with type 2 autoimmune hepatitis show a positive antiLKM-1 antibody, but the result is not deﬁnitive. A liver biopsy may be performed to help conﬁrm the diagnosis. If the anti-LKM-1 test is negative, but smooth muscle antibodies and/or antinuclear antibodies are positive, then it is likely to be type 1 autoimmune hepatitis. This patient is most likely suffering from PBC. E Bone marrow aspiration Bone marrow aspiration is non –speciﬁc for the diagnosis of PBC.

stem: A 42-year-old man presents with chronic right knee pain. He lives and works in Italy and only returns to the UK intermittently to see his family. He has a history of type 2 diabetes mellitus diagnosed last time he was in the UK, which is currently managed with diet. On examination, his BP is 142/82 mmHg, with a pulse of 76/min and regular. He looks particularly tanned. You count a number of spider naevi on examination of his upper chest and you notice that his pubic hair seems a little sparse. His BMI is 31. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal values Hb 129 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 8.1 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l PLT 190 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 139 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.5 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 134 μmol/l 50–120 μmol/l ALT 182 U/l 7–55 U/l Bilirubin 65 μmol/l 1.7–20.5 μmol/l Glucose 11.1 mmol/l 3.9–7.1 mmol/l Right knee x-ray chondrocalcinosis Which of the following tests would you carry out next?
explanation: B Serum ferritin The suspicion is that he has so-called bronze diabetes, or haemochromatosis, associated with chronic liver disease, diabetes mellitus and chondrocalcinosis. The condition occurs because of an inherited mutation on chromosome 6, which affects the way that the transferrin receptor binds to transferrin, and leads to iron accumulation. It is this which results in organ damage and consequent chronic liver disease and diabetes mellitus. The C282Y mutation is found in the majority of patients with haemochromatosis, and this can be screened for using a widely available genetic test. Ferritin is usually elevated in association with haemochromatosis, and is a useful initial screening test. It is not speciﬁc for haemochromatosis, however, as ferritin may be elevated in chronic liver disease per se. It is usually followed by transferrin saturation testing and genetic screening. C Serum copper Disordered copper metabolism is the cause of Wilson’s disease, where patients usually present at an earlier age either with unexplained abnormal liver function, psychiatric disturbance, or chorea, more marked on one side than the other. A Serum calcium Although hypercalcaemia is associated with chondrocalcinosis, it’s haemochromatosis which is more likely to be the primary cause here. D Urinary copper This is part of the work-up for Wilson’s disease, which presents at an earlier age with neurological impairment or unexplained abnormal liver function tests. E Hepatitis serology For viral hepatitis, presentation with diabetes mellitus or chondrocalcinosis would not be expected.

stem: A 31-year-old adopted man presents to his general practitioner (GP) with rectal bleeding and a change in bowel habit. Previous history of note includes osteomas of both tibia and skull osteomas. His brother is noted to suffer from ulcerative colitis and his uncle died at the age of 44 years from colon cancer. On examination, his blood pressure (BP) is 132/72 mmHg, pulse is 72/min and regular. His BMI is 22 and his abdomen is soft and nontender. He is anaemic with an Hb of 112 g/l. Which of the following is the most appropriate investigation in this case?
explanation:
C Colonoscopy This patient has altered bowel habit with rectal bleeding, coupled with the history of osteomas; it is therefore important to rule out colonic carcinoma as an underlying cause. The suspicion is that he has Gardner’s syndrome, which is an autosomal dominant condition characterised by multiple adenomatous intestinal polyposis, osteomas and soft tissue tumours (epidermoid cysts, ﬁbromas and lipomas). Individuals with the syndrome develop a multitude of colonic polyps. Colonic carcinoma develops in 7% of individuals with Gardner’s syndrome by age 21 years, 50% by age 39 years and 90% by age 45 years. Colectomy is recommended once polyps ap-

pear. D Barium enema Although barium enema is an option for patients who are unable to tolerate colonoscopy, colonoscopy is preferred because of a higher identiﬁcation rate for colon cancers, and the chance of making a tissue diagnosis. A Rigid sigmoidoscopy Rigid sigmoidoscopy is only useful to visualise the rectum and the distal portion of the sigmoid. It isn’t suitable in this case to rule out an underlying carcinoma. B Flexible sigmoidoscopy Flexible sigmoidoscopy can visualise the distal colon and rectum only. Genetic causes of colon cancer often result in right sided lesions, which means ﬂexible sigmoidoscopy is inadequate in evaluating this patient. E Barium follow-through Barium follow-through is most useful to visualise the small bowel, whereas colonic polyps are associated with Gardner’s syndrome.

stem: A 22-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department, complaining of intermittent diarrhoea and abdominal bloating. She is increasingly fatigued and suffers from ﬂitting muscle aches. She is very worried as her sister has recently been diagnosed with coeliac disease and wonders if she should try an exclusion diet as her sister’s symptoms have signiﬁcantly improved after going gluten-free. On examination, her blood pressure is 122/82 mmHg and her pulse is 75 bpm and regular. She looks well. There are no abnormal ﬁndings, and her body mass index (BMI) is 24 kg/m2. Investigations; Investigations Results Normal Values Hb 131 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 7.2 × 109/l 4–11 × 109/l PLT 189 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 137 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.3 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 100 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Albumin 39 g/l 35–55 g/l Anti-tissue transglutaminase (TTG) antibody: Negative. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: C Irritable bowel syndrome The normal physical examination and investigations, including negative anti-TTG antibody, make a diagnosis of coeliac disease, inﬂammatory bowel disease or Whipple’s disease extremely unlikely. It is likely she has presented because of anxiety related to her sister’s illness. She should therefore be reassured and discharged back to the care of her general practitioner. B Crohn’s disease Crohn’s disease is associated with abdominal pain and diarrhoea, although some evidence of small bowel disease, including anaemia or malabsorption (eg a reduction in albumin), would be expected here. A Coeliac disease Depending on the antibody assay, patients who are immunoglobulin A (IgA)-deﬁcient may present with negative anti-TTG and still have coeliac disease, but in such cases, other signs of anaemia/malabsorption would be expected. The normal haemoglobin and albumin seen here effectively rules it out. D Ulcerative colitis Ulcerative colitis is, by deﬁnition, associated with lower gastrointestinal symptoms, including bloody diarrhoea, and usually with left-sided abdominal pain. It does not ﬁt with the clinical picture seen here. E Whipple’s disease Whipple’s disease is associated with symptoms of small bowel malabsorption and joint pains. The lack of anaemia and normal albumin here count against signiﬁcant small bowel disease and favour irritable bowel syndrome over Whipple’s disease.

stem: A 29-year-old woman is admitted acutely with severe abdominal pain, nausea and vomiting. She has a history of poorly-controlled epilepsy. On questioning, she denies any unusual behaviour other than commencing a ‘low-carb’ diet 2 weeks previously. As well as her normal gabapentin, she has been taking paracetamol and aspirin for her abdominal pain. On examination, she has peritonism and appears to have some proximal muscle weakness. The nurses notice that her urine is dark and changes colour on standing. Tests reveal: Investigation Result Normal values Urea 15.0 mmol/l 2.5 - 6.5 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 85 µmol/l 50 - 120 µmol/l Sodium (Na+) 125 mmol/l 135 - 145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.0 mmol/l 3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l Blood glucose 5.0 mmol/l 3.9 - 7.1 mmol/l Full blood count (FBC) Normal Arterial pH 7.31 7.35 - 7.45 Computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen Normal Urinalysis Ketones ++ Urinary porphobilinogen 300 µmol//dl 0 - 18 µmol//dl Given the likely diagnosis, which one of the following is the most suitable therapeutic option?
explanation: C Intravenous haem arginate The presentation of severe abdominal pain in young people, particularly accompanied by neurological symptoms, should alert to the possibility of an acute porphyria. This diagnosis is conﬁrmed by the increased levels of urinary porphobilinogens although the type of porphyria cannot be determined by this test alone. Attacks can be precipitated by drugs, infections, smoking and crash dieting, particularly low carbohydrate intake. Symptoms include severe neuropathic abdominal pain (85–95%) vomiting (50–90%) paresis (40– 70%) and seizures (10–20%). Hypertension and hyponatraemia are often features, and should be corrected due to the increased risk of seizures. Paracetamol and aspirin are safe in porphyria as well as gabapentin (used to control seizure activity). Most other anti-epileptics (including clonazepam) may exacerbate attacks, as does metoclopramide (phenothiazines should be used to control nausea). The treatment of choice in acute porphyria is intravenous haem arginate, although high-glucose diets or infusions have been used for mild attacks of pain without neurological symptoms. B Discontinuation of paracetamol and aspirin Both paracetamol and aspirin are safe to use in porphyria and therefore there is no indication to stop them in this patient. A Intravenous insulin infusion Ketoacidosis is due to the high-protein low-carbohydrate diet, and in the presence of a normal blood glucose, does not respond to an insulin infusion. D Intravenous metoclopramide Metoclopramide may exacerbate an acute porphyria and therefore should be avoided. E Intravenous lorazepam Intravenous lorazepam would be indicated in the presence of status epilepticus and is safe to use in patients with porphyria but there is no indication that the patient is currently experiencing any seizure activity. Clonazepam should however be avoided is it can exacerbate an acute porphyria.

stem: A 30-year-old woman in her third trimester of pregnancy presents to the Emergency Department, feeling generally unwell with lethargy and nausea. There is no past medical history of note and she takes no regular medication. This is her ﬁrst pregnancy. On examination, she has a blood pressure of 165/90 mmHg and a heart rate of 96 bpm. There is palpable tenderness in the right upper quadrant. Her temperature is 37.4 °C. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Value Hb 61 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 6.7 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l PLT 47 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 138 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.4 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 100 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Bilirubin 57 µmol/l 2–17 µmol/l Alanine transaminase (ALT) 682 IU/l 5–30 IU/l ALP 280 IU/l 30–130 IU/l Gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase (γGT) 40 IU/l 5–30 IU/l What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Haemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes and Low Platelet (HELLP) syndrome
explanation:
C Haemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes and Low Platelet (HELLP) syndrome The syndrome HELLP is characterised by Haemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes and Low Platelet count. It is thought to represent a form of pre-eclampsia. Thrombocytopenia occurs as a result of microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia. This takes place within the sinusoids, resulting in ﬁbrin deposition, which leads to congestion, hepatic ischaemia and transaminitis. Treatment is with antihypertensive drugs, such as labetalol, to control hypertension, magnesium to prevent convulsion and prompt delivery. B Budd–Chiari syndrome Budd–Chiari syndrome (also known as hepatic vein thrombosis) causes sudden-onset abdominal pain, ascites and tender hepatomegaly. It is associated with prothrombotic conditions and it would, therefore, be a differential to consider in this patient. However, the signiﬁcantly deranged blood tests and raised blood pressure are more suggestive of HELLP syndrome. A Acute fatty liver of pregnancy Acute fatty liver of pregnancy is a rare complication of pregnancy that typically appears in the third trimester. Signs and symptoms

include abdominal pain, jaundice, nausea and vomiting, with signiﬁcantly deranged liver function tests (eg ALT > 500 IU/l). Although this patient has some of these features, the presence of anaemia and thrombocytopenia makes an alternative diagnosis more likely. D Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy occurs in approximately 1% of pregnancies, with most cases presenting in the third trimester. Symptoms include severe itching, commonly on the hands and feet associated, with a raised bilirubin level. It does not explain this patient’s examination ﬁndings or anaemia and thrombocytopenia. E Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura is a haematological condition characterised by a pentad of: microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia, acute kidney injury, fever and neurological dysfunction. Not all features need to be present to make a diagnosis, and pregnancy is a risk factor for the condition. However, the deranged liver function tests make HELLP syndrome more likely.

stem: A 31-year-old woman who is 34 weeks pregnant comes to the Emergency Department, complaining of intense itching accompanied by severe tiredness and jaundice. This is her ﬁrst pregnancy. Apparently, her mother suffered from a similar condition during her third pregnancy. She has no past medical history of note. Examination reveals a blood pressure of 110/70 mmHg and a pulse of 75 bpm and regular. She has jaundiced sclerae and extensive scratch marks. On further questioning, she reports her urine has become darker and her stools paler over the past few days. Investigations; Investigations Results Normal values Hb 108 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 10.4 × 109/l 4–11 × 109/l PLT 145 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 137 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.3 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 90 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l ALP 382 IU/l 30–130 IU/l Bilirubin 65 µmol/l 2–17 µmol/l ALT 85 IU/l 5–30 IU/l Albumin 40 g/l 35–55 g/l INR 1.0 1.0 Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
explanation: E Ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA) UDCA is the drug of choice for the treatment of ICP. UDCA at a daily dose ranging from 600 mg to 2000 mg has been shown in a clinical study to be effective at reducing pruritus, decreasing total serum bile acid, ALT and bilirubin levels and allowing delivery closer to term (37.8 ± 0.9 week versus 33.8 ± 7.1 weeks). D Loratidine Antihistamines merely reduce symptoms of itching and can accumulate in hepatic dysfunction. They will not improve hepatic function in this condition. A Cholestyramine Colestyramine positively impacts on itching in intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy (ICP). It has a much more modest impact on liver enzymes than ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA) and can be associated with vitamin K deﬁciency at high doses. It is therefore considered as a second-line therapy. B Dexamethasone Dexamethasone is associated with some efﬁcacy in the management of ICP. Side-effects of high-dose steroids are signiﬁcant and it is therefore not used as a ﬁrst-line therapy. C Induce delivery Delivery is considered from week 37 due to an increased risk for maternal and fetal death after this point. This patient is currently at 34 weeks, and therefore, she should be treated with UDCA and listed for an elective Caesarean section at 37 weeks.

stem: A 61-year-old woman is referred to the Gastroenterology Clinic with a 9-month history of dyspepsia and postprandial abdominal pain. She denies nausea, weight loss or a change in bowel habits. Her medical history includes mild hypertension, for which she takes amlodipine 5 mg once daily. On examination, she has a temperature of 36.4 °C, she has a heart rate of 88 bpm and regular and a BP of 135/90 mmHg. Her abdomen is soft, with mild discomfort in the epigastrium and left upper quadrant. Investigation Result Normal value Hb 109 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 10.5 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l PLT 271 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 142 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 3.9 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Urea 6.2 mmol/l 1.8–7.1 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 55 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l An endoscopy is performed and shows evidence of erosive gastritis with a visible mass within the gastric antrum; core biopsies show neoplastic inﬁltration of lymphocytes within the gastric mucosa and positive identiﬁcation of Helicobacter pylori; normal appearances of the duodenum and proximal jejunum. What is the most appropriate initial management for this patient?
explanation: A Amoxicillin, clarithromycin and omeprazole This patient has a likely diagnosis of gastrointestinal mucosaassociated lymphoid tissue (MALT) lymphoma. MALT lymphoma is characterised by dyspepsia and epigastric discomfort which may also be associated with constitutional symptoms of weight loss, fever and night sweats. Most patients present over the age of 60 years, and gastrointestinal MALT lymphoma is classically associated with H. pylori infection, as seen in this patient. The most appropriate initial treatment of gastric MALT lymphoma with positive H. pylori infection is to eradicate H. pylori with triple therapy which is amoxicillin, clarithromycin and omeprazole. D Gastric radiotherapy Gastric radiotherapy is a ﬁrst-line treatment option for gastric MALT lymphoma not associated with a positive H. pylori infection. In patients with H. pylori infection, gastric radiotherapy is used as a second line if H. pylori eradication therapy has failed. B Cyclophosphamide Cyclophosphamide is a chemotherapeutic agent used in the treatment of advanced gastric MALT lymphoma that has spread beyond the stomach. The normal appearance of the duodenum and proximal jejunum suggests that the disease is currently conﬁned to the stomach and, therefore, chemotherapy is currently not indicated as the initial treatment. C Gastrectomy A gastrectomy is a signiﬁcant operation with high risk and multiple lifestyle changes to consider. It is not generally considered as a treatment option for gastric MALT lymphoma, especially not in the initial stages. E Rituximab Rituximab is a third-line option used in the treatment of gastric MALT lymphoma. It can also be considered when gastric radiotherapy is inappropriate. However, it is not an initial management option for the condition.

stem: A 48-year-old man presents to his General Practitioner with symptoms of oesophageal reﬂux that he says has worsened over the past four years. There is no history of dysphagia or weight loss. He has no past medical history of note, although he smokes ﬁve cigarettes per day and drinks three bottles of wine per week. He is referred for a routine endoscopy that shows severe Barrett’s oesophagus with high-grade dysplasia. Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
options: Computed tomography (CT) chest, abdomen and pelvis
explanation: A Endoscopic mucosal ablation This patient has evidence of high-grade dysplasia on endoscopy and biopsy. Therefore, endoscopic intervention is needed at this stage. Options include endoscopic mucosal resection and surgical removal of precancerous cells or radiofrequency ablation where heat is used to destroy precancerous cells. E Computed tomography (CT) chest, abdomen and pelvis A CT chest, abdomen and pelvis is considered if a patient shows signs of established malignancy, to stage the disease by looking for invasion and metastatic spread. However, malignancy has not been diagnosed on this patient’s biopsy. B High-dose omeprazole and ranitidine therapy Although this may provide symptomatic relief from dyspepsia, this patient has evidence of dysplasia which requires endoscopic treatment to prevent progression to malignancy. C Six-monthly endoscopic surveillance Endoscopic surveillance is frequently used to monitor for the progression of Barrett’s oesophagus. Patients with metaplasia affecting ≥ 3 cm of the oesophagus are recommended to have 2- to 3-yearly endoscopies, while those with < 3 cm affected should have 3- to 5yearly endoscopies. Six-monthly endoscopic surveillance is not an option for managing patients with high-grade dysplasia, as treatment should be initiated following diagnosis to prevent the transformation of dysplastic cells to cancerous cells. The British Society of Gastroenterology guidelines recommends 6-monthly endoscopic surveillance for patients with low-grade dysplasia until either it transforms to high-grade dysplasia or there are two consecutive biopsies of non-dysplastic Barrett’s oesophagus, in which case the patient can then have 2- to 3-yearly endoscopic surveillance. D Oesophagectomy An oesophagectomy would be an option if this patient was diagnosed with an oesophageal adenocarcinoma, which this patient is at high risk of developing with a background of Barrett’s oesophagus and evidence of dysplasia. However, it is not a treatment of dysplasia.

stem: A 67-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis comes to the clinic for review, complaining of tiredness. She takes non-steroidal antiinﬂammatory drugs (NSAIDs), low-dose prednisolone and methotrexate for her rheumatoid, and additionally has hypertension, for which she takes amlodipine 5 mg daily. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal value Hb 110 g/l 115–155 g/l MCV 86 ﬂ 76–98 ﬂ Ferritin 400 μg/l 10–120 µg/l Iron 9 μmol/l (low) You are keen to differentiate deﬁnitively between iron deﬁciency anaemia and anaemia of chronic disease. Which of the following is most useful to differentiate between the two?
explanation: E Bone marrow biopsy Estimation of iron content in a bone marrow aspiration rules out iron deﬁciency anaemia if it is normal. Although the other investigations may be pointers to one or the other diagnosis, they don’t deﬁnitely rule out the alternative. A Erythropoietin levels EPO levels are reduced in anaemia of chronic disease, although for example in diseases such as chronic kidney disease, both iron deﬁciency anaemia and low EPO can co-exist. This makes it impossible to rule out iron deﬁciency anaemia on EPO levels alone. B Upper GI endoscopy Upper GI endoscopy may reveal ulcers, although this wouldn’t rule iron deﬁciency anaemia in or out, or rule anaemia of chronic disease out. C Small bowel follow-through We are given no indication of symptoms consistent with small bowel malabsorption. D Colonoscopy Colonoscopy is not indicated by a Hb of 110 g/l, although it may be required in the event that iron deﬁciency is conﬁrmed as the prevailing pathology.

stem: A 42-year-old man presents with pruritus, right upper quadrant (RUQ) pain and malaise. He has had ulcerative colitis for the past 10 years. He takes sulfasalazine and has had good control, with only two acute episodes since diagnosis. He now presents with a 6month history of itching. He drinks fewer than 10 units of alcohol per week. On examination, he has hepatosplenomegaly, spider naevi and scratch marks. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal values Bilirubin 150 μmol/l 1 - 22 μmol/l ALT 40 μ/l 7 - 55 u/l ALP 600 μ/l (45–105) 30 - 150 u/l What investigation is most likely to yield a diagnosis?
explanation: B Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography/magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography The history of a cholestatic illness (suggested by the itching) and evidence of chronic liver disease (cutaneous signs) against a background of inﬂammatory bowel disease suggests a possible diagnosis of primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC). This is an inﬂammatory obliterative cholangiopathy that can lead to chronic liver disease cirrhosis and liver failure. It is commoner in men and presents in the second to ﬁfth decade. A total of 3–10% of cases of ulcerative colitis will develop PSC. The diagnosis rests on the demonstration of destruction of the biliary tree and this is best demonstrated by cholangiopancreatography. The disease is progressive with recurrent episodes of cholangitis complicating cirrhosis. Liver transplantation is now used in end-stage disease. The risk of cholangiocarcinoma is high, and the development of cancer is a contraindication to transplant and associated with a poor survival. E Ultrasound scan (USS) Ultrasound would be useful to exclude an extra-hepatic cause for cholestasis, but would not lead to the diagnosis. It is far more useful in jaundice secondary to gallstone and to diagnose cholecystitis. A Liver biopsy Rarely only smaller bile ducts are damaged and diagnosis is made at liver biopsy when PSC is mistaken for more focal liver disease, although this is only in exceptional circumstances where the liver biopsy is performed because of apparent local changes only. C Anti-mitochondrial antibodies AMA is positive in 98% of cases of PBC, not in primary sclerosing cholangitis. ANA, SMA and ANCA may be positive, but these are unlikely to lead to a diagnosis. D Serum ferritin High levels of serum ferritin may suggest haemochromatosis, but may be slightly raised as an acute phase reactant in most inﬂammatory conditions.

stem: You are asked to review a 54-year-old woman on the Surgical Ward who received a 4-unit blood transfusion a 7 days earlier for an acute upper GI haemorrhage related to a duodenal ulcer. She has developed a number of petechial haemorrhages and her platelet count has fallen to 35 x109/l from 152 x109/l post op. Her BP is 121/82 mmHg; pulse is 75/min and regular. She has a laparotomy scar with dressing on her abdomen and has active bowel sounds. There is an extensive petechial rash over her abdomen and bruises affecting her arms and legs. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: D Post transfusion purpura The answer is Post transfusion purpura, (PTP) - The timing of this patient’s fall in platelet count and petechial rash ﬁts best with a diagnosis of PTP. The antigen most commonly implicated is human platelet antigen 1a, (HPA-1a). High dose IV immunoglobulin is the treatment of choice. Exchange transfusion and high dose corticosteroids have also been used, but they both take longer to impact on platelet count. E Haemolytic uraemic syndrome Haemolytic uraemic syndrome is incorrect it is strongly associated with E coli 0157 infection, we are given no indication of GI upset or worsening renal function here. A Disseminated intravascular coagulation Disseminated intravascular coagulation is incorrect, because the patient does not appear systemically unwell, we are also provided with no information that Hb or clotting are signiﬁcantly compromised. B Drug induced purpura Drug induced purpura is incorrect. Although Omeprazole is rarely associated with a fall in platelet count, the timing of the fall ﬁts perfectly with PTP. In addition, drug induced purpura is rarer in this situation versus PTP. C Idiopathic thrombocytopaenic purpura Idiopathic thrombocytopaenic purpura, is incorrect because of probabilities, it is a rare condition and even more rarely described post transfusion.

stem: An 18-year-old man is admitted to hospital with severe upper abdominal pain radiating to his back, associated with nausea and vomiting. He opens his bowels 3–4 times per day with loose stools and mucus. He was diagnosed with ulcerative colitis six months ago, and has had several ﬂare-ups of his disease requiring steroids over the last three months. He is a non-smoker and non-drinker. His current medications are azathioprine 50 mg daily, prednisolone 10 mg daily and omeprazole. He consulted his general practitioner with similar symptoms a few weeks ago and was started on high-dose steroids for exacerbation of colitis. On examination, he looks unwell. His temperature is 37.6 °C. Blood pressure is 100/50 mmHg, with pulse 100/and min regular. Chest and cardiovascular examination are unremarkable. There is tenderness in the left hypochondrial region and epigastrium with normal bowel sounds. Rectal examination is very tender but empty. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Value Hb 114 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 13.5 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l PLT 494 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 133 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 3.3 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 110 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Urea 8.2 mmol/l 2.5–6.5 mmol/l Bilirubin 43 µmol/l 2–17 µmol/l ALT 51 IU/l 5–30 IU/l ALP 170 IU/l 30–130 IU/l Albumin 35 g/l 35–55 g/l Corrected calcium (Ca2+) 2.08 mmol/l 2.20–2.60 mmol/l CRP 65 mg/l < 10 mg/l Chest and abdominal radiography Normal What is the most likely diagnosis to explain his current admission?
explanation: B Acute pancreatitis The diagnosis lies mainly in the symptoms, which are consistent with pancreatitis and one would expect his amylase to be high. Pancreatitis due to medications is an unusual event, but has been reported to be associated with drugs used for inﬂammatory bowel disease including sulphasalazine, 5- aminosalicylic acid compounds, 6mercaptopurine and azathioprine. The pathogenesis of druginduced pancreatitis may be due to an idiosyncratic response in some cases (e.g. 6-mercaptopurine, azathioprine). Drug-induced pancreatitis has no distinguishing clinical features. A high index of suspicion and careful drug history are therefore essential for making the diagnosis. The time course of developing the disorder depends upon the drug involved, and can vary from weeks to months. The prognosis of drug-induced pancreatitis is generally excellent. D Infective gastroenteritis Given the history of azathioprine use, coupled with epigastric and left-sided abdominal pain, acute pancreatitis should be ruled out ﬁrst as the underlying cause of his pain. Abnormal liver function tests would also be unusual in the context of acute gastroenteritis. A Steroid-refractory ulcerative colitis Given that this patient’s symptoms have been controlled by reducing doses of corticosteroids, this implies steroid responsiveness. Hence steroid refractory UC is an unlikely diagnosis. C Cholecystitis Cholecystitis is more commonly associated with right-sided abdominal and epigastric pain, rather than the left- sided pain reported here. E Peptic ulcer disease Peptic ulcer disease is associated with epigastric pain, and not with the abnormal liver function tests and mild hypocalcaemia seen here.

stem: You review a 48-year-old publican who is awaiting discharge from the Gastroenterology Ward after an episode of haematemesis related to oesophageal varices. He received injection sclerotherapy at the time. You review his investigations and decide on medication to reduce further bleeding. He is already on spironolactone. Investigation Result Normal values Hb 115 g/l 135 - 175 g/l WCC 6.1 × 109/l 4.0 - 11.0 × 109/l PLT 230 × 109/l 150 - 400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 137 mmol/l 135 - 145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 3.9 mmol/l 3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 90 μmol/l 50 - 120 µmol/l Hepatic ultrasound scan small shrunken liver Liver biopsy advanced cirrhosis Which one of the following would be most appropriate strategy to reduce portal blood pressure in this man?
explanation:
C Propranolol Propranolol is a non-selective beta-blocker with high hepatic ﬁrst pass metabolism and in clinical trials has been shown to be the most effective oral agent in long-term therapy for portal hypertension. Porto-systemic shunting is usually reserved for patients who re-bleed and have symptoms of worsening portal hypertension. D Furosemide Furosemide can drive symptomatic hyponatraemia and is less effective versus spironolactone in controlling ﬂuid balance in hepatic cirrhosis. A Atenolol Atenolol has greater B1 receptor selectivity than propranolol and lower ﬁrst pass hepatic metabolism, this makes it a less ideal choice for the treatment of portal hypertension. B Isosorbide dinitrate

Isosorbide dinitrate is less effective in controlling portal hypertension in this situation because of potential difﬁculties with postural hypotension, and tolerance to the effects of nitrates in the longterm. E Lactulose Lactulose and neomycin are usually used to prevent encephalopathy after a large GI bleed by reducing the ammonia load associated with a GI haemorrhage.

stem: A 22-year-old woman presents with a severe headache, peripheral oedema and indigestion. She is 32 weeks’ pregnant with her ﬁrst child. On examination, her BP is 140/90 mmHg and she looks tired; her ankles are swollen. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal value Hb 90 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 7.1 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l PLT 68 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 139 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.4 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 185 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l AST 205 IU/l 10–40 IU/l ALT 150 IU/l 5–30 IU/l ALP 301 IU/l 30–130 IU/l Bilirubin 80 μmol/l 2–17 µmol/l INR 1.0 < 1.1 Urine Protein++ Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: C Pre-eclampsia and HELLP syndrome The combination of severe headache, peripheral oedema, indigestion and proteinuria is very classical for pre- eclampsia. This patient has associated HELLP syndrome. Micro-angiopathic haemolytic anaemia, which accounts for the blood picture seen here, is typical of the situation. Of paramount importance is control of blood pressure and rapid assessment of the pregnancy by the obstetric team. The only way to resolve pre-eclampsia is delivery of the placenta, and hence the neonate. D Eclampsia Eclampsia is where seizures are seen on top of the picture of preeclampsia described here. A Acute fatty liver of pregnancy This is rare, occurring at around week 35 in pregnancy, and is associated with a moderate elevation in transaminases; bilirubin is also raised and clotting is abnormal, although the hypertension seen here is not present. B Cholestasis of pregnancy The main symptoms of cholestasis of pregnancy are itching and lethargy, which begin as early as week 25. E Idiopathic thrombocytopaenic purpura (ITP) ITP is not associated with the other features seen here, including hypertension, proteinuria, renal impairment and abnormal liver function tests.

stem: A 55-year-old man is admitted to the Emergency Department with large, fresh haematemesis. He has a history of alcoholic liver disease. He is known to have had grade 1 oesophageal varices on endoscopy three years ago. His only medication includes thiamine. On examination, he is unwell, with a blood pressure of 90/50 mmHg and a heart rate of 120 bpm. His abdomen is soft and non-tender. Rectal examination shows melaena. Investigation Result Normal Value Hb 76 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 12.5 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l PLT 99 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 133 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 5.5 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 70 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l MCV 101 ﬂ 76–98 ﬂ INR 1.8 < 1.1 Urea 9.5 mmol/l 2.5–6.5 mmol/l He is actively resuscitated with ﬂuids and blood products while awaiting urgent upper gastrointestinal endoscopy. During endoscopy, band ligation is performed to control the bleeding. Unfortunately, the bands do not stem the bleeding and the patient continues to ooze blood. Which of the following is the next best therapeutic option in controlling this patient’s acute variceal bleed?
options: Continue to perform variceal banding until the bleeding ceases
explanation:
E Transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPS) The combination of banding and terlipressin appears to be most effective in controlling acute variceal bleed, the rebleeding rate and early complications. In the event that banding does not control the bleeding, the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence guidance advises considering a transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt procedure.

D Variceal sclerotherapy and terlipressin Variceal banding is preferred to sclerotherapy because it achieves a resolution of large varices in fewer treatment sessions, compared to sclerotherapy. A Balloon tamponade and terlipressin Balloon tamponade does not directly target varices and is less effective than banding, although it can be used acutely to control catastrophic haemorrhage. B Continue to perform variceal banding until the bleeding ceases If banding fails to control bleeding, an alternative option needs to be sought. In the event that banding does not control bleeding, The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence guidance advises considering a transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt procedure. C Propranolol and variceal sclerotherapy Although non-selective beta-blockers and nitrates reduce portal pressure and the risk of rebleeding, they are not useful in the acute setting, because of hypotension, as is seen here. Sclerotherapy is also thought to have marginally less good outcomes, compared to banding.

stem: A 64-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with abdominal pain and distension and a 2-day history of persistent vomiting. He has had intermittent abdominal pain for the last 5 weeks and diarrhoea for 3 days prior to the onset of vomiting. He has not passed a bowel motion since. His past medical history includes hypertension and coeliac disease, from which he has been asymptomatic for the past 10 years although he admits to being poorly compliant with his diet. He has lost 4 kg in weight over the past 5 months. Physical examination shows a distended abdomen. Bowel sounds are tinkling in nature. What is the most likely cause of this patient’s symptoms?
explanation: D Small bowel lymphoma Coeliac disease is a common and underdiagnosed condition, which may present at any age. It is a hypersensitivity to gluten found in wheat, rye and barley. The gliadin fraction of the protein provokes an inﬂammatory response causing subtotal or total villous atrophy of the small bowel, resulting in malabsorption. It classically presents with a history of diarrhoea, weight loss, lethargy and anaemia (folate, B12 or iron- deﬁcient). It is associated with an increased risk of developing small bowel lymphoma, which thankfully only occurs in a very small proportion of coeliac patients. It is the rapid deterioration seen here, with weight loss, which points us towards malignant transformation of the coeliac to small bowel lymphoma. E Small bowel carcinoma The history of coeliac disease makes small bowel lymphoma a more likely cause than carcinoma of the bowel, although carcinoma of the small bowel can also cause weight loss and small bowel obstruction. A Adhesions There is no previous history of bowel surgery or abdominal surgery to suggest that adhesions may be present to cause small bowel obstruction. B Carcinoma of the colon The history of coeliac disease makes small bowel lymphoma a more likely cause than carcinoma of the bowel, especially in the absence of lower GI symptoms before the presentation with acute abdomen. C Meckel’s diverticulum Meckel's diverticulum is the most common congenital anomaly of the gastrointestinal tract. It results from incomplete obliteration of the vitelline duct leading to the formation of a true diverticulum of the small intestine. Meckel's diverticulum is a true diverticulum, containing all layers of the small bowel wall. It arises from the anti- mesenteric surface of the middle-to-distal ileum. The diverticulum represents a persistent remnant of the omphalo-mesenteric duct, which connects the midgut to the yolk sac in the foetus. Meckel's diverticula are uncommon and often clinically silent, particularly in the adult. Asymptomatic Meckel's diverticulum may be discovered during abdominal exploration for the evaluation of unrelated pathology. Less commonly, it is found incidentally on diagnostic imaging. When symptomatic, Meckel's diverticulum may present with abdominal pain or symptoms of gastrointestinal bleeding or bowel obstruction. In this scenario, the past medical history of coeliac disease makes Meckel’s diverticulum a less likely diagnosis.

stem: A 49-year-old man with a 20-year history of alcohol misuse is being investigated as an outpatient. He undergoes endoscopy and is found to have three columns of oesophageal varices that occlude the lumen. On questioning, he denies any previous episodes of melaena or haematemesis. He admits to still drinking 7–10 cans of lager per day. Physical examination reveals moderate ascites. There is no evidence of encephalopathy. His face is shown below. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Value Hb 150 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 6.5 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l PLT 120 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Bilirubin 45 µmol/l 2–17 µmol/l AST 80 IU/l 10–40 IU/l ALT 35 IU/l 5–30 IU/l Albumin 30 g/l 35–55 g/l PT 23 s 10.6–14.9 s Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment option with respect to reducing portal hypertension?
explanation: E Propranolol The blood results here are consistent with a diagnosis of alcoholic cirrhosis. Jaundiced sclera and ascites are signs of chronic liver disease. Portal hypertension is suggested by the low platelet count (due to hypersplenism) and varices at endoscopy.
