A systolic murmur over the left ﬁfth intercostal space is appreciated on cardiovascular examination. His abdomen is soft but distended, and there is palpable pelvic lymphadenopathy. Neurological examination reveals that cranial nerves are intact and peripheral power and sensation are normal in the upper and lower limbs, but there is clonus in the ankles bilaterally. When his gait is assessed, he has a broadbased stance and sways while mobilising from one end of the room to the other. Cognitive testing reveals an Abbreviated Mental Test Score (AMTS) of 8 out of 10. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
D Whipple’s disease This patient has Whipple’s disease, an infection caused by the pathogen Tropheryma whipplei. Classical symptoms include gastrointestinal symptoms that resemble other malabsorption syndromes, migratory arthralgia and fever. Sacroiliitis is common and the HLAB27 antigen is more commonly found among affected individuals. One-third of patients have cardiac involvement with pericarditis or endocarditis, which rarely causes signiﬁcant symptoms. Neurological features include ataxia, confusion, seizures, delirium and cognitive impairment. Diagnosis is made by intestinal biopsy and identiﬁcation of the organism. Periodic acid–Schiff staining shows foamy macrophages, and polymerase chain reaction will detect the bacterium. Treatment involves antibiotic therapy, with an initial phase of parenteral treatment, followed by 12 months of oral anti-

biotics. Relapse is common, often presenting with central nervous system (CNS) symptoms. A Coeliac disease This patient has Whipple’s disease which classically presents with migratory arthritis, intermittent diarrhoea and colicky abdominal pain. The main differential here would be coeliac disease, due to weight loss and diarrhoea. However, Whipple’s disease is the correct answer here because of the presence of systemic disease patterns (cardiac murmur indicating endocarditis, ataxia due to neurological involvement), due to the spread of the causative organism T. whipplei to other tissues. Coeliac disease may cause symptoms of malabsorption and other complications; however, it does not present with the typical features of endocarditis and neurological involvement seen here. B Friedreich’s ataxia Friedreich’s ataxia is an autosomal recessive disease, which usually presents in the teenage years with deafness, progressive spinocerebellar ataxia, optic atrophy and progressive muscle wasting. Patients may also present with cardiomyopathy; however, it is not associated with gastrointestinal symptoms, as in the case here. C Small bowel adenocarcinoma Small bowel adenocarcinoma may present with changes in bowel habit, anaemia, weight loss, abdominal pain and bowel obstruction but is now relevant here. E Wilson’s disease Wilson’s disease is an inherited disorder characterised by accumulation of copper in the body, which results in chronic liver disease, CNS abnormalities, including tremors, muscle stiffness, dysarthria, dysphagia and incoordination, and psychiatric symptoms such as anxiety, depression and psychosis. It is not associated with gastrointestinal symptoms, as seen in Whipple’s disease.

stem: A 72-year-old female is admitted with a 2-month history of diarrhoea. She has loose motions with no blood, four times per day. Her stool cultures are negative and her examination is normal. She has a background of rheumatoid arthritis for which she is in remission; hypertension, chronic renal impairment with a creatinine of 151 μmol/l and depression. Colonoscopy demonstrates mild diverticular disease. Biopsy shows evidence of colitis with lymphocytic inﬁltration. Her daughter ﬁnds a list of her medications that she is taking and shows them to you. Which one of the following medications is most likely to be causing her diarrhoea?
explanation: D Lansoprazole Many drugs contribute to causing diarrhoea and it is very important to get a good drug history when evaluating a patient with chronic diarrhoea. The list is endless and one must use the BNF to check whenever one is not sure. Drugs causing diarrhoea include broadspectrum antibiotics, antihypertensives such as diuretics, digoxin, some cholesterol-lowering drugs, sodium valproate, thyroxine, levodopa, antacids, theophylline, colchicines, non-steroidals and oral hypoglycaemic drugs. Mechanisms leading to diarrhoea are diverse, including effects on transit time, alterations in bowel ﬂora, and impact on colonic inﬂammation, such as the development of lymphocytic colitis seen with non-steroidals. With respect to lansoprazole it appears to result in the development of microscopic colitis. E Spironolactone Mild diarrhoea is a rare side effect of spironolactone therapy, although it isn’t as a result of microscopic colitis. A Ramipril Ramipril is associated with gastritis and pancreatitis, and in some cases diarrhoea, although this isn’t manifest as lymphocytic (microscopic) colitis. B Amlodipine Abdominal pain and intermittent nausea are the commonest associations with amlodipine use, and diarrhoea is uncommonly reported, although it isn’t thought to be due to microscopic colitis. C Furosemide Although loop diuretics have a recognised association with diarrhoea, this isn’t due to lymphocytic colitis. The changes in bowel habit are potentially due to an alteration in GI motility.

stem: A 47-year-old woman is referred to the Gastroenterology Clinic due to abnormal liver function tests which were a ﬁnding on a battery of blood tests checked by her GP. She attended the general practitioner (GP) because of increased fatigue and symptoms of itching. She was diagnosed with irritable bowel syndrome several years ago, but this has since become quiescent. She has no other signiﬁcant past medical history except for hormone replacement therapy and takes no regular medication. She is a non-smoker and drinks 6 units of alcohol per week. She has no risk factors for hepatitis. On examination she looked well, her BMI is 22. Some xanthelasmata were noted, but there was no jaundice, clubbing or lymphadenopathy. Her abdomen was soft and non-tender and the liver edge was palpable 1 cm below the costal margin. Cardiorespiratory and neurological examination was unremarkable. Investigation results are below: Investigation Result Normal values Haemoglobin (Hb) 130 g/l 135 - 175 g/l (WCC) 6.0 × 10 /l 4.0 - 11.0 × 10 /l Platelets (PLT) 220 × 10 /l 150 - 400 × 10 /l (MCV) 82 fl 80 - 100 fl INR 1.1 < 1.1 ESR 4 mm/h 1 - 20 mm/h Sodium (Na ) 140 mmol/l 135 - 145 mmol/l Potassium (K ) 3.8 mmol/l 3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l Urea 5.2 mmol/l 2.5 - 6.5 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 100 µmol/l 50 - 120 µmol/l Fasting glucose 4.1 mmol/l < 5.9 mmol/l CRP) < 4 mg/l < 10 mg/l Cholesterol 7.8 mmol/l < 5.2 mmol/ Bilirubin 16 µmol/l 1 - 22 µmol/l (ALP) 850 u/l 30 - 150 u/l GGT) 52 u/l < 50 u/l (ALT) 48 u/l 7 - 55 u/l Albumin 38 g/dl 35 - 55 g/dl Abdominal ultrasound Slight hepatomegaly, no other focal abnormality, no biliary obstruction Which further investigation would be most speciﬁc in making the diagnosis?
explanation:
C Anti-mitochondrial antibodies Clinical features are pointing towards a diagnosis of primary biliary cholangitis (PBC), which is a chronic progressive disorder with the gradual destruction of the intrahepatic bile ducts, leading to ﬁbrosis and cholestasis and ultimately hepatic cirrhosis. PBC is usually presented in middle-aged females with early symptoms of pruritis, fatigue, which can progress to the development of obstructive jaundice and portal hypertension. 50% of patients may be asymptomatic at the time of diagnosis and are detected by abnormal liver function tests especially elevated alkaline phosphatase. Anti-mitochondrial antibody has a sensitivity of 95% with a speciﬁcity of 98%. Treat-

ment options include colestyramine for pruritis (naltrexone and rifampicin may also help), ursodeoxycholic acid and liver transplantation for end staged disease (e.g. bilirubin > 100 µmol/L). Once jaundice develops, the survival rate is < 2 years without liver transplantation. B Computed tomography (CT) scan of abdomen CT scan of abdomen can be helpful in differentiating PBC from other biliary conditions e.g. carcinoma of bile duct, but not speciﬁc for PBC. There is a high risk of hepatocellular carcinoma in patients with PBC. A Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) MRCP can help to exclude chronic biliary obstruction (stone or stricture), however, it is not speciﬁc for PBC. D Hepatitis serology PBC must be differentiated from chronic hepatitis (due to viral infections) by performing hepatic serology tests. Hepatic serology is not speciﬁc for underlying possible diagnosis of PBC. E Anti-nuclear antibodies Patients with clinical and histological picture of PBC but negative anti-mitochondrial antibodies are referred to as antibody –negative PBC or autoimmune cholangitis, which is associated with high levels of anti-nuclear antibodies and smooth muscle antibodies. Almost all cases of SLE show a positive serum ANA.

stem: A concerned 29-year-old woman attends her general practitioner (GP) practice complaining of two days of painless rectal bleeding. There has been no change in her bowel habit. She denies any other constitutive symptoms and has no signiﬁcant travel history. She is particularly concerned since her mother, who is 48 years old, has recently been diagnosed with cancer of the bowel. On further questioning, it appears that her maternal grandfather also died after suffering from bowel cancer. The GP suspects that there may be an inherited tendency towards this disease and is especially concerned about familial adenomatous polyposis. What physical feature is most commonly found in this condition?
options: Hypertrophy of the retinal pigment epithelium
explanation: A Hypertrophy of the retinal pigment epithelium Familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP) is an autosomal dominant condition characterised by the presence of hundreds of adenomatous polyps throughout the colon. There is a wide phenotypic spectrum of FAP, with all phenotypes having an underlying germ-line mutation in the adenomatous polyposis coli gene. The average age of the polyposis is 16 years, with all patients having this syndrome developing colon cancer if left untreated. The average age of onset of colorectal cancer is 39 years. Physical features associated with this condition include congenital hypertrophy of the retinal pigment epithelium, dental abnormalities including supernumerary teeth and dentigerous cysts, osteomas of the skull and mandible, and ﬁbromas and epidermoid cysts in prepubescent patients. D Cutaneous lipomas Lipomas per se are not associated with increased risk of cancer, although weight gain is associated with a range of cancers including colon and breast cancer, which are linked to increased insulin resistance. B Early onset cataracts Early onset cataracts may be associated with decreased antioxidative activity, and have been shown in epidemiological studies to be associated with increased risk of head and neck cancer and hepatoma. C Axillary freckling Axillary freckling is identiﬁed in hereditary non-polyposis cancer, rather than FAP. E Pre-auricular skin tags Abnormalities of the ear cartilage are more commonly associated with renal and cardiac abnormalities. They are not thought to be associated with increased risk of colonic polyps.

stem: A 50-year-old Asian male, presents with a 3-week history of jaundice and pruritus. He has a 1-year history of diarrhoea which had been diagnosed as irritable bowel syndrome by his general practitioner. There is no history of foreign travel and he denies any illicit drug use or recent blood transfusion. On examination he appears jaundiced and has scratch marks on his trunk, but the liver is not enlarged and there is no evidence of ascites.
explanation: D Primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC) Periductal concentric ﬁbrosis (‘onion skin’) is a classic histopathologic ﬁnding of PSC on liver biopsy. The long history of diarrhoea should make you consider a diagnosis of inﬂammatory bowel disease (IBD), a condition strongly associated with PSC. In fact approximately 60-80% of patients with PSC have concomitant IBD. E Alcoholic liver disease There is no history of alcohol excess, and liver biopsy would usually show fatty change, cell necrosis and Mallory bodies. A Primary biliary cholangitis This typically shows a dense lymphocytic inﬁltrate in the portal tracts with granulomatous destruction and loss of medium-sized interlobular bile ducts, focal and variable within the liver. B Haemochromatosis When a liver biopsy is performed in this setting, Perls' Prussian blue stain would be performed to evaluate the degree and cellular distribution of hepatic iron stores. C Autoimmune hepatitis The ﬁndings on liver biopsy are described as interface hepatitis, formerly referred to as piecemeal necrosis. This is because portal inﬂammation is seen eroding through the limiting plate between the portal tract and liver parenchyma.

stem: A 44-year-old man presents with a 10-month history of pain in his lower back, hips, ankles and feet. He has tried osteopathy, acupuncture and diclofenac, but had no relief. He has also been feeling increasingly tired and breathless on walking up steep inclines. He had lost 10 kg in the last 6 months despite eating reasonable meals. He had no dysphagia or night sweats, but does report intermittent abdominal bloating and diarrhoea. He smokes 30 cigarettes/day and drinks two pints of beer 3 times per week. His past history includes hypothyroidism for which he takes thyroxine, and his mother is a tablet-controlled diabetic. On examination, his clothes ﬁt loosely and he looks pale. He has no clubbing or lymphadenopathy. He had normal cardiac, chest and abdominal examinations. On joint examination, there was pain when moving each joint but no obvious focus of the pain. Chest X-ray is normal, faecal immunochemical test (FIT) is negative. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Value Hb 71 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 6.5 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l PLT 512 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 136 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 3.8 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 71 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Urea 4.6 mmol/l 2.5–6.5 mmol/l Corrected calcium (Ca2+) 1.82 mmol/l 2.20–2.60 mmol/l Albumin 26 g/l 35–55 g/l MCV 71.2 ﬂ 76–98 ﬂ INR 1.5 < 1.1 Parathyroid hormone (PTH) 15 pmol/l 0.9–5.4 pmol/l What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
C Coeliac disease Coeliac disease is common, with a prevalence of 1: 100 and as much as 1: 30 in the west of Ireland. Only one- third of patients present with chronic diarrhoea and steatorrhoea. Malabsorption in this case has caused vitamin D deﬁciency with secondary hyperparathyroidism, low albumin, impaired clotting, iron deﬁciency anaemia and weight loss. The vitamin D deﬁciency has led to osteomalacia, causing the presenting feature of lower back and leg pain. Iron deﬁciency anaemia is the most common presentation of coeliac disease. Having other autoimmune conditions in coeliac patients is common, such as hypo/hyperthyroidism and type 1 diabetes mellitus (7%). B Metastatic caecal carcinoma Caecal carcinoma can present with anaemia, although it is much less likely to present with osteomalacia than coeliac disease. A Crohn’s disease Crohn’s disease is less likely to have an insidious presentation like this with predominant symptoms of osteomalacia, and is more likely to present with signiﬁcant diarrhoea and abdominal pain. D Whipple disease Whipple’s disease is associated with diarrhoea and malabsorption, but it is also associated with small joint polyarthritis and is signiﬁcantly rarer than coeliac disease. E Intestinal lymphangiectasis Intestinal lymphangiectasia is a protein-losing enteropathy and presents in childhood with symptoms of malabsorption and peripheral

oedema.

stem: A 32-year-old white bar owner returns from Spain and requires emergency consultation in the General Medicine Clinic. He feels lethargic and has not been able to maintain an adequate erection during intercourse or masturbation during the past few months. This is causing some marital difﬁculties. He also complains of swelling of his ankles and swelling around the abdomen. On examination, he appears tanned. There is a paucity of underarm and genital hair, and he has evidence of chronic liver disease and testicular atrophy. Past history of note includes arthritis and joint pain. He admits to drinking 12 units of alcohol per week (a glass of wine or half a pint of beer). Investigation Result Normal value Fasting glucose 8.2 mmol/l < 5.6 mmol/l ALT 183 u/l 7 - 55 u/l Bilirubin 125 μmol/l 1 - 22 μmol/l What would be the next best investigation to lead to this patient’s diagnosis?
options: Magnetic resonance imaging of the liver
explanation:
E Serum ferritin and transferrin saturation Symptoms of haemochromatosis usually begin in men aged between 30 and 50 years and include increased skin pigmentation (due to iron deposition and melanin), cirrhosis, diabetes mellitus, arthropathy, impotence in men and heart failure. First-line screening

involves measuring patients’ serum transferrin saturation and ferritin levels. Previously, liver biopsy with total hepatic iron estimation was considered the gold standard test for haemochromatosis. Now, however, genetic screening for the two identiﬁed mutations is seen as the next investigation of choice after transferrin saturation estimation. Around 10% of the Northern European population are heterozygous for each mutation (so-called compound heterozygotes), and this may account for the accelerated deterioration of liver function in patients with moderate alcohol intake corresponding to 15–30 standard drinks (units) per week. C Liver ultrasound scan A liver ultrasound scan is not indicated to diagnose haemochromatosis. Magnetic resonance imaging of the liver is the most sensitive and speciﬁc imaging modality for the measurement of liver iron deposition in haemochromatosis. A Glycated haemoglobin (HbA1c) This patient has a raised fasting glucose level, which is common in patients with haemochromatosis. Diabetes occurs in these patients due to iron deposition within the pancreas, affecting endocrine function, and/or liver cirrhosis. Although diagnosis and treatment of diabetes in these patients are important, HbA1c is not as accurate due to the increased turnover of red blood cells. Furthermore, HbA1c measurement will not lead to the diagnosis, making this an incorrect option. B Liver FibroScan Liver FibroScan is used to assess the degree of ﬁbrosis in fatty liver disease, hepatitis and cholestatic disease. It can be used in haemochromatosis but is not the next best step in conﬁrming this patient’s diagnosis. D Magnetic resonance imaging of the liver This patient likely has haemochromatosis, based on his symptoms, examination and investigation ﬁndings. Magnetic resonance imaging of the liver is a good, non-invasive investigation for measuring liver iron content in cases of haemochromatosis. However, the ﬁrstline investigations which can point toward the diagnosis of haemochromatosis are ferritin levels and serum transferrin saturations, which are both raised in cases of haemochromatosis.

stem: A 48-year-old man is seen in clinic with a 3-month history of chronic epigastric discomfort. The pain comes and goes and radiates to his back and his right shoulder tip at times. It is worse after meals but there is no relieving factor. He feels nauseous most of the time and has foul-smelling stools. He has lost 2 stones in weight. He also complains of intermittent light-headedness. He drinks a bottle of wine on most nights and smokes 20 cigarettes/day. On examination, he is thin and looks neglected. His abdomen is soft, but tender on deep palpation in the epigastric area. He has a 2 cm non-tender liver edge. He also has decreased sensation to light touch on both feet. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin (Hb) 102 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 12.1 × 10 /l 9 4.0–11.0 × 10 /l9 Platelets (PLT) 462 × 10 /l 9 150–400 × 10 /l9 Sodium (Na ) + 131 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K ) + 4.2 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 64 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Amylase 35 U/l < 200 U/l ALT 104 IU/l 5–30 IU/l ALP 121 IU/l 30–130 IU/l Bilirubin 24 μmol/l 2–17 µmol/l Corrected calcium (Ca ) 2+ 2.01 mmol/l 2.20–2.60 mmol/l Abdominal X-ray (AXR) Normal Oesophago-gastro duodenoscopy (OGD) Mild gastritis Campylobacter-like organisms (CLOs) - Ultrasound abdomen Mildly enlarged liver with fatty change Spleen & kidneys Normal He is referred for a secretin test, which reveals the following: Investigation Result Volume collected 110 ml Bicarbonate 52 mEq/l What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
A Chronic pancreatitis This patient has a history of excess ethanol consumption and chronic abdominal pain. In early disease there may be no X-ray calciﬁcation of the pancreas, and endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatogram (ERCP) and computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen can also be normal. Faecal elastase is in the mild-to-moderate pancreatic insufﬁciency range, and the most likely diagnosis therefore is chronic pancreatitis. Treatment acutely is as for acute pancreatitis, but chronic pain control is often difﬁcult and patients become opiate dependent. Pancreatic enzyme replacement is used. These patients also usually become diabetic and should be monitored for symptoms of hyperglycaemia such as polyuria, polydipsia, lethargy and dehydration. B Bacterial overgrowth of the gut Pancreas Partially obscured by overlying bowel gas Faecal elastase 110 µg E1/g of stool 200 to > 500 µg E1/g ofstool

Bacterial overgrowth syndrome presents with bloating, eructation and intermittent diarrhoea, weight loss is not as severe as that seen here, and faecal elastase remains in the normal range. C Coeliac disease Coeliac disease is associated with symptoms of malabsorption, positive anti-TTG antibodies, and faecal elastase remains in the normal range. D Vasoactive intestinal polypeptide-secreting tumour (VIPoma) VIPomas are vanishingly rare and are associated with large-volume diarrhoea, hypokalaemia and dehydration. The chronic excess alcohol consumption counts towards an alternative diagnosis here. E Caecal carcinoma Caecal carcinoma is often symptomless in the early stages, and presents late with iron deﬁciency anaemia or ultimately obstruction, rather than the chronic diarrhoea seen here.

stem: A 68-year-old woman is referred to the Cardiology Department with intermittent palpitations. She describes episodes of ‘feeling ﬂushed’ associated with a ﬂuttering feeling in the chest. She denies any chest pain or breathlessness. There are no risk factors for ischaemic heart disease or any history or rheumatic fever. She is also suffering from paroxysms of diarrhoea. On examination she appears well in herself. There are prominent vwaves noted on inspection of the jugular venous pulse. A pansystolic murmur is audible at the left sternal edge. The chest is clear on auscultation. A pulsatile liver is felt 2 cm below the costal margin on palpation of the abdomen. Which of the following investigations is most likely to yield the underlying diagnosis?
explanation: A 24 h urine collection for 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid (5HIAA) This patient presents with features of carcinoid syndrome. This is a paraneoplastic syndrome secondary to a carcinoid tumour. The most common locations for a carcinoid tumour are in gut and arise from the enterochromafﬁn cells. Carcinoid tumours secrete serotonin, which is metabolised by the liver. If the carcinoid tumour metastasises to the liver, serotonin enters the systemic circulation. Release of circulation is associated with ﬂushing, diarrhoea and bronchoconstriction. Continued serotonin exposure can result in restrictive cardiomyopathy secondary to ﬁbrosis. This can lead to valvular pa- thology (in this case the tricuspid valve). 5- HIAA is a degradation product of serotonin, which is excreted in the urine. A level of >25 mg per 24 is diagnostic. D Chest X-ray Carcinoid syndrome can occur secondary to a carcinoid tumour in the lungs (a common extra-GI site for primary carcinoid tumours). However, the features supporting tricuspid regurgitation point towards a liver metastasis as the serotonin source. A chest X-ray in this patient may only show non-speciﬁc changes or appear normal. B Echocardiogram This patient likely has tricuspid regurgitation secondary to the carcinoid plaques on the tricuspid valvular apparatus,seen in 50% of cases of serotonin syndrome. The echocardiogram would likely demonstrate these cardiac abnormalities. However, it is not the investigation of choice to reveal the underlying cause. C 24 h ECG Although this patient reports symptoms suggestive of palpitations (‘ﬂuttering feeling in the chest’), there are no features suggestive of a sinister arrhythmic event. This patient likely has carcinoid syndrome, which does not commonly affect cardiac conduction. E Abdominal ultrasound This patient has an enlarged liver on clinical examination. This may be due to hepatic metastatic spread of a GI carcinoid tumour or secondary to the apparent tricuspid regurgitation. An abdominal ultrasound may show a hepatic tumour, but it is unlikely to be able to differentiate between a carcinoid tumour and a metastatic adenocarcinoma. Although it is an important investigation, it is unlikely to be the key to the underlying diagnosis.

stem: A 42-year-old man from Bangladesh comes to the Emergency Department complaining of a 6-week history of weight loss, fever, night sweats and dull abdominal pain. He lives in a rural community in Bangladesh that is mostly farmland and has been visiting his daughter for the past week. He has a past history of hypertension, for which he takes nifedipine, but is otherwise well. On examination, his BP is 105/60 mmHg; his heart rate is 80 bpm and regular. Marked hepatosplenomegaly is noted on abdominal palpation. His BMI is 22 kg/m2. Investigation Result Normal value Hb 89 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 5.4 × 109/l 4–11 × 109/l PLT 89 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 137 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.3 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 102 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l ALT 188 IU/l 5–30 IU/l ALP 320 IU/l 30–130 IU/l Bilirubin 14 µmol/l 2–17 µmol/l Albumin 32 g/l 35–55 g/l LDH 121 IU/l 100–190 IU/l PT 12.1 s 10.6–14.9 s Which of the following is the most useful next step with respect to conﬁrming the underlying diagnosis?
explanation: C Direct agglutination testing The most likely diagnosis is visceral leishmaniasis, typically presenting with the syndrome ‘kala-azar’, which causes insidious progressive fatigue, weight loss and night sweats, along with splenomegaly and fever. Anaemia and liver dysfunction are common on baseline blood testing. This travel history from a rural area of Bangladesh increases the likelihood of sandﬂy bites that transmit the disease. Direct agglutination testing and recombinant kinesin antigen (rK39) testing have high levels of sensitivity and speciﬁcity. They should be considered as non-invasive investigative options before moving towards more invasive testing, such as bone marrow aspiration. B Dental scrapings The most likely diagnosis is visceral leishmaniasis. Dental scrapings are usually considered for the diagnosis of mucocutaneous leishmaniasis, which is not indicated here. Mucocutaneous leishmaniasis presents with nasal symptoms, mucosal bleeding and increased secretions. A Bone marrow aspiration Bone marrow aspiration could be considered in myeloproliferative conditions. However, the normal LDH level and travel history are pointers against this. There is the added risk of complications of bone marrow aspiration that should not be taken lightly. D Liver biopsy Liver biopsy is the gold standard for diagnosis but is not the most useful next step. It should be considered in cases where clinical suspicion is high and direct agglutination testing has not been suggestive of the diagnosis. There is the added risk of bleeding associated with this procedure and this should not be taken lightly. E Splenic aspiration Splenic aspiration biopsy, although it would provide a deﬁnitive diagnosis, is not the most useful next step in the management of this patient. It should be considered in cases where clinical suspicion is high and direct agglutination testing has not been suggestive of a diagnosis. There is the added risk of bleeding associated

stem: A 32-year-old nurse presents with iron deﬁciency anaemia. She prefers mainly white meat and ﬁsh but claims that her diet is sufﬁciently varied. She also reports frequent diarrhoea and weight loss of 6 kg in the past year. On examination, her BMI is 22, but no other abnormalities are found. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Value Hb 104 g/l 115–155 g/l MCV 80 ﬂ 76–98 ﬂ Serum ferritin 14 µg/l 10–120 µg/l Serum folate 1.4 µg/l 2.0–11.0 µg/l Albumin 34 g/l 35–55 g/l Immunoglobulin G (IgG) 15 g/l 5–16 g/l IgA 3.8 g/l 1.0–4.0 g/l IgM 2.6 g/l 0.5–2.0 g/l An OGD is performed, which shows some mild duodenitis. Small bowel biopsies are taken and are reported as showing subtotal villous atrophy. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
A Coeliac disease Coeliac disease is characterised by diarrhoea and malabsorption precipitated by sensitivity to gliadin, a protein fraction of gluten found in wheat, rye, barley and oats. Peaks of incidence occur in the third and seventh decades, there is a slight female preponderance and incidence is increased in Caucasian populations. Diagnosis is made by testing for tissue transglutaminase antibody (TTG) or small bowel biopsy, which shows the classical appearance of subtotal villous atrophy. Coeliac is also an important cause of iron deﬁciency anaemia caused by malabsorption of iron, as seen in this patient. Therefore, Option A is correct as it best ﬁts the clinical picture and biopsy ﬁndings. Note that this patient has a normocytic anaemia, as she is both iron deﬁcient (microcytic) and folate deﬁcient (macrocytic) giving an overall normocytic picture. Treatment for coeliac is avoidance of gluten- containing foods. C Small bowel lymphoma This is extremely rare, and usually occurs in older individuals and one would expect to see abnormal plasma cells on biopsy such as abnormal T-cell proliferation. B Crohn’s disease Although this can cause villous atrophy of the small bowel, the classical biopsy ﬁndings are non-caseating granulomas and transmural inﬂammation. This may also be associated with aphthous ulcers in the mouth. D Whipple’s disease This is a rare malabsorptive disease caused by the bacterium Tropheryma whipplei and occurs in conjunction with neurological, cardiac or rheumatological sequelae. This patient did not elicit any

of these symptoms. E Small intestinal bacterial overgrowth This usually gives a high folate as a result of bacterial synthesis, and is more commonly associated with patients who have diabetes or other autoimmune conditions such as scleroderma.

stem: A 55-year-old woman was admitted via the Emergency Department complaining of intermittent epigastric pain. She had had a cholecystectomy 1 year ago for these symptoms but continued to have pain after the procedure. The pain was severe, typically coming on when she was eating, radiating to the back and was accompanied by nausea and sometimes vomiting. It tended to last for several hours and did not vary in intensity. She has had ﬁve such attacks over the last year. Investigation Result Normal Values Bilirubin 21 µmol/l 1 - 22 µmol/l AST 100 u/l 10 - 40 u/l ALT 110 u/l 7 - 55 u/l ALP 176 u/l 30 - 150 u/l Amylase 220 u/l 23 - 65 u/l An ultrasound scan showed a moderately dilated common bile duct (12 mm) but no stones were seen. Consequently, she underwent an endoscopic retrograde cholangiogram which, again showed mildly dilated ducts. A sphincterotomy was performed along with trawling of the bile duct, again revealing no cause. Post- procedure she developed acute pancreatitis from which she recovered with conservative management. Subsequently, her symptoms resolved. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: D Sphincter of Oddi dysfunction The symptoms described by this woman and her response to sphincterotomy are characteristic of sphincter of Oddi dysfunction (SOD), which causes non-calculous obstruction of ﬂow of biliary and/or pancreatic ﬂuid. In SOD, the sphincter is hypertonic (>40 mmHg on manometry) and may also be dyskinetic. SOD typically occurs in middle-aged women, but may present in any age group, including children. The usual presenting symptoms are those of biliary-type pain, i.e. epigastric or right hypochondrial pain that is severe, steady and may radiate to the back or shoulder. Since the symptoms of SOD are usually so similar to that of gallstone disease, the diagnosis of SOD is often only made after cholecystec- tomy. SOD may also manifest as recurrent episodes of apparently idiopathic pancreatitis, but jaundice is rare. There are three categories of SOD: • Type I: People with typical biliary pain, abnormal liver enzymes and radiological evidence of impaired biliary drainage • Type II: People with typical biliary pain, with either abnormal liver enzymes or radiological evidence of impaired biliary drainage • Type III: People with typical biliary pain, but no other abnormalities. Deﬁnitive diagnosis of SOD is made by manometry, although delayed drainage of contrast at ERCP is also a classic sign (>45 min). Rates of post-ERCP pancreatitis are increased ﬁve-fold in people with SOD. Treatment of SOD with smooth muscle relaxants (such as nifedipine) improves symptoms in a proportion of affected people, but at rates similar to placebo overall. Endoscopic sphincterotomy is often effective in treating people with type I SOD, and may help people with type II SOD, but is usually of no beneﬁt in people with type III SOD. Botulinum toxin injection into the sphincter of Oddi may have a role in treatment, particularly for people with type III SOD. E Primary sclerosing cholangitis Primary sclerosing cholangitis only typically causes biliary pain in the presence of cholangitis, and is associated with a beaded pattern to the biliary tree on cholangiography. A Recurrent biliary stones Recurrent biliary stones may be ruled out given that none were seen on her ERCP. B Non-ulcer dyspepsia Non-ulcer dyspepsia does not explain this woman’s abnormal liver enzymes and imaging ﬁndings. C Chronic pancreatitis No typical risk factors for chronic pancreatitis are given, and it is unusual for chronic pancreatitis to cause such marked biliary dilatation.

stem: A 24-year-old man visited his general practitioner (GP) some 10 days after returning from holiday with his friends in Turkey. He admitted to drinking up to 10 pints of lager per day during his 2week holiday and frequently bought food from street sellers. Since his holiday, he has given up smoking as he said he did not enjoy it any more. There was a history of paracetamol use in the past few days for a sprained ankle sustained when slipping in the street, and there was some concern that he may have taken a couple of extra tablets while on holiday. Most recently, he has been suffering from fever and anorexia. On examination, he was jaundiced. Investigation Result Normal values Bilirubin 345 μmol/l 1 - 22 μmol/l (AST) 400 u/l 10 - 40 u/l Which of the following investigations is most likely to give the diagnosis?
explanation: D Hepatitis serology It seems likely that this man has an acute hepatitis. This is unlikely to be an acute alcohol-related phenomenon as he has taken some 10 days to present. The clue is in his visit to Turkey, where he is likely to have been exposed to hepatitis A. This is the commonest cause of viral hepatitis worldwide, transmitted via the faeco-oral route, and is associated with non-speciﬁc symptoms such as nausea, anorexia and distaste for cigarettes. Hepatitis A is not associated with progression to chronic liver disease. During the convalescent period, 5–15% of patients may have relapses of their hepatitis but these resolve spontaneously. Occasionally a more severe jaundice with prolonged cholestasis may occur over the course of 7–20 weeks. Mortality (due to fulminant hepatic necrosis) is rare at around 0.1%, but increases with age. C Paracetamol level In a patient presenting 10 days after his holiday, paracetamol levels are not of value in determining whether excess paracetamol during the trip contributed to his symptoms. A Conjugated bilirubin Given that transaminases are elevated, Gilbert’s disease can be ruled out as a cause of his symptoms. B Clotting screen Although this man has acute hepatitis, synthetic liver function is highly unlikely to be affected and clotting won’t reveal an underlying cause of liver disease. E Serum ammonia Serum ammonia is most useful in the evaluation of hepatic encephalopathy.

stem: A 40-year-old farmer is admitted to the Gastroenterology Ward with a 3-week history of intermittent abdominal pain, nausea, reduced appetite and 5 kg weight loss. He had no past medical history of note and has no allergies. On examination, his temperature is 37.9 °C with a heart rate of 99 bpm and a BP of 119/60 mmHg. There is tenderness in the right upper quadrant with palpable hepatosplenomegaly. Investigation Result Normal value Hb 140 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 10.7 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l Neutrophils 4.6 × 109/l 1.8–7.5 × 109/l Lymphocytes 4.5 × 109/l 1.0–4.0× 109/l Eosinophils 1.6 × 109/l 0.1–0.4× 109/l Sodium (Na+) 140 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.5 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Urea 6.5 mmol/l 1.8–7.1 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 109 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l An ultrasound scan (USS) liver is requested: What is the recommended management of this patient?
explanation:
E Albendazole and surgical resection This patient likely has hydatid disease, given the symptoms of abdominal pain, nausea, anorexia and weight loss, in addition to ﬁndings of eosinophilia and multiple liver cysts on ultrasound imaging. Hydatid disease is a zoonotic infection caused by the tapeworm Echinococcus granulosus which is commonly transmitted by infected dogs and foxes. Contact with animals is a risk factor for the infection and the occupational history of being a farmer is signiﬁcant in this instance. Importantly, unlike other causes of hepatic cysts (eg amoebic liver abscess), hydatid disease can remain asymptomatic for some time before being diagnosed. Treatment of hydatid disease involves a combination of albendazole, corticosteroids and surgical resection to ensure complete clearance of the infection. A Amphotericin B Amphotericin B is a potent antifungal agent used in the treatment of invasive Candida albicans and Cryptococcus neoformans. Fungal

infections do not typically cause eosinophilia as seen in this patient. Rather, it is much more likely that the patient is suffering from a parasitic infection (eg helminth) for which amphotericin B has no efﬁcacy. B Mebendazole Mebendazole is used in the management of parasitic infections, particularly threadworm, hookworm and roundworm. In contrast, albendazole is more commonly used in the management of hydatid disease with mebendazole reserved as the second line. Nevertheless, surgical cyst removal is generally necessary, making an antiparasitic agent used in isolation less likely to achieve complete clearance. C Metronidazole Metronidazole is an antibacterial agent with good activity against anaerobic bacteria. Therefore, it is generally a useful antibiotic to treat intra-abdominal infections. Metronidazole is also used to treat amoebic liver abscesses which can present very similarly to hydatid disease. However, some distinguishing factors include eosinophilia and the presence of multiple cystic liver lesions (representing daughter cysts) which are more common in hydatid disease. In contrast, an amoebic liver abscess is a smooth cystic mass without numerous daughter cysts. D Praziquantel Praziquantel is used in the treatment of helminthic infections including intestinal tapeworm infection. However, hepatic disease requires alternative forms of treatment including albendazole and surgical resection.

stem: A 45-year-old banker is referred by his general practitioner with abnormal liver function tests. He had a heart attack 2 years ago and is regularly seen in the Diabetic Clinic for poor glycaemic control. He currently takes metformin, atenolol and atorvastatin. He drinks socially and smokes 10 cigarettes per day. There is no history of blood transfusion or drug abuse. On examination, he is overweight and there is an enlarged, nontender liver. Ultrasound scan of the liver is reported as showing a generalised, hyper-echogenic appearance with no focal lesions. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Value Hb 130 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 8.0 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l PLT 240 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l MCV 83 ﬂ 76–98 ﬂ INR 1.1 < 1.1 Sodium (Na+) 136 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 3.7 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Urea 9.0 mmol/l 2.5–6.5 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 90 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Albumin 39 g/l 35–55 g/l ALT 96 IU/l 5–30 IU/l AST 70 IU/l 10–40 IU/l ALP 135 IU/l 30–130 IU/l Hepatitis and autoimmune serology Negative Ferritin Normal 20–250 µg/l What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: B Non-alcoholic steatohepatitis Most patients with non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH) are asymptomatic. The condition is usually discovered incidentally after abnormal liver tests. Diffuse fatty change can be detected on ultrasonography as a hyper- echogenic appearance. It is part of a metabolic syndrome and is commonly associated with obesity, diabetes mellitus, hypercholesterolaemia and drugs. In patients with NASH, the ratio of AST to ALT is usually <1, whereas in alcoholic liver disease the ratio is usually >2. Liver biopsy reveals macrovesicular steatosis. Treatment is that of underlying cause, encouraging moderate weight loss, exercise, improved diabetic control, treatment of hyperlipidaemia and avoidance of alcohol. Bariatric surgery is perhaps the best therapeutic modality in the presence of severe obesity. A Drug-induced hepatitis While statins can cause abnormal liver function tests, the history does not suggest that this has been recently commenced. Furthermore, a true drug-induced hepatitis would likely result in a more marked rise in liver enzymes. Given the risk factors, and ultrasound ﬁndings suggestive of fatty change, non-alcoholic steatohepatitis is a better answer. C Alcoholic-induced hepatitis The history does not suggest that the patient drinks alcohol to excess, and the ratio of AST to ALT is <1, suggestive more of NASH than alcoholic liver disease, where the ratio is usually >2. D Chronic active hepatitis There are no particular risk factors given in the history, and viral serology is negative. E Amyloidosis Hepatic amyloidosis occurs in the setting of primary (AL) or secondary (AA) amyloidosis. Hepatomegaly is present in 80% of patients, but one would expect the presentation to include other signs and symptoms of systemic illness such as weight loss, abdominal pain, anorexia, ascites, peripheral oedema and splenomegaly. ALP is frequently raised. Ultrasonographic ﬁndings of hepatic amyloidosis include heterogeneous echogenicity. The diagnosis of gastrointestinal amyloid requires a tissue biopsy with positive staining of amyloid by Congo red or the presence of amyloid ﬁbrils on electron microscopy.

stem: A 45-year-old woman with known rheumatoid arthritis complains of generalised pruritis. On examination, she is mildly jaundiced and has periorbital xanthelasmata. Abdominal palpation reveals hepatomegaly 2 cm below the right costal margin. She has no lymphadenopathy. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal value Hb 112 g/l 115–155 g/l MCV 89 ﬂ 76–98 ﬂ WCC 4.6 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l PLT 310 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l ESR 34 mm/hour 1–20 mm/hour Albumin 30 g/l 35–55 g/l Bilirubin 30 μmol/l 2–17 µmol/l ALP 260 IU/l 30–130 IU/ Which of the following tests would be most useful?
explanation:
A M2 subtype anti-mitochondrial antibody Primary biliary cholangitis is a slowly progressive inﬂammation and destruction of the intrahepatic ducts leading to eventual cirrhosis. The cause is unknown but it is thought to be an autoimmune disease, and there is a strong association with other autoimmune conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis, Sjögren syndrome and CREST syndrome. Most patients are diagnosed between the ages of 40 and 70 years, and 90% of patients are female. D M5 subtype anti-mitochondrial antibody Anti-mitochondrial antibodies are found in over 90% of patients, the M2 subtype being speciﬁc. Therefore M5 is not the most speciﬁc for primary biliary cholangitis. B Anti-smooth muscle antibody Autoimmune hepatitis is a chronic hepatitis characterised by immunologic and auto-immunologic features, generally including the presence of circulating auto-antibodies and a high total serum gamma globulin, usually conﬁned to the IgG fraction. The main circulating auto-antibodies, although not speciﬁc for the disease, are antinuclear antibodies (ANA) and anti-smooth muscle antibodies (ASMA) in type 1 disease and, in type 2 autoimmune hepatitis, antiliver-kidney microsome-1 antibodies (ALKM-1) and anti-liver cytosol antibody-1 (ALC-1). In this case, it is primary biliary chol-

angitis that we are wanting to diagnose so anti-smooth muscle antibody is not particularly useful. C Hepatitis serology Hepatitis serology is negative in primary biliary cholangitis and there is no association. E Serum electrophoresis Serum electrophoresis is abnormal in disorders such as multiple myeloma, but not in primary biliary cholangitis.

stem: A 50-year-old woman is being investigated for intermittent dysphagia and has had a normal upper gastrointestinal endoscopy. She undergoes oesophageal manometry and some of the results are outlined below. She has symptoms of Raynaud’s, and some skin thickening over her hands, but no other signiﬁcant medical problems. Investigation Result Normal values Lower oesophageal sphincter resting pressure 8 mmHg 17 - 36 mmHg Residual lower oesophageal sphincter relaxing pressure 7 mmHg < 8 mmHg Peristalsis: Investigation Result Normal values Proximal amplitude 80 mmHg 33 - 91 mmHg Distal amplitude 25 mmHg 64 - 154 mmHg Which one of the following is the most likely diagnoses?
explanation: A Scleroderma The ﬁnding of a low resting lower oesophageal sphincter (LOS) pressure is a requirement for a diagnosis of scleroderma-associated dysmotility. It may also be found in the hypocontractile oesophagus associated with reﬂux disease. However, in the presence of skin thickening and symptoms of Raynaud’s, the most likely diagnosis is systemic sclerosis. D Achalasia Absent distal peristalsis, high resting LOS pressures and failure of LOS relaxation would be expected in cases of achalasia. B Diffuse oesophageal spasm This is a condition characterised by uncoordinated oesophageal contractions, which can lead to pain on eating, dysphagia and regurgitation in some cases. C Globus Globus is a psychological condition which would only be diagnosed in the absence of abnormal ﬁnding on investigation. E Non-speciﬁc oesophageal dysmotility This is a disorder of peristalsis but would not be associated with the other features of systemic sclerosis (thickened skin and Raynaud’s) that are present in this case.

stem: A 46-year-old Malaysian woman with hepatitis C-related liver cirrhosis is seen in clinic for her 6-monthly follow-up. She remains well and a surveillance ultrasound shows two small focal lesions in the liver. Her alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) is 78 ng/ml (10–20). It was 30 ng/ml six months ago. Spiral computed tomography scan of the liver and thorax conﬁrms two liver lesions, both measuring 2.5 cm × 2.5 cm and no pulmonary lesions. What is the most deﬁnitive way to manage these two liver lesions?
options: Percutaneous ethanol injection of the lesions
explanation:
B Liver transplantation The only proven potentially curative therapy for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) remains surgical, either hepatic resection or liver transplantation. Liver transplantation should be considered in any patient with cirrhosis and a single small HCC (<5 cm) or up to three lesions (<3 cm). Hepatic resection should be considered as a primary therapy in any patient with HCC and non-cirrhotic liver. A rising alpha-fetoprotein indicative of a hepatoma and biopsy is not always necessary to avoid seeding of tumour. D Trans-catheter embolization of the lesions Chemo-embolisation can produce tumour necrosis and has been shown to affect survival in highly selected patients with good liver reserve, although in this case it would only be considered if liver transplantation was not an option. A Partial hepatic resection This is not advised because of the potential to generate new areas of dysplasia within the remaining abnormal liver. C Percutaneous ethanol injection of the lesions Percutaneous ethanol injection has been shown to produce necrosis of small HCC and is best suited for peripheral lesions. Given the

two lesions here are small, liver transplantation if possible is the preferred intervention. E Intravenous interferon Systemic therapies including interferon have a poor response rate in the treatment of hepatocellular carcinoma and would not be curative. Transplant is therefore preferred.

stem: A 64-year-old man presents to accident and emergency complaining of a 4-day history of upper abdominal pain which radiates to his back, along with nausea and diarrhoea. He has been admitted to hospital twice in the past 8 months with similar symptoms and has lost approximately 5 kg in weight over this time. His past medical history includes hypertension, gastric ulceration and a partial gastrectomy 12 years ago. His current medication includes atenolol 50 mg once daily and omeprazole 20 mg once daily. The following blood results were obtained: Investigation Result Normal values WCC 12.6 × 109/l 4.0 - 11.0 × 109/l Hb 124 g/l 135 - 175 g/l MCV 112 ﬂ 80 - 100 ﬂ PLT 110 × 109/l 150 - 400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 135 mmol/l 135 - 145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 3.2 mmol/l 3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l Urea 2.4 mmol/l 2.5 - 6.5 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 64 mmol/l 50 - 120 µmol/l Corrected calcium (Ca2+) 2.24 mmol/l 2.2 - 2.7 mmol/l ALT 64 u/l 7 - 55 u/l ALP 250 u/l 30 - 150 u/l Bilirubin 26 μmol/l 1 - 22 μmol/l Albumin 30 g/l 35 - 55 g/l Random glucose 18 mmol/l 3.9 - 7.1 mmol/l 3-day faecal fat excretion 21 g/day = 63 g total (normal < 30 g/3 days) Which of the following is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
explanation: A Alcohol abuse In view of this man’s history, the most likely diagnosis is recurrent pancreatitis secondary to alcohol abuse or gallstones. Alcohol is a cause of chronic pancreatitis, whereas gallstones may be associated with recurrent acute pancreatitis. Other causes of chronic pancreatitis include cystic ﬁbrosis, haemochromatosis and sclerosing chol- angitis. Chronic pancreatitis is an inﬂammatory condition which is characterised by irreversible damage to both the exocrine and endocrine pancreas. This patient’s faecal fat excretion is high (> 30 g/3 days) indicating pancreatic enzyme insufﬁciency. This is further supported by an elevated random glucose consistent with a diagnosis of diabetes mellitus. Initial further investigations in this patient should include abdominal ultrasound and, if indicated, abdominal CT or MRCP.. Chronic pancreatitis is treated with pancreatic enzyme supplementation and complete abstention from alcohol. Approximately 60% of patients survive two years. B Haemochromatosis There is an absence of other symptoms of haemochromatosis including increased pigmentation, endocrine dysfunction and costochondritis, and presentation at an age earlier than 64 years would be expected. C Sclerosing cholangitis Primary sclerosing cholangitis is strongly associated with inﬂammatory bowel disease, and usually presents at an earlier age than 64 years. D Gastric carcinoma Gastric carcinoma is less likely as the underlying diagnosis, given very gradual weight loss over the past 8 months, and no symptoms suggestive of gastric obstruction. E Coeliac disease Coeliac disease is a possible differential, but given the duration of symptoms, more pronounced anaemia and associated conditions such as dermatitis herpetiformis would be expected.

stem: A 31-year-old previously ﬁt and healthy woman is knocked over by a cyclist on the pedestrian crossing. She is admitted to hospital and has an abdominal computed tomography (CT) scan. This shows that the spleen and liver are normal except for a cyst in the pancreas. The cyst shows features of a 1 cm serous cystadenoma. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
explanation:
A Do nothing Serous cystadenomas (SCAs) are benign tumours of the pancreas commonly picked up on imaging. They are rarely >2 cm and usually remain benign, and therefore do not require follow-up. The differential in this case would be a mucinous cystadenoma, which has malignant potential (in about 25% of cases). CT and MRCP can differentiate between the two but occasionally EUS with FNA

of serous ﬂuid may be required. High levels of CEA are typically observed in a mucinous cystadenoma (but are normal in a serous cystadenoma). The international consensus guidelines (2012) recommend all mucinous cystadenomas should be resected. Other cystic lesions of the pancreas that may be noted incidentally include intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasm (IPMN), which also has a malignant potential and requires MRCP surveillance; pancreatic pseudocysts (in a patient with a history of pancreatitis); retention cysts (simple cysts, seen in association with Von Hippel–Lindau disease and polycystic kidney disease); and papillary cystic neoplasm (typically seen in young females, in the tail or body of the pancreas). E Resection of whole pancreas There is no malignant potential of SCAs. Pancreatectomy would be considered in mucinous cytadenoma or in IPMN with high-risk radiological features (see consensus guidelines mentioned above). B Annual follow-up As there is no malignant potential of SCAs, this is not recommended. Annual follow-up is recommended for patients with low-risk or stable IPMNs with MRCP and clinical examination. C Resection of cyst alone This is not recommended as there is no malignant potential for SCAs. A mucinous cystadenoma would be resected, but pancreatectomy with lymph node dissection remains the standard of care in these cases. D Resection of tail of pancreas There is no malignant potential for SCAs. This option could be considered in a patient with a papillary cystic adenoma, as this tends to occur in the pancreatic tail and metastasis is rare.

stem: A 45-year-old man presents with a 6-month history of progressive intermittent dysphagia to both solids and liquids, and a persistent productive cough. He is a long-term smoker but otherwise is ﬁt and well; he reports no signiﬁcant weight loss. Clinical examination is unremarkable and an upper gastrointestinal endoscopy report from another hospital is normal. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Value Bilirubin 19 μmol/l 2–17 µmol/l AST 22 IU/l 10–40 IU/l ALT 31 IU/l 5–30 IU/l Albumin 42 g/l 35–55 g/l Hb 148 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 9.0 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l PLT 258 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Investigation Result Normal values Lower oesophageal sphincter resting pressure 60mmHg 17–36 mmHg Residual lower oesophageal 12mmHg < 8 mmHg sphincter relaxing pressure Peristalsis reveals the following: Investigation Result Normal values Proximal amplitude 80 mmHg 33–91 mmHg Proximal duration 3 s 2.0–3.6 s Distal amplitude 0 mmHg 64–154mmHg Distal duration Absent 2.9–5.1 s What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
E Achalasia Achalasia describes a failure of relaxation of the lower oesophageal sphincter, and affects an estimated 10 in 10,000 people. Endoscopy is often normal but can show lower oesophageal dilatation and failure of the lower oesophageal sphincter (LOS) to relax. The hallmark feature of manometry is absence of peristalsis in the distal oesophagus, accompanied by failure of the LOS to relax during swallowing (i.e. a high residual relaxing pressure). These features may be accompanied by a high resting LOS pressure, but this is not necessary for a diagnosis. Achalasia often causes intermittent symptoms, with residual food and liquid in the distal oesophagus causing halitosis and recurrent chest sepsis due to nocturnal aspiration. B Nutcracker oesophagus Nutcracker oesophagus is an oesophageal dysmotility disorder characterised by dysphagia of both liquids and solids, with chest pain. In nutcracker oesophagus, there is oesophageal pressure exceeding 180 mmHg, which this patient does not have. A Scleroderma Scleroderma is an autoimmune connective tissue disorder which causes ﬁbrosis of organs. It can cause ﬁbrosis of the oesophagus leading to dysphagia, but is unlikely without other features such as calcinosis, Raynaud’s, sclerodactyly and telangiectasis. Scleroderma can also lead to reduced or occasionally absent distal peristalsis, but this is accompanied by low resting LOS pressures. C Diffuse oesophageal spasm Diffuse oesophageal spasm causes intermittent dysphagia and chest pain. A barium swallow can differentiate from achalasia by demonstrating abnormal oesophageal contractions such as a corkscrew pattern. In this patient there is interruption of peristalsis, which does not ﬁt. D Carcinoma of the oesophagus Oesophageal cancer is associated with male gender, smoking history, oesophageal reﬂux, Barrett’s oesophagus and achalasia. Man-

agement is via an MDT approach. The presence of intermittent rather than progressive dysphagia makes this unlikely, as does the abnormal manometry.

stem: A 42-year-old woman comes to the clinic complaining of chronic diarrhoea. She underwent an extensive small bowel resection for Crohn’s disease 2 years earlier and has not been well since. On examination, she has a BMI of 17, with multiple scars on the abdomen. Additionally she is suffering from dermatitis, glossitis and angular stomatitis. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal value Hb 104 g/l 115–155 g/l MCV 106 ﬂ 76–98 ﬂ WCC 5.6 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l PLT 232 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l ESR 12 mm/hour < 10 mm/hour Sodium (Na+) 139 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 3.9 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 100 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Albumin 29 g/l 35–55 g/l ALT 52 IU/l 5–30 IU/l Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: C Short bowel syndrome Short bowel syndrome has many causes, but in adult patients it is usually the result of extensive surgery undertaken for either Crohn’s disease or mesenteric infarction. We can see from the patient’s blood results that she has a macrocytic anaemia, likely indicating a failure to absorb B12. Her low albumin of 29 also suggests signiﬁcant malabsorption. Dermatitis is a feature of failure to absorb essential fatty acids (linoleic acid and linolenic acid). These patients also commonly exhibit dehydration and signs of hypovolaemia due to extensive gastrointestinal ﬂuid losses. In some individuals adequate oral intake may be impossible; parenteral nutrition may be the only option, but is associated with signiﬁcant long-term morbidity and mortality. A Reactivated Crohn’s disease The fact that the patient has a low ESR level makes a diagnosis of active inﬂammation unlikely. The chronicity of her symptoms going back 2 years also makes an exacerbation of her Crohn’s less likely as the answer here. B Coeliac disease Coeliac disease more often presents with generalised symptoms of tiredness, weight loss and iron deﬁciency anaemia, though it can present with features of ﬂorid malabsorption in severe cases. However, given that we already know that this patient has had an extensive small bowel resection, that represents a far more likely explanation for her clinical picture. D Bacterial overgrowth Bacterial overgrowth tends to present with chronic diarrhoea and/or steatorrhoea with anaemia. Given that both Crohn’s disease and extensive small bowel resection can predispose to the condition, it should certainly be considered in this case. However, the fact that the patient has evidence of chronic malabsorption is more easily explained by a loss of surface area for digestion and absorption caused by short bowel syndrome. E Cryptosporidium infection Cryptosporidium is a protozoal parasite and generally causes a short illness with voluminous watery diarrhoea and abdominal cramps. The exception is in severely immunocompromised patients such as those with AIDS, where it can develop into a serious chronic condition with persistent severe diarrhoea and weight loss. We are given nothing in the history to suggest that degree of severe immunocompromise in this patient.

stem: A 19-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with complaints of lower abdominal pain for the past day that has worsened over the past few hours. He had two episodes of vomiting on his way to the hospital. On examination, his blood pressure is 110/60 mmHg and his heart rate is 108 bpm. Abdominal palpation revealed tenderness in the right iliac fossa. There was no guarding or rigidity. After further radiological examination, the patient was taken up for surgery and the surgical specimen is shown below. Which of the following is the most likely pathology in this patient?
options: Infection of the terminal ileum resulting in granuloma formation
Inﬂammation of a congenital outpouching of the small intestine
Inﬂammatory bowel disease with stricture formation
explanation: B Inﬂammation of a congenital outpouching of the small intestine This is descriptive of Meckel’s diverticulitis. The surgical specimen shows the presence of a Meckel’s diverticulum, which is the most common congenital abnormality of the small intestine. The most common presentation is with bleeding, followed by diverticulitis which can be confused with appendicitis. In a large majority of cases, Meckel’s diverticulum may be incidentally found during surgery. A computed tomography (CT) abdomen may be helpful in the diagnosis, whereas a Meckel scan with technetium-99m pertechnetate may be more accurate in identifying it. D Inﬂammatory bowel disease with stricture formation This is descriptive of Crohn’s disease, which presents with chronic diarrhoea and weight loss, rather than with the acute presentation seen here. Besides, there are no strictures observed in the gross specimen presented here. A Infection of the terminal ileum resulting in granuloma formation This is descriptive of ileocaecal tuberculosis, which usually does not have such an acute presentation. Besides, an outpouching of the small intestine is suggestive of Meckel’s diverticulum. C Inﬂammation of the appendix This is descriptive of acute appendicitis. However, the gross specimen shows an outpouching of the small intestine in the antimesenteric border, suggestive of Meckel’s diverticulum. E Salmonella enteritis resulting in perforation Typhoid due to Salmonella infection can cause longitudinal ulcers which may result in intestinal perforation. However, intestinal perforation usually occurs after more than two weeks of illness. Besides, there is no evidence of perforation in the gross specimen shown here.

stem: A 35-year-old Iraqi student was admitted to the Emergency Department on a number of occasions with abdominal pain associated with arthralgia and fever. Previous medical history included appendicectomy and cholecystitis. Pain was often associated with constipation that became diarrhoea when the pain resolved. Clinical examination revealed a pyrexia of 38.5 °C, with generalised rebound tenderness in the abdomen and diminished bowel sounds. Bilateral swollen knees were noted and clear ﬂuid was aspirated from each joint. Computed tomography (CT) examination was unremarkable. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Value Hb 135 g/l Males: 135–175 g/l Females: 115–155 g/l WCC 10.0 × 10 /l 4.0–11.0 × 10 /l PLT 300 × 10 /l 150–400 × 10 /l Bilirubin 10 µmol/l 2–17 µmol/l AST 16 IU/l 10–40 IU/l ALT 21 IU/l 5–30 IU/l Albumin 40 g/l 35–55 g/l CRP 72 mg/l < 10 mg/l ESR 50 mm/hour 1–20 mm/hour Synovial fluid No organisms Urinalysis Protein+++ Urinary porphyrins Normal What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
A Familial Mediterranean fever Familial Mediterranean fever is an autosomal recessive disorder characterised by sporadic paroxysmal attacks of fever and serosal inﬂammation. Patients are recurrently admitted to hospital and undergo extensive investigation and often abdominal surgery, but no speciﬁc pathology is found. Constipation accompanying the fever is common and diarrhoea may follow its resolution. Synovitis has been reported in up to 75% of patients. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein are elevated, and serosal (peritoneal or pleural) or synovial ﬂuid may show large numbers of neoutrophils with no organisms. Amyloidosis manifesting as proteinuria can occur, particularly in Sephardic (Middle Eastern and North African) Jews. Therefore, Option A is the best answer here. A speciﬁc genetic test is now available to aid diagnosis, and the treatment of choice is colchicine. B Crohn’s disease It could explain many of these symptoms, including the abdominal pain with associated joint pains, as Crohn’s is associated with extraintestinal manifestations such as arthritis. However, this patient has a fever and, in the context of Crohn’s disease, you would be con-

cerned about an abscess or another complication of Crohn’s such as a perforation, which would usually be apparent on a CT scan. C Acute intermittent porphyria Normal urinary porphyrins effectively rule out acute intermittent porphyria. D Adult Still’s disease This condition is usually associated with a classic salmon-coloured rash and a raised ferritin. Splenomegaly can also be present. E Irritable bowel syndrome

stem: A 62-year-old man presents to the Colorectal Clinic for a review of his test results. He had presented earlier that year with a 6-month history of lower abdominal pain and constipation. An urgent CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis shows an ill-deﬁned mass in the lower rectum measuring 30 mm × 28 mm × 16 mm. A diagnosis of stage 2a colorectal adenocarcinoma is made. He has no signiﬁcant past medical history of note and is normally ﬁt and active. In the clinic today, the patient is keen to explore treatment options. What is the most appropriate initial management strategy for this patient?
explanation: E Surgical resection alone Surgical resection is the mainstay of treatment for stage 2a colorectal cancer, aiming for complete removal of the tumour with clear margins. Adjuvant chemotherapy is not routinely indicated in stage 2a disease, unless speciﬁc high-risk features are present. However, chemotherapy would be considered in stages 2b and 2c. D Palliative chemotherapy without surgery This would not be suitable for stage 2a colorectal cancer, which is potentially curable with surgery. Palliative chemotherapy is typically reserved for advanced or metastatic disease where surgery is not a curative option. Given that this patient is relatively young with a good performance status, surgery should most deﬁnitively be considered as an option for managing his cancer. A Adjuvant chemotherapy following surgery This is not the most appropriate initial management for stage 2a colorectal cancer. Adjuvant chemotherapy is generally not recommended for stage 2a disease, unless there are high-risk features such as poor histological differentiation or lymphovascular invasion. It would be considered in later stages of the disease such as stages 2b, 2c and 3. B Neoadjuvant chemotherapy followed by surgery This would not be appropriate for stage 2a colorectal cancer, as neoadjuvant chemotherapy is typically reserved for locally advanced (stage 3) or metastatic (stage 4) disease. Stage 2a patients usually undergo surgery as primary treatment without neoadjuvant therapy. C Observation with close surveillance While surveillance is important following treatment for colorectal cancer, including stage 2a disease, observation alone without surgical intervention is not appropriate as it does not address the primary tumour.

stem: A 62-year-old man with a long history of diabetes and previous cerebrovascular accident is admitted with early satiety, postprandial vomiting and abdominal distension. There is no history of haematemesis or abdominal pain. He opens his bowels regularly. He is on insulin therapy, digoxin and aspirin. On examination, he is overweight and he is in atrial ﬁbrillation. His abdomen is distended and tympanic, but is otherwise soft and nontender with active bowel sounds. Rectal examination reveals soft brown stool. Neurology examination reveals a residual right-sided paralysis. Investigation Result Normal values Hb 134 g/l 135 - 175 g/l WCC 12.7 × 109/l 4.0 - 11.0 × 109/l PLT 319 × 109/l 150 - 400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 133 mmol/l 135 - 145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 3.1 mmol/l 3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 117 µmol/l 50 - 120 µmol/l MCV 81 ﬂ 80 - 100 ﬂ INR 1.2 < 1.1 Urea 10.4 mmol/l 2.5 - 6.5 mmol/l Albumin 36 g/l 35 - 55 g/l Corrected calcium (Ca2+) 2.06 mmol/l 2.2 - 2.7 mmol/l Glucose 11.2 mmol/l 3.9 - 7.1 mmol/l Chest X-ray Normal Abdominal X-ray Dilated stomach Upper GI endoscopy is normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial therapy?
explanation:
E Trial of domperidone Gastric motility is frequently affected in diabetes mellitus, with a

reported prevalence of gastroparesis of 10%, although in reality this is probably signiﬁcantly higher. Patients should initially be investigated with an endoscopy to exclude anatomical lesions such as pyloric stenosis. Gastric emptying scans using solid-phase meals are usually necessary. Treatment is often difﬁcult and improving diabetic control can be beneﬁcial, but a prokinetic drug has the added effects of increasing locally released acetylcholine at the myenteric plexus. Domperidone is now the initial intervention of choice, with metoclopramide having fallen out of favour because of long-term neurological sequelae associated with its use. B Trial of high-ﬁbre diet High-ﬁbre diets may result in signiﬁcant residual solid material remaining within the stomach, exacerbating symptoms of gastroparesis. A Recommend less frequent meals Patients should be encouraged to eat smaller, more frequent meals with a lower potential residual solid component, to minimise solid food retention in the stomach. C Trial of nifedipine Nifedipine is a potential intervention for the treatment of oesophageal spasm in achalasia, but it has no role in the treatment of diabetic gastroparesis. D Trial of a gastric pacemaker Gastric pacemakers are viewed by NICE as a research intervention for patients with gastroparesis resistant to other interventions.

stem: An 18-year-old woman is seen to take a large quantity of paracetamol tablets following an argument with her boyfriend. At 72 h later, she presents to the Emergency Department with jaundice and vomiting. On examination, her BP is 105/72, pulse is 85 and regular. She is tender in the epigastrium and tells you she is passing only small amounts of dark urine. Which of the following would be the best indicator of her overall prognosis?
explanation: A Prothrombin time Paracetamol can cause liver failure even at relatively low doses (>7 g). The transplant criteria published by King’s College Hospital are based on prognostic factors from a large retrospective cohort of patients. In these criteria, coagulopathy (prolonged prothrombin time/increased international normalised ration (INR)) is an important prognostic indicator along with encephalopathy, development of kidney disease and acidosis not corrected by ﬂuid resuscitation. Maximal liver damage will occur approximately 72 h after ingestion when prothrombin time will be maximally prolonged – it will then either return to normal (recovery with no sequelae) or remain prolonged (acute liver failure – recovery unlikely). E Urea Creatinine, not urea is used as an indicator of impending acute kidney disease in paracetamol overdose. Measurement of urea is confounded as a measure of renal failure because of it’s absorption as part of a 'blood meal'. B Liver transaminases Transaminases are released by damaged hepatocytes and are always raised in signiﬁcant paracetamol poisoning, reaching levels of >10 000 IU/l. Transaminase levels are, however, not good indications of whether progression to acute liver failure will occur. C Serum paracetamol levels Although raised serum paracetamol levels at >48 h would suggest a large or staggered overdose, both more at risk of progressing to acute liver failure, the value has no prognostic role. D Bilirubin Although serum bilirubin is included in some prognostic indices in paracetamol poisoning, it is nowhere near as reliable as prothrombin time. Transaminases, γ-glutamyl transpeptidase (GGt), albumin and alkaline phosphatase are of no beneﬁt.

stem: You are asked to review a 42-year-old man with alcoholic cirrhosis who is an inpatient on the Gastroenterology Ward. His spironolactone has been withdrawn, but the nurses are concerned as his creatinine has risen to 180 µmol/l. He has received albumin infusions. On examination, his BP is 110/70 mmHg, with pulse 75/min and regular. He has marked ascites consistent with cirrhosis. You suspect hepatorenal syndrome. Which of the following is the most effective intervention with respect to his renal function?
explanation:
A Terlipressin The class of drugs known as splanchnic vasoconstrictors has been studied regarding treatment of individuals with hepatorenal syn-

drome. One of the drugs terlipressin, has a positive impact on both blood pressure and glomerular ﬁltration rate (GFR), when used in combination with albumin. Terlipressin is a non-selective V1 vasopressin agonist, with lower incidence of ischemic complications as compared to ornipressin. Also, terlipressin can be given as a bolus. Albumin is useful in expanding the plasma volume and maintenance of cardiac output. Liver transplantation is the ultimate deﬁnitive treatment of hepatorenal syndrome. Over the longer term, transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPS) may be of value, although ultimately liver transplantation is the most effective option. In a study by Sarwar et al. (see below), complete response to terlipressin–albumin therapy was seen in 58.3% patients, 29.2% achieved partial response with > 25% creatinine reduction, while 12.5% showed no response. E Midodrine Midodrine (an alpha-agonist) is used the treatment of postural hypotension and is non-selective in constricting splanchnic vessels, and thus cannot be used in this case. Where terlipressin therapy is not available, initial treatment with a combination of midodrine, octreotide and albumin is suggested. Investigations of midodrine alone or in combination have shown conﬂicting results for systemic and renal haemodynamics and renal function in patients with cirrhosis-related complications. B Lactulose Lactulose is used in the management of hepatic encephalopathy. It reduces ammonia production in the intestine. Lactulose is the mainstay of treatment and results in improvement in approximately 70– 80% of patients with overt hepatic encephalopathy. It would not be effective in this particular scenario. C Furosemide Furosemide, a diuretic, is not indicated as the patient is already on spironolactone and his blood pressure needs to be maintained at an optimal level. D Dobutamine Dobutamine is less selective in vasoconstriction of the splanchnic vasculature as compared to terlipressin, and would be ineffective in maintaining blood pressure in this situation.

stem: A 50-year-old man presents with shortness of breath. He is a known alcoholic and has a past history of ischaemic heart disease. On examination, he looks jaundiced but his abdomen is soft and nontender. His blood pressure is 109/82 mmHg, pulse is 80 and regular and his chest sounds clear with good breath sounds bilaterally. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Value Hb g/l (elevated reticulocytes) 135–175 g/l WCC 8.2 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l PLT 92 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 137 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 3.9 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 85 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Bilirubin 35 μmol/l 2–17 µmol/l GGT 400 IU/l 5–30 IU/l Cholesterol 10 mmol/l < 5.2 mmol/l Which of the following diagnoses do you think he has?
explanation: A Zieve syndrome Zieve syndrome occurs in patients with excessive alcohol consumption, with haemolysis and severe hyperlipidaemia, abdominal pain and transient mildly raised bilirubin. It usually occurs in males and resolves once alcohol consumption is stopped. D Gilbert syndrome Gilbert syndrome is a benign cause of isolated hyperbilirubinaemia episodes of jaundice can be triggered by illness, surgery or dehydration. B Whipple’s disease Whipple’s disease is a cause of gastrointestinal (GI) malabsorption, and is caused by the Gram-positive bacterium Tropheryma whippelii. It is also associated with joint pains. C Crigler Najjar syndrome Crigler–Najjar syndrome is a rare congenital disorder of bilirubin conjugation. It has two distinct forms, type 1 and type 2: type 2 patients can survive to adulthood without any neurological impairment, whereas this impairment is seen in neonates in type 1 cases. E Non-alcoholic steatohepatitis syndrome (NASH) NASH is fatty liver disease unrelated to alcohol exposure and is seen in obese patients with insulin resistance, including those with type 2 diabetes.

stem: A 24-year-old man comes to the Emergency Department for review. For the past four weeks, he has had increasingly frequent diarrhoea, opening his bowels up to eight times per day. Over the past few days, the diarrhoea has become increasingly mixed with blood. He has no past medical history of note and takes no regular medication. He tells you he has lost 5 kg in weight over the past few months and has suffered from intermittent night sweats. On examination, his blood pressure is 110/70 mmHg while his pulse is 85 bpm and regular. His abdomen is soft and he has mild left-sided tenderness. Bowel sounds are normal and PR reveals no masses. Repeated stool cultures taken by his General Practitioner are negative. Investigation Result Normal value Hb 133 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 10.1 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l PLT 421 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 137 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 3.8 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 100 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l CRP 189 mg/l < 10 mg/l ALT 42 IU/l 5–30 IU/l ESR 75 mm/1st h < 10 mm/1st h Albumin 31 g/l 35–55 g/l Bilirubin 17 µmol/l 2–17 µmol/l Which of the following is the most useful investigation to establish the diagnosis?
explanation: C Flexible sigmoidoscopy Given the history of chronic bloody diarrhoea, coupled with multiple negative stool cultures, ulcerative colitis is the main diagnosis to exclude. Bearing in mind that distal disease is always present, a ﬂexible sigmoidoscopy coupled with biopsy is the most useful step in establishing the diagnosis. Oral and rectal corticosteroids are the key to achieving remission, coupled with a 5-ASA compound. B Barium enema While a barium enema can show evidence of colonic pathology in ulcerative colitis, it is contraindicated in patients with acute severe colitis due to the risk of perforation and should not be performed here.
