A Abdominal X-ray An abdominal X-ray would not lead to a conﬁrmed diagnosis of the underlying condition (ulcerative colitis) which is the question here. It would, however, be useful in the work-up of patients presenting with an acute severe ﬂare of colitis, as is the case here, in order to investigate for toxic megacolon. Truelove and Witt’s criteria deﬁne acute severe colitis as more than six bloody stools per day along with any one of the following: • tachycardia > 90 bpm • fever > 37.8 °C • Hb < 105 g/l • Raised inﬂammatory markers. D Hydrogen breath test Hydrogen breath testing is useful in conﬁrming a diagnosis of bacterial overgrowth syndrome. Patients with bacterial overgrowth typically present with bloating and abdominal pain along with diarrhoea and ﬂatulence. E Ultrasound scan (USS) abdomen While a USS abdomen can be useful in the diagnosis of inﬂammatory bowel disease it cannot differentiate between ulcerative colitis and Crohn’s disease. It is a more useful in the investigation the of the hepatobiliary disorders which are complications in these patients. Ulcerative colitis is an important risk factor for primary sclerosing cholangitis and gallstone disease.

stem: A 31-year-old man who recently emigrated from China had some routine blood work by his general practitioner (GP). His hepatitis-B screen came back showing positive HBs and hepatitis-B IgG core antibodies. Anti-HBe was positive, but he is eantigen negative and s-antigen negative. The GP immediately referred the patient to your clinic, but before doing this sent some liver function tests. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Value Bilirubin 12 µmol/l 2–17 µmol/l ALT 42 IU/l 5–30 IU/l ALP 67 IU/l 30–130 IU/l Albumin 36 g/l 35–55 g/l HBV DNA Negative The patient seems to be in good health. What is the most appropriate management of this patient?
options: Start combined lamivudine and interferon therapy
Offer an HIV, Hep-C test and discharge the patient back to the GP if negative
explanation:
E Offer an HIV, Hep-C test and discharge the patient back to the GP if negative A patient who is HBs antibody positive indicates previous infection unless they have been vaccinated against Hep-B. The phenomenon of loss of HbeAg and seroconversion to anti-Hbe-positive status indicates a reduction of inﬂammation accompanied by histological change from active to inactive hepatitis. E-antigen negativity implies that he no longer has active infection. Guidance suggests that in this case it is worth offering an HIV test, as exposure to hepatitis

B may well indicate exposure to other blood-borne viruses. For indications for treatment, refer to NICE guidance CG165. D Start combined lamivudine and interferon therapy Antiviral therapy is not currently indicated for a man over 30 years old, with LFTs and negative HBV DNA. Antiviral treatments for HBe-Ag-negative chronic hepatitis-B include PEGinterferon alfa-2a (ﬁrst line), entacavir and tenoﬁvir. A Elective liver biopsy In patients with HBe-negative chronic hepatitis and mildly raised ALT, liver biopsy is usually only considered in those patients who have serum HBV DNA levels >2000 IU/ml, to determine whether treatment is warranted. This patient has nearly normal LFTs and negative HBV DNA. B Discharge back to the GP He should be tested for other blood borne viruses, and offered transient elastography testing. C Start interferon therapy Antiviral therapy is not currently indicated for a man over 30 years old, with normal LFTs and negative HBV DNA.

stem: A 50-year-old bar owner comes to the Gastroenterology Clinic for review. He has suffered from chronic diarrhoea for many years, accompanied by intermittent abdominal pain, and is ﬁnding it impossible to maintain his weight. He admits to drinking excess alcohol in the past, although now he claims to have reduced his intake to one glass of whisky per day. He also smokes 20 cigarettes per day. On examination, his blood pressure is 135/75 mmHg and pulse 80 bpm and regular. His abdomen is soft, although he complains of vague tenderness in the epigastrium. His body mass index (BMI) is 21 kg/m2. Investigations: Investigations Results Normal Values Hb 108 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 7.1 × 109/l 4–11 × 109/l PLT 151 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 137 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.3 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 90 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Albumin 29 g/l 35–55 g/l ALT 121 U/l 5–30 IU/l ALP 172 U/l 30–130 IU/l Bilirubin 17 µmol/l < 17 µmol/l You suspect him to be suffering from chronic pancreatitis. Which of the following is the best way to conﬁrm functional pancreatic insufﬁciency?
explanation: C Faecal elastase Faecal elastase measurement is the preferred approach to evaluating chronic pancreatitis because it requires a single random stool sample, with values of elastase of < 200 ug/g being suggestive of pancreatic insufﬁciency. D Lipase Like amylase, random lipase measurement is not useful in the diagnosis of chronic pancreatitis. It is only useful in diagnosing acute pancreatitis where patients usually present with acute epigastric pain and vomiting. A Amylase Random measurement of amylase and lipase is of no value in detecting either chronic pancreatitis or pancreatic insufﬁciency. Minor elevations may be seen in patients with obesity and diabetes, but this has no prognostic value with respect to pancreatic disease. B Faecal fat estimation Faecal fat estimation is both time-consuming and unpleasant in terms of collection and analysis. Qualitative staining for fat with sudan staining is not recommended. A quantitative approach looking at thresholds of > 7 g/fat excretion per day (possible pancreatic insufﬁciency) and > 10 g/fat excretion per day (likely pancreatic insufﬁciency) is therefore required. E SeHCAT test The SeHCAT test is used for determining bile acid malabsorption. It uses a radiolabelled taurine-conjugated bile acid analogue, and retention is measured at seven days using a gamma camera.

stem: A 24-year-old man was diagnosed with Crohn’s disease at the age of 17 years. He has been admitted to hospital on a yearly basis since his diagnosis with acute ﬂare-ups requiring courses of systemic corticosteroids. He has no extra-enteric manifestations of Crohn’s disease, but has had a problematic perianal ﬁstula requiring frequent courses of antibiotics. He is ﬁnding it difﬁcult to maintain attendance at work because of ill health. Which of the following steps is recommended next to maintain remission in this patient?
explanation:
A 6-Mercaptopurine

Thiopurines (azathioprine and 6-mercaptopurine) are the most effective agents in maintaining remission in Crohn’s disease long term. If not tolerated, methotrexate could be used as an alternative. Thiopurines are thought to be particularly effective in patients with ﬁstulating disease. Inﬂiximab is of value in long-term remission in ﬁstulating Crohn’s disease (and possibly in non-ﬁstulating disease) but is generally used alongside a thiopurine. Over the long term, it may prove a superior option to methotrexate, but currently it is still considered only after a traditional second line therapy has failed to gain control. E Sulphasalazine ASA (5-Aminosalycilic acid) compounds such as balsalazide and sulphasalazine have a role in maintaining remission and are generally well tolerated but are not as effective as thiopurines. B Polymeric diet This has most value in reducing the severity of acute ﬂares and their frequency, rather than resolving ﬁstulae. C Budesonide Steroids do not have a role in maintaining remission, their main value is in treating acute ﬂares of Crohn’s disease. D Ciclosporin Cyclosporine is of most use in the treatment of severe ulcerative colitis which is unresponsive to high dose corticosteroids and 5-ASA compounds.

stem: A 40-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with a 2week history of jaundice, nausea and right upper quadrant abdominal pain. There is no history of fevers or recent travel. He has a past medical history of rheumatoid arthritis, for which he has been taking methotrexate for the past four months. He drinks two glasses of wine three times a week and denies smoking or recreational drug use. Investigation Result Normal value WCC 10.2 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 135 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.2 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 90 µm/l 50–90 µmol/l Bilirubin 60 μmol/l 1–21 μmol/l ALT 150 U/l 1–40 U/l AST 180 U/l 1–40 U/l Albumin 40 g/l 35–50 g/l ALP 80 U/l 30–130 U/l GGT 50 U/l 1–54 U/l What is the most likely cause of this patient's liver injury?
explanation: C Drug-induced hepatitis The most likely cause of the patient’s liver injury is drug-induced hepatitis, given the recent history of methotrexate use. The patient’s blood results demonstrate evidence of acute hepatitis with raised AST and ALT levels, with a normal ratio, and raised bilirubin levels. Methotrexate, a commonly used medication for rheumatoid arthritis, is known to cause hepatotoxicity. It is important to promptly recognise and discontinue the offending medication in cases of drug-induced hepatitis to prevent further liver damage and facilitate recovery. Bilirubin levels of more than twice the upper limit of normal are indicative of severe hepatotoxicity and are associated with a 10–15% mortality rate. A Alcoholic hepatitis This patient’s history does not suggest signiﬁcant alcohol consumption, with six standard glasses of wine totalling 12 units across the week. This makes a diagnosis of alcoholic hepatitis less likely. Additionally, alcoholic hepatitis would typically cause a raised AST : ALT ratio of more than 2 and elevated GGT levels, which are not seen here. B Autoimmune hepatitis While autoimmune hepatitis is a consideration in patients with elevated liver enzyme levels and jaundice, the onset of symptoms within a short time frame from starting methotrexate makes druginduced hepatitis a more likely diagnosis in this case. D Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) typically presents with elevated liver enzyme levels and may progress to liver ﬁbrosis and cirrhosis. LFTs tend to show an AST : ALT ratio of less than one. Bilirubin levels are typically normal and are only elevated with decompensated disease. Adding to this, the patient’s history of methotrexate use makes drug-induced hepatitis a more likely explanation for the liver injury in this case. E Viral hepatitis The absence of fever or recent travel and a normal WCC make viral hepatitis unlikely. The history of recent methotrexate use with the LFT results seen above makes a drug-induced cause more plausible.

stem: A 35-year-old patient with a diagnosis of ulcerative colitis (UC) has suffered a number of episodes of pan-colitis over the last 11 years. He is currently managed with inﬂiximab and has stable disease. He has read on the Internet that people with UC have an increased risk of cancer and liver disease and wishes to discuss this. He has not had any weight loss or additional bloody diarrhoea. The general practitioner (GP) measures his carcino-embryonic antigen level (CEA) and alpha fetoprotein, and a surveillance colonoscopy is arranged. Which of the following is the correct advice to give him?
options: CEA is a useful screening test for bowel cancer
Faecal calprotectin elevation indicates a possible neoplasm
Cancers tend to present earlier in patients with UC and are therefore easier to treat
Alpha-fetoprotein is a good marker for primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC) in this case
He is at risk of PSC despite good control of his UC at the current time
explanation: E He is at risk of PSC despite good control of his UC at the current time Although this patient’s UC is currently well controlled, it won’t signiﬁcantly impact on future risk of PSC, which is strongly associated with inﬂammatory bowel disease. C Cancers tend to present earlier in patients with UC and are therefore easier to treat Due to the fact that symptoms may be confused with active inﬂammatory bowel disease, diagnosis is often made late. A CEA is a useful screening test for bowel cancer CEA is not reliable as a test for diagnosing early colon cancer, but is considered as a test for cancer recurrence in those who have undergone a surgical resection. B Faecal calprotectin elevation indicates a possible neoplasm Faecal calprotectin is a measure of active inﬂammatory bowel disease. D Alpha-fetoprotein is a good marker for primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC) in this case Alpha-fetoprotein is a marker for hepatocellular carcinoma, not for PSC.

stem: A 24-year-old woman comes to the Gastroenterology Clinic for review. She complains of weight loss, intermittent abdominal bloating and diarrhoea which has increased over the past few months. She also has a history of type I diabetes, for which she takes a basal bolus insulin regimen. Examination reveals a blood pressure of 110/75 mmHg; pulse is 85 bpm and regular. She looks pale and has a body mass index (BMI) of 20 kg/m2. Investigation Result Normal value Hb 101 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 9.7 × 109/l 4–11 × 109/l PLT 178 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 138 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.3 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 95 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Albumin 26 g/l 35–55 g/l ALT 85 IU/l 5–30 IU/l Bilirubin 17 µmol/l 2–17 µmol/l ALP 183 IU/l 30–130 IU/l Calcium (Ca) 2.15 mmol/l 2.2–2.6 mmol/l Anti-endomysial antibody (IgA) Negative Which of the following is the most useful next step given the negative anti-endomysial antibody result?
explanation: C Immunoglobulin electrophoresis Insufﬁcient levels of IgA lead to falsey negative coeliac serology (both IgA tTG and IgA endomysial antibodies). As IgA deﬁciency can coexist in up to around 5% of patients with coeliac disease. It is therefore necessary here, given the suspicious clinical scenario and concurrent autoimmune disease, to rule out IgA deﬁciency before excluding coeliac disease based on negative serology alone. Duodenal biopsy would be appropriate after IgA testing. A Duodenal biopsy Although anti-endomysial antibody is negative, this test requires sufﬁcient levels of IgA which has not been tested for. It raises the possibility of IgA deﬁciency and would be required for testing before a duodenal biopsy is clinically indicated. B Gluten-free diet Although this is a treatment option for coeliac disease, it may obscure the diagnosis if further requiring duodenal biopsy after IgA testing. A gluten-free diet is a signiﬁcant undertaking for which coeliac patients must strictly adhere to lifelong. It should not, therefore, be advised to be started without a diagnosis ﬁrst. D SeCHAT testing SeCHAT testing is not clinically indicated. This is a test of bile acid malabsorption which is common in inﬂammatory bowel disease. The clinical scenario would indicate she may have coeliac disease. E 24hr fecal fat collection 24-hour faecal fat collection is a test for fat malabsorption which is not currently indicated by the clinical scenario.

stem: A 46-year-old man complains of acute epigastric pain radiating to his back. This is associated with vomiting. The pain is improved when he sits forward. He drinks half a bottle of whisky per day. On examination, he is mildly pyrexial. He looks jaundiced and unwell. He is tachycardic and slightly hypotensive. There is generalised tenderness of the abdomen. There is no guarding or rebound rigidity. Bowel sounds are normal. Electrocardiography, erect chest and abdominal radiography are normal. Abdominal ultrasonography shows a small liver, normal bile ducts and minimal ﬂuid around the pancreas. Which of the following is an indicator of poor prognosis for his condition?
explanation:
C Serum calcium = 1.91 mmol/l The patient has acute pancreatitis secondary to alcohol (95% of acute pancreatitis is attributable to gallstones and alcohol). The pain in pancreatitis can be very severe and is relieved by leaning forward. In severe cases, patients are shocked. There are several severity scoring systems used to assess prognosis/predict mortality. The Ranson criteria use the following parameters (assessed at admission and 48h) to predict mortality in alcoholic pancreatitis: age > 55, WCC > 16.0 × 109/l, fasting blood glucose > 11 mmol/l, LDH > 350 IU/l, serum AST >250 IU/l; within 48 h of admission: haematocrit decrease by >10%, arterial Pa02 <8 kPa, serum calcium < 2.0 mmol/l, blood urea nitrogen increase > 1.8 mmol/l, base deﬁcit > 4 mmol/l, ﬂuid sequestration > 6 l. Mortality ranges from 1% for those with <3 criteria to 90% for those with >6 criteria. Other assessment systems include the Glasgow score and Acute Physiology and Chronic Health Evaluation (APACHE) II scoring system. There are limitations to most scoring systems (as most require 48 h to determine predicted outcome) and the patient needs to be aggressively ﬂuid resuscitated early to reduce the chance of progression to end organ dysfunction (250–500 ml/h isotonic crystalloid during ﬁrst 12–24 h). The most recent British Society of Gastroenterology guidelines are from 2005. For more recent guidelines see American College of Gastroenterology: Management of Acute Pancreatitis (2013), Am J Gastroenterol 2013; 108:1400–1415. E Serum creatinine = 150 mmol/l This creatinine may be indicative of early kidney disease, which is a marker of severe pancreatitis, but serum creatinine in isolation is

not in the recognised severity criteria. A PaO2 = 9.5 kPa In the Glasgow prognostic criteria for alcoholic and gallstone pancreatitis, a Pa O2 of <8kPa in room air is a marker of poor prognosis. Other criteria include: Age >55 Serum albumin <32g/l Serum Ca <2 mmol/l Blood glucose >10 mmol/l Serum LDH >600 units/l Serum urea nitrogen >16.1 mmol/l WBC >15 With a score <3, severe pancreatitis (deﬁned as the presence of persistent organ failure >48 h) is unlikely to occur. B Serum albumin = 34 g/l In the Glasgow prognostic criteria for alcoholic and gallstone pancreatitis, an albumin of <32 g/l is a poor prognostic indicator. D Aspartate aminotransferase = 98 IU/l An AST >250 would be predictive of severity in the Ranson criteria.

stem: A 55-year-old man was found on the street by the police. He complains of right upper quadrant pain and anorexia. He works at a building site but has recently lost his job. On examination, he smells very strongly of alcohol. He has icteric sclera. His temperature is 37.6 °C. There is spider naevi and palmar erythema. Heart sounds and chest examination are unremarkable. Abdominal examination reveals dull ﬂanks and a tender liver edge. There is no focal neurology but a hepatic ﬂap is present. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Value Hb 121 g/l 135–175 g/l White blood count (WBC) 17.0 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l PLT 80 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l MCV 103 ﬂ 76–98 ﬂ INR 1.6 < 1.1 Sodium (Na+) 132 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 3.3 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Urea 1.7 mmol/l 2.5–6.5 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 70 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Albumin 35 g/l 35–55 g/l Bilirubin 102 µmol/l 2–17 µmol/l ALT 45 IU/l 5–30 IU/l AST 100 IU/l 10–40 IU/l ALP 156 IU/l 30–130 IU/l Ferritin 987 µg/l 20–250 µg/l Hepatitis and autoimmune serology Negative What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: B Alcoholic hepatitis Alcoholic hepatitis commonly occurs after a prolonged period of alcohol abuse or return to alcohol after period of abstinence. It often presents with malaise, anorexia, mild fever, tender hepatolomegaly, and (if severe) jaundice. Investigations usually reveal mildly increased serum transaminases, macrocytosis, thrombocytopenia, poor hepatic synthetic function, leukocytosis irrespective of infection and increased acute phase reactants. Usually the AST : ALT > 2. The prognosis depends on its severity. Malnutrition, jaundice, ﬂuid retention and encephalopathy are associated with poor outlook. Histology can help to conﬁrm diagnosis. The mainstay of treatment is supportive in nature: • Alcohol abstinence • Prevention and treatment of alcohol withdrawal • Fluid management • Nutritional support • Infection surveillance • Prophylaxis against gastric mucosal bleeding The discriminant function (DF) can be used to identify patients for treatment. Those who have a value > 32 may beneﬁt from corticosteroids. If there is a contraindication to steroids, pentoxifylline is an alternative. A Hepatoma The development of a hepatocellular carcinoma in a patient with liver cirrhosis is a possible cause of decompensation. However, the history of alcohol, low-grade fever and high WCC, make alcoholic hepatitis a more likely cause. C Choledocholithiasis Acute gallstone impaction in the common bile duct is likely to present with right upper quadrant pain, with possible complicating cholangitis causing a fever. But this would not account for the macrocytosis, signs of chronic liver disease, and decompensation with jaundice, ascites and asterixis. D Viral hepatitis This could be the cause of chronic liver disease, which has now decompensated, but we are told that viral serology is negative. E Haemochromatosis There is no suggestion of other organ involvement, and haemochromatosis is less likely to explain the tender hepatomegaly, raised WCC, and mild fever. The raised ferritin in this case is likely due to alcoholic liver disease and not haemochromatosis.

stem: You are seeing a 25-year-old woman in clinic with a history of ulcerative colitis (UC). She had extensive colitis 10 years ago, which has improved with medical treatment. Last year, she had been diagnosed with early primary sclerosing cholangitis after an MRCP and liver biopsy. Her last colonoscopy was 6 months ago, which detected no active disease, and random biopsies were normal. She is remaining well and asymptomatic. Physical examination is unremarkable, with a normal BMI of 23. When should colonic screening be performed on this patient?
options: Colonoscopy should be performed only when there are symptoms of colitis
Colonoscopy should be performed in 10 years’ time
Colonoscopy should be performed in 3 years’ time
explanation: C Colonoscopy should be performed annually This patient has had ulcerative colitis (UC) for 10 years and has developed associated primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC) of the liver. Patients with concomitant UC and PSC are at a higher risk of developing colonic cancer, and it is recommended that they be screened annually with colonoscopy. Those with history of colon cancer in a ﬁrst-degree relative under 50 years of age should also be subject to annual surveillance. D Colonoscopy should be performed in 3 years’ time Those with intermediate-risk disease, extensive colitis with mild active endoscopic/histological inﬂammation or post-inﬂammatory polyps or family history of colorectal cancer in a ﬁrst-degree relative aged 50+, should be surveyed 3-yearly. A Colonoscopy should be performed only when there are symptoms of colitis Given there is signiﬁcant risk of colonic dysplasia and subsequent carcinoma, expectant colonoscopy only when there are symptoms runs the risk of missing a lesion that could be advanced at the point of diagnosis. B Colonoscopy should be performed in 10 years’ time Even those patients with low-risk disease (those with previous extensive colitis with no active endoscopic/histological inﬂammation or left-sided colitis or Crohn's colitis of <50% colon) should be surveyed 5-yearly. E Flexible sigmoidoscopy should be used 2-yearly Flexible sigmoidoscopy is inappropriate because it would fail to detect right-sided colonic lesions.

stem: A 68-year-old man complains of lethargy and progressive shortness of breath on exertion. He has a long history of intermittent heartburn and has occasionally passed some dark red blood mixed with his stools. Other past medical history includes hypertension and diet-controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus. He has not lost any weight recently, is an ex-smoker and drinks only occasional alcohol. Physical examination conﬁrms hypertension, blood pressure 150/90 mmHg, but is otherwise unremarkable. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal value Hb 84 g/l 135–175 g/l MCV 70 ﬂ 76–98 ﬂ WCC 9.5 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l Neutrophils 5.4 × 109/l 2.5–7.58 × 109/l PLT 258 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Renal and hepatic function are normal. Gastroscopy and barium enema are normal. Mesenteric angiography showed an abnormal vascular blush in the ascending colon. \ What is the most likely cause of his anaemia?
explanation:
B Angiodysplasia This patient has a microcytic anaemia and a history of gastrointestinal bleeding. The ﬁndings on mesenteric angiography, combined with a normal barium enema, suggest a diagnosis of angiodysplasia. Angiodysplasia may be found throughout the gastrointestinal tract, although it most commonly occurs in the caecum and ascending colon. It is a signiﬁcant cause of chronic anaemia and can also cause acute haemorrhage. Treatment is either by heat coagulation at endoscopy or by embolisation of the bleeding vessel during angiography. C Colonic varices Colonic varices would produce distension of the veins in the colon and would not appear as an abnormal vascular blush on mesenteric angiography. A Colonic carcinoma Barium enema would not be normal in colonic carcinoma – we would expect a colonic mass in carcinoma. The mesenteric angiography would be normal. D Meckel’s diverticulum

Meckel's diverticulum is the most common congenital anomaly of the gastrointestinal tract. It results from incomplete obliteration of the vitelline duct leading to the formation of a true diverticulum of the small intestine. Meckel's diverticulum is a true diverticulum, containing all layers of the small bowel wall. It arises from the anti- mesenteric surface of the middle-to-distal ileum. The diverticulum represents a persistent remnant of the omphalo-mesenteric duct, which connects the midgut to the yolk sac in the foetus. Meckel's diverticulum is uncommon and often clinically silent, particularly in adults. Asymptomatic Meckel's diverticulum may be discovered during abdominal exploration for the evaluation of unrelated pathology. Less commonly, it is found incidentally on diagnostic imaging. When symptomatic, Meckel's diverticulum may present with abdominal pain or symptoms of gastrointestinal bleeding or bowel obstruction. Mesenteric angiography is not abnormal as in this case. E Ulcerative colitis Ulcerative colitis is characterised by recurring episodes of inﬂammation limited to the mucosal layer of the colon. It commonly involves the rectum and may extend in a proximal and continuous fashion to involve other parts of the colon. Patients with ulcerative colitis usually present with diarrhoea, which may be associated with blood. Bowel movements are frequent and small in volume as a result of rectal inﬂammation. Associated symptoms include colicky abdominal pain, urgency, tenesmus and incontinence. Patients with mainly distal disease may have constipation accompanied by frequent discharge of blood and mucus. The endoscopic ﬁndings in patients with ulcerative colitis include loss of vascular markings due to engorgement of the mucosa, giving it an erythematous appearance. In addition, granularity of the mucosa, petechiae, exudates, oedema, erosions, touch friability and spontaneous bleeding may be present. More severe cases may be associated with macroulcerations, profuse bleeding and copious exudates. Mesenteric angiography is not abnormal as in this case.

stem: An 18-year-old man is admitted after celebrating his birthday with friends at a night club. He drank a large volume of vodka and beer and then proceeded to vomit copiously. After vomiting and retching for the third time, the vomit was seen to contain bright red blood. Endoscopy the following morning was normal. Which of the following is the next most appropriate management step?
options: Start intravenous proton pump inhibitor therapy
Start oral proton pump inhibitor therapy
Discharge the patient with reassurance and advise on safe alcohol consumption
explanation: E Discharge the patient with reassurance and advise on safe alcohol consumption The history of retching followed by bright red blood in the vomitus and the normal ﬁndings on endoscopy suggest a diagnosis of Mallory–Weiss tear. The patient is haemodynamically stable and requires no speciﬁc intervention, except reassurance and advice on safe consumption of alcohol. C Start intravenous proton pump inhibitor therapy This would be appropriate if a peptic ulcer was present, but with a normal endoscopy excluding ulceration, this is unlikely and the treatment isn’t therefore relevant. A Angiography of the coeliac axis This would be a possible investigation for mesenteric ischaemia. Mesenteric ischaemia is small bowel injury due to hypoxia following a thrombosis or embolus. It is associated with AF and causes sudden and severe pain with PR bleeding. This does not ﬁt, as the patient has vomited blood rather than passed it PR, and he lacks any relevant risk factors. B Repeat endoscopy in one month The absence of any abnormalities is unlikely to change. It would be appropriate to arrange repeat upper GI endoscopy in the presence of peptic ulcers to ensure recovery. D Start oral proton pump inhibitor therapy Oral proton pump therapy would be appropriate for gastritis, but the symptoms, demographic and endoscopy ﬁndings do not match this.

stem: A 36-year-old woman with a 15-year history of severe ileo-colonic Crohn’s disease is admitted for assessment and management of a severe ﬂare-up of her disease. Her symptoms are severe lower abdominal pain, diarrhoea, weight loss and lethargy. She has also recently developed a vesico-colic ﬁstula. She is currently taking mycophenolate mofetil (MMF), which had been controlling her symptoms for the last few months, but was now losing its efﬁcacy. Her treatment history consists of multiple courses of steroids which, when tapered off resulted in severe disease recurrence. She also failed on azathioprine and 6-mercaptopurine and an elemental diet. She had an ileal segmental resection with end-to-end anastomosis 8 years ago. Her blood tests show a normochromic normocytic anaemia, leucocytosis, elevated ESR and CRP and a low albumin. What is the most appropriate next line as steroid-sparing therapy?
options: Total colectomy with ileo-anal pouch formation
explanation: B Intravenous inﬂiximab Inﬂiximab is a biological therapy for Crohn’s disease and is a monoclonal antibody to the cytokine tumour necrosis factor-alpha. It is licensed for use in the management of steroid- and immunosuppressant-resistant Crohn’s disease. It is also particularly useful in healing ﬁstulae. It has been reported to induce a remission in 60– 80% of patients. If the patient responds to the initial dose, then the usual treatment regime is a further four infusions at 8-weekly intervals. Allergic reactions are seen in 5% of cases. It is important to exclude tuberculosis prior to starting this treatment as it can cause reactivation. C Total colectomy with ileo-anal pouch formation Surgery is a part of management for Crohn’s disease in those severely affected when medical immunomodulation has completely failed. Surgery is also necessary as an emergency treatment for GI obstruction from stricturing or bowel perforation. As surgery is never curative, it should be reserved after medical options have been exhausted. A Oral ciclosporin Ciclosporin is a treatment option for ulcerative colitis rather than Crohn’s disease. D Alpha-interferon therapy Alpha-interferon therapy is appropriate in CML, hairy cell leukaemia, follicular lymphoma and chronic hepatitis B and C. It is not useful in Crohn’s disease. E Intravenous cyclophosphamide Cyclophosphamide is a chemotherapeutic agent that can be used against rheumatoid arthritis, vasculitis and in various forms of leukaemia and lymphoma. It should not be used in Crohn’s disease.

stem: A 40-year-old woman presents with a history of chronic diarrhoea. She also complains of bone pain. On examination, she has a number of small blisters on the skin that are extremely itchy, as shown below over her shoulder. Blood testing reveals low corrected calcium, raised alkaline phosphatase and low albumin levels. She is also found to be anaemic. Which of the following represents the best treatment option for this patient?
explanation:
D Gluten-free diet The history of anaemia with associated hypoalbuminaemia, hypocalcaemia and raised alkaline phosphatase all point to a malabsorptive process secondary to coeliac disease and associated osteomalacia from vitamin D deﬁciency. There are dual peaks of incidence in the 3rd and 7th decades, and the disease is commoner in women. An OGD with duodenal or jejunal biopsy is the gold standard test, and demonstrates sub-total villous atrophy. Treatment is the commencement of a gluten-free diet, so Option D is correct. This will also help treat the skin rash from which the patient is suffering,

called dermatitis herpetiformis - a chronic blistering skin rash linked to coeliac disease. C Topical corticosteroids Topical corticosteroids have no role in the management of this skin condition. A Calcium and vitamin D supplementation It would help with the low calcium but would not treat the underlying cause, so is not the best option here and is therefore incorrect. B Intravenous albumin This is rarely used as a treatment strategy to correct hypoalbuminaemia and would not be the best treatment in this patient. E Oral 5-aminosalicyclic acid The diarrhoea is caused by malabsorption from coeliac disease. 5ASAs have no role in the management of coeliac disease and are more commonly used in the treatment of inﬂammatory bowel disease.

stem: A 60-year-old woman with systemic sclerosis complains of diarrhoea, abdominal bloating, lethargy and weight loss. On examination, she is pale. Respiratory and cardiovascular examinations are normal. The abdomen is distended, but soft and nontender. Bowel sounds are present. She has bilateral pitting ankle oedema. There is a proximal weakness of her arm and leg muscle. The tone, reﬂexes and sensation are normal. Blood pressure is 122/82, pulse is 75 and regular. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Value Hb 80 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 11.2 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l PLT 400 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 136 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.4 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 60 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l MCV 106 ﬂ 76–98 ﬂ Urea 2.5 mmol/l 2.5–6.5 mmol/l Albumin 34 g/l 35–55 g/l Serum B12 123 pmol/l 160–900 pmol/l Folate 22 μg/l 2.0–11.0 µg/l
explanation: A Hydrogen breath test Bacterial overgrowth is common in patients with jejunal diverticulae, which in this case has led to malabsorption of vitamin D and calcium and muscle weakness. The bacteria can also lead to B12 deﬁciency, although folate levels are not normally depleted. Bacterial overgrowth can be conﬁrmed by the hydrogen breath test after giving lactose or glucose. Small-bowel diverticula develop secondary to intestinal dysmotility and connective tissue disorders – for example, Marfan syndrome and systemic sclerosis. Patients are usually asymptomatic, but on bacterial colonisation they develop malabsorption. Treatment is empirical, and options include metronidazole and tetracycline. If this fails, jejunal aspiration is recommended to identify the organism. B Urea breath test The urea breath test is used to conﬁrm a diagnosis of H. pylori, which is associated with peptic ulceration, rather than the symptoms of malabsorption seen here. C Schilling’s test Schilling’s test is used to diagnose pernicious anaemia, but the jejunal diverticulae seen here drive us more towards bacterial overgrowth and malabsorption as the cause of the abnormal metabolic picture seen here, rather than pernicious anaemia. D Thyroid function test Stable pulse and blood pressure, coupled with normal reﬂexes, count against thyroid dysfunction as the underlying cause of this patient’s symptoms. E Faecal calprotectin Faecal calprotectin is a cytoplasmic protein from neutrophils which is almost always increased with colonic inﬂammation related to ulcerative colitis or Crohn’s disease.

stem: This chest radiograph is from a 36-year-old man who presented with severe abdominal pain, having collapsed at home. He has suffered from intermittent bloody diarrhoea, which has increased in severity over the past few months. On examination, his blood pressure is 100/70, pulse is 90 and regular. He is pyrexial at 38.4 °C. Abdomen is generally tender and rigid with guarding. His chest X-ray is shown below: What is the most likely underlying cause of his presentation?
explanation: A Ulcerative colitis The chest radiograph shows free air under the diaphragm, which is due to perforation of an abdominal viscus. Although the heart shadow looks a little large, remember that it is an AP ﬁlm. The most likely cause in this patient would be perforated large bowel secondary to ulcerative colitis, which ﬁts well with the previous history of chronic diarrhoea. C Acute cholecystitis Cholecystitis presents with epigastric and right upper quadrant pain, and gall bladder perforation is very rare. B Acute pancreatitis Acute pancreatitis presents with vomiting and epigastric pain, rather than the clinical picture seen here. D Ischaemic bowel Ischaemic bowel does cause diarrhoea, although it usually occurs in patients with a history of atherosclerosis and who are considerably older than 36. E Diverticulitis Diverticulitis is seen in a more elderly population, although it does present with left-sided abdominal pain and diarrhoea.

stem: A 63-year-old man with a history of COPD and severe arthritis presents to the Emergency Department of the university hospital with haematemesis. You get his old notes and ﬁnd that his lung function is quite poor. He is managed with both salmeterol/ﬂuticasone high-dose inhaler and tiotropium. Medication for his arthritis includes diclofenac. On examination, he is very unwell, with a pulse of 105/min and BP of 85/50 mmHg. You resuscitate him with ﬂuids and 2 units of blood and arrange an endoscopy; the endoscopist visualises a large bleeding duodenal ulcer, but he is unable to reach it properly to control the bleeding via the scope. The patient has a further large haematemesis. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal value Hb 89 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 5.4 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l PLT 130 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 138 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 5.1 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 189 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l ECG Lateral ST depression Which of the following represents the most appropriate management in this case?
options: Further ﬂuid resuscitation and delayed endoscopy
explanation: D Angiography and selective embolization This patient is a very poor surgical candidate, with severe COPD and an ECG which reveals signs of ischaemia, potentially related to hypovolaemia as a result of blood loss. In this situation a number of case series have demonstrated that selective arterial embolisation is an effective way to control bleeding from a duodenal ulcer, and leads to improved survival vs other potential interventions. C Fluid resuscitation and IV pantoprazole Although acute use of PPIs does reduce the risk of re-bleeding in peptic ulcer disease, given the size of the ulcer and continued bleeding on endoscopy it’s unlikely to impact here. A Further ﬂuid resuscitation and delayed endoscopy This risks further catastrophic bleeding from the duodenal ulcer. B Progression to open surgery Open surgery is not an option for this patient in his current state; he has an unstable blood pressure and is unlikely to avoid long-term ventilation because of his COPD. E Fluid resuscitation and IV terlipressin IV terlipressin is of value in controlling bleeding from oesophageal varices, not as a result of peptic ulceration.

stem: A 64-year-old vegetarian woman comes to the clinic for review. She has been referred by her general practitioner with unexplained iron deﬁciency anaemia which has not responded to iron therapy. There is no signiﬁcant past medical history, apart from hypertension which is controlled with 2.5 mg bendroﬂumethiazide. Speciﬁcally, there is no history of indigestion, change in bowel habit or blood per rectum. Examination reveals a blood pressure of 135/72 mmHg and a pulse of 75 bpm and regular. She has pale conjunctivae. There are no abnormal ﬁndings, and her body mass index (BMI) is 23 kg/m2. Investigations; Investigations Results Normal Values Hb 91 g/l 115–155 g/l MCV 78 ﬂ 76–98 ﬂ Ferritin 18 µg/l 10–120 µg/l WCC 8.1 × 109/l 4–11 × 109/l PLT 201 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 137 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.3 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 85 μmmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Albumin 30 g/l 35–55 g/l ALT 54 IU/l 5–30 IU/l Urine, blood and protein negative Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
explanation: C Coeliac antibody screening The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) Clinical Knowledge Summaries recommend coeliac screening for any patient who present with iron deﬁciency anaemia before beginning speciﬁc investigations. This is because of the recognition that underlying coeliac disease may present without the classical symptoms of abdominal bloating and diarrhoea. In this case, the low albumin level hints at chronic malabsorption, which may be due to an underlying small bowel disease. Following coeliac antibody testing, the patient should be referred for both upper and lower gastrointestinal investigations, with colonoscopy being a more deﬁnitive option (when preparation is adequate), compared to barium enema. B Barium enema This is not a ﬁrst-line investigation for imaging of the large bowel. If large bowel investigations are required, then patients should be referred for a colonoscopy. A Abdominal ultrasound scan (USS) An abdominal USS would be an appropriate ﬁrst-line investigation in patients with deranged liver function tests or abdominal pain. In this case, the patient importantly has no symptoms to suggest this and we are not provided with signiﬁcantly deranged liver function tests. D Colonoscopy Importantly, in this case, there are no red ﬂag symptoms. Therefore, it would be reasonable to screen the patient for coeliac disease before referring them for a colonoscopy. NICE guidelines do state that all patients over the age of 60 with unexplained iron deﬁciency anaemia should be referred for a colonoscopy on the two- week wait rule. E Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy This would be an investigation that could be considered if the patient had a normal colonoscopy and a normal coeliac screen.

stem: A 45-year-old man presents with a recent change in bowel habits. He had a colonoscopy which was normal. He is still concerned about colorectal cancer as a colleague has recently been diagnosed with metastatic colorectal cancer. He would like some advice on prevention. Which of the following lifestyle measures will have the most impact on reducing his risk of colorectal carcinoma?
explanation: D Stop smoking Colorectal cancer is the second commonest cause of cancer death, after bronchial carcinoma, in the United Kingdom. It is thought that just over half (54%) of bowel cancer cases in the UK are linked to lifestyle risk factors. Public Health England guidance currently advises the following, with regard to modiﬁable risk factors in bowel cancer risk: 1. Exercise regularly 2. Stop smoking 3. Reduce the amount of alcohol consumed 4. Maintain or achieve a healthy weight 5. Eat a healthy balanced diet Meta-analysis suggests that smokers have an 18% increased relative risk of developing colorectal cancer. A Reduce dietary sugar intake While weight gain has been shown to carry a 15-20% increase in relative risk of colorectal cancer, depending on when in life the weight is gained, current guidance does not draw a speciﬁc relationship between sugar intake and colorectal carcinoma. B Avoid contact sports Meta-analysis has shown an approximately 26% reduced risk of colon cancer when comparing the most- versus the least-active individuals. C Dietary supplement with micronutrients There is no evidence to suggest that dietary supplementation with vitamins / micronutrients has a signiﬁcant effect on bowel cancer risk. E Veganism Long-term consumption of red and processed meat appears to be associated with a raised risk of colorectal cancer. Public Health England advise limiting the amount of red meat consumed to 500 grams or less (cooked weight) per week, and limiting the amount of processed meats one consumes. The practice of veganism carries the risk of other nutrient deﬁciencies, and such a practice is not currently advised.

stem: A 38-year-old man with a 5-year history of ulcerative colitis pre- sents to the Emergency Department with complaints of severe abdominal pain, distension and bloody diarrhoea persisting for the past three days. He feels increasingly fatigued, with occasional nausea and vomiting. His vital signs are as follows: temperature of 38.6 °C, heart rate of 115 bpm, BP of 98/60 mmHg and respiratory rate of 24 breaths per minute. On examination, his abdomen is distended and diffusely tender, and bowel sounds are diminished. Investigations: An abdominal X-ray is shown below: Investigation Result Normal value Hb 125 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC PLT 16.2 × 109/l 390 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 132 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 3.8 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 82 µmol/l 60–120 µmol/l Based on the clinical presentation and ﬁndings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
D Toxic megacolon The patient’s symptoms, history of ulcerative colitis, systemic toxicity (fever, tachycardia, hypotension) and radiological evidence of colonic dilatation of more than 6 cm are classic features of toxic megacolon. This diagnosis requires urgent management to prevent complications. B Fulminant colitis

Fulminant colitis is a severe form of ulcerative colitis that can lead to toxic megacolon. However, toxic megacolon itself is characterised by colonic dilatation and is considered a complication of fulminant colitis. Radiographic evidence of signiﬁcant dilatation is key in diagnosing toxic megacolon over fulminant colitis alone. A Acute intestinal obstruction While bowel obstruction may cause abdominal pain, distension and vomiting, it is usually associated with hyperactive or high-pitched bowel sounds early on. Furthermore, it is not typically associated with fever or systemic toxicity, unless complicated by ischaemia or perforation. The patient’s history of ulcerative colitis also makes toxic megacolon more likely. C Perforated diverticulitis Perforated diverticulitis can present with fever, pain and leukocytosis, but it is more common in elderly patients and typically involves the left lower quadrant. Additionally, it does not usually cause the marked colonic dilatation seen in toxic megacolon. E Bowel ischaemia Bowel ischaemia can present with pain, fever and leukocytosis, but it is more likely to present with severe pain out of proportion to physical ﬁndings. Colonic dilatation is not a typical feature of ischaemic bowel disease without infarction or obstruction.

stem: A 72-year-old woman presents with dull abdominal pain and bloating. She tells you on further questioning that she has suffered intermittent episodes of abdominal pain after a heavy meal, and episodes of diarrhoea with dark blood over the past few months. She has a history of hypertension and is clinically in atrial ﬁbrillation. Her abdomen is distended and bowel sounds are absent. Blood tests show an elevated white cell count, renal impairment with a creatinine of 160 µmol/l and metabolic acidosis. What would be the most appropriate diagnostic test in the emergency situation?
explanation: D Contrast CT angiography This patient’s history and the investigation results are very suggestive of mesenteric ischaemia. The patient’s antecedent history of postprandial abdominal pain suggests there may be a degree of chronic ischaemia, and her atrial ﬁbrillation is a risk factor for acute mesenteric arterial embolism. Of the tests listed, mesenteric angiography is the gold standard, although it is much less obtainable in the emergency situation. Rapid diagnosis is essential among patients with clinical features and risk factors suggestive of acute intestinal ischemia to reduce the potential for intestinal infarction. The usual initial test for patients suspected of having mesenteric ischemia, such as in the case above, is contrast computed tomographic (CT) angiography. CT angiography has a high degree of accuracy for diagnosing mesenteric ischemia, and is also useful in excluding other causes of acute abdominal pain. The creatinine of 160, whilst being associated with an increased risk of contrast nephropathy, does not altogether preclude the examination, and attempts should be made to minimise the risk with optimal hydration. A Plasma lactates Although mesenteric ischemia is likely to cause a raised lactate, this is non-speciﬁc and non-diagnostic, as it will rise as a result of any cause of tissue hypoperfusion. B Plain abdominal X-ray In the context of mesenteric ischaemia, positive ﬁndings (ileus, small bowel obstruction, oedematous or thickened bowel walls and paucity of gas in the intestines) on plain abdominal radiography are usually late and non-speciﬁc. More speciﬁc signs, such as pneumatosis intestinalis, thumbprinting of the bowel wall and portal vein gas, are also late ﬁndings. C Conventional mesenteric angiography This has the advantage of offering therapeutic as well as diagnostic options, including administration of intra- arterial thrombolytic agents for acute arterial thrombosis. However, the investigation is highly invasive and unsuitable for critically ill patients; it often is not readily available, and may delay surgical management. Angiography also has a relatively high negative rate in patients presenting early in the course of acute mesenteric ischaemia. Arteriography can also precipitate acute ischaemia; thus, it is important to make sure that the patient is well hydrated. E Colonoscopy Colonoscopy, or ﬂexible sigmoidoscopy, is usually required to conﬁrm a diagnosis of ischaemic colitis, often after suggestive cross-sectional imaging. It does not carry any diagnostic merit in small bowel ischaemia, and is not an appropriate investigation in the emergency situation.

stem: A 50-year-old man presents to his General Practitioner with a 5month history of tiredness. He has no previous medical history and takes no medication. There is no history of weight loss or fever. He eats a regular healthy diet and has no urinary or bowel symptoms. His examination is unremarkable. Investigation Result Normal Value Hb 115 g/l 135 - 175 g/l WCC 10.0 × 109/l 4.0 - 11.0 × 109/l PLT 300 × 109/l 150 - 400 × 109/l MCV 70 ﬂ 80 - 100 ﬂ MCH 20 pg 27 - 33 pg Ferritin 10 µg/l 24 - 355 µg/l (male) Vitamin B12 500 ng/l 160 - 760 ng/l Folate 9 μg/l 2.0 - 11.0 μg/l Urinalysis: negative. Which investigation should be performed next?
options: Urgent referral to Colorectal Services under 2week wait
explanation:
B Faecal occult blood testing Faecal occult blood testing is appropriate in this patient. Indications for faecal occult blood testing include: • An abdominal mass Change in bowel habit Iron-deﬁciency anaemia • ≥40 years and over with unexplained weight loss and abdominal pain • ≥50 years with rectal bleeding and either: o Abdominal pain o Weight loss. • ≥Aged 50 years with any of the following unexplained symptoms: o Rectal bleeding o Abdominal pain o Weight loss. • ≥60 years with any anaemia. As this patient is 50 years old and has iron deﬁciency anaemia, a faecal occult blood sample is recommended. The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence recommends faecal immunochemical testing (FIT) as the primary method of testing. Anti-tissue transglutaminase antibodies and urinalysis would also be appropriate investigations here. A Capsule endoscopy This investigation is usually reserved for patients who have a normal OGD and colonoscopy but remain anaemic despite iron replacement therapy. This investigation is then performed to rule out a small bowel cause for their anaemia such as Crohn’s disease or angiodysplasia. It is not a ﬁrst-line investigation. C Oesophagogastroduodenoscopy (OGD) In all men, post-menopausal women and women aged over 50 years, mandatory investigations for iron deﬁciency anaemia include an OGD. However, more simple non-invasive investigations, such as a faecal occult blood sample, would be considered ﬁrst. D Outpatient colonoscopy This would be indicated, particularly to exclude malignancy as a cause for this patient’s anaemia. However, it would not be the next test performed as it is an invasive procedure. E Urgent referral to Colorectal Services under 2-week wait Urgent referral under the 2-week wait is not appropriate here. Criteria for a 2-week wait referral for colorectal cancer investigation include: • patients aged ≥ 40 years with weight loss and abdominal pain patients aged ≥ 50 years with unexplained rectal bleeding • patients aged ≥ 60 years with iron deﬁciency anaemia or change

in bowel habit • positive faecal occult blood • anal or rectal mass on examination • abdominal mass on examination • patients aged < 50 years with rectal bleeding and any: o abdominal pain o change in bowel habit o weight loss o iron-deﬁciency anaemia.

stem: An 82-year-old woman with poorly controlled chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is admitted to the Respiratory Ward with an exacerbation. She is managed with high-dose intravenous (IV) co-amoxiclav and makes an initially good recovery. There is no other past medical history of note. During her admission, she develops acute-onset abdominal pain and diarrhoea, passing up to 3–4 motions of loose stool per day. There is no vomiting or bleeding per rectum. On examination, her temperature is 37.8 °C. She has a heart rate of 94 bpm and a blood pressure of 115/64 mmHg. Her abdomen is distended and tender. Investigations show: Investigation Result Normal values Haemoglobin (Hb) 149 g/l 135–175 g/l White cell count (WCC) 14.0 ×10 /l 4.0–11.0 × 10 /l Platelets (PLT) 300 × 10 /l 150–400 × 10 /l Sodium (Na ) 138 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K ) 4.0 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 150 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Given the likely diagnosis, what is the recommended management for this patient?
explanation: C Oral vancomycin This is an elderly patient who has been treated with intravenous (IV) co-amoxiclav, associated with Clostridium difﬁcile infection, the cause of pseudomembranous colitis. The antibiotic associated with the highest rate of pseudomembranous colitis is clindamycin, which is used for bone infections, where rates of Clostridium difﬁcile infection are as high as 10%. Mortality related to pseudomembranous colitis is high and in elderly patients, it may be as high as 10%. Vancomycin has virtually no systemic absorption when administered via the oral route and is an ideal choice for the treatment of C. difﬁcile infection. Oral vancomycin is the recommended ﬁrst-line therapy. B Intravenous vancomycin and intravenous metronidazole The combination of vancomycin and metronidazole is reserved for life-threatening C. difﬁcile infection, characterised by a white cell count > 15, temperature > 38.5 °C, hypotension and partial or complete ileus or toxic megacolon. These features are not seen here. Furthermore, an oral preparation of vancomycin is given, rather than via the intravenous route. A Intravenous metronidazole The sole use of IV metronidazole does not play a role in the management of C. difﬁcile infection. Rather, it should be added in with oral vancomycin in severe diseases. D Oral ﬁdaxomicin Oral ﬁdaxomicin is used as a second-line agent in the treatment of C. difﬁcile infection. Therefore, it would be inappropriate to administer at this stage. E Oral rehydration with Dioralyte® Although antibiotic use can cause non-infective diarrhoea as a general side-effect, the presence of low-grade fever makes an infective cause, such as C. difﬁcile, more likely. Oral rehydration alone is not enough to overcome the illness.

stem: A 38-year-old woman with previously stable Crohn’s disease presents complaining of worsening diarrhoea. She is managed on a small dose of budesonide and mesalazine, and had no symptoms up until 6 months ago. Most recently, she has been taking a course of sertraline for depression. Currently she opens her bowels many times per day, with voluminous non-bloody diarrhoea. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Value Hb 129 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 5.0 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l PLT 203 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 139 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 3.9 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 100 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Colonic biopsies lymphocytic inﬁltrate Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
C Lymphocytic colitis Lymphocytic colitis may occur in patients with other forms of GI pathology, including Crohn’s and coeliac disease. Sertraline also appears to be associated with the development of lymphocytic colitis. Withdrawal of the offending agent is preferable, and loperamide is often used as ﬁrst-line therapy to reduce the severity of diarrhoea, with cholestyramine an alternative if there is additional evidence of bile salt malabsorption. Other alternatives include immunemodulating agents such as azathioprine, although a response to therapy may take many months to appear. Approximately 20% of patients have a spontaneous remission without speciﬁc intervention. D Ulcerative colitis UC biopsy shows inﬁltration of the mucosa and submucosa with neutrophils, crypt abscess formation, lymphoid aggregates, mast cells, eosinophils and shortening and branching of crypts. A Coeliac disease Coeliac disease does not lead to the colonic changes seen here, but does show subtotal villous atrophy within the small bowel. B Tropical sprue Like coeliac disease, tropical sprue is associated with villous atrophy rather than the colonic changes seen here. E Crohn’s reactivation In Crohn’s disease, transmural lymphoid inﬁltrates are seen alt-

hough there is also usually evidence of non- caseating granuloma formation. The proximity to prescription of sertraline is also a better pointer to lymphocytic colitis as the diagnosis.

stem: A 40-year-old man is admitted to the Emergency Department having taken a paracetamol overdose. On questioning he describes having taken 50 tablets of 500 mg of paracetamol over 30 min, with the intention of ending his own life. He did this 6 h ago and has been brought into hospital after being found by his girlfriend. She reports that she found him conscious and he agreed to go to hospital. During the journey to hospital he started developing abdominal pain, which has been progressively become worse since then. He has also vomited once. On examination he looks unhappy and downcast, and his RUQ is mildly tender. He is not jaundiced, and he has a GCS of 15/15. Which of the following investigations is the best indicator of the severity of liver failure?
explanation: D Prothrombin time Paracetamol overdose is one of the most common methods of selfpoisoning in the UK. Paracetamol is metabolised by glucuronidation in the liver. The toxicity of this analgesic arises from its saturable metabolism. Excess oxidation product, NAPQI (N-acetylbenzoquinoneimine) is produced, overwhelming the liver’s capacity to detoxify it by conjugation with glutathione. Serum paracetamol levels should be measured at least 4 h after ingestion. Initial symptoms of overdose are nausea and vomiting, with hepatic and/or kidney disease presenting at 24–36 h. Liver damage peaks at 3–4 days after ingestion. The PT is the most sensitive indicator of liver damage. A poor prognosis is indicated by a PT >100 s, serum creatinine >300 µmol/l and arterial pH <7.3. A Blood glucose In acute liver failure, gluconeogenesis fails. This can lead to hypoglycaemia, which is important to correct if found. However, this is an intermittent problem and a poor marker of liver failure as it ﬂuctuates easily following ingestion of food and IV treatment with glucose. Hypoglycaemia can also occur in sepsis, which is a common presentation in acute liver failure. B Creatinine Kidney disease is common in liver failure but can occur due to several causes, including acute renal injury and dehydration. C Alkaline phosphatase ALP is present especially in the liver, bile ducts, kidneys and bone. ALP is released in the liver and in diseases of elevated bone turnover. It can be very high in liver failure, especially if there is a biliary cause. However, it is not a marker of synthetic liver function and therefore not useful in direct assessment of liver failure. E ALT ALT is present especially in hepatocytes and is released on cell injury. It can be very high in liver failure, especially if there is a hepatic cause. However, it is not a marker of synthetic liver function and therefore not useful in direct assessment of liver failure.

stem: A 32-year-old woman who has a long history of Crohn’s disease comes to the clinic for review. She has undergone an extensive ileal resection some four months earlier and is coming to the clinic for a check up. Although she feels her general health has improved, she continues to be troubled by watery diarrhoea. Her only current medication is azathioprine to maintain her Crohn’s in remission. On examination, her blood pressure is 100/60 mmHg, her pulse is 70 bpm and regular. Her abdomen is soft and non-tender and there is a midline scar. PR is unremarkable. The body mass index (BMI) is 20 kg/m2. Investigation Result Normal Value Hb 99 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 7.1 × 109/l 4–11 × 109/l PLT 171 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l ESR 12 mm/1st hr 0–10 mm/1st hr CRP 15 mg/l 0–10 mg/l Sodium (Na+) 137 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 3.8 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 85 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Albumin 32 g/l 35–55 g/l ALT 15 IU/l 5–30 IU/l ALP 85 IU/l 30–130 IU/l Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
explanation:
B Cholestyramine Extensive ileal resections and normal inﬂammatory markers in a patient together suggest an alternative diagnosis to that of active Crohn’s disease. Following ileal resection, bile acid malabsorption is common and can result in chronic water diarrhoea. Bile acid malabsorption responds to cholestyramine which sequesters bile acids. Codeine can be added in addition, if there is no response. The SeHCAT (75-selenium homocholic acid taurine) test is an appropriate test to conﬁrm bile acid malabsorption.

A Codeine phosphate The most likely diagnosis is bile acid absorption. Codeine can cause constipation as a side-effect; however, as a ﬁrst-line option, it is not indicated. C Inﬂiximab Given this patient has normal inﬂammatory markers and generally feels well in herself, it would be unlikely she has active Crohn’s disease. Inﬂiximab is used in treatment of active severe Crohn’s disease or ﬁstulating disease, as an alternative to standard immunosuppressive therapies, and is therefore not appropriate here. D Mesalazine The most likely diagnosis is bile acid malabsorption, rather than an active inﬂammatory exacerbation of Crohn’s disease. Mesalazine can be considered a steroid-sparing treatment option when corticosteroids are contraindicated in a ﬁrst presentation of acute Crohn’s disease in the last 12 months. E Prednisolone Given the patient has had extensive ileal resection and normal inﬂammatory markers, the likelihood of active disease is low. The most likely diagnosis is bile acid malabsorption, and therefore, prednisolone would not be clinically indicated.

stem: A 51-year-old man with a history of ulcerative colitis comes to the gastroenterology clinic for review. Over the past 6 months, since his last appointment, he has felt increasingly fatigued and off his food because of problems with nausea. He has also lost 6 kg in weight over the past 3 months and noticed his stools have become increasingly paler, with dark urine and he has problems with generalised itching. On examination, his BP is 132/72 mmHg, his pulse is 75/min and his BMI is 19. He looks jaundiced. Abdominal examination reveals no palpable masses. Investgation Result Normal value Haemoglobin 109 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 8.9 × 109/l 4–11 × 109/l Platelets 182 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 138 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.4 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 110 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l AST 141 IU/l 10–40 IU/l Alkaline Phosphatase 387 IU/l 30–130 IU/l Bilirubin 188 µmol/l 2–17 µmol/l Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: D Cholangiocarcinoma This patient has a history of ulcerative colitis, which raises the possibility of underlying chronic liver disease related to primary sclerosing cholangitis. One outcome of primary sclerosing cholangitis is the development of cholangiocarcinoma, which presents often with only vague right upper quadrant pain, anorexia, jaundice and weight loss. It accounts in total for around 25% of biliary tract cancers. Ultrasound and MRCP are the initial non-invasive investigations of choice to conﬁrm the diagnosis. C Primary biliary cholangitis This is a disease found predominantly in females. It presents with fatigue, itch and jaundice. Patients usually have positive antimitochondrial antibodies. A Carcinoma of the gall bladder This is a rare diagnosis and although a carcinoma of the gall bladder could present with weight loss and obstructive jaundice you may also ﬁnd a painless palpable gall bladder. It is also not typically associated with ulcerative colitis and therefore is not the most likely diagnosis. B Pancreatic carcinoma Although pancreatic carcinoma would present with weight loss and obstructive jaundice, patients may also complain of abdominal pain radiating through to the back and an epigastric mass may be palpable. It is also not typically associated with ulcerative colitis. E Autoimmune hepatitis Autoimmune hepatitis typically presents with fever, jaundice, fatigue and right upper quadrant pain, and is predominantly seen in females and is associated with other autoimmune conditions. Patients usually have positive antinuclear, anti-smooth muscle and anti-liver kidney microsomal-1 antibodies.

stem: A 42-year-old man with known ulcerative colitis is admitted to hospital. His medication includes azathioprine and intravenous (iv) hydrocortisone. He initially improves on treatment after 3 days, but then his clinical condition deteriorates. Biopsies from a ﬂexible sigmoidoscopy are consistent with underlying ulcerative colitis, but they also show a signiﬁcant number of inclusion bodies. Which treatment is most likely to improve his condition?
options: Combination of rifampicin, pyrazinamide and isoniazid
explanation: E Ganciclovir The presence of inclusion bodies on colonic histology is suggestive of cytomegalovirus infection of the colon. Inﬂammatory bowel disease, and the history of immunosuppressive therapy with azathioprine and steroids, have put the patient at risk of CMV infection. CMV colitis increases the biological severity of colitis, and given this patient’s clinical deterioration, treatment with ganciclovir should be initiated. D Metronidazole Metronidazole can be of beneﬁt in the treatment of perianal Crohn’s disease and pouchitis. In addition, antibiotics are sometimes prescribed if systemic toxicity is present in the context of an acute exacerbation of colitis. However, the important histological ﬁnding of inclusion bodies points towards CMV disease. A Combination of rifampicin, pyrazinamide and isoniazid This would be the treatment for an underlying mycobacterial infection, the presence of which is not suggested in this case. B Methotrexate Methotrexate is not indicated in the setting of an acute exacerbation of ulcerative colitis (NICE guideline NG130). C Inﬂiximab Inﬂiximab is recommended as an option for the treatment of acute exacerbations of severely active ulcerative colitis only in patients in whom ciclosporin is contraindicated or clinically inappropriate (NICE guideline TA163).

stem: A 72-year-old woman presents with a long history of dysphagia for both liquids and solids. Food occasionally gets stuck, but this is relieved by drinking large volumes of ﬂuid. Chest X-ray reveals a dilated lower oesophagus with a ﬂuid level behind the heart. Barium swallow shows gradual narrowing of the distal end of the oesophagus, ‘swan-necking’. Endoscopy reveals food residue in the distal oesophagus. Routine bloods are entirely unremarkable. Her blood pressure is 132/82 mmHg, with pulse 62/min and regular. Which of the following would represent the most appropriate initial medical treatment in this patient?
explanation: B Nifedipine This patient has achalasia, a condition which can present at any age, of unknown aetiology, and which results in failure of relaxation of the lower oesophageal sphincter and oesophageal dilatation. Medical treatments include calcium channel antagonists such as nifedipine or nitrate donors such as isosorbide dinitrate. Botox is a potential option where patients fail to respond to systemic medical therapy. Case series (both treated and untreated) suggest that there is around a 7% increase in cases of oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma over 25 years in patients with achalasia. Therapeutic endoscopy with balloon dilatation and botulinum toxin injection are both effective treatments for achalasia, and are increasingly used in elderly patients. Where patients fail to respond to medical therapy or therapeutic endoscopy, cardiomyotomy may be considered. E Propanolol Propanolol does not have a role in the treatment of achalasia; its main role is in the treatment of portal hypertension in patients with cirrhosis. A Atenolol Beta-blockers to not lead to dilation of the lower oesophageal sphincter and therefore don’t have a role in the management of achalasia. C Diltiazem Although diltiazem is a calcium channel antagonist and therefore may have a role in dilatation of the lower oesophageal sphincter, given that it is cardioselective it may precipitate symptomatic bradycardia in this case. D Ramipril Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors have no role in oesophageal sphincter relaxation. Their main role is in the treatment of hypertension, renal protection and reduction of major adverse cardiac events.

stem: A 27-year-old lawyer is referred to the Gastroenterology Clinic in view of a strong family history of bowel cancer. He is otherwise asymptomatic. His general practitioner (GP) comments on a normal colonoscopy, which he had privately one week ago. He reports that his grandmother died of bowel cancer aged 68 years. His mother was diagnosed with bowel cancer aged 45 years and is currently receiving chemotherapy for endometrial cancer. His uncle had bowel surgery for cancer at the age of 49 years. He is still very concerned and would like some advice about whether he needs any further investigations. Which one of the following is the most appropriate management with respect to bowel cancer surveillance?
options: Arrange double contrast barium enema to reassess bowel
Computed tomography of the abdomen with contrast
explanation: C Repeat colonoscopy in 2 years This gentleman is clearly at risk of hereditary non-polyposis colorectal cancer syndrome (HNPCC) in view of the strong family history. It is an autosomal dominant syndrome characterised by early-onset colorectal cancer. It may account for 1-2% of all cases of colorectal cancer (CRC). In 55-60% of cases, cancers are right sided and affected individuals are also at increased risk of cancer of the endometrium, stomach, small bowel and genitourinary tract. Mutations responsible for HNPCC are found in DNA repair genes. The diagnostic criteria for HNPCC families are: a. Histologically veriﬁed CRC or HNPCC-related cancers in three or more relatives, one of whom is a ﬁrst- degree relative of the other two; b. CRC affecting at least two generations; c. One or more cases of cancer diagnosed before the age of 50 years. Individuals at risk should be offered colonoscopic screening at 2year intervals from the age 20-25 years, which should be continued up to the age of 40 years, when screening should be increased to an annual basis. The optimal interval between colonoscopic examinations is not known. There is some evidence that progression from adenoma to carcinoma is accelerated in this syndrome, thus colonoscopic intervals of 1-3 years are recommended. The above are based on retrospective observational studies and panel expert consensus. A Arrange double contrast barium enema to re-assess bowel Barium enema has less sensitivity versus a properly prepared colonoscopy in identifying colon cancer and is therefore not required given the recent colonoscopy. B Arrange ﬂexible sigmoidoscopy in 3 months This will add nothing to the colonoscopy conducted some 3 months earlier. D Repeat colonoscopy in 5 years This risks too long a delay, during which disseminated colon cancer may develop. E Computed tomography of the abdomen with contrast CT abdomen has less sensitivity to identify an underlying colon cancer versus colonoscopy.

stem: A 74-year-old man is referred to the Gastroenterology Department with a 4-month history of progressive dysphagia for solids and liquids. He also complains of early satiety and has lost ﬁve kg in weight. His past medical history includes hypertension, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and peripheral vascular disease that has led him to be wheelchair-bound. Examination reveals a blood pressure of 110/79 mmHg and a heart rate of 88 bpm and regular. His body mass index is 16 kg/m2, and he looks dehydrated. There is minimal wheeze on auscultation, with normal heart sounds. He has an irregular liver edge, and a large left supraclavicular lymph node is palpable. Investigation Result Normal value Hb 85 g/l 135 - 175 g/l WCC 12.3 × 109/l 4.0 - 11.0 × 109/l PLT 179 × 109/l 150 - 400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 137 mmol/l 135 - 145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.3 mmol/l 3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 151 µmol/l 50 - 120 µmol/l Urea 15.2 mmol/l 2.5 - 6.5 mmol/l Albumin 27 g/l 35 - 55 g/l ALT 282 u/l 7 - 55 u/l ALP 421 u/l 30 - 150 u/l Bilirubin 24 µmol/l 1 - 22 µmol/l Given the likely diagnosis, which of the following is the most appropriate next intervention?
explanation:
C Oesophageal stenting This patient has oesophageal carcinoma, given the progressive history of dysphagia, accompanied by weight loss, palpable Virchow’s node and anaemia. On examination, this patient has a palpable irregular liver edge and signiﬁcantly deranged liver function tests, suggesting metastatic spread. Oesophageal stenting can be used as longterm palliation for dysphagia. The primary goal of oesophageal stenting in patients with advanced disease is to relieve dysphagia and prevent malnutrition. In comparison to parenteral nutrition, endoscopic stent placement signiﬁcantly improves the quality of life of patients by restoring the ability of oral intake of ﬂuids and food. B Oesophagectomy Oesophagectomy is no longer considered for palliation of symptoms. Therefore, oesophagectomy cannot be used in this patient. It is more useful in the early stages of carcinoma. A Local mucosal resection The cancer has already progressed too far for this to be effective. Mucosal resection should be considered in patients with oesophageal mucosal cancer and those with early-stage carcinoma. The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guidelines also point out that the role of mucosal resection in patients with Barrett’s oesophagus and ablation of residual areas of dysplasia require further research. D Photodynamic therapy

Photodynamic therapy is used as a debulking option. However, because this patient has an advanced case and the disease has spread too far, this option would not be effective. Endoscopic therapies can be offered to patients with high-grade dysplasia and intramucosal cancer (T1a), as an alternative to oesophagectomy. These therapies include endoscopic mucosal resection and ablative therapies (radiofrequency ablation or photodynamic therapy). Radiofrequency ablation alone is considered for ﬂat, high-grade dysplasia. E Trastuzumab Trastuzumab is used in HER 2-positive cancers at the oesophagogastric junction, in combination with cisplatin/ﬂuoropyrimidine. There is documented improvement in disease-free survival and overall survival rates with the use of this regimen. However, chemotherapy is not the best option for this patient due to his poor

stem: A 55-year-old man attends the Acute Medical Unit with abdominal distension. He has been feeling generally unwell for some time, and his partner is concerned regarding the discoloration of his skin and eyes. On examination, you note scleral icterus and numerous spider naevi. He also reports bilateral knee pain and palpitations. He has a history of diet-controlled type II diabetes; he is a smoker of 15 cigarettes per day and has been a lifelong teetotaler. Investigation Result Normal Values Hb 115 g/l 135–155 g/l Blood glucose (HbA1c) 59.0 mmol/mol < 53 mmol/mol ALT 121 iu/l 5–30 iu/l ALP 301 iu/l 30–130 iu/l PT 15 s 10.6–14.9 s ECG Atrial ﬁbrillation (AF) with rapid ventricular response An X-ray of his knee is shown below: What is the most appropriate investigation to identify the underlying cause?
explanation: D Transferrin saturation This patient clearly has decompensated liver disease, with evidence of jaundice and ascites. The patient does not drink alcohol, and there are no obvious risk factors for viral hepatitis noted in the stem. There is a description of diabetes and AF, and the X-ray reveals chondrocalcinosis. This combination of pathology points to haemochromatosis, for which an initial investigation would be transferrin saturation. A Abdominal ultrasound This patient clearly has decompensated liver disease, with evidence of jaundice and ascites. While an abdominal ultrasound would be helpful in identifying cirrhosis, it would fail to identify the underlying cause. B Ascitic tap While an ascitic tap may demonstrate a high serum ascites albumin gradient (SAAG), pointing to cirrhosis, this is not particularly speciﬁc. It fails to explain the concurrent AF, diabetes and chondrocalcinosis shown on the X- ray. The most likely underlying multisystemic disease process is haemochromatosis, which an ascitic tap would not delineate. C Knee aspiration The knee X-ray shows chondrocalcinosis, which has numerous potential causes, including pseudogout, osteoarthritis, Wilson’s disease and hyperparathyroidism. The picture here, however, does not ﬁt an acute gout alone, given the chronic nature of the pain and the concurrent picture of cirrhosis, AF and diabetes. A knee aspiration will not be particularly helpful in identifying haemochromatosis, the unifying diagnosis. E Viral serology This patient has decompensated liver disease. As the patient does not drink alcohol, other causes of cirrhosis should be considered, including viral hepatitis. However, no obvious risk factors are described in the stem, and viral hepatitis would not explain the AF or diabetes as neatly as haemochromatosis.

stem: A 68-year-old man presents to the Accident and Emergency Department. He is unkempt and an alcoholic. He complains of fevers, weight loss and malaise over the past four months, and a dry cough with sputum which is occasionally blood-stained. On examination, he is febrile at 37.5 °C and has moderate ascites.
