The CXR ﬁndings show a pneumomediastinum, more likely to be secondary to oesophageal rupture from vomiting. C Mallory–Weiss tear A Mallory–Weiss tear is unlikely here, given the lack of haematemesis and the systemic response following the vomiting. D Perforated peptic ulcer A perforated peptic ulcer could explain the vomiting and abdominal discomfort but would not explain the CXR ﬁndings.

stem: A 32-year-old woman presents to Outpatients after noticing the whites of her eyes changing colour. She is 36 weeks’ pregnant with her ﬁrst child. She feels well in herself and has no relevant past medical history other than a transient episode of jaundice in her late teens, and takes no medication. There is no history of recent travel. Clinical examination reveals icteric sclerae and excoriations on the upper arms. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Value Bilirubin 150 µmol/l 2–17 µmol/l ALT 150 IU/l 5–30 IU/l ALP 600 IU/l 30–130 IU/l Albumin 40 g/l 35–55 g/l Urinalysis Bilirubin +++ Hb 110 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 5.0 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l PLT 350 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l PT 17 s 10.6–14.9 s What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: HELLP syndrome (haemolysis, elevated liver enzymes and low platelets)
explanation:
C Cholestasis of pregnancy Cholestasis of pregnancy is by far the most likely diagnosis. This condition is caused by a bile acid transporter defect and usually manifests in the last trimester. It is not associated with signiﬁcant constitutional symptoms for the mother, although the risk of stillbirth and postpartum haemorrhage is slightly increased. Milder episodes may have occurred earlier in life associated with hormonal contraception, and it recurs in subsequent pregnancies. Prothrombin time may be prolonged in any cholestatic process due to deﬁciency of vitamin K. Pre-eclampsia, HELLP syndrome and acute fatty liver of pregnancy form a spectrum of disease known as toxaemias of pregnancy. All are associated with constitutional symptoms and are potentially life-threatening. A Pre-eclampsia Pre-eclampsia is deﬁned as pregnancy-induced hypertension with proteinuria. There can also be oedema, but this is not essential for a diagnosis. It can become life-threatening and any organ can be affected. Blood pressure would by greater than 160/100 mmHg and proteinuria should be greater than 0.3 g/24 h. Eclampsia is evidenced by convulsions following features of pre-eclampsia. The patient may present with severe headache, new oedema, RUQ tenderness or visual disturbances, and examination can show oedema, clonus and papilloedema. Pre-eclampsia is associated with abnormal liver function tests (LFTs) in 20% of cases, but jaundice is unusual in all but severe cases and proteinuria would be expected. B HELLP syndrome (haemolysis, elevated liver enzymes and low platelets) The vast majority of cases occur with pre-eclampsia and this has similar clinical features, but with the addition of haemolysis, elevated liver enzymes and low platelets. The absence of a low platelet count excludes HELP. D Hepatitis E Hepatitis E is an enterically spread RNA virus, the epidemic form of which has a high (10–20%) mortality in pregnant women in devel-

oping countries. It is especially common in India, but in the absence of any travel history this is a very unlikely diagnosis. E Acute fatty liver of pregnancy This is a rare condition which tends to occur late in pregnancy and is associated with ﬁrst pregnancy and pre- eclampsia. It is associated with nausea, vomiting, fever, headache and pruritis and can present with jaundice on examination. Acute fatty liver of pregnancy is associated with abnormalities of synthetic function, and therefore serum albumin would be expected to be low. The absence of clinical symptoms as well makes this unlikely.

stem: A 38-year-old man presents with a 6-week history of feeling unwell and very lethargic. He is a known hypertensive. His wife tells you he has been rather stressed at work recently and is drinking fairly heavily. As a child, he was found to have an abnormality in the structure of his heart though she is not sure what this is, but she does know that he has had problems with palpitations. In Accident and Emergency, he has two generalised tonic-clonic seizures, which are treated with intravenous lorazepam. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Values Hb 134 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 12 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l PLT 122 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Neutrophils 8.4 × 109/l 2.5–7.58 × 109/l Bilirubin 44 µmol/l 2–17 µmol/l Cholesterol 6.0 mmol/l < 5.2 mmol/l ALP 647 IU/l 30–130 IU/l ALT 110 IU/l 5–30 IU/l GGT 540 IU/l 5–30 IU/l CRP 84 mg/l < 10 mg/l Total Protein 50 g/l 60–80 g/l INR 1.4 < 1.0 Albumin 28 g/l 35–55 g/l Which of the following drugs is the best choice for the longterm treatment of his seizures?
explanation: B Lamotrigine The most important intervention is for this patient to stop drinking, although this should take place under cover of a reducing course of benzodiazepines. Lamotrigine is an appropriate ﬁrst-line intervention for seizures: it has the advantage of not being a CYP450 enzyme inducer or inhibitor, and has data suggesting it may reduce long- term alcohol dependence. A Sodium valproate Sodium valproate should not be used in patients with hepatic dysfunction, because it is a CYP450 inhibitor. Additionally, MHRA advice (due to the risk of impaired fertility in men and teratogenicity in women) suggests that no patient under the age of 55 should be commenced on valproate unless two consultants agree that there is no suitable alternative treatment. C Gabapentin Gabapentin is a normal adjunctive therapy for patients with persistent seizures despite starting a ﬁrst-line agent; as such, it’s not the appropriate choice here. D Vigabatrin Vigabatrin is associated with peripheral visual ﬁeld defects in up to 1/3 of users. It is also associated with suicidal ideation, and is therefore not an ideal option in a patient with alcoholism. E Carbamazepine Carbamazepine is a potent CYP450 enzyme inducer, and it may also be associated with AV conduction defects and is therefore not ideal in a patient with congenital heart disease.

stem: A 42-year-old premenopausal woman presents to her General Practitioner (GP) with a 3-week history of epigastric pain that is occasionally retrosternal and worse at night. She has tried over-thecounter antacid preparations and esomeprazole which have achieved no relief. Her weight is steady and her bowel habits are normal. There is no history of gastric malignancy in the family. The examination is unremarkable, except for the fact that the patient is obese. The full blood count is normal. Which of the following describes the next best management step?
options: Arrange upper GI endoscopy if symptoms do not settle in two weeks on an alternative proton pump inhibitor (PPI)
Check repeat haemoglobin level in three months; if low, refer for upper GI endoscopy
Start an alternative PPI and perform a carbon-13 urea breath test; if positive, prescribe Helicobacter pylori eradication therapy
Stop esomeprazole and perform a carbon-13 urea breath test after two weeks
explanation:
E Stop esomeprazole and perform a carbon-13 urea breath test after two weeks The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guidelines state that in this age group, dyspepsia, in the absence of alarm symptoms, should be treated with lifestyle advice and a proton pump inhibitor (PPI) if needed. In the event that symptoms of

indigestion have not been relieved, H. pylori testing or upper gastrointestinal (GI) endoscopy can then be considered. However, PPI therapy needs to have been stopped for two weeks before H. pylori testing, due to the risk of a false-negative result. D Start an alternative PPI and perform a carbon-13 urea breath test; if positive, prescribe Helicobacter pylori eradication therapy Urea breath testing for H. pylori should ideally be conducted off PPI therapy for a period of at least two weeks. A Arrange upper gastrointestinal (GI) endoscopy A routine endoscopy would be considered where symptoms do not improve after one month of empirical proton pump inhibitor (PPI) treatment. B Arrange upper GI endoscopy if symptoms do not settle in two weeks on an alternative proton pump inhibitor (PPI) Patients with dyspepsia without any alarm features should ideally be tested for H. pylori infection before more invasive endoscopy is considered. C Check repeat haemoglobin level in three months; if low, refer for upper GI endoscopy This is the appropriate course of action where there are alarm features, including weight loss, persistent vomiting, dysphagia, anaemia and the presence of an epigastric mass.

stem: A 26-year-old woman presents with a 3-day history of progressively worsening abdominal distension, severe epigastric pain, nausea and vomiting. She was previously ﬁt and well with no signiﬁcant past medical history and the only medication she took was the oral contraceptive pill. There was no relevant family history. She smoked 10 cigarettes per day and drank approximately 12 units of alcohol per week. On examination, she was unwell, drowsy and deeply jaundiced. She was apyrexial. Her heart sounds were normal, her chest was clear to auscultation and she had peripheral oedema. Her abdomen was distended with shifting dullness and tender hepatomegaly. There were no focal neurological signs. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Value Hb 130 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 13.0 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l PLT 200 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 132 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.8 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 120 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l MCV 82 ﬂ 76–98 ﬂ Urea 7.2 mmol/l 2.5–6.5 mmol/l Bilirubin 120 μmol/l 2–17 µmol/l ALP 410 IU/l 30–130 IU/l AST 900 IU/l 10–40 IU/l GGT 850 IU/l 5–30 IU/l Albumin 29 g/l 35–55 g/l PT 30 s 10.6–14.9 s Ascitic ﬂuid analysis reveals the following: Investigation Result Protein 17 g/l Neutrophils 80 cells/mm3 Gram stain No organisms seen Amylase 100 IU/l Which investigation should be performed next?
options: Colour ﬂow Doppler ultrasound of the hepatic vasculature
explanation:
B Colour ﬂow Doppler ultrasound of the hepatic vasculature The diagnosis is Budd–Chiari syndrome. Doppler ultrasound will show obliteration of the hepatic veins and abnormalities of the direction of blood ﬂow in the remainder of the hepatic vasculature. Budd-Chiari syndrome is deﬁned as the obstruction of venous outﬂow from the liver caused by hepatic vein occlusion. The most common cause is thrombosis, usually in association with a hypercoagulable state, in conditions such as primary polycythaemia, thombophilias and leukaemia. There is also an association with the oral contraceptive pill. Other causes include malignancy (especially hepatocellular, renal and adrenal), radiotherapy, trauma and congenital venous webs. The cause is unknown in one-third of cases. It can present either acutely or chronically. In the acute from, there is abdominal pain, nausea and vomiting, ascites, tender hepatomegaly and sometimes fulminant hepatic failure. The chronic form presents more insidiously, with signs of cirrhosis and portal hypertension. Ascitic ﬂuid analysis will show a high serum ascitic albumin gradient (SAAG= serum albumin – ascitic ﬂuid albumin) and is classiﬁed as a transudate. . An enlarged caudate lobe may be seen on ultrasound/computed tomography (CT)/magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan of the liver. Liver biopsy usually shows centrilobular congestion with ﬁbrosis. Management includes treating the underlying cause, portocaval shunts and TIPSS (transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic stent shunt). Treatment with streptokinase and subsequent anticoagulation may be attempted if the thrombus is known to be of recent onset. Liver transplantation is the only option in the acute presentation, which has a very poor prognosis, with two-thirds of patients dead within 1 year. A Serum alpha-fetoprotein A rising alpha-fetoprotein may be seen in hepatocellular carcinoma, known to be associated with Budd-Chiari syndrome, but isn’t speciﬁc for the condition itself. C Liver biopsy Liver biopsy usually shows centrilobular congestion with ﬁbrosis which is related to pressure and ﬂow changes within the liver, but this isn’t the next investigation here.

D Anti-mitochondrial antibodies Anti-mitochondrial antibodies are positive in primary biliary cholangitis, a disease of insidious onset, which usually presents with tiredness, lethargy and itching, rather than the acute deterioration seen here. E Serum caeruloplasmin This is an investigation for Wilson’s disease, which presents with abnormal transaminases either picked up incidentally or associated with neuropsychiatric features, rather than the acute deterioration seen here.

stem: A 40-year-old woman presents with a history of abdominal pain and distension for the past 7 days. On examination, she is found to have jaundice, a smooth, 5 cm hepatomegaly and ascites. There are no stigmata of chronic liver disease and she does not take any regular medication. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Value Hb 150 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 11.0 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l PLT 200 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 140 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.7 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 200 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Urea 20 mmol/l 2.5–6.5 mmol/l PTT 50 s 23.0–35.0 s PT 13 s 10.6–14.9 s What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: D Budd–Chiari syndrome The prolonged APTT in the presence of a normal PT is suggestive of lupus anticoagulant, which would be consistent with antiphospholipid syndrome, well recognised as a cause of Budd–Chiari syndrome. Budd-Chiari syndrome commonly presents with a triad of abdominal pain, hepatomegaly and ascites. It is a rare condition caused by occlusion to the hepatic vein. Treatment is with anticoagulation, surgery or a transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPS) procedure. C Glomerulonephritis This would not explain the hepatomegaly and jaundice. A Alcoholic liver disease Although this could account for her presentation, there is no mention of excessive alcohol intake in the history and her presentation is far more typical of Budd-Chiari syndrome. B Right heart failure Although this might cause an engorged liver and ascites, it would not explain her clotting abnormalities. E Metastatic liver disease You would not expect to feel a smooth liver in this case, and the ascitic ﬂuid tap is more likely to be exudative in malignancy rather than transudative.

stem: A 69-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department claiming to have swallowed a foreign object four hours previously. He has a long history of mental health problems and had presented with a similar history in the past. He denies dysphagia, odynophagia or abdominal pain, and physical examination is unremarkable. His plain abdominal (anteroposterior view) X-ray is shown below: Which of the following should be the next step?
options: Colonoscopy and removal of the object
Laparotomy and removal of the object
Monitor with weekly X-rays to ensure passage through the GI tract
Oesophago-gastro-duodenoscopy and removal of the object
explanation:
E Oesophago-gastro-duodenoscopy and removal of the

object While most ingested foreign objects will pass through the GI tract without complication, there are certain instances where intervention is required. The presence of large objects that are unlikely to negotiate the duodenum, sharp objects, batteries and multiple magnets are indications for intervention. After four hours, these swallowed foreign bodies are still located proximally, which suggests that they cannot pass through the pyloric sphincter to the duodenum. Furthermore, the close contact of the two objects is suspicious for magnet ingestion. Urgent endoscopic intervention is required to remove these objects. (Of note, narcotic packages should probably not be removed endoscopically, because of the risk of accidental rupture.) C Laparotomy and removal of the object This is not the optimal course of action for this situation. Currently the object is easily accessible via endoscopy, given its proximal location. A Colonoscopy and removal of the object Colonoscopy is usually not indicated, as once the foreign object has passed distally, it is likely to pass naturally with a bowel motion. Furthermore, colonoscopy would only be indicated for a more distally located foreign body, which is not seen here. B Gastrointestinal stimulation with metoclopramide Because of where the object appears to be lodged, advising metoclopramide or other GI stimulants runs the risk of signiﬁcant pain and potentially even oesophageal rupture. D Monitor with weekly X-rays to ensure passage through the GI tract Where endoscopic removal is not possible or is contraindicated, an alternative strategy is for daily X-rays to monitor the progress of more distal objects, and for surgery to be considered for objects that do not move for 72 hours and/or people in whom symptoms develop. This would be the alternative strategy if the patient was deemed to have capacity and refused endoscopy.

stem: A 44-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department complaining of shortness of breath and tiredness. She recently started oral steroids prescribed by her General Practitioner for an intensely itchy, vesicular rash on the elbows, knees, buttocks and back. She also gives a history of mild diarrhoea and abdominal bloating and has lost a stone in weight. Investigation Result Normal Values Hb 56 g/l 135 - 175 g/l MCV 90 ﬂ 80 - 100 ﬂ WCC 5.8 × 109/l 4.0 - 11.0 × 109/l PLT 387 × 109/l 150 - 400 × 109/l RDW 22 % 11.8 - 14.5 % Sodium (Na+) 138 mmol/l 135 - 145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.4 mmol/l 3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l Urea 4.4 mmol/l 2.5 - 6.5 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 99 µmol/l 50 - 120 µmol/l Albumin 3.2 g/dl 3.4 - 5.4 g/dl Corrected calcium 2.0 mmol/l 2.2 - 2.7 mmol/l (Ca2+) Bilirubin 25 µmol/l 1 - 22 µmol/l Which of the following is most likely to be contributing to her anaemia?
explanation:
D Iron deﬁciency due to malabsorption The constellation of anaemia, weight loss, diarrhoea and bloating – together with a pruritic rash on the extensor surfaces – is highly suggestive of this patient having coeliac disease and dermatitis herpetiformis. Coeliac disease may present in various ways, but iron deﬁciency anaemia is not an infrequent presentation. In contrast, folate deﬁciency may also occur in the condition; B12 deﬁciency is less common, as this vitamin is absorbed in the terminal ileum. Hypocalcaemia may also occur due to malabsorption of calcium and vitamin D. Dermatitis herpetiformis is an intensely pruritic, vesicular rash that typically affects the elbows, scalp and extensor surfaces of the forearms and buttocks. It is more common in men and may occur at any age, although it tends to present in young adulthood. It is normally – if not exclusively – associated with gluten-sensitive enteropathy. Treatment of dermatitis herpetiformis includes strict adherence to a gluten-free diet. Dapsone may be effective in controlling the rash but is often associated with mild, dose-related haemolytic anaemia. Haemolysis can, however, be dramatic in people with glucose-6phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deﬁciency. Monitoring of liver function tests and a full blood count is advised, as dapsone may also rarely cause liver dysfunction and aplastic anaemia. Drug treatment can often be withdrawn after a period of adherence to a gluten-free diet. A Anaemia of chronic disease Anaemia of chronic disease is associated with normochromic normocytic anaemia but would only be entertained as a diagnosis once other causes of anaemia, including iron deﬁciency, have been ruled out. B Autoimmune haemolysis The clinical presentation here is much more consistent with coeliac disease, which is not associated with haemolysis. Although dapsone, occasionally prescribed for dermatitis herpetiformis, may lead to haemolysis, this is not seen with corticosteroids. C Bone marrow failure Bone marrow failure is unlikely in the context of an isolated anaemia. It would be more likely to be bone marrow failure if there were associated thrombocytopenia and leukopenia.

E Pernicious anaemia Pernicious anaemia is an autoimmune disorder characterised by atrophic gastritis and a reduction of parietal cells in the gastric mucosa, leading to vitamin B12 malabsorption. The MCV here is inconsistent with isolated B12 deﬁciency. The MCV of 90, together with increased RDW and symptoms of coeliac disease, is more consistent with a mixed picture of iron and B12 vitamin deﬁciencies.

stem: A 46-year-old man is admitted from the clinic with dysphagia and weight loss. Over the last few months, he has found that it has been progressively harder to swallow solids. He was able to swallow them but he had to regurgitate them about 30 minutes later. Over the last few weeks, he has been having increasing difﬁculty with ﬂuids. He has previously been in good health and never smoked. He drinks half a bottle of wine at weekends and the only other history of note has been long-term dyspepsia for which he uses antacids. On examination, there is nothing to ﬁnd except some mild tenderness on palpation in the epigastric area. Barium swallow – oesophagus appears dilated and the distal oesophagus is narrowed. Oesophageal manometry – incomplete relaxation of the lower oesophageal sphincter in response to swallowing with high resting pressure. Absent oesophageal peristalsis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: A Achalasia Achalasia is a primary oesophageal motility disorder characterised by failure of a hypertensive lower oesophageal sphincter to relax and the absence of normal oesophageal peristalsis. Oesophageal manometry will demonstrate ﬁndings as for our patient. An OGD should be carried out to make sure there is no cancer. The goal of therapy for achalasia is to relieve symptoms by eliminating the outﬂow resistance caused by the hypertensive and nonrelaxing sphincter. This can be accomplished by mechanical disruption of the muscle ﬁbres of the lower oesophageal sphincter (e.g. pneumatic dilation, surgical myotomy or per-oral endoscopic myotomy) or by pharmacological reduction of oesophageal sphincter pressure (e.g. injection of botulinum toxin, oral nitrates or calcium channel blockers). C Plummer–Vinson syndrome Plummer-Vinson syndrome is a triad of iron deﬁciency anaemia, dysphagia and a cervical oesophageal web. It is more common in women, and may be associated with glossitis, angular cheilitis, koilonychia, splenomegaly, an enlarged thyroid and symptoms of iron deﬁciency anaemia. Oesophageal webs characteristically cause intermittent solid food dysphagia. These typically arise from the anterior wall, or are circumferential, and are best seen on barium swallow as they are more easily missed on endoscopy due to their proximal nature. The barium swallow report for this patient is not consistent with an oesophageal web. B Oesophageal cancer The dysphagia is usually for solids, with the possibility of difﬁculty swallowing liquids in advanced disease. Barium swallow would show obstruction by the tumour, rather than the characteristic ‘bird’s beak’ appearance of achalasia, as described in this case. D Oesophageal candidiasis Oesophageal candidiasis is more likely to cause retrosternal odynophagia rather than a progressive dysphagia. Patients usually have a history of immunosuppression, of which there is no suggestion in this case. In severe cases, barium swallow may reveal an irregular, ‘shaggy’ appearance to the oesophagus due to pseudo- membrane formation. E Gastro-oesophageal reﬂux disease This patient has reported dyspepsia, suggesting possible gastrooesophgeal reﬂux. While barium swallow studies could reveal obstruction from a peptic stricture in the context of long-standing gastro-oesophageal reﬂux, the oesophageal dilation and abnormal manometry ﬁndings would not be present in simple gastro- oesophageal reﬂux disease.

stem: A 26-year-old woman with a history of ulcerative colitis comes to the Emergency Department with an exacerbation. She is opening her bowels some ten times per day with bloody diarrhoea. She tells you that she stopped taking oral mesalazine some eight weeks ago after she found out she is pregnant with her ﬁrst child. She is now 16 weeks pregnant. On examination, her BP is 105/70 mmHg and his heart rate 88 bpm and regular. Her abdomen is soft but generally tender. She has active bowel sounds. Investigations; Investigations Results Normal Values Hb 98 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 12.2 × 109/l 4–11 × 109/l PLT 387 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l ESR 75 mm/1sthour 0–10 mm in the 1sthour Sodium (Na+) 137 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.3 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 100 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Albumin 31 g/l 35–55 g/l Which of the following is the most appropriate way to manage her exacerbation?
explanation: C Oral Mesalazine and oral Prednisolone While no randomised controlled trials of 5-aminosalicylic acid (5ASA) compounds exist speciﬁcally in pregnant women, they are generally thought to be safe, with animal studies revealing no evidence of teratogenicity. As such, it is most appropriate to restart oral mesalazine and to add oral prednisolone to gain control of the exacerbation. A Azathioprine and Prednisolone Research suggests that azathioprine is less effective than mesalazine in controlling symptoms, although it is also an appropriate option from the point of view of safety for use in pregnancy. B Mycophenolate mofetil Mycophenolate mofetil use during pregnancy is associated with an increased risk for malformations and ﬁrst- trimester pregnancy loss. The most frequent malformations include external ear and other facial malformations such as cleft palate and lip. As we know that there are safer options in this case, mycophenolate mofetil should be avoided. D Prednisolone Prednisolone would be a reasonable option to control the exacerbation, but it should be done in conjunction with restarting mesalazine. E Rectal Mesalazine and Predsol enemas The generalised abdominal tenderness raises the possibility of more than just rectal disease. For this reason, rectal mesalazine and prednisolone are unlikely to be effective.

stem: A 40-year-old woman with a history of chronic alcoholism presents to the clinic with increased abdominal swelling. She has noticed increasing abdominal girth over the past 4-6 months. On examination, there are signs of chronic liver disease, including spider naevi and ascites, and she also has jaundiced sclerae. Her BP is 100/65 mmHg. Investigation Result Normal Values Hb 105 g/l 135 - 175 g/l MCV 107 fL 80 - 100 ﬂ WCC 5.6 × 109/l 4.0 - 11.0 × 109/l PLT 202 × 109/l 150 - 400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 136 mmol/l 135 - 145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 3.9 mmol/l 3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 85 µmol/l 50 - 120 µmol/l CA-125 65 u/ml < 35 u/ml What is the most likely cause for the increased CA-125?
explanation: E Cirrhosis The patient has clinical features of chronic liver disease and the alcohol history makes cirrhosis the most likely option. Cirrhosis with ascites is a well recognised cause of a false positive CA125. C Colonic carcinoma Colon cancer can produce a falsely positive CA-125. However, this patient clearly has signs of chronic liver disease. A Hepatitis B Hepatitis B infection is not strongly associated with an elevated CA125. B Ovarian carcinoma A patient presenting with ascites and a raised CA-125 raises the suspicion of ovarian cancer, however, there is a clear alcohol history and the patient has features of chronic liver disease. Although CA125 is often used to screen for ovarian cancer there are multiple conditions that also result in an elevated CA-125 (including cirrhosis and ascites, other intra-abdominal cancers, endometriosis, PID, ﬁbroids, pancreatitis and heart failure amongst others). If ovarian cancer is suspected, NICE recommend using the “Risk of Malignancy Index (RMI)”, which combines transvaginal US, menopausal status and CA-125 level to assess the risk. All women with a score >250 should be referred for specialist assessment. In women where there is a family history of ovarian carcinoma, genetic screening for BRCA1/2 is recommended as the preferred method for assessing future ovarian carcinoma risk. D Hepatocellular carcinoma HCC is not associated with a rise in CA-125 (although it may be elevated in a patient with HCC as HCC occurs as a consequence of cirrhosis). Alfa-fetoprotein can be elevated in HCC.

stem: A 33-year-old woman who has undergone multiple small bowel resections comes to the clinic for review. She is ﬁnding it virtually impossible to maintain her weight and suffers from chronic diarrhoea. On examination, her blood pressure is 103/80 mmHg; her pulse is 80 bpm and regular. She has a healed laparotomy scar on her abdomen. Her body mass index is 19. She was tried with total parenteral nutrition but unable to be weaned from it. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal values Hb 87 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 5.9 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l PLT 162 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 138 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 3.4 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 85 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l CRP 11 mg/l < 10 mg/l Albumin 22 g/l 35–55 g/l ALT 39 U/l 7–55 U/l Bilirubin 12 µmol/l 1–22 µmol/l Which of the following is the most effective next intervention?
explanation: D Teduglutide The answer is Teduglutide. Teduglutide is a glucagon-like peptide 2 agonist, which promotes small bowel mucosal growth; therefore, it is of value in the treatment of short bowel syndrome caused by multiple resections for Crohn’s disease. Six months after commencing therapy, patients with short bowel syndrome requiring total parenteral nutrition (TPN) top-ups achieved a reduction in their TPN requirements between 20 and 100%. A Codeine phosphate Codeine phosphate is incorrect. Although codeine phosphate may slow gastrointestinal transit and have an impact on the symptoms of diarrhoea, it is not likely to have a signiﬁcant impact on the symptoms of malabsorption. B Liraglutide Liraglutide is incorrect. Liraglutide is a glucagon-like peptide 1 agonist used in the treatment of type 2 diabetes; it has no signiﬁcant impact on small intestinal mucosal growth. C Loperamide hydrochloride Loperamide hydrochloride is incorrect. Like codeine phosphate, loperamide hydrochloride may improve the symptoms of diarrhoea, but it is not likely to improve the symptoms associated with malabsorption. E Vildagliptin Vildagliptin is incorrect. Vildagliptin is a dipeptidyl peptidase 4 inhibitor used in the treatment of type 2 diabetes.

stem: A 52-year-old man presented with an attack of acute upper abdominal pain associated with vomiting. On examination, he had epigastric tenderness and guarding. Serum amylase was 1300 IU/l. He was treated with intravenous antibiotics, ﬂuids and analgesia. His pain settled and he made a good recovery and was discharged from hospital several days later. Eight weeks later, he was readmitted with malaise and persistent abdominal pain. On examination, he had low-grade pyrexia and there was a tender mass palpable in the upper abdomen. His heart rate is 96 bpm and his blood pressure is 124/81 mmHg. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Value Hb 112 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 14 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l PLT 390 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l MCV 82 ﬂ 76–98 ﬂ CRP 200 mg/l < 10 mg/l Sodium (Na+) 137 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.3 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Urea 4.8 mmol/l 2.5–6.5 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 120 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Corrected Calcium (Ca2+) 2.50 mmol/l 2.20–2.60 mmol/l Bilirubin 22 μmol/l 2–17 µmol/l ALP 160 IU/l 30–130 IU/l (γGT) 78 IU/l 5–30 IU/l AST 42 IU/l 10–40 IU/l Amylase 1000 U/l < 200 U/l What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: A Pancreatic pseudocyst Pancreatic pseudocysts are an uncommon complication of acute pancreatitis, and are localised collections of pancreatic ﬂuid and debris, usually in the lesser sac. They are initially contained within a fragile wall of granulation tissue which eventually forms a ﬁbrous capsule. They cannot be diagnosed until more than 6 weeks after the acute attack, and may present with abdominal pain or a mass, fever and persistently raised amylase and liver function tests. Small pseudocysts usually resolve on their own, but those that are greater than 6 cm in diameter seldom disappear spontaneously and may lead to complications such as haemorrhage and infection. They are usually managed by endoscopic or percutanous drainage or surgical intervention. B Pyogenic liver abscess Liver abscesses mostly occur following peritonitis due to leaking of bowel content with spread to the liver by portal circulation. Alternatively, there can be direct spread from the biliary system or haematogenous seeding from systemic infection. Liver abcesses common- ly cause fever and abdominal pain, whilst patients can also have anorexia, vomiting and weight loss. The low-grade, as opposed to a high-grade, fever, as well as the very delayed timing, makes this an unlikely diagnosis. C Chronic pancreatitis Chronic pancreatitis occurs with progressive inﬂammatory changes causing permanent structural damage, which results in impaired exocrine and endocrine function. It can present as chronic epigastric pain with nausea and vomiting which radiates to the back, or with pancreatic insufﬁciency causing malabsorption and steatorrhea. The acute abdominal signs and elevated amylase make this a less likely differential. D Recurrent attack of acute pancreatitis Recurrent acute pancreatitis can occur, and in some patients this becomes a regular problem necessitating surgery if very severe. The presence of a tender and palpable mass makes this a less likely diagnosis. E Pancreatic carcinoma Pancreatic carcinoma is a cause of a painless epigastric mass and progressively worsening jaundice. The presence of pain and tenderness reduces the likelihood of this diagnosis, as does the absence of jaundice.

stem: A 45-year-old woman with a history of type I diabetes presents with a 3-month history of nausea, early satiety, bloating and intermittent vomiting, particularly after meals. She reports poor glycaemic control and frequently experiences hypoglycaemic episodes after eating. Physical examination is unremarkable. She has tried antacids and proton pump inhibitors, with no improvement in her symptoms. Investigation Result Normal value Hb 130 g/l 135–175 g/l PLT 300 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Fasting blood glucose 8.0 mmol/l 4.0–6.0 mmol/l HbA1c 9.5% Less than 7% Creatinine (Cr) 85 µmol/l 60–120 µmol/l What is the most appropriate diagnostic test to conﬁrm the suspected diagnosis?
explanation:
B Gastric emptying scintigraphy Gastric emptying scintigraphy is the gold standard for diagnosing gastroparesis, as it quantitatively assesses the rate of gastric emptying. In gastroparesis, delayed gastric emptying without mechanical

obstruction is a key feature, especially in patients with a history of diabetes. A Abdominal ultrasound While abdominal ultrasound can be helpful in ruling out other causes of abdominal pain, such as gallstones or biliary pathology, it does not assess gastric emptying function. This patient’s symptoms and history are suggestive of delayed gastric emptying, making gastric emptying scintigraphy more appropriate. C Upper GI endoscopy While an endoscopy can help to identify structural abnormalities, it cannot evaluate gastric emptying. Endoscopy may be helpful to rule out other causes of this patient's symptoms if gastroparesis is not conﬁrmed, but it is not the primary diagnostic tool for delayed gastric emptying. D CT of the abdomen A CT scan is useful for evaluating intra-abdominal pathology but does not provide information on gastric motility. It may help to exclude other causes but is not diagnostic for gastroparesis. E Hydrogen breath test The hydrogen breath test is used to diagnose small intestinal bacterial overgrowth or carbohydrate malabsorption disorders, which can cause bloating and discomfort but would not conﬁrm gastroparesis.

stem: A 22-year-old woman is admitted to hospital with severe abdominal pain, nausea and vomiting. She undergoes emergency laparotomy, which is normal. On further questioning, she reveals a family history of an aunt who has a light-sensitive rash and a diagnosis of porphyria. On examination, she is hypertensive, with generalised rebound tenderness. She responds to analgesia and once she is stabilised a porphyrin screen is sent. Investigation Result Normal Values Sodium (Na+) 125 mmol/l 135 - 145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.0 mmol/l 3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l Glucose 5.0 mmol/l 3.9 - 7.1 mmol/l Full blood count (FBC) Normal CT abdomen Normal Urinary porphobilinogen (PBG) 300 µmol/dl 0 - 18.0 µmol/dl Faecal porphyrins Normal (co-proporphyrins and protoporphyrins) Plasma porphyrins Markedly increased What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: A Acute intermittent porphyria Attacks of acute porphyria are often mistaken for surgical abdomens. Family histories may be misleading, as porphyria may be misdiagnosed or may not be manifest in other family members. Acute intermittent porphyria is correct as it ﬁts the clinical symptoms of gastrointestinal upset with abdominal pain and cramp with nausea and vomiting. Urinary porphyrins are raised in all three acute porphyrias (acute intermittent porphyria, hereditary coproporpyria and variegate porphyria), so these can often be impossible to distinguish clinically. Faecal porphyrins can be useful to differentiate the conditions, because they are elevated in coproporphyria and variegate porphyria. B Variegate porphyria Variegate porphyria is an autosomal dominant disease caused by a mutation of protoporphyrinogen oxide. It is characterised by symptoms of neurovisceral crises similar to those in a patient with AIP, but is also associated with a classic photosensitive skin disorder which this patient did not have. C Hereditary coproporphyria Similarly, hereditary co-proporphyria is also incorrect as it is associated with a blistering skin rash, particularly in sun-exposed areas. D Porphyria cutanea tarda Although it is the most common of all porphyrias, it is purely a skin disease, resulting from a deﬁciency of the enzyme uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase. E Lead poisoning This does not cause increase in urinary porphyrins. Lead poisoning predominantly affects the nervous system, with symptoms such as delirium, tremor and convulsions.

stem: A 52-year-old truck driver has been referred by his general practitioner (GP) to the rapid access upper gastrointestinal (GI) clinic with a 10-day history of intermittent epigastric pain and nausea. He has been prescribed a proton pump inhibitor (PPI) which he started taking 4 days ago with some relief. He has taken regular cocodamol for years for chronic back pain but otherwise has no previous medical history. His weight is stable and clinical examination is unremarkable. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Value Hb 147 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 3.6 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l PLT 212 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l MCV 86 ﬂ 76–98 ﬂ Which is the most appropriate next step in management according to available evidence?
options: Refer for routine upper GI endscopy and give symptomatic antacids in ﬁrst instance
Add metoclopramide 10 mg tds and review in 2 weeks
explanation: C Continue proton pump inhibitor This gentleman is <55 years old without ‘alarm’ features – weight loss, persistent vomiting, dysphagia – and does not take nonsteroidal anti-inﬂammatory drugs (NSAIDs). He is not anaemic and has no epigastric mass on examination. As he has gained some relief from the PPI it’s therefore appropriate to continue the medication. A Urgent upper gastrointestinal (GI) endoscopy Alarm features that prompt urgent referral for endoscopy include weight loss, persistent vomiting, dysphagia, anaemia and the presence of an epigastric mass on physical examination. B pylori eradication therapy H. pylori testing is useful, particularly where there is a limited response to PPI, although a 2-week wash-out should be accomplished if possible before breath testing is instituted. D Refer for routine upper GI endscopy and give symptomatic antacids in ﬁrst instance Before referral for routine endoscopy, a trial of PPI and/or H pylori breath testing should ﬁrst take place. E Add metoclopramide 10 mg tds and review in 2 weeks Although metoclopramide is a pro-kinetic and may improve nausea, its use is now discouraged because of dopamine antagonist-related adverse effects of therapy.

stem: A 45-year-old man presents with an upper gastrointestinal (GI) haemorrhage. He is a non-smoker and drinks only occasional wine. On further questioning, he admits to problems with indigestion over the past few months, for which he has tried over-the-counter Ranitidine tablets, and increasing diarrhoea. Upper GI endoscopy reveals multiple small gastric ulcers and helicobacter testing is negative. He is willing to have a short period off Ranitidine to be properly investigated. Which of the following is the most appropriate investigation in this case?
options: Fasting gastrin on three different days
explanation: B Fasting gastrin on three different days There is a suspicion that this patient may have Zollinger–Ellison syndrome as a result of a gastrinoma. The best initial screen is a fasting gastrin level on three separate days, as the secretion of gastrin is pulsatile. Three samples in the normal range make a gastrinoma unlikely. This is usually followed by basal acid output estimation and a secretin stimulation test. After this, patients usually move on to imaging studies. In the absence of metastases, surgical resection is advised. Octreotide, interferon and chemotherapy may be useful in non-surgically resectable lesions. D Secretin stimulation test Like basal acid output estimation, secretin stimulation test is an investigation which follows the three gastrin measurements. A Single fasting gastrin level Gastrin has a short half-life and release is cyclical, hence remeasuring on 3 separate days is recommended. C Basal acid output estimation Basal acid output estimation is a subsequent test after elevated gastrin has been established. E Protein meal test An arginine stimulation test is used in the evaluation of growth hormone deﬁciency.

stem: A 42-year-old woman is referred to the Hepatology Clinic with liver failure. She drinks no alcohol but over the past few months has suffered from increasing tiredness, upper abdominal discomfort, nausea, anorexia and itching. Most recently, she has noticed markedly increased bruising if she takes a knock on something. On examination, her blood pressure is 105/70 mmHg. You notice signs of chronic liver disease including scratch marks on her skin, spider naevi and evidence of mild jaundice. She also has extensive bruising on her limbs. Hepatomegaly is also present. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal value Hb 105 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 5.5 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l PLT 110 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 134 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.2 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 90 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l PT 27.3 s 10.6–14.9 s Albumin 22 g/l 35–55 g/l ALT 765 IU/l 5–30 IU/l Bilirubin 100 μmol/l 2–17 µmol/l Anti-soluble liver antigen antibody + Gamma-globulins Increased Liver biopsy Hepatic cirrhosis Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
E Autoimmune hepatitis Type 3 This patient has an autoantibody pattern consistent with autoimmune hepatitis type 3, and features of cirrhosis which are said to occur in around 75% of patients with the condition. It is commonest in those of the 30–50- year group, the vast majority being women. The prolonged PT is likely to be as the result of severe hepatic dysfunction. Corticosteroids achieve remission in around 2/3 of patients, although the relapse rate is as high as 80% after steroid withdrawal. Azathioprine is the main steroid-sparing agent used in the treatment of the condition. A comparison between subtypes of autoimmune hepatitis is listed below: A comparison between subtypes of autoimmune hepatitis is listed below: Clinical Features Type 1 Type 2 Type 3 Diagnostic autoantibodies ASMAANAAnti-actin AntiLKMP-450 IID6Synthet ic core motif peptides 254- 271 Soluble liverkidney antigenCytokeratins

and 18 Age 10y - elderly Paediatric (2-14y)Rare in adults Adults (30-50y) Women (%)

Concurrent immune disease %

Gamma globulin elevation +++ + ++ Low IgA No Occasional No HLA association B8, DR3,DR4 B14, DR3, C4AQO Uncertain Steroid response ++ ++ +++ Progression to cirrhosis

A Wilson’s disease Wilson’s disease presents at an earlier age and is usually associated with an asymptomatic rise in transaminases, psychiatric symptoms or a movement disorder. B Haemochromatosis Haemochromatosis presents later in women because of the natural blood loss afforded by the regular menstrual cycle. It also presents with other features such as diabetes and chondrocalcinosis, which aren’t seen here. C Autoimmune hepatitis Type 1 This is associated with anti-smooth muscle antibodies rather than the soluble liver–kidney antigen antibodies seen here. D Primary biliary cholangitis Primary biliary cholangitis presents with itching and lethargy and is associated with an obstructive picture on liver function testing.

stem: A 28-year-old woman presents to the Gastroenterology Clinic complaining of long periods of constipation interspersed with short episodes of diarrhoea. She has not lost any weight over the past year and continues to eat a varied diet. On examination, her BP is 122/82, her heart rate is 67 and regular and her BMI is 22.5 kg/m2. Full blood count and viscosity are normal. Flexible sigmoidoscopy is unremarkable. What is the next most appropriate management step?
explanation: D Soluble ﬁbre supplementation Normal clinical examination, stable weight and normal routine bloods make a sinister diagnosis unlikely. Irritable bowel syndrome is, therefore, the most likely cause of her symptoms. Psyllium or ispahula supplementation is of value in patients like this who have predominant constipation symptoms. A Colonoscopy Given the normal ﬁndings so far, there is little value in progressing to colonoscopy in this patient. Committing her to further investigation will only serve to increase anxiety. B Barium enema Like colonoscopy, progressing to barium enema would be considered over-investigation in this situation. C Lactose-free diet A lactose-free diet may be effective in reducing bloating associated with irritable bowel syndrome, but has limited impact on constipation. E Wheat-free diet There is no evidence this patient has coeliac disease. Some patients with bloating beneﬁt from reducing their wheat intake, although greater beneﬁt is usually found from lactose exclusion.

stem: A 20-year-old man presents complaining of diarrhoea for the past 2 days. It is watery and he has opened his bowels three times already today. He feels concerned as he thinks there was a small amount of blood mixed in with the stool on the most recent occasion. He does not feel too unwell and has been drinking plenty of ﬂuids. He has not eaten anything unusual or been travelling abroad in the last 6 months. He had an infected boil on his back, for which he received ﬂucloxicillin 2 weeks ago for one week in total. No one else in the household feels unwell. He has no past medical history and takes no medications. BP is 105/80 mmHg with a postural drop of 20 mmHg on standing. What would be the most appropriate next management step?
explanation:
E Oral rehydration salts NICE suggest that acute diarrhoea should be assessed for cause and the severity of dehydration should be established. The Table below is based on NICE guidelines to help divide the different features. Mild dehydration Moderate dehydration Severe dehydration Lassitude Apathy/tiredness Profound apathy Anorexia/nausea Dizziness Weakness Light-headedness Muscle cramps Confusion Postural hypotension Pinched face Shock Dry tongue or sunken eyes Tachycarida Reduced skin elasticity Peripheral vasoconstriction Postural hypotension Hypotension Tachycardia Oliguria Oliguria or anuria As his only feature dehydration is postural hypotension he can be managed for mild dehydration with oral rehydration.

C Loperamide Whilst infection has not been proven, it is suspected, especially as there is an element of PR bleeding. Loperamide should be avoided if infective diarrhoea is suspected. A Oral antibiotics According to guidance, antibiotics should be reserved for when a patient has a positive stool culture or is extremely unwell. This patient is very stable. He has noticed a small amount of blood on passing stool so it is deﬁnitely worth sending a stool culture. His short course of ﬂucloxicillin is very unlikely to have precipitated Clostridium difﬁcile infection in an otherwise healthy young man. B IV antibiotics As with the previous option there is no indication to treat with antibiotics, IV or oral, unless there is a speciﬁc pathogen identiﬁed or there is evidence of severe infection. This patient is well and no samples suggesting infection have yet been returned. D Sigmoidoscopy Endoscopic examination would be necessary if inﬂammatory bowel disease was suspected to be the underlying cause. There is not very much in the history or examination to support such a suspicion; absence of fever, chronic history, abdominal pain and systemic features. Should such features develop or his diarrhoea not settle then this could be a reasonable choice.

stem: A 28-year-old teacher presents to his General Practitioner with bloating, abdominal pain and weight loss. He also reports diarrhoea, which is very difﬁcult to ﬂush away and tends to ﬂoat on the toilet pan. On examination, his blood pressure is 115/72 mmHg and he looks pale. His BMI is 21 kg/m2 and his abdomen is soft and non-tender. Results of blood tests show iron deﬁciency anaemia and an elevated ALP level; his albumin level is low at 30 g/l. Given the likely diagnosis, which of the following associated complications will have the best response to treatment?
explanation: C Osteopenia The symptoms and iron deﬁciency anaemia in this scenario are suggestive of coeliac disease. Coeliac disease can be associated with deranged liver function tests. Serological tests for coeliac disease include immunoglobulin A (IgA) antibodies to tissue transglutaminase (TTG) (preferred and most widely available), anti-endomysial antibodies and gliadin antigen. The ‘gold standard’ for diagnosis remains a duodenal or jejunal biopsy. There are many recognised complications of untreated or undertreated coeliac disease in adults including depression, anxiety and eating disorders like nutritional deﬁciencies and anaemia due to malabsorption, reduced bone mineral density, hyposplenism malignancy and dermatitis herpetiformis. Some renal diseases, including IgA nephropathy, membranous nephropathy and chronic kidney disease, are associated with coeliac disease; however, this does not include renal cystic disease. A Dermatitis herpetiformis Dermatitis herpetiformis is the skin manifestation of active coeliac disease. Episodes can recur, even on a strict gluten-free diet, making it inappropriate here. In recurrence, treatment with dapsone, in conjunction with a gluten-free diet, may be helpful. B Infection with encapsulated organisms Hyposplenism and splenic atrophy are closely associated with the development of other complications and autoimmune diseases in patients with coeliac disease. This increases patients’ risk of infection with encapsulated bacteria and sepsis. Studies have shown that treatment with a gluten-free diet can reverse functional hyposplenism, but not splenic atrophy, making it inappropriate for this patient. D Non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma People with coeliac disease are at increased risk of cancer, including an estimated 2- to 4-fold risk of non- Hodgkin’s lymphoma. Increased risk of malignancy in coeliac disease has been shown to normalise following a few years of a gluten-free diet. As this risk takes longer to normalise, compared to osteopenia, it is not appropriate here. E Small bowel cancer Those with coeliac disease are at increased risk of cancer, including an estimated 30-fold risk of small bowel cancer. As the increased risk of malignancy in coeliac has been shown to normalise after a few years of a gluten-free diet, compared to osteopenia, this risk takes longer to normalise and is not appropriate here.

stem: A 58-year-old woman presents with a 4-day history of shortness of breath and cough. There is a long past medical history of indigestion, worse when she lies ﬂat on the bed, with occasional acid regurgitation. She may even wake at night occasionally with acid in her mouth and paroxysms of coughing. On examination, her body mass index (BMI) is 31, she is pyrexial with a temperature of 39 °C, there is an area of bronchial breathing over the right lung and a suggestion of increased shadowing on the chest X-ray at the right base. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause for this clinical picture?
explanation: E Gastro-oesophageal reﬂux disease (GORD) This woman has a long history of indigestion, particularly worse when lying ﬂat, and acid regurgitation, complicated by a chronic nocturnal cough. It is likely that an episode of regurgitation has led to right-sided lower respiratory tract infection. She is obese, which may well contribute to her symptoms. Other predisposing factors which increase the likelihood of GORD include smoking; hiatus hernia; medications which relax the lower oesophageal sphincter such as calcium channel blockers and beta-blockers; pregnancy; and foods such as chocolate and peppermint. Weight reduction would be the mainstay of management in this case, with the addition of proton pump inhibitors. D Benign oesophageal stricture Benign oesophageal stricture leads to regurgitation of food, often a mix of both solid and liquid meals, rather than the progressive dysphagia seen with oesophageal Ca. A Bronchiectasis Bronchiectasis is associated with longer-term shortness of breath and recurrent episodes of lower respiratory tract infection. B Exacerbation of asthma Given the long history of water brash and associated coughing, reﬂux is the more likely primary cause of her symptoms, and the CXR changes, rather than asthma alone. C Oesophageal carcinoma The long history of indigestion without progression to dysphagia and lack of weight loss doesn’t ﬁt with a diagnosis of oesophageal carcinoma.

stem: A 32-year-old woman has been referred to the clinic by her GP who suspects she may have irritable bowel syndrome. She suffers intermittent bouts of diarrhoea, problems with bloating, and ﬂatulence. On further questioning, it transpires that she has been feeling a little tired over the past few months. On examination, her BP is 125/72 mmHg, pulse is 72/min and regular. She looks a little pale, her BMI is 22. Abdominal examination is unremarkable. Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin 105 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 5.4 × 109/l 4–11 × 109/l Platelets 201 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 139 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.1 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 110 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Small bowel biopsy villous atrophy, increased epithelial lymphocytes Which of the following represents the most appropriate intervention?
explanation: C Gluten free diet This patient has symptoms consistent with coeliac disease. She is also anaemic, which likely reﬂects iron deﬁciency from malabsorption. Her small bowel biopsy shows increased intraepithelial lymphocytes and villous atrophy, which is characteristic of the condition. As such the most appropriate therapy is a trial of gluten free diet. Coeliac disease is caused by an immune response to gluten exposure causing a small bowel enteropathy in patients with a genetic predisposition. It is associate with HLA-DR3 + DQ2. Diagnosis is made on the basis of serology (IgA for endomysial or tissue transglutaminase (EMA/TTG) and duodenal biopsy. NB there is an association with IgA deﬁciency. In these cases patients should be tested for IgG to tissue transglutaminase. (TG2). The histological ﬁndings are not pathognomic and may also be seen in other disorders, such as immune deﬁciency, AI enteropathy, tropical sprue, Whipple’s disease and microscopic colitis amongst others so combination with positive serology is key to the diagnosis. B Lactose free diet Lactose avoidance may be of value in patients with symptoms of irritable bowel syndrome, particularly those of an ethnic origin where congenital lactase deﬁciency is increased. An increase in intraepithelial lymphocytes may be seen in cow’s milk hypersensitivity, but not villous atrophy. A Metronidazole Metronidazole would be used to treat giardiasis, a protozoal infection that can cause chronic diarrhoea with bloating and malabsorption. However, there is no history of travel and although one can see an increase in intraepithelial lymphocytes, villous atrophy is not typical. D Doxycycline Treatment with a tetracycline would be indicated in Whipple’s disease, which is a differential for the ﬁnding of villous atrophy on small bowel biopsy. However, one would also see PAS positive macrophages on histology. E Prednisolone Corticosteroids may be of value in Crohn’s, but are not used in the management of coeliac disease. Histology in small bowel Crohn’s might yield cryptitis or crypt abscesses in addition to intraepithelial lymphocytes.

stem: A 79-year-old man was referred by his GP with a 4 month history of dysphagia. He was unable to pinpoint the site of his symptoms accurately but noted that his dysphagia worsened as he ate. At times he would regurgitate food during his meals, which would temporarily relieve his symptoms. According to his GP, who had weighed him, he had lost 1 kg in weight over the past 2 months. His medications include Bendroﬂumethiazide for hypertension, and Ranitidine, which he takes intermittently for symptoms of gastro-oesophageal reﬂux disease.
explanation: D Pharyngeal pouch The barium swallow shows a pharyngeal pouch (or Zenker’s diverticulum). These occur predominantly in elderly men (male: female of 5: 1), and are rare before the age of 40 years. The aetiology is unclear, although they may be related to poor relaxation of the upper oesophageal sphincter. An association with gastro- oesophageal reﬂux disease has also been noted. Pharyngeal pouches commonly cause dysphagia, regurgitation and aspiration, and are a rare cause of halitosis. If large, they may cause a mass in the neck that gurgles on palpation (Boyce’s sign). Regurgitation of the contents of the pouch may temporarily ease dysphagia until the pouch reﬁlls with food and ﬂuid. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy is risky, since the pouches are thin-walled and easy to perforate; this is the reason why a barium swallow may be the preferable ﬁrst-line investigation in elderly patients with dysphagia. Treatment is surgical, with either an open or endoscopic approach. C Benign oesophageal stricture This would give a very different appearance on barium swallow to those of a pharyngeal pouch. Barium studies in those with benign oesophageal strictures typically produce a smooth, tapering narrowing of the oesophagus. A Schatzki ring This would give a very different appearance on barium swallow to those of a pharyngeal pouch. Schatzki rings are benign narrowings in the distal oesophagus. B Achalasia This would give a very different appearance on barium swallow to those of a pharyngeal pouch. Barium swallow in people with achalasia is associated with a very tight tapering at the gastrooesophageal junction, generating a so-called ‘bird’s beak’ or ‘rat’s tail’ appearance, together with a dilated oesophagus. E Post-cricoid web This would give a very different appearance on barium swallow to those of a pharyngeal pouch. Post-cricoid webs occur near the upper oesophageal sphincter and may occur in association with irondeﬁciency anaemia (Patterson-Brown-Kelly syndrome).

stem: A 26-year-old man presents to the Gastroenterology Clinic with a 6-month history of constipation. He has found some relief after taking a combination of lactulose and macrogol sachets. However, cessation of this medication leads to a return of his symptoms. More recently, he has experienced intermittent abdominal discomfort and nausea. His only past medical history is for multiple epidermoid cysts, for which he is under the care of the dermatology team. He is concerned as his mother has recently been diagnosed with colorectal cancer and his maternal grandfather died of the same. He is referred for a colonoscopy that shows multiple adenomatous polyps varying between 5 mm and 1 mm in size. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: B Familial adenomatous polyposis This patient has a likely diagnosis of familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP) given the young presentation of chronic constipation, abdominal discomfort and multiple adenomatous polyps on colonoscopy. FAP is an autosomal-dominant condition caused by mutations in the adenomatous polyposis coli (APC) gene, causing hundreds to thousands of adenomatous polyps throughout the colon. It comes with almost a 100% risk of colorectal cancer if not treated with a prophylactic pan-colectomy. The family history of colorectal cancer makes FAP an even more likely diagnosis. Extraintestinal features of FAP include dermoid cysts and lipomas and the recurrent epidermoid cysts lipoma is another hint towards FAP. Colonoscopy and biopsy form the mainstay of investigation for the condition. However, genetic testing for the APC gene is also a useful investigation to consider. C Hereditary non-polyposis colorectal cancer Hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer (HNPCC) (Lynch syndrome) is a hereditary syndrome associated with a genetic predisposition to having an increased risk of malignancy, including colorectal and endometrial cancer. Although it is certainly a diagnosis to consider, this patient is not yet displaying signs of malignancy on examination or colonoscopy. Furthermore, the young age of presentation and extraintestinal manifestations make FAP more likely. A Cowden’s disease Cowden’s disease is a hamartomatous polyposis disease that is inherited in an autosomal-dominant fashion. Hamartomas can develop in the bowel, breast, thyroid, uterus and brain. It is also associated with skin lesions including hamartomas of the skin and mucosa, which are seen in almost all cases, along with trichilemmomas and sclerotic ﬁbromas. The absence of skin changes makes this diagnosis unlikely. D Mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue lymphoma Gastrointestinal mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue lymphoma is characterised by dyspepsia and epigastric discomfort that may also be associated with constitutional symptoms of weight loss, fever and night sweats. It does not account for the colorectal polyps or chronic constipation. E Peutz–Jeghers syndrome Peutz–Jeghers syndrome is an autosomal-dominant hamartomatous polyposis syndrome associated with mucocutaneous pigmentation and gastrointestinal polyposis. It is associated with a high risk of malignancy including colorectal, gastric and small-bowel cancer. Extraintestinal disease is also common (eg breast and cervical cancer). Peutz–Jeghers syndrome can commonly present with smallbowel obstruction secondary to intussusception. Furthermore, the lack of mucocutaneous pigmentation makes this Peutz–Jeghers syndrome less likely than FAP.

stem: A 43-year-old woman comes to the clinic for review. She has peripheral calcinosis, sclerodactyly and multiple telangiectasia, particularly marked on her face. Her main complaint over the past few months has been of increasing indigestion. She occasionally has acid coming up in her throat. Which of the following is the most useful next step in managing the patient’s gastrointestinal (GI) symptoms?
explanation:
C Oesophageal manometry Patients with systemic sclerosis, the likely diagnosis here, given the presence of peripheral calcinosis, sclerodactyly and telangiectasia, suffer from oesophageal dysmotility because of a sclerotic process affecting the smooth muscle. Lower oesophageal pressure is commonly decreased in systemic sclerosis and can be measured using manometry. Prokinetic agents such as domperidone may be useful in relieving symptoms. Esophageal dysmotility can present as dysphagia or a sensation of food being stuck in the throat. In patients with persistent symptoms

despite twice-daily PPI therapy, we suggest a trial of prokinetic drugs (eg, metoclopramide, cisapride, domperidone, prucalopride) to relieve these symptoms. These drugs act by increasing esophageal sphincter pressure, improving peristalsis, and enhancing gastric emptying. Other very common disorder is GERD which require medical attention. D Trial of omeprazole Although proton pump inhibitors such as omeprazole may improve symptoms from oesophageal dysmotility in systemic sclerosis, prokinetic agents and calcium channel antagonists are likely to be more effective. A Breath testing Small bowel bacterial overgrowth is seen in patients with systemic sclerosis and can be diagnosed with hydrogen breath testing. Usual symptoms of bacterial overgrowth include abdominal bloating, eructation and anorexia, not the symptoms reported here. B Helicobacter pylori testing Although H. pylori is a recognised cause of epigastric pain and indigestion, the symptoms of waterbrash described here are more suggestive of oesophageal dysmotility. E Upper GI endoscopy Although upper GI endoscopy may reveal the presence of oesophagitis, it will not shed light on any underlying dysmotility as a result of systemic sclerosis.

stem: A 45-year-old woman with a long history of Crohn’s disease presents with increased lethargy, weight loss and diarrhoea over a period of several months. She had undergone a very extensive small bowel resection an unknown length of time ago and has recently returned from a period of work in Thailand. While abroad, she was admitted with an episode of renal pain due to kidney stones. On examination, she has a midline scar and is thin with a BMI of 18.5. Her BP is 125/72 mmHg. Investigations reveal: Investigation Result Normal values Blood count and film Features suggestive of megaloblastic anaemia Prothrombin time (PT) 21.2 s 11 - 14 s Albumin 28 g/l 35 - 55 g/l Corrected calcium (Ca ) 2.05 mmol/l 2.2 - 2/7 mmol/l CRP) 15 mg/l < 10 mg/l ESR 17 mm/h 1 - 20 mm/h Which of the following diagnoses ﬁts best with this clinical picture?
explanation: B Short bowel syndrome In patients who have removal of more than one-half of the small intestine, malabsorption syndrome may result. It may occur in patients with Crohn’s disease or those with ischaemic bowel who have undergone signiﬁcant bowel resection. Patients present with diarrhoea and steatorrhoea, weight loss, anaemia, osteoporosis/osteomalacia, electrolyte disturbances and hypovolaemia. In patients with more than 100 cm of jejunum, oral intake is still possible. Diarrhoea may reduce with lactose exclusion or with a course of metronidazole to eradicate bacterial overgrowth. In patients with less than 100 cm of jejunum, total parenteral nutrition is recommended as the only way to maintain adequate nutritional intake. A Active Crohn’s disease Active Crohn’s disease is unlikely given that both the CRP and ESR are only just above the upper limit of the normal range. C Coeliac disease Although coeliac disease can co-exist with Crohn’s disease, it is unlikely, and would not lead to increased risk of renal stones. Oxalate renal stones are a recognised consequence of short bowel syndrome. D Tropical sprue Tropical sprue presents with symptoms similar to those of coeliac disease, but is infective in origin and particularly occurs in patients who have spent time in the Caribbean. E Ulcerative colitis Ulcerative colitis is associated with bloody diarrhoea and is not associated with the oxalate renal stones seen here.

stem: A 52-year-old South Asian woman is referred to the Hepatology Clinic with progressive tiredness and lethargy, coupled with abnormal liver function tests. She has a history of hypertension, for which she takes Bendroﬂumethiazide, and she received a blood transfusion in 1989 after the birth of her last child in India but is otherwise well. On examination, her blood pressure is 115/85 mmHg; pulse is 70 bpm and regular. There is no organomegaly on palpation of the abdomen, although there is mild ascites. Her body mass index (BMI) is 28 kg/m2. She appears mildly jaundiced. Investigation Result Normal value Hb 114 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 7.9 × 109/l 4–11 × 109/l PLT 101 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 137 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 3.3 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 81 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l ALT 181 IU/l 5–30 IU/l ALP 278 IU/l 30–130 IU/l Bilirubin 45 µmol/l 2–17 µmol/l Glucose 6.2 mmol/l 3.5–5.5 mmol/l PT 19.2 s 10.6–14.9 s Which of the following is the most useful next investigation?
explanation: E Hepatitis C serology The blood transfusion in 1989 occurred before widespread screening for Hepatitis C was introduced to blood banks in the 1990–1992 timeframe. As such, presentations with chronic liver disease are consistent with chronic active hepatitis due to hepatitis C. Quantiﬁcation of hepatitis C RNA and genotyping are important to determining prognosis. Non-invasive imaging including ultrasound and ﬁbroscan, coupled with liver biopsy can be used to assess the extent of ﬁbrosis. The key to successful management of hepatitis Crelated liver disease is identiﬁcation and eradication of chronic carriage before ﬁbrosis and cirrhosis is established. A Autoimmune proﬁle Although an autoimmune proﬁle would be helpful to pick up potential diagnoses, the blood transfusion is signiﬁcant. Therefore, hepatitis C serology is more useful in terms of the next investigation. B Caeruloplasmin This patient has evidence of chronic liver disease; however, there are no symptoms or signs suggestive of Wilson’s disease. Patients often present by their mid-30s and although patients can be nonspeciﬁcally unwell, they will often have psychiatric symptoms, such as depression and personality change, at some point prior to diagnosis. C Ferritin This patient has evidence of chronic liver disease; however, there are no symptoms or signs that would suggest haemochromatosis as a diagnosis. In addition to deranged liver function, these patients often present with skin hyperpigmentation (‘bronze skin’) along with joint pains and symptoms related to a possible diagnosis of diabetes mellitus. D Hepatitis B serology

stem: A woman who is 34 weeks’ pregnant is admitted with anorexia, nausea and vomiting over the past few days. She is started on intravenous (iv) ﬂuids and ranitidine. Six hours later, her vomiting persists and she becomes confused. She is a non-smoker and does not drink any alcohol. On examination, she is afebrile. Her blood pressure is 130/80 mmHg and she is tachycardic. Cardiovascular and chest examinations are normal. Her abdomen is tender in the right upper quadrant but there is no rebound or rigidity. There are no focal neurological signs. Investigation Result Normal values Hb 120 g/l 135 - 175 g/l WCC 20.0 × 109/l (75% neutrophils) 4.0 - 11.0 × 109/l PLT 160 × 109/l 150 - 400 × 109/l MCV 82 ﬂ 80 - 100 ﬂ INR 1.6 < 1.1 Sodium (Na+) 133 mmol/l 135 - 145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.5 mmol/l 3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l Urea 13.0 mmol/l 2.5 - 6.5 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 124 µmol/l 50 - 120 µmol/l Bilirubin 40 µmol/l 1 - 22 µmol/l ALP 201 u/l 30 - 150 u/l ALT 520 u/l 7 - 55 u/l GGT 101 u/l < 50 u/l Albumin 32 g/l 35 - 55 g/l Glucose 3.9 mmol/l 3.9 - 7.1 mmol/l Blood ﬁlm Schistocytes seen Urinalysis 2+ protein Ultrasound scan of the abdomen shows fatty changes in the liver. She is given FFP and iv dextrose. Which of the following is the most appropriate next management step?
options: Urgent liver biopsy to determine prognosis
explanation:
E Prompt delivery by caesarean section This patient has acute fatty liver disease of pregnancy (AFLP) and disseminated intravascular coagulation. It is a condition of the third

trimester and is common in ﬁrst pregnancies and multiple pregnancies. The diagnosis is a clinical one and there is characteristically an elevated white blood cell (WBC) count, low glucose, low albumin and evidence of disseminated intravascular coagulation. The management involves aggressive correction of hypoglycaemia and coagulopathy followed by expeditious delivery which results in the dramatic recovery of the mother. The development of hepatic failure requires the patient to be transferred to a liver unit for assessment for transplantation. The haemolysis, elevated liver enzymes and low platelet count syndrome (HELLP) is associated with preeclampsia and there is a degree of overlap with haemolytic uraemic syndrome and thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura. A Broad-spectrum antibiotics There is no indication of acute infection and with hypertension, abnormal LFTs and evidence of haemolysis, broad-spectrum antibiotics are not of beneﬁt. B Urgent liver biopsy to determine prognosis There are inherent risks of liver biopsy with respect to bleeding in this patient, and the biopsy will almost certainly show evidence of fatty inﬁltration and hepatocellular necrosis. As such, it won’t contribute to the diagnosis. C Urgent abdominal CT with contrast There is no indication for CT with contrast here; the diagnosis can already be made by the clinical picture including BP, assessment of LFTs and full blood count. D Upper GI endoscopy The vomiting here is related to the underlying diagnosis of acute fatty liver disease of pregnancy. An upper GI endoscopy therefore is not indicated in this patients acute vomiting.

stem: A 20-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with abdominal pain and rectal bleeding. She has never experienced rectal bleeding previously and is concerned that it may be cancer. Her past medical history includes chronic constipation and a recent excision of a lipoma on her abdomen. She reports that her elder sister also suffers from chronic constipation and her grandmother died of colorectal cancer 15 years ago. On examination, her observations are within normal limits. She has a soft abdomen with mild, generalised tenderness and no guarding. Digital rectal examination is signiﬁcant for two rectal polyps and a small amount of bloodstained stool. What is the most appropriate investigation to conﬁrm the likely diagnosis?
explanation: B Colonoscopy and biopsy This patient has a likely diagnosis of familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP) given the young presentation of rectal bleeding, abdominal pain and rectal polyps. FAP is an autosomal-dominant condition caused by mutations in the adenomatous polyposis coli (APC) gene, causing hundreds to thousands of adenomatous polyps throughout the colon. It comes with almost a 100% risk of colorectal cancer if not treated with a prophylactic pan-colectomy. The family history of colorectal cancer and constipation makes FAP an even more likely diagnosis. Extraintestinal features of FAP include dermoid cysts and lipomas and the recent lipoma removal is another hint towards FAP. Colonoscopy and biopsy form the mainstay of investigation for the condition. However, genetic testing for the APC gene is also a useful investigation to consider. C Faecal calprotectin Faecal calprotectin is used in the investigation of inﬂammatory bowel disease (IBD) which is a useful differential diagnosis to consider given the onset of rectal bleeding at a young age. However, this typically presents with diarrhoea and weight loss and the absence of these features plus the family history of malignancy make IBD less likely. A Carcinoembryonic antigen testing Carcinoembryonic antigen testing is a tumour marker used in the assessment of colorectal cancer. Although FAP has a very high risk for becoming colorectal cancer, this is usually in later years (35–40 years). Furthermore, it would not aid in the speciﬁc diagnosis of FAP. Rather, if FAP had malignantly transformed into colorectal cancer. D Faecal immunochemical test Faecal immunochemical testing is used in the investigation of colorectal cancer. It detects the presence of blood within the stool using antibodies that are speciﬁc for haemoglobin. As this patient is presenting with haematochezia, this result is likely to be positive. However, it is much more likely that this patient has FAP rather than colorectal cancer or FAP that has already malignantly transformed into colorectal cancer. E Genetic testing for STK11 Genetic testing for STK11 is used in the diagnosis of Peutz–Jeghers syndrome, an autosomal-dominant hamartomatous polyposis syndrome associated with mucocutaneous pigmentation and gastrointestinal polyposis. It is associated with a high risk of malignancy including colorectal, gastric and small-bowel cancer. Extraintestinal disease is also common (eg breast and cervical cancer). Peutz– Jeghers syndrome can commonly present with small-bowel obstruction secondary to intussusception. Furthermore, the lack of mucocutaneous pigmentation makes this Peutz–Jeghers syndrome less likely compared with FAP.

stem: A 48-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with a 4-hour history of haematemesis. She admits that she went foraging for mushrooms ﬁve days earlier and cooked some that she found in the forest. There is no past medical history of note. On examination, she is jaundiced. Her blood pressure is 110/72 mmHg, her heart rate is 92 bpm and regular. She is tender in the epigastrium and right upper quadrant of her abdomen. There is dried blood around her lips and evidence of bruising on her arms and legs. Investigation Result Normal values Hb 101 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 10.5 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l PLT 121 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l INR 3.6 < 1.1 Sodium (Na+) 138 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.2 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 255 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Bilirubin 182 µmol/l 3–17 µmol/l Alanine aminotransferase 290 u/l 3–40 u/l Alkaline phosphatase 99 u/l 30–100 u/l Glucose 3.8 mmol/l 4–7 mmol/l What is the next step in the management of this patient?
explanation:
C Referral for liver transplant This patient has acute liver failure exhibited by jaundice, deranged liver function tests, elevated INR and hypoglycaemia. Her presentation with haematemesis indicates that her liver is decompensating. The history of eating wild mushrooms before symptom onset is the likely cause of liver toxicity. It is recommended that a referral for liver transplantation in patients with non-paracetamol-induced liver failure if any of the following are present: • Prothrombin time >100 s (INR > 6.5) or Any 3 of the following (irrespective of the grade of encephalopathy): • Age <10 or >40 years • Etiology: non-A/non-B hepatitis, drug-induced • Duration of jaundice to hepatic encephalopathy (HE) >7 days • Prothrombin time >50 (INR > 3.5) • Serum bilirubin >300 μmol/L D Rifaximin Rifaximin is used in the management of hepatic encephalopathy. It is an antibiotic that modulates gut ﬂora to reduce ammonia production. This patient has presented with acute liver failure, for which rifaximin is not indicated.

A Acetylcysteine infusion Acetylcysteine is the ﬁrst-line treatment for paracetamol overdose. However, evidence from a recent Cochrane review concludes that it is of no beneﬁt in non-paracetamol-induced causes of acute liver failure.
